title: Pound rises to its highest level since the Brexit referendum
content: Image source,Matt Cardy/Getty ImagesByFaisal IslamEconomics editorPublished1 hour agoThe pound has risen to its highest overall level since the Brexit referendum over a decade ago.Sterling has risen notably in recent weeks against the euro and the dollar, ahead of an expected rise in interest rates.The most-watched measure of the value of the British currency against a basket of 18 of the world's main currencies this week reached its joint highest level since the June 2016 referendum, according to Bank of England figures.The value reached 86.4 on an index where 100 equals the value in 2005. The Bank will officially confirm the calculation on Thursday.The value of sterling fell significantly after the Brexit referendum in June 2016, and reached further lows during the Brexit process, the Covid pandemic and the 2022 mini-Budget.Some traders said the UK was being seen in a different light given relative political stability, solid growth and the rapprochement with the European Union.Sterling has responded strongly to Brexit developments and political uncertainty in recent years.Jim O'Neill, an economist and former Treasury minister, said: "I'm not surprised. People were, and to a lesser extent, are, underestimating the improving momentum in the UK,"A stronger pound can help rein in inflation, and increase buying power for consumers on imports and on holidays.UK growth so far this year has outperformed all expectations, but there are signs that higher energy and fuel prices have now hit consumer confidence.The Bank's nine member Monetary Policy Committee faces an important decision on interest rates on Thursday, with the first rise in three years widely expected.Related topicsPound Sterling (GBP)UK economy

title: Crude oil prices fall below $90 a barrel as Vance blames GOP election defeat on Iran war
content:
Crude oil prices tumbled Wednesday after Vice President JD Vance blamed the war against Iran for Republican midterm election reversals.

U.S.West Texas Intermediatelost 8.3% to close at $88.12 a barrel.Brentcrude futures, the international benchmark, shed 8.7% to settle at $94.62.

"The reason we lost is the war,"Vancesaid in asocial media postWednesday. "The president himself said so last night."

Democrats swept the House and Senate in Tuesday's elections, giving the party leverage to pressure PresidentDonald Trumpto end the unpopular war that has spiked gasoline and diesel prices.

"The elections are leading the market to conclude that Trump might now be inclined to make a deal," said Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates.

The Democrats may try to restrict funding for the war, Lipow said. Trump's announcement earlier this week that the U.S. will cut some funding to Israel could force Jerusalem to accept Washington's decisions, he said.

Trump told the Financial Times on Tuesday that he has no immediate plans to strike Iran. The oil market had priced in the risk of a major escalation after the elections, gaining more than 10% in October.

Oil futures have fallen more than 14% this week as senior U.S. and Iranian officials indicated they're open to a diplomatic settlement of the conflict, which has disrupted global energy supplies for eight months.

The sell-off "could be getting a bit overdone," said Rebecca Babin, senior energy trader at CIBC. The market is in a "shoot first, ask questions" later mode as emotions run high after the unexpected election results, Babin said.

Many observers expected a Democrat tsunami could push Trump to escalate with Iran, Babin said. "Vance's commentary and the public lack of backing from key allies have challenged that assumption," she said.

But the odds still favor military escalation in the region, warned Bob McNally, president of Rapidan Energy and a former advisor to President George W. Bush.

"Iran is hardened in its uncompromising position," McNally said. "Trump, having now paid a huge price for his determination to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon, is unlikely to let go of this legacy goal and walk away."

title: Midterm elections 2026 live updates: Vance blames Iran war for Republican losses
content:
Democrats scored a seismic victory in themidterm elections, flipping both chambers of Congress from Republican control and setting the stage to challenge PresidentDonald Trump's policy priorities from a position of strength.

The Democratic victories spanning a surprising number of House districts and Senate seats mean the party will be able to launch congressional investigations with subpoena power.

Democrats could eye the financial windfall Trump, his family members and his political allies have enjoyed since he regained the White House. They will likely examine the president's controversial, heavy-handed enforcement of immigration, his use of the Department of Justice to target people he considers enemies and favorable business dealings.

As of early Wednesday morning, Democrats were projected to win at least 250 House seats, with Republicans winning a minimum of 160 seats, according to the CNBC Election Desk.

A number of Democratic candidates won in House districts that were redesigned by Republican-controlled state legislatures with the intention of easing the way for GOP candidates to win.

Democrats were on track to hold at least 54 seats in the Senate, with Republicans likely to hold at least 42 seats. The big Democratic winners on Tuesday night include James Talarico in the Texas Senate election. He overcame an unprecedentedflurry of $224 million in spendingbySpaceXCEOElon Muskto boost the candidacy of Republican nominee Ken Paxton, the state's scandal-plagued attorney general.

Just two uncalled Senate races left as final votes trickle inKatie Hobbs wins reelection for governor in ArizonaDemocrat Tina Kotek wins reelection for governor in OregonAaron Ford ousts Joe Lombardo in race for Nevada governor

Jeremy Allaire, CEO of crypto platform Circle, told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" he doesn't see pending Democratic control of Congress meaningfully affecting chances of crypto legislation, calling the technology a "bipartisan" issue.

"Circle is purple, and that's very important," Allaire told CNBC. "Our business and what we do in digital dollars are a bipartisan issue, and we want to work with leadership in every political party and in countries around the world."

"Policy will continue to iterate and get forged, and so we'll just continue to work with policymakers and governments like we have for the last 13,14 years," he said, pointing to Congress passing the GENIUS Act by a wide margin last year.

When pressed about notions that the crypto industry is more friendly to Republicans, Allaire said crypto's push into the mainstream has brought parties to the table that are important across the political spectrum.

"Everybody in capital markets, in banking, in payments and technology companies — they're all moving to build on this, and those all of those companies are important to political leaders no matter what side of the aisle you're on."

Democrats' sweeping midterm victorieswill reshape Donald Trump's final two years in the Oval Office.

Party leaders are planning a hard-charging legislative and investigative push shortly after they take majority control of the House and Senate.

Trump has strongly signaled he is ready to veto Democrats' bills. But with his grip on the Capitol shriveling and his approval ratings scraping record lows in numerous polls, it's unclear how much support he'll be able to muster to fight the coming political battles.

Click here to read more about what the GOP's stunning midterm defeat means for Trump.

Ted Leonsis, Monumental Sports & Entertainment founder, chairman and CEO, congratulated democratic socialistJaneese Lewis Georgeon her Washington mayoral win.

"Living and working in the nation's capital gives us a special appreciation for civic participation," Leonsis wrote in anX post.

Lewis George will succeed Mayor Muriel Bowser, a moderate Democrat who has held the role for over a decade. She defeated independent and Green Party candidates in Tuesday's election.

Lewis George campaigned on universal childcare, lowering costs, expanding housing and instituting a new Business Activity Tax, among other policies.

She has also pledged to stand up to Trump, who has previously labeled Lewis George a"communist."

"Our commitment to D.C. carries through every day of the year," Leonsis said in his post. "Through our teams, venues, and network we have an opportunity and a responsibility to create jobs, support local businesses, bring people downtown and open doors for young people across the city."

LinkedIn co-founder and Democratic megadonorReid Hoffmantook a victory lap Wednesday, responding to news that House Speaker Mike Johnson would not seek the minority leader post with ajab on X: "full resignation also an option."

Hoffman, who poured$8 million into Wisconsin Democratsthis fall, also weighed in on Silicon Valley's political loyalties, writing that "some have always stuck true to their principles" in an earlierpost Wednesday.

House Majority LeaderSteve Scalise, R-La., and House Judiciary ChairJim Jordan, R-Ohio, are both expected to vie for the job of leadingRepublicansin the minority next Congress, setting up a battle of two top GOP lawmakers.

Jordan sent a letter, obtained by CNBC, to the Republican caucus on Wednesday, announcing his plans.

"For too long, we have operated without a clear plan to survive the hour or the day in front of us," Jordan wrote. "That will not cut it against an emboldened and energetic Democrat majority."

Scalise, who has been the number two Republican in the House under Speaker Mike Johnson, is expected to announce his candidacy later on Wednesday, MS NOW reported, citing a House GOP aide who requested anonymity to discuss the private plans.

The intraparty battle takes shape hours after Johnson announced on Wednesday morning that he would not seek the leadership spot in the next Congress.

Theelectoral sweepby Democrats last night injects a new, unstable dynamic into the single biggest political risk to financial markets in the coming year:the debt limit. Unless a defeated Republican Party makes a swift and unlikely show of unity to take the issue off the table in their last few weeks in power, the protracted fight that will unfold is set to be nastier than ever, adding volatility to an already shaky bond market.

The debt limit is the definition of a must-pass bill, even more than issues like funding the government and the defense budget. That makes it potentially the one real chance the new Democratic majority in Congress has to extract concessions from a president who is already pledging to veto their agenda. Markets will hate the entire process, even if – as many expect – it ends in compromise.

Because it is Democrats who hold the leverage, unlike past episodes, the ultimate agreement is more likely to increasegovernment spendingthan lower it. With highbond yieldsweighing on the economy, and Americans expecting action from a newly empowered Democratic opposition, the fight could be particularly damaging.

Read more of our debt-ceiling analysis here.

Vice President JD Vance blamed the Iran war for Republican losses in the midterms in asocial media postWednesday.

"The president himself said so last night," Vance wrote.

"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so," the vice president said. "Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest.""But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there," he said.

Brentcrude oil is down more than 4% to $98.98 per barrel, whileU.S. crudeis 4.3% lower to $91.99 a barrel.

Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden, D-Ore., said the committee will focus on CEO accountability, a billionaire tax, healthcare and tariffs in a statement detailing plans for the upcoming session of Congress."Trump and Republicans have been running a smash-and-grab job on the American people. Under my leadership, the top priorities of the Finance Committee will be affordability for us, accountability for them," the statement read.

Wyden indicated much of the committee's focus would rest on accountability for billionaires and corporate executives, detailing plans for a "tax agenda that puts American families first and requires the ultra-rich to pay their fair share." He declared he was putting bank, insurance and pharmaceutical company CEOs "on notice," bringing those who have worked with Trump under the committee's scrutiny.

Wyden also declared expanding healthcare and asserting authority over trade policy as legislative priorities for the upcoming session. With Democrats projected to take control of the Senate and its committees, Wyden, who is currently the highest-ranking Democrat on Senate Finance, is expected to become chair.

House SpeakerMike Johnson, R-La., won't run to lead the HouseRepublicansfrom the minority nextCongress, his office confirmed on Wednesday.

Punchbowl Newsfirst reportedthat Johnson announced the decision on an all-staff call Wednesday morning, after the GOP suffered a drubbing at the hands of Democrats, losing their majorities in both the House and Senate.

Johnson became speaker in 2023 after his predecessor, Rep.Kevin McCarthy, R-Calif., was deposed amid an intraparty revolt. He led House Republicans through the first part of Trump's term, helping to shepherd through the president's sprawling2025 tax and spending packageand other legislative priorities

title: What Republicans' huge loss means for Trump
content:
Democratsjust put PresidentDonald Trumpin a bind.

The party is projected to win commanding majorities in theHouse and Senateafter thrashing Republicans in key races up and down the ballot across the country. Theblue tsunamiwill knock Washington on its head and crush the Republicancongressionalbulwark that both supported and shielded Trump through the first two years of his term.

Themidterm resultsnuffs out any chance Trump had of passing partisan legislation in the second half of his presidency. And many of the interests he has been able to pursue without Congress' input — includingtariffs, theIran warand an array of Washington-areaconstruction projects— are sure to face sudden pushback from newly empowered Democratic majorities.

The paradigm shift hardly leaves Trump helpless, however. As president at a time ofexecutive-power expansion, Trump wields singular authorities that could stymie Democrats' efforts to pursue their own agendas.

But with his grip on the Capitol shriveling and hisapproval ratingsscraping record lows in numerous polls, it's unclear how much support he'll be able to muster to fight the coming political battles.

Even before Election Day, analysts and pundits had contemplated a Democratic rout so decisive that it would force a reckoning for the GOP, and potentially even pose an existential threat to Trump's "Make America Great Again" movement.

Marc Short, chairman of Advancing American Freedom and onetime chief of staff to former Vice PresidentMike Pence, told CNBC on Tuesday afternoon that the GOP has moved away from its conservative foundations.

"We need a refresh right now," Short said in an interview. "We've lost our way."

Trump has been vague about what he hopes to achieve with the rest of his term. But he has shared a vision of how he might coexist with a Democratic majority, and it involves heavy use of the veto pen.

"It's one of the stronger powers that a president has," Trump said in a Fox News interview overnight. "They'll send over things that are insane, and I'll veto them."

"And after a couple of months of vetoes, they'll call and they'll say, 'How do we get this stuff done?' And we'll work together," he said, adding, "I have a lot of friends that are Democrats."

Trump has previously stated his willingness to veto reams of legislation that Democrats send across his desk. In a New York Post podcast interview released Monday, Trump said that if Republicans don't win, "I veto everything."

Pressed to detail his plans for the next two years, Trump touted his record and said, "The most important thing is to keep it going. It's going to get better and better and better, unless people come in that hate our country."

If that happens, "I guess I'll become Mr. Veto," Trump said.

He may soon get his chance: House Democrats, poised to be led by current Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, are planning to pass a flurry of bills as soon as they take the reins next January, CNBC has learned.

The legislative push, firstreportedby The New York Times, aims to show a united Democratic caucus taking quick action on the issues they were elected to solve, especially oppressively high costs on everything from gas to groceries.

In their first 100 hours after being sworn in, House Democrats plan to introduce bills reinstating the enhanced health insurance subsidies that expired under the GOP-held Congress, and reversing the Medicaid cuts Trump signed into law earlier this year.

Democrats also plan to push forward a bill that would undo Trump's sweeping tariffs and reassert Congress' role in setting import taxes. And they will again vote on legislation to end the war in Iran, or seek congressional authorization to keep it going.

But without Trump's approval, those bills may end up as little more than symbolic gestures, as Democrats will lack the two-thirds majorities in both chambers that are required to override a presidential veto without GOP help.

And there's no guarantee the bills will even make it out of Congress: Despite their landslide victories, Senate Democrats will still end up shy of the 60 votes required to bypass the chamber's filibuster rules for most legislation, giving Republicans key leverage in the minority.

Democrats also could feasibly benefit from Trump's vetoes in the long term. Forcing the president to shoot down numerous popular bills could give them fodder in the 2028 election.

It's far from clear whether Trump believes he can find compromise with Democrats on any of their initial legislative priorities.

But any potential for a working relationship with the opposition could be poisoned early on, as Democrats in both chambers are aggressively signaling their plans to launch politically charged investigations against Trump, his political and corporate allies and even his family members.

Winning control of House committees gives Democrats the ability to issue subpoenas under thecurrent rules.

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is likely to chair the House Oversight Committee in the next Congress, said his panel will target the Trump family's business dealings, corporate corruption and alleged abuses by federal immigration agencies. He also plans to return focus to the Trump administration's handling of files related to notorious sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

As results rolled in Tuesday night, Garcia summed up his plans in atwo-word statement: "Lawyer up."

It's not just Garcia. Other Democrats have already demanded records from the Trump administration on a range of issues. Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., for instance, last week accused Trump of using tariff exemptions to cut "sweetheart deals" for industries whose leaders have plied Trump withgifts.

Senate Democrats have sent similar signals.

"They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we'll be printing," Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., said in an X post late Tuesday in response to a post, appearing to refer to tech executives.

The investigations are widely expected to consume much of the rest of Trump's term.

Trump has ample experience being targeted by Democrats, who impeached him twice in the House during his first presidential term.

But with his base of support appearing to erode inside and outside of Washington, Trump may have to face his political foes with a smaller arsenal than he's used to.

"I'm not expecting Republicans to revolt" against Trump following the midterm losses, AAF's Short told CNBC. "But I'm expecting some of them to quietly distance themselves."

title: Trump hammers Fox News, blaming network for GOP losses as ratings slide
content:
President Donald Trumpturned against Fox News on Tuesday night in a string of posts on Truth Social while Democratic wins rolled in during a historicmidterm election.

Trump blamed the network, which he's long championed, for Republican losses, saying in one post on his social media network that it "bears responsibility for these losses by constantly and consistently putting on the Dumocrat opposition."

Democrats took control of both the Senate and House of Representatives, flipping seats in states usually favorable to Republicans, including Texas, South Carolina and Kansas.

Trump also pointed to Fox's recent ratings as evidence of the network's decline.

"FoxNews Ratings are way down (27%!) because they're spending too much time covering the Trump Deranged Dumocrats! All of those people who used to watch Fox, and no longer do, get it. It's them, not me," he posted.

Fox News did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In apress releaselast week, Fox News reported 1.1 million average viewers for October, down about 27% from the same month a year prior.

Fox Corp.CEO Lachlan Murdoch noted the decline during the company's quarterly earnings call on Monday, citing "viewer fatigue."

However, Murdoch said such a shift is expected in the lead-up to a midterm election with a second-term president and said it was not the result of viewers turning to competitors' coverage.

"Those viewers are not going to any other news channel. They're not switching to MS NOW or to CNN," he said. "They're just fatigued and watching slightly less television overall."

Versant-ownedMS NOWandSkydance-ownedCNNboth reported primetime viewership was up by double digits in October compared with the year-ago period. However, both networks still had smaller total-day average audiences than Fox News.

MS NOW had 588,000 average viewers in October across all day parts, and CNN had 402,000, according to Nielsen data cited by Fox.

Despite Fox News' year-over-year drop in viewership, the company reported anotherwise strong quarterin what Murdoch called an "outstanding start to fiscal 2027."

Fox Corp., which includes the linear TV networks as well as entertainment and sports assets and a streaming business, reported revenue for its fiscal first quarter of $4.57 billion, up 22% year over year.

The company pointed to strength in advertising revenue, which increased 47%, buoyed by strong political advertising and the FIFA Men's World Cup, which aired in part on Fox platforms across June and July.

Trump is a frequent critic of media companies, especially broadcasters that he views as being biased against him. While he's repeatedly taken aim at NBC andDisney-owned ABC, the president has had a much friendlier relationship with Fox and its networks.

Trumpappeared on Fox News' "Hannity" on Monday night ahead of the election.

Disclosure: CNBC and MS NOW are divisions of Versant Media.

title: Elon Musk’s record election bet backfired. The backlash may reach beyond one billionaire
content:
Democrats' sweepingmidterms victorymarked a major rejection ofElon Muskand the artificial-intelligence industry, as a broad backlash against U.S. PresidentDonald Trumpand his tech allies put their political influence — and the debt-fueled data center buildout — under sharper scrutiny.

Musk, who spent a record of at least$474 millionon the midterms, funneled $224 million, or nearly half, into Texas alone, according to a CNBC analysis of campaign finance records, only to see his favored candidates, Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton and Gov. Greg Abbott, trounced in a Democratic wave.

The defeats rattled markets overnight, sendingSpaceXandTeslashares lower, both of which havelong flourishedunder Abbott's business-friendly policies. Meanwhile, broadertech stockscame under pressure as Democrats secured control of Congress.

Across the country, voters pushed back against billionaire influence and the growing power of technology companies, electing critics of the AI industry and approving restrictions on data centers fueling its expansion.

"We must get big money out of our politics, so no billionaire or trillionaire can buy our elections," Democratic Senator-electJames Talaricosaid in his victory speech, without naming Musk. "We must unrig this economic system that only benefits the top 1%."

J.C. Lintzenich, a visiting senior fellow at the German Marshall Fund, pointed to Musk's massive spending in Texas, telling CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Wednesday that the results were "clearly a rejection of the Elon Musk aspect that has found its way into the Trump orbit."

Texas has grown to be homebase for much of Musk's Empire.Teslaoperates its largest U.S. vehicle factory outside Austin,SpaceXlaunches rockets from its Starbase complex in South Texas, and Musk is pursuing additional investments in AI and semiconductor manufacturing.

These operations rely heavily on state decisions regarding electricity, water, environmental permits, infrastructure, and tax incentives. Democratic Governor-electGina Hinojosa— who campaigned against generous corporate subsidies, and Musk himself — will wield significant influence over those decisions.

Hinojosa has called for a moratorium on new data centers, an end to industry tax breaks and requirements that developers cover their full electricity costs. In her victory speech Tuesday, she vowed to take power from the "powerful people who have gotten very comfortable running this state."

Republicans still control the Legislature, limiting Hinojosa's ability to overhaul state policy. But her administration could complicate Musk's expansion plans with a tougher approach to permitting and business incentives.

Nationwide, Musk'sAmerica PACspent nearly $87 million across 44 federal races, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings. By Wednesday morning, Republicans it backed had lost 29 contests and won just three, with 12 still uncalled. More than $80 million — or 93% of its spending — went toward races Republicans lost.

The outcome leaves Musk with fewer allies in a Democratic-controlled Congress that could investigate his federal contracts, his past leadership of Trump'sDepartment of Government Efficiencyand his companies' ties to Washington.

Congressional scrutiny may slowSpaceX's lucrative and fast-growing government contracts, but Trump still controls executive agencies and holds veto power, limiting Democrats' ability to reverse policies that benefit Musk's defense-tech businesses.

The defeats aren't the first time that Musk's political spending has failed to produce his desired result.

America PAC backed eight losing congressional candidates in 2024, and last year Musk spent over $20 million trying to elect a conservative in Wisconsin. Though Musk promised last year tospend "a lot less"on politics, he ultimately became the biggest known donor in the 2026 midterms.

Longtime Tesla investor Ron Baron warned in March 2025 that Musk's political activism risked driving away customers,telling CNBC: "I don't think it's a great thing to alienate half the population."

Others cheered Musk's close relationship with Trump, and his influence over everything from regulation to Pentagon tech spending.

Musk was not the only tech figure who spent big.

OpenAI President Greg Brockman and his wife, Anna, contributed $25 million to Leading the Future, a political operation seeking to shape AI regulation, according to FEC filings. Venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz contributed another $50 million.

While the industry secured some victories – such as defeatingNew York lawmaker Alex Bores, an advocate for tougher AI safeguards, in a Democratic congressional primary – winning over local communities proved far more difficult.

In Ohio, DemocratSherrod Browndefeated Republican Sen. Jon Husted after attacking his support for data centers. Democrats spent nearly $28 million on advertisements criticizing data centers, according to AdImpact.

In South Carolina, Democrat Annie Andrews defeated Republican Sen. Darline Graham despite a late advertising push by Building the Future, a new data center industry super PAC that made Graham its first candidate to back. The group reserved $1.5 million in ads supporting Graham, while Andrews campaigned for a two-year moratorium on new data centers.

Nationwide, campaigns and outside groups spent $173 million on ads about data centers during the 2026 general election, with the ads almost entirely negative, according to AdImpact. Democratic advertisers accounted for $140 million of that spending. Voters also considered 41 local data center measures Tuesday, with at least 10 communitiesapproving bans or restrictions.

The financial stakes are enormously high.

JPMorgan Asset Management estimates theAI infrastructure buildoutcould cost roughly $5 trillion through 2030, including about $2 trillion financed through investment-grade debt markets.

Projects cannot generate anticipated returns until fully operational. Permitting delays can postpone completion and revenue, while higher utility and borrowing costs can raise project expenses and make expected returns harder to achieve.

title: Analysis: The Democrats have one chance to extract concessions from Trump. Markets will hate it
content:
Theelectoral sweepby Democrats on Tuesday night injects a new, unstable dynamic into the single biggest political risk to financial markets in the coming year:the debt limit. Unless a defeated Republican Party makes a swift and unlikely show of unity to take the issue off the table in its last few weeks in power, the protracted fight that will unfold is set to be nastier than ever, adding volatility to an already shaky bond market.

Past episodes of brinkmanship around the need to raise the government's borrowing limit have involvedRepublicans in Congressdemanding budget cuts from a Democratic president as the price of their vote. This time it will almost certainly be the left seeking concessions from the right.

The debt limit is the definition of a must-pass bill, even more than issues like funding the government and the defense budget. That makes it potentially the one real chance the new Democratic majority in Congress has to extract concessions from a president who is already pledging to veto their agenda. Markets will hate the entire process, even if — as many expect — it ends in compromise.

Because it is Democrats who hold the leverage, unlike past episodes, the ultimate agreement is more likely to increasegovernment spendingthan lower it. With highbond yieldsweighing on the economy, and Americans expecting action from a newly empowered Democratic opposition, the fight could be particularly damaging.

Many in the markets are stuck on the outdated idea that Democrats are less assertive than Republicans, said Aniket Shah, head of the Washington policy team at the investment bank Jefferies.

"They have this sort of mental image of Biden-Harris 2024," said Shah. "I don't think they realize how aggressively Democrats plan to take 2027."

The debt ceiling is a quirk of the congressional budgeting process. It stops the government from borrowing funds that Congress has already ordered federal agencies to spend. And because Congress has run deficits for decades — this year at$1.99 trillion— the pile of debt periodically bumps into the debt ceiling.

Congress last set the limit in 2025, when it gave the Treasury Department the authority to borrow $41.1 trillion. The Treasury is likely to hit its maximum borrowing capacity by midsummer, according to theBipartisan Policy Center, a nonprofit that tracks the issue.

The Treasury can use budgeting techniques to extend the so-called X-date, when the U.S. would no longer be able to meet all its obligations, to sometime in the fourth quarter of 2027, according to Wall Street estimates.

A few technical hiccups aside, the U.S. has never meaningfully breached the debt limit. The results of the U.S. missing payments would be chaotic as damage ripples out across the financial system into the global economy. U.S. default would immediately call into question trillions in Treasury securities that are the lifeblood of the global financial system. Damaging them could send the U.S. and global economies into an economic tailspin with no obvious means of recovery.

Because the stakes are so high, Shah and many others on Wall Street have come to believe that the episode will produce volatility but will ultimately be resolved in compromise.

Fights under former PresidentsBarack ObamaandJoe Bidensaw Republican congressional majorities use the issue to ram through spending reductions. (The 2025 raise was less contentious, because Republicans held Congress and the presidency. It was passed along party lines.)

Still, the risk-taking in those episodes contributed to ratings firms' decisions to downgrade U.S. debt — and could again.

PresidentDonald Trumphas called for Republicans to resolve the issue in the next few weeks, before the new Democratic-majority Congress is seated.

That isn't likely. The 2025 debt limit increase only passed because it was tied to a package of tax cuts and other policy changes. Republican debt hawks complained but held their noses.

Republicans may attempt to raise the limit in the coming lame-duck session under a budgeting procedure called reconciliation, which would allow them to move ahead without Democrats' votes. But success would require unity among a fractured, fleeting Republican majority that also faces several other more pressing priorities.

The most likely path toward raising the debt limit is the incoming Democratic majority negotiating another temporary fix with Trump. But they aren't going to make it easy. The president has occasionally made noises about making deals, but the political incentives ahead of the 2028 presidential election are for both sides to dig in.

"[Democrats] are going to want to embarrass the White House, and they're going to want to get leverage," Shah said. Democrats will use that to push to reverse cuts to Medicaid spending passed in 2025 and to try to restore healthcare spending, he said.

Democrats could also seek to tie the debt limit to restraining signature Trump policies, such as limiting the war in Iran or rolling back tariffs, analysts at Goldman Sachs said in a research note Wednesday.

Another potential compromise being considered in some corners of Washington is for Democrats to tie an increase in the corporate tax rate to a debt-limit raise, said George Pollack, senior U.S. analyst with Signum Global Advisers. Trump has shown he can be surprisingly flexible on similar issues, Pollack noted.

That is what will make this debt-limit fight different. In the past, Republicans used it to try to win spending reductions they couldn't get through regular budget negotiations. Now Democrats will broaden it out into an all-purpose hostage. That effort is far more likely to raise overall government spending than cut it. "There's a very weird irony here," said Robert Sockin, chief U.S. economist at PGIM, an asset manager.

The path to compromise will likely be rocky. Sockin believes it may turn out like the 2025 government shutdown. That was the longest government-wide shutdown in history, even though Democrats weren't in control of either house of Congress. This time they will have even more power.

If the fight extends beyond the X-date, missing debt payments could do serious damage to the financial system.

"It's not our base case, but we think the risk is higher than ever that you could get a technical default from the government," Sockin said. That would see the U.S. miss a payment, even if the government eventually makes it up.

That would still hurt. "You'll get more downgrades to the U.S. sovereign, and those might bite more this time," Sockin said. Yields on longer-term Treasuries would rise to account for added uncertainty.

Crossing the red line could prompt a "very negative reaction in equity markets," he said.

The coming months will show just how close Democrats are willing to get to that line.

title: Americans have said 'NO TO WAR,' Iran speaker says as Democrats take Congress
content:
Iran's speaker of parliament Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Americans have said "NO TO WAR," as projections from U.S. midterm elections showed that Democrats have flipped both houses of Congress.

Posting on Xafter projections showed that Democrats will have a majority in the House and Senate over the coming two years, Ghalibaf said that "Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message."

"If the [U.S. government] betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare."

TheXaccount of Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei posted: "The process of the US's collapse has accelerated."

"If there are still those who entertain the slightest hope that the hegemonic system may change behavior or shifts in its political parties may bring about change, or that by making concessions to the US, they can persuade it to abandon its hostility, they're gravely mistaken," the account added.

Last Saturday, Khamenei had called for Tehran's armed forces to meet "any level or type of threat" with "an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."

The Iran war has been a central issue for voters in the midterms, after U.S. President Donald Trump launched joint strikes with Israel against the Islamic Republic in February. The conflict has pushed up energy prices across the U.S., which has led to cost of living concerns.

Trump is also blaming the Iran war in part for the Democratic sweep of both chambers of Congress, tellingthe Wall Street Journalthat "Iran was a piece of it" when asked if the war contributed to the Republicans losses.

However, he maintains that prosecuting the war was the right decision, saying, "I don't think about it. I did the right thing. I would have done it again."

Washington has not explicitly stated it plans to resume attacks on Iran, butreports from The Wall Street Journaland The New York Times indicate the U.S. is preparing forpossible renewed military actionsafter the midterm elections.

With their new majorities, Democrats might be able to push through a War Powers Resolution, which will direct Trump to end the conflict with Iran should Congress not authorize it.

In June, both chambers — which were then Republican controlled —passed a concurrent resolutionto end the conflict, although a concurrent resolution is not binding and does not have the force of law. Previous attempts to impose a binding War Powers Resolution had been defeated.

title: What Trump losing power over Congress means for Iran, Ukraine and foreign policy
content:
WithDemocrats taking control of Congress, U.S. President Donald Trump could intensify his focus on foreign policy in his final two years in office, while facing greater scrutiny over the wars in Iran and Ukraine, experts told CNBC.

Democrats will have a Senate majority, with the Associated Press forecasting they will flip seats from Republicans in Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina, and Texas.

Democrats also won control of the House, giving the party greater scope to scrutinize the administration, shape spending and challenge Trump's foreign-policy agenda.

"We are going to see a president that is somewhat constrained on matters of oversight and investigation, but on foreign policy, he does still retain a lot of latitude," Laurel Rapp, director of Chatham House's U.S. and North America Programme, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe."

Rapp said the Iran war was a "major issue" in this election cycle amid soaring fuel prices, food costs, and inflation. The war began when Trump launched joint strikes with Israel on Feb. 28.

"Republicans don't really have an off-ramp here at this stage. We know the Democrats will seek to take votes in the House and the Senate to constrain the Republicans, to restrain the administration on Iran war powers. But whether that will bind the administration is another matter," Rapp added.

She said that Democrats could exercise the "power of the purse" to limit spending on U.S. military and other Iran-related costs.

With control of both chambers, Democrats could pass legislation seeking to direct Trump to end U.S. involvement in the conflict. However, making such a measure binding over a presidential veto would require enough votes in Congress to override it.

In a Wednesday note, Berenberg's Chief Economist Holger Schmieding predicted a final round of bombing in Iran, with Trump ultimately striking a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz by 2027, as voters feel the sting from high prices and fuel costs.

J.C. Lintzenich, visiting senior fellow at the German Marshall Fund, said that the president is not a "lame duck."

"Remember that this election changes the Congress; it does not change the president," Lintzenich told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Wednesday.

"The President of the United States still has lots of power, lots of authority. We still have pending action in Iran. We still have an unresolved situation with Russia and Ukraine."

He added that while Congress has changed, foreign policy is still executed by the president and his appointed officials.

"What we'll now see is a little bit more congressional oversight, the application of funding, for example, Ukraine, that's required by statute and law," Lintzenich said.

Lintzenich said the outgoing Congress was "more willing to let the White House slide," but Democratic control of both chambers would mean a more assertive Congress, using its Article I powers over legislation, spending, and oversight to hold the White House more closely to existing law and congressional requirements.

There could be "more trouble ahead" as Trump loses control of the Senate, Berenberg's Schmieding warned.

"As a perennial attention seeker without a consistent long-term strategy, he may be even more eager to pursue dangerous geopolitical adventures," Schmieding said.

"Congress will most likely not grant him the money for an expensive campaign similar to the Iran war… We probably have to brace ourselves for significant foreign policy noise in the two final years of the Trump presidency," he added.

Schmeiding said that the Russia-Ukraine war will be the "tail risk," as Trump will likely try to pressure "Ukraine to de facto surrender to Russian demands" — but this is an unlikely outcome as the President has lost support on the matter from his own party, he added.

Trump's influence over the Republicans is likely to decline after the midterm defeat, especially as most Republicans, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, don't share his sympathy for Putin, according to Schmeiding.

"That can help to contain the risk of Trump trying to impose an unacceptable deal on Ukraine. We thus see it as a tail risk rather than a likely outcome."

title: 5 midterm election takeaways: Tech billionaires suffer as Democrats drub Republicans
content:
Democrats decisivelytook control of CongressTuesday night, delivering a stinging rebuke to PresidentDonald Trumpand his economic record as voters voiced deep frustration with rising prices, government corruption and theAI data center build-out.

The party scored an extraordinary pair of victories in traditionally Republican Texas. James Talarico defeated Ken Paxton, becoming the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from the state in nearly four decades. Gina Hinojosa defeated three-term Gov. Greg Abbott, making her the first Democratic governor of Texas since Ann Richards left office in 1995. Texas became the clearest measure of how far the blue wave reached: Democrats swept the state's marquee races in a Republican stronghold long considered beyond their grasp.

Follow CNBC's live coverage of the 2026 midterm election results

The victories were part of a broader wave of Democratic gains. In South Carolina, Democrat Annie Andrews upset Darline Graham in a race Republicans had expected to win. In Ohio, Sherrod Brown defeated Republican Sen. Jon Husted. Democrats also flipped Senate seats in Iowa and North Carolina and won key races in Georgia and New Hampshire.

The results marked a striking collapse for Trump's candidates. Paxton, Graham and Husted were among the president's prominent picks who lost after he made dozens of endorsements.

The election also sharpened the political fight over data centers andartificial intelligence infrastructure. Texas is a major center ofplanned data-center construction, and Hinojosa campaigned for a pause on new projects until the state adopts tougher rules. Her victory gives Democrats more influence over Texas' approach to the build-out, though the state Legislature remains in Republican hands.

The results also delivered a blow to the tech billionaires and corporate interest groups that pouredhundreds of millions of dollarsinto backing Republican candidates who might be friendly to the massive AI data center projects they hope to build around the country.Elon Musk,the world's richest man and the cycle's largest individual political donor, spent record sums in a failed effort to help Republicans retain power, including in Texas.

Musk's spending may have become a liability as voters raisedconcerns about government corruptionand the growing influence of billionaires in exit polls. Talarico repeatedly attacked Musk on the campaign trail, accusing him of trying to buy "his very own personal United States Senator."

"Tonight's results are a wake-up call for corporate special interests and billionaires who have been rigging the economy," said Rep. Chris Pappas, who defeated former Republican Sen. John Sununu to win an open Senate seat in New Hampshire.

The outcome is poised to reshape the technology sector's relationship with Washington. A more adversarial Congress is likely to intensify scrutiny of tech companies and the AI data center build-out. Markets reacted as the scale of Democratic gains became clear:Dow futuresfell andS&P 500 futuresslipped Tuesday evening.

Economic frustration was also central to Democratic gains. Many voters blamedTrump's tariffsand thewar with Iranfor worsening their economic situation, while the cost of living remained a persistent strain.

Democratic control of both chambers gives the party a powerful check on Trump in the final two years of his term, including the ability to block parts of his agenda and intensify congressional oversight. The results sent a clear warning: promises to bring down costs did not overcome voters' frustration with prices, corruption and the country's direction.

Silicon Valley spent record sums trying to shape the election. Instead, it got a Democratic House promising to haul its CEOs before congressional investigators.

Many of the winners ran against not just Trump, but the billionaire donors who helped bankroll Republicans. In North Carolina, Cooper told supporters that North Carolinians "will always matter more than the billionaires and the insiders."

In Texas, Talarico defeated Paxton despite more than $200 million from SpaceX CEO Musk to stop him. On the same ballot, Hinojosa defeated Abbott after blaming him for the rapid buildout of data centers across Texas, saying the governor for putting Big Tech interests ahead of local communities.

The GOP had a commanding advantage among the election's biggest donors. According to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission records, 14 of the 20 largest donor groups backed Republicans exclusively or nearly so. Crypto, AI, and online gambling interests poured more than $377 million into races.

Not all of Silicon Valley's money ended up on the losing side. LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman, one of Democrats' biggest donors, cast the results as"an overwhelming wave against Trump and his cronies"and took a direct shot at Musk.

"We should get money out of politics," Hoffmanwrote on Xlate Tuesday. "And while people like Elon are spending outrageous amounts to keep authoritarian clowns in power, those of us who believe in the ideals of America cannot yield."

With control of the House comes the power to launch investigations, issue subpoenas and examine the Trump administration and its allies. That's going to be a challenge for tech companies to navigate as they find themselves in Democratic crosshairs.

Democrats are already calling for AI executives to testify under oath.

Among the first to seize on the results was Rep. Greg Casar, the Texas Democrat who chairs the Congressional Progressive Caucus.

"The House Democratic majority must make it a top priority to protect Americans' jobs, freedom, and lives from AI billionaires," Casar said in a statement after Democrats were projected to win the House. "AI company CEOs should be called to testify under oath."

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., the presumptive next chair of the oversight committee, put it more simply: "Lawyer up," he said in a statement.

The results also present headwinds for the infrastructure undergirding AI.

The Texas results appear to be a warning sign for the AI industry in a state projected to overtake Virginia as the world's biggest data center market by 2030,according to JLL. Abbott had long courted data center development before shifting his position this year as the backlash grew. Talarico and Hinojosa both seized on that anger, winning over Republican voters fed up with data centers going up in their communities. Hinojosa has promised toforce lawmakers to regulate the industry.

In a CNBC Voter Poll, 56% of voters said data centers were a crucial or major factor in their decision, with Democrats ranking the issue higher than Republicans.

Trump personally pushed states to redistrict their congressional seats mid-decade to cement a Republican majority in the House. The effort largely flopped.

Many of the GOP's redrawn districts ended up falling to Democrats, despite the unprecedented effort to defend or flip them by redrawing boundaries mid-decade.

That includes seats in Texas, Florida and North Carolina, which Democrats won despite Republicans making them safer. In Texas, where Republicans began their redistricting war that then spread to other states, Democrats ended up winning most of the gerrymandered seats.

The redistricting push was always risky because no recent census was available when the maps were drawn.

Trump rolled out the red carpet for Paxton, only for Republicans to lose a Senate seat in Texas for the first time in over three decades.

Talarico's victory in Texas came after Trump endorsed Paxton over the incumbent Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who held the seat for decades. In endorsing Paxton, Trump said Cornyn had not been sufficiently loyal.

Paxton prevailed in a bitter primary, and Trump's move to tip the scales spurned Senate Republicans, who saw Cornyn as a better and less expensive candidate than Paxton — who had a laundry list of scandals that plagued his campaign.

Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., who Trump handpicked to replace her late brother Lindsey Graham, fell to Democrat Annie Andrews. And Republican Michael Whatley lost to former Gov. Roy Cooper in North Carolina.

Democrats linked voter concerns over the cost of living to corruption in government in the lead-up to their colossal victory. The mix of the two helped propel corruption to be a top voter issue rather than a downballot concern.

Public polling indicated before Tuesday night that the issue of corruption was landing with voters. CNBC's All-America Survey conducted in mid-October found corruption was voters' top concern. Exit polls on Tuesday also tied the two issues: 69% said benefits flow to the wealthy in CNBC's Voter Poll.

The issue of corruption has exploded into public view during the second Trump term, as reports of Trump family business deals and the president's own ballooning wealth while in office dominate headlines.

In victory speeches across the country, Democrats made clear they are committed to battling a "rigged" system — a line reminiscent of once-radical Bernie Sanders presidential campaigns.

"We must get big money out of our politics, so no billionaire or trillionaire can buy our elections. We must unrig this economic system that only benefits the top one percent,"  Talarico said. "The real fight in this country is not left versus right. It is top versus bottom."

title: Gold, silver and precious metals prices jump, dollar dips as Democrats take control of Congress
content:
Precious metals saw strong gains on Tuesday morning, while the value of the dollar fell, following the U.S. midterm elections.

Spot goldwas 2.64% higher at $4,031.98 an ounce by 3:37 a.m. ET, whilespot silverjumped 4.17% to trade at $51.8495 per ounce.

Front-monthgold futuresadded 2.53% to trade at $4,039.90, whilesilver futureswere up 4.21% at $51.85.

Other metals seeing notable gains on Wednesday morning includedplatinum, which jumped 2.82% to trade at $1,455.96, and palladium, which was 3.8% higher at $969.33.

The moves came as vote counting continued in the midterms, with the Democratsprojectedto have won control of the House and multiple governors' offices also turning blue.

U.S. stock futures broadlyfellas the results came in, while Treasury yields alsomoved lower.Oilprices were marginally higher, while theU.S. dollar indexshed around 0.3%.

Rhona O'Connell, head of market analysis for EMEA and Asia at StoneX, said in a note on Tuesday that if the Democrats won dual Congressional control, gold should find support as rates and the dollar would likely come under pressure.

She said it would result in "fiscal brinkmanship, institutional friction, both leading to uncertainty," adding that "the Iran war and a weaker dollar would compete with [the] impact of [a] hawkish Fed."

"Less fiscal stimulus argues for lower long yields and a softer dollar, offset by debt-limit premia in bills and a Fed leaning towards another hike," she said.

Both gold and silver enjoyed record-breaking rallies in 2025, surging 66% and 135% respectively over the course of the year as investors sought safe haven assets amid geopolitical uncertainty and broader market volatility.

But the momentum has come undone this year, with rising inflation, surging bond yields and hawkish central banks removing support from the metals. Gold is down more than 7% year-to-date, while silver has tumbled almost 28%.

Spot gold rose on Monday as oil prices retreated, and is now on course for a weekly rise of around 3.7%.

Daniela Hathorn, senior market analyst at Capital.com, said in a Tuesday note that the recovery remains fragile.

"The challenge for precious metals is that geopolitical uncertainty is not automatically translating into safe-haven demand when investors are also concerned about restrictive monetary policy," she said. "They also face the risk of liquidation during sharp equity selloffs, as investors sell profitable or liquid positions to raise cash."

title: No more rice grains in Kellogg's Rice Krispies due to changing weather
content: Image source,Bloomberg via Getty ImagesByOsmond ChiaBusiness reporterPublished4 November 2026, 01:14 GMTUpdated 38 minutes agoBreakfast cereal giant Kellogg's has stopped using rice grains in Rice Krispies and Coco Pops in the UK due to "changing weather conditions" that have disrupted supplies.Corn flour and rice flour are being used instead, a Kellogg's spokesperson said on Tuesday, adding that the updated recipes have been "carefully assessed" and the firm has taken customer feedback into consideration.Those ingredients are replacing rice grains as crops have been hit by dry weather in key producing countries in Asia, reducing harvests and driving up prices.The new recipes mean cereal packaging will now include a "contains wheat gluten" warning.Rice Krispies products in the US and Canada will continue to be made with real rice with no changes to their recipes expected, a spokesperson for Kellogg's North American business told the BBC.The recipe change in the UK will help "maintain consistent quality at a time when changing weather conditions are affecting the quality and availability of some of the rice and grains used in our cereals," a Kellogg's spokesperson told the BBC."We appreciate that even small changes to a much-loved product can feel noticeable and that's why we have approached this with a lot of care and consideration."The company also said that Rice Krispies and Coco Pops will continue to meet UK food standards on levels of fat, salt and sugar in food.The cereals also contain no artificial colours, flavours or sweeteners and the nutritional benefits in each bowl, such as fibre, Vitamin D and iron are staying the same, the spokesperson added.Watch: How does El NinÌo affect world weather?Published21 AugustThe Kellogg company separated into two distinct firms in 2023.The largest is Kellanova, which focuses on snacks, cereals, noodles and other food products like Eggo, Pringles and Pop-Tarts sold globally. It is now owned by Mars, which makes confectionery and pet food.The other business, WK Kellogg's, operates in North America and has since beentaken over by Italian chocolate giant Ferrero.Most of the world's rice comes from Asia, many parts of which has been impacted by droughts, floods and heatwaves due to the El NiÃ±o weather phenomenon.The weather event is expected to severely impact crop production from South East Asia in particular. The region produces more than a quarter of the world's rice.The World Meteorological Agency expects the record-breaking El NiÃ±o will last until at least 2027.Related topicsInternational BusinessFoodKellogg CompanyMore on this storyFive ways El NiÃ±o is affecting the weather around the worldPublished20 OctoberAre breakfast cereals really good for us?

title: Google responds to political backlash over removing search from schools that ban AI
content:
Googleis playing defense on Tuesday after a political backlash to its new policy surrounding use of artificial intelligence in schools.

In a blog post titled"Designing responsible AI for learning,"Google said it's bringing AI into its Classroom offering with a product called Guided Learning. The New York Timespublisheda story saying that the company will turn off search for schools that reject AI entirely.

Following the Times' story, prominent left-leaning politicians, includingSen. Bernie Sandersfrom Vermont and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani voiced their outrage on social media.

"Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools," Mamdaniwroteon X. Sanderswrotethat "Google is threatening schools," referring to the policy as "extortion."

Google responded later in the day. In apost on X, the company said its new policy was meant to give schools more choice over how students interact with AI. Google said its Gemini chatbot, Gemini Notebook and search are turned off by default, and that "schools are in control," with the ability to turn them as they see fit.

"We are also updating Search for schools to make it better for learning," Google wrote. "Specifically, AI Mode and AI Overviews will offer step-by-step guided learning through problems, so that students don't get quick answers to schoolwork."

The company's post didn't explicitly respond to the claim that access to search requires use of AI. However, Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told the Times that "Search and AI are deeply integrated."

A Google spokesperson referred CNBC to the X post when asked for comment.

Google's broader practices have come under fire in recent years, with the company losing antitrust cases over itssearchandadvertisingbusinesses. Former Federal Trade Commission Chair Lina Khan aggressively pursued Google and other tech giants, includingMetaandAmazon.

Khan said in apost on Xon Tuesday that Google's new AI for learning policy highlights "the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service."

It's the latest controversy related to the impact of technology on children and the role leading internet companies are playing in delivering information.

In August, Meta reached a landmark$16.7 billion settlement in its child safety trialafter a number of state attorneys general accused the company of misrepresenting the extent of child mental health harms caused by apps likeFacebook and Instagram.

The same month, OpenAI launchedChatGPT for Teensafter state attorneys generallaunched an investigationinto the company's safety practices, with Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, a Republican,filing a lawsuitin June.

The nonprofit Common Sense Media recently gave Google's AI overviews an "unacceptable risk" rating. Last month, Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., and Josh Hawley, R-Mo.,launched an inquiryover Google's push of AI into classrooms.

Google introduced AI overviews as a search functionin May 2024.

— CNBC's MacKenzie Sigalos contributed to this report.

title: Graduates are managing AI - but are they learning much else?
content: Image source,Lotte UnderwoodImage caption,Managing AI agents is a big part of Lotte Underwood's jobByMaryLou CostaTechnology reporterPublished2 hours agoRecent university graduate Lotte Underwood is a public relations executive with a twist - she spends more time using AI than actually doing PR.Underwood, 25, joined London-based PR agency Fight or Flight in November last year, in the new role of "AI associate" after completing a degree and then a masters in marketing.She's part of a recently established, dedicated AI team that has built around 30 AI agents. Specific tasks include industry research, client reporting, media interview preparation, helping clients create clearer briefs, and image generation.A big part of Underwood's job is to manage those agents, check their outputs and feed those to the team members who are dealing directly with clients and the media.Another key responsibility of hers is to monitor how clients appear in the responses from AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and others."A huge part is being in client meetings and calls to work out what is actually going to be most helpful from these agents," says Underwood.What is an AI agent?AI is seen as one of the main factorsbehind graduate job cuts, but companies are also creating dedicated AI-specific graduate roles like Underwood's.Dillan Patel, for example, joined engineering software company Stride 18 months ago as an intern. A business management graduate, he was put to work developing an internal chatbot designed to capture the knowledge of a senior staff member transitioning into retirement.Patel, 24, is now an AI automation analyst, tasked with developing further internal agents to provide specific information to individual teams, while also identifying which manual or repetitive tasks across the company could be done by AI."My role focuses on finding practical ways to use technology, automation, data and AI to improve how we operate," says Coventry-based Patel.Image source,ArvatoConnectImage caption,Debra Maxwell is looking for "AI disruptors"Such AI savvy graduates are also in demand from companies like ArvatoConnect, an outsourced contact centre company.CEO Debra Maxwell says the company's usual graduate intake is on hold this year, but she plans to resume it next year with a bigger focus on AI."We would be looking for more AI-disruptor type roles, where you can challenge us as an organisation to think more holistically about where AI can be applied and where we could grow our business from," says London-based Maxwell."We see our graduates as not filling administrative roles, but actually adding value to the organisation in a different way."Maxwell adds: "For example, one of our recent graduates is using AI to do deep dives on specific markets, and provide more information for when we're bidding [for new contracts]. It's basically giving him a more rounded role."If AI can make a graduate job bigger and more integral to the organisation, Maxwell argues that companies can create a more loyal, engaged workforce that is able to contribute more meaningfully, much earlier.Research from consultancy PwC found that some graduate roles are assuming more responsibilities because of AI, as it allows companies to demand more senior abilities from junior hires.For the consultancy's 2026AI Jobs Barometer,external, it analysed 2.4 million entry-level jobs in the US. It found that the entry-level roles most influenced by AI are now seven times more likely to require traditionally senior-level skills. These include motivational leadership, strategic decision making and team building.Those entry-level roles with higher expectations have in fact grown 35% since 2019, PwC found, while other entry-level roles actually shrank by 10%.Image source,Cian ClintonImage caption,Cian Clinton uses around ten AI agents for work tasksCian Clinton, who joined consultancy Valliance last September after graduating from a Bachelor of Science in 2024, says the incorporation of AI into his role makes him feel less like a graduate, and more like an equal team member. He uses around 10 AI agents daily for different tasks."Your ideas and your creativity are a lot more valued because you actually get to implement those firsthand, and the responsibility you take on is a lot greater because of that," says London-based Clinton, 23."I am now taking on responsibilities which would usually take me four or five years to get to."His career progression, he believes, will now be faster as a result."AI is killing the 'pyramid' approachâ¦progression is no longer based on your knowledge bank. Now it's more based on your critical thinking and understanding of the processes," says Clinton.'Learning the trade'There's no doubt Underwood, Patel and Clinton are developing valuable AI knowledge which can help them across their careers.But with their time at work so focused on AI, does it matter how much - or how little - time they're spending learning about the professional field they're supposed to be operating in?Underwood says she'd like to still pick up the traditional PR skills her role isn't currently focused on, but is confident of her future in the agency's growing AI team."There's certain things that I haven't had the chance to do yet, like directly pitching to the media. I absolutely plan to do this," she says.Graduates becoming too AI-centric is an issue for Simon Pratt, chief operating officer at Portman Finance Group. He says being able to use AI effectively is important, but the company's two-year graduate programme is fully centred on "learning the trade"."Our graduates rotate across four areas at six-month intervals, working directly alongside senior relationship managers to learn their trade," Northampton-based Pratt explains."They'll learn all of our financial products, how to draft credit papers for submission to lenders, and how to build meaningful relationships with our customers. They'll progress to running transactions from start to finish."Claire Reed, PwC UK's chief technology and innovation officer, believes graduate roles that are too AI heavy won't necessarily provide graduates long-term career progression."There will be no graduate job now that doesn't require a baseline of AI literacy," says Glasgow-based Reed."But AI skills on their own are not going to help you in your career. You've got to couple that with that sector knowledge of what that client actually wants."Back in Coventry, Dillan Patel is confident his AI work will continue to be valuable, and he wants to keep building on it."I don't think I'd want to explore different positions within the business. Through my involvement in AI-related projects, I already work closely with different areas of the business and I'm gaining valuable knowledge and experience along the way," he says.Related topicsInternational BusinessTechnology of BusinessArtificial intelligenceEmploymentTechnology of BusinessWhy are more roofs not made of solar tiles?Published9 OctoberX-planes: Are they needed in the new era of drones?Published25 SeptemberThe virtual worlds where robots are trainedPublished18 September

title: Poundland supplier 'will lose millions' if retailer collapses
content: Image caption,Adam Turner is sales director at Poundland supplier HillcrestByTom Espiner,ÂBusiness reporter,ÂEmma Simpson,ÂBusiness correspondentÂandÂOliver Smith,ÂBusiness reporterPublished2 hours agoOne of Poundland's suppliers has said it will lose millions if the firm collapses.While that supplier will stay afloat, it is feared that some small and medium-sized suppliers could go under.This is in addition to potentially thousands of job losses among staff.Politicians have been putting questions to representatives of Poundland owners Gordon Brothers this week seeking "clarity" on plans for the retailer.Adam Turner, sales director at Highcrest Retail Brands - a family owned Bradford business - told the BBC that Poundland was one of Highcrest's biggest customers, and that the firms have had a relationship for decades.Highcrest mainly sells confectionary to Poundland, and turns over about Â£50m.It will "lose a few million" if Poundland becomes insolvent, so it will have a gap in its balance sheet next year, he said.Highcrest was a "longstanding business that can stomach this", but other medium and small suppliers have told him that "if Poundland goes under, so do they", Mr Turner said.This echoes awarning from Poundland founder Steve Smithon Monday that two or three thousand suppliers to the firm, which only work for Poundland, would be directly affected by its collapse.Not only 12,000 Poundland staff would be affected, but also potentially tens of thousands more, he said.If Poundland's stores are sold to new buyers, some of the employees may get new jobs on the same premises. However, it is understood that buyers are only interested in about half the stores at present - meaning roughly 6,000 employees would not be re-employed.Poundland's founder offers to invest in firmPublished1 day agoHigh stock levelsMr Turner said that the last three months of the year is the "golden quarter" for retailers. In terms of sweets, Poundland will get its Halloween stock in from July, and Christmas stock in from September.These three months will be the time of year when suppliers will be owed the most by Poundland.If Poundland goes under, suppliers will be getting "pennies in the pound" back from the administration, he said, which is "very upsetting" - although he still hopes a deal can be done so Poundland can remain solvent.Poundland owners Gordon Brothers will be a secured creditor, which means they are first in line to get their money back, and suppliers "who have done nothing wrong" will take the financial hit."It's sad. It's a nightmare for us all to be honest with you. It's not just the suppliers, it's the staff at Poundland, some of these guys have been there for many years."It's from the warehouse staff all the way to the shop staff to everybody within head office. It's a massive ripple effect through the supply chain," he added.Mr Turner said he had no knowledge of whether Gordon Brothers had deliberately timed the process of Poundland going into administration so it could take advantage of having high stock levels, which it can then sell.One of the ways Gordon Brothers makes money is through stock liquidations - selling off stock from collapsed businesses.One insider familiar with the situation told the BBC that the timing of Poundland facing collapse was "odd" - most retailers don't fall over in the run-up to Christmas.Gordon Brothers was approached for comment.Ministers' questionsMeanwhile, business secretary Jonathan Reynolds will meet with Gordon Brothers later this week after he and Prime Minister Andy Burnham questioned why a solvent deal had not been made.Business minster Kate Dearden told MPs that government officials had also met with representatives from Gordon Brothers on Monday."I am deeply concerned about the uncertainty surrounding Poundland's future and the impact it could have on its staff and their families who are at the forefront of my mind," Dearden told the House of Commons."Poundland is not currently in administration and the business continues to trade, but this is a worrying time for employees, suppliers and communities", she added.The minister confirmed she would also be meeting with Poundland executives on Wednesday.She said the government doesn't want to interfere with "current ongoing commercial negotiations", but said ministers would be seeking "clarity" on the plans for the retailer."It's absolutely legitimate for this government to ask the business if they're doing everything they can to protect employees and suppliers up and down the country," she added.Dearden told MPs that the government would be ready to help the company's employees, should the current situation end in administration."We stand ready to support them if they need to move into new employment, however... our priority is always in protecting jobs and the Secretary of State and I will continue to engage with the company to secure the best possible outcome," she added.The head of Gordon Brothers' European operations reportedly told the government that the firm stood by its stewardship and had given Poundland Â£85m in additional financing since its purchase in 2025.Related title: Jim Cramer sees signs of life in tech stocks — but not from the usual winners
content:
CNBC'sJim Cramersaid Tuesday that a new group of technology stocks may be emerging as market leaders.

While heavyweights such asNvidia,Microsoft,AlphabetandMetahave struggled to sustain rallies in recent weeks, other companies are showing signs of strength. That was evident during Tuesday's session as gains fromBroadcomandMicronsupported the major averages — a sign that investors may be shifting toward a different set of tech winners.

"Tech's trying to make a stand here. It's just not the tech that's led us for the last few years," the "Mad Money" host said.

Cramer pointed to chipmakerAdvanced Micro Devicesand networking companyArista Networks— both of which reported strong quarterly results after the bell Tuesday — as examples of technology companies that could help lead the sector's recovery. He also highlightedOracle, whose shares jumped nearly 6% in Tuesday's session.

"I want to believe that non-magnificent tech can lead us," he said. "But I also know that there are concerns we must be aware of before we get too cocky about one session's set of positives."

One concern is growing opposition to data center development, as local communities push back due to fears about rising electricity costs and the facilities' water consumption. He said smaller developers such asIren,NebiusandCoreWeavecould be particularly vulnerable if projects are canceled or forced to relocate, while larger companies likeAmazonhave more resources to secure alternative locations.

The ongoing war with Iran is another source of uncertainty.Oil prices turned lowerTuesday on hopes there could be progress in U.S.-Iran negotiations. But Cramer cautioned that Wall Street has repeatedly underestimated the risk of further escalation, making it difficult to declare the conflict no longer a threat to markets.

He stopped short of saying that the sector had reached a lasting bottom. After months of failed rebounds, Cramer said he "would like to wait for the crescendo before I commit too much money back into tech."

title: CrowdStrike's new kill switch can stop rogue AI agents in their tracks, CEO says
content:
CrowdStrikeCEO George Kurtz said Tuesday that the cybersecurity company can now shut down rogue artificial intelligence agents.

CrowdStrike'snew kill switch, announced Tuesday at its Fal.Con Europe conference, allows security teams to terminate misbehaving agents, prevent them from restarting and cut off their network access. It is designed to give humans more power over artificial intelligence models and systems, as concerns about how to control agents grow.

"Everyone is building AI agents, but they never had the off button, and now they do," Kurtz told CNBC'sJim Crameron "Mad Money." "It's going to be an incredibly important part of making sure that AI agents run and operate safely."

The AI Kill Switch, as CrowdStrike calls it, is part of the company's Falcon Guardian platform, which monitors AI agents operating within an organization. The technology, which is available immediately, is aimed ataddressing AI safety concernssurrounding the rapid adoption of AI agents.

In September, Anthropic CEODario Amodeicalled forslowing AI developmentover safety concerns, a position backed byOpenAICEOSam Altman. Kurtz argued at the time that slowing AI development would not eliminate existing security risks, which he saidunderscored the need for safeguardsas companies deploy autonomous systems.

Kurtz said Tuesday that CrowdStrike's new kill switch represents a significant shift in cybersecurity, which has traditionally focused on protecting companies from external threats. As businesses rely more on AI agents, he argued that security providers must also ensure those systems operate safely within their own organizations.

"Enabling agents to work safely is a massive market opportunity for CrowdStrike," Kurtz said. "We have AI capabilities to prevent these breaches from happening on the outside, and we also have the capabilities to make sure that agents are basically doing what they are instructed to do."

The CEO compared the technology to airbags in cars, arguing that safeguards are necessary even when AI systems are designed to operate correctly.

"If they go outside of those guardrails at runtime, we can kill those agents," he said.

CrowdStrike is seeing growing demand for its security tools as businesses adopt AI. Kurtz pointed toCrowdStrike's partnershipwithAnthropicto protect its Claude Cowork product: He said enterprise customers had pushed for CrowdStrike's technology to be integrated before they deployed Anthropic's offerings.

"Our customers went to Anthropic and said, 'We need CrowdStrike before we can deploy AI,'" Kurtz said. "I think it says volumes that customers would not roll out AI without CrowdStrike."

Shares of CrowdStrike closed at a record high of $278.86 on Oct. 6 but have since fallen about 12% as tech stocks struggled in October and into November.
