title: Crypto firm Binance covers 90% of losses after $6.3bn hack
content: Image source,Bloomberg via Getty ImagesByImogen JamesPublished31 October 2026Updated 2 hours agoBinance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has covered 90% of the $6.3bn (Â£4.7bn)assets stolen in a hack on Thursday.The remaining 10% may take longer to source in the required amounts, the company added.Binance has consistently pledged to cover 100% of the losses from what is suspected to be crypto's biggest hack on record and said it has set aside more than $6.34bn in company funds to do so."Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the company said in a statement on Saturday.In an update on Sunday, Binance said withdrawals had been restored on several of its networks, after they were suspended following the hack.It previously said withdrawals would be resumed in phases.The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said on Saturday that North Korea was responsible for the attack.The FBI said it had observed hackers converting stolen assets into a type of cryptocurrency called Ethereum and that it is expected that the assets will then be converted again using decentralised finance and instant swap services.Two analytics firmspreviously told the BBCthey had robust intelligence pointing to North Korean state-backed hacking unit the Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor - which was specifically named by the FBI - as the likely culprits.Speaking to reporters on Saturday night,US President Donald Trump said,externalthe US is still unsure who the culprits are."We're learning about it. We don't know if it's North Korea - but if it is, we'll talk to North Korea about it," he said.Binance said it had replenished the stolen assets using various funds and its own corporate treasury.All holdings of the cryptocurrencies bitcoin, Ethereum and Tether are covered, along with seven other widely-traded crypto assets, the company said.From Bitcoin to Binance: Crypto terms and what they meanThe hack is believed to be the largest in history, eclipsing the record of a $1.5bn heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025 - for which the FBI also said North Korea was responsible.North Korea has always denied involvement in these attacks.Binance's initial investigation suggested an engineer's laptop was compromised, which allowed access to unauthorised withdrawals, but a later update said they had uncovered "additional points of breach".Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, said the hack was carried out by more than one person, and the hackers used sophisticated methods to hide their tracks, such as a "self-destruct mechanism".On Friday, the company said it had frozen around $3bn of stolen assets after working with law enforcement, intelligence firms and partners.The investigation is ongoing, it added. The US Secret Service said on Friday it is "working around the clock" with private sector partners "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds" stolen from Binance.Binance, founded in China in 2017, lets users buy, sell and trade digital assets - it is estimated to have hundreds of millions of users worldwide.Crypto is a digital asset, which doesn't exist physically and is instead accessed via digital wallets or computers.Related topicsCryptocurrencyCyber-crimeCyber-attacksMore on this storyWho could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so farPublished2 days agoCrypto giant Binance attempting to recover $6.3bn stolen in hack linked to North KoreaPublished1 day agoWhy North Korea's 'elite' hackers are the prime suspect in major Binance hackPublished1 day ago

title: Companies promised AI gains— here's how the payoff showed up in earnings
content:
Some companies are beginning to report financial benefits from artificial intelligence investments, as interest in the technology shifts from hype to measurable returns in the latest quarter.

Corporate AI investment has surged as companies look to boost efficiency and become more profitable, reaching $581.7 billion in 2025, up 130% from the previous year, according to theStanford HAI 2026 AI Index report.

As CEOs tout the tech's benefits and hyperscalers likeMicrosoft,Amazon,GoogleandMetaare expected to spend$700 billion combined this yearon its infrastructure, investors are looking for measurable gains.

Now, with third-quarter earnings season underway, some companies are beginning to put numbers around those benefits.

Spanish banking giant Santander said Wednesday that it saw AI initiatives generate 194 million euros ($216 million) in business value in thefirst nine months of 2026.

Santander Chief Financial Officer José García Cantera told CNBC that AI is helping the bank reduce low-value tasks so employees can focus on higher-value work.

"This affects both revenue and costs, so we are actually in the quarter where we can actually link directly to AI a positive contribution," Cantera said.

"AI is being embedded in all the processes that we are conducting at the bank, so it's really difficult to just say how much comes from AI, but clearly AI is improving the quality of our services to clients."

Swiss pharmaceutical giantNovartisCEO Vas Narasimhan told CNBC that AI was beginning to contribute to the company's bottom line.

Novartis reported third-quarter core operating incomeof $6.04 billion, up 10% year-on-year at constant currencies. The company did not quantify how much of that was attributable to AI but Narasimhan told CNBC: "I think this is the first quarter I've really seen AI start to improve actually our P&L on a tangible basis."

"We're working on R&D [research & development] to see if it can really increase R&D productivity," Narasimhan said on "Squawk Box Europe" on Tuesday.

"We're already seeing some of the productivity you saw in the bottom-line performance of what we can do with AI from M&S [marketing & sales]."

Meanwhile, Standard Chartered Chief Financial Officer Manus Costello told "Squawk Box Europe" on Wednesday that the company is seeing AI "appear everywhere across the business."

The bank reported third-quarter operating income growth of 14% at constant currency, excluding notable items.

"I think you can see it in the top line growth that we're delivering, and you can see it in that operating leverage that I talked about," Costello said, adding that AI is helping managers drive better relationships with customers and generate more income.

"We're also seeing that strong operating leverage that I talked about, where income is growing much faster than costs, and some of that is because we've been able to deploy AI tools to improve core processes and enable us to scale those up very efficiently," he added.

CarlsbergCEO Jacob Aarup-Andersen said on "Squawk Box Europe" this week that it's not seeing AI benefits at scale, but the technology has impacted internal processes, cost efficiency, commercial and pricing processes, marketing and its supply chain.

The company's revenue grew 4.9% in the third quarter.

Elsewhere, tech firms are also reporting gains. Meta said in its Oct. 21 earnings that its AI investments were delivering "substantial incremental advertising revenue," while total revenue jumped 26% in the quarter ended Sept. 30.

While Alphabet's Google Search revenue growth slowed amid concerns about AI competition,Google Cloud revenuemore than doubled to nearly $31 billion in the third quarter, it reported on Wednesday.

title: No more washing up: How Airbnb's new house rules have divided hosts and guests
content: Image source,Lisa ClewesImage caption,Airbnb host Lisa says her Welsh holiday let was left 'a complete mess' by a group of guestsByYasmin RufoPublished1 November 2026, 00:17 GMTWhen Lisa Clewes returned to her Welsh holiday let after a group of guests checked out, she was horrified by the mess.Just days earlier, she had met the group in person and helped with their luggage.But after a dinner party, the house was left "in a complete mess" with broken glasses, drinks cans on the floor, pans full of food on the table and fish guts left in the garden."It was really unbelievable. Had I had another booking the same day, I would have had to cancel or delay check-in," says Clewes.She charges a cleaning fee that covers around 75% of the cost of a cleaner and asks guests to empty the fridge, put rubbish in the bins and load the dishwasher.Image source,Lisa ClewesImage caption,Clewes says it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her property and fears that guests leaving more mess could mean increasing costsBut Airbnb's new rules mean hosts can no longer ask guests to do jobs normally carried out by cleaners, including washing and putting away dishes, stripping beds and taking rubbish off site.The updated guidelines, which apply to bookings made globally from 20 November, state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules and add other "reasonable" requests.Clewes says it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her three-bedroom property. She fears guests leaving more mess could mean hiring extra cleaners and increasing costs â expenses that may ultimately be passed on to her guests.Image source,AirbnbImage caption,The changes have come as a relief to guests like Jessica Newhook, who says she has been faced with lengthy checkout lists, often on top of hefty cleaning fees.She booked an Airbnb in Florida for a family reunion of 11 guests and says they had to "leave the property move-in ready for the cleaners", despite paying a $250 (Â£187) cleaning fee.Newhook says the host told them to wash and fold towels, clean the bedding and kitchen, and sweep and mop the floors. She was also warned by the host that their behaviour needed to improve or they could be told to leave, because they had left chairs blocking bins."We had rules about everything and it was not relaxing at all."While Newhook likes the home comforts of staying in an Airbnb, she says the combination of relentless rules and rising cleaning fees has taken away much of its appeal."It is getting to the point where a hotel is cheaper and I know what to expect."Krissi Foskett, 46, from Glasgow, runs a national cleaning company and regularly stays in Airbnb properties so "can see the issue from both sides".Image source,Krissi FoskettImage caption,Krissi says there's a difference between being a respectful guest and being expected to help run the business you've just paid to stay inDuring a recent stay in Stafford, she paid a Â£35 cleaning fee but was still asked to strip the beds, put on a wash, empty bins and carry rubbish down a long track to a recycling area."I don't particularly mind doing those things, but it did make me question what exactly I was paying the additional cleaning fee for," she says.For Foskett, there is a difference between being a considerate guest â "putting your dirty dishes in the dishwasher" â and being "expected to prepare the property for the next guests".Through her cleaning business, she has also seen the other extreme, with teams arriving to find broken furniture, vomit and pet urine.While she sympathises with hosts facing tight turnarounds and rising cleaning costs, these should not be passed on to guests, she says."If you're running an Airbnb as a business, professional cleaning is a cost of doing business."Anthony Marsh, who co-owns a cabin retreat in North Yorkshire with his husband, used to list five of their 12 properties on Airbnb, but says the new rules have prompted him to reduce this number to just two.His concern with the changes is that "Airbnb has effectively given guests permission to come and leave properties a tip, and a host can't do anything about it".Image source,Anthony MarshImage caption,Anthony and his husband used to list five of their 12 cabins in North Yorkshire on Airbnb...Image source,Gasp image coImage caption,... but will now list just two in light of the new rulesHe believes asking guests to wash their pots and put out the bins is hardly unreasonable and, with a small cleaning team and tight turnaround times, he worries extra mess could leave properties unready for the next arrivals."It's common sense and common decency," he says.His company does not charge a cleaning fee, and Marsh says most guests are respectful. But fees are more common than not. Some 63.2% of Airbnb listings charge a cleaning fee, with an average cost of Â£55 according todata from AirROI,external.Laura Lewis runs a directory that helps holiday-let owners market their properties and connect with potential guests.Many of her clients also list on Airbnb and she says most are unhappy with the new rules, arguing that asking guests to wash up is a matter of basic respect."Some people say it's factored into the cleaning fee, but I wouldn't leave a holiday let with all the washing-up to do. It's not the right thing," she says.Image source,Laura LewisImage caption,Laura Lewis says it's a matter of "basic respect" to wash dishes and take the bins outThe announcement has added to growing frustration among owners following increases in Airbnb's commission rates last year. Many are investing in their own websites and social media to attract direct bookings and avoid platform fees.Lewis has taken the same approach with the three treehouses on her farm â most of her bookings are already direct and she now plans to remove her listings from Airbnb altogether.Not all hosts are concerned about the changes, however. Matt Prosz, who hosts and manages other Airbnb properties full-time, believes the update will improve the guest experience without changing how most people behave.Image source,Matt ProszImage caption,Prosz joined Airbnb's co-host network during Covid and now leads a London community of about 3,000 hostsGuests at his property in south-west London are asked only to lock up and return the keys. "People sometimes strip the beds or do things without me asking, and that's nice for my cleaners, but I don't expect it."Prosz doubts the changes will lead to guests leaving properties in a worse state, pointing to Airbnb's mutual review system."If I put a big chore list, I wouldn't expect a five-star review and vice versa â if a guest leaves the place in a state, you're not going to give them a good review."He believes the system encourages both sides to behave reasonably, and that most guests will continue to treat properties with respect."Airbnb is trying to cut out the silly stuff because it's not a good guest experience."Related topicsAirbnbTravelHolidaysMore on this storyAirbnb hosts can no longer make guests strip beds and wash dishes under new rulesPublished21 October

title: OPEC+ agrees in principle to keep oil output targets steady in December, sources say
content:
OPEC+ oil-producing countries have agreed in principle to ⁠keep their December oil output targets steady at a meeting on ​Sunday, three people ​with knowledge ​of the matter told Reuters, in line with expectations that further output policy adjustments won't occur until next ⁠year.

Sunday's online meeting of seven core OPEC+ members — Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman — comes as Gulf members have been boosting exports disrupted for months by the war with Iran. Most, however, are still pumping well below their ​output targets.

All three people declined to be identified.

OPEC+ comprises the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies, including Russia.

In September, OPEC+ ⁠completed the phased rollback of a 1.65 million-barrel-per-day supply cut ‌first agreed in 2023. Disruption caused ‌by the Iran war has meant Gulf producers are falling below their quotas.

Reuters reported in July that OPEC+ was likely to make no changes to its targets during the fourth quarter as it turns its focus to 2027 quota negotiations.

The group still has one more layer of production cuts ​of about 2 million ‌bpd covering most members through the end of 2026.

OPEC+ needs to finalize a review of members' production capacity during the fourth quarter before setting the 2027 baselines that ​will determine future quotas and ‌shape plans to unwind those cuts, sources have said.

On Friday, oil pricessurgedmore than 2%, settling ​at their highest levels since the end of April as traders braced for a potential escalation in thewar.

Brent crudefutures for December, which expired on Friday, closed up $2.76, or 2.4%, at $117.64 a barrel, after touching a high of $118. The more active January contract gained $2.63 to $113.43.

U.S.West Texas Intermediate(WTI) crude futures ended $2.12, or 2.08%, higher at $104.12.

title: Trump defamation suit against Murdoch, WSJ over Epstein letter dismissed with prejudice
content:
A federal judge on Saturday dismissed PresidentDonald Trump'sdefamation lawsuit against media baronRupert MurdochandThe Wall Street Journalover the newspaper's reporting on a purported 50thbirthday letterto notorious sex offenderJeffrey Epstein.

U.S. DistrictJudge Darrin Gaylesin Miami ruled that Trump again failed to plausibly allege that the newspaper and other defendants acted with actual malice when they published the story in July 2025.

"Grasping at straws, the Amended Complaint attempts to manufacture flaws with the investigation," Gayles wrote in the 20-page ruling, which dismissed the lawsuit with prejudice.

The judge said the Journal had conducted a "thoughtful and detailed investigation" and rejected Trump's argument that the newspaper should not have published the story after he denied writing the letter.

Gayles did not determine whether Trump actually authored the disputed letter.

The ruling comes roughly six months after the court first dismissed the $10 billion lawsuit against Murdoch and the newspaper, which he owns.

By dismissing the suit with prejudice, Trump cannot file another amended version of the lawsuit in the district court. However, a spokesman for Trump's legal team told CNBC on Saturday that the president plans to appeal the ruling.

"President Trump will continue to press forward in his powerhouse lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and all of the other defendants. The President will continue to hold those who mislead the American People with Fake News and smears accountable for their actions," the spokesman said in a statement.

Spokespeople or legal representatives for the Journal and Murdoch did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Judge Gayles, as he did when dismissing the suit for the first time, noted Trump, who has adamantly denied sending theletter to his then-friend Epstein in 2003, had "not plausibly alleged that the Defendants published the Article with actual malice."

"As with his first attempt, he has failed," Gayles' Saturday ruling reads. "Grasping at straws, the Amended Complaint attempts to manufacture flaws with the investigation."

Plaintiffs who are public figures like Trump must show that a defendant acted with actual malice when making allegedly defamatory statements, according to legal precedent.

The amended lawsuit contained new details and claims, including that Murdoch told Trump "I will handle it" on a phone call about an article describing a birthday letter to Epstein that allegedly bore Trump's signature,Newsweekpreviously reported.

Gayles rejected each of Trump's arguments in the amended complaint, including that the Journal did not adequately investigate the letter, omitted relevant details, and published the letter after the president and his representatives denied it was authentic.

Gayles said the last argument would effectively allow public figures to block unfavorable reporting, which "runs afoul of the First Amendment" that protects freedom of speech and the press.

The Saturday ruling is the latest setback in litigation between Trump and the media. A different federal judge on Oct. 22 ordered Trump to sit for a deposition in his$10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBCby Dec. 11.

The Journalpublished an articleon July 17, 2025, saying a letter bearing Trump's signature was included in an album of letters Epstein was giving for his 50th birthday. The article said Trump sent the letter at the request of Epstein's close friend, Ghislaine Maxwell, who two decades later was convicted of procuring underage girls to be sexually abused by Epstein.

The Journal noted that the letter "contains several lines of typewritten text framed by the outline of a naked woman, which appears to be hand-drawn with a heavy marker."

"A pair of small arcs denotes the woman's breasts, and the future president's signature is a squiggly 'Donald' below her waist, mimicking pubic hair," Journal reporters Khadeeja Safdar and Joe Palazzolo said in the article.

"The letter concludes: 'Happy Birthday — and may every day be another wonderful secret,'" they wrote.

Trump angrily denied writing the letter, saying, "This is not me. This is a fake thing."'

"I never wrote a picture in my life. I don't draw pictures of women," the president said at the time.

title: OpenAI pares fundraising goal, now seeking up to $20 billion in latest round
content:
OpenAI is seeking to raise up to $20 billion in a new funding round, CNBC confirmed on Saturday, paring back its earlier target of up to $30 billion.

The funding round is still in progress and has not closed, so the figures are subject to change, a person directly familiar with the deal told CNBC, asking to remain unnamed as they were not authorized to discuss the details publicly.

OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Financial Timesfirst reported that OpenAI had reduced its target for the round by $10 billion, and said the company would seek a post-money valuation of $1.25 trillion. According to FT, the ChatGPT developer set a Friday deadline for investors to commit to ​the newest round, with some investors opting to reduce their allocations.

Investors from the United Arab Emirates areleading the roundalongside Coatue, as CNBC previously reported.

News that the ChatGPT developer slashed its funding round follows a week when investors asked whether big tech firms' spending on AI, especially to build out data centers and snap up GPUs, will deliver adequate returns.

AI-linked stocks sankon Friday, with chip makerInteldown 25% on lackluster revenue guidance,Microndown 5.5%, andNvidiafalling 4%.

Microsoft,Alphabet'sGoogle andAmazonhave been on aspending blitzin recent years to meet the surge in demand for AI infrastructure, but all three issued capex figures or forecasts last week that came in below analysts' estimates.

Alphabet saw its worst trading day ever on Thursday after its search revenuefell short of expectations. Philipp Schindler, the company's chief business officer, said theimpact on searchwas partly because of lower monetization within the company's AI Mode.

title: G20 foreign ministers end Atlanta meeting without consensus on key issues
content:
Top diplomats from the Group of 20 largest world economies wrapped up two days of talks Saturday without reaching consensus on several critical global security issues after divisions, notably over Russia's war with Ukraine, overshadowed the start of the Atlanta meeting.

As a result, the group did not release a joint communique but will rather rely on a chairman's statement summarizing the talks, which Secretary of StateMarco Rubiosaid he would release later Saturday.

"I wouldn't pretend to you today that we are close to finding universally accepted solutions to these problems," Rubio told reporters at a news conference marking the end of the meetings.

"But," he said, "I do think that among the G-20 represented here are countries that are working together to solve some of them, particularly in the realm of supply chains and critical minerals."

Rubio had said the first day of the session was "very productive" and hosted sideline talks with his counterparts from Australia, India and Japan on Saturday before leading the final G20 event. That discussion on supply chains examined freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red, Black and South China seas.

"I made clear to our partners that secure supply chains are essential for growth," Rubio said in a social media post on X. "Critical trade routes including the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb Strait must remain secure and open to commerce. And we must continue to strengthen and expand critical mineral supply chains to protect our future."

At a reception for G20 participants Friday night, Rubio sounded optimistic. "Together, I think that we are mapping a vibrant, dynamic, and bold economic future, one that will pioneer new horizons for the entire world," he said.

Rubio had opened the talks Friday with an appeal for unity, but then canceled the traditional group photo of the foreign ministers. European diplomats objected to including Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov and threatened to boycott or walk out of the snapshot.

Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski, who was representing his country for the first time as a guest at a G20 meeting, said he was not surprised by the failure to reach consensus.

"We have wars going on, and we have participants in those wars around the table, so it's very difficult to agree on a common line," he told reporters.

Other participants in the meetings, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the private talks, said they had all agreed to try to overcome their differences despite the long odds and to work to make next month's summit of G20 leaders, hosted by President Donald Trump in Florida, a success.

These diplomats said a chairman's statement had long been the plan because of the major differences among attendees, including over the Russia-Ukraine war, the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, U.S. tariffs, and Chinese moves in the South China Sea. All have contributed to spikes in global fuel costs, as well as uncertainty about trade.

They described the opening session as cordial but said Russia's position on Ukraine was unyielding — as was its opposition to Poland's membership in the G20. They said the disagreements also included the Trump administration's decision not to invite G20 member South Africa, despite others' objections.

Before the meeting began, some G20 countries had expressed concern that the U.S. invited Russia during its heightened attacks on Ukraine, especially after Trump pushed ties with Ukraine to new lows by waiving fresh sanctions on Moscow and temporarily limiting logistical and intelligence assistance.

The State Department, however, announced Friday that it had approved a proposed $2.1 billion sale of Patriot air defense interceptors for Ukraine.

Lavrov said Moscow would not allow a situation in which Ukraine poses a "military threat to legitimate security interests of the Russian Federation."

Lavrov has traveled only infrequently to NATO member states since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022 and resulting severe sanctions were imposed on Moscow. It is unclear whether Russian President Vladimir Putin will accept Trump's invitation to attend the summit at Trump's Miami golf club in December.

The prospect of new U.S. military intervention in Iran also hung over the G20 meeting. That has put the region, including G20 member Saudi Arabia, on edge. Rubio met on Friday with his Saudi counterpart, Prince Faisal bin Farhan, as well as Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, whose country has been a key mediator.

The Associated Press has reported that U.S. officials have told several Middle East countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military strikes against Iran after U.S. elections Tuesday and the possibility that Iran will retaliate.

title: SpaceX loses bid to toss NAACP lawsuit over Memphis data center air pollution
content:
SpaceX'sAI division, SpaceXAI, lost its bid to dismiss an NAACP lawsuit, which is proceeding in federal court in Mississippi, according to ajudge's opinionreleased late Friday.

The lawsuit claims that the AI division of CEOElon Musk'saerospace and defense tech conglomerate violated the Clean Air Act by using gas-fired combustion turbines to power its massive AI data centers in Greater Memphis.

The Colossus data centers and a power plant that SpaceXAI is also building in Southaven, Mississippi, have faced community backlash for years.

The Southern Environmental Law Center and Earthjustice filed the suit on behalf of the NAACP in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Mississippiin April 2026.

The suit alleges that between August and December 2025, xAI and its subsidiary MZX Tech, installed and operated 27 gas turbines in Southaven, Mississippi, "without an air permit or regard for the health and safety of people living nearby."

(SpaceXAI is owned and operated by SpaceX, which has rebranded it as SpaceXAI or SpaceXSI.)

The turbines emit smog-forming pollutants and particulate matter that can increase health risks and cause an unpleasant odor, among other unwanted impacts, according to the suit.

Lawyers for SpaceXAI argued in theirmotion to dismiss,filed in June, that the NAACP suit should be tossed because the company's use of the turbines, which it characterized as "mobile," was exempt from permitting requirements. They also argued that NAACP didn't have a right to sue under the federal Clean Air Act, and suits by such community groups were unconstitutional.

The judge presiding over the case rejected those arguments, writing: "Because the plaintiffs have statutory standing under the Clean Air Act, because the combustion turbines are not 'mobile sources' under Mississippi's SIP, and because the citizen suit provision does not violate Article II of the Constitution or the private nondelegation doctrine, the plaintiffs' claims will proceed."

The decision comes about two weeks after the same court rejected a Department of Justice'srequest to end the caseagainst Musk's company.

SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: Qatari mediators held talks in Tehran aimed at restarting direct U.S.-Iran negotiations, source says
content:
Qatarimediators have held talks withIranianofficials in an attempt to restart direct negotiations between Washington and Tehran, an official source familiar with the discussions told CNBC on Saturday.

Iran promised a "geographically unrestricted response" to any new attacks by the U.S.

Qatari mediators held more than 12 hours of talks in Tehran on Friday to reach a deal to avoid a possible resumption of American-led attacks on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections, the source said, speaking on condition of anonymity.

Axiosfirst reportedthe talks, which it said are set to continue in the Qatari capital, Doha, on Saturday.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said there areno plans to meet U.S. officials, adding that an Iranian delegation has headed to Qatar for talks with mediators, Qatari media outlet Al Jazeera reported.

"What is being circulated in this regard is merely media speculation," Al Jazeera quoted Araghchi as saying.

A preliminary agreement signed on June 17 between the U.S. and Iran to halt the fighting — which began on Feb. 28 with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iranian targets — broke down weeks later.

On Tuesday, U.S. PresidentDonald Trumpreiterated his claim that the Iran war will end "whenever I want it to." Trump said it "would be very quick, but we have to have an end properly,"with a "total statement" that Iran would never have a nuclear weapon.

The last confirmed U.S. strikes on Iran occurred on Sept. 1. Trump previously left open the possibility thatattacks on Iran would resumeafter the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which are set for Tuesday. Tehran has said it ispreparing a military responseto any U.S. strikes.

A statement posted on Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei's Telegram account Saturdaysaidthat "any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."

The Iranian Broadcasting Agency quoted a Hormozgan province official as saying Saturday that U.S. forces attacked two fishing boats off Masan near Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. The report has not been independently confirmed.

U.S. Central Command did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

It's the latest report of attacks on shipping in the economically crucial stretch of water.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre reported Friday that a crude oil tanker was hit by an unknown projectile as it was heading out of the strait.

Separately, Iran said Friday four tankers struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz and Yemen's Houthis claimed missile strikes on Saudi Arabia, escalating pressure on two fronts.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said three tankers caught fire after striking mines along what it called an "unauthorized southern route" near the Omani coast. Iran's army said a fourth burned east of the strait.

Oil pricesjumpedmore than 2% on Friday and settled ​at their highest levels since the end of April, as traders braced for a potential escalation in thewar.

Brent crudefutures for December, which expired on Friday, settled up $2.76, or 2.4%, at $117.64 a barrel, after touching a high of $118. The more active January contract gained $2.63 to $113.43.

title: Automatic 401(k) rollovers reduce cash-outs, research finds — but few accounts reach new employer plans
content:
Leaving a job can make asmall 401(k)hard to hold on to: Someemployers' plans cash out accounts under $1,000 or move slightly larger balances into an IRA.Taking the moneyin cash and moving on can feel like the simplest option, but it can have short- and long-term financial consequences.

A system backed by major 401(k) administrators aims to make it easier for those savings to follow workers to their next job. New research from one of those companies, Vanguard, shows it's helping fewer people cash out — although most of the money has yet to reach workers' new retirement plans.

Among workers with less than $1,000 in their 401(k), the share who cashed out within 10 months of leaving their job fell to about 9% from roughly 50% after their employers began participating in a new system called the Portability Services Network, according tothe Vanguard research. Among those with balances of between $1,000 and $7,000, the share cashing out fell to 31% from 39%.

Portability Services Network is a coalition of large401(k) administrators— including Vanguard, Fidelity Investments and Alight Solutions, among others — in conjunction with Retirement Clearinghouse and has been in operation since late 2023.

How it works: When a worker with a small 401(k) balance leaves an employer that participates in the network, the money is generally automatically rolled into a safe harbor IRA, where it remains until the network matches it with the worker's new employer plan. The balance then gets rolled into the new 401(k) from that interim IRA. The catch, however, is that the receiving employer must also participate in the network for the money to move to the next employer's plan.

In Vanguard's research, just 6% of accounts that have been transferred into IRAs as part of this automatic portability network successfully made it to a new employer's plan as of early 2026, largely because few employers have opted in. The rest generally remained in those interim IRAs, waiting to be matched with another employer plan that participates in the network. While workers can always roll over the money into their new 401(k) themselves, the point of the network is for it to happen automatically.

Of the roughly 220,000 outbound rollovers involving Vanguard participants analyzed, the median balance was just $200, and nearly three-quarters involved less than $1,000. The typical saver affected was 31 years old, earned about $20,000 annually and had worked for their employer for roughly six months, according to the research.

The cash-out analysis is based on workers at 83 employer-sponsored retirement plans administered by Vanguard that have adopted the automatic portability.

Typically, when you part ways with an employer, you can leave your money in its 401(k) plan if the account value is above $7,000. Balances under $1,000 usually result in the plan cashing you out and mailing you a check. For amounts between $1,000 and $7,000, most plans roll the balance over to an IRA if the former employee takes no action to move it themselves.

Cashing out a 401(k) when leaving a job, whether done by an employer or the employee, can have lasting financial consequences. Workers who withdraw their savings can owe income taxes on the money and may face a 10% early withdrawal penalty if they're younger than 59½. They also lose the opportunity for that money to grow over time.

Most workers — 84% — have changed employers at least once during their careers, while 53% have switched three or more times and 27% have made at least five moves, according toa new studyfrom Empower, a 401(k) recordkeeper and a founding partner of the portability network. The report is based on an online survey of 2,005 adults.

Additionally, 50% of Generation Z respondents and 45% of millennials said they may have retirement savings from a previous employer that they've lost track of, the survey found. That compares with 30% of Gen X and 14% of baby boomers.

Since the Portability Services Network's launch in November 2023, there have been 53,118 completed transactions, totaling $71.3 million in assets transferred from a previous employer plan to a new employer plan via automatic portability, according to Steve Holman, senior vice president of Portability Services Network strategy and development at Retirement Clearinghouse.

There are 23,787 plans that have adopted automatic portability, representing 7.73 million participants, Holman said. The overall estimate of participants in 401(k)s and similar workplace plans is about 96 million, he said.

There are 1.22 million eligible participants waiting to be matched with a new employer, up more than 25% since the beginning of 2026, Holman said.

Keeping the money in a safe harbor IRA can be better for investors financially than cashing out — but management fees may take a toll on small balances, especially when the money is in an interest-bearing cash account or other conservative investment.

"For many of these small accounts, earnings on the conservative default investment may not be sufficient to offset recurring account-level fees while the account remains unmatched, leaving the balance vulnerable to gradual erosion," the Vanguard study said.

Workers withRoth savingsface another complication. If retirement savings are in a traditional 401(k) — funded with pretax contributions and taxed when withdrawn in retirement — it goes into a traditional IRA. Likewise, Roth 401(k)s, funded with after-tax contributions and withdrawn tax-free down the road, go into Roth IRAs.

However, IRS rules don't allow for a Roth IRA to be rolled into a new employer's 401(k), even a Roth 401(k).

"We are advocating for future legislation to allow for Roth dollars to be eligible for auto-portability — our technology can support it today," Holman said.

title: Crypto industry pours more than $200 million into 2026 midterms to pressure Congress on favorable rules
content:
The largest group of single-issue super PACs in United States history is pouring millions of dollars into congressional races across the country.

Cryptocurrency groups outpaced online betting and data center development groups in federal corporate political spending this election cycle,according to Public Citizen. Crypto-tied organizations have contributed more than $200 million in this election cycle.

The industry is hoping to repeat the success of 2024, when super PACs spent $250 million to elect pro-crypto lawmakers and reshape Congress.

Crypto juggernaut Fairshake and its affiliated super PACs are throwing their support behind 33 House candidates — 19 Republicans and 14 Democrats — seen as key supporters of the industry's priorities.

The network is prioritizing six House incumbents by injecting a baseline of $1 million into their campaigns. Republicans Bryan Steil ofWisconsin, who chairs a digital assets subcommittee in the lower chamber, as well as French Hill ofArkansasand Bill Huizenga ofMichigan, who serve as the chair and vice chair of the House Financial Services Committee, respectively. Democratic lawmakers receiving at least $1 million from Fairshake include Reps. Janelle Bynum ofOregon;Derek Tran ofCalifornia;and Steven Horsford ofNevada.

Fairshake's spending spree has been supercharged by digital asset-focused companies, like cryptocurrency exchangeCoinbase Global.

Coinbase established itself as one of the largest corporate political donors in modern history in the 2024 election cycle, contributing $79 million to federal races,according to OpenSecrets. That included a $1 million dollar personal contribution from CEO Brian Armstrong to Fairshake in 2023.

Coinbase donated $25 million to Fairshake's midterm efforts in 2025, according to the super PAC.

"The ultimate goal is to make sure that we bring our 20th century financial system into the 21st century," Ryan VanGrack, vice chairman at Coinbase, told CNBC.

"In an era where affordability is top of mind for American voters, it's important that we find a way that we can move money more cheaply, that we can invest more easily, and that we can transact more quickly, and fundamentally that is not something that Democrats or Republicans should oppose," he said.

The industry faced pushback in the current Congress as it urged lawmakers to pass landmark crypto legislation. In September, the Clarity Act, a bipartisan set of market structure rules for digital assets,stalled in the Senateafter Democrats argued it didn't do enough to prevent top government officials from profiting off crypto ventures.

The stalemate over ethics comes as Americans grow increasingly gloomy toward government corruption. AGallup pollreleased in September found a record 89% of U.S. adults say government corruption is widespread.

Changing voter priorities also present a headwind for crypto's legislative efforts. The latestCNBC All-America Economic Surveythis month found only 20% of respondents rate the economy as excellent or good, down from 27% in July.

"Overwhelmingly, the issue right now is the affordability crisis," said Rep. Steven Horsford (D-Nev.), one of the three Democratic candidates Fairshake is giving more than $1 million.

Horsford, whointroduced bipartisan legislationin May to modernize federal tax laws for digital assets, said crypto is still on the minds of some voters, alongside economic uncertainty.

"It definitely comes up in town halls and community meetings, in forums that I have, especially with small businesses who are looking to use digital assets and bitcoin," said Horsford. "They're being asked more and more by their consumers whether or not they take those those payments for services and goods."

November's elections will test crypto's continued influence on Washington.

The crypto industry is laser-focused on the Ohio Senate race between Democratic nominee, and former Senator,Sherrod Brown, a longtime crypto critic, and Republican Jon Husted, who is pro-crypto and currently holds the seat.

Fairshake spent about $40 million to unseat Brown in 2024, when the then-Senate Banking Committee chairman had promoted tougher crypto regulation and stalled a House-passed market-structure bill. The super PAC this cycle told CNBC it has already spent $55 million to oppose Brown.

AMaristpoll conducted Oct. 15-18 showed Brown holding a four-point edge over Husted among likely voters statewide, within the margin of error of 4.5%.

"A lot of these races are going to be extremely tight," said Mason Lynaugh, executive director of the advocacy group Stand With Crypto, launched by Coinbase in 2023.

This election cycle,Stand With Cryptohas endorsed a total of 45 candidates, 42 in the House of Representatives and three in the Senate.

Lynaugh told CNBC one of the reasons the group endorses candidates is because of their legislative record.

"We want to show that when we execute our program and we turn out those thousands or tens of thousands of Stand With Crypto advocates in these districts we are credibly ensuring that they get what they deserve for supporting crypto from the community that supports them," he added.

Digital assets and infrastructure company Ripple spent a total of $63.65 million in federal contributions last election,according to OpenSecrets, and the company is spending millions again now. Ripple donated $25 million in 2025, according to Fairshake.

Asked if the crypto industry got a good return on its investment, Stu Alderoty, Ripple's chief legal officer, told CNBC, "I think compared to where the industry was two years ago to where the industry is today, yes, I would say that that is a very good return."

Alderoty pointed to the GENIUS Act, which established the first federal framework for dollar-pegged stablecoins. President Trump signed the bill into law in July 2025, the first-ever standalone crypto legislation in the United States.

Alderoty noted that the industry has gottenclearer rulesfrom both the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures and Trading Commission. He also pointed to advancements for the industry from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, noting that Ripplereceived final OCC approval this weekto charter Ripple National Trust Bank, a federally supervised national trust bank.

But the latest guidelines from these agencies aren't meant to replace legislation from Congress, and the window to pass new laws for crypto may be closing.

Former New York governor Andrew Cuomo, now a board member of the crypto exchange OKX, told CNBC that lawmaking is unlikely if Congress changes hands in January.

"You're going to have a Democratic Congress overseeing an administration, the Trump administration, where the regulators are making decisions under the scrutiny of a hostile Congress, and that is not a good place to be because the Congress will be at loggerheads with the administration," he said.

Horsford, the Nevada congressman, told CNBC that time is of the essence.

"Every stakeholder needs to stay at the table and to continue to make the case why legislation is needed," he said.

If the Clarity Act doesn't advance before the end of the year, Congress will have to start from scratch on a new market structure bill for digital assets. And crypto super PACs are hoping their spending still has the influence to shape which lawmakers work on the next round of legislation.

"Regardless of who is elected in Congress, we're going to continue to see more regulatory clarity in this space," Coinbase's VanGrack, a former SEC senior advisor, told CNBC.

"It may be an open question whether we get all the way across the goal line, but it's not an open question about whether we're going to have progress and continue to see progress in terms of regulatory clarity in crypto," VanGrack added.

— CNBC's Luke Fountain contributed to this report.

title: Binance’s $6.3 billion hack raises questions about crypto wallet safety
content:
Two high-profile security breaches this week – including thebiggest cryptocurrency theftin history – are raising questions on the safety of storing funds in a walleton a crypto exchange.

A security incident at digital asset exchangeBinanceon Thursday affected some $6.3 billion in client assets, making it the largest crypto theft on record.

Earlier that day, prediction market platformPolymarkettemporarilyhalted trading on its international exchangeafter a third-party data provider was hacked, resulting in at least $2.7 million being drained from users' wallets. The company's international platform operates on the Polygon blockchain.

Experts whom CNBC interviewed said the security incidents on the crypto exchanges aren't surprising, especially in light ofrecent artificial intelligence hacking incidents.

Most of these experts even said that observers should expect more security incidents, at least in the near term, as that problem worsens.

"I think it's extremely dangerous," said Tyler Moore, a cybersecurity professor at the University of Tulsa who has followed the asset class for more than a decade. "I think you should be very wary of leaving any significant amount of funds in an exchange… there are no built-in protections for when these inevitable hacks take place."

For instance, banking customers can rely on theFederal Deposit Insurance Corporationto insure deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, in the event of an institution's failure.

There is no similar form of coverage available for funds lost from a cryptocurrency exchange, noted Moore.

BinanceandPolymarketreassured users that they would make affected investors whole. That's a sign that users should feel confident in crypto exchanges, according toIdo Ben-Natan, CEO of blockchain security company Blockaid.

"I actually think no users will lose any money," he said. "Binance has said they're going to cover everything… I actually don't think it's a bad idea for users to put money in these exchanges. These exchanges need to work really hard to make sure they don't take another hit like this."

Ben-Natan noted that while he thinks more hacks are likely as the cybersecurity landscape changes due to AI, he said it will only make the crypto industry stronger.

As a result, a crypto wallet could ultimately become a safer place to hold funds compared to other options, since the industry will have the experience of how to handle these attacks, Ben-Natan said.

A key point is that while Binance experienced a security incident on its offshore platform, its regulated, centralized U.S. exchange did not have a similar issue. The same was true of Polymarket's domestic exchange.

U.S. regulated platformsCoinbaseandRobinhoodwere also unaffected by the security breach on Binance, though shares of both fell on Friday in the aftermath.

In a Friday appearance on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street," theCommodity Futures Trading Commission— the federal regulator of derivatives — ChairmanMichael Seligsaid that the offshore nature of these incidents was critical to note.

"They don't have the same sorts of safeguards that we have in our financial markets," he said. "We want to offer a federal option to these exchanges to come and register with the CFTC, and they would be subject to the same sorts of cybersecurity safeguards that we have in our markets today."

Brett Falk, a professor and director of the Crypto and Society Lab at the University of Pennsylvania, said that U.S. regulations likely wouldn't have stopped an incident like that of Binance on Thursday. That's because the hack may have involved a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, Binance said in apost on X.

"Most of the regulation doesn't touch the specific software stack you have to use to authenticate people," Falk said.

In another social media post, BInance later said its investigation uncoveredadditional points of breach, though the company didn't specify what they were.

Falk echoed the argument by Ben-Natan that individuals likely won't face losses, and that it's better for traders to leave funds with an exchange where they have the financial backing of a company rather than in a self-custody wallet where no one can refund their losses in the event of a hack.

Ben-Natan added that traders should feel secure based on how many incidents companies like his catch that don't become news. That's because the security technology often works and stops them before they become major incidents.

However, crypto may be a unique target for hackers in a changing cybersecurity landscape, these experts told CNBC. That's because of how much liquidity individuals can quickly access in the event of a successful breach.

It's why Ryan Kirkley, CEO of blockchain infrastructure company Global Settlement Network, thinks traders should be cautious leaving their funds in any wallet that's not backed by insurance until financial companies upgrade their security infrastructure.

"I do not think there's anything right now that is a common solution in the marketplace where your assets are truly safe," Kirkley said.

"Unless you are dealing with a reputable and firm broker-dealer that provides an asset insurance, you are risking your assets putting them into any ecosystem today just simply because there's so much unknown," he added.

title: Humans are still doing the work behind some AI agents
content:
The next time someone's supercharged AI agent attempts to make a phone call to negotiate a cable bill, it could be an actual human who haggles with customer service rather than the software.

That's because AI agents, powered by the bleeding-edge foundation models developed by companies likeMetaandOpenAI, still can't reliably take actions across the web, particularly those involving phone calls. Former Yahoo CEO Marissa Mayer, who now helms agent startup Dazzle AI, says current top-tier AI models excel at surfacing online home renovation services for consumers, but might blow it when they need to book and schedule a rooftop upgrade.

"We're relying on the frontier models to give us good suggestions and a good candidate list, but we're checking that over to make sure that we're really delivering the type of service that we can stand behind," Mayer said, referring to how Dazzle funnels certain tasks to human contractors.

Digital assistants driven by artificial intelligence are currently gaining renewed interest thanks to Meta, OpenAI and others that are pitching the technology as capable of tasks like scouting the internet for shoes.

Meta's Muse, OpenAI's Dotsand a host of other agents can accomplish a multitude of web-browsing feats, but it's still early days for the technology, and it often hits digital roadblocks. Those barriers typically involve tasks that would have an AI agent make a phone call, schedule a doctor's appointment on someone's behalf, or reserve a couch scrubbing from a local cleaning service, said Meghan Joyce, CEO of digital agent startup Duckbill.

For tasks that require real-world judgment, Joyce said humans still trump AI, and companies building consumer-grade digital assistants will need to patch in real people to take over. That's why Duckbill recently debuted an application programming interface, or API, intended for companies building personal agents to connect with human contract workers.

"We work on a model that is not dissimilar fromUber, where we boil tasks down into atomic bite-sized pieces," Joyce said, referencing the ride-hailing company where she previously worked.

Companies making agents can use Duckbill's API to delegate the tasks that the agent is likely to fumble. Duckbill translates those tasks into bite-sized pieces that the average adult can do consistently and reliably.

"And then we track what happens," Joyce said.

Mayer said that AI models can still lack common sense. She said a Dazzle AI super user attempted to have the technology simultaneously handle a series of home renovation projects involving a roof replacement, a broken window and the purchase of a glass tabletop.

But the AI agent, Mayer said, confused window glass with tabletop glass, resulting in the digital assistant "trying to figure out if he could make the tabletop fit in the window."

The mishap didn't last long, Mayer said, because Dazzle's technology flagged the task and outsourced it to a person to complete.

"Within a few seconds, the human had things sorted out. Whereas an agent would have burned a ridiculous number of tokens," Mayer said. "Or they may never have gotten to a good solution."

Shivani Poddar, CEO of personal AI agent startup Wajo AI, is also incorporating human workers to handle phone calls and evenCAPTCHA testsintended to fend off bots from sites.

"I think AI plus humans, collaborative AI, is what you need to actually get the job done," Poddar said, emphasizing that people will stop using the technology if agents can't complete tasks.

Chatbot and agent interactions can be ultra personal and users have good reason to be concerned about the humans stepping in, particularly if the company didn't tell them how it works.

Meta employees previously raised privacy concerns about the company's internal test usinghuman contractorsto handle phone calls on behalf of its Muse AI agent. A Meta spokesperson said in a statement at the time that this kind of testing is "core to the product development process."

Meta currently doesn't use humans to complete users' Muse requests.

Duckbill's Joyce said her startup does "full background checking" into the 1099 contractors it uses, comparing them to drivers for Uber and DoorDash, "people who live here in the United States and want a source of additional income." Duckbill also uses contract workers from businesses that typically offer contact center labor to companies.

Mayer said Dazzle conducts background checks and looks for contractors with the same qualities someone might look for in a human personal assistant.

"We generally are screening for people who we think are extremely discreet and have good taste and good judgment, both in terms of how they interact with our users, but just the ability to kind of forget and compartmentalize that information afterwards," Mayer said. "I understand it's a point of privilege, but I've had personal assistants for some time, and I know how I want them, and I know how I guide them."

Mayer said that while foundation models are still improving, the market is in a "transitionary period" until the technology can perform more involved web tasks and phone calls as efficiently as people.

"We're not even trying to hide it, we think the human in the loop is a benefit," Mayer said.

title: The rise of the 15-foot skeleton—how a viral novelty became a Halloween staple
content:
If it feels like there are a lot more giant skeletons around these days, you're not imagining it.

What began as a viral novelty just six years ago has become a Halloween staple, and a growing line of business, as big-box retailers have responded to demand with an expanding array of towering monsters each fall.

"In 2020, Skelly's debut really was … the genesis of these fully molded structures that people could put in their yards," said Tyler Pelfrey, a manager of brand communications at Home Depot.

What followed was a retail arms race of increasingly elaborate creatures — undead horses, zombie velociraptors — with shoppers hauling home 85-pound boxes of oversized bones that might not fit in the trunks of their cars.

The decorations aren't the only thing expanding. As shoppers spend more on Halloween, retailers are giving the holiday more room, with seasonal displays arriving earlier and occupying larger sections of stores.

Americans are expected to spend a record $13.5 billion on Halloween this year, up from $8.8 billion in 2019,according tothe National Retail Federation. Spending on decorations alone has risen from $2.6 billion to $4.3 billion over that period.

Home Depot introduced its 12-foot skeleton in 2020 for $299. Nicknamed "Skelly," it quickly sold out, with some fetchingaround $1,000on the resale market at the time.

Retailers responded by making more of them — and more things like them. By 2024, Home Depot had quadrupled production of Skelly from its first year and increased its assortment of giant Halloween decorations fivefold,according to Fast Company. It has introduced at least one new giant every year since 2021, Pelfrey says.

Other big-box retailersfollowed suit. Sam's Club now offers oversized animatronics reaching 12 feet tall, while Lowe's sells the 15-foot headless Skeleton Watcher, which holds its severed skull aloft and projects spotlight beams from its glowing eyes. Home Depot, meanwhile, has upgraded Skelly with new tricks: an app-controlled version can move its head and mouth, let owners speak through it in real time and display American-flag eyeballs, among other settings.

Oversized Halloween animatronics have proliferated with an almost Darwinian biodiversity: motion-activated 12-foot pumpkin kings, three-headed carnivorous plants studded with human bones and a 5-foot undead parrot that answers yes-or-no questions are all on sale this fall.

At Sam's Club, the 11-foot Towering Reaper is among its 10 best-selling Halloween items this year, with sales ahead of expectations and sellouts at some locations. Online visits to the retailer's Halloween décor listings rose 67% in July from a year earlier,according to Business Insider.

That growth is visible inside the stores, too. In 2013, Home Depot's Halloween merchandise occupied a single endcap — a display at the end of a store aisle. By 2026, its displays can take up more than 800 square feet of floor space.

Halloween shopping is starting earlier, too. Nearly half of shoppers planned to begin their Halloween shopping by September or earlier this year, compared with about a third a decade ago,according tothe National Retail Federation.

"Halloween has evolved from a discrete event into an extended consumption season," said Ross Steinman, a consumer psychology professor at Widener University.

One reason for the oversized monsters' appeal is obvious. They're really big.

And size was always the point: Home Depot's team wanted something "larger than life" that would feel overpowering when it began developing Skelly in 2019, Lance Allen, the retailer's senior product merchant, recalled in a 2024 Viceoral history.

"At one time, it was like, 'Ah, a 10-foot would be huge. That'd be empowering. Everybody would like 10 feet!'" Allen said. "And then it's like, let's just press everything, no limits! Let's go higher than everybody thought was possible."

The result was the 12-foot Skelly. And when it debuted in 2020, its visibility was well suited to the moment. It was the first Halloween of the Covid-19 pandemic, when people were social distancing and spending much more time at home.

"With everyone being at home, I think [Skelly] being so giant and being able to [be seen] from a far distance, really helped with him being so popular," Rachel Little, a former Home Depot product engineer who helped develop Skelly,toldThe Atlanta Journal-Constitution in 2023.

The popularity has endured, with owners sharing their creations on social media, often in tableaus that might include skeleton families or a giant skeleton walking a skeleton dog. But when the first Skelly came out, it was only designed for the Halloween season.

"One of the things we didn't prepare for was, we didn't know people were going to keep these up year-round," Allen told Vice.

Indeed, owners found reasons to keep Skelly on the lawn, dressing it for Christmas and Independence Day — enough of them that Home Depot eventually added UV protection and changed the resin to better withstand summer heat. The dress-up trend has even attracted brands: Arby's this year released a$46.66 "Meat Sweats" tracksuitspecifically designed to fit a 12-foot skeleton.

Some owners go even further, buying articulated elbows and other replacement joints designed and sold by independent sellers to give their Skellies more flexibility for elaborate poses.

Of course, you don't put a Hawaiian shirt on a 12-foot skeleton and pose it just for yourself. It's meant to be seen.

"Giant Halloween displays are directed outward towards a public and the front lawn becomes a stage, the homeowner becomes a producer, and neighbors and passersby become the audience," says Timothy Malefyt, a marketing professor and business anthropologist at Fordham University.

And putting something that conspicuous in the front yard can get neighbors talking. As more of life has moved online, Malefyt says opportunities for shared, real-world experiences have become more meaningful — and Halloween decorations offer one without requiring much formal social interaction.

"Large-scale displays transform a home from a private space into part of a shared neighborhood experience," Steinman says. "In that sense, consumers are purchasing an experience as much as a decoration."

title: Hong Kong telecom company agrees to halt U.S. operations under pressure
content:
HKT, a leading Hong Kong telecom carrier and subsidiary ofPCCW Ltd, on Friday agreed to halt its operations in theUnited Statesunder pressure from the Federal Communications Commission.

The FCC in October 2025 said it was moving to revoke the authority of HKT to operate in the United States, citing national security concerns and its affiliation withChina Unicom, which is a shareholder in PCCW. Under a consent decree reviewed by Reuters, HKT has agreed to stop international and domestic telecom services to and within the United States.

HKT must file an application with the FCC within 30 days to discontinue services and must discontinue US services by September 1, 2027. PCCW declined immediate comment.

The agreement means the FCC will not move forward with the revocation proceeding that could have offered more details on Washington's national security concerns.

The FCC has previously barredChina Mobile,China Telecomand China Unicom from providing ​international telecommunications services to the United States, citing broad national security concerns.

The Trump administration has continued an extensive crackdown on Chinese telecoms over the past year. The FCC on Thursday voted to ban all Chinese labs from testing US electronics starting from December 2028.

The telecom crackdown has sparked a strong reaction from Beijing. China said Friday it firmly opposes the FCC action on labs, warning ​it would take necessary ​countermeasures "if the US side persists in acting unilaterally."

The FCC also announced on Thursday it plans to soon ban Chinese telecom firms from direct access to US phone numbers on national security grounds. The plan would bar Chinese IP network service providers from direct access and those that use equipment from companies on the FCC's list that pose national security risks, including Huawei and ZTE.

Other measures under consideration by the FCC include barring Chinese telecom firms from connecting to US networks and from ‌operating their data centers in the US.

Concerns about the potential for spying and other harms to arise from Chinese access to US telecom data and infrastructure have grown in recent years.

In late 2024, Washington said a Chinese state-sponsored cyber espionage group known as Salt Typhoon stole consumers' call records and US call data and infiltrated US telecommunications and telecom infrastructure firms.

China has consistently denied any wrongdoing.

title: AI is coming to construction sites. But does it make workers safer?
content:
When Shelley Copsey was appointed by the Ontario Teachers' Pension Plan, one of the world's biggest infrastructure investors, her job was to find ways to use technology to solve problems across its portfolio.

She quickly learned that there were persistent problems facing front-line workers.

Four years later, Copsey is CEO of FYLD, a London-headquartered software company that uses artificial intelligence to support workers in construction, utilities and infrastructure.

It comes as AI plays an increasingly important role in some of the most physically demanding jobs, from maintaining roads and railways to working on construction sites.

The aim is to reduce both paperwork — and accidents.

According to Copsey, when fieldwork goes wrong, attention usually turns to budgets or cash flow.

"We always go to the back office and we're like: oh, if we could help them forecast the job better, maybe this wouldn't be a problem," she told CNBC. "I think that what nobody ever did was just sit and say: well, what goes on in those field workers' lives and how do we make the life of the front line easier?"

FYLD uses AI to predict which permits a project will need, helping workers avoid delays. Previously, workers often arrived at a site without all of the information they needed, Copsey said. The system can also help crews plan around the weather, for example, rescheduling heavy lifting from a day when strong winds are forecast.

Workers record short videos describing their day's tasks and safety concerns. AI analyzes the information to help workers and managers anticipate potential problems.

An additional benefit is a reduction in paperwork, according to Copsey. Field workers can spend around 20% to 25% of their time on site on administrative work, she said, whereas now, photos, video and job information can be used to generate draft reports, reducing a task that previously took around half an hour to two or three minutes.

Infrastructure services providerAmey announced in Marchthat it would roll FYLD out to 2,500 field workers as it looks to improve safety and give supervisors real-time visibility of work on the ground. Copsey said FYLD case studies have reportedreductions in incidents and injuriesof as much as 48%.

AI is also being used to reduce the need for physical infrastructure inspections.

Nathan Marsh, London-based senior vice president for Europe, the Middle East and Africa at U.S. software company Bentley Systems, told CNBC that the company's road maintenance platform, Blyncsy, analyzes images captured by drivers to spot problems, including damaged guardrails, overgrown vegetation and debris.

"Applying AI to existing imagery provides complete asset coverage in a fraction of the time a conventional survey would take," Marsh said.

Steven Elsham, U.K.-based CEO of Dutch maintenance software company Ultimo, told CNBC its AI tools can flag safety incidents that might otherwise go unreported.

The system scans work orders and shift logs for signs of incidents, then drafts a report for a person to review. Elsham gave the example of a warehouse door with damage that suggested it had been struck by a forklift.

"People should still report things themselves," he said. "This is there for what gets missed."

Waleed Umer, an assistant professor at Northumbria University, England, told CNBC that many studies so far have focused on what models can detect, rather than whether they prevent harm.

Construction sites change constantly, making it difficult for cameras to capture every hazard, he said. He also warned that false alarms can lead workers to ignore warnings, while overreliance on AI can create a false sense of security.

Billy Hare, a professor of construction management at Glasgow Caledonian University, Scotland, told CNBC that research projects and pilot studies have primarily focused on productivity gains, often assuming that less exposure to hazards means lower risks.

Bentley Systems, for example, said one rail project it supportedcut physical site visits by 50% and manual surveys by 70%using a digital twin, a virtual model of a physical asset.

It's reasonable to assume that less time spent in hazardous environments could reduce risks, Hare said, but establishing whether technology actually prevents accidents needs further investigation.

According to theU.K.'s Health and Safety Executive(HSE), the number of construction workers killed in work-related incidents in Great Britain fell to 25 in 2025/26, down from 35 the previous year and below the five-year average of 37.

"The U.K. has seen the lowest construction fatality figure ever recorded this year, but this may be due to economic slowdown," Hare said, which makes it harder to tell whether technology has made a measurable difference.

Human oversight may not be enough on its own,  Northumbria University's Umer said, especially if AI produces more information than supervisors can realistically review. In that case, recommendations could be approved without proper scrutiny.

"Treat AI as an extra pair of eyes, not a replacement for supervision," Umer said. "And be clear about what it can't see."

For Ultimo's Elsham, the bigger question is whether AI makes difficult jobs more manageable rather than squeezing more work out of the people doing them. That starts with how performance is measured, he said: companies need to decide what any time saved is for, and which parts of the job AI should support.

"Safety teams are already covering more hazards with the same headcount," he said. "If the only plan for the freed-up hours is more tickets per head, workers will see straight through it, and they'd be right."

Companies should instead measure what matters on the floor, he argued, including safety, first-time fixes and unplanned breakdowns, rather than just output.

"A well-run business benefits everyone in it, and the people doing the hardest jobs should feel it first," Elsham said.

title: Jim Cramer says it's time to look beyond tech. Here are 4 consumer stocks he likes
content:
Investors looking to diversify beyond the struggling artificial intelligence trade should consider consumer staples stocks, CNBC'sJim Cramersaid Friday.

TheNasdaq-100, which tracks the biggest tech stocks, ended October down almost 7%. Investors rotated into other more defensive areas of the market. TheS&P 500 Equal Weightgained roughly 5% for the month. (The equal weight index treats all the S&P 500 stocks the same, rather than weighting them by market cap.) Theconsumer staples indexsurged 11.4%, making it the second-best performing sector behind energy.

"You've got to take what the market is giving you, and until we sort out some of the issues for the tech sector, some other groups might be better bets for the time being," the "Mad Money" host said. "I like the idea of camping out in the staples for a bit."

Cramer highlighted four companies he finds particularly attractive in consumer staples — a group that features companies with household brand names that people tend to buy regardless of market conditions or economic environment.

title: Meta outlook revised downward by S&P on cash flow and capex concerns
content:
Meta'soutlook has been revised downward by S&P Global Ratings on concerns surrounding cash flow and AI spending.

The credit agency said Friday that the outlook reflects "uncertainty" about Meta's elevated capex and its negative free cash flow.

Meta's credit rating was revised from AA- stable to AA- negative, S&P said. S&Ps highest credit rating is AAA. Anything below BBB falls into the junk bond category.

The agency questioned "Meta's ability to monetize its AI investments" relative to its peers, which are also spending heavily on data center buildouts and goingcash flow negativein the process.

Although Meta has recently debuted its Muse AI agent app and related foundation models, S&P said "it is unclear when these revenue streams will generate material contributions that exceed their rising costs over the next few years."

A Meta spokesperson pushed back on the revision.

"We respectfully disagree with S&P's assertion about Meta's AI monetization capabilities," the spokesperson said in a statement. "We see significant product and business opportunities ahead of us, supporting our very strong credit profile."

Meta said in its third-quarter earnings report last week that it expectsfull-year capexto come in the range of $135 billion to $145 billion. The company also posted negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion, going in the red for the first time.

Investors sent Meta shares down 7% followingthe reportdespite a revenue beat. The stock finished October down 15%, its worst month in four years.

The company said on Monday that it plans toraise $95 billionto help fund its AI initiatives, with plans to first raise $35 billion in underwritten public equity offerings, followed by an additional $60 billion through an at-the-market program.

S&P said that while it expects Meta's capex growth to start "flattening out beginning in 2028," the agency is "less certain that it will curtail its spending as previously anticipated."

title: Cramer’s week ahead: Expect more volatility as tech earnings, midterms loom
content:
CNBC'sJim Cramerwarned on Friday that volatility on Wall Street may not be over.

Stocks endured a turbulent week as renewed concerns about the artificial intelligence trade weighed on technology shares. The tech-heavyNasdaq Compositeclimbed 2.3% through Wednesday before plunging 2.9% Friday, ending the week down 2%. TheS&P 500followed a similar pattern, rising 1.6% through Wednesday before tumbling 1.8% Friday to finish the week down 0.6%. TheDow Jones Industrial Averagealso reversed course, gaining 0.5% through Wednesday before slipping 1.1% Friday to end the week down 0.9%.

"After a brutal week for tech, don't assume the worst is behind us," the "Mad Money" host said. "We've got the election, uncertainty overseas, the jobs report and another slew of earnings."

"My advice?" he added. "Don't try to call the bottom in the Nasdaq just yet. Pick up some high-quality companies that are being thrown away, and remember, in this market, even great earnings might not be enough to send a stock higher."

With that backdrop, Cramer turned to the week ahead.

Applereports after the bell. Shares recently hit an all-time high, helped by enthusiasm for its latest products, including the upcoming Duo foldable phone. Cramer remains bullish on the company but acknowledged that its valuation of almost 40 times earnings leaves little room for disappointment. "You can trade it, but I am going to own it," he said.

Cramer also expects encouraging results fromPalantirwhen it reports, citing strong customer feedback about the value of its AI software.

The midterm elections take center stage, with Cramer watching whether a shift in congressional control could threaten planned data center projects. He warned that growing political opposition to the facilities could delay construction and hurt companies whose growth depends heavily on AI infrastructure spending. However, he's "not going to write off the data center entirely because there are plenty of states that will welcome them."

On the earnings front,Advanced Micro Devicesreports, offering another important test for the semiconductor sector followingIntel'sdisappointing results. Cramer expects AMD to report better numbers than rival Intel.

DrugmakersPfizerandAmgenalso report. Cramer said both could benefit from renewed investor enthusiasm for pharmaceutical stocks.

CVS Healthreports, and Cramer remains intrigued by the company's position in the healthcare sector. However, he expressed concerns about its pharmacy benefit management business. "I wish it could disengage with that business; its stock would go higher," he said.

McDonald'searnings will also be in focus. Cramer wants to see whether the company's restaurant improvement strategy is gaining traction amid reported concerns from franchisees.

Kimberly-Clarkreports, with Cramer optimistic about the consumer products company's prospects following its planned merger withKenvue. The stock has benefited from investors rotating into consumer staples, and Cramer remains bullish on the company. "If this one falls before then, I think you should pick some up," he said.

The monthly jobs report will provide another important test for markets. Cramer expects strong hiring but limited wage growth, a combination that could help ease inflation concerns and explain the relative stability in Treasury yields.

The CNBC Investing Club will also hold its annual meeting, where Cramer and Jeff Marks will discuss the portfolio, market risks and their biggest investment winners.
