title: Criminal investigation of Alaska Senate race is 'ongoing,' U.S. Attorney says
content:
The U.S. attorney inAlaskasaid Friday that there is an "ongoing" criminal investigation of the state's U.S. Senate race in connection with the presence of a second candidate with the name Dan Sullivan on the ballot.

The probe is occurring as the Department of Justice pursues a related civil lawsuit to potentially block quick certification of that race's result because of possible voter confusion due to retired schoolteacher Dan Sullivan being on the ballot with the incumbent Republican senator of the same name.

The DOJ's suit claims the "sole purpose" of the non-incumbent Sullivan running was to benefit the campaign of Democratic nomineeMary Peltolaby reducing the number of votes for Sen. Sullivan. The DOJ says that if Sen. Sullivan loses by a share of voters that could be attributable to confusion about which Sullivan voters meant to select, an investigation should be conducted to determine voter intent.

"We will not let anyone or any group undermine this election," said U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman at a press conference in Anchorage, which was held just four days before Election Day.

"There is both a civil investigation and a criminal investigation that is ongoing," Heyman said. "There is a surge of FBI resources and resources in this office."

"Every Alaskan deserves a fair election, and they're going to get one," the prosecutor said.

He said that the criminal probe has been underway for months. Heyman had previously recused himself from the probe because he was being considered for a judicial nomination, but that recusal was rescinded Thursday because he was no longer under consideration.

Heyman said the criminal investigation has been accelerated because of a New York Times report on Wednesday that said aides Peltola's campaign and senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee helped recruit the retired teacher to enter the Senate race with the hope of drawing votes from the incumbent Sullivan.

"When credible information comes out, we are committed to pursuing that information … and we will act on it," Heyman said.

Peltola's campaign and the DSCC deny being involved in the retiree's Senate campaign.

Heyman, when questioned by reporters, would not say what criminal statute might have been violated

Earlier Friday, a federal judge kept on a fast track efforts to dismiss the DOJ's suit.

Judge Sharon Gleason ordered theDOJto respond by 1 p.m. Alaska Time to the new dismissal motions, which were filed hours after the department amended its suit in U.S. District Court in Anchorage on Thursday to add a new legal claim.

The DOJ's updating of the civil complaint forced Gleason to rule the prior dismissal motions were moot.

Gleason gave state election officials, the campaign of Democratic nominee and other groups until noon Saturday to reply to the DOJ's response.

The judge's order leaves open the possibility that she will rule on the dismissal motions before Tuesday, which is Election Day, as both the state and Peltola's campaign have requested.

The state, the campaign, and other intervenors in the suit argue the DOJ has no legal authority to block certification of an election because two candidates on a four-candidate ballot happen to share the same name.

The winner of Alaska's race could determine which party holds a majority in the Senate starting in January. Republicans currently have 53 seats in the 100-member chamber.

Alaska's election uses ranked-choice voting. If no candidate obtains more than 50% of the vote in the first count, then the fourth-place finisher will be eliminated, and the second choice on that candidate's ballots will be allocated to the remaining candidates.

Only Peltola and Sen. Sullivan are considered likely to draw large shares of the votes.

The DOJ's suit seeks to delay certification of the Senate election if Sen. Sullivan loses by a margin that could be attributable to voter confusion over the presence of the other candidate, who is listed as Daniel J. Sullivan, on the ballot.

The amended complaint, which updates the suit filed Oct. 23, added a claim under the Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution to the first claim, under the National Voter Registration Act.

It also contained added details from the Times article.

Peltola's campaign, in its dismissal motion filed Thursday, said, "Rather than defend its indefensible legal claims as it was ordered to do, the Department of Justice ... has filed an Amended Complaint that does nothing to address the fatal problems that preclude it from bringing this case or obtaining the relief that it seeks."

"The U.S. Constitution leaves the regulation of federal elections exclusively to the States and to Congress, and DOJ has no statutory authority to bring this case," the motion said.

In their own dismissal motion, state election officials said the amended lawsuit "rests on the same meritless theory that the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA) — a voter registration law — governs this case, which has nothing to do with voter registration."

"Because this reading of the NVRA fails, the amended complaint fails," the motion said.

title: Trump admin again loses bid to block California from counting alleged noncitizen votes
content:
A US appeals court on Friday rejected the Trump administration's request that it temporarily block California from counting any mail ballots for the November 3 midterm elections from more than 20,000 registered voters the Trump administration alleges are likely noncitizens.

The decision marked the second time this week that the San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals had denied an emergency request in the case from the Justice Department.

The decision comes as President Donald Trump's fellow Republicans are battling to retain majorities in both houses of Congress in the midterms. Trump's administration has sought to pressure state election officials over alleged noncitizen voting, which all available evidence shows is exceedingly rare.

In 2-1 decision denying the Justice Department's request for an order blocking California from counting the votes while the case plays out, a panel of 9th Circuit judges pointed to a lower court's finding that the Trump administration's list may not be fully reliable.

"There is a material risk that granting the United States its requested relief would result in disenfranchisement," wrote US Circuit Judges Mark Bennett, who was appointed by Trump during his first term, and Gabriel Sanchez, an appointee of Democratic President Joe Biden.

The case stems from a lawsuit the Justice Department filed on October 15 asking a federal judge to order California to separate any ballots it received from people on the administration's list and to not count them until it had verified that the people who cast the ballots were citizens.

US District Judge David Carter denied the Trump administration's request for a temporary restraining order, writing on October 28 that it would "wreak havoc" on the election and potentially disenfranchise thousands of lawfully registered voters.

California has said the state's safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust. It said the Justice Department's assertions relied on "suspect data" and that complying with its demands would risk disenfranchising eligible voters.

title: Bilt simplifies its rewards program and eases Bilt Cash restrictions. Here’s what to know
content:
Earlier this year, fintech and loyalty program Bilt sunset its original credit card andintroduced three new cards. It also overhauled its rewards program and tweaked how you earnBilt Points— a change that some customers considered complex and confusing.

Now, Bilt is further simplifying its program and making certain features easier to use. This comes after afirst round of changes the company made in January, shortly after the announcement of the new-and-improved program.

Bilt Points remain one of the most valuable credit card currencies on the market, so there's good incentive in exploring the program. And while Bilt is changing several program features with this update, there is a way to be grandfathered into the old system if you open a card before Dec. 31, 2026.

CNBC Select takes you through the latest update to Bilt's rewards system and who the changes might benefit most.

The largest change to Bilt Cash is a positive one: Effective immediately, Bilt Cash will no longer expire at the end of the year or roll over. Instead, the Bilt Cash you earn will now expire 12 months later. So any Bilt Cash you earn throughout November 2026 will now expire on Nov. 30, 2027.

In the previous system, all but $100 in Bilt Cash would expire at the end of a year. Now, you have a lot more time with your currency, and you can better plan how to use it instead of panic-spending before your rewards expire.

The rest of the Bilt changes — which we cover below — are set to happen in 2027, though you have the option to opt out of some as an existing cardholder. If you accept a Bilt Card offer on or after Jan. 1, 2027, you'll get the perks immediately. If you're a cardholder before this date, you'll get them on your first card account anniversary.

One downside to the changes to Bilt Cash is how often you can use it for hotel bookings through Bilt Travel. As of now, Bilt members with Blue and Silver status can redeem up to $50 in Bilt Cash toward eligible stays each month (Gold and Platinum members can redeem $100). This is shifting to just twice a year starting Jan. 1, 2027.

Additionally, new redemption limits apply based on your membership status:

One silver lining for owners of theBilt Palladium Card(seerates and fees) is that the maximum amount of Bilt Cash you can use at one time is increasing. But the total amount you'll be able to use over the course of the year is being slashed heavily.

Previously, provided you had enough Bilt Cash, Gold and Platinum members could redeem up to $100 Bilt Cash per month toward a qualifying Bilt hotel stay, or $1,200 over the course of the year.

The Bilt Palladium Card offers consumers a way to earns up 1.25X points for rent and mortgage payments with no transaction fee, and earns 2X points on everyday spend, without having to track categories

Earn 50,000 points, Gold elite status and $300 Bilt Cash if approved

Seerates/feesandrewards/benefits. Terms apply.

The Bilt Palladium Card earns 2X Bilt Points on everyday purchases, and your choice of up to 1.25X on rent and mortgage payments

Highlights shown here are provided by the issuer and have not been reviewed by CNBC Select's editorial staff.

Bilt is also attempting to streamline the annual credits its three cards provide, removing hotel-specific credits in favor of flat Bilt Cash.

Currently, the Palladium earns $200 in Bilt Cash and a $400 Bilt Travel Hotel credit. (For the hotel credit, get up to $200 in statement credits from Jan. 1 to June 30 and up to $200 in credits from July 1 to Dec. 31 on hotel bookings of two nights or more booked through Bilt Travel.) In January, these perks will be replaced with a blanket $600 in Bilt Cash each year.

TheBilt Obsidian Card's (seerates and fees) $100 Bilt Travel Hotel credit (applied twice a year as $50 statement credits for qualifying Bilt Travel Portal hotel bookings) will also be replaced with $100 in annual Bilt Cash.

The Bilt Obsidian Card offers you the choice of 3X Bilt Points on groceries (up to $25,000 per year) or dining, 2X points on travel and 1X points on everyday purchases. Your 3X category choice remains in effect for the entire calendar year.

Seerates/feesandrewards/benefits. Terms apply.

The Bilt Obsidian Card offers 3X Bilt Points on key everyday categories, like groceries (up to $25,000 per year) or dining (your 3X category choice remains in effect for the entire calendar year). It also comes with a $50 Bilt Travel Portal hotel statement credit semiannually.

Highlights shown here are provided by the issuer and have not been reviewed by CNBC Select's editorial staff.

If you're disappointed with the changes being made, Bilt gives you the opportunity to opt out of several changes, which we'll touch on in the next section.

Currently, Bilt offers two ways to earn housing rewards: You can earn 4% Bilt Cash on all your purchases, or you can earn up to 1.25X points per dollar spent on your housing payments. But starting Jan. 1, 2027, the Bilt Cash option will be removed for new cardholders.

This makes the decision-making process a lot easier for prospective cardholders, but what if you were really invested in earning that Bilt Cash? If you're a cardholder by Dec. 31, 2026, you can opt out of this change and instead continue to earn Bilt Cash. This also means you'll keep any eligible annual credits (like the hotel credit), but you won't be able to switch between the flexible Bilt Cash and housing-only mode anymore.

The main factor to consider is how much you value the 4% Bilt Cash perk. If that's a make-or-break feature of the card for you, just make sure you opt out before your card's anniversary date.

Bilt is gamifying day-to-day spending with the introduction of Daily Rewards. Launching Jan. 15, 2027, every on-time monthly rent or mortgage payment made through Bilt will earn a Daily Reward. Completing one daily activity with a qualifying Bilt neighborhood partner, like eating at a partnered cafe or a qualifying hot yoga class, will also provide you with a Daily Reward.

Each Daily Reward will provide you with two options to choose from. The rewards will vary drastically, from instant prizes like Bilt Points or Bilt Cash to collectibles that build toward a chance to win a grand prize*. Some examples of grand prizes include:

*All prizes subject to terms, to be provided before Jan. 15, 2027.

You don't need a Bilt card to partake in the Daily Rewards (you can participate as a Bilt member), but having one can significantly increase the amount of Bilt Points you can earn. TheBilt Blue Card(seerates and fees) is a great starting point for someone curious about the Bilt program, and Bilt now lets you easily upgrade and downgrade between the cards.

The Bilt Blue Card is a $0 annual fee card, offering 1X points on everyday spend and the ability to earn up to 1.25X points on your rent or mortgage payments with no transaction fee.

Seerates/feesandrewards/benefits. Terms apply.

The Bilt Blue Card offers a solid entry card to the world of Bilt, offering 1X on everyday purchases without charging an annual fee.

Highlights shown here are provided by the issuer and have not been reviewed by CNBC Select's editorial staff.

Bilt is making a conscious effort to simplify how its program works. From removing the Bilt Cash reward option to dropping the hotel credit in favor of blanket Bilt Cash, it's clear that streamlining the user experience was top of mind.

Many of the changes, such as the Bilt Cash expiration timeline, are positive. Other changes, like losing the ability to earn 4% Bilt Cash on purchases, could be painful, especially if you value theBilt Points Boost feature.

One downgrade that existing cardholders will have to work through is the limitations applied to using Bilt Cash for hotel bookings, as the maximum amount you're able to redeem in a calendar year is being slashed.

title: Crypto giant Binance attempting to recover $6.3bn stolen in hack linked to North Korea
content: Image source,Getty ImagesByJaroslav LukivÂandÂJoe Tidy,ÂCyber correspondent, BBC World ServicePublished30 October 2026, 16:03 GMTUpdated 34 minutes agoBinance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has frozen around half of the funds stolen in a "complex" hack,after $6.3bn (Â£4.7bn) was accessedin what is believed to be a record heist.The firm said $3bn of its stolen digital assets had been secured - but many were still in the hands of unidentified hackers. It initially thought an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals, but later said the attack was wider.Several analytics firms have linked the hack, which eclipses a $1.5bn (Â£1.12bn) heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit.The US Secret Service said it was "working around the clock" "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover" stolen funds.America's lead federal agency for investigating financial crimes added that it would "identify the cyber criminals responsible and bring them to justice", while Binance also said it was working with the FBI.While Binance said its US-facing exchange was unaffected, the US would still have jurisdiction to investigate the hack and help track down stolen funds - an effort which generally involves a global law enforcement effort.The hack also involved some US-linked assets, such as stablecoins Tether and Circle â cryptocurrencies pegged to the dollar.Binance told its users "your money is safe, and we're covering every loss".It had initially suspended all deposits and withdrawals - but then said in an update that "deposits remain unaffected".Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so farPublished8 hours agoBinance's co-CEO Richard Teng said: "This was not carried out by one person. Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach."Teng also describes how the hackers used "a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and traces as they went, making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate".Initially, the company had indicated the breach "may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop" but later statements have pointed to a broader breach.The Binance hack spooked cryptocurrency markets on Friday. The price of Bitcoin was down 5% to $76,800 in Friday afternoon trading in New York.Cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase was down 12% as investors also reacted to earnings results in which the firm reported revenue slightly below expectations. Robinhood, a financial services company that trades in cryptocurrency, was down 7.8%.Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.The company said in 2024 that it had more than $160bn in assets under its custody.A lot of the fear right now from Binance users - and the crypto industry at large - is whether or not Binance will actually be capable of covering this enormous financial loss.The company has said repeatedly that customer funds will be covered and that the firm is strong enough to weather the storm.But crypto history watchers have been pointing out online that this is exactly the kind of message that FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried gave before his crypto exchange collapsed in 2022, leading to huge losses for customers and the industry.Several experts have warned customers not to regard Binance's promise to cover losses as legally binding and said they may need to pursue litigation to recover them.Daniel Tunkel, of the London-based Edwin Coe law firm, said that would "come down to what [customers] have been promised in their contracts", and "where Binance can be sued for non-performance, if it comes to it".Binance has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world.Meanwhile, AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said that several elements of the attack resembled earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack.In the last five years the crypto industry has been beset by enormous losses from hackers.In nearly all cases investigators have blamed hackers from North Korea, pointing to the infamous Lazarus Group - also know as TraderTraitor. The names refer to clusters of cyber criminals accused of working directly for the regime.Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, said it had "high confidence" that a North Korean is linked to the hack.North Korea is an impoverished country with very little industry and heavy international sanctions and experts say the regime uses cyber crime as a way to bring money in.North Korea has always denied this, but the wealth of evidence from cryptocurrency flow analysis and insider interviews from defectors is compelling.It makes North Korea likely to be the only nation that uses hacking as a way to raise public funds.Related topicsCryptocurrencyCyber-attacksCyber-securityCyber-crimeMore on this storyAI gold rush draws crypto firms away from BitcoinPublished26 AugustMeet the crypto billionaires building a world where money buys you a votePublished11 July

title: Binance loses $6.3 billion in crypto heist—what happens to your money when an exchange gets hacked
content:
Arecord-breakinghack at Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, is a reminder of the risks investors take when trusting a company to hold their digital tokens.

Binance said Friday that the security breach affectedabout $6.3 billion in client assets, making it the largest crypto hack on record. Around $3 billion of the affected assets has been frozen on blockchain networks, and the exchange says it has begun recovering some of them.

Binance's initial investigation suggests hackers gained access to the firm's withdrawal systems and were able to make unauthorized transfers from the exchange's crypto wallets,according to the company. The company says it has found no evidence that the private keys controlling those wallets were leaked and is still investigating the full scope of the breach.

The company says it willcover customers' losses. Binance maintains a roughly $1 billion emergency fund known as SAFU, which was created to protect customers in the event of a security breach. The company initially saidSAFU and company funds would cover the losses, and hassince saidit has set aside more than $6.3 billion of its own funds.

For crypto investors, the Binance breach highlights one of the risks of keeping assets on an exchange. While exchanges make it easier to buy, sell and store crypto, what happens after a hack can vary widely, including whether customers get their money back.

Crypto exchange hacks aren't uncommon. Hackers stoleroughly $1.5 billionfrom Dubai-based exchange Bybit in 2025, while Seychelles-registered Bitget lostmore than $387 millionin a hack in September 2026.

But a hack doesn't necessarily mean customers will lose their money permanently. Stolen assets can sometimes be recovered or frozen — preventing the hackers from moving or cashing them out — and exchanges may also have insurance, dedicated emergency funds or other company resources available to cover losses.

In Binance's case, roughly half of the affected assets have already been frozen, preventing some of the stolen crypto from being moved. Itsroughly $1 billionSAFU emergency reserve provides another backstop, if needed.

Customers don't always recover stolen digital assets quickly. New Zealand exchange Cryptopia was forced into liquidation months after a 2019 hack in which aboutNZ$30 million in cryptowas stolen. The liquidation process stretched on for years, with the first distributionsfinally beginning in 2024.

"When you leave crypto on an exchange, you are relying on that company's controls and its balance sheet," says Martin Mulyadi, YHB Endowed Chair in Accounting and professor of accounting at Shenandoah University. "A pledge to make customers whole is only as strong as the resources behind it."

When considering where to transact in and hold crypto, start by researching the exchange itself. TheSecurities and Exchange Commission recommendssearching for customer complaints and checking how the exchange is regulated.

U.S. customers can also check whether an exchange is registered with the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, or FinCEN, usingits online database. Registration can help confirm that you're dealing with an identifiable business operating within the U.S. regulatory system, though FinCEN cautions that registration isn't an endorsement of the company.

Crypto experts also recommend reading an exchange's user agreement or terms of service. Some exchanges might have separate custody agreements or risk disclosures that are worth checking, too, Mulyadi says.

Look for language explaining who owns your crypto and what the exchange can do with it. Phrases such as "you retain title" or assets being "held for your benefit" are good signs, Mulyadi says. Check whether customer assets are kept separate from the exchange's own, which can offer extra protection if the company fails. And find out whether the exchange can lend or otherwise use your crypto, which can expose your assets to additional risk.

In the user agreement, check the exchange's limitation-of-liability section, Mulyadi says, and look at what insurance coverage the exchange offers and what it actually covers.

"If a refund after a hack is at the exchange's discretion, it's a goodwill gesture, not a promise," Mulyadi says.

Even strong language in the terms isn't a guarantee that your assets will be safe. FTX, the popular crypto exchange that collapsed in 2022,misappropriatedbillions of dollars in customer funds even though its terms said those assets belonged to customers, Mulyadi says.

If you don't want to hold your crypto through an exchange, there's another option known as "self-custody."

With self-custody, you use your own crypto wallet and control the private keys used to authorize transactions on the blockchain. Wallets typically come with a recovery phrase — essentially a master password that can be used to restore access to the wallet if you lose it.

That gives you control of your crypto without relying on an exchange, but it also makes you responsible for keeping that information safe.

And for anyone who's ever lost or forgotten a password, the risks of self-custody are real. With self-custody, there is "no help desk if you lose your recovery phrase," Mulyadi says.

For many investors, Mulyadi says a middle ground is keeping only what they actively trade on an exchange and holding longer-term assets themselves, as long as they understand how to safely store and recover them.

"Coins on an exchange are a promise from a company; coins in your own wallet are a responsibility you can't hand off," Mulyadi says.

title: Binance hack: Investigators in a 'cat and mouse game' to recover $6.3 billion in stolen funds
content:
Crypto firms and law enforcement are racing to recover more than$6 billion worth of cryptocurrency stolen from Binancebefore hackers manage to hide the funds.

The firms say they're in a "cat and mouse game" against alleged North Korean hackers who are using a combination of crypto obfuscation techniques and professional global money laundering networks to turn their digital coins into fiat currency, according to experts who spoke to CNBC.

These moves underscore how hard it can be to recover the stolen funds after a crypto hack.

"Ultimately, they're [hackers] trying to off-ramp it [crypto] to fiat. And that becomes the challenge, that's sort of this race against time," Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs, one of the companies investigating the Binance hack, told CNBC on Friday.

Binance pledged to cover losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users.

Both TRM Labs and Chainalysis have attributed the Binance hack to a North Korean state-backed hacking group called TraderTraitor, which has a history of crypto cyberattacks.

After the hack, several stablecoin issuers, includingCircle, which issues USDC, and Tether, which issues USDT,moved to freeze the funds. Stablecoins are digital coins that represent a currency, such as the dollar, 1-to-1 and are backed by assets such as government bonds or fiat.

Binance estimates that around $3 billion worth of cryptocurrency has been frozen so far.

The issuers of the stablecoins could burn and reissue the tokens and potentially recover those losses. In this scenario, a company like Circle or Tether would effectively destroy the frozen stablecoins, making them inaccessible to hackers. They could reissue new stablecoins that could be held in a legal government entity and then given back to Binance.

The hackers were one step ahead. They quickly moved to sell USDT to market makers and borrow the cryptocurrency ether against the stablecoin, according to TRM Labs. Ether is harder to freeze, and the entity the hackers borrowed from would be left with the stolen stablecoin.

"The attackers knew that route would be closed to them and so got out ahead of that," said Joe Hancock, a partner and head of cyber risk and complex investigations at law firm Mishcon de Reya.

Hackers have used sophisticated tactics to evade law enforcement and keep authorities from seizing the roughly $3 billion that remains.

Cryptocurrencies run on blockchains, which are public ledgers of transactions. That means crypto forensic firms can track the movement of crypto across different online wallets. So hackers use various techniques to throw investigators off their trail.

Crypto mixer services obscure the trail of cryptocurrency by mixing funds from different users, making it harder to track the money.

Jonathan Levin, CEO of Chainalysis, told CNBC there are no signs of this happening yet.

Instead, his company observed "laundering patterns we have not seen before," with hackers using automation to send funds back and forth between different wallets to throw investigators off their scent.

"Rather than simply moving funds onward, they repeatedly circulate them among addresses, often sending funds back to addresses involved earlier in the sequence," Chainalysis wrote in ablog post.

If hackers swap stablecoins into cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum, it's not possible to freeze the assets.

Levin told CNBC that the hackers moved a lot of money to different Tron addresses. Tron is a blockchain.

"We've got teams working around the clock to continue to follow that," Levin said. "We also have automated mechanisms now to track that. It's not just manual work."

All of these tactics will make it harder for companies to track the stolen crypto, but TRM Labs' Redbord said his company is getting "better and better" at identifying these techniques.

"It's this continued cat and mouse game where bad actors are trying to obfuscate their transactions and we are trying to track and trace them," Redbord said.

Hackers are increasingly using Chinese money laundering organizations to turn crypto into fiat, according to Chainalysis' Levin and TRM Labs' Redbord.

"So we are not necessarily only chasing North Korean on-chain, often we're chasing these professional money laundering networks," he said.

On-chain refers to transactions on blockchains, while off-chain refers to transactions not recorded there. That could be because it involves fiat currency.

Levin explained that money laundering organizations will offer to buy the stolen crypto over the counter for a large fee. They would then launder the money and get it back to the hackers, potentially in some form of stablecoin, which can then be exchanged for fiat currency.

When it gets to this stage, it becomes harder to recover stolen funds.

"As you get further and further away, the amount of seizure opportunities go down," Levin said.

title: Meta settles with teen during trial testing claims social media caused depression, eating disorders
content:
Meta Platformshas settled with a teen plaintiff who accused the company of designing Instagram and Facebook to be addictive, causing her mental health problems and disordered eating, attorneys for the plaintiff said ⁠on Friday.

The settlement came after jury selection began on Wednesday for a trial that was slated to test the claims of ​two teens, identified as S.J. and ​K.D.B., against Meta and Snapchat ​parentSnap Inc. Meta had settled with S.J. days before the trial, so Friday's settlement with K.D.B. means the trial is expected to proceed against Snap only.

"We remain committed to improving safety for kids on social media apps ⁠and ‌holding tech companies accountable, and we are pleased to have brought ⁠this matter to a just resolution on behalf of our client," Emily Jeffcott, an attorney for K.D.B., said in a statement.

The trial is the second in Los Angeles state court over claims brought by young people who say they became addicted to social media ‌after Meta, Snap, TikTok andAlphabet'sYouTube designed their platforms to encourage compulsive use.

S.J. and K.D.B. had previously settled with TikTok and YouTube.

The case was selected among the thousands of ​pending lawsuits as a test case, so the jury's verdict could influence how the companies and plaintiffs resolve similar cases.

S.J., a 16-year-old girl from Illinois, and K.D.B., an 18-year-old from Mississippi, say they began using YouTube as early as age 3 and the other platforms around age ⁠9, developing compulsive habits they blame on features such as autoplay and infinite scroll.

The companies have rejected claims their platforms were designed ‌to addict young people, and say they have taken action to make ‌the apps safe places for young people to express themselves.

Social media companies face thousands of lawsuits in federal and state courts by individuals, school districts, municipalities and other government entities alleging the companies knowingly sought to addict children to their platforms, contributing ⁠to a youth mental health crisis involving anxiety, depression and suicide.

In the first case to go ⁠to trial, which ended in March, a Los Angeles jury foundMeta and YouTube ⁠had been negligentand awarded a young woman $6 million in damages.

The next two teens whose cases were selected for trials either settled or dropped their claims against the ​companies.

The first school district chosen for trial settled with ‌all of the companies.

In August, Meta strucksettlements worth up to $18 billionwith nearly every state and US territory to resolve lawsuits brought by attorneys general over the platforms' harm to teens and agreed to make changes to how Instagram and Facebook work for teens.

Earlier this month, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta topay a $25 billion penaltyafter ​a jury found the company misled Facebook users ‌about the privacy of their data and how it handles hate speech. The company has said it will appeal.

title: Tankers defy sharp escalation of Iranian attacks to keep crude oil flowing through Strait of Hormuz
content:
Within 24 hours of the U.S. and Israel going to war with Iran, Tehran responded with awave of attackson commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz to cut off one of the world's main sources of crude oil.

Iran's campaign was initially successful, with crude exports plunging nearly 90% to 1.8 million barrels a day in March compared with 16 million bpd in February, according to data provided by Kpler.

But crude flows have rebounded over the past eight months as the U.S. militaryprovides protectionto tankers transiting Hormuz. Tehran has responded byescalating its attacksinrecent weeks.

More commercial ships have come under attack in October than at any other point in the war. Yet in contrast to March when exports cratered, tankers have continued to ferry substantial volumes of crude oil through Hormuz in a sign that the shipping industry has adapted to wartime in the Persian Gulf.

As of Oct. 27, at least 30 vessels, mostly oil tankers, were hit this month leaving at minimum 16 seafarers injured, according to data from theInternational Maritime Organization, a United Nations agency. Ship attacks doubled in October compared with 15 confirmed incidents in September.

"It's a difficult situation. Ships are attacked really on a daily basis," said Jakob Larsen, chief safety and security officer at Denmark-headquartered BIMCO, one of the big international shipping trade associations.

Crude prices have surged more than 13% this month as security conditions have deteriorated in the Persian Gulf. The internationalBrent contracttraded above $117 a barrel on Friday. That's just shy of its wartime closing high of $118.35 during Iran's big wave of ship attacks in March.

Yet actual crude exports through Hormuz stood at nearly 11.1 million bpd on average in October, only about 2% lower from September despite the sharp escalation of violence, Kpler's data shows.

"On balance in terms of oil coming out, there hasn't been a massive impact," said Mary Melton, senior tanker analyst at Braemar, a ship broker headquartered in London.

Crude flows through Hormuz are highly volatile on a daily basis with exports near prewar levels one day while falling well below such levels another day. The final leg of October has seen flows decline to 7.3 million bpd for the week ended Wednesday, more than 40% below the prewar baseline, according to Kpler.

Oil flows are more resilient now because the shipping industry has adjusted its operations to the threats, Larsen said. Freight rates have soared, making it "more attractive for the risk takers in the industry to actually carry out these voyages," he said.

"And when the cost of oil goes up that also means that there's more commercial incentives to get the oil out and sell it in the global market," Larsen said.

Shippers have adapted by setting up a shuttle system to reduce the risk of attack. Tankers load crude at Persian Gulf ports, sail through Hormuz with their transponders turned off and transfer the cargo to tankers waiting in the Gulf of Oman that then deliver it to refiners in Asia. This reduces insurance costs for the ships waiting outside the strait, Melton said.

The shuttle system has been effective at getting oil out with flows through Hormuz surging more than 70% since July, according to Kpler. But this system is also inefficient, logistically complicated and expensive, Melton said.

It requires more equipment, ships and experienced crews, the analyst said. About 20% of the world's supertanker fleet is tied up helping to shuttle oil out of the Gulf, she said.

Tanker rates have exploded as a consequence. It cost $249,000 per day to hire a supertanker to make the journey from the Gulf of Oman to Asia in early September, Melton said. By the first week of October, the price had surged to more than $900,000 per day. This translates to about $21 in transportation costs per barrel of crude oil compared with $6.50 a barrel in September, the analyst said.

"If you're an importer in Asia, you're used to paying almost nothing for freight," Melton said. "Then you're facing 20% to 30% of the actual delivered cost of crude is going to freight.

"That really starts impacting your margins as a refiner," the analyst said.

More Gulf oil producers are now covering the cost and risk of shipping through Hormuz in a bid to claw back market share in Asia from the U.S. and other Atlantic producers, she said. And they are increasingly using their own tankers to run the gauntlet through the strait, she said.

It is unclear how long the complex and expensive shuttle system can sustain current export levels. The tankers transiting Hormuz are totally dependent on air support from the U.S. military for their security, Larsen said.

"I don't think there would be many shipowners willing to take the risk if they didn't have that air cover from U.S. fighter jets and helicopters and drones," he said.

It is also uncertain how long the U.S. military will remain engaged, particularly if Democrats regain control of Congress after Tuesday's elections and demand that the president end the war.

The U.S. has told several Gulf Arab nations to be ready for a short but intense military campaign following the Nov. 3 midterm elections, people briefed on the conversations toldThe Wall Street Journal. The U.S. Navy, which is enforcing a blockade against Iran, has warned ships that don't need to transit the Persian Gulf, Hormuz and Gulf of Oman to steer clear of the region.

"Due to the current geopolitical situation, vessels which do not need to transit the area are advised to remain well clear to avoid unnecessary delays to their voyage," the U.S. military told vessels Wednesday through a notice issued by theJoint Maritime Information Center.

title: Why bitcoin held up better after the record Binance hack
content:
Binance has suffered thebiggest hack in crypto history, but that's done little to shake confidence inbitcoin, according to market analysts and researchers.

On Thursday, the world's largest exchange by daily trading volume said that roughly $6.3 billion were affected in an exploit. Security firmTRM Labs linkedthe security incident to North Korea.

The hack sparked a slight sell-off inbitcoin. On Friday, the cryptocurrency traded at $77,065 around 1:34 p.m. ET, down about 4% on the day.

By comparison, the token has fallen 8.3% on average in the first 24 hours following past crypto exchange exploits, according to data from institutional crypto platform Anchorage Digital.

The digital asset has remained relatively resilient because the hack on Binance had nothing to do with the security of the bitcoin network itself, according to Sam Callahan, director of bitcoin strategy and research at crypto treasury firm OranjeBTC.

"Investors recognize an important distinction: Bitcoin itself was not hacked," Callahan told CNBC. "This was a security breach at a centralized exchange, not a failure of the Bitcoin network."

Although Binance has suffered the largest hack in crypto history, it's far from the only digital asset exchange to fall victim to bad actors and lead bitcoin to tumble.

In the early 2010s, bitcoin exchange Mt. Gox was hacked a handful of times, wreaking havoc on the price of bitcoin. The token fell as much as 23.7% in the first 24 hours after an attack on Mt. Gox in February 2014, per Anchorage Digital data.

More recently,crypto exchange Bybit suffered roughly $1.5 billion in lossesdue to an exploit targeting its trading platform. Last month, crypto platform Bitget was drained ofmore than $350 millionin digital assets.

What's different about the Binance hack is that it hasn't sparked the same loss in confidence in crypto markets that occurred after other major crypto security incidents, according to Spencer Hallarn, head of markets at crypto trading firm GSR.

Binance said it has started recovering affected assets, which has likely assuaged some of investors' concerns, according to Spencer Hallarn, head of markets at crypto trading firm GSR.

"The speed of Binance's response, its deep financial resources, and its assurances that no user funds would be lost have helped restore market confidence and prevent potential panic," Hallarn told CNBC.

Tether, Circle and several other crypto firms said they had frozen roughly $3 billion in funds stolen in the heist. That should help mitigate losses tied to the attack, the executive noted.

Binance also has a $1.2 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users to offset losses from security breaches and other events. The firm could also be eligible for loans that would minimize its solvency risks, if history is any indication, according to investment bank Compass Point.

"We believe Binance has more than enough liquidity to cover the hole and we expect the exchange to remain solvent while reimbursing user funds," Compass Point analyst Ed Engel said Friday in a note to clients. "ByBit also received a bridge loan after its $1.5bn hack last year; therefore, we believe Binance has financing options."

GSR's Hallarn noted that this latest rotation out of technology stocks may also be to blame for some of the pressure on bitcoin.

"Since the exploit, bitcoin has largely traded in lockstep with other risk assets, including equities, which sold off overnight amid concerns over AI-related earnings," Hallarn told CNBC.

TheiShares A.I. Innovation and Tech Active ETF (BAI)was down more than 8% on the day.

Still, Anchorage Digital head of research David Lawant noted that current holders of bitcoin are more likely to hold their tokens through short-term headwinds than holders of other risk-on assets at the moment.

Just 6% of bitcoin is held in exchange-traded funds, according todatafrom bitcoin analytics platform Bitbo. That suggests many bitcoins are still being held by long-term believers in the asset and its cypherpunk origins, Lawant said.

"Bitcoin and crypto are not these hot-topic [assets like tech stocks] that investors are fleeing in and out," Lawant said. "The current holder base is a pretty strong one that is able to look at these things with a slightly longer-term view. That's playing a big role in how bitcoin is behaving well in this negative market environment."

title: Chevron and Exxon hit all-time highs as refining profits soar in reaction to Iran and Ukraine wars
content:
ChevronandExxonMobilon Friday reported profits that soared in the third quarter, as their U.S. refineries ramped up production to take advantage of high diesel fuel prices.

Chevron shares are up nearly 2% while Exxon is more than 1% higher. Both touched all-time highs Friday.

The world is facing a fuel crisis as Ukraine, Iran and Houthi militants attack refineries in Russia and the Middle East, reducing global capacity by millions of barrels per day. Importers have increasingly turned to U.S. Gulf Coast refineries for diesel supplies as a consequence.

ExxonMobil's profits doubled to $15.4 billion, or $3.72 a share, compared to $7.5 billion, or $1.76 a share, in the same period in 2025. When adjusted for one-time items, it posted earnings of $4.23 a share, soundly beating Wall Street's expectations.

"Refining capacity is very tight today," Exxon CEO Darren Woods told CNBC in an interview. "Frankly, diesel is the key crunch point here because it is so critical to economic growth [with] very inelastic demand."

U.S. diesel stood at a national average of $6.32 per gallon on Friday, an increase of more than 70% compared to the same period last year, according to AAA. Prices in the U.S. hit a record high in September.

Chevron's net income surged nearly 200% to $9.9 billion, or $5.06 a share, compared to $3.5 billion, or $1.82 a share, in the same period last year. When adjusted for one-time items, it reported earnings of $5.28 per share, also beating the Street's expectations of $4.89.

"The system is under stress," Chevron CEO Mike Wirth told CNBC in an interview. "We remain in an environment that is fairly fragile."

Here's whatChevronandExxonearned, compared with estimates from analysts polled by LSEG:

High profits from the largest oil companies at a time of war is politically controversial. President Donald Trump said in August that Chevron and Exxon "were making too much money based on a shortage." The supply disruption began in March after the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran.

Profits from Chevron's refining division surged more than 300% to $4.9 billion compared to $1.1 billion in the same period in 2025. Its oil and gas production generated earnings of $5.7 billion, up 70% from $3.3 billion in the year-ago period.

Chevron's U.S. refineries processed record amounts of crude oil at just above 1 million barrels per day, as the facilities ran at 98% capacity. Diesel and jet fuel yields rose more than 10%, Wirth said.

Exxon's refining division generated profits of about $7.2 billion in the quarter, outpacing its production business' earnings of about $7.1 billion. Its refining profits have surged nearly 200% to $11.4 billion so far this year compared to $4 billion during the first nine months of 2025.

Exxon's Gulf Coast refineries operated at 100% capacity utilization. Those refineries produced "record volumes of diesel" in the quarter, Woods said.

Chevron's oil and gas production actually declined slightly to 3.9 million barrels per day compared to about 4 million bpd in the same period last year. The decline was in its international segment due in part to the conflict in the Middle East, while output was largely flat in the U.S. year over year.

Exxon has produced about 4.5 million bpd this year, a more than 2% decline from nearly 4.7 million during the first nine months of 2025.

title: Gamble on democracy: Inside suspicious election-contracts trading on prediction markets
content:
Spencer Pratt appeared to be a shoo-in to win the June primary in the Los Angeles mayor's race, based on millions of dollars wagered on prediction markets aiming to call the race.

Pratt was an unlikely candidate for mayor. The former reality TV star had never held elective office, but after the Palisades fire destroyed his home, he turned his criticism of the city's response into a campaign rallying cry.

Using prediction markets including Kalshi, Polymarket U.S. and Polymarket International, speculators flocked to the race, which drew more than $47 million in trades, making it the most heavily traded mayoral contest of 2026. On the eve of the June primary, one market gave Pratt a78% chanceof advancing to the November runoff.

The prediction markets were wildly off base, and Pratt finished third.

Pratt supporters, though, used the failed speculation to cast doubt on the integrity of the election. That drew a response from the city: "Prediction markets can add to that confusion when people treat their projections as more authoritative than the actual votes being counted," Dean Logan, the registrar-recorder for the Los Angeles County Clerk's Office, said in a statement to CNBC.

Prediction markets' failure to call the election correctly also raised the possibility that markets can be manipulated to make candidates appear to have more support than they really do. Exclusive reporting from CNBC shows that this risk is real.

The dissonance between voter polling, speculation-fueled prediction markets and the actual outcome has grown in importance as election wagers become a prominent feature of elections. Odds and gambling platforms do not use methodologies used by traditional political polling, and therefore are not substitutes for political polls.

Polymarket and Kalshi are the two largest prediction market platforms. They let people speculate on almost anything — from which team will be the 2027 NBA champions to whether the U.S. will confirm that aliens exist.

Already, on these platforms the amount wagered on contracts related to the 2026 congressional elections has more than tripled wagers on the 2024 races, according to the Anti-Corruption Data Collective, or ACDC, a nonprofit based in Washington, D.C. And people are increasingly using the platforms as a source of information. For midterm election markets specifically,Kalshi reportsthat viewers outnumber actual traders by a 5-to-1 ratio.

Despite the Pratt race being a heavily traded, liquid contract,Kalshi detected and reported on price spikes that occurredduring trading on that race in a case study it published in July. A price spike is a temporary but large price jump that can make an outcome look more likely to happen, according to experts. Price spikes can happen for a variety of reasons, such as new information changing trader expectations or a trader buying a large number of contracts, which can drive up contract prices as cheaper ones get bought up.

On May 20, the company said, a trader on Kalshi spent $1.25 million on "Yes" contracts on Pratt becoming LA's next mayor. One of the trades caused the price of contracts on Pratt's victory to jump from 29 cents to 45 cents, suggesting that traders saw his chances of winning rise from 29% to 45%. However, according to Kalshi's case study, within nine seconds, the price reverted to earlier levels and the markets self-corrected.

"You can absolutely guarantee there are rational traders in that market willing to take those trades and bring that price right back down to where it belongs," said Robert DeNault, the head of enforcement at Kalshi, who is tasked with tracking unusual activity on the platform. "And by the end of the day, his price was lower than when it began."

But during the LA mayoral race, there were numerous price spikes across Kalshi and Polymarket International that pushed the odds in Pratt's favor, according to an analysis for CNBC by ACDC. The group didn't consider trades from Polymarket U.S. in its analysis.

Data that ACDC collected confirms Kalshi's findings. In the case study, Kalshi provided insight through about 30 minutes after the large order was placed. However, the group found that if you expand the time frame to three hours after the spike, the price lands three cents higher and that level is sustained for about two hours. In the long term, the price does correct. But according to ACDC's research, the longer a price increase lasts, the greater the risk of that information being interpreted as market sentiment.

And as ACDC's research suggests, election contracts are vulnerable to unusual price spikes — similar to those in the Pratt race.

The group found that of 167 congressional markets across Polymarket International and Kalshi worth more than $100,000, 38 markets — or about 23% — experienced price spikes moving the contract price 30 cents or more.

One example of such a spike was the Kalshi contract on whether Juliana Stratton would be the Democratic nominee for the Senate in Illinois. On March 3, according to ACDC, two purchases stood out as large — the median order was $12 before election day.One buyer spent $5,000 on contracts that favored the longtime public official's candidacy, taking the price from 47 cents to 79 cents. The price normalized after three seconds, going back down to 47 cents, but about one minute later, it shot back up to 99 cents after $3,000 of additional contracts were purchased. The price eventually sank back to 52 cents — 5 cents more than where it started — meaning a person or persons spent $8,000, and, in the process, drove up the price that made a Stratton victory look more likely.

Two weeks later, Stratton won the Democratic primary. Stratton declined to comment on this story, but a spokesperson from her office pointed CNBC to a poll from Public Policy Polling released on the same day as the price spike. It showed Stratton leading.

In a statement to CNBC, a spokesperson for Kalshi wrote, "As is common on Kalshi, the market corrected quickly to a price near fair value."

ACDC said it's impossible to know the motive behind these wagers. While profit could be a factor, it is an imperfect one. On prediction markets, participants can buy and sell contracts valued between $0 and $1, with the price reflecting how likely traders think an event is to happen. The more expensive a contract, the smaller the potential payout. Winning contracts settle at $1, while losing contracts become worthless. So traders buying in at 99 cents expect to earn only 1 cent if their predicted outcome happens, and transaction fees charged by prediction markets can also eat into that profit.

"If the theory is that prediction markets are accurate because of a price motive, [a lack thereof] begs the question: What type of goal does someone making a trade like that really have for themselves?" said Michelle Kendler-Kretsch, a researcher at ACDC.

Influencing election outcomes may be an answer.

Voters were between 10 and 20 percentage points more likely to believe a candidate would win if prediction markets favored the candidate, no matter what the polls reported, according to anew study funded by the Brennan Center for Justice, a New York City-based left-leaning advocacy organization. That survey, which took place in September, included the perspective of 1,994 registered voters.

Data ACDC shared with CNBC also shows shifting the odds is even easier and cheaper in markets where not many wagers are placed. Across 18,000 active congressional markets on Polymarket International, Polymarket U.S., and Kalshi, 88% could have their prices moved by 10 cents with a single wager under $1,000.

Still, Kalshi market outcomes are often correct. "Across U.S. elections since 2024, when Kalshi's markets favored a candidate to win, that candidate went on to win roughly 9 times out of 10," the company wrote ina website post. Further, The Washington Post examined 268 candidates in this year's primaries who received a 70% to 80% chance of winning on Kalshi or Polymarket on any day in the two months before the primary election. Three-quarters of them won.

Kalshi says it's working to assuage election distortion concerns. Itadded new transparency-centered featuresto its midterm election markets earlier this month to help users understand how much confidence to place in a contract's odds, including labels for markets with little trading activity and live feeds showing individual trades. Polymarket also rolled out its ownelection-specific surveillance system"to detect potential attempts to manipulate election markets, distort probabilities, or manufacture apparent market consensus."

Kalshi told CNBC it uses algorithms to generate alerts based on parameters for unusual trading activity, including fishy trading times and volumes as well as price jumps. It's unclear if Kalshi's internal protocols alerted over the Pratt trades; the company didn't respond to CNBC's request for clarity.

Both Kalshi and Polymarket U.S. are governed by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, or CFTC, an independent federal agency whose rules are designed to prevent market manipulation and insider trading. Trading prices and activity are publicly visible, and at least in the case of Kalshi, its order book is public on derivatives exchanges and people can escalate and flag unusual trades to the exchanges. In addition, Kalshi and Polymarket U.S. collect "know your customer" information including full legal names and Social Security numbers.

The outside world, however, has no insight into who is behind each trade.

title: Musk and Zuckerberg echo Trump's push to rebrand AI as 'super intelligence' on earnings calls. Others do not
content:
A month afterPresident Donald Trumporderedthat "super intelligence" replace the term artificial intelligence within executive branch departments and agencies, his leading tech allies,Elon MuskandMark Zuckerberg, followed suit on earnings calls. Their fellow tech CEOs were less eager to do the same.

Trump's declaration took place on Sept. 29, while he was hosting an AI luncheon at the White House for industry leaders. At the time, he was working to ensure the growth of AI in the U.S. with limited regulations. The president this week announced on Truth Social that he'sbanningthe use of the terms "AI" and "artificial intelligence" in "all relevant documents" and "everything else."

SpaceXandTeslaadhered to Trump's wishes on earnings calls last week after Musk, earlier in October, changed the name of his rocket company's AI division to SpaceXSI. Speaking onTesla's callabout his work on humanoid robots, Musk said, "Some of them look very impressive, but they're not really using any kind of advanced AI or SI."

Zuckerberg was equally compliant on Meta'searningscall on Oct. 21, emphasizing his company's "goal of delivering personal superintelligence to everyone." However, Meta was already using the term, havingcreateda unit called Meta Superintelligence Labs last year.

While Musk and Zuckerberg have been perhaps the fiercest supporters of the Trump administration among tech's CEOs, they're by no means outliers. Leaders of all the tech giants have contributed to Trump'sinauguration festivitiesor his plan for theWhite House ballroom, and some have been intentional aboutgetting ridof diversity, equity and inclusion, or DEI, programs that the president opposed.

But, for now at least, they're holding out when it comes to eliminating the term AI.

AmazonCEO Andy Jassy peppered his call with use of "AI" onThursday, uttering the abbreviation well over a dozen times in his introductory remarks. A day earlier,MicrosoftCEOSatya Nadellasaidone of the company's three points of focus is "designing AI to empower people." AndAlphabetCEOSundar Pichaiwas seconds into his quarterlyearningscommentary when he said the search giant's "AI investments are driving increased usage and overall user growth."

Trump's attempted rebrand comes just ahead of the midterm elections next week, with the Republican Party in jeopardy of losing control of both the House and Senate. Trump's job approval has been dropping and hiseconomic approvalrating just hit an all-time low, according to the latest CNBCAll-America Economic Surveyreleased last week.

That's not to suggest tech execs sticking with "AI" on this week's earnings calls are openly defying the president. Trump's preferred term is seeping into other correspondence and documents. Microsoft'sannual report, filed last week, included eight mentions of "super intelligence," starting at the top of the letter to shareholders.

"For Microsoft, the central question as we enter this Super Intelligence era is not just how big the opportunity becomes, but how we deliver the real-world outcomes that every country, community, and company demands and deserves," Nadella wrote.

IBMCEO Arvind Krishna, who didn't attend Trump's September lunch, used "SI" alongside "AI" during his company'searnings calllast week. "Technology innovation in both hybrid infrastructure and super intelligence is leading to better business performance," Krishna said, adding that IBM is advancing as a "software-led hybrid cloud and AI platform company."

Lip-Bu Tan, CEO of chipmakerIntel,saidThursday the supply shortage the chip industry is navigating has been "driven by the unprecedented demand for super intelligence."

Some in the tech industry have been explicit in their support of Trump's terminology ahead of their forthcoming earnings reports next month.

Palo Alto NetworksCEO Nikesh Arora repeatedly referred to "SI"on CNBC, and posted onXon Sept. 30, "The meeting at the WH on SI was an epic moment."

Then there'sNvidia'sJensen Huang, who runs the world's most valuable company and the chipmaker that's powered much of the AI boom. Along with Musk and Zuckerberg, Huang has been one of Trump's most vocal supporters in tech and the president'stop allyon the AI safety debate.

Like Arora, Huang took toXafter last month's AI meeting to praise the "White House Accord on Super Intelligence."

"Super Intelligence offers an extraordinary opportunity to advance discovery, productivity, security, health, and prosperity," Huang wrote. "The future of Super Intelligence will be shaped not only by what it can do, but by the confidence it earns."
