title: What we know about Binance's $6.3bn hack
content: Binance, the world's biggest crypto exchange, has been hit by a $6.3bn (Â£4.7bn) hack - thought to be the biggest in history.Half of the assets have been frozen but many remain in the hands of the hackers, the cryptocurrency giant said. It later added that it has "begun recovering" some funds.Two analytics firms have attributed the incident to a North Korean hacking unit, though no one has claimed responsibility. Binance did not directly respond to questions about the incident's potential links to North Korea.BBC cyber correspondent Joe Tidy explains more about the hack and what to do if you are affected.Follow our live coverage of the hack.SubsectionBusinessPublished3 hours agoShare pageAbout sharingRelated topicsCyber-crimeCyber-securityCryptocurrencyBitcoinCyber-attacksComputer hacking

title: Wall Street braces for Democratic gains as 2026 midterm election nears
content:
Investorsexpect a blue wave in next week'smidterm election, asDemocratssurge in polls and PresidentDonald Trump's approval rating remains low.

Public pollingsuggests Democrats are likely to take control of the House of Representatives, and analysts who parse what politics means for investors are in overdrive to tell their clients how to prepare for what Congress will look like after the Tuesday election.

Concern about the spending plans and priorities of a Democratic-controlled Congress permeates analyst reports reviewed by CNBC. But because Trump has another two years of his presidency, a divided government would likely create gridlock that would prevent congressional leadership in opposition to the president from getting much done, analysts are advising their clients.

Most analysts believe Democrats are also within striking distance of a Senate majority, though that outcome is significantly less likely than a House flip according to the polls. Next Tuesday's elections will determine which party controls both chambers ofCongressfor the remainder of Trump's presidency, after two years of fullRepublicancontrol.

Divided government typically makes must-pass legislation, likegovernment fundingand raising thedebt ceiling, harder to enact. A debt ceiling standoff — or first-ever default on federal debt — could be particularly damaging.

Wall Street watchers are also expecting Democrats to try to advance an ambitious and expensive agenda should they gain control of Congress. An Oct. 29 report from Piper Sandler analyzing Congressional Budget Office data projected that policy proposals from Democrats "would add $5 trillion to the deficit over the coming decade." The analysis assumes repeals of Trump's tariffs and reversing cuts to Medicaid, nutrition programs and Affordable Care Act subsidies.

Major policy swings — and big spending packages — become less likely as a divided government is unlikely to agree on issues. That's a dynamic the market typically enjoys. Trump's veto power would effectively block major Democratic policies from becoming law.

"A blue House is the obvious consensus base case," Wolfe Research said in an Oct. 27 report. The firm surveyed 138 investors and found 96% of those polled believed Democrats would prevail in House control.

"The scale of polling error that would be required for Republicans to retain House control would be unprecedented in modern history, well above the polling error in the famously bad 2020 cycle," Wolfe wrote.

Wolfe is less bullish on a Democratic Senate, though investors clearly see a possibility that Democrats regain control of both chambers of Congress.

Fifty-eight percent of investors the firm surveyed believed Democrats would gain control of the Senate, while 42% believed Republicans would retain control of the chamber. The investors surveyed were more bullish than Wolfe itself, which puts the chances of a Democratic Senate at 49%.

Other analysts are largely coalescing around the potential for a good night for Democrats.

"A blue wave scenario has become our base case," an Oct. 20 report from TD Securities reads. An Oct. 23 Raymond James report says "Democrats are in a solid position to win a majority in the House of Representatives and are increasingly likely to win enough seats to capture a Senate majority."

Even if Democrats sweep both chambers, protracted battles could still play out as Republicans maintain the White House and the Senate must still surpass the 60-vote filibuster threshold.

Democrats winning control of the Senate could allayconcerns about the Federal Reserve's independencefrom Trump, TD predicted.

That's because any new Fed members would need to be confirmed by the Senate, which would be unlikely to support a nominee who wouldn't support the central bank charting its own course.

Democrats are also expected to investigate companies that have done business with the Trump administration should they win control of a chamber. The majority party in Congress holds subpoena power on committees. Some Democrats have alreadytelegraphed their investigative prioritiesahead of the election.

Thedebt ceilingis likely the most critical sticking point for the economy that lawmakers will need to address during the next Congress, unless Republicans raise it during the lame-duck session between the election and the start of the next Congress in January. TheBipartisan Policy Center expectsthe U.S. will reach the so-called X-date — the point at which Treasury runs out of cash under the debt ceiling — between late-winter and mid-summer 2027.

"While negotiations around the debt ceiling may come down to the wire, a Democratic Congress would make it slightly more likely that a bill is passed than a divided Congress," TD said.

If Congress does not raise the debt ceiling by the X-date, the U.S. could default on its debt, causing catastrophic economic consequences.

Democrats, should they control one slice of government, are expected to demand concessions from Republicans in exchange for their votes to raise the debt ceiling. That sets up a potential standoff, which analysts note Republicans could avoid if they lose next week and raise the debt ceiling during the lame duck.

"[R]aising the debt limit before January could substantially reduce leverage Democrats have over healthcare, Medicaid, SNAP, and broader domestic spending priorities in the next Congress," Raymond James told its clients.

title: Amazon falls 7%, Intel plunges 25% in premarket trading, as pressure mounts after earnings
content:
AmazonandIntelshares were down in premarket trading on Friday after they reported September quarter numbers that disappointed investors, dragging Nasdaq futures down 2% and capping off a week of rough tech earnings.

Amazon shares were down 7% in premarket trading, while Intel was down 25%.

Amazon reported athird-quarter miss on the top and bottomline while maintaining its capital expenditure forecast for 2026 of $220 billion this year. Amazon also reported negative free cash flow for the second consecutive quarter, much larger than the previous period.

Intel issuedweaker-than-expected guidance, citing ongoing softness in the PC market.

Chip stocks includingMicron,NvidiaandArmwere lower in premarket trade in the U.S., while major European semiconductor names, includingASML, saw sharp declines.

Investors are nervous about the massive AI spending from the tech giants and whether that will pay off.

On Thursday,Alphabetshares closed 13% lower, itsworst single-day drop in historyafter it too reportedballooning negative free cash flow.

Microsoftshares rose after it remainedcash flow positive in the September quarter.

Nasdaq-100 futureswere down 2% in early trading as tech stocks remained under pressure, which could put the tech-heavy index into negative territory this week. Even with the recent fall, the Nasdaq Composite index is up more than 12% year-to-date as of Thursday's close.

"I don't think this is a moment of reckoning but I think it's a moment where investors should take a long thought about how positioning across the space still remains crowded even though the fundamentals are strong," Matt Orton, chief market strategist at Raymond James, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Friday.

"While the here and now can be painful … the fact of the matter is the fundamentals by and large still remain in place, especially across the AI capex beneficiary part of the market."

Orton said he is "generally okay" with these companies turning free cash flow negative as it's for a "temporary period."

title: BP’s third-quarter profit nearly quadruples to $8.5 billion as refining margins surge
content:
Oil majorBPsmashed third-quarter expectations on Friday, as volatile energy markets and high refining margins saw profits nearly quadruple year-on-year.

The company reported $8.5 billion in underlying replacement cost profit, used as a proxy for net profit. That was above the $6.191 billion forecast by analysts in an LSEG-compiled consensus andup from $2.2 billion a year ago.

Operating cash flow hit $28.55 billion across the first nine months of the year, up from $16.89 billion in 2025, while net debt fell to $13.87 billion from $26.05 billion across the same period.

The result primarily reflects better performance in gas and marketing trading, and "significantly higher" realized refining margins, BP said.

"These are dynamic times with volatility and disruption to trade flows continuing to define energy markets," BP CEO Meg O'Neill said in a statement.

"The industry as a whole has been showing remarkable adaptability. Refineries have been running close to capacity to make up for shortfalls, shipping has been taking different and longer routes, and releases from strategic and commercial reserves are helping to bridge supply gap."

RivalsShellandTotalEnergieson Thursday said their refining margins — the amount earned from processing crude oil into products like diesel, jet fuel and gasoline —hit historically high levels.

Outages and damage to refineries from global conflicts, from the Russia-Ukraine war to the Middle East, have created tightness in global fuel markets this year,pushing product prices sharply higher relative to crude.

Benchmark crude prices have also been hugely volatile this year as traders reacted swiftly to unpredictable newsflow coming from the U.S. and Israel's war with Iran, and remain nearly double their level a year ago.

Analysts have been questioning when and if high energy prices will ultimately drive demand destruction, easing pressures on constrained refineries, as the premium for refined products over crude remains at decade-highs.

BP CEO O'Neill told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Friday that BP's refining indicator margin for the quarter of $46.7 a barrel was "incredibly strong" and "indicative of demand for the products we produce," boosted by refining reliability of over 96%.

"We've been able to adapt and try to adjust our refining runs to meet... the needs for the product that is most in demand," she said.

"Now, if we roll forward, we are seeing refining margins start to soften a bit ... third quarter is always a big driving period and a big holiday period. So, fourth quarter demand typically drops off. That is bringing the refining margins down a bit."

"But again, what we control is our ability to run our facilities safely and reliably to try to capture the opportunity that presents itself."

BP announced a new strategy last year that sees the energy giant pivot back towards its traditional oil and gas operations and away from renewables. It also announced a consolidation of its leadership structure and debt reduction.

O'Neill told CNBC on Friday that BP was focused on strengthening its balance sheet to give shareholders "confidence that they can be rewarded through the cycle."

"So, oil prices today are strong. They will not always be strong. I've got 30 years in the industry, and the prices go up and down. And at some point, they will fall again. So we need to design a company and a financial frame and a balance sheet that allows us to reward shareholders through the cycle."

That includes addressing its financial obligations, including the $5.9 billion it still owes the U.S. government and states for settlements over theDeepwater Horizon oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico in 2010, which it intends to ringfence extra cash for, she said.

"Deepwater Horizon was an incredible tragedy, and it has shaped BP. We will not forget the 11 men who lost their lives, or the impact that we had on the Gulf Coast and the environment there," she said.

"So we have deeply embedded those lessons, but we're in a position now where we want to take care of those financial obligations going forward to ensure we're a more resilient company in future years."

title: Trump, Vance scrap planned appearances in final stretch of midterm campaign
content:
President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance canceled several planned appearances across three states, in the final days of a midterm campaign that could see Republicans lose control of Congress.

Trump canceled two weekend rallies in Kansas and Iowa and will instead hold a flurry of tele-rallies, addressing voters by phone. The Republican National Committee said the president would reach at least 19 states in a "72-hour sprint" before Tuesday's elections.

The canceled stops were part of a midterm blitz in which Trump said he would travel to 35 locations to boost Republican turnout. He had been scheduled to appear in Kansas on Saturday and Iowa on Sunday.

"Voters across the country want to hear from President Trump before Election Day, and this 72-hour sprint will be a huge boost in the closing days,"RNC Chairman Joe Gruters saidin a statement.

Trump has campaigned at 25 rallies this month and acknowledged the strain following a dense schedule of back-to-back rallies. Sounding hoarse in Corinth, Mississippi, on Monday, he said: "God didn't make your vocal cords to do a rally every day."

On Thursday, after campaigning for Senator Darline Graham in Rock Hill, South Carolina, Trump snapped at a Reuters reporter who asked how he felt after weeks of rallies and whether he was tired of traveling. "You've been following me for two weeks," Trump, 80, said. "I feel perfect."

Hours later on the same day, Vance also called off a Friday news conference in St. Cloud, Minnesota, on the administration's "War on Fraud," though the reason for the cancellation remains unclear.

Vance, who leads the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, was scheduled to appear with other members to make an announcement on the administration’s 'War on Fraud” effort, according to the White House.

The scrapped appearance came as Trump's approval rating hasfallen to historic lowsamid growing frustration over high gasoline prices and the prolonged war with Iran.

Forecasters and prediction markets see the Democratsfavored to sweep Congress, flipping both the House and Senate blue. TheNBC News average of national pollsshowed 52% of surveyed Americans preferred Democratic control of Congress, compared with 43% who favored Republican control.

Trump is still scheduled to hold a rally in Daytona Beach, Florida, on Friday, and no events have been announced for Monday, the final day of the campaign.

title: Binance's $6.3 billion hack: What we know and what comes next
content:
Binance washackedwith an estimated impact of $6.3 billion, raising questions about the recovery of stolen funds and the broader fallout for crypto markets. Around $3 billion in cryptocurrency assets have been frozen so far.

The exchange pledged to cover all losses, while blockchain investigators linked the attack to North Korea and analysts assessed the potential financial risks.

Freezing cryptocurrency prevents it from being transferred, but recovering the funds requires a separate legal process, according to Ari Redbord, global head of policy at blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs and a former U.S. federal prosecutor and Treasury official.

"A freeze stops the money from moving, and recovery follows through legal process," Redbord told CNBC.

Redbord said law enforcement typically obtains a court order or seizure warrant before working with stablecoin issuers to release or reissue assets and return them to their rightful owners.

"Stablecoins are the most recoverable asset class in crypto because the issuer controls the token contract," he said. "Tether and Circle can freeze, burn and reissue, which allows frozen USDT and USDC to be returned to a victim."

But recovering bitcoin and ether is more challenging because they have no issuer that can directly freeze the assets. Instead, investigators must trace funds through exchanges and other crypto services where they can potentially be intercepted, added Redbord.

Eric Jardine, head of research at blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis, said returning frozen assets requires coordination among law enforcement, exchanges and token issuers.

"There is no standard recovery timeline. A technical freeze may happen quickly, while returning funds can take months or years," Jardine told CNBC.

Jardine added that while bitcoin and ether cannot be frozen by an issuer, they can still be traced and potentially recovered. Investigators can trace the funds on public blockchains and intervene when they reach a cooperating exchange or another centralized platform, he said.

TRM Labsattributedthe attack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored hacking unit, based on on-chain and off-chain intelligence.

The FBI previously identified the same group as responsible for the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025, according to the company's insights.

TRM Labs said the Binance attack shared characteristics with previous North Korea-linked incidents, including preparations made well before the theft and transaction signatures obtained in advance.

The firm estimated that approximately $6.36 billion in digital assets were moved from Binance wallets across 10 blockchains, with most transferred within about 20 minutes.

TRM Labs said preparations for the attack began at least 36 hours before the theft, with the attackers using Tornado Cash, a cryptocurrency mixing service, to fund their wallets ahead of the breach.

Chainalysis also pointed to North Korea, with co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levinsayingthe firm assessed that the $6.4 billion Binance hack was likely carried out by TraderTraitor, citing links to previous attacks.

The attack does not currently appear to pose a significant solvency risk for Binance, according to Sean Farrell, head of digital asset strategy at Fundstrat Global Advisors.

"The most important takeaway for markets is that this does not currently appear to create meaningful solvency risk for Binance," Farrell said.

Farrell estimated that around $3.3 billion in assets remained unfrozen. Assuming frozen stablecoins are eventually returned, Binance's SAFU emergency fund, worth approximately $1.2 billion, could cover roughly a third of the remaining losses, with the balance coming from the exchange's own funds.

Farrell said the key indicators to watch were how quickly Binance resumes withdrawals and whether outflows remain orderly. He added that a shortfall in customer assets could force the exchange to sell reserves, potentially triggering broader selling across crypto markets.

"I do not think that is the setup we are dealing with, but the key tell will be how quickly withdrawals resume and whether outflows stay orderly," Farrell said.

The Binance hack underscores the need for stronger cybersecurity standards and greater coordination among governments, according to Chris Perkins, head of Franklin Crypto at Franklin Templeton.

Speaking to CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia," Perkins said the industry must address cybersecurity challenges to reach its full potential, calling for stronger defenses and policies to hold cybercriminals accountable.

"We need to make sure standards are incredibly high, but we have to really focus on the criminals," Perkins said.

Perkins called for greater international cooperation to address cybersecurity threats, pointing to regulatory coordination among G20 countries following the global financial crisis as a potential model.

He also said AI could help improve cybersecurity by identifying and addressing vulnerabilities, even as the technology is used by both attackers and defenders.

title: Foxconn hopes to own 50% of the global AI server market within a couple years
content:
Taiwanese electronics giantHon Hai Technology Group, or Foxconn, is looking to expand its artificial intelligence server market share and boost manufacturing in the United States, as demand for AI infrastructure shows little sign of slowing, Chairman Young Liu told CNBC.

In an interview with CNBC's Christine Tan, Liu said Foxconn's share of the global AI server market could reach 50% in a couple of years, potentially rising to around 45% next year.

"I think we can grow up to 50 percent," Liu said, referring to Foxconn's share of the global AI server market, which currently stands at around 40%.

Formally known as Hon Hai Precision Industry, the company is best known as a major assembler of Apple's iPhones but has increasingly turned to AI infrastructure as a key growth driver.

Liu expects AI infrastructure to account for 60% to 65% of Foxconn's revenue in the next three to five years, excluding edge AI devices — which run AI and machine learning algorithms directly on local hardware.

Foxconn's production capacity was already fully booked for at least the next year and a half, Liu said, pointing to sustained demand for AI infrastructure.

He said demand so far has come largely from AI model developers and cloud service providers, while governments and enterprises have yet to fully embrace the technology. AI demand remains “quite strong,” he added.

Foxconn is looking to expand its U.S. manufacturing footprint, with Liu saying the company plans to move further up the supply chain to better serve the U.S. market.

"What we are going to do is we're going to move up the supply chain," he said, explaining that a broader manufacturing presence would allow Foxconn to respond more quickly to rising demand.

However, higher manufacturing costs in the U.S. mean the company will initially focus on products with stronger margins, including AI server racks and data center equipment.

Liu said greater production scale in the U.S. could eventually help lower manufacturing costs.

The expansion comes as Foxconn seeks to strengthen its position across the AI infrastructure supply chain, from servers and racks to entire data centers and computing services.

However, even as AI demand continues to grow, Liu emphasized the importance of managing investments carefully.

"Overinvestment will kill the company," he said, adding that Foxconn would keep a tight rein on spending as it expands its AI business.

Liu said Foxconn could spend more than its planned $3 billion to $5 billion a year on AI, depending on how far it expands its vertical integration.

Asked how the company would respond if major customers cut back on AI spending, Liu said weaker demand from one customer could be offset by growth elsewhere.

However, an industry-wide slowdown would pose a much bigger challenge for Foxconn and the broader AI supply chain.

title: Iran claims four tankers struck mines in Hormuz as strike fears grow after U.S. midterms
content:
Iran said four tankers struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz and Yemen's Houthis claimed missile strikes on Saudi Arabia, escalating pressure on two fronts as the U.S. reportedly weighs renewed military action against Tehran after Tuesday's midterm elections.

The flare-up is fueling concern among regional officials and analysts that fighting could resume around the Nov. 3 vote, even as Vice President JD Vance seeks to reopen talks with Iran.

The developments underscore the competing diplomatic and military tracks now shaping the conflict, which now in its ninth month.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said three tankers caught fire after striking mines along what it called an "unauthorized southern route" near the Omani coast. Iran's army said a fourth burned east of the strait.

The UK Maritime Trade Operations agencyreported a small boat attaching two explosive devices to a tanker about 25 nautical miles northeast of Khasab, Oman. The blasts sparked an engine-room fire that disabled the vessel, the agency said, adding that the crew was safe.

Separately, Iran's Revolutionary Guards on Thursday alsochallenged a U.S. Central Command statementthat American forces had cleared mines from the primary transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz. The vital waterway carried about one-fifth of the world's energy supplies, and has seen traffic plummet to single-digit daily passings since the war started in late February.

"Prove the claim that the Strait of Hormuz has been cleared of mines with independent evidence, not a statement," IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebi said. "The reality of the Strait of Hormuz is determined in the air, on land and at sea, not on social media and in America's media war rooms."

Iran-backed Houthi forces said they launched six military operations across Saudi Arabia, targeting airports and oil facilities, despite a rare meeting of Saudi and Iranian senior officials in Tehran earlier this week. The two sides had agreed to resolve regional differences through dialogue.

Saudi authorities have not confirmed the attacks but said their air defenses have intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone launched toward the holy Mecca region.

Earlier this week, Vance sent a letter via Qatari mediators to Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, proposing a framework for talks.

President Donald Trump, when asked whether he directed the outreach, said "no," framing it as Iran needing "help with medical supplies and various things." "He [Vance] asked me what I thought. I said, 'if you want to do that, that's OK,'" Trump said.

Reports have emerged that the Trump administration may resume military actions in the Middle East after the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

Adm. Brad Cooper, top U.S. commander in the region briefed Trump on military options for Iran in a rare in-person visit to the White House,the Wall Street Journal reportedlate Thursday, citing unnamed U.S. officials close to the matter.

The meeting, joined by other cabinet members, covered other topics including the continuing U.S. blockade, according to the report.

title: How Poundland grew from a market stall to a high street giant
content: Image source,Getty ImagesImage caption,Poundland has been a recognisable presence on high streets for more than 35 yearsByAndrew Dawkins,ÂWest MidlandsÂandÂRachael Lewis,ÂReporting fromin WalsallPublished30 October 2026"When I told people what I wanted to do, open shops on the high street selling things for one pound, they said, 'how will you find products to sell for a pound, what about inflation, it will never work.'"That is how Steve Smith, the founder of Poundland, describes the genesis of the budget giant - which went on to employ thousands of people and see over a million customers a week -on his own website,external.But now the West Midlands-based retailer is teetering on the edge, after its US-based owners Gordon Brothers cut off a vital funding supply and rejected a takeover offer from Irish firm Martin Property Group.More on this storyPoundland staff protest after chain approach administratorsPublished1 day agoBurnham 'ready to support' Poundland staff as retailer faces collapsePublished1 day agoThe curious case of why Poundland is struggling during a cost-of-living crisisPublished21 November 2025Having spent time on his parents stall since the age of two Wolverhampton-born businessman Smith started out in the very same place - selling items for Â£1 from his own stall.After a Â£50,000 loan from his parents he opened the first Poundland shop, in The Octagon Shopping Centre in Burton-upon-Trent, Staffordshire, on 13 December 1990.That first day, with a range of 624 products, the store took more than Â£13,000 - "and Poundland was born," Smith said.Smith and his wife, Tracy, now based in Shropshire, owned the company for 16 years.In 2006, he decided the time had come and he sold his final shares in the business for Â£250m, but later said the sale felt it was "as though somebody had died".Image source,Steven SmithImage caption,Steven Smith founded Poundland in 1990 with the help of his father, Kevin SmithBut by 2025,the Walsall-based company was itself sold for just Â£1.Its owner, Polish firm Pepco, confirmed it had sold the brand for a "nominal" sum to US investment firm Gordon Brothers.At the time Poundland had more than 800 stores across the UK and Ireland and employed around 16,000 staff."I did pick up the phone when I heard it was for sale but I was a bit too late," Smith said after the sale.Now, the retailer's bosses have filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, which will give the business 10 days to find a rescue deal.A protest was held outside the Poundland HQ on Thursday, Claire Sutcliffe - who has been at the company for nearly a decade - among those demonstrating.Image caption,Sutcliffe said she was "very sad" to hear the newsQuestioned about how she felt, the 49-year-old replied she was "very sad", adding: "Nine years is a lot working for Poundland and they've been really good to me as a Poundland family, really supportive."Sutcliffe added that some had worked for the business for 20 years and "it's just very sad for us all".Asked what her message was to owners Gordon Brothers, she replied: "Please just sell."Save our jobs, we've all got families to feed and it's... near Christmas."Image caption,About 25 people took part in a protest at Poundland in Walsall on ThursdayProfessor Sarah Montano, a retail expert from the University of Birmingham, said: "The real problem for Poundland is, when they first started it was really great because everything was Â£1, that was a really unique selling point for them."[Today] there's competitors which are offering very similar prices and for quite a lot of products they're offering them cheaper."She added that some competitors had "really got their finger on the key trends".In a statement, the board of Poundland Limited said it had been "working on a formal sale process for Poundland" and despite "enormous efforts it has not been possible to identify an acceptable offer for the business as a whole"."The process has however attracted several established retail operators who have made formal offers, collectively these cover a significant part of the business, and we believe offer the best available prospects for shareholders, creditors and to preserve jobs," they said."We recognise any sale process creates uncertainty and particularly when set against a challenging UK economic environment."They also thanked "staff, suppliers and customers for their continued support".Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Birmingham and the Black CountryContact formFollow BBC Birmingham onBBC Sounds,Facebook,external,X,externalandInstagram,external.Related topicsWolverhamptonWalsallBurton-upon-TrentPoundlandRelated internet linksPoundland

title: Crypto worth billions frozen after suspected Binance hack
content: Image source,VCG via Getty ImagesImage caption,Binance is the world's biggest cryptocurrency trading platformByOsmond ChiaBusiness reporterPublished30 October 2026, 00:37 GMTUpdated 39 minutes agoCryptocurrency giant Binance said on Thursday that it has frozen digital assets worth around $3bn (Â£2.24bn) to prevent them from being stolen while it investigates a security issue.The company said as part of a series of alerts online that all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while its teams conduct security checks and that the firm will "cover all losses".Two other major crypto platforms, Tether and Circle, said they have also frozen a total of about $2.4bn of assets in response to the potential Binance hack.Binance has not said how much was potentially stolen but some crypto experts have put the figure at over $5bn.The security incident concerns Binance.com, while much smaller crypto platform Binance.US which provides trading services specifically for American residents, said its platform is not affected by the issue."It does look like a hack," Binance's former boss Changpeng Zhao said on X.Zhao, who is also known as CZ, no longer manages the firm but remains a key shareholder.Glassnode, a digital asset advisory firm, estimated the hack concerns a total of $5.3bn in crypto.Meanwhile, New York-based blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis estimated that more than $5.9bn has been stolen.That amount is nearly four times the value of crypto stolen from Dubai-based crypto exchange Bybit in 2025 - a record-breaking incident that has been attributed to hackers linked to North Korea.Binance said the amount of funds frozen may continue to increase as its teams work closely with law enforcement and other partners to trace and seize additional assets."We are working around the clock and will share a full post-mortem once the investigation is complete. Please rely only on official Binance channels for updates," the firm said, adding that users' funds are safe.Binance is the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes.Bitcoin dropped by around 5% following the alerts. The price of other major cryptocurrencies including Ethereum and Solana also fell sharply.Image source,Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption,Binance's former boss Changpeng Zhao, who is also known as CZ, said the incident looked like hackCircle chief executive Jeremy Allaire said his firm is "closely tracking reports of a potential exploit involving Binance" and that his company has frozen more than $800m in assets linked to the incident.Circle is the issuer and co-creator of the USDC, one of the world's largest US dollar-backed cryptocurrencies.Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino said his firm has frozen around $1.6bn "related to a potential Binance exchange hack.""Protecting the industry and our partners is our main priority," said Ardoino, whose company issues a cryptocurrency known as USDT.Several crypto industry observers had flagged concerns about a potential hack on Binance hours before the exchange confirmed the security issue.Binance, which was founded in China by Zhao in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.The exchange has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world.The company said in 2024 that it has more than $160bn in assets under custody.Related topicsInternational BusinessCryptocurrencyCyber-attacksMore on this storyAI gold rush draws crypto firms away from BitcoinPublished26 AugustMeet the crypto billionaires building a world where money buys you a votePublished11 July

title: Microsoft plans to raise $25 billion in debt as it pursues AI buildout
content:
Microsofton Thursday announced plans to raise $25 billion in bonds, taking advantage of its healthy credit rating to support its infrastructure expansion.

The software maker holds a top-tier AAA rating with S&P, a credit agency. Management is targeting $170 billion in 2026 capital expenditures, as the company looks to meet heavy demand from artificial intelligence labs Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as other clients.

"Microsoft intends to use the net proceeds from the offering for general corporate purposes,  which may include, among other things, funding for working capital, capital expenditures, repurchases of capital stock, acquisitions, and repayment of existing debt," according to astatement. The offerings should close on Nov. 4, the company said.

AmazonandAlphabethave engaged the bond market to support infrastructure projects this year, and AI-focused cloudCoreWeavehas also relied on the debt market to broaden its data center footprint. Investors have turned more skittish on companies with tall debt piles as central bankers raise interest rates to fight inflation.

Microsoft will access additional funding sources to complement its own cash flow generation when conditions are attractive, Amy Hood, its finance chief, said on thecompany's earnings callon Wednesday.

"There's a form of financing called leasing, and we've been using that one as a vehicle," she said. "We're fortunate to have access in the debt markets, given where our ratings are, and we haven't yet tapped that."

Microsoft reported positive free cash flow on Wednesday,differentiating itselffrom Alphabet, whose cash flow was negative for the second quarter in a row. Last weekMetasaid it had negative free cash flow, and on Thursday Amazon reported negative free cash flow.

Also on Wednesday,Oracleunveiled plans to raise$10 billionin new debt and said it anticipates a return to positive free cash flow in the second half of its 2028 fiscal year.

title: From workshops to the catwalk - why mended clothes are going mainstream
content: Image source,Alice Brown/MaybeArtUKImage caption,Alice Brown uses felt animals to cover holes and stains on her clothesByLucy HookerBusiness reporterPublished2 hours agoIf Alice Brown is browsing in second-hand shops and finds a jumper with a hole, that won't stop her buying it."I see it as challenge," says the 27-year-old forest ranger from Lincolnshire.She is a champion of the growing fashion for eye-catching repairs.Over the last year she has developed her own unique style, needle-felting cute animals and insects to cover moth holes, stains and other imperfections, winning her a huge following online."The natural place for decoration is in the centre at the front. If the hole is under the arm or on the shoulder, it forces you to think about the design," she says.Often dubbed "visible mending" the trend is spreading from hobby crafters and community workshops, even drawing in fast-fashion brands and reaching the designer catwalks this year.Image source,Jayne Eagle / The Stitching MagpieImage caption,Some mends are designed to be eye-catchingAt one Saturday morning workshop in Brighton, Jayne Eagle shows her students how to attach a patch of fabric behind a tear so the cat-face design peeps through.Then she instructs them in stitching techniques inspired by the traditional Japanese methods Boro and Sashiko. Instead of matching the thread colour to the garment, they make the mend highly decorative using geometric patterns in large white stitching.She also offers classes in darning using contrasting vibrant colours that celebrate, rather than disguise, the repair.Image caption,Jayne Eagle sees repair as an "act of rebellion" against fast fashionOne student, Nicola, has already used her newfound skills to stitch over sunscreen marks on a T-shirt "making a feature of it" and is now delighted that people "stop seeing the stains and just see the decoration".Another student, Lisa, says her mother's generation would never have wanted the mends to show. "Now part of it is being proud of what you've done," she says.Lisa bought a second-hand jacket online, but snipped the fabric with the scissors when she was opening the package. She managed to patch it in a way that "looks intentional"."I was actually pointing it out to people," she laughs.Image caption,Lisa says she's so proud of her mends she wants people to notice themIn the past mending was primarily about saving money, by wearing clothes for longer, rather than buying new. But visible mending is about celebrating that choice.The trend took off about six years ago, Jayne says, and has boomed since.An era of "throwaway" fast fashion from the 1980s onwards undermined the tradition of looking after and mending your clothes and people lost the skills, she says.The revival of interest feels to her like a backlash against overproduction in the fashion industry and the damage it causes: the pollution, carbon emissions, water use, and poor labour conditions.So perhaps it is surprising just how popular mended style is proving among retailers, with brands from Ralph Lauren to ultra-fast-fashion firm Shein currently selling stitched and patched garments, albeit in both of those cases brand new off the peg.Other High Street chains are adopting a more authentic approach, offering in-house repairs and workshops."We want to give customers practical ways to extend the life of the clothes they already love, rather than simply replacing them," says Uniqlo's head of sustainability, Maria Ledous.Image source,Oscar Elliot/UniqloImage caption,Uniqlo offers decorative mending using Sashiko techniques, in keeping with the brand's Japanese heritagePrimark, often seen as a fast-fashion retailer due to its lower prices, has also joined the trend."We don't think that affordability and durability should be opposites," says Vicki Swain, the brand's longevity lead.Outdoor brand Finisterre says around a fifth of the mends it provides for customers are designed to be eye-catching, while premium artisan clothing store Toast says around a third of customers go for that option.Part of the "magic" is that customers can bring in a garment and "choose what they'd like it to become next", says Toast chief executive Suzie de Rohan Willner.Image source,Sukhi Dhanda/ToastImage caption,Toast has a team of 14 in-house "repair artists" providing a range of creative mendsToast's repair services are free, but off-the-peg "renewed" pieces fetch higher prices than the originals to reflect their unique character.Levi's, which boasts probably the longest tradition of being fixed up by its fans using anything from rhinestones to fringed cuffs, is rolling out a workshop programme this year.The firm says its research shows younger customers in particular want to repair more but don't know how.For now, Levi's' workshops focus on traditional mending skills, such as sewing on a button and hemming, rather than visible mends, and at a recent launch event in London, that seemed to be what its Gen Z participants were looking for."I'm from East London. If you have holes in your clothes people are like 'Ha ha! You're poor!'," says 16-year-old school student Bianca.Image caption,At a workshop run by Levi's, Nicholas (r) says he prefers mending not to show, while Bianca (centre) says people still see it as a sign of povertyTheo, 19, says he'd rather learn how to mend without it showing."I would want [the jeans] to look how I originally bought them," he says.He has a side hustle selling clothes at car boot sales and thinks traditional repair skills would make it more lucrative.His friend Nicholas, also 19, says most people want to look "fresh"."No-one wants to look like they came out of a dumpster," he says.Still, Paul Dillinger, Levi's head of global design innovation, thinks more creative repairs will win them over as they pick up more skills."No-one has time for that perfect 'straight from the shop' thing. That's not cool."People crave agency," he says. "Mending is a demonstration of humanity: it's not a mustard stain, it's a memory of a great day in the ballpark."Related topicsEnvironment

title: DOJ amends Alaska Senate suit to suggest Peltola campaign misled court over Sullivan candidacy
content:
The Department of Justice on Thursday updated its lawsuit over Alaska'sSenaterace to reflect aNew York Timesreport that people from Democratic nomineeMary Peltola's campaign and senior advisors at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee worked to recruit retired schoolteacher Dan Sullivan to run to draw votes from incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan.

The DOJ, in its amended civil complaint, suggests that Peltola's campaign and the DSCC misled a federal judge by saying in court filings they lacked knowledge about why the retiree Sullivan entered the race earlier this year.

"But the New York Times has reported that Alaskans For Mary and the DSCC were well aware of the purposes of Daniel J. Sullivan's candidacy: they orchestrated his sham campaign for the purpose of misleading Alaskan voters and getting Peltola elected," the DOJ said in its amended complaint in U.S. District Court in Anchorage, Alaska.

The amended suit also notes that Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, late Wednesday ordered the state Department of Public Safety to investigate whether the alleged recruitment of the retired teacher violated criminal or civil laws. Dunleavy cited the Times' report as the reason for that probe.

Thelawsuitseeks to block the state from immediately certifying any Senate election result "that may be impacted by voter confusion ... pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan."

PresidentDonald Trumphas said he ordered theDOJto file the suit.

Peltola's campaign and the DSCC, which have previously denied involvement in the retiree Sullivan's campaign to CNBC, did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the amended DOJ suit.

The campaign, the DSCC and state election officials have asked Judge Sharon Gleason to dismiss the DOJ's lawsuit before Election Day, Nov. 3.

The political stakesin the Alaska Senate race are potentially momentous. The winner could determine the power balance in the Senate, where Republicans hold a six-vote majority.

Dunleavy, in announcing his order of investigation, noted that Alaska's Division of Elections had investigated concerns that the retired teacher's entry into the Senate primary was designed to confuse voters, which led the division to block him from that ballot. A state court judge reversed the order, and the Alaska Supreme Court upheld that ruling, allowing him on the ballot.

"The new reporting substantially supports the Division's findings," Dunleavy said in a post on X.

"I am therefore directing the Department of Public Safety to investigate whether this scheme violated Alaska's laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted," Dunleavy said. "The evidence will determine what happens next."

"Alaskans have a fundamental right to vote for the candidate they actually intend to support," he said. "Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections. Anyone or any organization found to have broken the law must be held accountable."

Peltola's campaign, in a statement to CNBC on Thursday in response to Dunleavy's announcement, said, "Mary got in this race because Alaskans deserve a champion who is fighting to lower their costs and put Alaska first, and no tweet or threat from any politician will keep her away from that fight."

"The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign," the campaign said.

Gleason on Wednesday ordered the DOJ to respond by late Thursday afternoon to motions to dismiss its lawsuit by Peltola's campaign, the DSCC, the League of Women Voters of Alaska and the advocacy group Common Cause, whom the judge also had allowed to intervene in the case.

Gleason said those groups needed to file any response to the DOJ's response by early Friday afternoon.

Trump, before flying to South Carolina for a campaign rally Thursday morning, was asked by a reporter whether Senate Republicans should try to block Peltola from taking the seat in January if she wins Tuesday's election.

"Well, you're going to have to see what happens," Trump said.

"It's hard to believe that she can even be allowed to run. Frankly, I don't know how you can allow somebody like that to run," the president said.

Trump said the retired teacher Sullivan "was just put there as a fraud."

"But people aren't going to know that, so nobody's going to know what to do," Trump said.

Both Peltola's campaign and the DSCC have argued that Trump and other Republicans are being hypocritical in their claims about the Senate race.

"Republicans have a long history of recruiting and propping up candidates in an attempt to boost their own campaigns — including recruiting a prisoner with a New York address to run against Mary Peltola and spending nearly half a million dollars to secure a spot on the ballot in Alaska for an Arizona resident in the Senate race this cycle," a DSCC spokesperson said Wednesday.

The DSCC pointed to instances of Republicans promoting third-party and dark horse candidates in the current election cycle and past ones to increase chances of a GOP candidate winning a race.

Alaska election officials in a court filing have said the Division of Elections "has taken significant steps to distinguish" between the two Sullivans on the ballot, "so that voters can easily determine which candidate is which."

The retired teacher's name on the ballot is spelled out "Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr." with no other words next to it.

Directly below his name, Sen. Sullivan is listed as "Sullivan, Dan. S." with the words "Registered Republican, incumbent" next to his name in parentheses.

Alaska election officials said in their court filing that "the United States lacks authority to intervene in state elections at all, much less in support of a favored candidate."

title: Circle, Tether freeze funds impacted by potential Binance 'security issue'
content:
Several crypto firms, includingCircle Internet Groupand Tether, on Thursday froze roughly $1.8 billion worth of funds tied to a potential hack on cryptocurrency exchange Binance.

The world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes has not explicitly confirmed that it has suffered an exploit as of writing time. In a social media post, the company said it was investigating "a potential security issue" on its trading platform.

"Our teams are aware of reports of a potential security issue and are actively investigating," a Binance spokesperson said. "Rest assured that user funds are completely safe. Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official Binance channels as soon as we have verified information."

Circle CEO Jeremy Allaire said Thursday evening in a social mediapostthat the company had frozen more than 800 million in USD Coin associated with the incident. USDT stablecoin issuer Tether CEO Paolo Ardoinoalso said inon Xthat his firm had frozen more than 1.5 billion of its stablecoin that may have been related to a potential breach.

Later, Binance co-founder Yi Hesaidin a statement that the XRP and RLUSD-tied firm Ripple helped halt the movement of $200 million worth of funds linked to the possible attack.

But those frozen funds could represent only a fraction of the ones impacted. Crypto data provider Arkham Intelligencelinkednearly $6 billion in digital assets — includingbitcoin,ether,solanaand various stablecoins — to 55 wallet addresses it has linked to the potential exploit.

Arkham identifies, tracks and flags crypto wallets by analyzing publicly available blockchain data. It also solicits tips from its community members.

Bitcoin — the most widely followed cryptocurrency in the world — slid more than 3% following the executives' statements, breaking below $80,000. Ether fell nearly 4%, while solana shed about 3%.

Shares of Circle also tumbled about 5% in after-hours trading on Thursday.

title: Intel stock plunges 21% as chipmaker blames PC slowdown for weak guidance
content:
Intelshares plummeted more than 20% in extended trading on Thursday after the chipmaker issued a weak fourth-quarter forecast, citing continued softness in the global PC market.

Here's how the company did in the third quarter, compared with estimates from analysts polled by LSEG:

Revenue climbed 21% from $13.7 billion a year earlier, the company said in a press release.

However, revenue in Intel's client computing and physical AI group fell 5% from the same quarter a year ago to $8.1 billion, missing estimates, even as data center and AI revenue jumped 78% to $7.3 billion.

Global PC shipments declined 4% in the second quarter from a year earlier due to soaring costs for memory and other components, according toCounterpoint Research.

For the current quarter, Intel said it expects adjusted earnings per share of 25 cents on revenue between $15 billion and $16 billion. Analysts were expecting revenue of $17.1 billion and EPS of 43 cents, according to LSEG.

"We see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," Intel finance chief David Zinsner, said in the release. "We will continue making disciplined investments in capacity and working capital to increase supply and support future growth."

Intel's forecast reflects the effects of an explosion at a fab in Israel that killed two workers and seriously injured a third earlier this month.The incident will cost the company about $600 million in lost revenue over two quarters, Zinsner said on Thursday's earnings. CEO Lip-Bu Tan said the explosion, which he called an "unfortunate and tragic accident," caused an "extended shutdown" at the plant, impacting shipments of 10-nanometer chips.

Intel's stock has been on an upward tear, up about 150% so far this year prior to the earnings report, although it's down roughly 23% in October overgrowing concernover the size of the artificial intelligence buildout.

"We will remain disciplined as we invest, and we will not spend $1 of capital unless we have confidence in the health of our products and process technologies, and clear evidence of customer demand," Zinsner said on the call.

Nvidia, which has become the world's most valuable company thanks to its dominance in graphics processing units, or GPUs, is scheduled to report results in mid-November.Advanced Micro Devices, a maker of GPUs and central processing units, or CPUs, reports next week.

Known best for its industry-leading CPUs, Intel has been a beneficiary of the rise in agentic AI. While chatbots and large models rely heavily on graphics processors from Nvidia and AMD, agentic applications such asMeta's Muse and OpenAI's Dots lean on CPUs to help orchestrate tasks and data from a computer operating in the cloud.

"Despite near term headwinds affecting the broader PC industry, we continue to see robust demand for CPUs and more broadly, for all our computing platforms in the long term," Tan said in the press release.

Intel's foundry business, meanwhile, has struggled to find its footing.

Intel is the only U.S.-based manufacturer of advanced logic chips, and is now in high-volume production of its most advanced 18A chip out of its new fab in Arizona, providing an alternative toTaiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. Its next fab in Arizona is expected to begin operations by the end of 2028.

For now, Intel has no major external customers for its new chips.

"We're going to have a couple of customers ready to announce the next two quarters," Tan said on the call, adding that Intel is making "tremendous progress" on its coming 14A chips.

The Trump administration took a 10% stake in Intel last year after the company had fallen behind on its 7- and 10-nanometer technologies. Nvidia andSoftbankalso invested billions in Intel last year.

Tan has taken a more cautious approach to foundry spending than his predecessor, Pat Gelsinger, who launched an ambitious revival of the foundry business.

Last week, Intel said crews have installed the first structural truss at its huge Ohio fab that was originally expected to deliver chips in 2025.

In September,reportssurfaced that the world's leading maker of high-bandwidth memory,SK Hynixmay team up with Intel in Ohio to lease some foundry space to make memory chips at the new site. Neither company would confirm any plans.

"We continue to evaluate unique and highly differentiated opportunities to accelerate our Ohio build out, and I hope to share more on this in the near future" Tan said on the call.

Intel completed a $23 billion equity offering in August. Tech giants have spent trillions of dollars in recent years to meet insatiable demand for AI and the infrastructure needed to support it.

Tan said he's"disappointed that we were not able to meet strong customer demand in this quarter."

title: Google value plunges by $500bn as AI fears rattle Wall Street
content: Image source,EPAImage caption,Google CEO Sundar Pichai has backed the company's massive spending on AI.ByKali HaysTechnology reporterPublished29 October 2026, 21:29 GMTUpdated 1 hour agoGoogle parent Alphabet lost just over $500bn (Â£374bn) in value on Thursday after it rattled Wall Street with its last update of the year on its business operations.Google spooked investors so badly that its stock hit a six-month low, after it revealed its artificial intelligence (AI) summaries on search were affecting ad revenue.Microsoft and Amazon also updated investors this week, and joined Google in plans to keep spending astronomical sums of cash in an ongoing AI race.But investors appeared dismayed at the impacts these plans are having on the ability of each to keep growing their core lines of business.Google AI is eating its core business - searchAt first glance, the quarterly results of Alphabet, the parent company of Google, were not at all bad.Total revenue grew 25% compared to last year, hitting $127.6bn. It was buoyed by the ongoing success of Google Cloud, where revenue grew by 103% to almost $31bn.However, profits at the company fell by a considerable 25% during the quarter. And forthe second time in its historyas a public company, it showed negative free cash flow, this time in excess of $9bn. That's almost twice the loss of cash Alphabet showed just three months ago.Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments, meaning Alphabet is now spending more money than it is bringing in. That new level of spending is almost entirely dedicated to Google's AI investments.By the end of Thursday, the company's total stock market value had fallen to $3.46 trillion from $3.97 trillion the day before.Google's omnipresent search engine now defaults to AI summaries of a person's query, and that hit the number of advertisements it was able to sell during the quarter.The sale of ads that appear alongside Google Search results is the vast majority of Alphabet's business.Tracy Woo, a principal analyst at Forrester, said Alphabet's disappointing search business results "highlights the challenge of funding massive AI investments while maintaining the strength of established businesses."Although Phillip Schindler, Google's chief business officer, said on Wednesday that he felt "very good about our trajectory" with an AI-focused version of the search engine, the company's stock fell by almost 13% on Thursday, its second lowest showing this year.Investors not buying Amazon's trillion-dollar business hopesAmazon's stock also took a hit on Thursday after it shared results that disappointed investors. Shares of the company fell 6% in after hours stock trading.Alongside quarterly sales growth of 11%, hitting $201bn, the company shared a staggering cash flow figure of negative $42bn.That number shows that Amazon is not only spending more money than it makes, but that spending has increased six-fold over the span of three months.Chief executive Andy Jassy claimed the business was spending in part because it had the chance at, not one, but two businesses that could end up bringing in $1 trillion for Amazon the future.Jassy did not specify what two Amazon businesses those may be. But during a call with financial analysts he repeatedly mentioned the financial opportunity presented by Amazon making and selling its own computer chips, as well as its AI developer platform Bedrock, which offers paying users access to most major AI models and tools."One of the lessons we've learned over 20-plus years is that there is not one tool to rule the world," Jassy said. "People always assume whatever is in the lead early on will be the only thing that people use - it's never true."As Jassy was asked several times to explain the company's spending, he admitted it "would be more convenient" if it were spread over the next 25 years. "That's not the world we live in," he added."We can fund this plan, and I think it will forever change the size, the revenue, the free cash flow of Amazon."Microsoft begs the question of AI's real valueWall Street reacted less enthusiastically to Microsoft's update, with shares falling by less than 1% on Thursday.The company, which is also one of OpenAI's largest investors, spent around $5bn less on investments dedicated to AI. It also revealed earlier this weekplans to cut thousands of workers, which will further reduce the company's costs.Meanwhile, its revenue grew 19% from a year earlier, hitting $92.3bn for the quarter. Its crucial cloud business grew by 30% to $63bn.Chief executive Satya Nadella said the use of Copilot, Microsoft's AI chatbot and tool, has seen "automated tasks nearly double since July" as daily users grew by 500% from a year ago.Usually lower spending and growing sales earns a positive reaction from investors.But Woo said Wall Street is trying to look farther into the future when it comes to which businesses will truly make good on their big promises around AI."Microsoft's results reinforce that enterprise demand for AI remains strong, but they also highlight a much bigger question facing the technology industry, where AI value will ultimately be captured," Woo said.Related topicsGoogleAlphabetMicrosoftAmazonArtificial intelligenceStock markets

title: Amazon AWS posts 39% revenue growth as cloud rivals also accelerate
content:
Amazon'scloud-computing unit reported more rapid third-quarter growth than analysts had projected.

Revenue came in at $45.98 billion, up 39% year over year and above the $45.29 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount, according to astatement. Growth in the second quarter came in atabout 37%.

"Our core compute and storage revenue grew at their fastest rates in several years," Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said on a conference call with analysts. The AWS growth rate was the highest since the fourth quarter of 2021.

Amazon remains the top cloud by revenue, but growth has also sped up at rivals Alphabet and Microsoft. On WednesdayAlphabetsaid the Google Cloud business, which contains infrastructure and Google Workspace subscriptions,more than doubledin the third quarter.

All the major clouds have been racing to build data centers that can accommodate high artificial intelligence demand. During the quarter, AWSannounced plansto expand its portfolio ofNvidiagraphics processing units that can handle AI workloads.

AWS alsoacquireddata analysis startup DuckLabs and signed deals with Meta and OpenAI, according to the statement.

The AWS segment generated $17.77 billion in third-quarter operating income, up 55% and more than the $16.97 billion StreetAccount consensus.

The unit now accounts for almost 23% of Amazon's revenue, a record.

On Wednesday, Microsoft publishedits first earnings reportthat contained revenue from its Azure cloud in dollars. Azure is 72% the size of AWS, up from 58% two years ago.

AWS came before Azure and the Google Cloud Platform, with its first services appearing in 2006.

"With our continued pace of innovation, new core and AI functionality, enterprises wanting to run their core and AI workloads in AWS, and the amount of capacity that we're adding each year, we believe that AWS can grow north of 40% in each of 2027 and in 2028, and be a trillion-dollar revenue business in the next five to 10 years," Jassy said.

Google has been pumping up its cloud revenue by making itstensor processing unitsfor AI available outside its own facilities. Now Amazon will adopt the strategy with its Trainium chips for training models, starting in late 2027.

"With Trainium demand so strong, customers continue encouraging us to make it available outside of AWS. We intend to do so late in 2027," Jassy said.

title: Rivian third-quarter earnings beat estimates as software revenue, R2 deliveries rise
content:
Rivian Automotivebeat Wall Street's third-quarter earnings expectations as it ramped up production of its new R2 entry-level SUV that the company has promised investors willlead itto profitability.

Here's how Rivian performed in the period ended Sept. 30, compared with average estimates compiled by LSEG:

Shares of Rivian were up roughly 7% during afterhours trading Thursday, after hitting a new 52-week low of $11.38 earlier in the day. The stock closed at $11.45 a share, down 1.9%

The electric vehicle maker also revised its 2026 guidance to mark expected improvements in its vehicle deliveries, pre-tax adjusted earnings and capital expenditures.

The new guidance calls for a pre-tax adjusted loss of between $1.75 billion and $1.85 billion — a $100 million improvement at the midpoint from its prior guidance — vehicle deliveries of between 67,000 and 70,000 units, up from at least 65,000; and capital expenditures of between $1.4 billion and $1.5 billion, $300 million less at the midpoint.

Rivian attributed the improvement in its pre-tax adjusted earnings guidance to better-than-expected revenue related to its sales of regulatory credits, an IEEPA tariff refund receivable in the third quarter and its expected increase in vehicle deliveries.

The R2 — the first deliveries of which arrived to customers in June — has become Rivian's best-selling model and was responsible for "much of the gain quarter-over-quarter," the company said.

Rivian delivereda record 19,248 unitsfrom July through September. The company does not disclose deliveries by vehicle.

The EV maker remains unprofitable overall but continued to narrow its losses during the quarter. The company reported a net loss attributable to common stockholders of $913 million, compared with a loss of $1.17 billion during the third quarter of 2025.

Rivian's gross profit, which is closely monitored by investors, was $176 million during the third quarter, up from $24 million a year earlier. Its adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization was a loss of $435 million, a $167 million improvement from the same period last year.

The company reported that its software and services segment continues to grow, generating $605 million in revenue and a gross profit of $256 million, a 42% margin. That compares to its automotive operations, which recorded nearly $1.55 billion in revenue and a gross loss of $80 million.

Also on Thursday, Rivian reiterated that it expects the R2,a smaller and less expensive siblingto its current luxury R1S SUV, to have a positive gross margin by the end of the year. CEO RJ Scaringe has said the company needs to scale beyond current R2 production plans of 160,000 units in order to achieve overall profitability.

"That ramp-up is critical for us getting to positive gross margin on R2 and that ultimately will contribute to positive gross margin for the business," Scaringe told CNBC's Phil LeBeau during an interview Thursday. "We're going to see that through the end of the quarter and the unit economics will continue to grow … into Q1 of next year as well."

Rivian on Thursday said its cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments balance was $5.5 billion, up from $5.3 billion to end the second quarter.

title: Starbucks sales miss expectations, but its U.S. turnaround is gaining steam
content:
Starbuckson Thursday reported mixed quarterly results as its international cafes underperformed expectations.

However, its U.S. turnaround continues to take hold, as its home market topped expectations during the coffee giant's final quarter of fiscal 2026.

"We enter fiscal 2027 with momentum, a clear set of priorities and higher ambitions for what Starbucks can become," CEO Brian Niccol said in a video shared on the company's website.

Starbucks is ahead of schedule to meet the fiscal 2028 targets laid out at itsinvestor dayin January, he said on the company's earnings conference call.

For fiscal 2027, Starbucks is projecting adjusted earnings per share in a range of $3.15 to $3.25, above Wall Street's expectations of earnings per share of $3.14. However, its anticipated revenue decline of 1% is weaker than expected; analysts were forecasting net sales growth of 1.4%.

Starbucks is projecting North American same-store sales growth of 4% for the fiscal year.

The company's earnings and revenue outlook includes an additional week and the effects of the shift in its China business to a joint venture business model. Starbucks is also projecting slight deflation in coffee pricesand slowing net new North American cafe openings, which will both weigh on its full-year revenue, according to CFO Cathy Smith.

Shares of Starbucks fell nearly 2% in extended trading.

Here's what the company reported for the quarter ended Sept. 27 compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Starbucks reported fiscal fourth-quarter net income attributable to the company of $677.2 million, or 59 cents per share, up from $133.1 million, or 12 cents per share, a year earlier.

Excluding restructuring and impairment costs and other items, the company reported earnings per share of 80 cents.

Net revenue fell 4% to $9.14 billion, reflecting the joint venture deal in China.

The company's global same-store sales increased 7.2%, fueled by growth in average ticket, and beating Wall Street estimates of 6%, according to StreetAccount. Transactions grew 1.8% in the quarter.

Starbucks' U.S. cafes reported same-store sales growth of 7.7%, topping StreetAccount estimates of a 6.5% increase.

Under Niccol's "Back to Starbucks" strategy, the company has focused on improving service, making its cafes more welcoming and sharpening its marketing. The changes have helped to win back customers.

"Starbucks brand affinity is at near record levels as our menu innovation, marketing and merchandise continue to create moments that drive culture and bring people into our coffee houses," Niccol told analysts.

The company said its North American rollout of its fall menu, which includes the iconic pumpkin spice latte, was the company's strongest ever autumn launch day. And matcha is now a $1 billion drink for Starbucks.

Outside of North America, the company's international comparable sales ticked up 0.9%, as traffic declines offset an increase to average ticket. That growth fell short of analyst estimates of a 3.2% increase, according to StreetAccount.

After its China business transitioned to a joint venture, Starbucks has shifted most of its international business to a licensed model, allowing local operators to take charge. The company is also exploring selling a majority stake in its Japan business,Reuters reportedin September.

Starbucks opened 303 net new cafes during the quarter. In September, the company announced it would close about 1% of its North American footprint, or about 250 locations, as part of its turnaround.

By the end of its fiscal year, across the U.S. and Canada, the company also completed more than 1,700 cafe uplifts, meant to make its stores more welcoming to customers. The company has said locations that receive a makeover, with tweaks like increased seating and softer lighting, see higher transactions in the aftermath.

title: Alphabet tanks nearly 13% for worst day ever, losing $500 billion in value
content:
Alphabetshares plunged the most since Google went public in 2004, dropping 13% on Thursday, wiping out roughly $500 billion in market cap.

In its earnings announcement late Wednesday, Alphabet reported negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion for the third quarter, compared to the $2.7 billion analysts expected. The Google parent maintained its full year capital expenditure guidance of between $195 billion and $205 billion.

Microsoft, meanwhile, traded largely flat as investors focused on the tech giants' latest spending andfree cash flownumbers in the third-quarter earnings report.

Microsoft reported $45.2 billionin capital expendituresand finance leases during the quarter, which was 30% higher than a year ago, but below analyst projections of $50.67 billion. Free cash flow fell 27% to $18.63 billion but remained positive.

The earnings reports come as investors scrutinizeAI spending plansof tech companies and are focusing on the returns on those investments.

"Microsoft is building out its architecture in a measured way and as such contains fewer surprises," Ben Barringer, global head of technology research at Quilter Cheviot, said on Thursday. "Alphabet, by contrast, saw its share price hit after hours as a result of a fairly messy set of results and a poorly handled earnings call" .

Alphabet's biggest source of revenue, search advertising, grew 12% in the September quarter to $63.35 billion, but missed analyst expectations, adding further pressure to the company's shares.

Philipp Schindler, Alphabet's chief business officer, said theimpact on the search businesswas partly because of lower monetization within the company's AI Mode. He added that Alphabet is now "scaling" ads within its AI Overviews and AI Mode products, including in international markets.

Google's search business has faced headwinds from the rise of other AI chatbots like OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude. People may be carrying out more search queries outside Google. Gemini, Google's own AI chatbot, has failed to keep pace.

"The problem for Google is it faces an innovator's dilemma and doesn't know whether to protect its core business or look to join the disruption. As such, Google has lost its edge with Gemini and is behind peers on agentic AI," Barringer said.

Google's dominant market share in the search business, however, could ultimately give it a leg up over its peers, Rosenblatt Securities analyst Scott Devitt said.

"I don't think it's a sea change," Devitt told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Thursday. "If it's a problem for Alphabet, it's a problem for any consumer-facing AI agent or LLM as well. And so, it's a problem that I think is ultimately going to be resolved. And when it does, Alphabet, with its 4 billion search customers that become AI customers, is in an enviable position."

-CNBC's Robert Hum, Samantha Subin, Jordan Novet and Caleigh Keating contributed reporting.

title: ServiceNow shares plunge 27% to worst day ever after earnings revive AI disruption fears
content:
ServiceNowshares sank 27% on Thursday and recorded their worst day on record after the enterprise software company'sthird-quarter resultsunderwhelmed, reignitingartificial intelligencedisruption concerns.

"This was a little bit uncharacteristic for ServiceNow standards, just in terms of the lack of upside," Citi's Tyler Radke told CNBC on Thursday.

Revenue grew more than 20% during the period to $4.11 billion, which was roughly in line with a $4.10 billion estimate from analysts polled by LSEG. Adjusted earnings came up short at $1.00 per share, compared to a forecast of $1.02.

The results did little to overturn recent "SaaSpocalypse" fears, or concerns that new AI capabilities will upend traditional software business models.

The stock drop came even after the company slightly lifted its full-year 2026 subscription revenue outlook to between $15.78 billion and $15.79 billion. Net new AI average contract value jumped 65%.

One factor spooking investors is the lack of immediate payoff for the company's investments in its newly formed forward-deployed engineering team that embeds in enterprises to build AI solutions, Radke said.

"It's just going to be a little bit longer of a waiting game, and so I think the market, you know, wanted to see something a little bit sooner," he said. "I think you got to wait until next year to really see that inflection."
