title: Cruise companies aim to keep fuel costs down. Their strategies for doing so differ
content:
Carnival,Royal CaribbeanandNorwegian Cruise Line Holdingsposted strong earnings for their most recent quarters despite rising fuel prices. How the leading cruise companies navigate fuel costs boils down to starkly different strategies.

Oil prices have skyrocketed since the U.S.-Israel war with Iran began on Feb. 28. Brent crude oil reached asix-month highon Friday, settling at $116.72 per barrel. Withno clear end in sightfor the conflict in the Middle East, the pressure affecting cruise ships' lifeblood seems poised to last into the holiday travel season and beyond.

Both Royal Caribbean and Norwegian practice "hedging," or a strategy of using derivatives to reduce exposure to swings in the price of fuel, to account for sharp increases.

Carnival CEO Josh Weinstein, on the other hand, told CNBC in an interview last month that cutting fuel consumption is the best way to avert the effects of expensive fuel.

"At the end of the day, fuel is an input cost for us. The best thing that we can do to control that cost is to use less," Weinstein said at the time.

Jefferies analyst David Katz told CNBC in an interview that companies that hedge do so primarily to manage the cost of fuel, but also to manage Wall Street expectations and prevent hectic stock trading based on fluctuations in the price of fuel.

"When you're public, the Street will trade your stock around based on the price of fuel," Katz said. "The Street's argument is that volatility puts pressure on your multiple."

"While it is mathematically most likely true that over the long term it is more expensive," he explained. "The benefit of having less fuel volatility in the model and less trading volatility is [it's] good for your multiple."

Despite the potential positives of the strategy, Carnival has maintained the stance it has held since 2019: Cutting fuel consumption works better than hedging.

And Carnival's third-quarter earnings report last month suggests the strategy may be paying off.

Carnival beat analysts' expectations on both the top and bottom lines for its most recent quarter and reported an all-time high net income of $1.9 billion.

Weinstein told CNBC in an interview on "Squawk on the Street" following the release that the company has been "maniacal" about cutting its fuel consumption, saying it's slashed its unit fuel consumption rate by 26% since 2019.

"We estimate we've saved about $700 million in 2026 based on that consumption savings rate going down since 2019," he said.

Carnival spent $615 million, or about 7.3% of its revenue, on fuel in the third quarter, according to its most recent earnings release. That's an increase from the $425 million, or 6.7% of revenue, that the company spent on fuel in the fourth quarter of 2025, before fuel prices spiked.

Carnival projects its fuel costs will rise to $640 million in the fourth quarter, according to its earnings release.

Royal Caribbean similarly beat analyst expectations for earnings per share for its third quarter, reported Tuesday. However, it narrowly missed on revenue.

CEO Jason Liberty attributed the company's beat in part to its hedging strategy during an interview on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" Tuesday morning.

"We're a little bit over 60% hedged here for 2026, and so that's helping insulate us from some of the impacts on the rising fuel costs," he said.

"It's obviously still impacting us," Liberty said. "[High fuel prices] evaporated a good chunk of our Q3 earnings beat into the full-year guide. But we're continuing to hedge, and we watch."

Royal Caribbean spent about $347 million on fuel in the third quarter, or about 6.2% of its revenue, according to its earnings release. That compares with $293 million, or 6.8% of revenue, spent on fuel in the fourth quarter of 2025, which ended on Dec. 31.

The company projects fuel costs will continue to rise to $379 million in the fourth quarter.

Liberty pointed out that high fuel prices have not dampened demand from consumers for vacations.

"It's not that we don't see points of challenges, but really what we've seen is that even in those points of challenges, the consumer comes roaring back," he said.

Royal Caribbean reported strong bookings for the third quarter and said reservations for 2027 are already up by a high-teens percentage.

Norwegian Cruise Line Holdingsbeat on both the top and bottom lines for its third-quarter earnings, reported on Thursday, with revenue of $2.9 billion and adjusted earnings per share of $1.12.

The company has hedged approximately 48% of its fuel consumption for 2026, according to the earnings release.

Norwegian spent about $196 million on fuel in the third quarter, or about 6.6% of its revenue, according to its most recent earnings release. That's a lower share of revenue than the 7.4% — totaling $167 million — spent on fuel in the fourth quarter of 2025, which ended on Dec. 31.

The company projects fuel consumption to rise slightly in the fourth quarter, up to 255,000 metric tons from 239,000 metric tons consumed in the third quarter.

The company is in the midst of a turnaround effort. And despite facing added challenges from the macro environment, Chief Financial Officer Mark Kempa said he is reassured by this quarter's results on an earnings call on Thursday.

"These results reinforce our confidence in the appeal of our products and the opportunity to translate stronger revenue performance and disciplined cost management into improved profitability," Kempa said.

title: Rare Stanley Druckenmiller post sends crypto-linked stock surging
content:
The post appeared seemingly out of nowhere. Stanley Druckenmiller, the legendary hedge fund manager who brought the Bank of England to its knees in the 1990s, and whose annual returns are the envy of Wall Street, posted a simple message on an otherwise sparse X feed announcing his involvement with a new type of decentralized exchange. The post caused bedlam on social media and moved shares of a leading crypto treasury company and its token.

TradeXYZ, the primary developer of perpetual futures, or "perps" markets, on exchange Hyperliquid, announced a partnership Thursday withIntercontinental Exchange (ICE)to bring its popular perpetual futures onshore into the U.S.

Shortly after the two said they are seeking regulatory approvals, Druckenmiller said on X that he is "excited to be an investor in trade(xyz)," and that he is "looking forward to to using their innovative product to enhance my investment process." Representatives for Druckenmiller confirmed thestatement to the Financial Times.

Options traders pounced on the closest publicly-traded play to the news:Hyperliquid Strategies (PURR), the company that invests in the HYPE crypto token that powers the Hyperliquid exchange.

More than 111,000 options traded on Hyperliquid Strategies Thursday, more than six times the 30-day average, as underlying shares surged 19% to the highest in three weeks. The flows leaned bullish, with almost 86,000 calls and under 27,000 puts trading. Almost four times as many calls were likely initiated by buyers than puts, and of the top 10 trades, only one involved put-buying, Cboe LiveVol dat show.

"We are thrilled to see ICE partnering with Trade.XYZ to bring the markets and liquidity of Hyperliquid to American investors," David Schamis, CEO of Hyperliquid Strategies, said in a text. "ICE is a cornerstone of traditional finance and the ideal partner."

Schamis added that the deal shows demand for perp-futures trading and is a step forward toward regulated trading of the asset class.

In August, President Donald Trump said in a surprise comment to reporters that regulators were working to bring the exchange onshore.

The most popular trades by volume in PURR were selling the 13-strike put expiring Dec. 18, and buying the 13-strike call expiring Nov. 6. Taken together, the two resemble a "risk reversal" strategy, a bullish trade looking for a short-term continuation of the rally, paired with long-term confidence the stock won't be below $13 by year-end.

title: Amazon to report Q3 earnings after the bell with AI spend under scrutiny
content:
Amazonis slated to report third-quarter earnings results after the bell on Thursday.

Here's what analysts are expecting, according to LSEG:

Wall Street is also looking at other key revenue numbers:

Investors expect to see robust growth in Amazon's cloud segment. AWS sales are predicted to grow 38%, according to StreetAccount, compared witha 37% gainlast quarter. It would mark AWS's fifth consecutive quarter of revenue acceleration.

That momentum isn't expected to slow down. CEO Andy Jassy said Amazon's cloud capacity is "largely sold out" for next year, and it's received significant commitments for 2028 as well.

"We always leave a certain amount for on demand and our inference service Bedrock or EC2, but largely sold out all the big chunks," Jassy said on anAndreessen Horowitzpodcast last week. "A good chunk of '28 is sold out."

Wall Street will be listening for any commentary from Amazon executives around AI spending.

Last quarter, the companyhikedits capital expenditure forecast for 2026 to $220 billion, up from $200 billion. Analysts surveyed by StreetAccount expect Amazon's capex to creep up more than $280 billion in 2027.

Amazon has rushed to bring more data centers online to meet surging demand for AI computing power. The aggressive spending has eaten into the company'scash flow. In July, the company reported negative free cash flow of $7.6 billion for the trailing twelve months, compared with positive free cash flow of $18.2 billion one year earlier. It's expected to be cash flow negative in the current quarter, with an outflow of $9.9 billion, according to FactSet estimates.

Alphabetand Meta both reported negative free cash flow in their latest quarterly earnings reports.Microsoftsaid Wednesday its free cash flow declined27%in the fiscal first quarter, but its cash flow remained positive, unlike its hyperscaler peers.

As Amazon shells out more on AI, it's steadily trimmed its headcount. The company haslaid offmore than 57,000 staffers since 2022, or roughly 16% of its corporate workforce. Thejob cutshave continued on a rolling basis this year via smaller rounds of layoffs.

The company on Wednesday laid off some staffers in its device software and services team to "operate more efficiently and better align with our product roadsmap," an Amazon spokesperson confirmed to CNBC. Fewer than 250 employees were let go as a result of the job cuts, the company said.

During the third quarter, Amazon made headlines when it blockedMeta'sMuseAI agent from shopping on its platform. The company said it was not given advance notice that Muse would access its webstore, and it never agreed to participate.

The move is in line with Amazon's broader stance on third-party agents accessing its site. Amazon hasblocked dozensof external agents, includingPerplexity, which the company sued last year over allegations that the startup concealed its AI shopping bots.

While it locks down its site from third-party agents, Amazon has increasingly invested in its own tools. In May, Amazonrebrandedits Rufus AI shopping chatbot to Alexa for Shopping.

On Thursday, Amazonsaidmore than 400 million shoppers have used the assistant, and the number of people using Alexa for Shopping's agentic features has "grown more than eight times since the start of the year."

The tool now has more than 100 shopping-related capabilities, the company said, including the ability to build gift lists, manage subscriptions and handle account changes.

As rivals Meta andOpenAIpush deeper into AI shopping tools, analysts have said the services could pose a risk to Amazon's digital advertising business. Users are turning to services like Muse and ChatGPT to research products, or in some cases, handing off purchases to AI agents, which means they're bypassing sponsored ads on Amazon's site.

"We expect Amazon to eventually develop its own agentic shopping offering, with its proprietary purchase data and commerce infrastructure positioning it well," Deutsche Bank analysts wrote in a note last week. "The key question is whether Amazon can accommodate third-party agents on terms that preserve attractive monetization."

title: Faisal Islam: This Budget was micro and that was deliberate
content: Image source,Getty ImagesByFaisal IslamEconomics editorPublished29 October 2026, 14:58 GMTUpdated 4 hours agoIt was not a mini Budget, but it was rather small. It might be called the "micro Budget".Small does not necessarily mean bad, but it clearly falls short of radical action to create a promised new economic model.A new "theory of growth" was not unveiled as promised by the prime minister Andy Burnham.It was preamble, roadmap, consultation, perhaps the starter to the main course, which appears to be the PM's 10-year plan next month.It went unsaid, but the clear stategic aim of Healey's statement was to be the "anti-mini Budget".This "steady as she goes" predictable fiscal event set out to avoid the aftermath seen following Liz Truss's mini-budget, in which unexpected and unfunded tax cuts spooked the bond and currency markets.The markets didn't even flicker on Healey's announcement of Â£65bn of extra borrowing over the next five years - government interest costs have actually fallen since Wednesday, against the backdrop of market turmoil due to the US-Iran war.The core of the Budget was to get Downing Street through the impacts of the Middle East conflict shock on energy and borrowing costs.If these pressures prove enduring there are some unpalatable decisions that will have to be grasped within the next year. The can will have to be picked up rather than kicked down the road again.It buys more time, more "breathing space", as it were, for the government and the prime minister's long-term strategic plans.The detail may come more quickly than feared. On welfare, the Milburn Review process is clearly heading for some sort of welfare-to-work scheme, even a separate system for younger workers.It will cost money up front to subsidise work opportunities and hope to save more from welfare bills in the future. The chancellor saw at close quarters Gordon Brown do this twice two decades ago.The Office for Budget Responsbility's (OBR) economic forecast showed the sheer rise in the welfare bill, which is set to jump to Â£431bn in 2031, if pensioner support is included.There are two further areas where the chancellor laid down markers, with little fiscal cost, in terms of the long term plan.On energy, there is some significance to the "cheaper power" mission announced, reshaping what had previously been a focus on clean power.While still committed to Net Zero, a series of technical changes to powers over levies and renewable auctions, will seek to turn the tide on additional pressures on energy costs.On devolution, the plan to allow local mayors to keep some extra business rate and income tax revenues, are more radical than expected.There are trade offs here, but it essentially provides incentives for regional leaders to grow their economies, workforce and tax base, that are normal elsewhere, but have not existed in the UK's very centralised tax system.How the PM will square other aspects of his "theory of growth" with the chancellor's spending constraints is the other significant challenge.Can he announce a 10-year plan without detailing the Liverpool to Manchester high speed train line, or a rebirth of some cancelled HS2 lines he championed a year ago?Away from the long term, the OBR forecast point to a very tricky economic backdrop until the spring, and a trickier spending review, given the need to accommodate the new defence target of 3% of national income by 2030.The PM's insistence he will not call an election for a year are eminently believable given the risk of 5% inflation and declining household income.A "focused" Budget at an uncertain time achieved its narrow aim of a bit of "breathing space" for households and also for the government itself.But the evident gaps in the Budget will need filling in come the PM's upcoming 10-year plan.Related topicsUK economyEconomic growthHM TreasuryJohn HealeyUK government spendingUK taxes

title: Bereaved families will not face tax bill over pension delays under new rules
content: Image source,Getty ImagesByBecky MortonPolitical reporterPublished4 hours agoBereaved families will no longer be hit by an unexpected tax bill because of severe delays paying out civil service pensions, following a change in Wednesday's Budget.Under previous HMRC rules, certain lump sum pension payments had to be paid within two years of the pension scheme being notified of a death to remain tax-free.Campaigners had warnedsome families could face an unfair financial penalty because of delays which were not their fault.The government has now changed the rules so payments will no longer become taxable solely because more than two years has passed.The Civil Service Pension scheme manages the pensions of 1.7 million public sector workers in the UK.Outsourcing firm Capita took over the administration of the scheme from a company called MyCSP in December 2025, saying it inherited a backlog of more than 86,000 cases.Despite a two-year transition period to prepare for the takeover, problems have persisted and by February the backlog had grown to 120,000 cases.Retired civil servants and bereaved families have been left waiting months for pension payments, with some struggling to pay bills.According to the latest figures up to 30 September,external, 1,643 outstanding cases of bereavement or death in service are more than 100 days old.The Cabinet Office, which has overall responsibility for the Civil Service Pension Scheme, previously said only a small number of these cases were approaching the two-year threshold.However the PCS union, which represents civil servants, had warned there were "serious questions" over how long cases would remain unresolved.Civil service pension backlog 'overwhelmed' Capita, boss saysPublished12 FebruaryEmergency loans offered to civil servants waiting on pensionsPublished29 JanuaryRetired civil servants left in pension limboPublished23 JanuaryRob Wassell, 58, had to wait more than two years following the death of his brother until he finally received the lump sum from his civil service pension on Tuesday.After his case was highlighted by the BBC last week, Rob says he got a call from the pension scheme's complaints department who told him the payment was on its way.However, because it was made after two years it was taxed at 45%, amounting to thousands of pounds.If the payment was made after the rule change, it would not have been subject to tax.Rob told the BBC he was pleased the government had addressed the issue in the Budget as this would mean others in his situation would not face a tax bill.While he said he was happy to finally get his payment it was "a bitter pill to swallow" as he is now waiting for the outcome of a complaint review to find out if the tax will be reimbursed.Rob said he was hopeful he would get the money back, adding: "I don't want to have to fight it anymore, it's been an ordeal already."Image source,Rob WassellImage caption,Rob Wassell was taxed on the payment from his brother's civil service pensionPensions minister Torsten Bell confirmed the rule changein a letter to the chairman of Parliament's Public Accounts Committee,external, Conservative MP Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who had raised concerns about the issue after it was highlighted by BBC Radio 4's Money Box Live programme.Bell said the move would "make the position fairer for all grieving families and friends where there are delays in the payment of death benefits, whether in the Civil Service or any other pensions scheme".He added: "Removing the tax deadline does not remove [a pension scheme's] wider duties to administer schemes prudently and without avoidable delay."Under the previous rules, if someone died before the age of 75, a pension lump sum death benefit was only tax-free if it was paid within two years of the pension scheme first becoming aware of the death, and if the value was below the deceased's Lump Sum and Death Benefit Allowance.However, the government has now removed the two-year deadline so payments will no longer become taxable solely because they were made more than two years after a pension scheme was notified of the death.The change applies to payments made from 28 October.In his letter, the pensions minister said people who had already been impacted by avoidable delays and been taxed as a result could seek compensation through the pension scheme's complaints process and the Pensions Ombudsman.Sir Geoffrey welcomed the announcement but said it does not "absolve Capita from processing and making payments to members of this scheme in a timely manner".Fran Heathcote, general secretary of the PCS union, also welcomed the change but said "this situation should never have arisen in the first place".She added: "Bereaved families must not pay the price for failures in the pension system."Capita is not off the hook, it continues to fail members and their families, which is why the scheme must be brought back in-house."Capita has previously apologised for the impact of delays on pension scheme members and their families.The company has said it is working to resolve outstanding cases as quickly as possible, with a particular focus on people who have been waiting the longest and those facing financial hardship or challenging circumstances.Sign up for our Politics Essential newsletterto keep up with the inner workings of Westminster and beyond.Related topicsCivil ServicePensionsCapitaCabinet Office

title: DoorDash to buy Instacart in $17bn deal it says will expand customer options
content: Image source,Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesByRachel ClunBusiness reporter,ÂReporting fromNew YorkPublished4 hours agoDoorDash will acquire grocery delivery firm Instacart in a $17bn (Â£12.8bn) deal, creating a behemoth that will bring more meals, quick-need purchases and big weekly shops directly to customers.DoorDash said the deal, expected to be final in about a year, will expand options for customers and let more sellers use the companies' services.Instacart shoppers will be able to buy from 150,000 stores, up from the current 100,000, while DoorDash will reach beyond restaurants into retail, the firms said."Together, we can accelerate innovation across the grocery industry and make online grocery more seamless and affordable for the millions of households we serve," Instacart's chief executive said."Over the last 14 years, Instacart has transformed online grocery by helping retailers of all sizes compete and grow, and joining forces with DoorDash allows us to do even more," CEO Chris Rogers also said.For DoorDash, the acquisition will allow it to use Instacart's grocery selection and substitution expertise, the company's co-founder and chief executive, Tony Xu, said."Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online. Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you'd choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts," Xu said.He added that "Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day".The deal, expected to be done by the end of 2027 or first six months of 2028, is DoorDash's biggest acquisition to date, and could help it take on delivery giants like Amazon.Morningstar analyst Martin Szumski told Reuters that the growth area in food delivery was shifting."Restaurant delivery is maturing, and growth now lies in more frequent, higher-value orders: weekly grocery shops, convenience items, and retail," he said.In the agreement, DoorDash will acquire Instacart for a value of $65 a share, which would be a 26% premium on the closing price of Instacart stock on 22 October - the price before news of the potential merger first emerged. The deal will be at least 75% cash, DoorDash said.DoorDash plans to keep Instacart's brand, app, and technology products. The delivery services will keep operating as independent companies until the deal is concluded.The merger may raise antitrust issues with government regulators, Reuters also reported.New York City's commission on consumer and worker protections, which last month reached a $131.5m settlement with DoorDash over allegations of underpaying workers, said in a statement: "This proposed merger continues a troubling trend of mega-corporations consolidating.""Whether or not this merger proceeds, we will fully enforce delivery workers' rights," it added.Related topicsRetailingDelivery servicesOnline shoppingMergers and acquisitions

title: Poundland's future hangs in the balance as chain edges towards collapse
content: Image source,Getty ImagesByEmma Simpson,ÂBusiness correspondentÂandÂTom Espiner,ÂBusiness reporterPublished29 October 2026, 09:46 GMTUpdated 8 minutes agoThe future of Poundland hangs in the balance as the discount chain edges towards collapse.The retailer's bosses have filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators which will give the business 10 days breathing space to find a rescue deal.The move comes after Poundland's managing director Barry Williams wrote a memo to his 12,000 staff saying the chain's US owner had limited Poundland's access to funding despite strong sales.It is understood the firm's owner, Gordon Brothers, wants to break up the firm, with rivals Poundstretcher, B&M and Lidl interested in potentially buying up stores.Gordon Brothers bought Poundland, which had been struggling, from the Polish retail group Pepco in June last year for a nominal Â£1, but a little over a year later it put the business up for sale.Irish firm Martin Property Group (MPG) put forward a bid to take the business on as a going concern, which was the preferred option for management, but it is understood this did not meet Gordon Brothers' expectations.Gordon Brothers wants to recoup a Â£30m shareholder loan it inherited from the previous owners as part of a its deal, but it is understood the Martin Property Group offer was for Â£5m, with the rest of the payment deferred.It means Poundland is now heading towards an insolvency process.Gordon Brothers could secure a new owner through what is known as a pre-pack administration.But the most likely option for the business to be broken up and for parcels of stores to be sold.Poundland was founded in 1990 with a store in Burton-upon-Trent, and has around 20 million customers per year.It has across its 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, where it trades as Dealz.It sells low-cost everyday products, general merchandise and fashion on local high streets.Business secretary Jonathan Reynolds said the government was "keeping a close eye" the future of Poundland thought said the government had "no standing role" in the process."This is a business that has been turned around, it employs thousands of people," he told the BBC."If there is a potential owner that can continue that progress, obviously that naturally sounds like the best way forward so if that hasn't been accepted I want to know that is the case."The curious case of why Poundland is struggling during a cost-of-living crisisPublished21 November 2025Poundland in rescue talks as owners seek buyerPublished13 OctoberA Gordon Brothers insider said breaking the firm up would allowcreditors to recover more money, and that this process would ultimately offer the best outcome for staff.The US investment firm's position is that current employees may be able to get employment with new store owners.If this type of insolvency happens, it would let interested parties firm up offers.These include Poundstretcher owner, Fortress, which according to one insider is interestedin takingon between 200 and 250 stores.Another large retailer is understood to be interested in buying up more than 100 other sites.More than half a dozen retailers, include Iceland, Lidl, and B&M, have expressed interest in Poundland's store estate.Situation 'wholly avoidable'However, there is a split between the owners and the management running Poundland, who described the situation as "unexpected, unwanted and wholly avoidable"."As you all know, our sales are strong and our recovery is taking root. This business simply does not deserve to go into any kind of administration," the chain's managing director Williams said in a message to staff this week.He revealed that Gordon Brothers had limited Poundland's access to funds which help it run its day-to-day business."I'm disappointed to have to tell you that Gordon Brothers have given instructions that restricts our access to funds that we would, in normal circumstances expect to access fully under our existing loan agreement," he added.In the memo, seen by the BBC, Williams said the offer from Martin Property Group was a "fully funded, ready to go bid that would have kept the business intact and able to continue the remarkable progress we've made".Three independent directors who were appointed earlier this month to help oversee a sale resigned with immediate effect after disagreeing with Gordon Brothers' decision not to accept MPG's solvent offer.Gordon Brothers has lined up AlixPartners as administrators.Get in touchDo you work for Poundland? Share your experience.Contact formRelated topicsPoundlandCompaniesRetailingUK High Streets

title: Steve Eisman gets more conservative with portfolio as AI trade nears 'tipping point'
content:
Steve Eisman of "The Big Short" fame thinks the artificial intelligence trade is near a "tipping point," but he's not ready to outright bet against it yet.

"I've gotten much more conservative in my own portfolio. We have shorted against the box a whole bunch of our positions, so that our risk is much, much, much lower. But I'm not, like, net short any," he told CNBC's"Squawk Box"on Thursday.

Eisman's primary concern pertains to the frontier algorithm models, which are exploiting a climate of fear around their technologies, he believes, in order to set up a competitive regulatory moat against more cost-efficient products and to obscure some faltering fundamentals. Bigwigs in the tech industry have issued similarwarnings.

Anthropic left its latest revenue figures blank in its initial IPO filing, but Eisman believes they will show a significant deceleration from the prior quarter. Other figures in the report point to capital efficiency issue, he said.

The ratio of revenue-to-equipment-expense was 2.08 in the second quarter and 1.7 in the third, marking a significant change in trajectory, Eisman said, citing an analysis he'd been given.

Yet, Eisman said he was scared to make a definitive bet against the AI trade because of how intertwined it is with the market as a whole, calling it "impossible" for the technology sector to be siloed away from the broader equity market and the rest of the economy.

"So much of the market is on the other side, and it's still reading tea leaves. I think we're getting closer. I think the numbers from Google scared people," he said.

Alphabet'sstock tanked after reporting earnings on Wednesday, following a big pullback in its core advertising business as AI queries supplant internet search across its various products.

Google executives said Wednesday they were running experiments to figure out what to do about it.

"It's worth noting the strong growth in AI mode queries had an impact because of the lower monetization we are seeing in AI mode," Philipp Schindler, Google's chief business officer, said. "Our ad experiments have shown promising results."

Portions of Anthropic's recently filedS-1struck Eisman as "extremely negative" in light of the fact that it didn't contain many metrics for the upcoming quarter that would give a clearer picture of the company's financial situation.

title: Eli Lilly hikes sales outlook, as CEO says there's room for 'dramatic' obesity market expansion
content:
Eli Lillyon Thursday reported third-quarter earnings and revenue that blew past estimates and hiked its full-year sales outlook, as demand for its blockbuster weight loss drug Zepbound and diabetes treatment Mounjaro soared again.

Despite that strength, sales of its new GLP-1 obesity pill Foundayo, which launched in the U.S. in April, were under Wall Street's expectations for the quarter.

The pharmaceutical giant now expects 2026 revenue to come in between $91 billion and $92 billion, up from a previous guidance of $85 billion to $87 billion.

Lilly projects its full-year adjusted earnings will be between $35 and $36 per share, which compares with a previous outlook of $35.50 to $36.50 per share. The company said it raised the underlying profit guidance by $4.07 per share at the midpoint, but noted that it is offset by $4.57 per share in charges tied to deals in the quarter.

The company's shares rose about 9% on Thursday.

Lilly's massive diabetes and obesity windfall – and market share lead over chief rival Novo – shows no signs of slowing down, even as the company grapples with lower net prices in the U.S. The pharma giant is converting its massive profits into a dealmaking spree, most recentlystriking an agreementto buy Merida Biosciences to develop a new class of treatments for serious autoimmune and allergic diseases.

Here's what Eli Lilly reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Resilient demand for Zepbound and Mounjaro has helped fuel several strong quarters for Lilly despite lower prices for the medications in the U.S., which came aftera drug pricing dealstruck with the Trump administration last year. In a release, Lilly also pointed to expanded U.S. coverage for obesity care, referring to Medicare's decision to start covering GLP-1s for weight loss in July under a temporary pilot program.

"This is a program that's really working," Lilly CEO Dave Ricks said on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." "We're pleased with the early uptake and access, and I think doctors and patients are as well."

Mounjaro's worldwide revenue rose 65% to $10.72 billion for the quarter, including U.S. sales of about $5 billion. That surpassed the $10.10 billion in worldwide sales and $4.79 billion in U.S. revenue that analysts were expecting for the quarter, according to StreetAccount.

Mounjaro notably saw strength internationally, with sales outside the U.S. jumping 93%.

Zepbound, which entered the market roughly three years ago, posted $5.35 billion in revenue for the third quarter. That's up 49% from the year-earlier period, as demand for the drug also rose while realized prices dropped. The vast majority of those sales came from the U.S.

Analysts were expecting $5.09 billion in global sales for Zepbound, including $4.99 billion from the U.S., according to StreetAccount.

Lilly's newly launched obesity pill, Foundayo, which won U.S. approval in April, took in $184 million in sales for the third quarter. That fell under analyst forecasts of around $229 million in sales, StreetAccount estimates showed.

It marks the second earnings report that includes revenue from the GLP-1 pill, which is competing head-to-head witha rival oral drugfrom Novo that launched in January.

Lilly is working to maintain its dominance in the booming market for GLP-1 drugs, with the company holding 63% share of the U.S. obesity and diabetes drug market in the third quarter, according to an earnings presentation on Thursday. Novo's market share in the quarter was 36.6%.

Ricks told CNBC that he estimates 3% to 10% of eligible patients access obesity care in the U.S., but said the "room for expansion here of this market is dramatic." Lilly is at the front of that push, he added.

Internationally, Lilly held 58.4% share of the market, while Novo had 41.6%, the presentation said.

Eli Lilly's revenue in the U.S. climbed 34% to $15.1 billion. Lilly said it saw a 41% increase in volume — or the number of prescriptions or units sold — for its products, primarily for Mounjaro and Zepbound. That was partially offset by a 7% decrease in realized prices, primarily driven by Zepbound.

Lilly's quarter was also boosted by a sales-based milestone payout of $410 million for its Type 2 diabetes medication Jardiance, related to the company's collaboration with Boehringer Ingelheim.

Sales outside the U.S. jumped 47% to $9.3 billion, propelled by a 76% surge in volume and partly offset by a 29% drop in realized prices.

The pharmaceutical giant booked net income of $6.45 billion, or $7.22 per share, for the third quarter, which includes the $4.57 per share deal charges. That compares with net income of $5.58 billion, or $6.21 per share, a year earlier.

Excluding one-time items associated with the value of intangible assets and other adjustments, Eli Lilly posted earnings of $7.48 per share for the third quarter.

title: Analysis: Kevin Warsh is keeping Wall Street guessing. It may be his most powerful tool.
content:
Kevin Warshis done proving himself.

The Federal Reserve chairman's press conference Wednesday was sharply different from hisearly appearancesin the job, when he often seemed backed into a corner. He's shown he is willing to let the markets guess where he is going — at least to a point. And he has started using his authority to reshape the institution.

Warsh was appointed by apresidentwho said cutting interest rates was a litmus test for his choice for Fed chair. When the Federal Open Market Committee opted to hold rates flat in June and July, even with inflation well above the Fed's 2% target, a swarm of commentators questioned the new chairman's credibility. The FOMC's subsequent decision inSeptemberto raise rates came with such a hawkish reading of the economy by Warsh that the markets swung sharply in the opposite direction. Investors thought the Fed might be locked into a rate hike this week until a pair of top officials came out and appeared to deliberately temper market expectations.

This week, Warsh put all that behind him. He disavowed any expectation that the Fed is on a set course: "If we had a firm conclusion about the conduct of monetary policy, we'd announce it to much fanfare today," he said.

But Warsh also gave a strong signal that his current lean is toward higher rates. "While overall financial conditions are tighter, I'm unwilling and unable to call them tight," he said.

He was preserving his options while laying the intellectual groundwork for a hike in December, should inflation remain stubborn.

Warsh declined to confirm the widespread assumption in the markets that the officials who had talked down the markets had done so at his direction.Fed insiders have saidthat the Fed's vice chairs usually coordinate messaging with the chair.

"To suggest somehow that I am some kind of all-knowing person sending messages out, that's not the committee of the FOMC that I know," Warsh said. And yet the market got the message that the Fed wouldn't hike this week. If Warsh wants to give otherwise taboo forward guidance through his lieutenants, he now has plausible deniability.

This is Warsh's MO: He is intellectually flexible and highly focused on achieving his goals.

For instance, one of the goals of the task forces he has assembled to kick-start policy changes is to change the way the Fed measures inflation. But that was impossible while his commitment to fighting it was in question. September's rate hike does a lot to answer the skeptics who said he wasn't serious about slowing price increases, and he is willing to deliver more rate increases, if necessary.

"If you think that we're tolerating some inflation target somewhere in the twos, let us disabuse you of it," Warsh said Wednesday. The target is 2% flat. His remarks are a recipe for higher rates as long as the economy stays strong.

Warsh and the FOMC will have a raft of new data before the next meeting, in December, to make their case. That could, alternatively, help him make the case that productivity is rising, allowing for more growth without inflation.

Meanwhile, Warsh's other changes at the Fed are starting to take effect. He announced a plan Wednesday to reduce the number of times the FOMC is scheduled to vote on interest rates over the next two years. The Fed will keep meeting eight times a year, but will skip a vote on whether to change rates at one meeting in 2027 and two in 2028. That move has the effect of devaluing a good chunk of Fedspeak. The market won't pay much mind to a marginal regional Fed president's comments when they come as much as three months ahead of a rate decision. Regional presidents also get one fewer scheduled vote in their year-long rotations as decision-makers on the FOMC.

The Fed chairman retains the authority to call an impromptu meeting at any time should he see the need to change rates.

But there are risks to Warsh's way of doing business, especially as he recedes further behind the curtain. The advocates for Fed transparency believe that sunlight adds more rigor to officials' arguments.

That could already be a problem, said Robert Sockin, chief U.S. economist at asset manager PGIM. He is in the camp that thinks inflation is running too hot to justify the Fed's decision not to raise rates this week.

"While more data is always better, Warsh did not sufficiently explain why this backdrop did not justify a rate increase, particularly given his comment that while he thinks financial conditions have tightened, he would not say they are tight," Sockin said.

It was a "policy mistake" to hold, "and a gradual Fed likely means one that has to hike higher, mechanically raising recession risk," Sockin said.

The full consequences of Warsh's approach may not become clear for months. That gives him room to maneuver as he reshapes the Fed. But it also means the consequences of waiting to tighten may not become apparent until it's too late.

title: 'Painful' years ahead, think tanks warn, as living standards set to fall
content: Image source,Getty ImagesByLucy HookerBusiness ReporterPublished29 October 2026, 12:50 GMTUpdated 1 hour agoPeople are facing a "painful" and "depressing" few years ahead, economic think tanks have warned, after forecasts showed growth in living standards grinding almost to a halt.Typical working-age households would see their disposable income fall by Â£1,050, or 3%, between now and 2029, according to the Resolution Foundation, while the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the current decade would be the worst for household income growth on record.Chancellor John Healey said his Budget offered "breathing space", but said the government could "never remove completely" cost of living pressures.The UK's official forecaster said its latest economic forecast painted a "pretty grim picture".The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), blamed the difficult financial situation facing the UK on higher borrowing costs and inflation caused by the US-Iran war.In response to rising energy prices, Healey has announced measures, including a Â£100 support payment, aimed at easing pressure on household finances.But that would not be enough to offset the impact of higher energy bills, the Resolution Foundation said."This parliament is increasingly looking like one of two halves," said the think tank's chief executive, Ruth Curtice."The first half has been marked by rising living standards, solid economic growth and extra funding for public services," she said.However, the second half of the parliament would be "tough going", she said.Treasury will not commit to reducing welfare bill before next electionPublished3 hours agoWhat we now know about the UK economy in four chartsPublished18 hours agoYour pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects youPublished21 hours agoIn response the government had provided a "scattergun" Budget that did not do enough to address the challenges facing the country, Curtice said.Over the course of this parliament, incomes for non-pensioner households, after taxes, benefits, and housing costs are taken into account, will have risen by "a paltry" Â£600, the Resolution Foundation said, with the gains made in the first five years.Even after the extra support provided by the government, households will be left paying higher energy bills than during the last energy crisis in 2022, according to its analysis.The Resolution Foundation said the support should have been more targeted at the poorest households.Lost decadeAlongside the Budget the OBR issued its economic forecast indicating aslowdown in GDP growth from 1.2% in 2026 to 1% in 2027.The forecast for next year is sharply lower than what was predicted at their last assessment in March.The OBR also put its forecast for inflation for 2027 up from 2% to 3.4%.Frozen tax thresholdsare also eating into people's take-home pay.However, the OBR also emphasised the difficulties in economic forecasting, highlighting uncertainty over the future path of inflation, in particular, which could turn out to be either significantly higher or lower than their predictions.While the Resolution Foundation focused its forecast for living standards on working age households, the OBR looks at all households, including pensioners and reflects a 10-year rolling average growth to take into account short-term fluctuations.The OBR found that by the end of the decade living standards for all households would have barely grown, by less than 0.1% per year."This decade looks set to be the worst decade for growth in household incomes on record," added the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS)."No amount of temporary cost of living packages will fix that. We need a stronger economy."'Fragile' financesIFS director Helen Miller said there would also be growing pressure on the government's spending plans over the parliament."Spending plans look extremely tight. They don't look to me like plans that this government would want to deliver," she said."Whether or not they are delivered matters because the spending plans underpin the plan to bring down borrowing," she added.Miller said she was left with the impression that Healey was hoping the economy would improve to take the pressure off those spending decisions.Healey, speaking on the BBC's Today Programme, said "economic storms", including the Iran war and Russia's invasion of Ukraine, were affecting countries around the world and the government was seeking to help where it could.He said energy bill help would create "breathing space" for most households.Around 20 million households are set to receive the Â£100 payment based on which council tax band they are in.But Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said the Budget had left the public finances "more fragile" as Healey had reduced the "headroom" of the amount of buffer the country has between what it takes in revenues and what it spends.Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey said the Â£100 energy payment would be identified as the best item in the Budget for many people, but said that it was "not good enough" when you considered the "stealth tax rises" that were taking money out of people's pay packets.Related topicsJohn HealeyUK economyUK government spendingCost of LivingOffice for Budget Responsibility

title: Alphabet earnings miss reflects first real sign that AI is taking a bite out of search
content:
InAlphabet'sacross-the-boardearnings miss, one segment stood out above all else: search.

Revenue in the search and other segment grew 12% from a year ago to roughly $63 billion, but came in below estimates for the second straight quarter. At the same time, Google said search query growth on the platform was the strongest it's been in five years.

The gap between usage and revenue within the search giant's flagship business is becoming harder to dismiss as more people turn to artificial intelligence bots and agents, including tools offered by Google. Since the early days of ChatGPT, analysts have predicted that traditional search will get eclipsed by AI, and warned that Google will have to figure out new ways to make money. While search remains a massive business, early signs of a shift are appearing.

"These things are going to be a force," Deepwater Asset Management's Gene Munster told CNBC's "Fast Money" after the earnings report, referring to new AI-powered services. Munster said that if "personalized bots" take off, "that will become for a lot of people the starting point of commerce, which impacts where Google is."

Alphabet executives said foreign exchange was the biggest factor behind the deceleration in search revenue in the period, and said the currency impact would be even greater in the fourth quarter.

The stock plummeted about 10% in extended trading, reflecting the weaker-than-expected earnings report and negative free cash flow of $9 billion for the quarter, three times the estimated deficit. In the second quarter, Alphabet's free cash flow went negative for the first time in its history as a public company, at $5.9 billion.

Google has spent much of the past year telling investors that it needs to pour money into AI infrastructure and services to meet unending demand from consumers and businesses. Google's Gemini model has allowed the company to stay competitive withAnthropicandOpenAI, and its Gemini-poweredenterprise serviceshave proven to be a hit with customers.

The company also says that Gemini is strengthening its core digital ads business, as it uses AI to improve its ability to understand user intent and make advertising more relevant.

“We continue to accelerate the deployment of Gemini models across our entire ads infrastructure to boost performance,” Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler said on the earnings call.

The company made what Schindler called its “biggest update to product listing ads in a decade” during the third quarter, adding new AI capabilities.

“Overall, AI is accelerating our ads development and drives the majority of our product launches,” Schindler said.

Advertisers are also rapidly adopting AI tools. In the third quarter, Gemini models helped advertisers generate more than 1.5 billion campaign assets, up more than sevenfold from a year earlier, Schindler said.

But none of that addresses revenue growth for search, which slid from 19% in the first quarter to 17% in the second, before falling to 12% in the third.

Analysts at UBS wrote in a note that the results are "going to bring Search cannibalization fears right back to the forefront." AndMizuho analyst Jordan Klein said the numbers are an issue for search and YouTube.

"This elevates the fear around AI and agentic taking share from Search and YT and hurting their AI monetization narrative," Klein wrote in a note after the earnings report.

Where Alphabet's AI bet is very much paying off is in its cloud business.

Revenue in that division, which is racing to catch up toAmazonWeb Services andMicrosoftAzure, more than doubled in the quarter to nearly $31 billion. Cloud backlog also reached roughly $560 billion, reflecting enormous contracted demand for AI infrastructure. Management said it expects just more than half of that backlog to be recognized over the next 24 months.

In Microsoft's quarterlyearnings report, which also landed after the bell Wednesday, the software maker said Azure revenue increased 48% from a year earlier to $33.2 billion.

Cloud demand is a big reason for Alphabet to keep spending.

The company maintained its full-year 2026 capital expenditure forecast of $195 billion to $205 billion and said spending will increase significantly in 2027. Some of that is for itstensor processing units, or TPUs, which compete withNvidia'sgraphics processing units. Alphabet just started selling them to outside customers in the second quarter.

Customer agreements first show up in Google Cloud’s backlog, and the company has to spend money building the systems before it can deliver them and recognize the associated revenue.

“You see cash going out and we’re building up the inventory base,” Alphabet CFO Anat Ashkenazi said on the earnings call. “As we start delivering and billing customers for these TPU systems, then you see cash coming in.”

Still, Google has to contend with concerns about its longtime cash cow. Gil Luria, an analyst at D.A. Davidson, said the fears that existed from 2023 to 2025 about the AI effect appear to finally be showing up in Google's business.

"Investors will now worry that the miss in Search, YouTube and Subscription, leading to a profit miss, are an indication that AI has finally come for Google," Luria wrote in an email. "We would not rush to conclusions based on one quarter, but will definitely need to reassess what the world of agentic commerce means for Google."

WATCH:Google Cloud surges as search slows

title: Judge says Trump's bid to set aside California ballots would ‘wreak havoc’ on democracy
content:
A U.S. judge strongly rebuked the Trump administration on Wednesday by rejecting a request by the Justice Department to temporarily block California from counting mail ballots for the midterm elections from more than 20,000 registered voters the department alleges are likely noncitizens.

The decision marks the latest setback for President Donald Trump's effort to boost the federal government's role in elections ahead of the November 3 midterms, with his Republican Party locked in a tight battle to retain control of both houses of Congress.

US District Judge David Carter issued the decision after a hearing on Tuesday in Los Angeles federal court over the Justice Department's request for a temporary restraining order barring officials from counting any ballots from the individuals it flagged.

The Justice Department's lawsuit, filed on October 15, was a rare intervention in the voting process weeks before an election and signaled the Trump administration's willingness to contest the midterm results in court.

"Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch," Carter wrote on Wednesday.

The judge, an appointee of Democratic President Bill Clinton, said the Justice Department's last-minute request to exclude over 20,000 ballots ran afoul of "longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections."

Carter warned that a ruling in the Trump administration's favor would "wreak havoc" and cause thousands of registered voters to "potentially lose the right that generations of Americans have fought to preserve."

"Eroded trust in our democracy is irreparable," Carter wrote. "Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred. If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger."

The Justice Department swiftly appealed the decision to the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals.

"Every day, more ballots are processed by election officials," Justice Department lawyer Bill Essayli said in a statement. "This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution."

California has said the state's safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust. It said the Justice Department's assertions relied on "suspect data" and that complying with its demands would risk disenfranchising eligible voters.

California is the most populous US state and a Democratic stronghold. It has more seats in the House of Representatives — 52 — than any other state.

Trump has made California a focal point of his sweeping immigration crackdown since returning to the White House, accusing it of undermining public safety through its "sanctuary state" policies that ‌limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.

Trump has repeatedly insisted that states are not doing enough to stop voting by noncitizens, which he says is widespread despite multiple studies and state audits showing it is rare.

Carter ruled two days after a federal appeals court on Monday rejected an unusual emergency request by the Justice Department asking the appeals court to temporarily block California from counting the ballots before Carter had the chance to rule.

The Justice Department did not indicate how many of the more than 20,000 people it flagged in California had actually submitted a mail ballot.

It had argued that a restraining order was necessary to ensure that California did not impede prosecutors' ability to enforce a federal law that makes it illegal for noncitizens to vote in federal elections.

But Carter said the Justice Department never explained why counting ballots would impair any prosecutions under the law, as states are not required to help the federal government investigate and prosecute crimes.

Apart from California, the Trump administration has sought to intervene in elections in two states that are home to competitive races.

In Alaska, the Justice Department last week asked a judge to prevent certification of election results if the Republican incumbent senator loses by a slim margin, alleging that the presence of another candidate with a similar name on the ballot could confuse voters. Alaska has urged that the case be dismissed, arguing it has taken steps to distinguish the two candidates on the ballot.

In Washington state, the Justice Department on Monday sent a letter asking officials not to count any ballots received from 400 voters it said may not be citizens. Washington's top elections official said the timing of the request indicated it was intended to cast unfounded suspicion on election results.

California had 23 million registered voters as of December 2025, while Washington had 5 million registered voters as of 2024, state records show.

Voting rights activists have expressed concern that the federal government's methods for scrutinizing state voter lists to identify noncitizen voters risk wrongly flagging naturalized citizens for removal from the rolls.

title: Billionaire Ambani cries tears of joy as Jio Platforms becomes the second most valued Indian firm
content:
Billionaire Mukesh Ambani has become the owner of the two most valued companies in India, after a stellar listing ofJio Platforms, the country's largest telecom operator and digital services firm.

The share of Jio Platforms continued to climb higher on Thursday, opening 3.3% higher a day after its market debut.

TheMeta- andGoogle-backed company listed on Wednesday at a premium of over 25% to its IPO price, leading to a market capitalization of 13.05 trillion rupees ($137.1 billion).

Ambani's flagship company,Reliance Industries, also the most valued company in India, owns more than a 64% stake in Jio Platforms after the initial public offering.

Ahead of the listing, thepatriarch of the Ambani familyteared up as his three children shared the journey of building Jio and vowed to create value for investors over the next 50 years.

Analysts expect Jio's free cash flow to improve significantly as the funds from the initial public offering will be used to repay legacy telecom debt, and the company's 5G investment cycle is slowing down.

However, they cautioned that most of the value has been priced in after the listing gains, with the company now being valued on par with some of the global telecom giants.

With just 3% share dilution, Jio has wiped out nearly 300 billion rupees of debt, said Anurag Singh, founder and managing partner of U.S. based Ansid Capital, told CNBC. He added Jio's current market cap puts it in the league of American telecom giants such asAT&TandVerizon Communications.

AT&T has a market cap of $139 billion and Verizon of $179 billion, as per LSEG data.

In the next 10 years, Jio will "democratize every technology that can transform Indian lives," Akash Ambani, the eldest son of Mukesh and the managing director of Jio Platforms, said on Wednesday, ahead of the listing.

The 35-year-old scion listed out artificial intelligence, Cloud, connected devices, and "connectivity from even space," as some of the key areas for future growth.

The company's plans to launch satellite communicationsdrew the ireof trillionaire Elon Musk, who blamed the Ambanis for the delays in the launch of Starlink in India earlier this month.

"Jio brings a rare scale to Indian equities," with a customer base of more than half a billion, operating margins of 52% and net leverage of 0.36 times, Vaqarjaved Khan, senior analyst at Indian broking firm Angel One, told CNBC.

He added that at a price-to-earnings of 34 times, much of the "quality" is priced in and future returns will be driven by improvement in average revenue per user and AI services.

Meanwhile, after Jio's listing pop, Reliance Group'smarket value of 30 trillion rupeeshas surpassed that of Tata Group's 25 trillion rupees, making Ambani family business the top conglomerate in the country, as per a Bloomberg report.

title: Over 41,000 U.S. Homeland Security officials' details apparently exposed after massive data breach
content:
The identities of over 41,000 officials from the Department of Homeland Security have allegedly been exposed in a massive data breach by a hacktivist group calling itself the Department of Peace.

Late Wednesday stateside, the database was posted on Distributed Denial of Secrets, a nonprofit dedicated to news leaks, with claims that it was obtained from an Okta single sign-on service used by the DHS.

It appears to reveal employee names, offices, contact information and assignments, and is searchable.

Okta didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

DDoS said that "this is not a comprehensive list of all DHS employees," quoting cofounder Emma Best saying, "Rather than an indiscriminate directory of every DHS employee, Icepick identifies many of the architects and drivers of DHS policy and operations."

DHS didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. The agency told the Washington Post that it was "aware of a potential breach" and was"working to address the situation swiftly and effectively."

The searchable database appears to include employees from Immigration and Customs Enforcement, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, Customs and Border Protection and the DHS headquarters.

The hacker group said the leak was carried out in response to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullinreportedly sayingon July 17 that ICE will be "turning up the heat on the streets" by intensifying immigration arrests and traffic stops.

In U.S. President Donald Trump's second term, the backlash to his efforts to intensify arrests and deportations of suspected illegal immigrants has increased as ICE agents have been documented using physical force during operations.

DHS completed 980,000 deportations in the first 18 months of his term, according to theMigration Policy Institute.

title: Trump methane policy rollback may have minimal impact on crude prices, EPA says
content:
U.S. President Donald Trump'sproposed rollback of methane emissions rules would do little to lower oil and natural gas prices, according to the Environmental Protection Agency’s own economic modeling.

Trump and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldinannounced the proposalTuesday in Lubbock, Texas, in a bid to lower regulatory costs and support domestic energy production.

“When owners and operators can produce, America benefits with lower prices,” Zeldin said in EPA’s announcement.

TheEPA projectsthat the changes would lower U.S. crude prices by 11 cents a barrel in 2027, or 0.14%, while increasing domestic oil production by 0.09%. That amounts to roughly one extra barrel for every 1,000 the U.S. would otherwise produce, according to CNBC's calculations.

CLSA energy research analyst Baden Moore said uncertainty over implementation and the policy’s durability across administrations could constrain producers’ investment decisions.

That “limits the upside to current production rates in the near term,” including in 2027, he told CNBC.

He added that the changes could instead slow declines in existing production by allowing some wells to remain operational when environmental compliance costs would otherwise make them uneconomic.

Moore anticipates that the policy would affect only a small proportion of the U.S. shale market.

With CLSA expecting oil prices to remain above $80 a barrel, many wells would already be commercially viable, limiting the number whose continued operation would depend on regulatory relief.

The proposal could help many well operators while having a limited effect on overall supply.

Marginal wells — wells that produce small amounts of oil and gas — account for around 80% of active U.S. wells, but less than 10% of production,according to the International Energy Agency.

The EPA is considering lighter methane requirements based either on a well site’s production levels or whether it uses conventional or unconventional extraction methods.

The agency would also scrap its Super Emitter Program, which relies on approved third-party monitors to identify major methane releases. Separately, operators could manage gas produced alongside oil through flaring that destroys 95% of the methane.

The EPA projects the proposal would result in an additional 60 million short tons of methane emissions from 2027 through 2050.

The agency told CNBC it estimates the changes would save the U.S. economy about $45 billion over that period, including roughly $42 billion in lower compliance costs.

The EPA also expects operators to capture less gas for sale or use, resulting in about $4.2 billion in lost revenue. That figure is already reflected in its estimate of $42 billion in compliance savings.

This proposal remains subject to the rulemaking process, including a public-comment period and further EPA review, before any changes can be finalized.

It comes as the Trump administration has also moved to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports as part of efforts to address fuel prices. Energy Secretary Chris Wrighttold CNBC Tuesdaythat additional shipments could be permitted depending on Moscow’s actions.

title: China’s tech darlings are losing their shine. Here’s what’s behind the sell-off
content:
China's technology stocks are losing their luster as investors question whether the country's artificial intelligence boom can deliver profits strong enough to justify lofty valuations.

TheSTAR 50 Indexplunged over 40% from its July peak as concerns mount over returns on AI investments. The index tracks 50 of the largest and most liquid companies on Shanghai's technology-focused STAR Market — home to semiconductor, artificial intelligence and other high-tech firms.

Even battery giantCATL, long considered one of China's technology success stories, has come under pressure, falling 37% since the start of the year.

What started as profit-taking after a strong rally has turned into a broader reckoning over whether earnings can support current valuations.

"I think the sell-off primarily started as a valuation correction and some profit taking, but now there is a critical look happening at whether earnings can justify the AI excitement," said Benjamin Cavender of China Market Research Group.

China’s technology rally accelerated after DeepSeek emerged in early 2025, fueling optimism that domestic companies could challenge U.S. counterparts in artificial intelligence.

That optimism has since faded as investors question how quickly companies can turn heavy AI spending into profits.

Tai Hui, Asia-Pacific chief market strategist at JPMorgan Asset Management, said investors want to see how China's tech giants translate their AI spending into earnings, noting that several AI initial public offerings attracted strong initial demand before enthusiasm faded.

However, the challenge extends beyond technology.

China's prolonged property downturn has battered household confidence, while weak consumption continues to weigh on the advertising and e-commerce businesses of major internet platforms.

Vey-Sern Ling, senior equity advisor at Union Bancaire Privée, warned that rising AI investments could further pressure near-term earnings, with longer-term monetization prospects still uncertain.

"Chinese tech stock valuations have reached multi-year lows, which should limit downside, though upside catalysts remain elusive," he said.

The pressure is also evident among China's battery champions.

CATL, a major beneficiary of the global electric-vehicle and energy-storage boom, posted roughly 59% revenue growth in the third quarter, while net profit rose only about 15%.

Competition, shifting product mix and changes to taxes and rebates are squeezing profitability despite its dominant global position.

"CATL's problem is the gap between growth and profitability," Cavender said.

Ling also warned that lower unit profitability could weigh on near-term earnings, even as CATL maintains its global leadership.

The gap between rapid growth and slower profit gains highlights a broader challenge for Chinese technology manufacturers: rapid expansion is not necessarily translating into stronger margins.

Not all Chinese technology stocks face the same pressures.

Brendan Ahern, chief investment officer at KraneShares, noted that Shanghai's STAR Board companies are benefiting from semiconductor spending by Chinese and American tech giants.

Hong Kong-listed stocks, meanwhile, remain more exposed to sluggish domestic consumption, due to their heavier weighting in consumer-facing internet platforms.

Meanwhile, JPMorgan's Hui said China's property downturn remains a fundamental obstacle, with households increasingly parking savings in cash rather than equities.

He nevertheless saw limited downside for broader Chinese benchmarks, citing relatively undemanding valuations and light positioning among international investors.

Some strategists even believe the sell-off may be creating opportunities.

Jason Hsu, chairman and chief investment officer at Rayliant Global Advisors, said the sell-off in Chinese technology stocks has deepened alongside weakness in U.S. equities, as investors grow more skeptical about returns on AI spending.

A recovery in American technology stocks could therefore provide support for Chinese equities.

But cheaper valuations alone may not be enough, according to Cavender, saying that a sustained rebound would require stabilizing earnings, clearer returns on AI spending and stronger domestic demand.

For investors, China's technology sector is no longer about how fast companies can grow, but whether that growth can turn into sustainable profits.

title: Samsung Electronics third-quarter profit in line with estimates amid rising demand for AI memory chips
content:
South Korean tech giantSamsung Electronicson Thursday reported third-quarter operating profit that is broadly in line with analysts' expectations, as demand for advanced memory chips used in artificial intelligence applications continued to grow.

Here are Samsung's third-quarter results compared with LSEG SmartEstimates, which are weighted toward forecasts from analysts who are more consistently accurate:

Samsung's revenue rose 126.88% year-on-year and 13.85% from the previous quarter, while operating profit rose 783.11% from a year earlier.

title: Microsoft profits surge days after announcing major job cuts
content: Image source,Getty ImagesImage caption,Microsoft boss Satya NadellaByOsmond ChiaBusiness reporterPublished29 October 2026, 00:36 GMTUpdated 13 minutes agoTechnology giant Microsoft says its profits for the three months to the end of September jumped to more than $36.6bn (Â£27.5bn), just days after announcing plans to cut its workforce by more than a quarter.On Monday, the Windows developer said it would offer buyouts to around 60,000 of its workers to cut costs as it pours billions of dollars into artificial intelligence (AI).Like other tech firms, Microsoft is investing heavily in the infrastructure that powers AI even as questions remain over whether such huge spending will pay off.Microsoft shares rose by almost 2.9% in after hours trading in New York on Wednesday.The recent financial results of tech companies have been closely watched by investors as they gauge whether the heavy spending on AI is sustainable.Microsoft said on Wednesday that its quarterly revenue rose to $92.3bn - title: Inside India newsletter: New Delhi approves $22 billion in military spending amid China border tensions
content:
Hello, this is Priyanka Salve, writing to you from Singapore.

Welcome to the latest edition of"Inside India"— your one-stop destination for stories and developments from the world's fastest-growing large economy.

India, the world's fifth-largest military spender, shares a contentious relationship with two of its nuclear-armed neighbors — China and Pakistan. Last year, New Delhi carried out military strikes against alleged terrorist infrastructure in Pakistan, and last week an Indian official confirmed some border clashes with China.

As tensions at its borders simmer, India this week announced plans to spend billions of dollars on procuring modern warfare equipment. From whom will it get the goods?

Any thoughts on today's newsletter?Share themwith the team.

The world's second-largest arms importer, India, is pouring billions of dollars into modernizing its military as it seeks to counter the technological advancements of neighboring China, with whom it shares an uneasy peace.

Last week, an Indian military officialsaidthat confrontations with Chinese soldiers were ongoing across several locations along the country's north-eastern border.

Shatrujeet Singh Kapoor, the director general of a division of India's central armed forces, the Indo-Tibetan Border Police, also called China the "biggest adversary" and urged for modernization of defense equipment. "It will be difficult to compete with China using traditional methods," Kapoor said.

Following Kapoor's comments, India approvedspending 2.12 trillion rupees($22 billion) to modernize its defense equipment on Monday. The country plans to spend on long-range kamikaze drones, surveillance and strike systems, counter-drone technologies, short-range air defense, artillery, helicopters and naval platforms.

Experts told CNBC that New Delhi increasingly views Beijing as a threat, especially given the Sino-Pakistan military ties, and the latest purchases were aimed at bridging the technological gap with China.

A spokesperson for India's foreign ministrysaidon Friday that "the situation in the India-China border areas gets disturbed from time to time when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns." Beijing responded, saying it "strictly abides by the relevant agreements and common understandings reached between the two countries."

India's military policies are largely driven by its long-standing conflict with Pakistan, and an "increasing perception of China as a threat," Pieter Wezeman, senior researcher at the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, told CNBC.

According to a SIPRI report earlier this year,61% of Chinese arms exportswere supplied to Pakistan between 2021 and 2025.

India's latest weapons purchases will involve importing components and technology from South Korea for the artillery, engines and avionics from France for the helicopters, and drones from the U.S. and Israel, Wezeman said.

Collaboration with Russia and Japan could also be on the cards, given India's need for a technological upgrade.

Since April, India has greenlighted military spending totaling 3.7 trillion rupees, which is more than 50% of the 6.73 trillion rupee worth of approvals — a 10-year high — in the financial year ended March 2026, Citi said in a report on Tuesday.

While New Delhi has said it plans to procure 82% of the defense equipment from local industries, foreign companies are likely to play a key role in providing technology crucial for military modernization.

Foreign partnerships remain important for technologies that India does not yet produce independently, Arpit Chaturvedi, South Asia advisor at strategic advisory firm Teneo, told CNBC. India relies on imported technologies for specialized components such as aircraft engines, propulsion systems, sensors and electronic subsystems, he explained.

"American, Israeli, and Russian defense manufacturers are likely to find substantial opportunities in India's expanding defense market," through joint ventures, co-production and technology partnerships with Indian companies, Chaturvedi said.

India was the world's second-largest importer of major arms in 2021–25 with an 8.2% share of total global imports, even as its reliance on overseas suppliers dropped by 4% during the same time due to growing local design and production abilities, according to SIPRI.

New Delhi is also the world's fifth-largest military spender, with $92 billion, but this is less than 30% of Chinese military expenditure and around a 10th of America's, Wezeman of SIPRI pointed out.

India faces some practical challenges in matching China's scale of military modernization, but the conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine have shown that mass-produced systems like drones can address asymmetry, Collin Koh Swee Lean, a senior fellow at Singapore's Nanyang Technological University, said.
