title: 'I live with a ghost': Japan's haunted homes attract bargain hunters
content: Image caption,Ryua says that she shares her Tokyo apartment with a ghostByMichael FitzpatrickBusiness reporter,ÂReporting fromTokyoPublished1 hour agoFrom the moment Ryua first walked into her rental apartment in Tokyo she believed it to be haunted."When I visited the place for a viewing there was a man standing there, glaring at me," she says."Since the estate agent couldn't see him, I realised he must be a ghost."While someone more squeamish would probably have quickly left the flat never to return, Ryua chose to go ahead and move in."I'm a bit of a contrarian, so I decided I wanted to become friends with this glaring male ghost," adds Ryua, who works as an aidoru, a young entertainer, and who doesn't wish to share her surname.Four years later, and still in the same apartment, she says she continues to experience paranormal activity on a daily basis. She says she hears endless footsteps and the ghost talking.Image caption,The previous occupant of Ryua's apartment, pictured here, sadly took their own lifeAlthough Japan has increasinglymarked Halloween,externalin recent years, many Japanese people take ghosts seriously all year round. The country has a word, "yuurei", which means a lingering, troubled spirit.These are the ghosts of people who died in violent or tragic circumstances - those who were murdered, killed themselves, or simply were lonely and died alone. If they died at home, then the belief is that their yuurei won't go away.For house hunters who are not superstitious or squeamish it means there are big bargains to be found. There is a whole category of dwellings called jiko bukken, which means "stigmatised" or "incident" properties.Under guidelines issued by the government in 2021, Japanese estate agents must disclose suicide, murder, death by fire, and any death where the body was not discovered for an extended period of time.For rental properties this information must be disclosed for three years, and it must be revealed indefinitely for any property offered for sale.By contrast, in the UK there isno legal requirement,externalto reveal that a person died in a property. And in the US, itdiffers from state to state.,externalFor example, in California you have to reveal if a person has died in the property in the past three years, while in Arizona and Oregon you do not.Ryua was told that a man had killed himself in her apartment. It meant that she gets an almost 30% discount on her rent on her tiny, 25 sq m bedsit in the fashionable ward of Setagaya. She says she pays 45,000 yen ($285; Â£213) a month, instead of what should have been 62,000 yen.While a house where there had been a murder or suicide would probably be harder to sell or rent out anywhere in the world, Tokyo estate agent Erik Oskamp says that Japanese people are particularly superstitious and averse to stigmatised properties."[Even] an apartment next to a cemetery will be difficult to rent out, especially if you can see the tombs from the kitchen," explains Oskamp. "The worst thing is if a suicide has happened in the apartment. Even if somebody has jumped from the roof, many renters will move out. Other issues are a serious crime or a lonely death."The latter issue, that of a person dying alone, would not generally affect the price of a property in, say, the UK or the US.But in rural Kagoshima, in Japan's southwest, it enabled Diane Tincher to buy a large three-bedroom house for about half of what would have otherwise been the asking price.'If there is a ghost I'm thankful to her'The 79-year-old American has lived in Japan for nearly 40 years, working as a tour guide. She says that the estate agent had been straight with her â there was a heavy discount as an elderly lady had died alone, thereby stigmatising the property.Tincher paid 20m yen for the house, in a location where similar properties usually sell for up to 45m yen."I don't believe in ghosts. But I know that the Japanese are very superstitious," she says. "If there is a ghost I'm thankful to her every day... to live in such a splendid and affordable home."Image source,Diane TincherImage caption,Diane Tincher says she got a 50% reduction on her home in rural JapanResearching the house, Tincher had found it on a website called Oshimaland, which lists jiko bukken properties, giving details of the events that occurred. It was launched in 2005 covering Tokyo, before expanding across Japan and then internationally in 2011.It is crowdsourced, meaning that members of the public add the homes and their details.Teru Oshima, the founder of Oshimaland, says that in the past such properties were "not very attractive options" in Japan.Yet as house prices have surged in the country in recent years, as well as a big increase in thewider cost of living,one 2025 survey found that more than half of Japanese people would now rent a jiko bukkenif it was cheap.,externalBack in Setagaya, Ryua says she is happy living with her ghostly flatmate. "I believe that ghosts were once living human beings, so they deserve our respect," she says.For support and more information on any of the topics raised in this article, help is available on theBBC Action Line.Related topicsInternational BusinessWorld of BusinessHalloweenJapanHousing marketMore on this storyThe Sabrina Carpenter clip that helped a 22-year-old make Â£120,000 a yearPublished13 OctoberI paid Â£30,000 for an 'influencer' degree. Here's whyPublished29 SeptemberWe're saving Â£100 a month for our kids but they won't get it until they're 57Published6 OctoberThe grads ditching the UK for a fresh start abroadPublished7 days ago

title: As Waymo expands overseas, it remains a niche cash-burning business
content:
Waymo is dominant in the U.S. and expanding overseas, but it remains immaterial in terms of revenue to parentAlphabet, which is pouring cash into its growth.

In Alphabet'sthird-quarter earnings reporton Wednesday, the company said its Other Bets segment, which includes Waymo, generated $372 million in revenue, up 8% from a year earlier, and accounting for just 0.3% of total sales.

That revenue comes at a steep price. Operating loss in the Other Bets segment widened to $2.05 billion during the quarter from $1.43 billion a year ago. The unit also houses drug design research business Isomorphic, which is using Google's Gemini 4 Argon AI models.

CEOSundar Pichaitouted Waymo's expansion toward the end of his introductory remarks on the earnings call. The company has a commanding lead in the U.S. robotaxi market, where it faces emerging competition fromAmazon'sZoox andTesla. Waymosaidin August that it plans to roll out robotaxi rides in Germany in 2027, marking its third international market and first in the EU.

"Waymo now operates in 15 major U.S. cities and just recently opened up service to the public in San Antonio, San Diego and Tampa with planned expansions into Canada, Germany, Singapore and Spain," Pichai said on the call.

Waymo's steepest competition on the global stage comes fromBaidu'sApollo Go, which is based in China.

For years, Alphabet was able to operate Waymo as a side project while its core online ads business racked up tens of billions of dollars in annual profit and threw off mounds of cash. But with the company now investing heavily in artificial intelligence, free cash flow has turned negative and Wall Street has shown signs of concern.

Alphabet reported an earnings and revenue miss on Wednesday, sending the stock down almost 10% in extended trading. The company maintained its full-year capital expenditures forecast at between $195 billion and $205 billion, largely for AI infrastructure, and reported negative free cash flow of over $9 billion for the quarter.

Earlier this month, Waymo announced that it hadcloseda $5 ‌billion term loan, its first debt financing. In February, the robotaxi businessannouncedthat it had raised $16 billion at a $126 billion valuation in a funding round led by Alphabet that included support from Andreessen Horowitz, Fidelity, T. Rowe Price, Sequoia Capital, Kleiner Perkins and others.

Last week Waymostarted offeringdriverless rides to and from the Las Vegas airport, after previously announcing airport service in five other cities, including San Francisco and Phoenix.

"Waymo is on a great trajectory," Pichai said on Wednesday. "We have now driven more than 300 million fully autonomous miles."

Tesla says on its website that driverless vehicles in its Robotaxi network have completed about 3.8 million miles "unsupervised," or without a human driver at the wheel. CEOElon Musksaid on the company'searnings calllast week that the Robotaxi business should become a "meaningful" revenue contributor by the second half of 2027.

title: Here are five key takeaways from the Fed rate decision and Warsh news conference
content:
TheFederal Reservevoted Wednesday tohold its benchmark interest rate steady. At the press conference that followed, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh disclosed some of his thinking about where the U.S. economy stands, and how that affects monetary policy. But for Fed wonks, the big news may have been Warsh's disclosure of some procedural changes ahead.

"The Fed is leaning into patience. It seems they prefer to wait for more information on the appropriate level of rates, as uncertainty reigns supreme in light of recent geopolitical developments."—Phil Camporeale, chief investment strategist, JPMorgan Wealth Management.

"The Fed has time on its side ... But the direction of travel remains clear. The Fed is still taking back some of last year's rate cuts, and the two dissents underline that tightening bias. We expect a hike in December and another in early 2027." —Seema Shah, chief global strategist, Principal Asset Management.

"We hesitate to characterize his communication as particularly dovish or hawkish ... The bottom line is that the Fed policy reaction is not a black-and-white, binary thing ... The market has adjusted to Warsh's communication style, but there might be a ways to go before they are fully on the same page." —Thomas Simons, chief U.S. economist, Jefferies.

title: Bessent says 'not necessarily' a mistake if the Fed hikes again
content:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Wednesday that further Federal Reserve rate hikes wouldn't necessarily be a mistake.

After CNBC's Brian Sullivan asked if rate increases in the future would constitute a monetary policy error, Bessent responded: "That's not necessarily so."

Bessent's comments came hours after the Fed announced it wouldkeep interest rates unchangedat its October gathering, as the market widely expected.

Bessent is a key confidant of President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly called for lower interest rates. Trump pressured Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh's predeccesor, Jerome Powell, over the issue during Powell's final months at the helm of the central bank.

But Bessent said Wednesday that both he and Trump believe Warsh is doing well and can strike a balance between ensuring full employment and stable prices.

"I think Chair Warsh is off to a great start," Bessent said. "As I often say, I have great confidence in him."

The Fed's decision to hold rates steady came a month after it lifted borrowing costsfor the first time in three years.Fed funds futures traders widely expected the central bank to return to rate hiking when it meets again in December.

Bessent said he would like to see the Fed have an "open mind" about the supply shock from energy prices having a "transitory nature." The U.S. war with Iran has led to a sharp drop in global crude production volumes, in turn leading annual inflation readings to move further from the Fed's target of 2%.

Bessent also said the U.S. efforts to isolate the Iran economy, dubbedOperation Economic Outcast, have been "very successful." He said internal estimates show that Iran's economy could contract by as much as 25% in the span of a year.

When asked about bond yields on artificial-intelligence related debt, the Wall Street veteran said "we monitor" it, but that it didn't need to cause concern.

Bessent specifically referencedneoclouds, a type of company providing specific cloud infrastructure supporting AI that hasrecently struggledin the market.TeslaCEO Elon Muskwarned on Sundaythat more than 200 neocloud firms "are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation."

"I don't think it's problematic at all," Bessent said. "The neoclouds are a small component of the overall ecosystem, and we're still seeing the financing getting done. We're still seeing the deals get done."

Bessent told CNBC he expects the third-quarter GDP data expected Thursday to be "strong." But he clarified that "I haven't seen it yet."

title: 10-year Treasury yield creeps higher even as Fed keeps rates the same
content:
Bond yields moved higher on Wednesday as investors digested the Federal Reserve's decision tohold interest rates steadyat its October meeting.

The10-year Treasury noteyield — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — was more than 3 basis points higher at 5.026%.

The yield on the2-year Treasurynote, which more closely follows short-term Federal Reserve rate decisions, slipped more than 3 basis points to 4.704%.

The yield on longer-dated30-year U.S. Treasury— which tend to move on geopolitical events — was also up by more than 4 basis points to 5.354%.

One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.

Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said the bank remained focused on "price stability" despite the pause and that the employment picture has been "quite positive."

Despite the hold for October, expectations for a 25 basis points hike at the central bank's next meeting on Dec. 9 currently stand at 85.7%, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

More economic data is due Thursday. Personal consumption expenditures index — the Fed's preferred inflation gauge — as well as the quarterly GDP growth rate and personal income and spending data will offer investors additional insights into the domestic economy and inflation picture.

That data will be critical to determining where the Fed may go from here, according to TruStage chief economist Steve Rick.

"Holding rates steady doesn't necessarily mean the Fed is finished raising them, especially if inflation doesn't start to cool," he said. "Policymakers will want to see whether these price pressures are temporary or becoming more widespread throughout the economy."

—CNBC's Alex Harring contributed reporting.

title: Chipotle earnings miss estimates, but same-store sales increase for third straight quarter
content:
Chipotle Mexican Grillon Wednesday reported mixed quarterly results as its restaurant-level operating margin shrank.

Here's what the company reported compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Chipotle reported fiscal third-quarter net income of $339.9 million, or 27 cents per share, down from $382.1 million, or 29 cents per share, a year earlier. The company's restaurant-level operating margin fell from 24.5% to 23.3%.

Excluding restaurant asset impairment charges and stock-based compensation, the company earned 27 cents per share.

Net sales rose 9.6% to $3.29 billion, fueled by the chain's new restaurants. During the quarter, Chipotle opened 84 company-owned restaurants and five international locations run by licensees.

In the second half of July, Chipotle said it started to see sales pull back as diners grew concerned about consuming raw lettuce due to cyclospora, although its own supply was never tied to an outbreak. Then in August, the chain disclosed that it had temporarily pulled jalapenos from Minnesota restaurants after learning its supply was potentially linked to a salmonella outbreak.

Still, the chain was able to report same-store sales growth for its third straight quarter, shaking off last year's traffic woes.

Sales at stores open at least 13 months increased 2.1%, lifted by a 1.3% bump in average check.

For the full year, Chipotle reiterated its previous forecast that its same-store sales will increase by a low single digit percentage. Looking ahead to 2027, the company is projecting that it will open between 340 and 360 new company-owned locations in the U.S. and Canada and around 15 to 25 international restaurants.

title: Bond investor Jeff Gundlach on Fed's rate pause: 'What are you waiting for?'
content:
DoubleLine founderJeff Gundlachtold CNBC's "Closing Bell" on Wednesday that it's unclear why theFederal Reserveis waiting to hike rates further.

"What are you waiting for? You just upgraded the economy right here," he said, referring to Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh's comments about astrong macroeconomic environmentduring the central bank's post-decision news conference. "We're headed to 4% handle headline CPI. The commodity index is rising in a bull market, and I don't understand why the Fed is so reluctant to move."

His comments come after the central bank decided toleave interest rates unchangedat its October meeting.

Following the Fed's decision to hike rates by 25 basis points at its September meeting, Gundlach told CNBC that the central bank should haveraised interest rates by even more. He argued back then that the bank needed to raise rates by 50 basis points, rather than hike them gradually over various meetings.

"I just think that the Fed is a little bit behind the curve right now," he said Wednesday. Gundlach noted that the Fed's 3.75%-4% overnight rate is significantly below that of the2-year Treasurynote, which trades around 4.7%. That is a sign the Fed needs to hike more than it already has, he said.

Despite holding rates steady, there is still an 85% chance the Fed raises interest rates by 25 basis points at its December meeting, according to CME'sFedWatch tool. The Fed said in a statement it will use further information to determine the correct policy to ensure a return to the Fed's inflation goal of 2%, though Warsh at a press conference reiterated future policy decisions can't be determined at this time.

"Absent a crack in the oil price, I think they have to hike in December," Gundlach said.U.S. oil pricescontinued to trade above $100 per barrel on Wednesday.

He also said his investment strategy remains unchanged after the decision, with 30% of his portfolio allocated to equities — where he particularly favors theequal-weight S&P 500to avoid too much exposure to what he calls potential artificial intelligence "problems" — 30% to bonds, 20% toward commodities and 20% in "dry powder."

Warshalso announcedthat one meeting in 2027 and two in 2028 of the scheduled eight Fed gatherings will focus on policy strategy, and no vote on the fed funds rate will take place. Gundlach said the move wasn't surprising, adding he was in favor of having only six rate-setting meetings starting immediately.

"I don't think eight meetings is really necessary," he said. "It seems like they come up really quickly ... at least you have a couple months worth of data to filter in."

title: Dharshini David: Healey buys himself some time, but big questions still unanswered
content: Image source,Getty ImagesImage caption,While earnings are rising, forecasters predict that is not compensating for higher prices and taxesByDharshini DavidDeputy economics editorPublished28 October 2026, 17:32 GMTUpdated 1 hour agoJohn Healey talked of charting a new course for Britain, but this Budget was more about course-correcting than charging down a new path.It was abundantly clear that the financial fallout from that conflict in the Middle East has hampered the finances of households and businesses â and the government's ability to help.While the government targeted those impacted by higher energy and fuel bills, the "breathing space" it aimed to provide was limited; it is a pill that doesn't fully alleviate the pain.The most telling evidence was that official forecasters predict that while earnings will rise, that is not compensating for higher prices and taxes.Even after the extra help is taken into account, households' incomes after inflation and tax are set to be typically lower across the next two years than the start of the parliament. On that basis, it could be the second worse parliament for living standards, after the last one, since the 1950s - a sign of how far the war has blown prosperity off course.But it can't be all be blamed on the war. Taxes haven't helped. Although there were few major measures aimed at households, the policy of previous chancellors of freezing the thresholds at which different rates of tax on income apply - fiscal drag - has been maintained in the background, scooping more money out of pay packets.Overall, this Budget has the tax burden - the proportion of the nation's income going to the tax office - rising to a new historic high of 38.6%However, a more generous package of help would have been hard to pull off. The impact of higher inflation and debt have increased borrowing costs by Â£14bn in the past year alone.The Chancellor had to prove to the markets which lend the government money that he has a plan to bring down future debt to avoid those costs climbing further.As it stands, debt interest repayments are due to be Â£160bn in 2032, more than double the amount spent on schools in England.And the plans Healey has unveiled already eat into wiggle room he has within the public finances. He says he was right to do so - that's what such safety margins are there for - in times of strife. But the great uncertainty that remains made going further very risky. Energy prices remaining high, for example, could easily chew up all the spare cash.So the result was what some have termed a beige, safe Budget. As Healey strove to prove his fiscally sound credentials, there wasn't even the customary rabbit pulled out of the hat, the end-of-speech sweetener.The markets seem reassured â even if some of his tax raising plans involve clamping down on loopholes and those not paying the right tax, which is always highly uncertain.Budget 2026: Key points at a glancePublished4 hours agoYour pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects youPublished4 hours agoSo the chancellor appears to have bought himself some breathing space. But that means some big questions have been postponed until another day, not least on public services.Higher-than-expected inflation may mean that if areas such as health and defence are prioritised, budgets for some other "unprotected" areas â justice and higher education for example â are set to lag behind inflation after 2028.There was a hint too from John Healey that he'd tap into some of those budgets to help out defence spending. To maintain those budgets in 2030 would means finding tens of billions of pounds.And issues around the other big area of spending â welfare â remain unresolved. Between 2025 and 2032, spending there is set to increase by Â£100bn.The official forecasters also noted the rapid rise in sickness and disability caseloads since the start of the pandemic. They warn if that trend continued, spending on such benefits would rise by a further Â£13bn.Any suggestion of welfare reform has been postponed until the forthcoming review into the plight of workless young people.Then there's the issue of boosting growth. There was a bit more detail on the plans for devolution â but there is much to be fleshed out.And on another key part of the growth strategy, housebuilding, there was disappointing news. Even though first-time buyers are set to get more help, their first home may be more elusive.Between regulation and higher costs â in part, related to the war - the OBR estimates that 190,000 fewer homes will be built by 2032 compared to what it thought in March, a significant setback.So the chancellor may have unveiled 98 (relatively small) measures but the to-do list gets longer.With his official forecasters warning that, in a very uncertain world, his finances face exceptional risks, playing a wait-and-see game feels like a prudent move.The risks go both ways: the OBR points out that a swift resolution to the war and an improvement in the economy could spell a significant boost to the public finances.So the chancellor has more reason than most to keep his fingers crossed that happens rapidly.For as it stands, the official forecasters say incomes after inflation, living standards, are set to be only 1% higher at the end of the decade than at the start.A series of economic shocks outside out control could thwart plans to turbo-boost prosperity . And as today shows, breathing space only extends so far.Related topicsUK economyHM TreasuryJohn Healey

title: Elon Musk is a 'real genius', Putin says after satellite talks with SpaceX boss
content: Image source,ReutersImage caption,Russian President Vladimir Putin has promoted the country's own satellite internet project.ByKali Hays,ÂTechnology reporterÂandÂLaura GozziPublished2 hours agoElon Musk is a "real genius", Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Wednesday after revealing the two are in "close" contact about satellite technology.The remarks came during the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, during which Putin discussed Russia's own satellite internet project Rassvet, which provides internet connections to people from satellites."He's a genius, a real genius," Putin said of Musk, according to a translation of his remarks by the BBC. "We are in close contact with our American partners, including Mr. Musk."Starlink is part of Musk's company SpaceX. The company did not respond to a request for comment.Putin added that it was important for Russia to be in contact with Musk so Rassvet and Starlink satellites do not "interfere with each other in orbit"."We and our American partners value this mutually, and despite all the political questions, we are working hard," he said.Starlink has launched roughly 13,000 of its satellites, according to the company. By contrast there are only a couple of dozen Rassvet satellites currently in orbit, according to online satellite trackers.The Russian Embassy in South Africa said on Wednesday Rassvet is "Russia's Starlink alternative" and "marks only the country's first steps in this field"."Russia maintains close contacts with the US on space, including with Elon Musk," the embassy wrote.Putin's comments about Rassvet and Starlink were made as the US and Russia appear to be growing closer, even as it approaches five years since Putin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.Ukrainerelied on Starlinkinternet in its efforts to keep Russia's forces at bay. But its military last week suddenly suffered Starlink connectivity problems, somethingMusk has admittedSpaceX did intentionally.US President Donald Trump earlier this month said he'd struck a deal with Russia toimport dieselin an effort to lower gas prices that have skyrocketed due to the US war with Iran.Then Trumpwaived certain sanctionsagainst Russia that were set to take effect.Not long after, a US citizen wasreleasedfrom Russian custody, with US envoy Steve Witkoff referring to Putin as a "humanitarian".Musk was born in South Africa and then immigrated to Canada before settling in the US. All of his business ventures, including Tesla, SpaceX and Starlink, are based in America, with most operating out of California and Texas.The billionaire, and off and on again trillionaire, has been one of thebiggest political alliesand financiers of Trump and other Republican US politicians.Related topicsElon MuskSpaceXVladimir PutinRussiaUkraineDonald Trump

title: Healey tells departments to make 1% cuts to fund defence
content: Image source,Press AssociationImage caption,Members of the Finnish army and British army on a training exercise on Nato's border with RussiaByKate Whannel,ÂPolitical reporterÂandÂJack Fenwick,ÂPolitical correspondentPublished28 October 2026, 17:32 GMTUpdated 2 hours agoChancellor John Healey has told every government department to find 1% cuts in their capital budgets to fill a Â£4.7bn hole in the funding of the Defence Investment Plan.The reductions come on top of the 1% cuts departments were asked to make earlier this year in order to pay for the initial Â£10.3bn of the plan's overall Â£15bn price tag.The plan boosted defence spending; however the chancellor continues to come under pressure to explain how he will meet a further target of spending 3% of national income on defence by 2030.Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused the chancellor of only offering "a plan to have a plan" adding: "I bet [Vladimir] Putin's really scared now."Setting out his Budget, Healey hinted that meeting that goal would require further cuts, telling MPs it would involve "looking hard at public spending".He said he would set out how the UK would reach the 3% target by 2030, as well as 3.5% of GDP by 2035, at next year's spending review.Government departments have yet to decide what will be cut from their capital budgets.Capital budgets are focused on long-term investments, rather than day-to-day spending. For example, earlier this year, when departments had to make capital budget cuts to fund the initial defence spending rise, a number of major road improvement schemeswere scrapped.Badenoch criticised Healey for not using his Budget to explain how he would boost defence funding to 3%."He is the man who is making our country less safe. He has failed his own test. This is on him, and no one will ever forget," she said.The Conservatives have previously urged the government to pay for defence by making cuts to the welfare budget.Nato secretary general Mark Rutte said the UK was on "a credible path towards meeting the commitment made by all Nato Allies in The Hague - to ensure we're all investing what's needed to remain ready & able to deter aggression and defend our freedom and security".Chair of the Commons defence committee - and Labour MP - Tan Dhesi said "some of the key decisions on defence spending have lamentably been delayed until next year's spending review".He added: "There is a cost to inaction. Investment in our nation's defence and security cannot be kicked into the long grass."Former Nato secretary general Lord Robertson told the BBC the Budget was "pretty good news for defence generally" but warned there would be "battles ahead with the spending departments" to reach the 3% target.Earlier this year, Healeyresigned as defence secretary,accusing the then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer of not providing enough money to keep the UK safe.In a scathing resignation letter, he specifically emphasised his belief in the importance of reaching a 3% target by 2030.Now chancellor, Healey told the House of Commons on Wednesday: "At the spending review next year, I confirm that I will set out the details of how we will meet our Nato commitment to spend 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035, with a target date for 3% in 2030."And today, I am getting work under way to get there in a fiscally sustainable way."In addition to looking at public spending, Healey said he also wanted to use "more innovative financing alongside the private sector and our international allies".The chancellor said this would include:starting treaty negotiations with Finland, Poland and Netherlands to set up a "multilateral defence mechanism" which would allow allies to share resourcesincreasing the amount of private investment in defence through public-private partnershipsdirecting the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank to put Â£5bn into "defence, dual-use technology and sovereign capability"The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates that the UK government's target to increase defence spending to 3.5% of GDP by 2035 will cost Â£35bn.Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said: "Increasing investment in defence companies may contribute to the target but it is unclear how much this will lead to an increase in UK defence capabilities."There is much further to go to get to 3% of GDP on defence and it is hard to believe that this government will want to get there without topping up spending totals."Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back - with Starlink playing a key rolePublished16 OctoberZelensky says Ukraine has right to defend itself after Trump calls latest strikes a 'disgrace'Published16 OctoberBurnham treads carefully with Zelensky visit, balancing Trump and UkrainePublished14 OctoberIn his Budget speech, Healey also announced Â£10bn of economic and military support for Ukraine, in the form of loans and export guarantees.The funding includes Â£5.5bn of loans through World Bank guarantees and a grant contribution to the World Bank International Development Association's crisis facility.A further Â£3bn will be made available to Ukraine through loans facilitated by UK Export Finance, a government export credit agency.Healey told the House of Commons that the week had started with Russia launching a "brutal ballistic missile attack" and that the extra money would send "a clear message to Moscow".He said that when he told the Ukrainian leader about the additional support in a phone call, President Volodymyr Zelensky had said: "You've made my day."Later on social media, Zelensky welcomed the money, saying: "Every step to strengthen Ukraine brings Russia closer to realising that it must end this war of its own making."The money comes on top of the UK's pledge to provide Ukraine with Â£3bn of military support until at least 2030-31.Sign up for our Politics Essential newsletterto keep up with the inner workings of Westminster and beyond.Related topicsJohn HealeyUK defence spendingUK government spending

title: Tax thresholds remain unchanged - here's what it means for your pay
content: Image source,Getty ImagesByLucy HookerBusiness reporterPublished26 November 2025Updated 3 hours agoIncome tax thresholds, which have been frozen under successive chancellors, will stay at current levels until April 2031 as planned. But after that they are expected to start to rise again with inflation.John Healey may not have mentioned the end of this policy in his Budget speech - after all, it is still some way off - but according to the documents released by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) the freeze, which has been shaving additional tax off people's take-home pay for the past five years, is scheduled to end.The proportion of your income that is taken in tax will continue to go up over the next four years in line with decisions made in previous Budgets.But then the personal allowance - the point at which you start to pay tax - and other thresholds, where you tip into paying a higher rate of tax, will rise again with inflation, meaning you keep more of what you earn.Freezing thresholds is often dubbed a stealth tax because, unlike raising the headline rates, it is not as obvious on your payslip.It has been a useful way for chancellors from Rishi Sunak onwards to raise more money to help pay for things like defence, the NHS, schools and support for the sick, disabled and the elderly.The amount of extra money brought in by freezing tax thresholds has risen steadily every year, and is due to reach Â£58bn by 2030-31, more than the UK government spends on transport and not far off current defence spending.Who is affected by frozen thresholds?They hit you hardest if your income is close to one of the tax thresholds, but anyone who gets a pay rise is affected, as long as you earn enough to pay tax. Only people earning under Â£12,570 - the personal allowance threshold - pay no income tax.By 2031 an extra 6.8 million people will be paying tax who wouldn't have if the personal allowance had not been frozen, the OBR calculates.The state pension is currently just below the personal allowance threshold, and pensioners looked set to be drawn into paying tax from next April, when the basic state pension rises to Â£13,036.However, the chancellor is putting in place a new separate Pension Tax Allowance, which will ensure that low-income pensioners, with income up to the value of the full new state pension,will not pay income tax.The personal allowance threshold is set for the whole UK, so people in Scotland will also be affected, although othertax bands there vary,external.National Insurance Contributions (Nics) are levied according to the same thresholds.Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects youPublished4 hours agoBudget 2026: Key points at a glancePublished4 hours agoHow does it work?Wages usually go up year-on-year to cover the rising cost of living. Normally tax thresholds would also be raised in line with rising prices. Currently that isn't happening - the thresholds have been "frozen" at 2021 levels.So, as your pay rises, a bigger proportion of it ends up above the threshold where you start to pay tax.If the personal allowance had risen with inflation over the last five years, you would now be able to take home the first Â£16,070 of your salary without paying any income tax. Instead you pay 20% on anything you earn above Â£12,570.Will I pay the higher rate?As incomes rise, frozen thresholds also mean more and more people are dragged into the higher, 40%, tax bracket.An extra 5.4 million will be higher rate taxpayers by 2031, thanks to the freeze, according to the OBR.If thresholds had risen with inflation you would have had to be earning Â£64,470 this year before you tipped into the higher tax bracket.As it is, with thresholds frozen at 2021 levels, you pay the higher rate on anything you earn over Â£50,271.If you were already earning more than the threshold and you get a pay rise, a bigger proportion of your earnings will be taxed at the higher rate.Almost one in four taxpayers will pay some of their tax at the higher rate by 2031, according to the government's official forecaster.The same principle - that rising income can push you into a new tax bracket - applies to the additional, 45%, rate that is charged on a person's income over Â£125,140.Will I be better off after 2031?Wages have risen sharply to keep up with inflation in recent years, making the impact of the first five years of this policy quite noticeable, and that is set to continue.The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) says if Healey had unfrozen the personal allowance this week, instead of keeping it in place until 2031, basic rate taxpayers would have saved up to Â£198 in tax a year.Higher rate taxpayers would save Â£395 a year.However, for people in the middle of the earnings range, a cut to Nics introduced in 2024 has offset the higher income tax bill.How much of a difference "unfreezing" thresholds will make in four years' time depends on how fast wages are going up at that point.There is no fundamental principle at stake, no point that is the "right" level for tax thresholds. Before the financial crisis the personal allowance was much smaller than today, and it was allowed to grow until the pandemic hit. Even in 2031 you'll be able to take home a bigger proportion of your earnings before income tax than you could back in 2008.Related topicsUK economyTaxIncome taxBudget 2025

title: Fed meeting live updates: No hike expected, but investors watching Warsh for what's next
content:
TheFederal Reserve's interest rate decision Wednesday likely will be short on suspense, with markets expecting the central bank to stay on hold even with inflation tracking well above target.

Markets are pricing in less than a 10% chance that the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee follows up its quarter-percentage-point hike in September with another increase, according to the CME Group'sFedWatchtool.

Assuming that sentiment is correct, it will leave the Fed's benchmark interest rate in a range between 3.75% and 4% — and shift investor attention to Fed ChairmanKevin Warshand whatever clues he chooses to provide in his post-meeting news conference.

Traders expect the Fed to follow up the October skip with a hike at its next meeting in December.

While the Federal Reserve is largely expected to stand pat on its key interest rate on Wednesday, consumer rates have edged higher since policymakers pushed through their first hike last month.

The average 30-year fixed rate mortgage now sits at 7.33%, up from 7.12% last month, according to MND. Mortgage rates are closely tied to movement in the 10-year Treasury yield, which is now just below 5%.

The cost of borrowing against the equity in your dwelling – a home equity loan – has also risen and is now at 8.77%, versus 8.28% in September, according to Bankrate.

Savers have seen some marginal gains in the past month since the Fed lifted its rate by a quarter percentage point in September. The average money market annual yield is now at 0.45%, up one basis point from last month, according to Haver. The annual percentage yield on a five-year certificate of deposit is at 1.83%, up eight basis points from September, per Haver.

Fed funds futures traders now widely expect the central bank to keep rates unchanged today. But that wasn't always the case.

Futures indicate a nearly 93% likelihood that rates are holding steady, according to the latest data from CME's FedWatch tool. A month earlier, traders were forecasting a less than 30% probability of rates staying unchanged.

The market adjusted expectations as Fed officials signaled that the central bank can take its time before making another move.New York Fed President John Williams said "there is no need for urgency" after its September hike, which was the central bank's first in three years.Philip Jefferson, the Fed's vice chair, said members of the central bank would "need to come to our own judgment, which may take more time." Jefferson noted that yields increased following the Fed's September decision, indicating that investors are watching macroeconomic shifts.

The Federal Reserve's decision to raise rates at its last meeting boosted borrowing costs, and the expectation that more rate increases are in the pipeline means consumers are unlikely to see much relief anytime soon. Those elevated borrowing costs are adding to existing affordability challenges, particularly for lower- and middle-income consumers.

As long as the Federal Reserve keeps rates at the current target range of 3.75% to 4%, consumers are unlikely to see much relief. Elevated borrowing costs are adding to existing affordability challenges, particularly for lower- and middle-income consumers.

Higher rates continue to affect credit cards, auto loans and mortgages. Credit card rates have climbed to their highest levels since late 2025, while 30-year mortgage rates have remained above 7%, making homeownership less affordable. Auto loan rates have also stayed near 7%, with even higher rates common in the used-car market.

One bright spot is savings. High-yield savings accounts continue to offer relatively strong returns compared with traditional bank accounts.

Some experts suggest consumers can ease budget pressures by paying down high-interest debt, negotiating better loan terms and taking advantage of higher yields on savings.

The Fed's big problem today is explaining why it's holding rates steady when theinflation ratehas worsened since its last meeting – and several indicators suggest more bad numbers to come.

Start with tomorrow's PCE price index, the Fed's preferred inflation indicator. Both Wall Street and the Fed are able to use the CPI and PPI to pretty much peg the change in the PCE. The headline isexpected to rise 0.5% for September, which will boost the year-over-year rate to 3.7% from 3.4%. The Fed could look past that, assuming it's driven by the continued rise in energy prices. But the core rate is seen rising 0.3%, raising the annual rate by a tenth to 3.1%.

What about the much-touted three-month annualized rate, which many doves have promoted as showing that inflation is under control? It fell to 2.05% last month, almost spot on with the Fed's 2% target. Time to cut, right? Not so fast. Model in a 0.3% rise in the core and the 3-month annualized rate shoots up to 2.7%. The Cleveland Fed's inflation nowcasting gauge sees core PCE in October running at 0.25%. Model that number in and the three-month annualized rate would rise to 3.24% in October. The takeaway: the gauge is so volatile that it serves as a poor guide for monetary policy.

The Cleveland Fed's trimmed mean, which removes extreme price changes from the CPI, has hovered between 2.6% and 2.7% for most of this year, showing little change. The Dallas Fed's trimmed mean has stood mostly alone in supporting a dovish take on inflation at 2.2%. It's worth noting, however, the Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan has herself cautioned that the measure may do too extreme a job of trimming away inflation.

Another problem the Fed faces: a seasonal pattern of inflation spiking up at the beginning of the year. Goldman Sachs sees inflation easing next year as pressures from tariffs, the AI buildout and energy abate. But it worries, "companies could take the opportunity provided by start-of-the-year price increases to pass along their higher costs, resulting in a larger 'January effect.' "

The danger of a hold today amid current inflationary pressures is that the Fed may need to do more in coming months. TD Securities writes: "It only takes one notably bad inflation report and/or a collection of strong labor market data for the market to start pricing larger odds of a 50bp rate increase in upcoming meetings."

Markets were taking a cautious approach ahead of the Fed rate decision, withmajor indexes mostly positiveand Treasury yields also higher.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average is up less than 100 points, while the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq were around the flatine.

In the fixed income market, the benchmark 10-year note added about 3.6 basis points to yield 5.03%, while the 2-year note added 3.7 basis points to 4.774%.

Since Kevin Warsh took over as Fed chairman in May, stocks have generally fallen on Fed meeting days, then posted gains the day after, according to DataTrek Research cofounder Nicholas Colas. The S&P 500 in particular has rallied at least 1% on the three post-meeting days of Warsh's tenure.

The Fed's decision Wednesday follows a string of reports indicating that inflation is reaccelerating.

September'sconsumer price indexshowed annual inflation ticked up to 3.7%, driven byhigher energy costs.The CPI is currently onone of its longest streaksof annual readings above 2% on record.

Theproducer price indexrose to 6.3% year over year in September. It was the steepest 12-month increase since 2022 for the index, which acts as a gauge of inflation on wholesalers.

The Fed won't get the latest from its preferred inflation reading, the personal consumption expenditures price index, until the September number is released Thursday morning. Wall Street economists use CPI and PPI use to estimate PCE, and they expect itto riseas well.

The Federal Reserve is following a different reaction function as it sets monetary policy, according to Stephen Miran, a former chair of the Council of Economic Advisers and governor at the central bank.

"There's a completely new reaction function in town," Miran said Tuesday on CNBC's"Squawk Box."

That new reaction function is "leading them to forecast additional hikes," said Miran, who's now senior strategist at Hudson Bay Capital.

Fed meeting minutes from the September gathering showed officials anticipatedanother increase, but did not signal when. Fed funds futures traders are anticipating the central bank holds rates steady on Wednesday before raising them in December, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

Miran said inflation expectations in financial markets have been "cool as a cucumber" about hitting the Fed's inflation target. He said no one was willing to bet that the Fed was not committed to getting inflation to its 2% target.

Goldman Sachs economists think Fed watchers may be disappointed if they expect any major revelations from Warsh. The firm thinks the Fed has decided to take an every-other-meeting approach to hiking, and Warsh, who disdains providing forward guidance on policy, isn't likely to offer much new insight.

"We do not expect significant new information from the press conference," Goldman economist David Mericle said in a note. "The seemingly strong support for hiking every other meeting means there is likely a high bar to deviate from that plan through the end of the year, which should limit the impact of Fed communication for now."

Moreover, "even if the FOMC decides to change course in the future and wants to communicate this to markets, Warsh's decision not to hint at the slower pace at his September press conference suggests he might prefer to again leave that to others," Me

title: Alphabet set to report Q3 earnings after the bell as shaky AI trade looks for signs of strength
content:
Alphabetis set to report third-quarter results after the bell on Wednesday.

Here's what analysts expect, according to a consensus of estimates compiled by LSEG:

Revenue is expected to increase 25% from a year earlier, which would mark the fastest rate of growth for any period since 2021.

Still, the report arrives at askittish momenton Wall Street, with investors growing more concerned about the costs tied to the artificial intelligence buildout.

Shares of the Google parent have dropped in five of the past six sessions through Tuesday and are down about 7% in October. In July, the companyliftedits full-year forecast for capital expenditures to between $195 billion and $205 billion, up from prior guidance of as much as $190 billion. At the same time, the company reported negative free cash flow for the first time.

For the third quarter, analysts are expecting Alphabet to show capex growth of 130% from a year earlier to $55.2 billion, according to FactSet. Annual capex is expected to top $200 billion before exceeding $300 billion in 2027.

Meanwhile, analysts see negative free cash flow of $2.27 billion in the third quarter, and expect that gulf to widen for each of the next four quarters.

As Google continues to open its wallet to fuel expansion, it's getting rewarded with revenue growth in its cloud division, home to its AI offerings. The company is projected to show cloud growth of 90% to $28.7 billion, as Google continues taking market share from larger rivalsAmazonWeb Services andMicrosoftAzure. Microsoft also reports earnings on Wednesday, followed by Amazon on Thursday.

Google is aggressively adding its Gemini models and services to its enterprise offerings, and is also ramping up sales of its customtensor processing units(TPUs), which compete withNvidia'sgraphics processing units (GPUs). At the same time, Google's core business is under pressure fromOpenAIandAnthropicas well as from a blitz of newagentson the market.

"Google continues to be well-positioned across AI," analysts at Citizens – who recommend buying the stock – wrote in a report last week. "That said, execution risk exists, and we are incrementally cautious on Search as we believe competition is increasing with agents and requires another pivot."

Company executives are scheduled to hold a conference call with analysts at 4:30 p.m. ET.

title: Trump is using tariffs as a 'tool for grift,' Raskin says in demand for donor records
content:
A topHouse Democraton Wednesday accused PresidentDonald Trumpof usingtariffsas a "tool for grift and self-enrichment," pointing to what he says are suspicious import-tax exemptions for industries whose leaders have curried Trump's favor withgiftsanddonations.

"You took care to cut lots of sweetheart deals with corporations and industries that won carve-outs from your tariffs when you saw you could get something good in return," Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., told Trump in a fiery letter obtained first by CNBC.

Raskin, the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee and the former top Democrat onthe House oversight committee, highlighted three such tariff carve-outs — forBrazilian meat,diamondsandsmartphones— that he says "make little to no sense" under the criteria set by the Trump administration.

"They do, however, make sense when factoring in the now world famous Trump Tariff Discount," Raskin wrote, coining a term to describe the president's alleged willingness to cut breaks for his allies and benefactors "when the price is right."

The letter asks Trump to hand over multiple categories of records spanning his second term, including communications between the White House and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, or USTR, related to any form of tariff relief for more than a dozen industries.

It makes a similar request for communications involving private-sector representatives, includingAppleexecutive chairmanTim Cookand Rolex CEO Jean-Frederic Dufour. Raskin asked for those records by Nov. 11.

Raskin's pugnacious letter directly accuses Trump of "profound corruption," asserting that his heavy-handed use of tariffs is really about clinching "levers of power that you could maliciously pull to extract exciting concessions for yourself."

The missive — which cites the Judiciary Committee's "jurisdiction over corruption, conflicts of interest, and effective enforcement of criminal and civil laws" — could offer a preview of how Democrats will flex their oversight powers against Trump should they win majority control of the House or Senate in themidterm election.

Raskin also drew a link between Trump's alleged misuse of tariffs and Americans' affordability concerns, connecting two of voters' top concerns in the final stretch of the election cycle.

"While you have protected your personal investments and crocodile skin connoisseurs from the giant bite of your tariffs, the American people are suffering. Independent analysts expect that your latest round of tariffs will cost an average of $820 per U.S. household this year," he wrote,citing datafrom the nonpartisan Tax Foundation.

The most recentCNBC All-America Economic Surveyfound voters are most concerned about government corruption, followed by high grocery and gas prices. Democratic candidates have deliberately tailored their campaign messaging to make connections between corruption and high costs.

The White House and the USTR did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment on Raskin's letter.

Raskin homed in on the far-reaching tariffs the U.S.imposed in Julyusing Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.

The Trump administration says those duties, which apply to more than 80 countries and cover nearly all U.S. imports, are meant to crack down on foreign forced-labor practices. But Raskin and other critics, including plaintiffs in amajor lawsuitchallenging the tariffs, argue they are actually intended to replace the sweeping "liberation day" duties the Supreme Court struck down in February.

"One could be forgiven for doubting the sincerity of your Administration's sudden concern for the victims of forced labor," Raskin wrote.

He pointed to Trump's decision last year to lift forced-labor-related restrictions on Dominican sugar producer Central Romana, despiteallegationsthat the company's abusive practices persisted.

Central Romana's owner, José Francisco "Pepe" Fanjul,reportedlyhosted a $50 million fundraiser for Trump in 2024, and his family corporation that yeardonated $1 millionto a pro-Trump PAC. He has also beenlisted as a donorto Trump's White House ballroom project.

The USTR only offersexemptionsto the Section 301 tariffs in certain cases, including where additional duties would not help reduce forced-labor practices. But the trade office's exemption list "contains conspicuous —and suspicious — carve-outs for a few industries," Raskin wrote.

Raskin referenced tariff exemptions for beef and bovine products, which took effect despite opposition from U.S. cattle producers whostrongly opposedthe move, citing "the well-documented use of forced labor in the Brazilian cattle sector and the documented surge of Brazilian beef."

In late August, Trumpreportedlymet in the Oval Office with Brazilian billionaire Joesley Batista, co-owner ofJBS, the world's largest meat processor. The next day, Trump announced the U.S. would allow the import of up to300,000 metric tonsof "product for ground beef" below market prices.

"Coincidentally, JBS's U.S. subsidiary, Pilgrim's Pride, made a $5 million donation to your 2024 inaugural fund, the largest donation of any single company!" Raskin wrote.

Diamond jewelry is also exempt from the Section 301 tariffs, which Raskin called "laughably indefensible" becausethe precious stones are identifiedby the U.S. Labor Department as a good produced using forced or child labor.

Raskin suggested the exemption was the result of Belgium's Antwerp World Diamond Centre gifting Trump an opulent gold ring — studded with 321 natural diamonds and 75 other gemstones — in June. The company'spress releaseabout the ring said it was given to Trump as a symbol of "the historic trade relationship between Antwerp and the United States" and in honor of the 250th birthday of the U.S.

"A diamond is truly the President's best friend!" Raskin quipped in his letter.

He also wrote that USTR exempted Chinese smartphones from the Section 301 tariffs, even though "abusive working conditions are a hallmark of smartphone manufacturing, including the Apple iPhone."

He listed multiple examples of Cook's flattery toward Trump, includingreportedlydonating $1 million to Trump's inaugural committee in 2025 and gifting Trump a gold plaque in the Oval Office. Raskin also noted Apple's donation of $25 million to Trump's White House ballroom project, a tie for the largest contribution.

"The exemptions above only scratch the surface of your profound corruption," Raskin wrote.

title: Microsoft earnings will land after the close
content:
Microsoftis set to report quarterly results after the market close on Wednesday.

Here's what analysts are expecting, according to LSEG:

For the fiscal first quarter, which ended on Sept. 30, Microsoft will be reporting under two operating segments for the first time since 1998. For the past 11 years it had three segments that divided up its Azure, Office and Windows businesses.

title: Wendy's shares jump 15% as Nelson Peltz's Trian offers $1.4 billion to buy burger chain
content:
A group of investors led by Nelson Peltz's Trian Fund Management has offered $1.4 billion to buyWendy's, according to a regulatory filing Wednesday.

The group has offered $7.35 per share in cash to take the burger chain private, paying a 20% premium to Tuesday's closing price. In addition to Trian, it includes investment firms BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners, plus Flynn Group, one of Wendy's largest franchisees.

Wendy's shares spiked about 15% in morning trading following the offer.The Wall Street Journal first reportedPeltz's proposal.

Wendy's did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNBC. Trian declined to comment beyond the filing.

The take-private deal offer comes after a tough two-year stretch for the burger chain. Wendy's stock has tumbled 65% over that period, including Wednesday's gains. For six straight quarters, the company has reported same-store sales declines.

Wendy's is scheduled to report its third-quarter earnings before the bell on Nov. 5.

Wendy's challenges have made the company a cheaper acquisition target for Peltz, whose history with the brand dates back to an activist campaign he led more than two decades ago.

Budget-conscious diners have been eating out less often, and Wendy's and its rivals have leaned into discounts to lure consumers into restaurants. Wendy's has also dealt with a revolving door of chief executives, who have had different ideas about turnaround strategies for the struggling chain.

"In our view, a take private makes sense as Wendy's turnaround is likely to be prolonged given the challenged state of the lower income consumer and soft state of the quick service burger category," TD Cowen analyst Andrew Charles wrote in a note to clients on Wednesday.

In May, former Potbelly CEO Bob Wright joined Wendy's as its latest chief executive, after his former employer went private. In his first earnings conference call with analysts in August, he was candid about what he views as the chain's biggest issues, like muddled value offerings, inconsistent execution at its restaurants and too many one-off promotions.

Trian previously explored atakeover of Wendy'sin 2022, but later decided against it. The firm and affiliated parties own a 16.25% stake in Wendy's, according to the regulatory filing, making them the company's largest shareholder.

title: The 'Magnificent Seven' is no more. Time to pick winners and losers as group's correlation breaks down
content:
The "Magnificent Seven" doesn't trade as a monolith anymore, challenging investors to be more discerning when picking through the market's biggest stocks rather than viewing them as a single trade.

CNBC calculated the rolling 60-day correlation of daily returns for each of the 21 unique pairs among the Magnificent Seven — which comprisesAlphabet,Amazon,Apple,Meta Platforms,Microsoft,NvidiaandTesla.

The average of those correlations recently fell to its lowest level in more than a decade, suggesting the group is trading less like a cohesive block than it has historically. This marks a departure for a group that's often discussed together because of its size and influence over the broader market.

The companies "all have different exposures to AI," said Gil Luria, analyst at D.A. Davidson. "This requires a much more granular approach to which of the largest mega-caps an investor wants to own as opposed to just owning them wholesale," he added.

The dislocation has led the group as a whole to lag the broader market. TheRoundhill Magnificent Seven ETF(MAGS) is up 7% year to date, while theS&P 500has gained 12%. Tesla and Meta are the two names in the cohort down in 2026, while Nvidia and Apple are the only ones outperforming the S&P 500.

Microsoft and Alphabet report results after the bell Wednesday. Amazon will post earnings after the close on Thursday.

The growing divergence among the Magnificent Seven reflects investors' deeper focus on companies' "independent fundamental growth drivers," said Thomas DiFazio, ETF strategist at Roundhill Investments. "They have varying levels of success, when you put them in the totem pole of AI winners and losers."

He added that "investors are focusing on the micro factors," such as company-specific news that can signal whether the business can flourish in the AI world.

For Microsoft, the market is watchingAzure's cloud growth. For Meta, it's assessing the potential of itsconsumer AI applications. Apple'sappealis with its devices and services. Meanwhile, Alphabet'ssuccessis tied to its Google Cloud business, its AI model Gemini and its leadership in Search. Close eyes are also on Amazon'scloud business growth, while the market is centered on evaluating thedurability of demandfor Nvidia's chips. For Tesla, it's less aboutelectric vehiclesand more about its pivot to AI, robotics and robotaxis —potentially in a merger withSpaceX.

"These are the best stocks to still be in, but they're starting to kind of separate and go in their own direction," said Jay Woods, chief market strategist at Freedom Capital Markets.

The dispersion within the Magnificent Seven doesn't point to deteriorating fundamentals. Overall, Wall Street remains largely bullish on each individual stock. For Apple, 58% of analysts have a buy or strong buy rating on the stock, according to LSEG. That number is a whopping 97% for Amazon; 92% for Alphabet; 97% on Microsoft; 89% on Meta; 97% on Nvidia; and 50% on Tesla.

Apple illustrates how investors' assessment of AI exposure has shifted.

The iPhone maker, which had been punished for not spending high levels of capital expenditures in the AI arms race, is now being rewarded for it. In 2025, Apple was the second worst-performing Magnificent Seven name, returning 8.9%. Amazon was in last place, gaining 5.2% in 2025. Alphabet was the best performer, delivering 65.8%.

In 2026, however, Apple's 28% gain leads the Mag-7 pack.

"The one stock that got criticized the most over the last two years about not having an AI strategy is now the leader of this cohort, and that is Apple," Woods said.

"They're continuing to hit on what they do best, which is the products and the App Store," Woods explained. To him, Apple is the "consistent tortoise of this race."

D.A. Davidson's Luria described Apple as "the place to hide from the AI trade," while Woods referred to the company as a "technology utility" and a "consumer staple" since its devices and services are embedded into everyday life.

Nvidia has been volatile lately amid concerns about the durability of chip demand and investor anxiety over a pullback in capex spending.

As the biggest stock in the semiconductor sector – and the world – the stock is bound to be subject to massive price swings. The stock peaked on Oct. 6 but since then, shares have fallen by over 13%.

Still, Woods said its valuation is "relatively [and] historically cheap." Right now, the stock is in a "digestion phase." He favors Nvidia's setup, pointing to continued demand for chips.

Alphabet's chart has weakened following its run from March to May, according to Woods, putting greater emphasis on earnings and guidance come Wednesday evening when the company reports its third quarter earnings.

While its search business remains a strength, Woods is watching competition from other AI platforms and whether the stock can gain upward momentum.

Amazon has been "slow and steady," but the stock's trend hasn't been consistent, said Woods. "It's not doing poorly; it's not doing great. It's just there."

The key for the company is its cloud computing business, Amazon Web Services, which deliver a majority of its profits. Revenue from Amazon's cloud segment grew37% year over yearin the second quarter. While growth is solid, it lagged Azure's43% year over yeargrowth last quarter and Google Cloud, which jumped82% year over yearlast quarter.

Meta stock surged in September onexcitementover its new personal AI assistant Muse after App Store downloads were off the charts.

Roundhill's DiFazio noted how investors are keen on how Muse adoption could translate into revenue and profits and credited the new consumer application with potentially helping the stock's trajectory.

But after the Facebook and Instagram parentreportednegative free cash flow while raising the floor of its full-year capital expenditures in its third quarter earnings last week, the stock turned negative over concerns that attracrtive returns on all its capex could be further away.

Microsoft has recovered from earlier concerns about AI disrupting its software business, but now faces a technical test, according to Woods.

"The fears that AI was going to disrupt this thought were definitely overblown," Woods said.

He identified the $530-$550 range as resistance and said that selling pressure could potentially threaten further gains.

DiFazio identified Azure as the growth driver investors are watching.

Upcoming earnings and guidance, set to be delivered on Wednesday evening, can help determine whether the stock can break above that range.

When discussing Magnificent Seven stocks, Tesla "has been left in the dust," Woods said. Tesla's investment case increasingly rests on opportunities beyond electric cars, including robotics, he said.

D.A. Davidson's Luria is also skeptical of its inclusion in the Magnificent Seven, arguing its valuation carries an "Elon premium."

— CNBC'sNick Wellscontributed reporting.

title: Mortgage rates fell for the second straight week, but more borrowers still sought savings in riskier loans
content:
Mortgage rates fell for the second straight week, and that finally brought consumers back to their brokers. A growing share, however, applied for riskier loans at even lower rates.

Total mortgage application volume rose 3.4% last week compared with the previous week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association's seasonally adjusted index.

The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances, $832,750 or less, decreased to 7.37% from 7.41%, with points increasing to 0.76 from 0.75, including the origination fee, for loans with a 20% down payment.

"The decline in rates gave borrowers some relief, with applications rebounding slightly, particularly conventional applications," said Joel Kan, vice president and deputy chief economist at the MBA, in a release. "Mortgage rates are still more than a percentage point higher than the same week last year and most homeowners still have rates much lower than prevailing market rates."

And that is why refinance is still running well behind where it was last year. Applications to refinance a home loan climbed 3% for the week but were 61% lower than the same week one year ago. About half of all borrowers today have a mortgage rate below 4%, according to data from the Federal Housing Finance Agency's National Mortgage Database.

Applications for a mortgage to purchase a home rose 4% for the week but were still 18% lower than the same week one year ago. While mortgage rates have pulled back some in the last few weeks, they are still much higher than they were just a few months ago, and home prices are still rising. Potential homebuyers are also worried about the broader economy, and, anecdotally, some agents say buyers are waiting to see the results of the midterm elections.

CNBC's Property Play with Diana Olick covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, delivered weekly to your inbox.

Subscribe here to get access today.

As borrowers search for savings, more are opting for adjustable-rate mortgages. The ARM share of applications increased to 11.3% last week, the highest level in more than a year. The average contract interest rate for 5/1 ARMs decreased to 6.41% from 6.46%. ARMs are considered riskier because they adjust to whatever the current market rate is at the end of their fixed term.

Mortgage rates haven't moved at all to start this week, according to a separate survey from Mortgage News Daily. That is because there has not been much economic data for the bond market to react to. While the Federal Reserve is not expected to announce any change in its interest rate at Wednesday's meeting, markets could move onany commentary fromFed ChairmanKevin Warsh.

title: At least 30 people reported dead in high-speed Spain train crash
content:
At least 30 people are reported to have been killed in a collision between two trains in the Spanish province of Toledo.

The high-speed trains collided shortly before 9:15 a.m. local time (4:15 a.m. ET), when emergency services were deployed to the scene. It occurred on the Madrid to Seville line, with a stationary vehiclereportedlybeing hit by the other at a speed of over 100 kilometers per hour (62 miles per hour).

Authorities said they would open a local sports hall to provide assistance to those affected, with an Advanced Medical Post being set up at the site of the crash to triage the injured, provide medical care and transfer those requiring further treatment to hospitals. It is currently unclear how many people suffered injuries.

Railway infrastructure manager Adif is investigating the sequence of events surrounding the accident, Spanish news agency EFEreportedon Wednesday.

Adif said in aposton X on Wednesday morning that traffic on the Madrid to Andalucía high-speed line had been interrupted.

Newspaper El Paisreportedthat officials fear the number of confirmed fatalities may rise, with sources telling the outlet that the collision could have a worse outcome than a high-speedcrashin southern Spain that killed 45 people earlier this year.

"We don't have a figure, but it's going to be a major tragedy," Spain's Health Minister Mónica García told a television news station, according to El Pais.

Officials currently do not know for certain what caused the collision, but local reports said initial analyses pointed to human error. Government sources told El Pais that it appeared an Adif operator made a mistake when railway signaling systems failed. The systems are automated, but they rely on manual operation when signals fail.

The trains were operated by AVE and Iryo, according to local media, with at least two carriages said to have fallen down an embankment after the crash. More than 500 passengers were on board the two trains, El Pais said.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said in aposton X that he was "shocked" by the accident.

"Emergency services are working on the ground to assist those affected and ensure their safety, in coordination with all the involved administrations," he said, according to a translation. "My affection, solidarity, and support to all the victims and their families."

Sanchez's political future will betestedin a snap election next month, which he called following widespread unrest over Spain's housing crisis.

Santiago Abascal, leader of the far-right Vox party — which is expected to make gains when Spain goes to the polls — pointed the finger at Sanchez's government over the train accident on Wednesday.

"Tragedy again. Rage again over the neglect, the ruin, and the betrayal suffered by the Spanish people," he said in aposton X.

—CNBC's Charlotte Reed contributed to this article.

title: Google alters its cloud playbook, enlisting partners to sell more AI chips
content:
Googlehas spent years pitching customers on the advantage of buying its chips, models and cloud services in one place, offering a full stack that rivalsAmazonandMicrosofthave tried to replicate.

Now, the company is pushing its equipment outside of its own walls to reach more customers and build a bigger business around artificial intelligence chips, a market thatNvidiahas dominated.

A day ahead of its third-quarter earnings report, Alphabetsaidon Tuesday thatOraclewill offer Google's tensor processing units, or TPUs, the custom chips the internet giant has been developing since2013. It's the first time customers will be able to access TPUs outside of Google's infrastructure, and shows that cloud boss Thomas Kurian, who previously spent more than 20 years at Oracle, is looking elsewhere for growth.

"They're a very strong competitor, and it's very possible that they could eventually take market share from Nvidia," said Chris Ballard, managing director of Check Capital Management, referring to Google's position in chips.

Kurian, whojoined Googlein late 2018, is operating from a position of strength. Analysts expect Google Cloud revenue to jump about 90% from a year earlier, after growing 82% in thesecond quarter, with TPUs contributing to its momentum.

"Google was great at doing its own thing, but it was never able to serve customers," said Uday Cheruvu, a portfolio manager at Harding Loevner, which owns Alphabet shares. "That mindset has changed."

Google opened up TPUs to outside data centers in the second quarter, before this week's announcement with Oracle.

Estimates for the TPU business vary widely, but they all point to significant growth. TD Cowen models $9.4 billion in TPU sales for the second half of this year and $62.5 billion for 2027. Wells Fargo expects about $9 billion in third-quarter sales and $99 billion next year.

CFO Anat Ashkenazi said on the last earnings call in July that only a small portion of TPU revenue from existing agreements will be recognized this year, with the "vast majority" coming in 2027. She also said Google planned to use more outside capacity in the third quarter while the company builds out its own infrastructure.

With $25 billion in second-quarter cloud revenue, Google trailed Amazon Web Services at $42 billion and Microsoft Azure at $29 billion.

But Google is growing the fastest.

"It's almost like the bigger the pie is getting, the faster they're accelerating into it," said Ballard, whose firm owned about $236 million in Alphabet stock as of June 30.

While Kurian aims to get more TPUs into the market by turning to outside partners, he has to balance the benefits of building the customer base with his company's own technology needs.

At aGoldman Sachsconference in September, Kurian said Google's AI servers pay for themselves in under two years, and servers running its own silicon reach payback in roughly half that time.

"It's because we can optimize that whole stack," Kurian said.

Industry research SemiAnalysis estimates that Google's latestIronwood TPUcosts about 44% less to own and operate than an Nvidia GB200 server.

There's also the margin hit that comes with external TPU sales. TD Cowen estimates a 20% operating margin on TPU sales, compared with an overall cloud margin of about 35% last quarter. Cheruvu said he doesn't think Google's cloud operating margin could widen much beyond the mid-30s.

Google's biggest TPU customer is one of its top AI competitors.

Anthropic, whose Claude models compete with Gemini,agreed last Octoberto use up to 1 million TPUsin a deal worth tens of billions of dollars. Mizuho says that agreement brings nearly a gigawatt of capacity online this year and describes the relationship as Google "arming its closest model competitor."

OpenAI is also planning to buy TPUs from Google, CNBC confirmed afterThe Informationfirst reported on the ChatGPT maker's intentions on Tuesday.

Anthropic is getting outside help to finance its Google silicon. This week,Broadcom, which works with Google on TPUs, detailed a $63 billion vehicle backed by Blackstone and three big banks that will buy TPUs and networking gear from Broadcom and lease them to Anthropic for five years. According to analysts from William Blair, the financing plan covers about half of Anthropic's 2027 needs, which suggests more financing is coming.

In itsIPO filingon Monday, Anthropic said it uses silicon from Google, Amazon, Nvidia andAdvanced Micro Devices, allowing the company to "select chips based on the best price-performance and efficiency characteristics for each workload."

Regarding Google and Broadcom, Anthropic said the partnerships "provide us with access to compute capacity powered by Google TPUs across multiple generations of the TPU platform."
