title: Early third-quarter earnings show a 'resilient' U.S. consumer, with signs of strain
content:
One word keeps appearing in third-quarter earnings reports: "resilient."

That's the early read on U.S. consumers from various companies that released their results this week. Many businesses say Americans are still spending despite inflationary pressures, though not every company has enjoyed the same success.

The commentary comes amid fears that diesel fuel prices, which hit anall-time highof $6.52 per gallon in September, woulddrive up prices on consumer products. Economistsalso worriedthat more expensive regular gas, combined with high borrowing costs and continued tension between the U.S. and Iran, would spur a pullback in consumer spending.

Retail salesrose 0.8% in September, following a jump of 1.3% in August. Sales in September were boosted by rising gas station spending. Despite all those challenges, some corporate executives say the headwinds aren't yet affecting sales.

"There's been a lot of noise in the market this year. There's a lot of geopolitical stuff,"Royal CaribbeanChairman and CEO Jason Liberty said on the company's earnings call on Tuesday. "But I look at our business [and our results], and I think that really talks to the resilience of the business, the resilience of the consumer."

Royal Caribbean reported an increase in bookings during its third quarter, whileSherwin-Williams'sCEO said the quarter was evidence of the company's strength.

Here's how companies are reading the consumer in the most recent three-month period:

The food and beverage companybeat analysts' expectationsfor third-quarter earnings and revenue despite what CEO Henrique Braun called an "uneven environment."

Coca-Colareported that North America unit case volume was flat, indicating demand was steady in the face of higher prices. The company's overall unit case volume was helped by higher demand outside of North America.

"The underlying momentum remains quite strong," CFO John Murphy told CNBC. "Consumer sentiment is largely unchanged in the sense that, wherever you are on the income scale, you're looking for value, and I think our system here has done a good job interpreting that."

The company increased its full-year forecast and now expects its comparable earnings per share to grow at least 11%, up from a prior forecast of growth between 9% and 10%.

The cruise company beat Wall Street's expectations for earnings per share and narrowly missed on revenue.

"Our third quarter results reflect continued strong consumer demand for our vacation experiences and the accelerated momentum across our industry leading brands," CEO Liberty said in therelease.

The company reported that the number of guests served in the third quarter increased 9% year over year to 2.7 million vacationers and said booking volumes for 2027 were already "up in the high teens," pacing ahead of historical levels and indicating high travel demand.

"It's not that we don't see points of challenges, but really what we've seen is that even in those points of challenges, the consumer comes roaring back as relates to the vacation experiences," Liberty told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" following the report.

Royal Caribbeanshares closed up more than 5% on Tuesday.

Sherwin-Williams beat analysts' expectations for revenue but fell short of expected earnings per share.

Sherwin-Williams CEO Heidi Petz said in the company'searnings releasethat the paint retailer's performance demonstrated "the resilience of our Company and the strength of our strategy in a challenging demand environment."

"Despite muted underlying market volumes, we continued to win new customers, increase share-of-wallet and deliver sales growth across all three reportable segments," she said.

Net sales increased 7.9% from the same period last year. The company attributed the gain to higher selling prices, but the benefits to profits were partially offset by increased costs of raw materials and supply-chain related expenses.

And the company maintained full-year guidance, saying "customer sentiment and the leading indicators we track point to muted demand over the remainder of the year and into 2027."

UPSbeat Wall Street expectationsfor both earnings per share and revenue in the third quarter.

Revenue in the U.S. rose 4.5% during the period to $14.86 billion.

CEO Carol Tomé told investors on the company's earnings call that consumers remain "resilient" ahead of the holiday season, the company's busiest period. She said the company expects that average daily shipping volume will grow next quarter at a rate consistent with last year. However, fourth-quarter domestic average daily volume will likely fall due to reducing deliveries with Amazon, she said.

UPS has been in the midst of unwinding its partnership with Amazon at the same time it's executing a broad turnaround effort to operate more leanly.

The company raised its full-year forecast for the second quarter in a row, projecting consolidated revenue of approximately $92.6 billion, up from its previous expectations of $91.2 billion.

Shares closed up more than 5% on Tuesday.

Not every company is seeing the same spending trends, however.

Appliance makerWhirlpoolmissed on both the top and bottom lines for its third quarter and cut its full-year revenue guidance.

Net sales in North America fell more than 8% year over year during the period ending on Sept. 30.

Even still, the company cited its own read on "resilience."

"Through disciplined working capital management, we are protecting our year end free cash flow andour balance sheet resilience to navigate challenging market conditions," CFO Roxanne Warner said in theearnings release.

Shares closed up more than 3% on Tuesday.

— CNBC's Amelia Lucas and Laya Neelakandan contributed to this report.

title: Robinhood shares fall 5% as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses
content:
Robinhoodshares fell in after-hours trading as investors digested a mixed third-quarter report in which transaction-based revenue missed Wall Street expectations despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.

Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. It wasn't immediately clear if Robinhood's earnings were comparable with LSEG estimates.

Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.

Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting the focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity.

Robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly important sources of transaction revenue, while the company has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.

Transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million.

Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.

Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.

Net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.

—With reporting from CNBC's Kate Rooney.

title: Speaker Mike Johnson calls election-transfer concerns ‘absurd’
content:
U.S. House SpeakerMike Johnson, R-La., committed to a peaceful postelection transfer of power, calling concerns that PresidentDonald Trumpand congressionalRepublicanscould contest the results ifDemocratswin control ofCongress"absurd."

"We're going to follow the Constitution. The Constitution says when a state certifies the election of members of Congress, then they're administered the oath. That's what I'll be doing on Jan. 3 to everybody who's there," Johnson said Tuesday during a campaign stop with New York Republican Rep.Mike Lawler, one week before theNov. 3 midterm election, in response to a question from MS NOW. "I may not like some of those outcomes, but that's our system. And for anybody to suggest otherwise is absurd."

Democrats and voting rights advocates are bracing for potential challenges if control of the House flips, as iswidely projected to happen, or control changes in the Senate, which ismore closely contested. Republicans have a majority in both chambers of Congress.

Trump, who has continued to falsely claim thatwidespread fraud cost him the 2020 election, has fueled those fears by calling to"nationalize" electionsearlier this year and repeatedly questioning the security of mail voting, while also suggesting noncitizens could vote in large enough numbers to skew results. His administrationsued California on Oct. 15in a fight over noncitizens voting.

The Department of Justice alsosued Alaska on Oct. 22to block the certification of its results in the event of voter confusion. GOP Sen.Dan Sullivanwill appear on the ballot beside Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher whom Republicans have said is on the ballot only asa spoiler candidate.

Johnson, who in the wake of the 2020 election was akey congressional allyof Trump's in his quest to overturn results, on Tuesday said questions about a peaceful transfer were "a little silly."

"Of course we'll have a peaceful transfer of power. But it will not be transferring, because we are going to keep the majority and I'm going to be the speaker of the House and I will keep steady hands at the wheel," Johnson told reporters.

title: AI debt fears ease ahead of Oracle, Alphabet and Amazon updates. Here's what to watch.
content:
Fears over artificial intelligence debt have eased after a bout of volatility. But more tests for AI debt are coming.

Oracle holds its Investor Day on Wednesday. And hyperscalersAlphabetandAmazon.comare scheduled to report quarterly results after the market close on Wednesday and Thursday, respectively.

Credit markets are on edge over a flood of AI debt, though fears have eased up a little lately.Meta Platforms' plans for a$95 billion stock offering, announced on Monday, helped bring down its credit-default swap spreads. Those spreads had risen last week when the company reported negative free cash flow in the third quarter. Other CDS spreads had moved higher too, though they have since backed off.

Investors had expected Meta to bring a large bond deal to market shortly after its earnings announcement, said Richard Cheng, head of Nuveen's investment-grade corporate sector team. The fact that it wasn't announced came as a relief.

"Just the absence of the bond deal itself is a direct catalyst for AI-related spread tightening," he said.

A credit spread is the difference in the yield between the corporate bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. When spreads tighten, it means investors are becoming more confident about the bond issuer.

The market action over the last few days shows that investors are recognizing that "credit fears may have been overblown," said CNBC contributor Paul Meeks, head of technology research at Freedom Capital Markets.

"I expect that these better feelings, maybe not good but better, may continue as companies announce their quarters over the next few weeks."

Still, spreads on CDS remain wider over the past year due to a surge of debt issuance and free cash flows turning negative across the AI space. Meta's CDS spread, for instance, is still up 177% year to date, while Amazon's spread has gained 129%.

Bond yields also remain elevated.

"It's not necessarily fundamentals," said CreditSights analyst Jordan Chalfin. "It's more, I'd say, 80% driven by technicals and sentiment."

Alphabet and Amazon pose the next big hurdle for tech bonds as they update their capex plans and free cash flow forecasts.Microsoft's earnings are also due Wednesday, but the company has yet to issue any bonds to pay for its AI spending.

Both Amazon and Alphabet reported negative free cash flow in the second quarter and analysts expect that trend to have continue.

Analysts expect Alphabet to report free cash flow of -$2.3 billion while spending $55.2 billion on capital expenditures in the third quarter, according to FactSet consensus estimates. Amazon is expected to report -$9.9 billion in free cash flow against capex of $58.7 billion.

S&P Global Ratings estimated in an August report that the hyperscalers will have negative free operating cash flow in 2026 and 2027.

More critical will be their outlooks, Cheng says. "The singular focus on the investors' minds is really what the capex guidance trajectory looks like across the hyperscaler space."

Meeks believes elevated capex is a sign of strong AI demand. The hyperscalers have "decided that with all the evidence they have — and they have more than you and me — that this is worthwhile spending, and not just worthwhile; it's required," he said.

CreditSights' Chalfin doesn't expect the hyperscalers to announce major new bond issuance around their earnings reports. Oracle's updates may be more critical for credit markets. The company has issued $117 billion in long-term debt and is clinging to an investment-grade credit rating of BBB-1, the lowest level of investment grade above junk, according to S&P.

"It's the most important IG tech credit, just given how it's a bit more stressed relative to the A-rated names," he said. "It's trading more like a high-yield credit, even though it's IG, and so there's just a lot of investor concern on that one."

One wrinkle to the AI debt story: balance sheets don't reveal the whole picture. The companies are using complicated off-balance sheet arrangements for data centers and chip financing, and they aren't fully transparent, S&P Global said in a September report.

"There are commitments they are entering into, for example, into data center leases or purchase commitments on chips that aren't necessarily treated as debt," Mark Habib, digital infrastructure sector lead at S&P Global Ratings, said on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" Monday.

S&P is trying to provide the market with more visibility on those commitments "to give a fuller picture of what kinds of obligations they're actually entering into," he added.

Oracle aside, hyperscaler credit ratings are all comfortably above A levels — reflecting the fact that they have broadly diversified revenue streams, ample coverage for interest payments, and capacity to add leverage if they choose.

Nuveen's Cheng isn't concerned, pointing out that while there has been some credit repricing, there is no credit crisis.

"They continue to have exceptional credit profiles, strong cash generation liquidity," he said of the largest hyperscalers.

"The market is really not concerned about credit quality at this point," Cheng added. "It's really just the trajectory of the capex needs and the supply of debt to fund that. Both of those are pointing in one direction — and that's up."

title: Amazon's anti-tokenmaxxing memo says engineers should be pickier about using AI
content:
Amazonlaid out its AI usage guidelines for software engineers in a memo to staffers, and discouraged employees from turning to "tokenmaxxing" in their push to embraceartificial intelligencetools.

Thememo, which was circulated internally in September and posted to the company's website on Tuesday, revises how the company defines the role of software development engineers and managers in the age of AI.

"We're just seeing the beginning of AI's effect on software engineering," the company wrote. "While we have a vision for what the future looks like, there's a lot that's still emerging. We are certain that whatever future best practices are, AI will be at the center of software engineering practice."

Under CEOAndy Jassy, Amazon has rapidly integrated AI across the company's sprawling business operations.Jassyhas previously predicted that AI will "change the scope and speed" of day-to-day work, and potentially shrink its corporate workforce in the next few years through automation, though he's noted it will also create "other jobs."

As employees rush to adopt AI tools, companies have grappled with the technology'ssurging costsand how to reliably measure whether the technology leads to a productivity boost or other valuable returns on investment.

Companies have recently cracked down ontokenmaxxing, in which developers use AI as much as possible with little regard for output. Some companies have set limits on employees' usage of tokens, or the units of data that are processed and generated by AI models, in a bid to slow rising AI bills. Others have switched to cheaper, open-source models for certain tasks.

An Amazon spokesperson said the company hasn't instituted caps on employees' token usage. Amazon in May shut down aninternal leaderboardafter discovering employees were tokenmaxxing to climb the ranks.

In the memo posted Tuesday, Amazon said metrics like token usage, the rate of adoption of AI tools, and code changes or reviews remain "deeply flawed" ways of measuring teams or organizations' AI usage, adding that they can lead to higher costs and too much complexity.

It stopped short of telling staffers to ignore those metrics altogether, however. Token usage and code generation should be considered "with care and judgment" alongside other data, Amazon said.

"We believe that it is best to measure, and be measured by, long-term outcomes," the company wrote.

Marc Brooker, a vice president and distinguished engineer at Amazon Web Services, told CNBC in an interview that the company has looked to metrics such as "feature velocity" to measure how AI is improving engineer productivity.

The metric looks at things like, "how many launches are we doing, how many successful changes are we making in production," he said.

"Broadly, we think about this as a return on investment," Brooker said. "If there is an important problem to solve for our customers, important problem to solve for our business, we're going to invest tools, time, tokens, human effort, etc. into those."

He added, "What we don't want to see is wasted effort where we are going and spending those tokens solving problems that don't matter and sometimes it's hard to know, so we do need to have some appetite for experimentation."

Amazon also discouraged staffers from using AI when it doesn't make sense for a given task.

"If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing," Amazon said in the memo.

The company added, "An engineer who can explain where AI does not yet help their work is demonstrating the judgement we are asking for."

title: Margin debt growth slows sharply as stock market warning signs build
content:
The pace at which investors are borrowing money to invest in stocks has cooled substantially, raising concern that the stock market may be due for a fall.

Recent FINRA data shows the annual growth in margin debt fell to 31.4% in September from 53.7% in May, Bank of America technical strategist Paul Ciana pointed out in a Friday note. Ciana warned that slowing borrowing momentum from extreme levels has been associated with previous market peaks.

May's growth rate in 2026 was the fourth highest since 1998, according to a BofA analysis. The three higher extremes took place in 2000, 2007 and 2021 — all of which preceded stock market declines.

Earlier this year,borrowing was increasing much fasterthan stocks were rising. Analysts view high borrowing levels as a contrarian signal, similar to bull-bear sentiment indicators.

At $1.48 trillion, margin debt in September is 1.5% below June's record of $1.5 trillion.

High leverage can have snowball effects in a market downturn. Lower prices trigger demands for additional collateral or forced sales, which accelerate a downturn.

Individual investors can be hit hard.Teslainvestor Hy Luu, for example, refinanced his home toraise $30,000 to pay down margin debtduring the stock's 2022 decline.

BofA sees other market warning signs, including widening high-yield credit spreads and a rotation toward defensive sectors like healthcare and consumer staples.

Paradoxically, the rotation into those sectors has pushed them to "bubble-risk levels," BofA's equity derivatives team said in a note on Tuesday. Similar shifts occurred in the late 1990s dot-com era and Covid rally, they added. "These dynamics provide further evidence that markets continue to move towards a more bubble-like state."

The bull case is that the midterms could alleviate some of the market's uncertainty and trigger a relief rally, Ciana noted. "Typically, risk assets such as the S&P 500 rebound after midterms unless more severe downside risks materialize."

title: Oracle integrates ChatGPT, Codex into apps and expands cloud chip lineup
content:
Oracleon Tuesday announced an expanded collaboration withOpenAIthat brings theartificial intelligencelab's ChatGPT and Codex into the software maker's applications to make databases more actionable.

Mahesh Thiagarajan, Oracle's president of Cloud Infrastructure, told CNBC at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas that usingChatGPT"allows anybody to build an application, deploy it, manage it."

OpenAI CEOSam Altmanis set to join Oracle co-CEO Clay Magouyrk on stage for an Oracle AI World keynote on Tuesday at 12:40 p.m. ET.

For OpenAI, the announcement represents another example of the frontier lab's push into the enterprise market, just one day after its key competitor,Anthropic, filed itsS-1as it heads toward aninitial public offering.

Oracle's database plays a crucial role in underpinning businesses across healthcare and finance in logging and securing data.

Thiagarajan said his team observed OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra model get trained at Oracle's Stargate data center campus in Abilene, Texas, and could see the real-time benefits.

"More businesses are choosing OpenAI as we make it easier to put AI to work through the tools and systems they already use," said Greg Brockman, president and co-founder of OpenAI, in the press release.

Oracle also said Tuesday that it is making different hardware accessible on its cloud infrastructure, includingGoogle's tensor processing unit AI chips and OpenAI's Jalapeño chip.

"Now customers can actually have infinite possibilities in terms of how they can drive AI," Thiagarajan said.

It is the first time Google's custom chips will run on another hyperscaler's cloud, and illustrates how the companies are increasingly looking for opportunities to get their hardware in the hands of the frontier labs.

Thiagarajan added that the scarcity of chips remains an ongoing issue and that customers like OpenAI can benefit from having different accelerators to choose from. When asked whether this marks a pivot away fromNvidiaGPUs, Thiagarajan said no, adding that Nvidia chips are "the best, most fungible," and that the AI market remains incredibly large.

OpenAI's Jalapeno chip andCerebraswill also run on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The Cerebras deal is material, but the AI chipmaker won't be disclosing the scale because it's in a quiet period, a Cerebras spokesperson said.

Cerebras stock climbed about 8% following the news. Oracle shares were up nearly 5% on Tuesday.

The announcement comes seven months after market-leading cloudAmazonWeb Services announced plans to bring Cerebrashardware into its data centers, a major point of validation.

Thiagarajan also addressed Oracle's multibillion New Mexico data center dubbed Project Jupiter and the ongoing pushback it's receiving from the local community. He said Jupiter represents just one of the 30-40 different data center projects in development, per quarter, for the company.

"We're actually not too worried about what we're doing because I think we're building global infrastructure," he said.

A hearing to address air quality permitting is scheduled for Dec. 7 in Sunland Park, where the controversial data center has already broken ground. The political pushback tied to the project prompted Oracle to deliver a force majeure notice to its backerBlue Owl Capitallast month. Right now, Oracle maintains that the project is on schedule.

Investors are now counting down to Oracle's investor day, where investors will want to see if the company can back its fiscal year 2030 revenue targets and if the margin profile of its cloud deals has changed due to the rising cost of capital.

Bank of Americaanalysts wrote to clients that updates on Oracle's major data center projects are among the topics they expect clarity on at the meeting.

Oracle shares are down more than 30% this year due in part to concerns about how the company plans to finance its ambitious digital infrastructure pipeline.

—CNBC's Jordan Novet contributed to this article

title: Lula’s election win leaves Brazil facing a fiscal tightrope
content:
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's surprise re-election asBrazil's presidenton Sunday prompted a sharp market reaction — and showed the tightrope he must walk between pleasing his grassroots base and nervous investors who could fuel a fiscal crisis.

The country's benchmark stock index tumbled 13.9% on Monday, the sharpest daily decline since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, and theBrazilian realfell nearly 8% against the U.S. dollar, the most since 1999.

The yield on Brazil's 10-year government bond rose 2.46 percentage points to its highest level in more than a decade.

The moves wiped out a rally in Brazilian assets that followedFlávio Bolsonaro, seen as the more market-friendly and fiscally disciplined of the candidates, winning the first-round vote in early October.

Lula, who has been in office since Jan. 1, 2023 and was president before from 2003 to 2011, now faces a host of challenges, including a heavily right-wing Congress opposed to many of his policies andhostility from the White House.

Economic issues will be top of the pile.

Growth is slowingin Latin America's biggest economy, andinflationandinterest ratesare high.

Lula has promised expensive measures that appeal to his grassroots base. Those include protections of existing benefits, minimum-wage increases ahead of inflation, expansions of housing and education support programs, tax cuts on food essentials and a reduction in the country's long working week to 40 hours without pay cuts.

His ability to deliver will "revolve around a central tension," Rafael Ch, senior analyst for Latin America and emerging markets at Signum Global Advisors, said in a note Tuesday.

Voters want "tangible improvements in household finances," and the election result will be seen as an endorsement of higher social spending, Ch said.

But bond markets are already uneasy with Brazil's growing debt-to-GDP ratio, and are likely to demand an ever-higher premium if public spending rises significantly. The Brazilian Treasury on Monday canceled two planned bond auctions scheduled for this week amid concerns over demand and soaring yields.

"Insufficiently funded fiscal expansion could leave the central bank cutting [interest rates] less, offsetting part of the relief Lula hopes to deliver," Ch said.

"We believe Lula will manage this tension through sequencing: reassure markets initially, capture the benefits of monetary easing, and subsequently seek greater fiscal flexibility to deliver his legacy agenda," he added.

Reassurance will come through signals that he is preparing measures to increase the 2027 primary surplus, including a possible constitutional amendment expanding spending freezes, and appointing a market-conscious finance minister, Ch added.

A key question will be whether markets view any fiscal discipline as temporary and whether Lula embarks on a spending spree ahead of the 2030 elections if support for the left falls, Ch said. "Even a limited easing cycle could weaken his commitment to restraint once some of its economic benefits have materialized," he said.

Lula is facing a potential fiscal crisis "largely of his own making," Elizabeth Johnson, managing director of Brazil research at TS Lombard, said on Tuesday.

Johnson also said that market-calming measures should be expected, including the curbing of civil-service benefits, reducing subsidized credit and the presentation of a proposal for a new "sin tax" — on goods such as alcohol and cigarettes — in the coming days.

Meanwhile, the president will rush to approve reforms before the new legislature convenes in February, Johnson said, which "hinges on Lula's willingness to cut spending."

"Our base case is that Lula will advance a modest fiscal reform, helping avert a major fiscal crisis in 2027," Johnson said.

In the short term, Brazilian stocks would nonetheless suffer, according to Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell.

"Who will foot the bill for Lula's proposed welfare spending and debt moratorium for small enterprises remains to be seen, but the 10-year bond yield is likely to rise first and ask questions later, a development that can only serve to make Brazilian equities relatively less attractive," Mould said in a Tuesday note.

Brazil's Ibovespa had been the best-performing major stock market index this year, he said, buoyed by Bolsonaro's expected victory and the country benefiting from higher commodity prices.

The latest decline "in turn may not help wider pan-Latin American indices, which investors can easily access via exchange-traded funds (ETFs). The MSCI Latin America index hit a 12-year high this year, helped by the political rightward swing, which Brazil had been expected to join," Mould said.

title: CNBC Workforce Executive Summit live updates: AI and the future of work
content:
Today's workplace faces a litany of challenges. Whether it's shifting power dynamics between employers and employees, the accelerating impact of artificial intelligence on how we work and the skills we need, or the financial stresses that employees of all ranks are feeling, these issues and more are challenging the cohesion of workplace communities.

To address these issues, CNBC is convening its premiere council of human resource executives in New York City on Tuesday for the annual CNBC Workforce Executive Summit. The event is exclusive to members of CNBC's Workforce Executive Council.

For more about the WEC and to apply for membership,visit www.cnbccouncils.com/wec.

There are many forces changing the workplace. But few are having the impact that AI is, shifting roles and job expectations, as well as headcount.

Microsoft announced this weekthat it is offering voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees, a measure that comes as the company strives to balance a costly AI build-out with efficiency.

The software company has been ramping up its spending on data centers to accommodate high AI computing demand as it supplies cloud services to a number of AI companies. The offer follows a voluntary retirement program announced at Microsoft this past spring and 4,800 jobs cut in July.

American Expresssaid last week that it would be cutting thousands of employees as the leading credit card company prepares for artificial intelligence to take over more of its internal processes.

Amex is eliminating 5% of its global workforce and taking a $336 million restructuring charge, CEO Stephen Squeri told analysts Friday on the company's third-quarterearningscall. The firm had almost 77,000 employees at the end of 2025.

Chief Financial Officer Christophe Le Caillec told CNBC in an interview that the restructuring was to make American Express "leaner, more agile, and also to prepare for AI."

"You don't want to automate processes that are not optimally structured," Le Caillec said. "So what we're doing here is to reduce layers and increase spans of controls, so that we can automate and take advantage of AI in the coming quarters and the coming years."

The Amex announcement reflects a broader trend across financial services, where banks are working to replace repetitive roles with AI automation. On Thursday,Barclays confirmed plansto trim 5,000 jobs — also roughly 5% of its staff — in another tech-driven cost initiative. The moves come even as the sector is enjoying robust profits from growing consumer spending and resilient credit.

Skydance also announced voluntary buyoutsfollowing its $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, a step driven largely by the consolidation, but it also comes asexecutives acknowledge that AI will transform the company.

In addition,Qualcomm cut jobsearlier this month as the company pivots towards AI data centers and non-smartphone markets.

Earlier this month, the New York City Council held a legislative investigation concerning artificial intelligence safety risks, with senior leaders fromAnthropic,OpenAI,GoogleandMetatestifying under oathabout the potential dangers of the technology and outlined current safety measures.

The hearing took place amid the intense debate surrounding the risks posed by advanced AI models. It also came as the questions over who is responsible for keeping the technology in-check also grow.

With concerns over the federal government's oversight of AI abound, cities are stepping up. New York City Council speaker Julie Menin opened that hearing by singling out the federal government's light-touch approach to AI after President Donald Trump signed a voluntary accord withtech leaders in Washingtonlast week.

"The idea that artificial intelligence is going to self-regulate defies all reason," she said at the hearing.

Menin, who is appearing at today's Workforce Executive Summit, told CNBC's Kelly Evans on "The Exchange" following the hearing that one of the biggest takeaways was that the AI labs "really weren't able to answer some of the most rudimentary questions, such as what is the risk of a cataclysmic event happening? What do they feel the risk is? Will they agree, for example, not to release any new model that hasn't passed an internal or third-party validator safety check?"

"I think what really came out of the hearing is the need for regulation," Menin told Evans. "We have to remember that the pharmaceutical industry doesn't self-regulate; they have the FDA. The airline industry doesn't self-regulate; they have the FAA, and similarly, we need to ensure that with artificial intelligence, we have smart safeguard rails in place."

Menin told Evans that much of the responsibility when it comes to legislating AI will fall to localities, and she hopes that some of the legislation New York City is putting into effect will serve as a blueprint for other jurisdictions.

"We certainly hope the federal government will opt to regulate," she said, adding that she sees one of the most important regulations as the issue of third-party regulation. "You cannot have these companies self-select a validator," she said.

Menin added that she does not want to stifle innovation, but cautions that "with innovation, really comes responsibility, and I think it actually instills faith and confidence in the products that these companies are releasing, the new models that they're releasing, if we have smart and sensible safeguards in place."

CNBC has convened workforce leaders and industry experts to discuss the variety of forces changing the workplace.

Here are some of the discussions on today's agenda:

Steve Cadigan,Human Advantage Framework creator and author, is joining CNBC's Leslie Picker for a conversation about how AI is reshaping a workforce ready for change, how leaders can bolster the people skills AI cannot provide and ways to equip employees to successfully adapt and adjust to the rapid pace of change.

Nelson Chai,DailyPay CEO, will join CNBC's Sharon Epperson to discuss the challenges employees face staying financially afloat amid the rising costs of groceries, gas and everyday personal expenses. Chai will share ways employers can help workers deal with ongoing financial strain.

Maren Waggoner,Walmart's chief people officer of digital & associate experience, will speak with CNBC's Leslie Picker about why Walmart is "people-led and tech-powered," why AI is a work design issue and not a technology issue and how talent leaders can ensure that they're not just deploying AItoemployees but rather giving them the ability to use AI to redesign their own work.

Jill Bruning,Amentum chief technology officer andJacob Pat,Lovesac chief technology and digital transformation officer, two members of CNBC's Technology Executive Council, will join CNBC's Susan Caminiti to share their tech-centric perspectives on how companies can harness the power of AI while keeping the human needs of the workforce front and center.

James Lucania,HealthEquity CFO, joins CNBC's Annika Kim Constantino for a discussion on ways CHROs and benefits managers can use AI to streamline healthcare costs, and at the same time, make out-of-pocket payments easier for employees to understand and manage, all while helping each of them get the care they need.

Wes Burke,Care.com CHRO,Kerri Eskin,Cotiviti chief people officer, andAmy Segal,The Team managing director, join CNBC's Sharon Epperson to discuss how AI is redefining what makes a great employee and how they're attracting the right workers in this tech-powered moment.

Julie Menin,New York City Council speaker, recently brought leaders from the biggest AI companies together to answer questions under oath on safety and the risks of things going wrong. She'll join CNBC's Leslie Picker to discuss what cities can do if the federal government fails to act.

Dan Harris,author, podcaster and former ABC News anchor, will join CNBC's Susan Caminiti to discuss how we can turn down the volume on our inner critics, let go of the relentless push to do more and learn to be a little kinder to ourselves while still being effective.

title: Fed expected to hold rates steady, but Warsh may point way to more hikes
content:
Federal Reserve officials enter this week's policy meeting amid a critical debate over what the central bank can, should and will do to address an inflation problem that shows no immediate sign of going away.

When the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee does release its decision Wednesday, markets overwhelmingly expect no change in benchmark interest rates following September'squarter percentage point rate increase.

Investors will be looking closely, though, for clues about future moves from policymakers, and ChairmanKevin Warshin particular.

Brett Ryan, senior U.S. economist at Deutsche Bank, said he'll be watching what Warsh will signal about future policy moves — something the Fed chairman has said he is highly reluctant to do as he seeks to move the central bank away from the "forward guidance" practice of most of the 21st century.

The chairman "is likely to signal that recent inflation data reinforce expectations from the September meeting that further tightening will likely be needed over time," Ryan wrote in a note to clients. "However, skipping October allows officials more time to assess trends in the data."

CNBC survey: Markets expect more rate hikes, but not yet

Recent inflation data has offered little respite from the price pressures that intensified earlier this year.

Theconsumer price index, a widely cited inflation barometer, showed the annual rate at 3.7% in September, driven largely by soaring energy prices. Even stripping out volatile gas and groceries costs, the core CPI pointed to a 2.6% rate — still well above the Fed's 2% mandate and heading in the wrong direction after climbing 0.3 percentage point from August.

At the same time, recent economic data has shown thehousing market strugglingfurther under the pressure ofmortgage ratesabove 7%. The labor market, meanwhile, has settled into alow-fire, low-hirepattern where layoffs are around their lowest levels since the late 1960s, while people out of work struggle to find jobs.

Calibrating policy under current conditions is complicated by Warsh's push for a more mercurial Fed that avoids signaling where policy is heading, preferring for markets to take their own signals from incoming data.

A pause this month could give the Fed more time to assess what impact the prior rate hike had on the economy and financial conditions. However, signaling tighter policy could put more strain on the housing and labor markets. Warsh and his colleagues must show they are prepared to contain inflation while avoiding a premature commitment to how far or how fast rates will rise.

Essentially, the Fed can use its interest rate to influence inflation. It almost certainly will hold off doing so as it evaluates current conditions. Markets and economists, though, are at odds over what it should do.

The chance of a mistake under those circumstances is significant, according to Krishna Guha, head of economics and central bank strategy at Evercore ISI.

"It ought to be possible for Warsh – who is alert to market risks even though he professes not to like mollycoddling investors – to show a calming steady hand," Guha said Monday in a note. "But there is material execution risk."

For instance, the Fed's lack of detail on how it sees the risks to its dual mandate of low inflation and full employment as well as how it views both the pace and tightening of monetary policy poses substantial challenges.

While inflation data has been hot, theunemployment ratehas been fairly steady.

The Fed also weighs financial conditions when figuring policy. TheChicago Fed's index of financial conditionshas shown a slight tightening since the September hike, a product ofstock market volatility, among other factors.

Recent chatter out of key Fed officials, such as Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed President John Williams, points to the likelihood of hikes at every other meeting. But how far the Fed will need to go remains a mystery.

Guha interpretsremarks Warsh gaveto the World Bank and International Monetary Fund in Bangkok recently as aligning "with the central view" on the FOMC. In practice, that's a Fed moving "at a deliberative and methodical baseline pace of once per quarter without prejudice to what it learns along the way and how far it might ultimately have to go and whether at some point later down the line it might need to speed up."

"If inflation continues to disappoint and/or growth momentum fails to moderate, the Fed will add more hikes," he added.

Trading in the fed funds futures market points to about a 10% chance that the FOMC will raise rates this week, but a better than 80% probability of an increase in December, according to the CME Group'sFedWatchtool. The market sees the likelihood of another hike in March 2027, then about a 50-50 chance of a final move before the end of next year.

To be sure, there's considerable debate among economists on whether the Fed should be tightening policy at all. Citigroup economists, for instance, think easing inflation data in the months ahead will give the Fed reason to stay on hold and perhaps begin cutting next year, though the firm is forecasting a hike this December.

Mohamed El-Erian, chief economic advisor at Allianz, said he expects further increases but believes that's a mistake as they will hurt vulnerable areas such as housing and worsen economic disparities.

"My sense is that the market is right in saying that they'll do nothing. [Warsh] will have to package it in quite a hawkish language because the [inflation] data all [have] come hotter than expected," El-Erian said Monday on CNBC's "Squawk Box." "My problem is that it's the wrong policy measure right now."

The solution to worries about inflation and higher Treasury yields should be "fiscal containment, not monetary tightening," he added.

"But we're going to get monetary tightening, and it's going to be what I call the one minus 'X' problem. 'X' is tech; it won't be impacted that much," El-Erian said. "It's going to be the rest of the economy: housing, consumer car loans, consumer loans. That's what's going to be hit."

Correction: Warsh gave remarks to the World Bank and International Monetary Fund in Bangkok. An earlier version misstated the name of one of the organizations.

title: Honda warns 50% Canada auto tariffs would be catastrophic for auto industry
content:
DETROIT — The automotive industry faces a "catastrophic" scenario if the U.S. and Canada cannot reach a new trade deal by the end of this year, an executive withHonda Motorwarned Tuesday.

PresidentDonald Trumphasthreatened to double tariffson Canadian vehicles and parts from 25% to 50% on Jan. 1 if the two countries don't reach a deal.

"That really would be catastrophic for the entire industry," Jennifer Thomas, senior vice president of corporate affairs at American Honda Motor Co., said during a Reuters automotive conference in Detroit.

Thomas said, ideally, the countries would also include Mexico in the arrangement and reach a trilateral deal, like the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, or USMCA. Trade associations representing Honda, as well as every major player in the U.S. automotive industry, have been advocating for that more comprehensive accord and against bilateral arrangements between two countries.

Her comments come months after U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer announced that the U.S. would not automatically extend USMCA, moving the trade pact intoan annual review processinstead of a 16-year trilateral extension.

Trump negotiated USMCA to replacethe North American Free Trade Agreement during his first term and it took effect in 2020. He later soured on it and accused Canada of "ripping off the United States of America for years."

Thomas said she is "cautiously optimistic" that cooler heads will prevail to avoid the doubling of tariffs, which Trump threatened in August if no deal can be reached.

She said she's encouraged by recent reports that the U.S. and Canada have reestablished trade talks, including easing levies on critical materials such as aluminum.

"Our message has been clear: We need that trilateral agreement to stay in place in order for the U.S. industry to be competitive," Thomas said. "It's integral to our success."

Honda is thesecond largest producerof vehicles in Canada behindToyota Motor, but many automotive officials have voiced concerns about the lack of a North American trade deal and tariff uncertainty due to the number of parts that regularly cross the borders for vehicle production.

While Honda has established large operations in Canada, the company reports that more than 60% of the vehicles it sells in the U.S. are manufactured domestically across multiple U.S. assembly plants.

"I never thought I would see the North American region be put at a disadvantage like this," Thomas said, adding that some overseas countries have better tariff rates.

The Trump administration has negotiated trade deals with other countries such as Japan and South Korea, which are major exporters of vehicles to the U.S., that include 15% tariffs on vehicles.

title: Coca-Cola hikes earnings outlook, even as it sees lackluster demand in North America
content:
Coca-Colaon Tuesday raised its full-year outlook for the third straight quarter, despite lackluster demand in its home market.

For the full year, Coke now expects comparable earnings per share to grow at least 11%, up from its prior forecast of an increase in the range of 9% to 10%. The beverage giant also anticipates that its organic revenue will climb at least 5%, a slight increase from its previous outlook of approximately 5% growth.

Shares of the company rose about 1% in premarket trading.

Here's what the company reported compared with what Wall Street analysts surveyed by LSEG were expecting:

Coke reported third-quarter net income attributable to shareholders of $4.01 billion, or 93 cents per share, up from $3.7 billion, or 86 cents per share, a year earlier.

Excluding transaction gains and other items, Coke earned 91 cents per share.

Net sales rose 7% to $13.4 billion.

title: Boeing is set to report earnings before the bell. Here's what Wall Street expects
content:
Boeingis set to update investors on how quickly it can increase aircraft production in the coming months when it reports quarterly results before the market opens Tuesday.

Wall Street is expecting Boeing to post a smaller loss for the quarter than it did last year as it hands over more aircraft to airlines and other customers after years of safety and manufacturing crises. The company posted a net loss of $5.34 billion in the same period in 2025.

But an investor focus is how quickly the company will be able to ramp up production of its planes, including of the best-selling 737 Max.

Boeing has been producing about 47 of its 737 Max planes a month, but is aiming for more. CEO Kelly Ortberg told investors last month thatproductionis taking "a little bit longer" than expected to stabilize, and the company expects to increase its output of the planes next year.

Aircraft production and deliveries are key to Boeing's recovery since the bulk of an aircraft's price is paid when the customer receives it.

Here's what Wall Street analysts are expecting the company to report, according to consensus estimates from LSEG:

The manufacturer had some wins lately. The Federal Aviation Administration last week signed off on the737 Max 10, the largest in the Max family. That followed the approval of the737 Max 7in August and marked the final certifications for the aircraft line.

title: Anthropic's IPO is risky business
content:
Anthropic'smuch-anticipated initial public offering is giving potential investors some perspective on the risky business of artificial intelligence.

More than 90 pages ofAnthropic's IPO prospectus, revealed Monday, center on the AI lab's multitude of corporate risk factors, many of which go beyond the kinds of boilerplate scenarios typically found in corporate filings.

From the end of humanity to the company's current clash with the Trump administration, Anthropic's IPO document underscores how one of the most well-capitalized startups in history foresees the future of its operations.

The Claude maker's risks include a laundry list of ways its models can cause harm, including potentially "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity."

It's imperative for Anthropic to emphasize AI safety because failure to do so could adversely affect its "brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations," the filing said. But fierce competition, market pressure and stakeholder expectations make the task of safely developing and implementing bleeding-edge foundation models particularly challenging.

Anthropic can't guarantee that its AI safety efforts will be adequate, as the technology's inherent complexity makes it difficult for the company to plan for and predict every potential scenario.

The public'ssouring position on data centersposes a major risk for Anthropic, which relies on an ever-expanding portfolio of state-of-the-art computing facilities to train and maintain its prized foundation models.

And with the midterm elections approaching, the tech industry's massive data center buildout has turned political, with lawmakers in 16 states considering moratoriums, according to theNational Conference of State Legislatures.

"Opposition to data center development  has also become more organized and coordinated across jurisdictions and our public profile may draw particular attention to projects associated with us," the filing said.

Anthropic's future success depends not only on building giant data centers, but also on the electrical and related power infrastructure needed to juice those computing facilities.

The lack of "sufficient electrical power" across the nation and world poses big risks to Anthropic and its rivals, the filing notes. Even if energy becomes more readily available through "on-site natural gas-fired generation," that power could becomemore expensivewith so much demand, the filing said.

Rivals like OpenAI andMetahave come under fire from lawmakers and plaintiffs' attorneys over allegations that the design and implementation of their AI models and apps have fostered certain child-safety-related harms. Meta recently agreed to pay roughly$17 billion in a settlementwith multiple state AGs in litigation involving child mental health and technology addiction.

Thus far, Anthropic has largely avoided scrutiny, but the filing noted that the company could potentially face its own legal headaches. Based on its terms of service, minors aren't allowed to access Claude and related products.

Anthropic knows it has work to do protecting children "as adoption of our models grows, including by minors and other vulnerable users, notwithstanding our efforts to restrict such access."

The company calling topace the frontieralso says it's a risk to move too slowly.

Anthropic needs to keep racing and needs the rest of the business world to keep up. If companies curb their AI spending, Anthropic could feel the burn.

"If the market for our models, platform, and applications develops more slowly than we expect or declines, our growth may slow or stall, and our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected," the filing says.

The prospectus also cites reduced demand for frontier models as a risk. Customers might find thatlower-cost modelswork fine for them and that "incremental performance gains at the frontier do not justify the additional cost," instead choosing cheaper, or open-source alternatives.
