title: Man charged with assisting ‘foreign intelligence service’ after incident at UK base used for Iran strikes
content:
The U.K. has said it had charged a man with an offense of assisting a "foreign intelligence service" over an incident at a military base used by the U.S. for strikes on Iran.

Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, has been charged under the country's National Security Act "following an incident involving RAF Fairford," an air base in the west of England,prosecutors announced on Tuesday.

Between Aug. 31 and Sept. 28, Abdulkarim is alleged to have engaged in "conduct that would likely materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out U.K.-related activities", the Crown Prosecution Service added. The foreign country was not named.

Prosecutors also charged 24-year-old Nouman Essghir with "entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK".

The men are due to appear in court in London on Tuesday.

Five people werearrestedon suspicion of explosives and terrorism offenses near RAF Fairford on Sept. 28. The base had been used as the U.S. Air Force's command outpost for operations from Europe and for American strikes on Iranian missile sites.

Announcing the charges, Frank Ferguson, a chief prosecutor for the Crown Prosecution Service's Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division, said that they followed "a Counter Terrorism Policing investigation into a high-profile incident involving RAF Fairford."

"We will continue to work closely with our partners as this complex investigation continues," he said.

After the arrests, U.S. President Donald Trumpsaidthe U.S. had moved its long-range bombers out of the U.K. in response to a threat "linked to Iran."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham told lawmakers earlier this month that the incident was "highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard."

Over the summer, Iran's Revolutionary Guard warned it saw any military base involved in launching airstrikes on Iran as a legitimate target.

Tehran denied any involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford.

title: UPS beats quarterly expectations, raises full-year guidance again
content:
United Parcel Serviceon Tuesday reported third-quarter results that beat Wall Street expectations and raised its full-year guidance.

The guidance raise comes after the company already upped its outlooklast quarter. UPS now said it's projecting full-year consolidated revenue of approximately $92.6 billion, up from its previous expectations of $91.2 billion, as well as fourth-quarter revenue of $25.7 billion.

Shares of UPS rose slightly in premarket trading.

Here's how the company performed in its third quarter, compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

For the quarter ended Sept. 30, UPS reported net income of $1.16 billion, or $1.37 per share, down slightly from net income of $1.31 billion, or $1.55, the year prior. Adjusting for one-time expenses, UPS reported earnings per share of $1.69.

In its domestic segment, the company said it saw a 4.5% increase in revenue, while its international segment saw a 7.1% rise in revenue. Its supply chain solutions business saw an 18.2% revenue increase, which UPS said was primarily driven to growth in forwarding and logistics, includinghealthcare.

The company had previously said it expected its third-quarter domestic revenue to be flat and for domestic average daily volume to fall due to seasonal declines and the glide down withAmazon.

"As momentum builds, we are entering the holiday shipping season from a position of strength, with the most automated and efficient network in our history," CEO Carol Tomé said in a statement.

UPS has been in the midst of a turnaround under Tomé's leadership, working to create a leaner business model and leveraging automation to position the company for growth.

title: Mbappé dropped by major Chinese brands as backlash grows over Mao joke
content: Image source,Getty ImagesImage caption,A backlash has erupted on Chinese social media over MbappÃ©'s comments on a "Chinese dictator"ByKelly NgPublished27 October 2026, 07:15 GMTUpdated 54 minutes agoSeveral Chinese brands have dropped French footballer Kylian MbappÃ© following a backlash over alleged comments referring to the late Chinese leader Mao Zedong.MbappÃ© reportedly told a French talk show The Bridge the meme "that makes me laugh the most, it's the one where there's a video of a guy, I think it's a Chinese dictator..." As he trails off, a meme of his face superimposed on an image resembling Mao appears.It's a play on the Real Madrid forward's nickname - "the dictator" - which he earned because of his huge influence in football. It has become a running joke, and the source of many memes involving MbappÃ©.But the joke did not go down well in China, where Mao is revered by the Communist Party, despite his chaotic and often violent rule that left millions dead.There have been a few people who have come out in support of MbappÃ© on Chinese social media. But theirs is a rare response given China's tightly controlled internet, where people are expected to toe the party and government line on sensitive topics.And few topics are as sensitive as Mao.The BBC has reached out to Mbappe and Real Madrid for comment. The Bridge is hosted by MbappÃ©'s Real Madrid teammate AurÃ©lien TchouamÃ©ni.The original video is not available on the show's YouTube channel, and it's unclear when the interview first aired. In the unverified clips that have been circulating online, MbappÃ© does not identify Mao by name. He says he "uses [the meme] with friends all the time".The furore appeared to kick off on Monday night after Chinese football forum Dongqiudi drew attention to the comments in a statement, saying they were "inappropriate" and "hurt the feelings of Chinese people".Screengrabs of the clip and meme have since spread quickly on Chinese social media, with people echoing this sentiment and even calling for a boycott of both the French striker and his club, Real Madrid.But some have blurred the meme itself as well as the part of the comment they found offensive, when Mbappe refers to "a Chinese dictator".Dongqiudi said in its statement that it was "unable to translate" his comments because they were "offensive to China and the Chinese people".So, many people are also wondering what exactly Mbappe said and have responded to the angry posts and comments with questions, wanting to know more.Image source,WeiboImage caption,Weibo users are recirculating the clip by blurring the meme and redacting references to MaoWhat is the reaction in China?Chinese fans are criticising MbappÃ© â who is popular in China and has huge brand endorsements â of "profiting from the Chinese market yet making remarks that offend the Chinese public"."International public figures, in particular, should show greater respect and sensitivity, as national sentiment must never be taken lightly," reads another comment on Weibo.As the anger online grew louder, Chinese brands began to cut ties, although they did not explicitly refer to the video.The country's largest dairy producer, Mengniu, said it "firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people".Drinks giant Dongpeng issued a similar statement:"Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments."According to state-owned newspaper The Global Times, state broadcaster CCTV's news apps will not feature content related to the French striker. CCTV will also stop showing La Liga matches, Chinese media reported on Tuesday. Real Madrid is one of 20 clubs that play in the Spanish football league and is the most decorated team with 36 league titles.China's foreign ministry has also weighed in, with spokesperson Lin Jian saying: "We have noted the relevant reports. Words and deeds that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with opposition from all sectors of Chinese society."Image source,Getty ImagesImage caption,MbappÃ© has a significant commercial presence in ChinaChina is a major market for international sports stars and homegrown brands have signed multimillion-dollar endorsement contracts with MbappÃ©, Norwegian striker Erling Haaland, and NBA player Stephen Curry.By 14:00 local time on Tuesday, five of the top 10 trending topics on Weibo centered on MbappÃ©, with the hashtag "multiple brands terminate partnerships with MbappÃ©" topping the list."Don't ever come to China," read one of the top comments on Weibo.Why is Mao a sensitive topic?Mao founded the People's Republic of China in 1949 and ruled through tumultuous decades in the 1960s and 1970s.His attempt at rapid industrialisation, which he called the Great Leap Forward, led to a famine that killed tens of millions. Then came the Cultural Revolution: a violent purge of anyone seen as a threat to Communism, which included Chinese intellectuals, landowners, artists and often rivals within the Party.His death in 1976 brought a new era for China, which began to open its doors to the global economy. Even as the country moved away from Mao's rule, he continued to be hailed by the party as a national icon whose legacy was beyond reproach.So jokes or memes about Mao are seen not just as an insult to the party but also its closely-guarded narrative about the country's past.It's unclear when the MbappÃ© meme involving Mao began but his nickname, "the dictator", has made the striker the subject of many memes and jokes online.In 2024, he sued a French influencer and kebab shop owner for using his name in the description of one of the shop's sandwiches, leading to more jokes about the nickname.France teammate Ousmane Dembele jumped on the trend during the 2026 World Cup, calling MbappÃ© Mobut â a reference to Mobutu Sese Seko, the dictator who ruled the Democratic Republic of Congo, formerly Zaire, for three decades.In an interview with France Football in September, MbappÃ© acknowledged the light-heartedness behind many of these memes, but said they "sometimes reveal a lack of political and human awareness among people"."There's a side that's a bit less funny, because we know the damage people like that have caused throughout history," he said."Being compared to people who murder others, or who have made millions upon millions of people miserable... I don't think I've done that in my life."Additional reporting by Fan Wang and Osmond ChiaRelated topicsChina

title: Melania Trump-brokered local ceasefire begins as Russia continues attacks on Ukraine
content:
As a ceasefire brokered by First Lady Melania Trump took effect in a city in southern Ukraine, Russia continued pounding Ukraine's cities overnight.

The local ceasefire, due to last until Saturday in Russia-occupied Oleshky near the Crimean Peninsula, began at 3:00 a.m. local time to permit humanitarian aid to reach the city's inhabitants who are stranded amid shortages of food, water, and medicines.

But it came as Kyiv reported Russian ballistic missile and drone attacks targeting some of Ukraine's biggest cities overnight.

As many as 16 ballistic missiles and 280 drones were launched by Russia, resulting in casualties, Ukrainian PresidentVolodymyr Zelenskyysaid early Tuesday.

"Almost everywhere, Russia's targets were the energy sector, logistics, and ordinary urban infrastructure," Zelenskyy said.

"Strikes are taking place every day. Russia is constantly taking new steps toward escalation."

The developments come ahead of a new round of trilateral peace talks between Ukraine, Russia and the U.S.

Following avisit to Europe by U.S. special envoy Steve Witkofffor separate talks with Zelenskyy and Putin, the leaders emphasized that they wereopen to negotiations, but security guarantees were essential.

Bloomberg reported Tuesday that Putin is preparing for talks with the leaders of neighboring Finland and Norway to discuss a possible peace agreement, citing people familiar with the matter. Talks, which would be held over the phone, may happen as soon as Tuesday, the report said.

title: Nvidia to invest $3 billion in Meta as tech giants deepen AI partnership
content:
Nvidiahas said it will invest $3 billion inMetaafter the social media and AI giant announced plans to raise $95 billion to support its investments in artificial intelligence infrastructure.

Meta on Monday said it wouldinitially raise $35 billionin underwritten public equity offerings, before raising an additional $60 billion with an at-the-market program.

The announcement said Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices, andBroadcomwere interested in purchasing up to $5 billion in shares.

Nvidia announced its investment on Tuesday, adding that Meta would expand Vera Rubin and Vera CPU deployment, and that the two companies would deepen their partnership on Muse, the social media giant's AI agent that launched last month.

"AI agents represent a new computing paradigm — software that understands our goals, reasons, uses tools and gets work done on our behalf," said Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in a statement.

"This changes how we use computers, from operating applications to working with intelligent agents."

"We're excited to keep working with NVIDIA to deliver the best personal agents and frontier models for billions of people," said Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

Both companies' shares were flat in premarket trading on Tuesday.

Nvidia has been rapidly building up stakes in companies powering the AI boom, investing in OpenAI, Anthropic, Intel and XAI.

The chip giant has participated in 121 investment rounds so far this year, according to Dealroom, up from just 13 in 2022.

title: Rise in sales of radios and tinned foods, say retailers, after call to stock up
content: Figure caption,UK prepper stores see massive sales following government campaignByNicholas Watt,ÂPolitical editor, NewsnightÂandÂBernadette KehoePublished27 October 2026, 03:48 GMTUpdated 4 hours agoSome retailers have seen a dramatic increase in sales of essential goods after the government called for people to stock up in case of a crisis, according to figures obtained by Newsnight.The Iceland supermarket chain said it was "clear" consumers had listened to warnings after it saw a 40% increase in sales of tinned products over the weekend.The rise in sales cameafter Defence Secretary Wes Streeting saidthat people should stockpile goods to prepare for an emergency such as a cyber attack or an extreme weather event.Robert Dyas reported a 160% increase in sales of radios compared with last week, while Maplin said sales had increased by 92% in radios, 284% in torches and 106% in power banks.The Maplin figures cover the period since the government's announcement last week compared with the same period last month."Within hours of the Be Ready announcement we saw people reach for the basics - a torch, a wind-up radio, a power bank. Torch sales nearly quadrupled and radio sales almost doubled in three days," said Ollie Marshall, managing director at Maplin."These are simple, affordable products that keep a household connected and informed when the power goes out, and it's encouraging to see people taking the advice seriously."On 22 October, Streeting said that people should ensure they have three litres of water per person per day; tinned goods in the cupboard; baby food; battery powered torches and mobile phone charging packs.Many of the items cited by Streeting appeared in the list of goods gathered by Newsnight whose sales have shot up.In response to the increase in retail sales of certain items, the defence secretary told Newsnight: "It's encouraging that people are taking practical steps to be ready. Having a few everyday essentials at home, from tinned food to torches, helps households prepare for disruption, whether that's flooding, power cuts or burst pipes. We can all play our part in making Britain more resilient."An Iceland spokesperson told the BBC programme: "It's clear consumers have listened to the government's message as we have seen a 40% increase in sales of tinned products over the weekend and strong sales of bottled water too. Our supplies of these products remain healthy."Image source,Getty ImagesImage caption,Sales of torches and radio have risen sharply for some UK retailersNewsnight also spoke to independent retailers who reported a spike in sales of goods highlighted by the defence secretary.Josh Pringle, from Sgt Prepper's online store, said his sales had increased tenfold: "We were a small outfit on Wednesday. And then the government launched the Be Ready campaign and we couldn't believe what we were seeing â order after order after order. Most of them were for a wind-up radio."Lincoln Miles, founder of Preppers Shop UK, told Newsnight of a 650% increase in sales after the government announcement. "Everything about off grid seems to be the key of what people are buying for the minute."Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day.Sign up here.Related topicsWes StreetingStockpilingAndy BurnhamMore on this storyWhy should I stockpile and what will I need?Published3 days agoBurnham suggests stocking up on tinned food and bottled waterPublished3 days agoPrepare for supply chain disruption from cyber or climate emergencies, Streeting warnsPublished4 days ago

title: Oil falls as renewed diplomatic efforts to end Mideast conflict ease supply concerns
content:
Oil prices fell Tuesday as renewed diplomatic efforts to end the U.S.-Iran war raise hopes of a de-escalation in the wider regional conflict that has seen Tehran-backed Houthis target Saudi Arabia.

Futures for international benchmarkBrent crudefor December delivery slipped 0.87% to $114.80 a barrel. U.S.West Texas Intermediate futuresfor June declined 0.86% to $100.88 per barrel.

The pullback followed talks between Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan and Iranian officials in Tehran on Monday, as they stepped up efforts to defuse tensions across the Middle East.

Riyadh said the discussions were aimed at keeping diplomatic channels open and preventing another escalation in hostilities. The four countries agreed to continue to engage to advance regional peace and security, according to Iranian state media.

The diplomatic push comes as U.S. President Donald Trump said in an interview with Fox News on Sunday that he was approaching a decision on whether to strike a deal with Iran or intensify military operations, suggesting that additional attacks remained an option.

Representatives from Qatar, which has helped mediate negotiations between Washington and Tehran, also traveled to the Iranian capital on Sunday, Reutersreported.

Prospects of a diplomatic breakthrough have helped temper fears of further disruptions to global energy supplies, putting downward pressure on crude prices.

Still, losses remained limited as the prospect of a lasting resolution appeared fragile, with Iran-backed Houthi militants continuing their attacks on Saudi Arabia over the weekend.

—CNBC's Justina Lee contributed to the report.

title: Morningstar CEO Kunal Kapoor on making career choices that help you grow
content:
Kunal Kapoor faced a choice early in his career: accept a higher-paid job in banking or join a little-known investment research firm called Morningstar.

Despite encouragement from those closest to him to take the more secure option, Kapoor trusted his instincts and chose Morningstar. Nearly three decades later, he's still there — having risen through the ranks to become CEO.

In the latest episode ofExecutive Decisions, Kapoor tells CNBC's Steve Sedgwick why he believes it's important to find opportunities for personal growth, how his approach to leadership has evolved and what he learned from hiring mistakes earlier in his career.

He also discusses Morningstar's expansion into private markets, the challenges of leading through technological change and why AI is forcing businesses to rethink how they operate.

Subscribe to Executive Decisions with Steve Sedgwick wherever you get your podcasts.

title: China industrial profits post strongest growth in three months as tech boom widens economic divide
content:
China's industrial profits grew at their strongest pace last month since June, as a boom in manufacturing tied to artificial intelligence offset drag from persistently weak domestic demand.

Profits at large industrial firms rose 14.4% in September from a year earlier, according todata released Tuesday by the National Bureau of Statistics. For the first nine months of this year, industrial profits climbed 15.5%, slightly below the 15.7% rise in the January-September period.

The strength comes as industrial earnings swung to double-digit growth earlier this year, following a modest gain in 2025 after three straight years of declines, helped by Beijing's efforts to curb rampant price wars across sectors and surging demand for AI-related equipment.

The global AI boom and higher commodity prices stemming from the war in Iran have lifted earnings for miners, chipmakers and raw-material suppliers this year, even as downstream manufacturers face rising input costs and weak domestic demand.

The uptick in earnings came as factory-gate prices rose at theirfastest pace since mid-2022, driven by higher energy and raw material prices amid the Middle East conflict.

Earnings growth in high-tech sectors, such as AI and robotics, has been outperforming profits in consumer-related industries, including clothing, autos and furniture, underscoring the increasingly bifurcated momentum in the economy.

NBS Chief Statistician Yu Weining attributed earnings growth mostly to surging profits in electronics and advanced-technology manufacturing sectors. Electronic special materials manufacturers saw profits more than triple, while they jumped 51.7% for semiconductor device equipment makers, as demand for AI computing power and storage over the nine months remained robust.

The buildout of AI computing power and data centers sent profits at optical fiber manufacturers more than sixfold higher, while those at cable makers more than doubled in the January-to-September period from a year earlier, according to Yu.

Raw material producers for copper and aluminum also benefited from rising demand from AI-related and renewable industries, with profits rising nearly 45% over the nine months.

High-tech manufacturing investment and electronics capacity utilization remain resilient, supported by the global AI cycle and domestic policy priorities, said Shena Yue, senior economist at Oxford Economics. Overall investment and industrial utilization are still subdued, she said.

Household demand is the weak link as the property downturn continues to weigh on housing purchases and related durables, Yue said. "China's export strength isn't able to fully offset its domestic weakness," she said.

Consumption remains soft, with retail sales growing 1.1% in September, beating forecasts but only marginally above August's weak reading.

China's economy expanded 4.5% in the third quarter from a year earlier, slightly faster than the previous quarter, taking growth in the first nine months to 4.6%, within the government's full-year target range of 4.5% to 5%.

Beijing has so far held back from major new stimulus for domestic demand, with concerns mounting over local government debt and the benefits of consumer trade-in subsidies fading.

Policymakers see no urgency to act, said Dan Wang, China director at Eurasia Group. Falling prices have raised purchasing power even as deflationary pressure builds, and officials are betting on tech exports to hit this year's growth target, she said.

But the strains are mounting among businesses and consumers. Most manufacturers make "very thin" profits, some even running at a loss, Wang said, while consumers continue to save up instead of spending, at a time when China faces its most severe employment crisis in decades.

Local governments across the country, saddled with debts, are also wary of spending as Beijing works to rein in local debt and excess capacity, Wang said. "A lot of money they should have spent is not spent because the officials are so afraid of being held accountable for new projects that they have approved."

Pessimism over the breadth of businesses' profitability has also gripped Chinese stocks, driving thebenchmark CSI 300 Index into a bear marketlate last week, as a prolonged consumption slump and intense competition have taken a toll on earnings.

title: China and Russia are redrawing Arctic trade. Can Europe fight back?
content:
China and Russia are tightening their grip on Arctic shipping routes, turning the rapidly warming region into a new geopolitical battleground with Europe.

Moscow and Beijing last weekhave agreed to expand freight traffic along Arctic shipping corridors, increase services between their ports and deepen cooperation on building polar vessels.

The agreement came after theEU unveiled a new Arctic strategyaimed at countering growing Russian and Chinese influence in the region.

Although the competing moves underscore how the once-remote region is turning into a strategic prize, analysts said that Europe's ability to challenge the emerging China-Russia partnership remains limited, given Moscow's control over the main shipping corridor and Beijing's growing commercial clout.

That's because Moscow controls the Northern Sea Route, including shipping permits, transit fees and a vast fleet of nuclear icebreakers, while Beijing provides the cargo, vessels and industrial capacity needed to develop the corridor, she added.

Europe, by contrast, has limited icebreaker capacity and Arctic infrastructure, leaving it with little leverage to challenge the partnership despite its position as a major destination market.

The Northern Sea Route offers itself as an increasingly attractive alternative, as Middle East disruptions expose vulnerabilities in established shipping corridors.

Cargo traveling between Asia and Europe through the Northern Sea Route could have its journey shortened to between 18 to 22 days, down approximately 35% from the 28 to 35 day journey through Suez, according to data provided by Fertmax FZCO.

For Moscow, the route offers an opportunity to redirect energy exports toward Asia as Western sanctions constrain its access to European markets, said industry watchers whom CNBC spoke to.

On the other hand, it provides Beijing another trade artery that could reduce reliance on traditional maritime chokepoints.

David Roche, a veteran strategist at Quantum Strategy & Geonomics, said the Arctic's importance lies less in its potential to transform global shipping than in the deepening economic dependence between Russia and China.

"The significance of the arctic route is for Russian energy shipments to China, which will increase China's control over Russia in terms of Russia's dependence on China to sell its energy to compensate for losses of its gas markets in Europe," Roche highlighted.

The EU has acknowledged the growing challenge, highlighting the region's strategic value in its strategy, as mentioned byEU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas last week.

Europe isn't entirely without leverage.

TheEU's new strategycalls for expanding European icebreaker capacity, strengthening maritime surveillance and developing infrastructure linking Arctic trade networks to European markets.

It also proposes a maritime security hub and greater protection for undersea cables, reflecting growing concerns about Russian military activity and threats to critical infrastructure.

Yet those strengths may not be enough to overturn the structural advantages enjoyed by Moscow and Beijing, said experts.

Garcia-Herrero said Europe's leverage largely rests on its position as a major destination market and the presence of large shipping companies that have avoided the Arctic because of environmental and commercial risks.

Europe also faces a strategic dilemma: engaging with the emerging corridor could deepen its reliance on Russian-controlled infrastructure, even as it seeks to reduce Moscow's economic influence.

Fertmax FZCO's former global head of research, Daeijin Lee said Western operators face sanctions, insurance and compliance complications that make the route considerably less attractive than it is for Chinese companies.

"The Arctic gives diversification, not independence," he said.

For all the geopolitical attention, the Arctic remains a marginal player in global shipping.

Roche estimates Arctic trade accounts for roughly 0.3% of global shipping today and could reach about 1% by 2030.

Data from Russian state nuclear corporationRosatomand CNBC calculations based onUN Trade and Development figuressimilarly supports the 0.3% figure, with 37.02 million tonnes of cargo transiting the Northern Sea Route in 2025 compared to the 12.72 billion tonnes of global seaborne trade in 2024.

Only 3.2 million tonnes of that cargo, or less than a tenth, involved vessels transiting the entire route, rather than shipments originating or terminating in the Russian Arctic, according to theCentre for High North Logistics.

But traffic may be picking up, the latest September 2026 CHNL data showed.

The route recorded 104 confirmed transit voyages carrying an estimated 3.7 million tonnes of cargo by the end of September, exceeding the 3.2 million tonnes recorded during the entire 2025 navigation season.

Much of the existing traffic consists of Russian oil, liquefied natural gas and other commodities rather than international container shipments.

However, the route also faces significant commercial hurdles. Ice conditions restrict navigation for much of the year, while specialized vessels, insurance premiums and Russian transit fees can erode savings from shorter voyages.

Matthew Wright, an analyst at Kpler, said the route remains poorly suited to replacing established shipping corridors because operators need reliable, year-round services.

Lee similarly expects the Arctic to develop primarily as a seasonal express route for selected high-value cargo rather than a replacement for Suez.

However, climate change could shift the balance in the long-term.

A study published in theWMU Journal of Maritime Affairsprojected that melting Polar ice could increase the Northern Sea Route's annual transit capacity to between 127 million and 463 million tonnes by 2050.

title: Bank of Japan is expected to hold rates this week — but stay hawkish: CNBC survey
content:
The Bank of Japan is expected to keep the policy rate unchanged at 1.25% at the end of its two-day meeting on Friday, according to a CNBC survey, with the possibility of a hike very much alive in the coming months.All 16 respondents expect the BOJ to stand pat, given the bank raised rates last month to their highest level in 31 years. All respondents said they expect the BOJ to set the stage for a rate hike in December or January next year, as domestic inflation and wages continue to rise.Macroeconomic factors support the BOJ's additional policy tightening, said Homin Lee, senior macro strategist at Lombard Odier. "But there may not be sufficient consensus in the policy board for successive rate hikes given the fragility in the domestic bond market," he added.

Sosuke Nakamura, an economist at Citi Research, said he sees no clear signs of inflation accelerating to a degree that would justify consecutive rate hikes.

Japan's core inflation, excluding fresh foods, for September rose 2.1% from a year earlier, reaching its highest this year as a weak yen raises import costs and elevated energy costs feed through to higher prices, even as government subsidies absorb rising costs of energy for consumers.

Japan'sinflation-adjusted wages rosefor the eighth month in a row in August, climbing 1.5% from a year earlier, according to the most recent government data, signaling potential wage-growth-driven inflation as well.Finance Minister Satsuki Katayamareportedly told lawmakerslast week that Japan was "on the cusp of shifting to a period of sustained inflation driven by rising wages," while acknowledging that higher import costs were also pushing up prices.

The BOJ is expected to declare that its "underlying inflation" target of 2% has been met at this meeting, according to reportsby ReutersandThe Japan Times.

Ryutaro Kimura, senior fixed income strategist at BNP Paribas Asset Management, said he was waiting to see if the BOJ changes its phrasing about inflation in the monetary policy statement this week from "underlying CPI inflation has been approaching 2 percent" to it "has reached 2 percent."As for the yen, nine respondents expect it to trade between 157 and 158 against the greenback over the next one month. Respondents' outlook for the three-month yen target was more scattered, ranging from 150 to 160.

"BOJ normalization, higher domestic yields and shifting institutional flows should gradually narrow the rate differential and pull capital back toward Japan," said Masahiko Loo, senior fixed income strategist at State Street Investment Management. But he added, "Elevated U.S. yields should prevent a straight-line yen rally."

The yen strengthened against the dollar, and Japanese government bond yields fell last week due to safe-haven demand amid a sell-off in AI stocks — a reversal from earlier in the month, when Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's spending plans and a global bond sell-off pressured those assets.Nine respondents said they expect the yield on the benchmark 10-year JGBs to be between 3% and 3.1% by the end of the year, up from the current 2.809%. Seven respondents said they expect the yield on the 30-year JGB to rise to 4% to 4.1% from 3.829% as of Tuesday.That forecast comes as analysts expect the BOJ will resume tightening after an anticipated pause in October.Takuji Aida, chief Japan economist at Credit Agricole, said the next rate hike is likely to happen in January, when the BOJ is scheduled to release its quarterly outlook report that assesses economic activity and prices.Thirteen respondents said they expect a terminal rate, or the level at which the BOJ is expected to stop its tightening cycle, of 1.75% to 2% by around mid-2027.Macroeconomic data shows the policy rate is closer to the neutral level of 2%, the BOJ's inflation target, said Masato Koike, senior economist at SOMPO Institute Plus. But "given the state of the Japanese economy and the need to avoid excessive downward pressure on growth, I expect the BOJ to stop raising rates at around 1.75%," Koike said.

The CNBC survey was conducted from Oct. 14 to 26 among 16 economists and analysts.

— CNBC's Lim Hui Jie and Sri Jegarajah contributed to this report.

title: Stock futures are little changed after Wall Street starts the week on a winning note: Live updates
content:
Stock futures were little changed on Monday night following a winning session on Wall Street, with traders looking ahead to a slew of corporate earnings while the Federal Reserve gets set to begin its two-day policy meeting.

Dow Jones Industrial Average futuresslipped 8 points, or less than 0.1%, whileS&P 500 futureswere marginally lower.Nasdaq-100 futuresadded 0.1%.

In Asia, Japan'sNikkei 225rose 1.7% while the Topix gained 0.4%. South Korea'sKospiadvanced 3.8% and the tech-focused, small-cap Kosdaq gained 2.9%. Australia's benchmarkS&P/ASX 200was 0.32% lower.

Wall Street kicked off the week on a solid note. TheDowclimbed 146.42 points, or 0.3%. TheS&P 500gained 0.7%, while theNasdaq Compositeadvanced 0.8% as tech shares outperformed. The artificial intelligence trade got a boost afterAnthropic filed to go publicat the Nasdaq. This would mark another major tech IPO for 2026, following SpaceX's blockbuster listing in June.

Teslashares advanced more than 5%, whileNvidiaclimbed 2%.MicrosoftandAmazonalso rose on the day.

Those gains come as the artificial intelligence trade has faced pressure from investors worried companies in the space are borrowing too much cash to fund their AI build-outs.

On Tuesday, traders will pore through a deluge of third-quarter earnings reports. Coca-Cola, Robinhood and Boeing are among the companies set to post results. Tech giants Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon are due out later in the week.

The Fed is also set to kick off its latest monetary policy meeting. While the central bank is expected to keep rates unchanged, traders will look for clues on whether another rate hike will take place before year-end.

"If, as expected, there is no change in rates, it will still be interesting to see what the vote is after the swings in the last two meetings," wrote Thomas Block, Washington policy strategist at Fundstrat. "While the Fed views itself above partisan politics, it would be unlikely that the Fed would move rates a week before a national election."

On the economic front, traders will be watching for durable orders, consumer confidence data and the new home sales report.

Asia-Pacific markets traded broadly higher early Tuesday.

Japan'sNikkei 225rose 1.7% while the Topix gained 0.4%. South Korea'sKospiadvanced 3.8% and the tech-focused Kosdaq gained 2.9%.

Australia's benchmarkS&P/ASX 200was 0.32% lower.

Asia-Pacific markets were set to open broadly higher on Tuesday, tracking U.S. stocks that kicked off the week on a solid note with optimism around the Anthropic IPO filing lifting the tech sector.

Futures for Japan'sNikkei 225in Chicago were at 63,060 and their Osaka counterpart last traded at 62,890, compared with the index's previous close of 62,189.65.

Hong Kong'sHang Seng indexfutures were at 23,233, compared with the index's last close of 23,211.81.

Australia'sS&P/ASX 200opened 0.17% lower.

Tensions continue to simmer between the U.S. and Iran. U.S. forces in the Middle East are prepared to start operations against Tehran within 96 hours of an order from Trump,CNNreported.

Whirlpool— The home appliance maker dropped almost 9% after slashing its full-year revenue guidance to $14.5 billion from $15 billion. Revenue in the third quarter also fell short of estimates, coming in at $3.68 billion versus the $3.92 billion LSEG consensus estimate. The company also lost an adjusted 21 cents per share, while analysts expected a profit of 80 cents per share.

JetBlue Airways– The air carrier surged 7% after the company said that it expects further margin expansion in the fourth quarter even as fuel prices are anticipated to be 85% higher than a year earlier. JetBlue reported an adjusted loss of 60 cents a share in the third quarter, compared to the 55-cent loss analysts polled by LSEG had sought. Revenue narrowly missed expectations, as well.

Dow Jones Industrial Average futuresslipped 24 points, or about 0.1%.S&P 500andNasdaq-100 futureshovered around the flatline.

title: From Wall Street to Silicon Valley, Anthropic IPO poised to have massive 'trickle-down effect'
content:
The tech industry needs this to go well. So does Wall Street.

Anthropic'sIPO filingon Monday puts the Claude creator in position to pursue what could be the largest initial stock offering in history. Investors are already measuring the 5-year-old company's potential market cap in the trillions, putting it in a category with the world's most valuable companies.

It's a critical moment for the whole tech sector, as the artificial intelligence boom has been largely driven by two companies: Anthropic and OpenAI. The latter has confidentially filed to go public, but has said adebutlikely won't take place until 2027.

Meanwhile, the stock market is showing signs ofjitterson the AI trade. Neoclouds and data center companies have been getting pummeled, prompting Australia's Firmus to withdraw its IPO plans and forSK Hynix'sU.S.-based Solidigm unit to do the same.

Now, all eyes turn toAnthropic, which is betting that investors will look past over $80 billion in losses in the first half of the year, and see the 14-fold increase in revenue as a reflection of seemingly insatiable demand for the company's leading models and services.

"If it underperforms expectations, it'll be a little bit of a house of cards," said Jai Das, co-founder of Sapphire Ventures whose career in tech investing dates to the 1990s.

Anthropic's business is deeply entwined with tech megacaps. Close to half its revenue comes from Claude being sold through cloud divisions atMicrosoft,AmazonandAlphabet, which all hold investments in the company. In the IPO, some $77 billion in notes can be issued toAmazon,BroadcomandGoogle, whileMicrosoftandNvidiaagreed toinvest $15 billionas the company builds up its computing capacity. Chips from Nvidia,Advanced Micro Devices, Amazon and Google are powering Anthropic's development.

Cloud providers are ratcheting up capital expenditures to meet demand, and memory manufacturers are fighting shortages to prioritize AI chips. And there's the debt factor. Alphabet, with its investment-grade credit rating, committed tobackstopping Anthropicfor a data center in Texas.Broadcom, which helps Google develop chips for AI labs, is creating financing pools to help Anthropic and OpenAI deploy high-performance models, CEO Hock Tan told analysts earlier this year.

For public market investors, more than one-third of the value of the S&P 500 comes from tech's trillion-dollar companies, which are all, to varying degrees, going deep in AI. Beyond that, there are software giants likeAdobeandSalesforcethat have integrated with Anthropic's Claude assistant.

And in the private markets, check sizes have ballooned but IPOs are few and far between. Bessemer Venture Partners and Menlo Ventures both told CNBC that Anthropic is their biggest investment ever.

"If they don't perform well, they will become the bellwether for AI," said Brad Bernstein, a managing partner at growth equity firm FTV Capital. "Their valuation will reflect that performance variation, and then it'll just be a trickle-down effect to all the stuff going on with the excess capital that's getting poured into the venture AI world. Everything is going to have to sort of be reset."

Anthropic will be the third company to go public with a valuation above $1 trillion, after Saudi Aramco andElon Musk'sSpaceX, which debuted in June. OpenAI could be the fourth.

Revenue at Anthropic has been multiplying at a staggering pace as businesses adopt the company's coding and productivity tools. Second-quarter revenue soared to $11.56 billion from $787 million a year earlier.

The company held almost $132 billion in cash, equivalents and short-term investments at the end of June. And after five quarters of operating losses, Anthropic reported $974 million in operating income for the second quarter.

"It is, I think, better than feared," said Rohit Kulkarni, partner and chief AI officer at Burnham Park Capital Markets, referring to the financials. "There could have been more negative tidbits."

One source of concern in some corners of the investing universe is the emergence of so-called open-weight models, which are cheaper for businesses to access and allow for customization and flexibility in terms of where users access the models.

In the prospectus, the only two competitors Anthropic named were OpenAI and Google, though the company said it faces competition from a "broader set of model providers," including open-weight or open-source models.

Anthropic says it's all very early, with Fortune 500 companies committing less than 0.1% of their total expenses to its models and services in the latest quarter. Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager at Founder ETFs, says that's part of the investment thesis.

"I think there's going to be room for frontier models like Anthropic and OpenAI and SpaceX, and I think there will be room for open-weight models," Monaghan said. "It's way too soon to say that one is going to disintermediate the other."

With hyperscaler spending on AI infrastructure set to reach into the trillions of dollars, Sapphire's Das said there's understandable concern about a market glut. But he compares it to the telecommunications and dot-com bubble of the late 1990s, when companies flooded the market with fiber-optic equipment. Eventually, the infrastructure got used, although plenty of companies went belly up in the interim.

"Long term, I don't think there is a lack of demand," Das said.

A lackluster debut could push out OpenAI's offering even further and cause investors to rethink its lofty valuation. At the same time, rising interest rates mean it's getting costlier for companies to raise debt.

David Trainer, CEO of financial research firm New Constructs, wrote in a report last month that the AI boom has been built on the view that cheap credit and access to the capital markets will be "readily available."

"If AI liquidity dries up, and there are clear signs it is, we see large, 20%, downside risk in the S&P 500, with most of that concentrated in the valuation of AI-related stocks," Trainer wrote.

Industry experts take a different approach, focusing on the power and rapid proliferation of the technology. Claude Opus 5.5 Max performs better than any other model on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, anindustry benchmark.

SnowflakeCEO Sridhar Ramaswamy said the technology is only becoming more essential.

"Anthropic and OpenAI have by now demonstrated their ability to stay at the frontier of AI and keep pushing innovation," Ramaswamy said. "They're incredible companies that are doing a big service to humanity by expanding the frontier of what is possible, and we are very much rooting for them to be public and very successful companies."

Still, Snowflake is experimenting with low-cost open-weight models from China's Moonshot AI, DeepSeek and Zhipu.

"We spend a lot on internal AI because we want to get as much efficiency as we can," Ramaswamy said.

end to the so-called cliff-edge for those receiving carer's allowance payments and higher tax-free mileage rates being made permanent.But the Conservatives said the offer of "cheaper gherkins" was "an insult to families hammered by Labour's tax rises".Ahead of the Budget, the government said it is removing tariffs on more than 100 "family favourite" products, while supporting farmers facing higher fertiliser costs and households reliant on heating oil.The government says the changes could save households up to Â£21 per year when combined with existing tariff suspensions on products including pasta, fruit juice and tuna.Healey's Budget needs to sustain the stronger economy through gathering cloudsPublished1 day agoMarmalade, for example, will see a 20% tariff, plus an additional Â£19 charge per 100kg imported, suspended.Healey said the ongoing wars in Iran and Ukraine had "hit families here at home through higher everyday costs"."We can't control global events, but we can act title: Jim Cramer warns this overlooked danger could threaten the market rally
content:
CNBC'sJim Cramerwarned Monday that a wave of massive initial public offerings and capital raises could threaten the bull market.

Anthropic, the company behind Claude,filed its IPO prospectusMonday, moving one of Wall Street's most anticipated public debuts a step closer. Investors have long awaited public offerings from AI leaders Anthropic andOpenAI, but Cramer said that their potentially massive fundraising needs could strain an already crowded market. With$148 billion raisedthrough IPOs so far this year, he fears the influx of new shares could outstrip investor demand and derail the rally.

"Politics can weaken the bull, higher rates can choke it, but if you want to slay the darn thing, use the IPO lance and stab it again and again," the "Mad Money" host said. "It just gets weaker and weaker until it is weak enough to be slaughtered with the ease of a bad quarter, a rate hike and a run on the margin bank."

Cramer emphasized that his concerns aren't about the viability of AI itself. Unlike the speculative internet startups that collapsed during the dot-com bust in 2000, many of today's leading technology companies have established businesses and genuine demand for their products.

"This time around the companies are real. They tend to make big money. We trusted them before this moment. We will trust them after," he said.

But Cramer sees one troubling similarity between the two periods: the enormous amount of capital being raised. During the dot-com boom, a flood of stock offerings eventually exhausted investors' buying power, contributing to the market's collapse. Supply outpaced investor demand.

He fears a similar dynamic could emerge as companies includingMeta,Alphabet,SpaceXandOracletap capital markets. Cramer warned that these massive fundraising efforts could absorb investor dollars that might otherwise flow into theS&P 500and other stocks, putting pressure on the broader market even as corporate fundamentals remain strong. Cramer'sCharitable Trust, the portfolio run by CNBC's Investing Club, owns shares of Meta and Alphabet.

"I think both the debt and the equity markets are running out of money," he said.

That means the market could run out of the money companies need to finance their ambitions before investors see the payoff. "I am not calling a top," he said. "I am just saying that I do not like what I see."

title: Bessent dines at Cheesecake Factory, slams Obama over Trump joke
content:
Treasury SecretaryScott Bessenton Monday became the latest right-wing critic to accuse former PresidentBarack Obamaof elitism for mockingly comparing PresidentDonald Trump's ostentatious White House renovations to theCheesecake Factory.

But Bessent, a former hedge fund manager whose net worth has been estimated at around$600 million, put his money where his mouth is — dining at the chain restaurant and praising its food before giving the Democratic ex-president a slice of his mind.

"This is the man who built the museum [that] looks like Darth Vader's tomb," Bessent told a Fox Business reporter who asked about Obama's remark as he left the restaurant. Bessent was apparently referring to theObama Presidential Center, a monolithic structure thatopened in June.

"I had a great meal, always have a great meal, and I would just tell the Martha's Vineyard set to give it a try," Bessent said. Obama vacationed on Martha's Vineyard as president, and he and his wife Michelle now own an estate on the exclusive island.

Bessent said he ordered "what I always have: the French Dip Cheeseburger."

That's a "Charbroiled Cheeseburger Served on a Toasted Brioche Roll with Grilled Onions, Sriracha Mayo and Au Jus for Dipping," one of the "Glamburgers" on Cheesecake Factory's famously sprawlingmenu. The burger, which comes with french fries or a green salad, currently costs $22.95 at the restaurant's downtown Washington location.

"I recommend the Cheeseburger Spring Rolls," Bessent added in a follow-uppost on Xdirected at Obama.

Bessent's biting comment followed those of other Trump allies who claim Obama sneered at working-class Americans when he tore into Trump over his extensive White House construction and decoration projects.

"I don't know if you've noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovations. He should be on HGTV!" Obama said of Trump during a speech at an Ohio rally for gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton and Senate candidate Sherrod Brown on Saturday.

"There's gold everywhere. What's up with the gold?" Obama went on. "He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory."

The crowd erupted in cheers and laughter at the remarks from Obama, who haspreviously poked fun atTrump's gold-heavy remodel of the White House.

Since retaking office, Trump has devoted significant amounts of time to discussing his renovations, including in the Oval Office, which now features heaps of gold leaf among many additional decorations. He has also built a White House helipad, the still-under-construction White House ballroom and an array of other projects.

Trump on Monday afternoon defended his White House redesign at length while claiming Obama had failed to address needed repairs."We have to explain to Obama that the White House is a symbol of America, and it has to be maintained properly," Trump said as he headed to Mississippi for a campaign rally. "Guys like Obama don't see it. You don't see dirt. He doesn't see filth. He doesn't see broken ornaments on a building.""It has to be clean," Trump continued. "The columns can't be broken. The bricks can't be falling off from under the plaster. And for you to say it's a cheesecake factory, that just shows why you were a lousy president."

Detractors insisted Obama's use of the Cheesecake Factory as an example of cheap, gaudy decor amounted to no less than class warfare.

"Classic Obama snobbery," Republican commentator Matt Whitlockwrote on X. "Cheesecake Factory is a great option for people who can't afford a private chef at their Martha's Vineyard estate."

GOP pundit Scott Jenningscalled Obama"undefeated at condescending to regular folks," while claiming the former president "has never been in a Cheesecake Factory."

That backlash quickly sparked its own backlash.

"This is actually a condescending view of working-class people," wrote Derek Guy, a popular menswear influencer,on X.

"I grew up in a working-class immigrant family and we ate at Red Lobster and The Cheesecake Factory for 'fancy nights out.' But even we understood that the White House should not look like the inside of a Red Lobster," Guy wrote. "Working-class people are not culturally illiterate just because their experiences are shaped by their limited means."

The food fight is taking place just days before theNov. 3 midterm election, where most polls and analyst projections indicate Democrats are poised to make significant gains in Congress.

The election cycle has been defined by Americans' widespread unhappiness with high costs, which has dragged Trump's approval ratings to new lows and imperiled Republicans' majorities in the House and Senate.

The Cheesecake Factory is set to report its third-quarter earnings on Tuesday.

title: JetBlue posts bigger loss on fuel costs, but CEO says margins improving
content:
JetBlue Airwaysreported a bigger loss in the third quarter compared with last year, but the New York carrier said strong travel demand is helping to offset higher fuel prices as it seeks to calm investors after shares fell to a new low Monday.

JetBlue stock soared roughly 11% in after-hours trading Monday.

JetBlue on Monday posted a net loss of $257 million for the three months ended Sept. 30, compared with a loss of $143 million a year earlier. The carrier's fuel bill rose 61% to $868 million.

"Resilient demand and strong yields drove revenue well ahead of our initial expectations, allowing us to recapture more of the increase in fuel costs than we initially expected," CEO Joanna Geraghty said in an earnings release. "That momentum has carried into the fourth quarter, and Fort Lauderdale continues to deliver exceptional results even as we significantly grow capacity."

JetBlue's average fares rose more than 19% to $245.11 in the third quarter from $205.67 in the year-earlier period.

JetBlue executives are set to hold an earnings call on Tuesday at 10 a.m. ET, where they will face questions from analysts about the company's long-term health amid sustained losses. A group of the airline's senior creditors isreportedlyworking with restructuring adviserPJT Partners, the Wall Street Journal reported Friday.

The carrier said it ended the quarter with $2.2 billion in liquidity and that its unencumbered asset base is now $7 billion, including $2.8 billion in aircraft and engines.

JetBlue had total debt of $8.4 billion as of Sept. 30, the carrier said in its earnings filing Monday.

"Importantly, we believe we have the liquidity and financing options to create a strong bridge to at least $1 EPS and positive free cash flow in 2028," CFO Ursula Hurley said in a statement. "We remain focused on disciplined cost execution and capital management as we work toward sustained profitability and positive free cash flow."

Here is what JetBlue reported in the third quarter compared with Wall Street estimates compiled by LSEG:

JetBlue last posted an annual profit in 2019. The airline is in the middle of a multiyear turnaround plan that includes cutting cuts and boosting revenue by investing in premium seats, like a new domestic first class section that recently went on sale.

Fuel costs have eaten into airline profits across the board. JetBlue said travel demand has remained strong despitehigher fares, which are up more than 20% this year.

JetBlue has struggled not just with higher costs but also with competition from larger rivals.

It sought to acquire now-defunct carrier Spirit Airlines, but that deal wasupended by a federal judgewho ruled it was anticompetitive. A judge also blocked a regional partnership between JetBlue andAmerican Airlines, which the airlines argued would help them compete better against carriers in the congested Northeast U.S. JetBlue now has a partnership withUnited Airlines.

title: Apple responds to user reports of broken iPhone Duo screens on new foldable phone
content:
Apple'sfirst foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, hit store shelves on Friday to considerable lines and long wait times for pre-orders.

But some customers who were lucky enough to get the $1,999-and-up phone on its first weekend have been reporting a pretty big problem: The inner screen of the phone can break, showing horizontal bright lines emanating from the phone's hinge.

Apple on Monday said it was aware of the issue, which it said affected a "small number" of phones, and that it would replace the devices under its AppleCare warranty.

"We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units," an Apple representative told CNBC. "If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement."

Applesays on itswebsite that an inner-screen repair will be $999 for iPhone Duos that are out-of-warranty.

Most of the reports are from anonymous customers on online forumssuch as RedditandX, and there are fake images online as well. But well-respected device repair firm iFixit weighed in on Sunday, after tearing down the new device and testing its resistance to dust, and theorized the issues may have to do with Apple's hinge design.

"Many of these damage reports describe folding or unfolding the phone, hearing a crunch, and pushing past it," said iFixit technician Shahram Mokhtari inits teardown video. "Right where the damage is happening, the hinge is shaped a little differently."

"The hinge is actually dozens of parts, with ludicrous precision," iFixit CEO Kyle Wienspostedon X. "A manufacturing variance or grain of sand can kill the fragile display panel it protects."

Breaking screens have been an issue with foldable phones going back to 2019, and have been seen as one of the major roadblocks to the technology's widespread adoption. That year, Samsung released one of its first folding devices, andreviewers quickly foundthat its inner screen cracked during normal use.

Earlyreviewers praisedthe experience of using the iPhone Duo when unfolded, especially for multitasking or media, but said that many apps had not been updated to take full advantage of the phone's larger and wider screens.

Apple said on Monday that apps were already being updated for the new foldable device.

"The response to iPhone Duo from early users has been incredibly positive, and we are seeing exciting things from developers who are rapidly updating their apps to take advantage of its unique form factor," an Apple representative said in a statement.

title: Microsoft offers voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees as AI leads to efficiency push
content:
Microsoftsaid Monday that it's offering buyouts to a wide swath of employees as it strives to balance a costly artificial intelligence infrastructure build-out with capital efficiency.

The software maker announced a new voluntary exit offer for certain workers in the U.S., Canada, India and the United Kingdom at its experience level of 70 or below.

Around 60,000 people are eligible, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named while discussing an internal matter. The effort affects about 27% of Microsoft's total workforce of 223,000 people.

Microsoft has been ramping up spending on data centers to accommodate high AI computing demand, supplying cloud services to Anthropic, OpenAI and a slew of other companies. That put a strain on Microsoft's finances. In April, it announced a first-evervoluntary retirement programthat around 7% of U.S. employees were eligible for. Then, in July, Microsoft announced plans to lay off4,800 employees.

"The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we're evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter," Amy Coleman, Microsoft's executive vice president and chief people officer, wrote in amemo to employees. "This builds on what we learned earlier this year through the Voluntary Retirement Program."

In the second quarter, Microsoft's cloud rivals, Alphabet and Amazon, both reported negative free cash flow, but Microsoft showed$19.64 billionin positive free cash flow for the period, down 23% year over year.

Some marketing, sales and engineering teams have decided not to participate in the new buyout, the person said. Employees must decide whether to take the offer in December, and those participating will leave on Dec. 31, the person added.

More than 30% of those who could join the voluntary retirement program went ahead with it, Microsoftsaid in July. But that was open to those at the senior director level and below, while the new initiative goes higher, to the vice president level, said the person briefed on the new plan. The person said Microsoft does not have a target in mind this time around.

On Wednesday, Microsoft is scheduled to report third-quarter results.

title: Anthropic IPO live updates: Prospectus sheds new light on Alphabet, Amazon stakes
content:
Anthropicis officially headed for the public market in what is expected to be a historic offering for a 5-year-old company that's been at the heart of the generativeartificial intelligenceboom.

In a Form S-1 filing with theSecurities and Exchange Commission, Anthropic said it plans to list on the Nasdaq under ticker symbol "ANT."

The company behind Claudeconfidentiallyfiled with the SEC in June, giving the agency time to review its financials before they were made available to the public and prospective investors.

Anthropic CEODario Amodeico-founded the company in 2021 after he and a small group of researchers defected fromOpenAI, now its chief rival. Anthropic's Claude model and services have captivated the corporate world, as companies have opened their wallets in an effort to crack new growth opportunities and find internal efficiencies.

Expansion has accelerated in 2026, driven largely by the popularity of AI coding toolClaude Code, and powerful models including ClaudeFable 5andMythos 5. The company has been racing to maintain an edge over competitors like OpenAI andGoogle, and faced sharp criticism over itspositionson safety, regulation and national security, leading to two high-profile disputes with the U.S. government in recent months.

Anthropic's offering, if it doesn't get derailed, will land just a few months afterElon Musk'sSpaceXdebuted on the Nasdaq in by far the biggest IPO on record, ultimately raising $85.7 billion. It's been a volatile stretch for SpaceX shares, which finished last week slightly below where they opened in June.

As it prepares to hit the market, Anthropic has to contend with severe jitters on Wall Street as concerns grow over whether spending on AI services will justify the trillions of dollars in expected infrastructure costs. So-called neoclouds likeCoreWeaveandNebiushave beenhammeredof late, losing over 30% of their value in October ascredit riskis rising across the data center space.

What you need to know about the IPO:

CNBC's reporters are covering Anthropic's IPO from bureaus in San Francisco and Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey.

In its Form S-1 filing, Anthropic said Claude's capabilities should facilitate progress in scientific research, particularly drug discovery.

This could add momentum to theinnovation boomhappening in the biotech industry.

Anthropic's AI model Claude is already being used in drug discovery, helping researchers and scientists automate workloads and analyze large data sets.

That suggests the AI lab could benefit from the $2 trillion in expected annual global spending by pharmaceutical companies in 2026.

In the filing, Anthropic explained that Claude could enable AI agents to operate lab and manufacturing equipment like microscopes, liquid handlers and off-the-shelf robotic arms.

Anthropic's filing lands at the start of a big week for tech on Wall Street.

Microsoft and Alphabet are scheduled to report quarterly results on Wednesday, followed a day later by Amazon. The other hyperscaler,Meta, reportedthird-quarter resultslast week. Revenue topped estimates and Meta issued a strong forecast, but the stock dropped on concerns about costs as the company turned cash flow negative.

Anthropic needs investors to stay confident in the cloud giants so they can continue investing in the AI infrastructure required for the development of new models and services.

In its IPO filing, Anthropic warned investors that ongoing issues with the Trump administration and U.S. Department of Defense could cause "material revenue losses or business disruptions."

As CNBC previously reported, the department labeled Anthropic a "supply chain risk to national security," and in February, President Donald Trump alsoordered the U.S. governmentto stop using the company's models.

In March,Anthropic filed a complaintin a federal court in the Northern District of California challenging that label as illegal, and at the same time, filed a petition for review in the U.S. Court of Appeals in D.C.

The California federal court ruled in Anthropic's favor, finding that the Pentagon's actions were "retaliatory acts meant to punish" the company. The court also found the actions violated the company's First Amendment rights, and had violated the AI company's Fifth Amendment rights to due process, the company noted in its IPO filing.

But the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled in favor of the DOD, saying the supply chain risk designation was allowed under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act.

Anthropic said in its filing that it is "evaluating its next steps" with respect to the D.C. appeals court decision. The company has asked the full D.C. circuit torehear its appeal.

Today, the U.S. filed anotice of appealto try to invalidate the decision from the Northern California district court.

Matt Witheiler, head of late-stage growth for private markets at Wellington Management, said the AI lab's focus on enterprise was 'absolutely' important in making it stand out.

"The scale at which they've been able to capitalize on the enterprise opportunity is really something that's been impressive," Witheiler told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street."

"I think what Dario [Amodei] and team are trying to build is really the next generation of great enterprise company," with products like Claude Code and Claude Science, Witheiler added.

Anthropic said its pool of computing power includes Nvidia's GPUs, AMD's GPUs, AWS Tranium, and Google TPUs.

Anthropic treats all AI chips as a "single fungible pool" and it has developed technology that routes its AI models to whatever chip is the most efficient at the time.

It's a sign that Anthropic won't tie itself to any one chip provider. OpenAI, which mostly uses Nvidia compute, has made similar moves to diversify the AI chips it uses.

"Our multi-chip compute approach provides us with substantially greater chip access than relying on one platform and enables us to opportunistically capture the price-performance benefits of each chip family and generation," Anthropic said in its filing.

All four of Anthropic's primary chip designers have large stakes or options to buy stakes in Anthropic, highlighting the strategic ties between chipmakers or hyperscalers and the AI labs.

Anthropic's filing left the amount of total money it has committed to spending on compute blank, but the frontier lab signaled it will spend heavily.

Separately, Anthropic detailed long-term commitments with SpaceXAI, Nscale, and Lambda to secure access to Nvidia chips. The company also said it could buy more than $20 billion in AMD chips. It said it was committed to spending on Amazon's Trainium chips at $110 billion through 2036, and $114.5 billion on Google TPUs through 2033.

"We anticipate making significant investments for the foreseeable future, including in compute and infrastructure, to ensure we have the technological resources to maintain and expand our position at the frontier of AI," Anthropic said in the filing.

Anthropic reported its cost of revenue as $2.38 billion as of June 30, 2026, booking $16.29 billion in revenue during the same period and implying a gross margin of 85%.

That's an explosion from the implied 12% gross margin the company generated during the same period last year, on just over $1 billion in cost of revenue and $1.16 billion in revenue booked.

However, Anthropic's S-1 states that operating margin and adjusted operating margin are expected to "fluctuate over time, particularly in periods when substantial incremental compute is delivered to us and we incur the associated expenses."

The prospectus also reveals that "substantially all of cost of revenue" is associated with compute and infrastructure costs, adding that smaller personnel and overhead-related costs are also factored in.

Amazon remains one of Anthropic's biggest backers and strategic partners. The company has poured $13 billion into Anthropic since2023, with the potential to invest $20 billion more.

According to the filing, Amazon has separately agreed to provide up to $15 billion in financing, which will become available to Anthropic in $5 billion tranches. Each draw is tied to Anthropic hitting certain compute capacity milestones.

Amazon holds $6.2 billion in outstanding convertible notes that could be worth $1.84 billion once Anthropic goes public. Amazon's stake is capped at 12% of the company, the filing states.

Amazon holds nonvoting shares and it doesn't have a board or observer seat at the startup.

The companies have continued to deepen their partnership, with Anthropic becoming a key customer of Amazon's cloud computing and chips businesses. Amazon last year opened an $11 billion AI data center campus dedicated to training and running models from Anthropic, called Rainier.

In April, Anthropic said it committed to spend at least $110 billion with Amazon for cloud services through April 2036, "regardless of actual usage."

The agreement is "non-cancelable," except for in the event of a "material breach" by Amazon, the filing says. If Anthropic's actual spend falls short, it's required to pay Amazon the difference as a true-up.

The filing doesn't state how much Anthropic has spent on Amazon's cloud services and Trainium AI chips to date.

Anthropic made $4.5 billion in international revenue during the first half of 2026, more than 13 times the $343 million recorded during the same period a year earlier. That's 27.8% of the company's total revenue.
