title: Anthropic warns of 'catastrophic risk' to humankind ahead of blockbuster share listing
content: Image source,Getty ImagesByRachel Clun,ÂBusiness reporter,ÂLiv McMahon,ÂTechnology reporterÂandÂKali Hays,ÂTechnology reporterPublished26 October 2026, 13:27 GMTUpdated 52 minutes agoAnthropic has warned artificial intelligence (AI) could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" as it unveiled details of its planned blockbuster stock market listing in the US.The firm's valuation is expected to exceedthat of SpaceX, which was the biggest-ever listing at aninitial valuationof about $1.8 trillion in the summer.Anthropic has not yet disclosed the number of shares to be released, their price range, or a date for the listing.The Claude chatbot developer reported $16.3bn (Â£12.2bn) of revenue in the first half of the year, with losses of more than $80.7bn.Anthropic, which said it will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT, will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public, making it a test case for the future of the technology.In a filing ahead of its listing, Anthropic said concerns had been raised by policymakers, regulators and researchers as well as by people within its organisation that AI systems posed a significant risk to humanity.It said advanced AI systems "could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy".Anthropic was founded five years ago by chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela Amodei and five others, and announced itsintention to go publicin June.Its main rival, OpenAI, quickly followed suit. That listing is now expected to occur early next year, according to a person familiar with OpenAI's plans.Those announcements were followed by a wave of cyber-security and other technological breaches involving their AI agents - bots designed to operate somewhat autonomously.Current and former staff of both companies also warned AI technology was being developed without the ability to protect humanity from possible future harms enacted by AI tools.As Anthropic revealed its stock debut plans on Monday,the owners of the rights to Elvis Presley's music sued the AI firmaccusing it of using hundreds of the rock-and-roll star's songs to train its chatbot Claude.'Bold but sane'In Anthropic's new documents, it reiterated promises it has made in the past to develop AI in a way that is beneficial to people, while at the same time warning investors of its dangers.Anthropic detailed losses in its financial filings that exceeded its revenue for the first half of the year, but said it would often make forward investments "that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance"."In general, we will aim to be bold but sane, and to win trust with a track record of successful bets," the tech giant said.Its success depends largely on its ability to develop the most advanced AI models, Anthropic said, adding, "any failure to do so could adversely affect our business".Across about 90 pages detailing possible risk factors, Anthropic set out the potential threats to its ability to safely and competitively develop AI.Anthropic warned it relies on a cluster of cloud computing providers, Taiwanese chipmakers already facing huge demand and data centres concentrated in the US.It also warned of "regulatory action arising from harms associated with our AI models"- citing concerns over AI being used by children or individuals at risk of suicide - and uncertainty about where and how it might be held liable for actions taken by its systems.However, Anthropic also used the filing to laud the potential benefits of the tech itself, envisioning it unlocking "millions of virtual agents with the ability to revolutionise every area of human endeavour" across a range of fields."We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history," the firm said.Anthropic said AI would also "profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine", potentially finding cures to diseases including cancer and Alzheimer's.The firm added it could also establish "sustained acceleration in economic growth" by boosting productivity.'Significant milestone'Matt Orton, chief market strategist at investment management firm Raymond James Investment, said investors expected to see rapid growth as well as rapid financial losses in Anthropic's finances, so Monday's filing would not come as a surprise."Getting the details from this filing, I think will help provide the market with more visibility, because we need to know where its revenue growth is coming from," he told the BBC.Peter Andersen, founder of Andersen Capital Management, told Reuters that Anthropic's plans to list was "a significant milestone in the development of artificial intelligence".He added that the outcome of its stock market debut would be "fairly indicative of the sentiment" among investors to continue ploughing cash into AI development.Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they?Published17 SeptemberOwners of Elvis music rights sue Anthropic for copyright violationsPublished2 hours agoMusk and Anthropic pledge public share giveawaysPublished7 days agoAI giant Anthropic woos potential investors ahead of stock market debutPublished15 OctoberSign up for our Tech Decoded newsletterto follow the world's top tech stories and trends.Outside the UK? Sign up here.Related topicsArtificial intelligenceCompaniesCyber-securityNASDAQStock markets

title: Investors are doing just as well this year by shunning AI. How to invest if the tech trade keeps fizzling
content:
Aversion of the S&P 500 without AIbriefly pulled ahead of the traditional index this year and is now neck-and-neck as investors rotate into other areas of the market.

A proprietary Goldman Sachs index tracking theS&P 500without stocks classified as "AI enablers" was up 12.4% through Oct. 22, edging ahead of the standard S&P 500's 12% gain. The Goldman index is now neck-and-neck with the S&P 500 as tech rallied in Monday trading.

Tech and AI-related companies make up about45% of the S&P 500. That heavy weighting has helped power the index for years, but it's turned into a liability lately; the S&P 500 tech sector is down about 7% this month while other sectors have held up.

Investors have soured on debt and equity issued by companies likeCoreWeaveandOracle. Shares ofMeta Platformssank almost 7% Thursday after it outlined more plans to spend heavily on capex and issue additional shares.

Companies supplying power and equipment for the buildout have been hit hard — names likeGE Vernova,Bloom Energy,VistraandQuanta Servicesallsuffered steep declinesduring the recent selloff.

Goldman, which launched the measure earlier this year with S&P, uses the S&P 500 as its starting universe and excludes companies perceived to be enablers of AI before applying S&P 500 Index weighting methodology to the remaining universe of companies.

The ex-AI index lagged the S&P 500 for most of the year as investors continued tofavor chipmakers, cloud-computing companiesand other firms benefiting from heavy AI spending. However, that advantage has been narrowing and it disappeared last week.

Meanwhile, investors are rotating into defensive areas. ETFs likeState Street Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF,State Street Health Select SPDR ETFandState Street Utilities Select Sector SPDR ETFare up 7% to 10% this month. Energy is ahead 10% too, though that's more related to the war in Iran.

Some analysts recommend sticking with non-AI companies for diversification and protection against more pain in tech. The "AI pendulum has swung back in favor of non-AI exposure over the last two weeks," Oppenheimer technical analyst Ari Wald said in a note on Oct. 24.

Two industries that Oppenheimer favors now are commercial services and insurance. The firm upgraded those industries to overweight last week, recommendingRepublic Services,Cintas,Verisk Analytics,Broadridge Financial Solutions,MetLifeandArthur J. Gallagher.

Berkshire Hathawayis also capitalizing on the rotation out of tech. Its Class B shares are up 8% this month, though it's still lagging behind the S&P 500 this year.

Berkshire owns a wide swath of operating companies, including insurance giant Geico and Burlington Northern Santa Fe railroad. It also has a $364 billion stock portfolio including companies likeApple,Coca-Cola,AlphabetandBank of America. That diversification may help Berkshire continue to outperform if the tech sector drags down the S&P 500.

Trivector Research sees potential in "non-tech compounders." Healthcare giantEli Lillyis one idea. The stock is up 22% on the strength of Lilly's weight-loss drugs. The companyhas more in the pipeline, including a next-generation obesity drug that Lilly plans to file for FDA approval early in 2027.

Viking Holdings, a cruise operator, is also proving durable. The company said on its August earnings call that 40% of its river capacity and 60% of its ocean capacity was already booked for 2027. "Based on recent events, we've seen our guests have proved to be resilient and are continuing to book 2027 and future seasons," the company told investors.

Viking stock is up 15% this year but it may still have upside. The average Wall Street target is $109, above recent prices around $82. Barclays recentlyupgraded the cruise operatorto overweight with a $102 target, citing the company's "compelling risk/reward."

title: Salon owners urge Budget VAT cut as staffing pressures grow
content: Image caption,Marcus Perkins said rising costs were making it harder for salons to employ staff and train apprenticesByLouise Brierleyin Brierley HillPublished26 October 2026, 06:14 GMTUpdated 11 minutes agoAfter 22 years running a salon, Marcus Perkins says he is increasingly worried about the future of the hair and beauty industry.Rising costs are making it harder for businesses to employ staff and invest in apprenticeships, he says, while more salons are turning to self-employed models to survive."Seeing salons close on the high street is very scary," he said. "I'm very scared myself. Luckily it hasn't happened yet but who knows what the future holds?"Perkins is among more than 2,000 salon owners who have signed an open letter calling on the Chancellor John Healey to cut VAT on hair and beauty services from 20% to 10% in this week's Budget.The letter is backed by the British Hair Consortium (BHC), which argues rising business costs are placing increasing pressure on traditional salon employers.However, the industry has also seen growing numbers of stylists move into self-employed arrangements, with hairdressers often renting a chair within a salon rather than being directly employed.With salon ownership perceived to be out of reach for many, self-employment offered independence, flexibility and higher earnings,industry research suggested,external.A Treasury spokesperson said hair and beauty businesses played an important role in supporting jobs, apprenticeships and thriving high streets.They added that the sector had benefited from reforms to business rates.While traditional salons said they faced rising pressures, a recent reportfrom the British Beauty Councilfound that hair and beauty salons and shops made up almost a third of all leisure sites across UK retail centres.It added that those businesses now accounted for greater share of smaller high streets and were equivalent to pubs, bars and cafes combined.Image caption,Stylist Trearna Hart fears fewer salons will be able to train the next generationSalon owners say they have also been affected by increases in wage, pension and National Insurance (NI) costs.The government's changes to employers' NI contributions and increases to the minimum wage have been defended by ministers as part of wider efforts to improve pay, support public services and drive economic growth.The BHC said a reduction in VAT would help businesses take on more staff, invest in training and keep more salons trading on the high street.What is the Budget and what could be in it?Published8 hours agoChancellor says he will cut 'pointless paperwork' to save businesses up to Â£800mPublished3 days agoPerkins believed it would make a significant difference."We can grow the business and employ more people," he said.The salon owner runs M&M Spa in Quarry Bank, near Brierley Hill, where he says he has trained more than a dozen young people over the past two decades.Among them is 21-year-old stylist Trearna Hart, who said many of her peers had struggled to establish careers after leaving college.She said she was fortunate to find an employer willing to invest in her development.Image caption,Dorothy Senior says visiting her salon is about more than having her hair and nails doneThis year alone, Perkins said he had spent about Â£2,000 on courses and travel costs to support her training."It's upsetting really," he said. "We help people, we train, we nurture, we mentor. We help the next generation because if we don't help the next generation, what happens to our future?"The BHC claimed apprenticeship numbers had fallen sharply and warned the trend could worsen if pressures on employer-run salons continued.Financial pressures and concerns over inconsistent training standards had led salons to take on fewer apprentices, with 53% of salon ownersreporting a reduction,externalin the number they trained, according to a Future of Hairdressing report.Perkins believes businesses that employ and train staff are increasingly competing against models centred on self-employed workers.He argues that creates an "unlevel playing field" because traditional salons often shoulder the costs of training future hairdressers.Hart said the number of salons disappearing from high streets was a concern."At the rate it's going we're not going to have many salons left open and there's no-one going to be able to do hair," she said.The challenges facing the sector are also worrying some customers.Research from the British Beauty Council highlighted the role hair and beauty businesses play in supporting local high streets, encouraging spending and providing opportunities for social connection.Dorothy Senior has visited M&M for hair and beauty treatments for the past 20 years.She said the salon was about much more than appearances."Every time I come in I go home feeling so much better," she said. title: Neocloud stocks fall as Elon Musk says more than 200 of them face 'guppy-level death'
content:
Shares of major neocloud stocks fell on Monday afterElon Musksaid that more than 200 companies in the sector could collapse.

Nebius,CoreWeaveandIrenall dropped more than 4% in early premarket trading, adding pressure to a sector already facing investor concerns about debt-fueled expansion and whether the large AI infrastructure buildout will generate returns. However, these stocks have since pared some of the losses and are now trading between 2% and 3% lower.

"As of the past few weeks, debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn't have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers," Musk, CEO ofSpaceXandTesla, said on a post onXon Sunday.

"That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation. Some will make it through, but not many," he added.

Musk's SpaceX operates its own data centers through which it sells computing capacity. SpaceX is a direct competitor to the neoclouds which also rent compute.

Musk was replying to a post onXby Chamath Palihapitiya, the founder of Social Capital, who laid out his views on the state of the data center buildout. He suggested that there will be "a lot of partially stranded compute and compute sitting in inventory in 2027 than is currently forecasted," which will be "bought and paid for but effectively underearning (below total cost of capital) or collecting dust."

"2027 will be a turbulent year because it will clear out a bunch of wrong/bad bets. It will also be a consolidation year for a few," Palihapitiya said.

Neocloud stocks have taken a hammering over the past month, with CoreWeave and Nebius down more than 30% while Iren has tanked 40%. The sell-off started earlier this month after thespread on CoreWeave's five-year credit default swapshit levels generally viewed as signs of distress. The yields on CoreWeave's bonds also climbed.

Investors have grown jittery over companies that are borrowing heavily to fund the purchase of expensiveNvidiachips, build data centers, and rent out computing power.

Nvidia, an investor in several neoclouds, looked to shore up the sector last week at its GTC event in Berlin, Germany.

In aninterview with CNBC, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said the demand for neoclouds is "off the charts."

"What is missing in the middle is the working capital to fuel that growth… because there's just so much demand across so many sectors of AI, there's a scarcity of capital," Huang said.

"The demand of the capital is much greater than the availability of the capital. That's going to get solved," he added.

Marc Boroditsky, chief revenue officer at Nebius, distanced his company from concerns surrounding CoreWeave, saying "we're not carrying the kind of debt that they are," in an interview with CNBC. Boroditsky said that if the AI infrastructure company brought its 2027 capacity online, it would sell out. And there could be "the same type of dynamic" in 2028.

Iren Co-CEO Daniel Roberts also defended demand.

"We understand the increased focus from investors, but when we're talking from customers, nothing has changed. The demand is still there," Roberts told CNBC last week.

"Next year, we are having conversations with customers covering multiples of all the capacity we possibly bring online, and in the last month or so, 2028 is now coming into focus. But the demand is there," he added.

title: Oil slides over 2% as traders weigh Saudi attack risks, demand destruction
content:
U.S. crude oil fell over 2% on Monday as investors weighed the threat of further attacks on Saudi Arabian energy infrastructure against concerns that elevated prices could eventually erode demand.

U.S. West Texas Intermediate futuresslid 2.19% to $101 a barrel, whileBrent crude futuresdeclined 1.89% to $114.51 a barrel.

The pullback followed a sharp rally on Friday after attacks by Yemen's Houthi militants on Saudi Arabia reignited fears of disruptions to global energy supplies.

Tensions remained elevated over the weekend as the Houthis said they had targeted Saudi Arabia's main airport in Riyadh and oil facilities on Saturday. Saudi authorities said Sunday that they had intercepted additional missiles and drones.

The kingdom partially resumed operations at its main airport on Sunday despite damage from earlier attacks, even as the Houthis threatened further strikes.

The continued hostilities have heightened concerns about the vulnerability of Saudi Arabia's energy infrastructure, with traders increasingly focused on the risk of a major disruption to production, refining or export facilities.

Speaking to CNBC, Michael Alfaro, chief investment officer at Gallo Partners, estimated that geopolitical uncertainty had already added roughly $20 a barrel to oil prices.

A substantial strike on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline or additional refining infrastructure could send prices sharply higher, he added, but further gains could eventually undermine consumption.

"What we would likely see if oil pushed above 120, 130, 140 dollars a barrel for Brent, that is, you're going to see more demand destruction," Alfaro said.

Beyond the immediate threat to crude supplies, damage to refining infrastructure could pose a more persistent challenge to global energy markets.

"The real challenge is refining capacity," he said, warning that the disruptions could develop into a longer-term structural problem extending into 2027 and beyond.

Meanwhile,Saudi Arabia plans to begin storing crude oilin Singapore from the second half of 2027, according to energy ministers from both countries, in a move aimed at strengthening the resilience of its Asian supply chain.

In the U.S., the Energy Department on Friday authorized the release of up to 400,000 barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to address a supply disruption at a Louisiana refinery.

Still, the prospect of additional supply from American producers remains uncertain, with companies reluctant to commit to major new investments amid volatile prices and geopolitical risks.

Alfaro added that U.S. producers were adding some drilling rigs, but remained cautious about substantially increasing capital expenditure.

"We're not really seeing major capex additions to bring new rigs on or bring new production online," he said.

title: SoftBank reportedly plans $50 billion tech investment in aspiring 'AI nation' Malaysia
content:
SoftBank Groupplans to make $50 billion of investments in Malaysia, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said, according to a Bloomberg report.

Anwar said Saturday that Son had identified locations in Kuching, Sarawak, and peninsular Malaysia for the planned investments following a video conference between the two earlier in the week,the report said.

The country's prime minister said the planned investments would focus on artificial intelligence, new technologies and data centers, according to the report.

The planned investment comes as Malaysia seeks to become an"AI nation" by 2030, with the government launching a national AI action plan earlier this year to strengthen the country's AI capabilities and infrastructure.

Earlier this month, SoftBanksigneda framework agreement with Singapore-based Grab and Malaysia's Petroleum Sarawak Berhad to explore AI and digital infrastructure development in Sarawak, including AI computing services and advanced technologies.

SoftBank is not alone in pursuing technology investments in Malaysia. Googleannounceda $2 billion investment in 2024 to build its first data center and cloud region in the country, while Amazon Web Services said itplannedto invest $6.2 billion through 2038. Microsoft alsoannounceda $2.2 billion investment in cloud and AI infrastructure and other digital initiatives.

The countryrecorded385.7 billion ringgit ($94 billion) in data center-related investments between 2021 and the first half of 2026, according to the Malaysian Investment Development Authority.

SoftBank did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

title: SpaceX closes $40 billion debt deal for AI chips, Elon Musk says
content:
Elon Musk saidSpaceXhas closed $40 billion in debt financing to purchase graphics processing units, or GPUs, used to power artificial intelligence systems.

In aposton X on Sunday, Musk said SpaceX had closed the financing, adding that the company was investment grade and generated revenue from its Starlink satellite internet and rocket launch businesses.

In afollow-up post, he added that the financing, primarily consisted of callable debt for graphics processing units, is expected to arrive in the first and second quarters of 2027.

Bloombergreportedearlier, citing people familiar with the matter, that SpaceX was in talks with banks and investors to raise $40 billion to purchase Nvidia chips.

The proposed financing would use a special purpose vehicle to keep the debt off SpaceX's balance sheet and preserve its investment-grade credit ratings, according to Bloomberg.

Goldman Sachs was leading talks with investors, including Apollo Global Management, over the financing structure, according to Bloomberg.

The financing underscores the enormous capital requirements of the AI boom, as technology companies pour billions of dollars into advanced chips and data centers to support increasingly powerful AI models.

SpaceX hasexpandedaggressively into artificial intelligence this year, referring to the business as "Super Intelligence," or SI.

The segment has become the company's largest business unit, with third-quarter revenue surging ninefold to $7.56 billion from $813 million a year earlier, according to its latest earnings release.

Musk also said that debt markets have largely shut off access to financing for companies without substantial revenue outside AI data centers.

He predicted that more than 200 so-called neocloud companies, which provide cloud computing infrastructure specifically designed for artificial intelligence and machine learning workloads, would face widespread failures and consolidation, with only a small number surviving.

title: Healey's Budget needs to sustain the stronger economy through gathering clouds
content: ByFaisal IslamEconomics editorThere have been almost no Budget leaks.The chancellor's aides are using intelligence-style security measures to guard its secrets: the Budget has been split into "compartments" with very few given access to all of them. There are codenames. The IT has been locked down and ministers viewing the plans have to sign a digital promise not to brief media.Such security is a response to the feeling that speculation around the last Budget, sometimes informed by insiders, was economically destabilising.As a recent former defence secretary, Chancellor John Healey has embraced such strict procedures, and has approached most of his public engagements and interviews with a sturdy refusal to break the Budget omertÃ , akin to his fellow Yorkshireman Geoffrey Boycott's at times ultra-defensive stance on a cricket pitch.The economic news has been good - growth has been better than expected and the International Monetary Fund has endorsed the UK for "standing out" among the G7 countries for at least planning to cut borrowing.Image source,ReutersImage caption,John Healey has embraced strict security procedures to keep this year's budget secretThe bond market's reverse beauty contest, in which investors single out the countries they distrust most, has moved on from Britain. Traders I occasionally hear from who were once focused on UK borrowing costs are now more preoccupied with "le spread" - the widening gap between French and German borrowing costs (the former being higher than the latter) - and with America's long-term debt outlook.And yet there are clouds on the horizon. The inflation rate rose more than forecast to 3.5% in September, and borrowing numbers were also higher than forecast. This means an imminent Bank of England rate rise is very much on the cards, with the resultant rise in mortgage repayments for some.Credibility with investors requires not just that Budget maths add up on Wednesday, but also belief that growth plans are realistic, and the perception that Downing Street can actually convince MPs to pass its Budget.The question for John Healey is whether he can deliver a Budget that can sustain the revival in growth and offer the help with the cost of living that his backbenchers demand. At the same time he needs to reassure the markets that his budget will keep a check on borrowing.The curious case of the UK economy"Is it resilient, or is it actually strong?" has been the tone of the debate among economists about the curious case of the UK economy ahead what is a vital Budget.The UK is the fastest growing G7 country so far this year, at 0.6% in Q1 and 0.5% in Q2. The widespread assumption of stagnation in the second half is being defied with Q3 heading for 0.6 to 0.8%.Each quarter has seen growth twice as fast as predicted by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) in March and independent forecasters. This is the fastest growth in the first eight months of a year since 2017, ignoring the post-lockdown re-opening.It's more resilient than it was in 2022. Back then, the Ukraine war, massive energy bailouts, and Liz Truss' mini budget all culminated in the UK facing the highest borrowing costs in the G7, in what was derided in financial markets as a "moron premium".Then last year, with constant policy u-turns, UK borrowing costs rose the most of the G7.This year the gap has narrowed, as uncertainty about the US and France takes centre stage, but all advanced economies are feeling the heat from the Iran war energy shock.Inflation has risen, but not just in Britain. Reforms to the electricity market have weakened the link between gas and electricity prices, meaning spikes in gas prices have less impact on electricity bills than they used to and helping to keep inflation lower than it otherwise might have been.The fact that up until now the Iran war has been more of an oil shock than a gas shock (where the UK is more exposed) has been another saving grace. Meanwhile, the significant amount of AI and tech investment in the UK is another boost to the economic numbers.The net result is that doom-mongering predictions of recession, of being hit worst by the Iran war, and, in some quarters, of imminent national bankruptcy, have been defied.That economic defiance of the early part of 2026 has persisted in the first three months of the Burnham-Healey tenure in Downing Street, buoyed by a lull in the Iran war and the energy price shock.Image source,EPA-EFE/REX/ShutterstockImage caption,Post Liz Truss' mini-budget the UK faced the highest borrowing costs in the G7Burnham was advised upon entry to Downing Street that if consumers could at least feel more confident, they might save less and spend more and therefore help boost growth.So far Burnham and Healey appear to be relying on a series of relatively inexpensive "feel-better" policies - such as capped bus fares and a temporary VAT cut on household energy bills - that have improved confidence without significantly increasing spending.But there isn't a lot of spare money, which limits just how much can be offered for "temporary and targeted" measures. And come January, the clouds on the horizon could be overhead, with typical energy bills predicted to rise by 16%, interest rates potentially up and an enduring fear that the AI bubble could burst.Healey's essential judgementAt a gleaming hi-tech robotics research facility in Coventry last month, John Healey sought to set out the broad contours of his approach to the economy. On a walkabout at the Manufacturing Technology Centre, I asked him if there had been too much doom-mongery."I know the global conditions mean that it is hardâ¦ we have huge latent potential in this country. Great talent, and deep capital markets."The challenge now is to make sure that we balance the books, we manage and control public spending, and the prime minister and I are in lockstep in our determination to meet the fiscal rules with a buffer," he said.The giant orange robot arms whizzing around were being trained by AI to use lasers to carve the most intricate metal shapes for prototype parts for the jet engines of the future. The Budget manoeuvres required by Healey may require even more precision.The essential question is whether he has chosen to impress the markets and explain himself to his MPs, or impress his MPs and explain himself to the markets. Judging by my three interviews with him in recent weeks, it is more the former than the latter.Image source,ReutersImage caption,At Labour conference Healey wore the same tie once worn by Gordon BrownThe answer may not be found in his speech at all, but in the borrowing tables that will reveal how much money the government expects to borrow over the coming years, published in the OBR's forecast released - assuming no repeat oflast year's disaster- when Healey sits down in the House of Commons around 13.00.Just after that, as Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch is delivering the Opposition's response, the real reaction the chancellor's team will be looking for is whether the markets move, particularly when the Debt Management Office publishes the "gilt remit" - the detail of any changes to its plan to sell UK government bonds to investors.My sense is that every effort is being made to minimise this number, and help guide down medium and long-term borrowing rates for the government and for mortgages. (It was at this moment in 2022 that markets vomited at the prospect of how much extra they thought the government would need to borrow after Liz Truss' mini budget.)From Healey's first day in office, the prudence message was practically tattooed to his head. He has spent more time working in the Treasury than any recent chancellor. He spent five years from 2002 to 2007 as a junior minister when Gordon Brown was chancellor - five finance bills, five Budgets, pre-Budget reports and two Spending Reviews.Image caption,Healey says he will take on some of the challenges Rachel Reeves found tricky to resolveFor his Labour Party conference speech, Healey sported Brown's old conference tie. But the Treasury he returned to this year is a changed place in important ways. When his predecessor wore the tie, the Treasury was running an annual surplus, not a Â£120bn deficit adding to a Â£3 trillion total national debt.I asked him just afterwards, and just before he was whisked off to a meeting of the government's emergency COBR committee on RAF Fairford, if he was going to have another go at some of the things that proved so difficult for his predecessor, former Chancellor Rachel Reeves.He replied: "100%. I was very clear to the conference today and the public beyond. There isn't the money that there was in the 1990s. People understand that. The public aren't daft."Running through the Budget I deliver must be fiscal discipline and the maintenance of control on the public finances, because otherwise we won't get on top of the debt costs."One intriguing element of what we may see on Wednesday is that this theoretically more left-leaning Labour government appears to believe they have the political capital to save money on welfare payments.The aim is to get some of the 1.35 million people currently off work with mental health issues back into jobs.Some reporting suggests some affected younger people may see benefits payments cut, with the government instead investing more in getting them into jobs and keeping them in them through the offer, for example, of in-work therapy.A constrained ChancellorBack in Healey's time under Gordon Brown, there was no OBR. Back then it was not unknown for late budget maths problems to be settled with an optimistic tweak of a forecast, a date change to the economic cycle, or choosing a stronger rate of long term growth.The OBR's verdict is crucial no
