title: Blanche defends Trump-ordered lawsuit over Alaska Senate election certification
content:
Attorney GeneralTodd Blanchedefended the Justice Department'slawsuiton Sunday seeking toblock certificationof Alaska's Senate election if Republican incumbent Sen.Dan Sullivannarrowly loses.

The lawsuit, filed last week, cites what it argues is likely voter confusion over the name Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher also on the ballot. The DOJ said confusion over the two Sullivans could help former Alaska Democratic Rep.Mary Peltola, who is narrowlyahead in pollsjust over a week from Election Day, win the election.

"What we're asking the court to do is make sure that after the election, if it's clear that there was confusion, if it's clear, and that's for a court to decide at a later date if there's litigation ... and that confusion led to an unjust, improper result that is not the will of the Alaskan voter, we want to make sure that the Alaskan system and the Alaskan state courts and the Alaskan electoral process can understand that in a way that lets them do the right thing," Blanche said on CNN's "State of the Union."

"Never before have opponents gone to such lengths to try and thwart and cheat in an election as they're doing in this case," he said.

The DOJ's lawsuit says that the potential for voter confusion exists and Alaska should not certify the election if "(1) Senator Sullivan does not win the election; and (2) had all votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan been cast instead for Senator Sullivan and Alaska's rank-choice process played out accordingly, Senator Sullivan would have won the election."

Alaska applies a top-four primary system to select candidates for the general election. The November general election uses ranked-choice voting.

Ranked-choice voting lets voters rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate receives a majority of votes in the first round of counting, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated. Voters who ranked the eliminated candidate first then have their second choice counted and added to that candidate's total. This continues until a majority winner — or the candidate with more than half of the vote — wins.

Republicans have argued for months that Daniel J. Sullivan is a Democratic plant intended to confuse voters and have sought to remove him from the ballot. Democrats have maintained they have no connection to the candidate, and Sullivan himself has denied running to confuse voters.

The Alaska Division of Elections briefly removed Daniel J. Sullivan in June, before a state court ordered his name returned to the ballot. The state Supreme Court upheld that decision.

PresidentDonald Trump, who has long made claims of voter fraud without evidence, said he ordered the DOJ's lawsuit himself.

Democratic groups and voting rights advocates, including Peltola's campaign, areseeking to jointhe lawsuit to stop the DOJ's effort to block certification of the election if Sen. Sullivan loses. The groups argue the executive branch lacks the legal authority to intervene in state-run elections and is attempting an unprecedented override of state election administration, with early voting already underway.

"In an unprecedented pre-emptive strike on democratic elections, the Department of Justice—acting on the President's personal orders—demands that this Court enjoin the certification of the ongoing U.S. Senate election, but only if the President's preferred candidate loses," the motion to intervene reads. "But the federal government has no power to impose that Hobson's choice on the people of this State."

Alaska is seen as one of the best chances for a Democratic flip in the Nov. 3 elections, which will determine control of Congress for the remainder of Trump's term. Trump has been barnstorming competitive states in recent weeks as the polls favor Democrats to win control of the House of Representatives and potentially flip the Senate.

Democrats and voting rights advocates have long feared that Trump — who denied his election loss to former PresidentJoe Bidenin 2020, leading to a violent riot at the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021 — would attempt to meddle in the midterm contest to save narrow Republican majorities in Congress.

Blanche bristled on Sunday when asked whether the lawsuit aimed to sway the election in Alaska toward Republicans.

"That is crazy," Blanche said, pressed on CNN about whether the president is laying the groundwork for a "doomsday" scenario in which he tries to overturn election results.

"We're not laying any groundwork for the president to do that ... the groundwork that we are laying is for the state of Alaska, if it becomes an issue after the election, will have the ability to determine whether there was confusion that violates the law in determining who the senator should be."

title: Ukraine disputes Elon Musk’s claim that its military violated Starlink terms during drone operations
content:
A Ukrainian official disputedSpaceXCEOElon Musk's claimthat Ukraine's military violated Starlink's terms of service, prompting the company to restrict Ukraine's access to the high-speed satellite technology.

Serhii Beskrestnov, a defense technology advisor to Ukrainian PresidentVolodymyr Zelenskyy,wrote an online poston Sunday contesting Musk's reason for temporarily throttling Ukraine's access to high-speed service from SpaceX's Starlink satellite communication systems.

Ukrainian officials previously said the restrictions disrupted the country's military drone services and left the countryvulnerable to Russian attacks.

Musk on Saturday claimed in apost on Xthat the "Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people."

Beskrestnov pushed back on Musk's allegation, arguing that pre-existing restrictions on the systems would have made it "physically impossible" for Ukraine to use Starlink in the types of strikes the SpaceX CEO described.

"It is very strange that Elon Musk is unaware of the operational limitations of Starlink in Ukraine," Beskrestnov wrote in apost on Telegram, noting that Starlink's civilian system in Ukraine "does not function over the territory of Russia" and that Ukrainian drones operating with Starlink have had a speed restriction of 70 to 90 km/h (roughly 43 to 56 miles per hour) for months.

"Consequently, it is PHYSICALLY IMPOSSIBLE for us to use commercial Starlink for deep-strike or medium-range strike operations," Beskrestnov wrote.

Ukraine officials acknowledged on Saturday that high-speed service for SpaceX's Starlink and Starshield satellite communications systems had been restored. The country has blamed that restricted service for disrupting its drone air defense capabilities during frequent Russian air attacks.

Starshield is SpaceX's military-focused satellite network for government and national security use, built on technology developed for Starlink, the company's broader commercial satellite internet network.

Before Musk acknowledged that he had restricted the systems, confusion and speculation abounded over who ordered the high-speed service changes.

At one point, Musk wrote in asocial media postthat the U.S. government was behind the decision, though PresidentDonald Trumpclaimed he hadno knowledge of the decision. Ukrainian officials have also said Starlink or the U.S.had imposed the restrictionswithout warning, leaving the country blindsided.

Musk has not explained the reported lack of notification to Ukraine before his company implemented the restrictions.

Musk and SpaceX did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment.

The restrictions on Starlink and Starshield in war-torn Ukraine have drivenUkraine and its alliesto seek or build alternative, "sovereign" satellite communication systems.

Poland's Deputy Minister of National Defense, Cezary Tomczyk, discussed his country's plans on apodcastcalled Influence Zone (Strefa Influenceów) earlier this month. Ukraine also announced partnerships with Norway andFinland's mobile giant Nokia, as well as satellite maker ICEYE, to develop alternatives.

Beyond Ukraine,several countriesare also exploring sovereign systems. The European Union is buildingIRIS², a constellation of hundreds of satellites, but it doesn't expect its first launches until 2029.

SpaceX's Starlink generated $5.25 billion in revenue in the third quarter of 2026, up from $3.1 billion a year earlier. Revenue from consumer Starlink subscribers totaled $3.12 billion, while the company generated $2.13 billion from government and enterprise customers during the quarter.

A wide array of customers, including non-government entities, the governments of Poland and France, and the Pentagon, have paid SpaceX to provide its Starlink and Starshield hardware and wireless internet services to Ukraine.

title: Audi defends plans for a $4 billion Georgia plant amid VW restructuring, tariffs
content:
DETROIT — Audi's CEO defended the carmaker's plans for anew $4 billion plant in Georgiaon Sunday, calling it a business decision aimed at growing sales and reducing exposure to U.S. tariffs.

The plant, set to be Audi's first in the U.S., wasannounced Saturdayby PresidentDonald Trumpduring a rally in Georgia, near where theVolkswagen-owned luxury brand plans to build the new SUV-producing facility.

"We have significantly greater ambitions for Audi in America," Audi CEO Gernot Dollner said during a media roundtable Sunday. "The United States is the second largest premium market in the world, and today we are not fully exploiting this potential. We are changing that."

The announcement comes amid anintense restructuring of its VWparent company, including plans to cut 50,000 jobs andclose four German plants, including an Audi facility, between 2031 and ​2034.

Dollner, who joined Trump at the rally, said the decision for a plant in the U.S. was years in the making, with more than 70 locations evaluated over "many months" and "intense" negotiations with public officials.

"This is not a decision against Germany. Germany remains the backbone of Audi," Dollner said. "We develop our cars here. Our technologies are created here, and Georgia does not take any task away from us in Germany."

Dollner said localized production is the best decision for the brand, which has struggled in sales this decade amid rising operational costs andTrump's tariffs on vehiclesfrom Germany and other countries into the U.S. Current tariffs on vehicles from Germany are 15%, down from 25%.

Last year, U.S. tariffs cost Audi 1.2 billion euros ($1.4 billion), as it imports all its vehicles for the U.S. market from Europe or Mexico.

Dollner said the Trump administration asked Audi to announce the new plant at the Georgia rally promoting Republicansahead of Nov. 3 midterm elections.

"It was … a three-year project that, at the end, by coincidence, led to that moment yesterday," he said Sunday. "With respect of the office and country, we joined the invitation."

Dollner noted Audi is the last major German luxury brand to establish U.S. production after Mercedes-Benz and BMW.

The company said the Georgia plant is expected to begin production of Audi's Q7, Q8 and Q9 in the early 2030s. The plant would have the capacity to produce up to 200,000 vehicles annually, roughly half of which the automaker said will be exported outside the U.S.

"This is to make Audi obviously a significant player here in the U.S. market," said Audi of America President Vito Paladino during the roundtable. He also said additional details on U.S. investments and production are forthcoming.

Audi's U.S. deliveries were roughly flat through the third quarter of this year, following a 16% decline from 2024 to 2025.

title: In pictures: Initially peaceful protests across France over inequality again descend into violence
content:
Mostly peacefulprotestsacrossFranceover a worsening cost-of-living crisis and growing inequality descended into violence for a second straight weekend.

France's Interior Ministry said 410,000 people took part in protests in several major cities, including Paris.

After rioters set fire to the historic city hall in Limoges and looters smashed supermarkets and luxury boutiques in Lyon last weekend, French authorities greatly stepped up security ahead of Saturday's protests.

In Paris on Saturday, riot police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse a group of around 500 hooded youths who hurled stones at officers, Reuters quoted a security official as saying.

In France's second city, Marseille, youths dragged large metal sheets to block a street, set fire to rubbish bins, and hurled rocks and bottles at riot police. The confrontations continued after sunset, and police said looters raided two jewelry shops, according to a Reuters report.

Clashes also flared in Lyon, Bordeaux and Grenoble, while police fired volleys of tear gas at demonstrators in Clermont-Ferrand, Lille, Nantes and Nice, according to the agency.

However, the violence was still less intense than a week ago, when looters and vandals went on the rampage in a number of French cities.

The demonstrationsbegan last monthas a group of high school students in suburban Paris lamented poor school conditions, including teacher shortages and unsatisfactory facilities. The demonstrations have since grown and evolved into nationwide protests.

France's economic and political woeshave sharply raised the cost of government borrowing. The yield on its10-year bondrose above 5% for the first time since 2002 this week, settling around 5.03% on Friday.

Some investors fear the country's debt problems could spread tothe rest of the euro zone.

title: Saudi Arabia says it intercepted missiles and drones from Iran-backed Houthis
content:
Saudi Arabiaintercepted drones and missiles headed for several cities, including the capital Riyadh, fired byIran-aligned Houthis on Sunday, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said.

The ongoing fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Yemen-based Houthis, combined with remarks by President Donald Trump last weeksuggesting that the U.S. and Israel are planning fresh strikeson Iran after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, drove oil prices to a six-month high Friday.

The official Saudi Press Agency quoted the spokesperson of the Saudi-led Coalition to Restore Legitimacy in Yemen, Turki Al-Maliki, as sayingtwodronesand aballistic missilewere "intercepted and destroyed" as they headed toward Riyadh.

The agency quoted Al-Maliki as saying that10 ballistic missileslaunched by the Houthis toward the southern region of Saudi Arabia were also intercepted, as was acruise missileheaded for the city of Khamis Mushait.

The Houthissaidin a Telegram post that they "carried out seven qualitative military operations using a number of ballistic missiles and drones."

The targets included Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and oil giant Saudi Aramco's facilities in Yanbu on Saudi Arabia's west coast as well as other airports and energy installations around the country, the Houthis said.

King Khalid International Airport said in a notice to travelers that it was resuming operations Sunday, using its Terminal 1 for domestic flights and Terminal 2 for overseas routes.

The airportsuspended operationson Oct. 10 following a strike that killed at least 13 people and injured around 300 others, making it the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.

Saudi Aramco did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

While the Houthis and Saudi Arabia have been exchanging strikes in recent weeks, concerns have been mounting among investors that the U.S. could soon resume its attacks on Iran.

The U.S. ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia last week amid the Houthi attacks.

Trump said Wednesday that the U.S. was not negotiating with Iran and something would happen "fairly soon."

The president's cryptic remarks came as U.S. officials told The New York Times that the U.S. and Israel have plans for fresh strikes on Iran after the midterm elections.

"I think there's more and more fears of escalation in the Middle East," Amrita Sen, Founder and Director of Energy Aspects, told CNBC's Squawk Box Europe on Friday.

"We keep getting asked by clients: 'Is it going to be before the midterms? Is it after the midterms?' So it's not a question of 'if.' People are asking if it's a question of 'when.' Our view remains that it's more likely after the midterms than before."

Rising tensions, worries about supply disruptions and concerns about possible fresh U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran helped push Brent crude to a six-month high Friday.

Brent futuresgained 3.1% to close at $116.72 a barrel, the highest international benchmark settlement since April 29. U.S.West Texas Intermediateadded 3.8% to settle at $103.27 a barrel. Brent added 6.2% for the week, the third consecutive week of gains. WTI advanced 2.3% for the week.

title: JetBlue creditors are working with restructuring adviser PJT Partners, WSJ reports
content:
A senior creditors group forJetBlue Airwaysis working with restructuring adviserPJT Partners, The Wall Street Journalreportedon Friday, citing people familiar with the matter.

A surge in jet fuel expenses due to the Iran war has pressured margins for U.S. airlines despite higher airfares and steady demand for air travel.

The carrier's shares, which are down 42% this year, closed 0.94% lower at $2.62 on Friday.

JetBlue is undergoing a financial and operational overhaul to cut costs and plans to expand its premium offerings.

As of June 30, JetBlue had $1.66 billion in cash and cash equivalents along with $8.5 billion of debt and finance lease obligations, according to its filings.

"JetBlue remains confident in its JetForward strategy and the progress being made toward returning to sustained profitability," the company said in an emailed statement.

PJT did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Read the complete Wall Street Journal report here.

title: Lula, Bolsonaro rally supporters on final day before Brazil presidential runoff
content:
BrazilianPresident Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro wrapped up their campaigns on Saturday ahead of Sunday's presidential runoff vote, mobilizing supporters and making a final push for undecided voters.

The two candidates have remained neck and neck in polls following astronger-than-expectedperformance by the right-wing senator in the first round. On Saturday, a CNT/MDA poll showed the senator with a 1.3-point lead.

Lula, who is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, kicked off his last day of campaigning with a march along Rio de Janeiro's iconic Copacabana beach, where thousands of supporters joined the leftist incumbent under a blazing sun.

"We're going to win the election for one simple reason: it's true that the people want change, (but) they want to move forward. They don't want to go backward," Lula told journalists before the rally.

Later, the president led another march in Sao Paulo, passing along Paulista Avenue, a traditional venue for political demonstrations in Brazil's largest city.

"It's so exciting to see everyone here. This is the kind of energy we want for Brazil. Brazil is ours," said Gisele Passos, a 61-year-old businesswoman at the Sao Paulo rally.

For many Lula supporters, the rallies carried a bittersweet undertone. The 80-year-old president and former union leader is widely expected to be making his final bid for office, lending the campaign's closing events the feel of a farewell tour.

"He's one of a kind. He has had an incredible, remarkable, and hard-fought journey. We're very proud of that," said Olga Leal, a 62-year-old retiree in Sao Paulo.

Bolsonaro, meanwhile, joined a motorcycle caravan in Belo Horizonte, the capital of Minas Gerais, a key battleground state. No candidate has won the presidency without carrying Minas Gerais since the country's return to democracy in the 1980s.

The senator led Lula by around 5 percentage points in the state in the first round.

"The time is almost here. There are only a few hours left before we shape the future of our nation for the next 30 or 40 years," said the lawmaker, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, in a social media video.

He later took part in a campaign march in his home state of Rio de Janeiro, which he has represented in the Senate since 2019.

The younger Bolsonaro was first backed by his father to run for the presidency last December. The former president was sentenced to over 27 years in prison for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 presidential election to Lula.

On Friday, Lula and Bolsonaro met for a final debate on TV Globo, the country's main free-to-air television channel, where they sparred over the cost of living and traded personal attacks.

title: Four ways Labour could raise money in the Budget without hiking income tax
content: ByBen ChuPolicy and analysis correspondentPublished3 hours agoWe're likely to hear a lot about the chancellor's "headroom" in this Budget.That is the cash buffer the government has to help meet its own fiscal rules and reduce borrowing.Economists think the buffer might have halved in the last six months from around Â£24bn to as low as Â£11bn, in part because of rising interest rates the government has been paying to borrow money from private investors.The Chancellor, John Healey, might need to raise money to restore it, which would show the government's plan to reduce borrowing by the end of this Parliament is still on track.At the same time, he is under pressure to find money to help people with the rising cost of living and to fund spending on defence. However, Labour's 2024 election manifesto pledged not to raise the rates of income tax, VAT or National Insurance.Increasingtaxes on capital gainsor extending the mansion tax had been raised as possible options but have since been ruled out by government sources.BBC Verify has looked at what other options could be on the table for the chancellor toraise some more money,externalon Wednesday.1. Increase taxes on banksBanks in the UK have seen profits rise in recent years because they have been able to charge people higher interest rates when borrowing money.And there iswidespread belief among bank bossesthat the chancellor is preparing to raise taxes on banks in this week's Budget.Think tank Tax Policy Associates estimates,externalthat increasing the surcharge that banks pay on corporation tax from 3% to 5.5% could potentially raise an additionalÂ£1bn to Â£2bna year for the Treasury.A higher tax would initially reduce the profits that banks have to distribute to their shareholders.Some shareholders will be wealthy investors. The banks have warned that additional taxescould deter them from investing in the UK,external, which could reduce jobs.And ordinary savers could be indirectly affected too, if theirpension investments include bank shares,external.Banks could also pass some of the tax burden on to their customers by offering lower savings rates or higher borrowing costs,research suggests.,external2. Higher taxes on gambling machinesFormer Prime MinisterGordon Brown has called on Healeyto hike the tax on electronic gaming machines - such as those found in betting shops and adult gaming centres which can offer payouts of Â£500 per game - citing the social harm imposed by problem gambling.The Social Market Foundation (SMF)think tank has estimated,externalthat doubling tax on these machines from 20% to 40% could raise could raise betweenÂ£275m and Â£460m- depending on how gamblers reacted to it.People who use gambling machines could also end up having the tax passed on to them through worse odds on games, though anti-gambling groups argue this could help discourage more people from using them.Research from the SMF found that gambling machines are increasingly clustered on some of the UK's most deprived high streets, and that one in four people who play casino games on these machines gamble at risky or harmful levels.Thegambling industry has argued,externalsuch a tax hike could cause betting shops, which own and operate the machines, to close down, by making them less profitable.It has also argued that betting shop closures couldreduce the money bookmakers contribute to horse racing,external, potentially putting jobs in that industry at risk too.3. Get online marketplaces to collect VATReports suggest the chancellor is preparing to announce that big online marketplaces such as Amazon, Ebay and Temu will bemade responsible for collecting taxowed by retailers selling on their platforms.The Treasury estimates it ismissing out on around Â£12bn a year,externalin VAT revenues that should be paid by companies, which it calls the "VAT tax gap".Tax experts say that part of the problem - although not accounting for the full Â£12bn of the VAT gap - is that some online sellers fail to comply with VAT rules, either by not charging VAT when they should or by failing to pass on VAT collected from customers to the government.Enforcement can be difficult because some firms that use platforms like Amazon to sell their products are based overseas and falsely present themselves as UK-established businesses.Others close down and reopen under different company names to escape their tax liabilities.Reports suggest that this move to make big online marketplaces responsible for collecting the tax - rather than the individual retailers - would clamp down on this form of tax evasion and could raise around Â£1bn in extra VAT a year.Amazon, which supports the move,has estimated it could raiseÂ£700m,externala year in VAT for the government.Some sellers could respond by raising prices or leaving the platform, which could have an impact on some shoppers.However, it would also level the playing field for online sellers, ensuring those businesses who charge VAT are not illegally undercut by those who break the rules and do not.4. Cut welfare spendingThe above three tax measures together would raise a maximum of only around Â£3.5bn a year.That would be small relative to the sums of money the chancellor might well need to restore his headroom and pay for any new spending.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in the summer he wanted a "fair and lasting" reduction to the UK's welfare bill, while the government is under pressure from opposition parties to find savings from working-age benefits.TheConservatives claim they could make savingsof Â£36bn a year by restricting people's access to welfare payments.Reform say they would save Â£50bna year in this way, although independent analysts say there are questions about how realistic it is to make such large savings.Working health and sickness benefits have risen sharply since the Covid pandemic and the overall cost is projected by the Office for Budget Responsibility to increase from Â£68bn this year to Â£81bn in 2031.Keir Starmer and Rachel Reevesattempted to reduce spending on these benefits,externalby Â£5bn a year by 2030, but wereforced to reverse courseafter a revolt by backbench Labour MPs.Independent welfare experts and economists say savings from the working age welfare budget are possible but would likely require upfront spending to help people into work, which could cancel out any near-term savings for the Treasury.Cuts to health and disability welfare wouldreduce the incomes of people who currently receive those payments,externaland/or those who would otherwise receive them in future - and campaigners warn of the risk of people being pushed into poverty.However, if more welfare claimants were also supported into work, their overall incomes could be maintained or even rise.Graphics by Callum Thomson and Lewis McBlane.What do you want BBC Verify to investigate?Get in touchWhat are you hoping for from the Budget? What questions do you have?Contact formRelated topicsUK economyLabour PartyJohn HealeyHM TreasuryUK taxes

title: Rosebank: Life on the oil field at the centre of a political storm
content: ByJames CookScotland editor,ÂReporting fromRosebank oil fieldPublished1 hour agoWhen we landed by helicopter at Rosebank, this oil field was at the centre of a political storm - and set to be in the path of a real one.We arrived on Wednesday morning, just a few hours after the UK government had granted consent for the production of gas from the Jackdaw field in the North Sea.But already attention was shifting to this wild and windy patch of the North Atlantic â the next big decision for Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh.Rosebank is bigger than Jackdaw, it would generate higher greenhouse gas emissions, and it could be far more lucrative for its owners, Adura and Ithaca.Image caption,Nicola Boyd loves her job on the Petrojarl Rosebank vesselThis summer, along with a camera crew, I travelled to Jackdaw, 150 miles east of Aberdeen.Now we were the first journalists to visit Rosebank.We came here - days before Storm Boelo arrived with strong winds and heavy rain - to scrutinise a controversial project which is at the heart of a national debate about climate change, energy policy and the economy.But we also hoped for a rare glimpse into life offshore."It's good fun, it's interesting, every day can change," said Nicola Boyd, who runs the helideck, and greeted us as we struggled out of our lifejackets and survival suits.Boyd has worked offshore for nearly a decade, including a year on Rosebank - where she spends two weeks at a time followed by three weeks' leave."It's a job I love," she added.Image caption,The Petrojarl Rosebank is moored in the North Atlantic waiting to see if production gets the go-ahead from the UK governmentIt's also a job that calls for steady legs and a strong stomach.Unlike the fixed Jackdaw platform, this installation â 80 miles north west of ShetlandÂ âÂ is a large ship, a floating production, storage and offloading vessel (FPSO) named the Petrojarl Rosebank.It's been chartered by the field's owners from Aberdeen-based Altera and, during my 48 hours on board, it was constantly but gently rolling on the North Atlantic swell.Those conditions may be misleading.With the understatement typical of an Orkney islander, lead mechanical technician Ewan Leonard told me the winter weather could be "a bit of a challenge.""Last week we had a 30m heave coming through," he said, referring to the swell, "so we'll probably suffer more of that as the winter goes on."Altera CEO Chris Brett told me that in the industry the environment west of Shetland is considered "as harsh as you get anywhere in the world."Whatever your view on that industry, the sheer scale of what humans have achieved in such conditions is impressive.Image caption,Ewan Leonard says the winter weather can be "a bit of a challenge"The deep reserves of skill, ingenuity and engineering prowess among the 122 people on board are obvious.The jobs are well-paid and, according to Ewan Leonard, the facilities are excellent."We have single-man cabins, there's good gym facilities, there's a lot of rec rooms here."Douglas Hogge, a production supervisor in charge of a team responsible for the safe extraction of oil and gas, agrees."There's the gym, the sauna," he said, adding "you can obviously go and get some fresh air. There's plenty of fresh air out there."There's even a cinema.Image caption,Food on board the ship was described as "fantastic""As you've seen yourself, the food is fantastic on board, so no complaints." added Leonard.Everyone we spoke to agreed with that, praising the talented chefs who sent out all sorts of delicious dishes, from braised ox cheek to mackerel to pork loin, day and night.As dusk gathers and the nightshift get ready for work with a strange breakfast of fillet steak and chocolate brownie pudding, the vessel begins to glow in the gloom.It is a strange sight, the decks criss-crossed by a bewilderingly complex array of pipes, valves and bright yellow steelwork.Image caption,The ship is an array of pipes, valves and bright yellow steelworkThe ship doesn't move far, rotating around a fixed central point called the turret to face into the weather, making life a little easier for those on board.If production is approved, oil and gas will be pumped up through the turret from wells in the field below, which contains an estimated 300m to 500m barrels, enough for perhaps 25 years."For myself and a lot of the guys, that would see us out to retirement," said Douglas Hogge."We need to see this approved," he added.Environmental campaigners strongly disagree. They've been trying to stop Rosebank for years, with some success."The future of the energy sector in the UK is renewable energy," said Tessa Khan, executive director of the campaigning group Uplift.Consent for production at Rosebank was first grantedunder the Conservative government in 2023.But in 2025, after a challenge by Greenpeace and Uplift,the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled the approvals of the UK's largest known untapped oil field and Jackdaw were unlawfulbecause they had failed to take into account the climate impact of actually burning the fossil fuels in cars, homes and factories.The judge, Lord Ericht, said the fields' developers could carry on with work short of producing oil and gas while they provided more detailed environmental assessments for the government and regulators to consider."We think Rosebank would be a disastrous decision and a terrible deal for ordinary people across this country," said Khan, urging prime minister Andy Burnham to prioritise renewables in his quest to re-industrialise the nation."If the government's interested in building investor confidence, giving the green light to a major new oil field is going to do the opposite," she argued.Whatever happens with Rosebank and Jackdaw, the long-term trend for the industry is clear and it is one of decline.It's a quarter of a century since oil production peaked and in recent yearsjobs in oil and gas have been disappearing much faster than they're being created in renewable energysuch as wind and solar power.The timeline of Jackdaw and RosebankThe oil from Rosebank would be loaded onto tankers via a gigantic hose and nozzle, which looks like the super-sized pump of an enormous floating filling station.From there it would be sold on the international market and, most likely, taken to continental Europe for refining.Opponents say that proves the project is of little benefit to the UK and should be rejected.Supporters argue that's not the case because UK and European energy markets are co-dependent, adding that Rosebank will generate millions in tax for the Treasury.Neil McCulloch, chief executive of Adura â which owns 80% of Rosebank and is a joint venture between Shell and the Norwegian state energy firm, Equinor â is optimistic.He points out that Rosebank contains not just oil but gas which would be piped to Shetland and on to the St Fergus terminal in Aberdeenshire, with the potential to heat 500,000 British homes at peak production.Approval of this project, argues McCulloch, could pave the way for four more Jackdaw-sized gas developments in the waters west of Shetland â Tornado, Tornado East, Tobermory and Suilven."We would like to proceed with them," he said.A surge in fossil fuel production if Rosebank is approved is exactly what campaigners fear.It would, argues Tessa Khan, exacerbate the deadly and damaging impact of climate change for British teachers, nurses, firefighters and families worried about their children while making "huge profits for companies that are already incredibly profitable".Image caption,The oil from Rosebank would be loaded onto tankers via a gigantic hose and nozzleWhen it comes to the impending UK government decision â which sources have told BBC News should come before Christmas â there is a strange mood at Rosebank.The decision in favour of Jackdawhas clearly encouraged many on board but it has also highlighted the jeopardy they are facing.For now, most workers we spoke to said they were just focusing on the job, with its strange rhythms and unusual restrictions â no ability to pop to the shops, no alcohol, a lot of special occasions missed.And for some on board, very particular cravings.For steward Liam Davidson, it is a desire to see his French bulldog, Bailey, at the end of his fortnight on board."My wee dog's at the heliport when I arrive," he said, "I do miss her."Image caption,It is hoped the decision on Rosebank will be made in the next few weeksFor Nicola Boyd, it's her double bed and a pizza delivery."I love seeing the family, but for me, it's the pizza," she told me.But this time there might be a delay in delivering Boyd herself.She is coming to the end of her fortnight but, as she helped us into our survival suits, the Met Office issued an amber weather warning for much of Scotland.For Rosebank, it seems, there are stormy seas ahead, one way or the another.Related topicsScotlandNorth Sea oil and gasOil & Gas industryClimateMore on this storyI will make final decision on Rosebank oil field, energy secretary insistsPublished2 days agoBurnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licencesPublished3 days ago

title: Obama, in Ohio, assails 'cruelty' and indecency from Trump and his allies in the midterm campaign
content:
Former PresidentBarack Obamaon Saturday seized on what he described as cruelty and indecency coming from PresidentDonald Trumpand his Republican allies, stepping into one of the nation's ugliest midterm fights as he worked to rally Democratic voters in battleground Ohio.

Obama specifically targeted Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who has doubled down on an ad featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Dr. Amy Acton. Trump and Vice PresidentJD Vancehave also defended the ad, even as Republican leaders across Ohio, including Gov. Mike DeWine, have called for its removal.

"In recent days, we've seen there is no line he will not cross, no low he will not sink to," Obama said of Ramaswamy, noting that Acton has "spoken movingly about her painful childhood and all she's experienced: abuse, neglect and homelessness."

"There's a decency we should expect out of our public officials," Obama continued. "And I don't know what's happened where the standards of behavior are so low that somebody could run an ad like that."

Obama, 65, remains the Democratic Party's best motivator nearly a decade after leaving the White House. He was set to campaign in Michigan later Saturday night, lending the Democratic Party his star power in midwestern battlegrounds that will help determine the balance of power in American politics next week.

Obama shared the stage with Acton and former three-term Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, who is looking to unseat Republican Sen. Jon Husted.

Although Ohio has become more reliably Republican, it's been a hotly contested battleground this year. Trump and Vance have both visited the state in recent weeks to drum up support for Husted and Ramaswamy. And the controversy over Ramaswamy's ad has ratcheted up the already high temperature.

Ramaswamy has defended his decision to press ahead with the ad as fair game. Trump aggressively defended the ad, which has become a national flashpoint in the final days of the midterms, as he voted in West Palm Beach on Saturday.

"This is a disgrace," Trump said. "The mother said that Amy Acton is a liar and she's no good. And you know what? I don't think you can get a better reference on that." He added that if his own mother had said anything bad about him, it would be front and center.

The Ramaswamy campaign video features Acton's birth mother, Donna Arthur, calling her "a liar" and insinuating she has mental health issues.

Acton, Ohio's COVID-19-era health director, has made no secret of facing homelessness and abuse as a child. Arthur lost custody of her children after their stepfather, Arthur's husband, was indicted on a charge of rape involving Acton.

The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978. Cledith Arthur failed to appear in court and became a fugitive. Donna Arthur remained married to him until his death in 2004.

Appearing before Obama, Acton spoke as if addressing Ramaswamy directly.

"My opponent has chosen to exploit, intentionally, my childhood to save his stumbling campaign, but it's not going to work," she said. "Decency still matters." She added: "Mr. Ramaswamy, you are not just out of touch, you are out for yourself and you are a danger to my state. Apparently there is no low to which you won't stoop."

After wrapping up in Ohio, Obama headed to a rally in Detroit for Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official working to unite the Democratic base in Michigan after winning a divisive primary by less than a percentage point. El-Sayed is running against former Rep. Mike Rogers, a Republican.

Obama's appearance in the city, which is three-quarters Black, could bolster El-Sayed's support among Black voters. In the primary, his opponent Haley Stevens won Wayne County, which includes Detroit, by about 6 percentage points. Former Vice President Kamala Harris, the first Black and South Asian vice president, campaigned for El-Sayed in September.

El-Sayed criticized Obama after his 2012 reelection for not following through on all of his progressive campaign promises, writing that Obama "was not the right choice — he just wasn't the wrong one."

El-Sayed told reporters earlier this month that he appreciated the former president, calling him "foundational" to his ability to run for office, but he still disagreed with elements of Obama's presidency.

Michigan also has open races for governor, attorney general and secretary of state. Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic nominee for governor, is slated to appear on the ballot alongside others. Benson is running against Republican Rep. John James.

Obama will headline a rally in Georgia next week with Sen. Jon Ossoff and gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms. Trump is slated to speak in Georgia Saturday.

In Ohio, Obama also criticized Trump for failing to lower costs, a key campaign promise, saying the president has instead focused on building a new White House ballroom and helipad on the South Lawn.

"I don't know if you've noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovation," he quipped. "He should be on HGTV." He went on: "There's gold everywhere. He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory."

The former Democratic president acknowledged that the nation has Trump for another two years, until his term ends. But voters are not stuck with Trump's allies, he said.

"We're not stuck with a spineless Congress and Republican governors who are handling lawlessness and carelessness and cruelty and indifference for working people," Obama said. "After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence … you get a chance to say enough is enough."

title: Trump casts his midterm election ballot early in Florida
content:
President Donald Trump cast his ballot in the midterm elections Saturday, saying he voted for all Republicans in Florida before speaking at a Georgia rally.

Trump and first lady Melania Trump arrived together at their West Palm Beach polling location, the Palm Beach County Supervisor of Elections office, after the president spent the morning at his nearby golf course. Trump has been criticized for voting by mail despite his long history of railing against that method of submitting ballots.

Asked if he voted the party line, Trump, who was wearing an "I Voted" sticker, said, "Very much so."

Speaking to reporters at the poll site, Trump again defended an ad from Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy. The ad has faced intense blowback for featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Dr. Amy Acton, who lost custody of her children after her husband, the children's stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton when she was 12.

Trump also defended his decision to instruct his administration to file its lawsuit toblock certificationof the U.S. Senate race in Alaska if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses over the inclusion of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot.

As for the war in Iran, he said, "I may have to finish it off. Or maybe they'll make a deal, but I'm not sure. Either way, we win."

Melania Trump, who this week brokered a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the ravaged, Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky so that humanitarian aid could be delivered and civilians evacuated, was asked whether she might travel to Ukraine.

"We will see," she told reporters.

In Florida, Trump has endorsed Republican Rep. Byron Donalds, who is running against David Jolly, a Republican-turned-independent-turned-Democrat, to succeed term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis.

He has also campaigned for Republican Sen. Ashley Moody, who is running to fill the last two years of Secretary of State Marco Rubio's former Senate term against progressive state lawmaker Angie Nixon.

title: Violence flares in Paris after massive, largely peaceful protests across France
content:
Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators marched in France on Saturday, with largely peaceful rallies giving way to clashes in Paris and Marseille as night fell despite a huge security operation aimed at preventing a repeat of last week's unrest.

The Interior Ministry said 410,000 people took part in protests nationwide, though unions said the true figure was twice as high.

The main demonstration took place in Paris, where around 110,000 people marched on the capital's southeastern fringes, denouncing rising living costs and growing inequality.

The atmosphere deteriorated sharply after the rally ended. Riot police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse a group of around 500 hooded youths who hurled stones at officers, a security official said.

In France's second city, Marseille, youths dragged large metal sheets to block a street, set fire to rubbish bins, and hurled rocks and bottles at riot police.

The confrontations continued after sunset, and police said they raided two jewelry shops.

Clashes also flared in Lyon, Bordeaux and Grenoble, while police fired volleys of tear gas at demonstrators in Clermont-Ferrand, Lille, Nantes and Nice.

However, the violence was still less intense than a week ago, when looters and vandals went on the rampage in a number of French cities.

Authorities deployed 70,000 police officers and gendarmes, 10,000 more than a week earlier, after conceding they had underestimated the scale of the unrest on October 17.

"We have to be ultra, ultra responsive," Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told reporters on Saturday, accusing far-left activists and criminal gangs of seeking to foment violence.

Much of central Paris looked like a city under lockdown, with shopkeepers boarding up storefronts, museums closing their doors, and more than 20 metro stations shut.

Business groups urged retailers to stay closed after thousands of shops and businesses across France were damaged or looted last weekend.

"There are hardly any customers, so it's not really worth staying open," said Oskar, manager of a Kiton boutique in Paris.

Several of the capital's best-known cultural institutions, including the Louvre, the Musée d'Orsay and the Paris Opera, closed for the day as a precaution, leaving tourists frustrated.

"Everything's boarded up and we're not quite sure where we should be," said Xavier Dolliole, a tourist from the US city of New Orleans.

The nationwide unrest began last month with small student demonstrations in suburban Paris to denounce school conditions. As it spread into a broader protest against France's economic situation, it also prompted demonstrators to take to the streets in neighboring countries.

On Saturday, Belgian police used tear gas and pepper spray as they clashed in Brussels with anti-government demonstrators, while protests took place in a number of Italian cities for a second weekend.

Leftist leaders in France denounced a government move to limit the number of authorized marches in many cities, as well as a last-minute decision to shift the Paris event to the southeastern fringes of the capital.

Hard-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who joined the Paris rally, hailed what he called a "magnificent mass display of collective discipline and self-restraint."

He predicted the protests would continue until President Emmanuel Macron, whose mandate expires next year, addressed France's social malaise, one of the world's richest nations, but with a growing debt mountain that has alarmed investors.

"Given the current situation, I think he will come to understand that this will happen again every week. There is still time for (Macron) to give in. After that, the only thing left to him will be the exit door," Melenchon told reporters.

Many demonstrators have accused the government of overreacting, as soldiers were dispatched to patrol the Champs-Élysées, a grand boulevard lined with luxury shops and restaurants.

"We shed tears for shops, not for the people who are being impoverished all year round," said Clara Lebbadi, a 22-year-old arts student.

"My friend and I almost didn't come because we were scared, but we came precisely because it's important not to let repression win," she added.

The first authorized march on Saturday passed off peacefully in Orléans, around 120 km (75 miles) south of Paris, where demonstrators rallied against Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally, which is holding a party congress in the city.

A shooting west of Paris on Friday heightened tensions. A gunman suspected of acting out of Islamophobic hatred killed one person and wounded four others, including a 12-year-old girl.

"We have come to tell the far right, face-to-face, that we are not afraid," said Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of Saint-Denis and a member of Melenchon's France Unbowed party.

title: American embassies tighten security as Iran threat warnings intensify ahead of U.S. midterm elections
content:
U.S. embassy officials were on heightened alert around the Middle East as new reports said Iran is in the "advanced stages" of planning attacks against Americans Friday.

A memo from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said agencies received intelligence that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" in the region, according to aNew York Times report, and that the threats applied to "certain other countries" as well.

The warnings come after theU.S. ordered non-emergency government employeesto leave Saudi Arabia this week, as attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis have worsened and the broader war between the U.S. and Tehran nears its eighth month.

The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said itdestroyed two ballistic missilesfired by the group Saturday, aimed towards Taif and Yanbu.

Despite rising tensions, an Iranian official told The Associated Press on Saturday that Tehran remains open to talks with the U.S. under the former Pakistan-brokered deal that was agreed to in June. Reza Amiri Moghadam, Iran's ambassador to Islamabad, said Iranian officials are prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the Trump administration lifts its naval blockade, AP reported, but he said Washington has rebuffed the proposal.

The Trump administration has vowed to put off military strikes on Iran after the midterm elections on Nov. 3, as the fallout from the war in Iran has caused a major disruption in the U.S. economy — with inflation and affordability the top concerns for voters who will decide control of Congress early next month.

Rising Middle East tensions sent oil prices soaring this week. BenchmarkBrent crude futurestopped $116 a barrel, asix-month high. U.S.West Texas Intermediaterose 3.8% to settle over $103 a barrel.

title: Retail investors are not more sophisticated than 30 years ago, says former hedge fund manager
content:
Retail investors who are trying to beat the market by buying individual stocks and complex exchange-traded funds may be better off with broad market index funds, according to Elm Wealth's Victor Haghani.

"I'm not sure that investors are that much more sophisticated than they were 30 years ago," the firm's founder and chief investment officer told CNBC's"ETF Edge"this week. "We still are human beings and we're subject to certain kinds of biases — particularly extrapolation bias where whatever has happened recently in the past we tend to believe that it's going to continue into the future."

Haghani, who was a founding partner at hedge fund Long-Term Capital Management, emphasizes cost-effective investment strategies as a priority at his current firm.

"It's an environment that continues to be tough for individual non-professionals to generate alpha," he said. "[Retail investors are] just very well served by having some exposure to broader index funds overall."

According to Haghani, access to elaborate strategies doesn't necessarily provide advantages.

"Whether it's Citadel or Jane Street or Hudson River Trading, they're just minting money every single day. So, it's an opportunity-rich environment — if you happen to have a billion dollars to spend on tech each year," he said. "If you're a retail investor sitting at home and trying to find opportunities, you have to realize that probably on the other side of your trades is [Citadel CEO] Ken Griffin or whoever, and it's probably not going to end all that well."

However, RBC Capital Markets' Valerie Grimba sees sophisticated funds playing a strategic role in retail investors' portfolios.

"More choice is ultimately a good thing," the firm's director of global ETF strategy said in the same interview.

She said funds holding 10 to 15 stocks can help investors participate in specific investment themes without having to identify their eventual biggest winner, while derivative-based products can be used to generate income in various ways.

But Grimba also emphasized that investors need to understand the holdings and trade-offs of the strategies they choose.

"It's more important than ever for an individual investor to understand what they're buying," she said. "You should be able to explain to your friend what it is in the ETF and what you're buying."

title: Fact vs. fiction: Doctors share whether peptides are safe and effective
content:
From YouTube influencers to Reddit threads, the health and wellness side of the internet is full of talk about peptides.

The term refers to a class of chemical compounds made up of short chains of amino acids. In the wellness market, synthetic peptides are often sold to consumers as injectables, which some health influencers say can bring a wide range of health benefits from muscle recovery and longevity to improved sexual function. Some peptides, including GLP-1 drugs commonly used for weight loss or diabetes, are heavily researched and federally approved for medical use. Many other forms of peptides are not.

Yet even some lightly researched peptides may be on their way to pharmacy shelves. The Department of Health and Human Services isreportedlyplanning to allow specialty pharmacies to compound certain synthetic peptides that have the support of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., whotold podcaster Joe Roganthat he is a "big fan" of the injectables in a February 2026 interview. As reported, the move would be an interim access policy covering some specific peptides not currently approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

Such a move would be controversial from a regulatory point of view: Multiple peptides, including one of the compounds reportedly included in the health department's proposal, appear on an FDA list of injectables that "may present significant safety risks." That compound, known as BPC-157, has shown potential anti-inflammatory effects in some animal and lab studies but has not yet been subject to large-scale human testing for safety or effectiveness.

"There are a few reasons why, but one of the main ones is the absence of evidence," including robust human studies on safety and effectiveness, saysDr. Caleb Alexander, a professor of epidemiology and medicine at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.

Yet consumer interest and regulatory momentum for peptides are growing. So here's what you need to know about peptides, from why they're the subject of such conversation to whether or not they're safe or effective to use.

Peptides are "kind of like the building blocks of proteins," saysDr. Alison Dempsey, a dermatologist at the Weill Cornell Medicine and NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital.

Several different types of peptides are naturally found in the body, like insulin and endorphins. Peptides can also be synthesized in labs, according toHarvard Health Publishing. GLP-1s, like Ozempic, are FDA-approved synthetic peptides, Dempsey says.

Injectable variations of synthetic peptides that haven't been approved by the FDA — such as BPC-157 and GHK-Cu, the latter of which has been marketed as a potential anti-aging drug — are the peptides that are making headlines at the moment, saysDr. Pieter Cohen, an associate professor at Harvard Medical School and internist at Cambridge Health Alliance.

One likely factor behind synthetic peptides gaining more attention has been the success of drugs like Ozempic at addressing health concerns such as obesity and diabetes, according to Cohen. "That probably opened up [the idea that] there must be this magical world of these other peptides that we can have access to, that will do these sort of similar magical things in other areas," he says.

However, Cohen and other health experts have their concerns. After all, a compound's status as a peptide "doesn't mean it's close to Ozempic in any way, shape or form ... in terms of both its chemical structure or its effects on the human body," says Cohen.

Synthetic peptides advertised on social media and sold on the so-called gray market — often produced by overseas sellers and sold to U.S. consumers outside the normal American drug regulatory system — come with marketing claims such as boosting longevity, improving sleep quality, strengthening the immune system and even enhancing skin health and sexual function, according to Alexander.

Particularly among the people who consider GLP-1s a form of miracle drug, consumers may simply want to believe that the weight loss medicine's chemical cousins could have similar effects on other elements of human health. "Unfortunately, when it comes to peptides marketing, word of mouth has strongly surpassed where we are with any type of research," Dempsey says.

The health experts who spoke with CNBC Make It recommend against using any injectable peptides that aren't approved by the FDA, especially if you're unsure where or how they were produced. Always consult with a medical professional before making any major changes that can affect your health.

"My recommendation is not to use any of the novel, unstudied injectable peptides because we simply do not know if they work. And if they do work, if they're safe," Cohen says. When buying peptides on the gray market, you can receive entirely different compounds or doses, and some may be contaminated with bacteria or other concerning materials, he says.

"There's concerns both about the potential risks, but also about the unclear level of benefit from these products," Alexander says.

"We have a great regulatory system governing prescription drugs in the United States," Alexander adds. "For advocates of these products that really believe in them, I hope that they'll put their money where their mouth is, and do the studies that are necessary so that we can understand the true safety and effectiveness of the products."

title: Ukraine says Starlink and Starshield high speed restrictions have been lifted
content:
Ukrainesaid Saturday that high-speed service has been restored forSpaceX's Starlink and Starshield satellite communication systems, a day after declaring that they remained throttled. Ukrainian official said the service disruption left the country vulnerable to Russian attacks.

"The monitoring systems of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine officially record the restoration of the speed of Starlink/Starshield," it said in astatement. "The connection remains stable [while equipment is moving] at speeds over 400 km/h (249 miles per hour)."

"Previously, monitoring systems recorded limitations in the operation of Starlink/Starshield. Now the speed indicators have been restored," the ministry added.

Starlink is SpaceX's broader commercial satellite internet network, while Starshield is the company's government operations built on Starlink technology.

SpaceX did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

Since Oct. 14,Ukrainian officialshave accused Elon Musk's SpaceX of undermining the country's ability to defend itself byimposing speed limitson Starshield, the military-grade offering of its Starlink satellite internet service. Officials said any drone traveling above 100 mph lost its connection, disrupting some missions.

Despite recent comments from U.S. PresidentDonald Trumpindicating service was restored, Ukraine's Starshield terminals continued to experience problems on Friday, said Dmitri Alperovitch, chairman of the Silverado Policy Accelerator, a Washington, D.C., think tank focused on energy, defense tech and global trade.

Ukrainian PresidentVolodymyr Zelenskyysaid in a Fridaypost on Xthat the restrictions on Starlink and Starshield "are still there," and added, "The speed has not been restored." He noted that the country is also waiting for the U.S. to deliver missile interceptors "that were already agreed on."

"Things have become harder — partly because of the Starlink and Starshield policies and speed limits," Zelenskyy wrote. "But our frontline is still holding and I am proud of how strong our people are."

Ukraine's Ministry of Defense said it continues to monitor the systems' operations.

"This result is, above all, important for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics, and communications," Defense Minister Yevgeny Khmara said in the statement.

Lawmakers in the U.S.fromboth partieshave called for a formal probe into Musk and SpaceX over alleged unilateral changes the company made to its services in Ukraine.

title: Why popular airplanes are getting scrapped years early
content:
GOODYEAR, Ariz. — An Airbus A320neo, one of the world's most popular planes, rolled off the Mobile, Alabama, factory line in July 2022, painted bright yellow for its next destination: Spirit Airlines.

It was built to fly for decades. But this May, less than four years later, it was stripped for parts worth millions and crushed, the steel teeth of an excavator tearing through its fuselage at a facility on the outskirts of Phoenix.

More aircraft are getting dismantled years, if not decades, earlier than expected, industry executives told CNBC. It is the result of a shortage of parts, none more precious and expensive than aircraft engines, that has exasperated airlines and driven up costs foryears.

Even after the engines are removed, firms are looking for parts as varied as landing gear and antennae to sell.

"It's the first time in my career that involved purchasing an aircraft that's less than five years since date of manufacture," said Bill Thompson, vice president who leads aircraft and engine acquisition for the Americas at aviation asset management and trading firmEirTrade Aviation, which bought the less than 4-year-old Airbus A320neo earlier this year.

He said the company paid "single-digit" millions each for that airplane and a similarly aged one, and it expects to make a profit from selling the more than 1,000 parts it took off them before they were crushed.

"I don't know if you're going to sell the coffee makers but you never know. Sometimes you do," he said.

Twenty-one newest-generation aircraft were torn down from June 2025 through this past August, according to aviation data and advisory firm IBA Group. The scrapped planes were 6.4 years old on average, and included mostly Airbus but also someBoeingplanes. That compares with an average retirement age for narrow-body airplanes of 21.7 years, IBA said.

"Anytime that you end up with any period of market softness in aircraft availability, engine availability, it's going to cause investors to look at other options," said Simon Goodson, CEO of AerFin, a company that buys, sells, repairs and leases aircraft and parts. "We always say to our aircraft and engine traders, 'Please don't fall in love with the metal.'"

Hundreds of aircraft are retired each year as manufacturers ramp up production for airlines, so older planes are swapped out for newer, more fuel-efficient models.

But aside from retiring aging planes, some owners don't want to wait around for replacement parts or repairs on younger jets.

"A year might not sound that long, but does three or four years?" said Dave Querio, CEO of Ascent Aviation Services, a company that repairs, modifies, stores and disassembles aircraft, based in Marana, Arizona, outside of Tucson. "That's the issue for the aircraft that came in in '23, '24 and '25."

In some cases, owners can reap more for the parts than they can selling the plane or paying storage costs and waiting for it to get back in the air again.

Querio said he hasn't seen "the volume of younger aircraft being torn down as I'm seeing today."

A major reason for the young retirements is the long wait and rising prices for jet engines.

One problem is that cutting-edge engines that burn hotter and use less fuel arecoming up for maintenancefar earlier than airlines expected.

The maintenance requests have kept engine repair and overhaul facilities backed up, from those owned by manufacturing giantsGE AerospaceandRTXunit Pratt & Whitney to smaller, independent ones. Airlines and leasing firms have been hunting for spare parts and engines anywhere they can find them, like here in Goodyear, Arizona.

The trend has added more fuel to the already hot secondhand parts market. An engine fan blade could cost $50,000 or even more than $100,000 for bigger jets, Goodson said. Engines that power some Airbus A320neo aircraft have 20 of those blades. A disc for the engine, meanwhile, could cost between $1 million and $2 million.

An enginerecallbecause of a manufacturing defect has backed up repair shops and grounded hundreds of Airbus planes around the world.Spirit Airlinesbore thebruntof that problem in the United States, years before the airlinecollapsed.

The engine is made by Pratt & Whitney, which issued the recall in 2023 after discovering contaminated powdered metal used in making some parts. Those engines are worth close to $17 million this year at the high end, up 60% from the upper end of the range in 2019, according to IBA.

Airlines are removing some engines off retired planes to keep current aircraft flying while they wait for engines to come back from the shop.

"So you're just playing Legos and moving engines on and off aircraft," said Mike Stengel, a partner at AeroDynamic Advisory, an aerospace consulting firm.

The problems are driving up the cost to buy or rent one of the popular engines to record levels.

Renting one is ranging from about $160,000 to $180,000 a month, according to IBA data. A competing engine for the A320neo family made by CFM International, a joint venture ofGE Aerospaceand France's Safran, is far from a bargain,renting in a similar range of $130,000 to $180,000 a month.

The problems with young retirements predate Spirit's collapse.

The 4-year-old Airbus plane that was torn down outside Phoenix in May is a key example. The aircraft was put in storage because of the engine recall, and it stayed until it was torn apart.

But the company's demise has brought more of its Airbus fleet to the market, forcing owners to figure out if it's worth the wait for engines or other parts.

CNBC visitedAerSale'sfacility in Goodyear on a scorching day in late June, less than two months after Spirit collapsed, where dozens of the idle yellow planes were stored. It was so soon after the airline's demise that a former Detroit-based Spirit captain, Glenn Zecchin, popped in and asked about opportunities toferry Spirit's aircraft to the desert, and to peek in on his former airline's planes.

"I knew the airplanes were there, and I wanted to see what happened," said Zecchin, who is now flying corporate jets.

A jet parked at the storage facility and maintenance hangar still had Spirit in-flight menus and safety cards in the bungee cord seatbacks. Pilot manuals were still in the cockpit.

Not all of these aircraft will be destroyed. Some companies that owned Spirit's planes before bankruptcy will just sell their parts, but some may keep the planes in storage. Other aircraft may go on to fly for other airlines, with potential carriers ripping out Spirit's tight 28-inch seat pitch for something roomier.

But as long as they're not flying, it means paying storage fees, which vary by aircraft type. Some planes in desert facilities — selected because the arid climate can preserve the aircraft better and avoid corrosion — can sit for decades.

Others won't make it back into the air if there's enough demand for the parts and too long of a wait to get the plane flying again.

"After you get rid of all the valuable equipment and sell it back into the aftermarket, what's really left is just a metal carcass that you will literally take a crane and crush," said AeroDynamic's Stengel. Then the owner can "sell it to recyclers that will make of it what they will, maybe into beer cans or something outside of aerospace."

Ascent's Querio said some owners opt to take that route.

"It's a little melancholy to watch it at times," he said. "But sometimes, it's kind of a thrill to ... see how fast an aircraft can be crunched up and sent off to the smelter."

— CNBC'sErin Blackcontributed to this report.

title: Berkshire shares shake the Buffett blues with new all-time highs
content:
(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign uphereto receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)

After almost 18 months, Berkshire Hathaway shares have entirely erased all the ground they lost in the wake ofWarren Buffett's surprise announcementat the 2025 shareholders meeting that he would step down as CEO at the end of that year.

On Friday, May 2, 2025, theClass Ashares closed at $809,350. TheClass Bshares finished at $539.80.

The meeting was the following day, Saturday, May 3.

On Monday, May 5, BRK.A dropped 4.9% and BRK.B lost 5.1%.

CNBC.com noteda14% drop in Q1 operating earnings, also announced that Saturday, may have contributed to the declines.

It also relayed some reassurance from analysts like Brian Meredith at UBS who predicted the company's culture and strategy would "remain unchanged" under new CEO Greg Abel.

"Buffett leaves a company that is less reliant on his investing capabilities, with an array of leading businesses with strong cash flows."

Investors, however, were apparently not reassured.

As the stock fell, there were fears a "Buffett premium" was evaporating.

Three months later, at their lowest closes of the year, BRK.A had lost 14.3% of its value and the more widely held B shares were down almost 15%.

Since then, they've rallied by 18%, and on Tuesday this week both classes topped their pre-announcement levels to set fresh all-time closing highs.

They were higher still on Thursday, setting new closing highs of $820,500 and $546.97.

Friday they lost almost 1% but remain roughly one-half of a percentage point above their highs just before the 2025 meeting.

Berkshire's gains have reduced its year-to-date deficit against the benchmark S&P to less than four percentage points.

A majority of the net gain in points between the August 2025 low and now has been racked up this month.

Berkshire's B shares have gained almost 9% since the start of October, strongly outperforming theS&P 500'sdip of 0.4% and an almost 4.8% drop for theequal-weightNYSE Fang+ index, which tracks10 megacap tech names, includingMeta,NVIDIA, andAlphabet.

Investors have been rotating out of high-flying tech and AI stocks in recent weeks amid growingconcerns their massive spending on computing infrastructure won't produce the sustained profits they envision.

Berkshire, by contrast, is "the ultimate anti-AI play,"according to aBarron'sheadlinethis week.

"With more than $350 billion in cash and equivalents on its balance sheet and close to $50 billion of annual after-tax earnings from a diverse group of businesses, Berkshire arguably is the most defensive megacap stock in the market."

And onCNBC's"Morning Call" Monday morning, Adam Patti of VistaShares, which runs anETF that tracks Berkshire's portfolio, said the market's turn away from its long-running "momentum-driven frenzy" comes at a good time.

"The market spent a year pricing Berkshire without Buffett. I think it's finally decided Abel can, in fact, run it" and likes that he's taking advantage of the company's cash.

"Berkshire is a coiled spring. When it comes back, it comes back fast and furious."

But, as Patti notes, Berkshire isn't completely separated from the AI world.

CEO Greg Abel has said providing energy to the growing number of AI data centers is a "significant opportunity for Berkshire and Berkshire Hathaway Energy" as long as rates don't rise for its other customers.

AndBerkshire has a now $34 billion position in Alphabet, one of AI's biggest players.

Some links may require a subscription:

Charlie Munger and Warren Buffett admittheir biggest errors are often "mistakes of omission" that don't appear in Berkshire's balance sheet.

AUDIENCE MEMBER: Mr. Munger, I know you're fond of evoking humility to promote rational thought. So my question is, what's the most recent business mistake that you've made, Mr. Munger, and why did it occur? (Laughter)

WARREN BUFFETT: I'm going to take notes on this one. (Laughter)

CHARLIE MUNGER: The mistakes that have been most extreme in Berkshire's history are mistakes of omission. They don't show up in our figures. They show up in opportunity costs.

In other words, we have opportunities, we almost do it. In retrospect, we can tell that we were very much mistaken not to do it.

In terms of the shareholders, those are the ones in our history that it really cost the most. And very few managements do much thinking or talking about opportunity costs.

WARREN BUFFETT: Billions and billions and billions. I might as well say it. (Laughter)

CHARLIE MUNGER: Right, right. And we keep doing it. (Laughter)

WARREN BUFFETT: Some might say we're getting better at it. (Laughter)

CHARLIE MUNGER: I don't like mentioning the specific companies, because the — you know, we may, in due course, want to buy them again and have an opportunity to do so at our price.

But practically everywhere in life, and in corporate life, too, what really costs, in comparison with what easily might have been, are the blown opportunities. I mean, it just — it's an awesome amount of money...

WARREN BUFFETT: I might add that when we speak of errors of omission, of which we've had plenty, and some very big ones, we don't mean not buying some stock where we — a friend runs it, or we know the name and it went from one to 100. That doesn't mean anything. It's only —

We only regard errors as being things that are within our circle of competence.

So if somebody knows how to make money in cocoa beans, or they know how to make money in a software company or anything, and we miss that, that is not an error, as far as we're concerned.

What's an error is when it's something we understand, and we stand there and stare at it, and we don't do anything.

Or worse yet, what really gets me is when we do something very small with it. We do an eyedropper's worth of it, when we could do it very big.

Charlie refers to that elegantly when I do that sort of thing as when I'm sucking my thumb. (Laughter)

And there really — I mean, we have been thumbsuckers at times with businesses that we understood well.

And it may have been because we started buying, and the price moved up a little, and we waited around hoping we would get more at the price we originally started — there could be a lot of things.

But those are huge mistakes. Conventional accounting, of course, does not pick those up at all. But they're in our scorebook.
