title: Nvidia's role as AI financier faces first big test as neoclouds take market hit
content:
Nvidia'semergence as financier for the global AI buildout is facing its first major stress test as credit markets tighten for key partners.

After creating the chips that powered the early stages of the generative artificial intelligence era, Nvidia turned to using its financial prowess to fund AI model developers, data center companies and a host of so-called neoclouds. CEOJensen Huang'sstrategy has been to not only build the most advanced technology but to provide customers with investment as well as help them take out loans so his systems can reach many more hands.

That's meant taking full advantage of Nvidia's investment grade credit rating and providing backstop guarantees on mega-projects for OpenAI so that buildouts can get funded at lower interest rates.

As of its last quarterlyfinancial filingin July, Nvidia had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, in addition to its guarantee on up to $105 billion for chips, land and power at a proposed 10 gigawatt OpenAI data center in Ohio. The company signed as a tenant for $20 billion in future data center leases, which will later be assigned to third parties.

For the vast majority of these deals, Nvidia won't have to pay up unless participants in the project default.

"If the demand for compute doesn't meet these really super lofty expectations, we're going to have a problem," said David Trainer, founder and CEO of financial research firm New Constructs, in an interview.

Nvidia declined to comment for this story.

Market conditions may soon test Nvidia's mettle. Shares of neocloudsCoreWeave,NebiusandIREN, all cash-burning companies in Nvidia's portfolio, are down at least 30% this month. CoreWeave, the biggest of the group, has seen the spread on its credit default swaps soar past 11%, as investors are forced to pay up for insurance against default.

Nvidia has backed other neoclouds that have run into challenges.

The company is an investor in Australian AI cloud provider Firmus, which abruptlywithdrewits IPO plans this month, as well asNscaleout of the U.K. and SoftBank-backedSB Energy. Both of those companies filed to go public in the U.S. in September but haven't provided updates on their plans in weeks.

Nvidia wrapped up a third straight down week on Wall Street on Friday, with its stock now off 7.6% in October, on pace for its worst month since November of last year.

Huang reiterated his confidence in the market this week, telling CNBC on Thursday that demand for neoclouds is "off the charts."

"What is missing in the middle is the working capital to fuel that growth," HuangtoldCNBC's Arjun Kharpal on the sidelines of the company's GTC conference in Berlin. "Because there's just so much demand across so many sectors of AI, there's a scarcity of capital."

Nvidia has taken equity stakes in dozens of companies, including big investments in OpenAI and Anthropic. Its portfolio is worth $99 billion as of the second quarter.

Investors told CNBC that a big question surrounding Nvidia is how the company can use its cash and $5 trillion market cap to get more chips into customers' hands, and how much risk it will assume in the process.

Nvidia graphics processing units are critical for training and deploying AI models. Revenue in the latest fiscal year hit $216 billion, up roughly eightfold since OpenAI launched ChatGPT in late 2022.

Before the AI boom, Nvidia sold graphics cards that could fit into a standard server rack or PC. Its newest systems are much larger and more expensive. Nvidia's flagship Vera Rubin product is a seven-foot rack containing 72 GPUs and weighing as much as a pickup truck. It costs more than $7 million, according to aMorgan Stanleyestimate.

While Nvidia still dominates the AI chip market, competition is emerging from the likes ofGoogle, which rents out tensor processing units (TPUs) inside its massive cloud offering, andAdvanced Micro Devices, which launched its first AI rack calledHeliosin July.

Cash is Nvidia's other great advantage. The company generated $70 billion in free cash flow in the first half of this year, while AMD totaled just over $4 billion and Google parent Alphabet wentcash flow negativein the second quarter to fund its buildout.

That's a big edge for Nvidia in building out its ecosystem. The company is now offering a full-service platform complete with software, services, integrated hardware and, for many customers, financing assistance.

Nvidia's most recentquarterly financial filingin August outlined over $500 billion in off-balance-sheet commitments over the coming years, with a majority maturing through fiscal 2029. That same month, Huang announced a partnership with six large asset managers on a $500 billion financing push designed to treat compute infrastructure as an asset class.That agreement, which promised financial firms up to $125 billion in residual value guarantees on GPU financings, was in addition to the stakes Nvidia has taken as a limited partner in private equity funds. The company seeded $2 billion in Brookfield's inaugural AI Infrastructure Partners Fund, which aims to raise $10 billion in total capital, as well as other unconfirmed sums in KKR's Helix Digital Infrastructure (an $11 billion vehicle) and Valor Equity Partners' $5.4 billion dedicated compute fund.

"We used to build chips that we sell, and these are technology components that people buy and use," Huangtold CNBC,in announcing the agreement in August. "But now, Nvidia's AI factory platform is really an investable asset."

Huang has adopted a marketing mantra to reinforce the unique value of its equipment.

"We're the most rentable. We're fungible, and we're durable," he said on apodcastwith investor Brad Gerstner published last week.

While Nvidia waits for Wall Street firms to pull in investors to expand the GPU loan pool, the chipmaker is already actively fostering record-sized deals in the AI infrastructure space.

Nvidia's biggest single guarantee is for OpenAI's forthcoming facility in Pike County, Ohio, which could be the largest data center in the world. That deal requiresuse of Nvidia hardware for at least 20 years.

The shiftfrom chips to capitalcarries significant risks should OpenAI run into trouble.

If OpenAI misses payments or faces insolvency, Nvidia can take over the lease, find a new tenant, or ask the landlord, SB Energy, to sell the facility, guaranteeing to pay the difference for the latter two arrangements up to $105 billion if the release or sale falls below a minimum price. Nvidia could also pay SB Energy a lump sum. On the other side, if OpenAI posts its own collateral, or achieves a high enough credit rating, Nvidia's guarantee ends.

At CoreWeave, Nvidia's investment includes equity and a commitment to buy up to $6.3 billion of its compute if it can't find another taker.

Nvidia's backstops can take many forms, such as guaranteeing a minimum resale price or a minimum hourly offtake price for the chips in the event the lender has to recoup the assets. With Sharon AI and other neoclouds, Nvidia's deals have come with revenue-sharing agreements.

"We believe these AI cloud partners have strong customer demand and robust sales pipelines but are constrained by the large-scale infrastructure that is required to meet that demand," Nvidia said in its quarterly filing.

Huang said this week that CoreWeave doesn't need Nvidia's backstop and that the neocloud'scost of capitalis decreasing. CoreWeave has roughly $51.6 billion in total debt, including about $35 billion in notes, bonds and loans. Yields on its bonds maturing in 2031 and 2032 topped 15%.

Brian Stutland, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, said the market jitters reflect concerns about the stability of the business.

CoreWeave and other neoclouds "will sign contracts into the future, and that all looks fine and dandy in their earnings reports, but is that contract going to be stable?" Stutland said. "Is it going to break at some point?"

Nvidia says its financial support can help customers build the infrastructure needed to meet strong demand for its chips. More computing capacity could also help AI labs develop new models and services, creating further demand for Nvidia products.

"They'll do $700 billion in revenue next year," Deepwater Asset Management founder Gene Munster told CNBC last month. "That affords them the ability to finance some of their customers."

Nvidia's credit backstops have mostly kicked in over the past six to 12 months. Its lastannual filing, published in February, makes no mention of AI cloud agreements.

Warren Hosseinion, co-founder of AI infrastructure startup Compute Labs, said Nvidia doesn't want to be in the position of insurer, "but they're willing to play that role while the market and the industry catches up."

"They kind of control how things move," said Hosseinion, whose company tokenizes GPUs in order to open up pools of capital for neocloud operators. "They have to be very careful about how they release their technology at what pace, because a lot of that will dictate how the market moves around it."

Nvidia is actively looking for insurers to bear some of the risk associated with the potential loss in value of GPUs.

"Insurers are not yet a complete panacea to this problem," said Tom Hoad, executive director of product innovation at global insurance group Howden. "But they are probably going to turn up and be helpful in the right situations, and therefore open up some commercial transactions."

title: Trump is pushing a massive AI buildout. His own voters are wary of what comes with it
content:
PresidentDonald Trumphas cast America'sartificial intelligencerace withChinaas a national-security imperative, pushing faster development of the technology and an immense buildout of the data centers andpower infrastructureneeded to fuel it.

But the newCNBC All-America Economic Surveyreveals a growing political tension beneath that agenda:Republicanvoters broadly support the push for AI development, but many oppose building the sprawling infrastructure needed to power it in their own backyards.

Nearly 55% ofMAGA supporterswant companies to keep developing advanced AI while Congress works on regulations, versus 27% who favor a pause. But only 29% would support adata centerwithin 10 miles of their home, while 40% oppose one. Among all Republicans and Republican-leaning voters — not just those who identify themselves with the MAGA movement — those who say they would support a data center near their home falls to 24%.

Across the electorate, 63% don't want a nearby AI data center and just 13% support one.Democratslead the opposition: 80% oppose nearby facilities while just 4% support them.

That resistance is increasingly forcing Trump and vulnerable Republicans who once championed data centers to recalibrate as they head into a bleakmidterm electionenvironment for the party.

"Many people are annoyed by these data centers," saidBrad Carson, a former Democratic congressman from Oklahoma and co-founder of Public First Action PAC, an AI-industry-backed political group pushing for stronger regulation and safeguards. "People are also strongly insistent upon reasonable guardrails of AI, and that's going to be hard to beat."

The CNBC survey of 1,000 registered voters nationwide was conducted Oct. 14-18 by Hart Research Associates and Public Opinion Strategies and has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1 percentage points. The data-center proximity question was asked of a half-sample of roughly 500 voters, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.38 percentage points.

Read the full survey results here.

The politics have shifted from the early AI boom, when Washington andSilicon Valleysold the technology as an avenue for investment, growth and American dominance.

But as the buildout accelerates, its physical costs are becoming harder to ignore. Communities are fighting data centers over spikingelectric bills, soaring electricity and water demand, noise,land useand taxpayer subsidies. Coupled with job-displacement fearsfrom AI, opponents now point to the facilities as a physical symbol of who benefits from the boom and who gets stuck with the bill.

The industry rejects that framing.

“The data center industry provides significant, tangible benefits,” said Dan Diorio of the Data Center Coalition, pointing to jobs, investment and tax revenue while adding that operators are committed to “paying for the energy we use."

But when asked their top concerns if Republicans retain Congress, 18% of voters in the survey cited a failure to regulate AI and data centers. That tied continued military efforts in Iran and outranked continued Immigration and Customs Enforcement deportations at 15%, cuts to health insurance subsidies at 10% and an extension of Trump's tariffs at 5%.

Even among voters who want Republicans to retain control, 17% cited weak AI and data center oversight — second only to a failure to bring down prices.

GOP strategists have taken note.

In August, the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned AI companies that data center backlash was threatening Sen.Jon Husted'sreelection in Ohio, calling the issue a midterm "sleeper" that could sour politicians nationwide on future projects, Axiosreported.

As Ohio lieutenant governor in 2024, Husted helped announce a $10 billion Amazon Web Services expansion, calling AI facilities "crucial to America's economic superiority." Now, in a tight Senate race against DemocratSherrod Brown, who has made data-center opposition a campaign issue, Husted is promotingstalled legislationto make large facilities cover their own grid and generation costs rather than pass them on to residential ratepayers.

Texas tells a similar story.Less than a year after Gov.Greg Abbotthailed the state as an "epicenter of AI development," hehalteddata center permits pending grid- and water-impact reviews and called for ending state tax incentives.

Trump himself is showing signs of the political pressure. In a Truth Social post Wednesday, he said data center developers should pay host communities afinancial "dividend"and generate their own power, arguing that local payouts can turn unpopular projects into popular ones.

For now, Democrats hold a modest edge on managing the issue: 32% of voters trust them to handle data center expansion, versus 24% for the Republicans. But 27% said neither party would do a better job than the other.

And the CNBC survey indicates this skepticism runs deeper than local zoning. Overall, 52% of registered voters want advanced AI development paused until Congress passes safety regulations, compared to 32% who favor moving ahead to keep pace with China. Democrats remain far more cautious: 70% favor a pause, while just 18% support pushing forward.

"The debate has shifted dramatically," Carson told CNBC. "A year ago, there were many people who said, 'Let it cook, no regulation at all, exempt the companies from normal rules.'" Carson said sentiment toward AI has "deteriorated a lot over the last six months."

title: America by the numbers: How voters feel about the economy, inflation, AI and Trump
content: With the U.S. midterm elections looming, Americans are nearly as gloomy about the economy as they were when the nation was emerging from the pandemic.

title: What a day in customer service looks like — as AI changes everything
content:
For Kaylee Harris, who works in customer service for a credit card company, a day at work now looks very different.

Her hours used to be filled with calls, note-taking and lengthy card disclosures. Now, thanks toartificial intelligence, she can focus more on each customer, Harris told CNBC.

For Shannon, AI has also changed things — but not in a good way. She works in customer service for a telecommunications company in Cardiff, Wales, and did not want to share her surname for fear of being identified by her employer. She told CNBC that AI-generated notes at her current workplace are often riddled with errors, "so I just write my own."

At her previous employer, a property services company, senior management told staff to "ChatGPT it" if they didn't know the answer. AI agents booked appointments, but when they couldn't offer a customer the requested date, they passed the case to a human.

Staff were "constantly fighting fires," Shannon said. "All the complicated cases came to us, causing a lot of burnout."

In theory, automation in customer service should mean human agents spend less time on admin and more time helping customers with problems that require human judgment, empathy and experience.

Nikola Mrkšić, CEO and co-founder of London-headquartered PolyAI, which develops voice AI systems for customer service, said contact-center agents can face "maximum abuse for minimum wage."

They often deal with frustrated customers while working under strict performance metrics, sometimes without the authority or information to resolve problems, he told CNBC. He sees AI agents as a way to help shoulder that load.

"It's a really, really difficult job," he said. "I think with AI, we have a shot at bridging the gap to make it better for both [customers and employees]."

British telecom and media company Virgin Media O2 launched an AI voice agent in September, which it said was designed to do just that. The agent handles routine issues so human advisors can spend more time on complex or sensitive cases.

At U.K.-based customer experience company ArvatoConnect, CEO Debra Maxwell told CNBC the company aims for 70% of interactions to be handled by technology and 30% by people.

One AI tool it developed for the U.K. government's procurement agency, the Crown Commercial Service, generates draft supplier viability assessments with 97% accuracy, she said, reducing the need for hours of manual data extraction.

As AI takes on routine tasks, human agents may be left dealing with a greater share of complicated cases — and be required to pick up the slack when the technology fails.

The pressure on customer-service staff comes amid reports of rising workloads across the industry.

According to MaxContact's 2025/26U.K. Contact Centre KPI Benchmarking Insights Report, more than half of surveyed contact-center decision-makers said agent workloads had increased, up from around 40% in 2024, although the survey doesn't establish what is driving the rise.

Amanda Jones, who researches organizational behavior and the future of work at King's College London, specializes in work intensification — the process by which jobs become more demanding over time. She told CNBC that AI could make call-center work even more intense if human agents are increasingly left with the toughest interactions.

"Some customers may already be frustrated by the time they reach that human," she said. "One thing we sometimes overlook is that relatively straightforward tasks can provide a bit of psychological respite between more demanding ones. If those disappear, the intensity of the working day could increase considerably, even if the overall volume of work doesn't."

Jones cautioned that productivity gains may also bring more intense performance targets. And as routine tasks are automated, workers could lose opportunities to develop the experience needed for more demanding work.

"So, we could end up expecting people to perform more demanding work while simultaneously reducing the experiences that traditionally helped prepare them for it," she said.

ArvatoConnect's Maxwell argued that average handling times may need to increase as employees take on more complex cases.

"We assess whether [human] agents understood the customer's needs, exercised sound judgement and reached the right resolution," she said. "Not whether they followed a script or hit an arbitrary time target."

Harris sees the upsides of AI tools, despite occasional system glitches that create more work. But she worries that the push to automate is coming, ultimately, at the expense of customer experience.

"As a country, I think we are focusing on getting things done faster and choosing quantity over quality … resulting in customers being fed up with the way AI is being pushed on everyone," she said.

Shannon also sees the potential benefits of using AI, but doesn't think it should ever replace real customer service.

"I believe people buy from people; with AI you don't get to experience that," she said. "I go the extra mile. Can AI give that feeling? Can it feel genuine?"

title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab
content: Image source,Getty ImagesByLiv McMahonTechnology reporterPublished1 hour agoThe UK says it will establish a national AI Biosecurity Lab (AIBL) to help strengthen its defences against emerging biological threats.As part of Wednesday's Budget, the government will commit Â£100m to establishing the new, "world first" institute with the support of leading AI firms.The chancellor will also pledge millions of pounds in spending across a range of initiatives aimed at shoring up the UK's ability to respond to evolving cyber, biological and AI-enabled threats."AI will transform daily life: every firm, community, hospital, school, and every aspect of our economy can benefit," John Healey said."I understand and share the concerns of working people, so I am setting out a distinctively British approach to AI."One that doesn't leave workers behind and defends our national interest, while ensuring the benefits of AI-enabled growth are felt right across the country."The full details about the role and remit of the new lab are yet to emerge.But the AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said it would be a "major new global institution" that brings together "world-leading scientific expertise" to ensure the UK can safeguard its citizens and goals as AI develops."That means staying ahead of emerging threats, from cyber attacks to biological risks, while building more of the critical technology our security depends on," he said."By backing British science, advanced chips and our own AI companies, we can strengthen our national security, rebuild Britain's industrial strength and create good, skilled jobs across the country."The AI Biosecurity Lab's creation will also be supported by leading AI developers, with OpenAI and Anthropic providing Â£200m worth of AI model credits that can be spent on the use of their models.What is AI, how does it work and why are some people concerned about it?Published14 SeptemberDon't leave AI to tech bros and oligarchs, UK's AI minister saysPublished20 hours agoThe Chancellor's plans to boost AI spending will also see an additional Â£120m committed to the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI).Established by the former Conservative government in 2023, the lab evaluates the risks of the most advanced and powerful models - and has been championed for its role in helping build a collaborative and open approach to AI testing.The additional funding announced by the Chancellor will aim to help ensure the lab can continue its efforts and work, particularly amid growing calls for technical standards and guardrails for AI development.It will come alongside a Â£60m investment in what it coined a "National Cyber Shield" which it said would use agentic AI to boost cyber-defences, and Â£70m funding towards a National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre.This, it said, would harness AI tools to detect cyber vulnerabilities across the UK's critical infrastructure and economy.It comes after the UK government revealed it wasamong organisations around the world to have taken some sites offlineas a precaution after critical flaws were surfaced in a popular programming language.Researchers who helped surface the vulnerabilities in PHP - a popular server-side scripting language used in web development for decades - warned platforms which use it could be exposed to potential hacks.There have been no reports of any successful exploits of the flaw, coined php2shell, so far.But experts have warned that the incident shows how quickly and easily bugs which have lain long dormant may be surfaced - and potentially exploited - using AI.Sign up for our Tech Decoded newsletterto follow the world's top tech stories and trends.Outside the UK? Sign up here.Related topicsCyber-securityArtificial intelligenceUK governmentNational securityMore on this storyAI minister warns 'likely' UK's cyber defences will be breachedPublished12 OctoberAnthropic blocks possible attempt to use AI to make biological weaponsPublished11 SeptemberChinese AI tool told researchers how to make bioweaponsPublished30 September

title: Are California voters about to impose 'world's first' tax on billionaires?
content: Image source,ReutersBySareen HabeshianLos AngelesPublished24 October 2026Few places on the planet have as many ultra-wealthy residents as California, a US state known for glamour, coastal mega-mansions, and being home to the rich and famous.Now voters are about to decide whether the mega-rich among them - including media mogul Oprah Winfrey, Meta head Mark Zuckerberg, Skims cofounder and reality television star Kim Kardashian, and filmmaker George Lucas - should hand over billions of dollars to pay for improvements to healthcare.Proposition 40 is aimed at levying a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of all of California's billionaires.There are a little more than 200 such individuals in the state - but that hasn't stopped the measure from dividing leaders and causing some of its ultra-wealthy residents to flee. One billionaire businessman says he's brought jobs to California, but the proposition made him feel "a little bit like I wasn't wanted".What are the US midterms? A simple guidePublished6 OctoberBut the vote is also offering regular residents a voice on an issue that has roiled politics for decades."I believe this is the first billionaire tax - meaning a wealth tax that is targeting a very extreme percentile of the wealth distribution," says Francesco Trebbi, a public policy professor at the University of California, Berkeley. He noted the measure's historic nature and how it could help even out California's wealth gap.The state has the largest economy in the country and boasts the fourth largest global economy, bigger than India and the UK. And it is home to one of the highest concentrations of billionaires in the world. But it also has the largest share of homeless people in the nation and one of the highest wealth gaps.Those who back the measure have argued it helps ensure that the ultra-wealthy are contributing their fair share and will help backfill gaps in the state's budget. The move aims to raise $100bn (Â£75bn) to make up for federal funding cuts to the state's health-care system.Suzanne Jimenez, chief of staff for Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, which helped lead the charge for the initiative, says the measure is a "short-term solution" for massive federal funding cuts coming to California as a result of US President Donald Trump'ssweeping tax and spending bill."If we do nothing, we're going to see a collapse of our healthcare system, while we figure out a longer-term solution to fund our healthcare," she tells the BBC.Image source,Getty ImagesWhile the ballot measure has many supporters - including some billionaires like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang - it has faced fierce opposition from a variety of figures, from billionaires to the state's liberal governor.Google co-founder Sergey Brin has given more than $100m to a political organisation funding ballot measures that could block the wealth tax,the Los Angeles Times reports,external.California Governor Gavin Newsom, whose tenure is coming to an end, is perhaps the most notable political leader opposing it. He has voiced concerns that the measure could cause the wealthy to leave the state and drive out their crucial income tax revenue.ASeptember poll,externalfrom the Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and the Los Angeles Times found the proposition has not clearly won over a majority of voters, with 45% of likely voters in favour of the tax, 42% opposed and 13% undecided.The statewide ballot measure would need to be approved by a majority of residents.California is not the first place to toy with the idea of taxing the rich. Also on the West Coast, voters in US state of Washington are considering whether to accept or reject a "millionaires tax" - a 9.9% tax on income over $1m a year.While wealth taxes were once a fairly common form of taxation in Europe, they have rapidly fallen out of favour and now only exist in three European countries â Spain, Norway and Switzerland, says Dr Kristian Niemietz, head of political economy at the Institute of Economic Affairs.Niemietz believes wealth taxes are "more trouble than they are worth" because they cause administrative issues, suppress investment, lead to capital flight and, in the end, do not raise much revenue.In the case of Norway, a local news organisation found that an increase in the wealth tax led to more super wealthy people leaving the countryin 2022,externalthan in the preceding 13 years combined. Astudy on Switzerland,externalfound that a 0.1 percentage point increase in a wealth tax reduced taxable wealth by 3.5%.GUIDE: What are the US midterms?IN DEPTH: The real reasons there are so few young US politiciansEXPLORE: How the US midterms will be won and lostVERIFY: How the US economy is really doing under TrumpNEWSLETTER: Sign up for Anthony Zurcher's analysis in your inboxThe California measure, if approved, would apply retroactively to those with a net worth of at least $1bn who resided in California as of 1 January 2026. At least six of the state's 200 plus billionaires have reportedly left California ahead of that deadline to avoid the tax.They include Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin, venture capitalist Peter Thiel, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick and Hankey Group founder Don Hankey.Hankey, a Los Angeles billionaire who has lived in California all his life, told Forbes he left for the state of Nevada as a result of the proposed wealth tax."I think we've created a lot of jobs in California. We have a few thousand people working for us and we have a profit sharing plan. And I have to leave the state," he said, adding that the measure made him feel like he wasn't "wanted" in the state.Image source,Getty ImagesImage caption,Google co-founder Sergey Brin has reportedly given more than $100m to a political organisation funding ballot measures that could block the wealth taxMeta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg told the company's board last month that he was thinking of moving his primary residence out of California over the proposed tax.To prevent him from leaving the state - where the company is headquartered - Metaagreed to a new stock dealthat gives Zuckerberg, whose wealth is estimated to exceed $200bn, even more shares in the company to make up for the billions he would lose if the measure passes in November. Estimates say he could owe as much as $12.5bn.DoorDash cofounder Andy Fang, who has an estimated net worth of $1.6bn, has called the measure "stupid" and wrote on X that "proposals like this make it irresponsible for me not to plan leaving the state".Zuckerberg wins Meta deal to help him foot bill for possible California billionaire taxPublished2 days agoMeanwhile, businessman Tom Steyer, who ran an unsuccessful bid for California governor earlier this year, is one of the few billionaires who hassaid,externalhe would vote in favour of the tax. Steyer said that although he believed the way the measure was written was "problematic", it was necessary to protect vulnerable Californians.Huang, too, has expressed support of paying the levy."I don't mind paying taxes. The more you make, the more taxes you pay. I'm okay with that," the Nvidia chief said in an interview with the BBC's US partner CBS. "I am the ultimate American Dream."Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, a vocal champion against income inequality, has campaigned in support of Prop 40.While at a Los Angeles rally, Sanders said billionaires "believe, like the monarchs of the 19th Century, that they have a God-given right to rule"."They have all the wealth, they got all the power, and who the hell do you think you are challenging them? Well, I think on November 3 they're going to learn a very powerful lesson."Image source,Getty ImagesImage caption,US Senator Bernie Sanders speaks at the "Ballots Over Billionaires" rally on 5 October in Los Angeles.Income inequality in the US is at some of itshighest levels,externalin over three decades, with the top 1% of households owning nearly 32% of all US wealth in the third quarter of 2025. It is also near historic highs in California.Economic inequality is a concern among most Californians, with 72% believing that the gap between the rich and poor is widening and a similar share holding that state government should do more to reduce the gap, according to astatewide survey,externalfrom the Public Policy Institute of California.Trebbi says it is an "anti-elite, anti-system sentiment" driving the policy."This is really not about Prop 40," he says, but rather about trying to "re-balance the scale a little bit".Correction 24 October: An earlier version of this article contained a graphic which incorrectly said median income in California was $288,000. This has been corrected to median household net worth.Related topicsUS midterm elections 2026CaliforniaLos AngelesSilicon ValleyBillionairesUnited StatesWorld of Business

title: Turmoil hits AI build-out as neoclouds face pressure, credit risks mount and Solidigm pulls IPO
content:
Neoclouds tanked. Credit default swaps soared.Metaturned cash flow negative. AndSK Hynix'sSolidigm unit canceled plans for its initial public offering.

It's been a rocky week for the AI infrastructure trade.

The Nasdaq followed Thursday'sbeatingwith an additional drop on Friday to end the week down 0.7%. Among the hyperscalers, the worst performer wasAlphabet, shares of which sank 6% ahead of the internet giant's third-quarter earnings report next week. Microsoft and Amazon are also on the docket, and they each saw shares fall less than 1%.

While the tech market has thus far avoided a dramatic across-the-board sell-off, the artificial intelligence build-out is showing signs of strain.

Shares of neocloudsCoreWeave,NebiusandIRENall fell sharply this week, bringing their losses for October to well over 30% each. CoreWeave, the leader of the pack,has seen spreadson its CDS widen past 11%, generally viewed as a distress level, as investors have to pay up for protection against default.

Meanwhile, yields on the company's 2031 and 2032 unsecured notestopped 15%.

"What investors are doing is throwing every baby out with the bathwater and saying anyone who is a neocloud" will be devalued, Roundhill Investments CEO Dave Mazza toldCNBC's "Squawk on the Street"on Thursday.

Fears aren't limited to the U.S. market. Shares of Elice Group, a South Korean cloud provider,dropped 30%in their market debut on Tuesday, and shares of Australia'sNextDCplunged 39.5% on Wednesday after the data center operatorslashedits annual earnings forecast.

AI optimism has been the major market driver for the past couple of years, as unrelenting demand for new models and services pushes the world's biggest tech companies to spend on infrastructure at historic rates. However, skeptics are getting more vocal in their concerns that returns on AI investment won't justify the capital expenditures.

Analysts at research and advisory firmGartner predict that 80% of neocloud companieswill either cease operations or be absorbed by 2030.

NvidiaCEOJensen Huang, perhaps the leading AI evangelist remains bullish. Huang said this week at a company conference in Berlin that "demand for the neoclouds is off the charts."

"The demand of the capital is much greater than the availability of the capital," Huangtold CNBC's Arjun Kharpal. "That's going to get solved."

Wall Street isn't convinced. On Thursday, South Korean memory giantSK Hynix, one of the biggest winners in the AI boom, said it'spulling an IPOfor its U.S.-based Solidigm unit, citing market volatility. SK HynixpurchasedSolidigm, which makes NAND and SSD storage for data centers, fromIntelin 2021.

"While an IPO was expected to ease investment burdens and expand capacity for shareholder returns, the review has been discontinued in light of market conditions and share price trends," SK Hynix said in arelease.

Despite the turmoil, all of tech's mega-caps have maintained their investment-grade rating even as they've opened their wallets to fuel their build-outs, including through debt. Even with that group of companies, the market is showing some jitters.

Meta saw its stock plunge 7% on Thursday after the company reported negative free cash flow in thethird quarterof over $2 billion while raising the floor of its full-year capex to $135 billion from $130 billion. Meta also said it plans to spend about $825 billion over the coming years on various leases and contracts, with over $450 billion of those leases being non-cancellable take-or-pay agreements.

Spreads on Meta's five-year CDS reached all-time highs of over 124 basis points. CDS onNvidiaandOraclealso touched records, with their spreads hitting 126 basis points and 343 basis points, respectively, this week. Oracle's stock has lost over one-third of its value this year, and now the companyfaces risks of a credit rating downgrade.

John Williams, who leads the derivatives practice at law firm Milbank LLP, says investors are seeking numerous ways beyond buying CDS to hedge their bets with respect to the AI trade.

"There's so much investment going into it that it's just very appropriate to look for risk management tools, completely regardless of whether you're bullish or bearish," Williams said. "It would be crazy for people not to be looking for appropriate risk management tools for it."

Brian Stutland, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments,told CNBC's "SquawkBox Asia"last week that it's "all kind of tied together," referring to AI's impact on the whole market.

"Can you drop a bowling ball in one part of the pool and not get any waves downstream to the rest of the Nasdaq?" he said. "I don't know. I have some concern about that."

—CNBC's Katie Tarasov contributed to this report

title: In hunt for Starlink alternative, Ukraine partners with Nokia and satellite maker ICEYE
content:
AfterSpaceXrestricted use of its Starlink and Starshield satellite internet services in Ukraine, causing fast-moving drones to disconnect and drop out of the sky, Kyiv is looking for alternatives.

Ukraine's Ministry of Defense said on Thursday that it has signed a letter of intent to develop new defense and satellite communication capabilities in partnership with Finnish tech companies Nokia and ICEYE, which makes satellites.

"Modern warfare has proven that reliable communications are a matter of national security," Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in astatement. "We must all rely on capabilities that we can control."

Zelenskyyalso announceda partnership with Norway this week to jointly develop air defense and communications systems that could serve as an alternative to Starshield.

Chad Anderson, founder and CEO of Space Capital, which tracks industry deals, said such an alternative could be "two to three years away" and that "matching Starlink's scale is a longer road."

SpaceX has around around 11,000 satellites in orbit, according todata tracked by astronomer Jonathan McDowell.

Anderson said Starshield may be an even tougher service to replace. "The Pentagon's own contracting documents say SpaceX is the only provider that can meet some of its needs through 2026. Capital isn't the constraint any more. Launch is."

Even Starlink competitors have relied on SpaceX launches to put their satellites in orbit.

As of Friday, Ukraine officials said the country is still experiencing restrictions on Starlink, which cut connectivity for drones or other aircraft traveling at speeds over 100 mph.

Both the Trump administration and SpaceX CEOElon Muskhave shirked responsibility for the unannounced Starlink service changes that Ukraine reported more than a week ago.President Donald Trumptold reporters at the White House on Friday that he would call on Musk to lift the restrictions.

SpaceX executives didn't respond to a request for comment.

Lawmakers in the U.S.fromboth partiesare calling for a formal probe of Musk and SpaceX regarding the alleged unilateral changes the company made to its services in Ukraine.

Jay Shambaugh, a senior fellow at Brookings and professor of economics and international affairs at George Washington University, told CNBC in an email that the sudden Starlink changes are "part of a pattern since Trump came back into office of the United States acting as an unreliable ally."

Shambaugh cautioned that, "over time, that can reduce U.S. exports to the EU if those countries don't want to be dependent on something where the U.S. can cut them off."

Rivals to Starlink are on the horizon, includingAmazon'sLeo, France'sEutelsatand a forthcoming service from Jeff Bezos'Blue OrigincalledTeraWave, which has yet to deploy its first satellites.

Beyond Ukraine,several countriesare looking into sovereign satellite communications systems. The EU is buildingIRIS², a constellation of hundreds of satellites, but its first launches aren't expected until 2029.

Since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, venture and private equity investors have poured about $8 billion into Starlink and Starshield alternatives, according to research by Anderson. About $3.9 billion of that funding has gone to potential Starlink competitors, mostly Spacesail and China SatNet.

Virginia Burger, senior defense policy analyst with the Project on Government Oversight, told CNBC in an interview that the problem today is there's no drop-in replacement for Starlink, and combat is moving more into "unmanned systems, drone warfare and other systems that require high-speed internet."

— CNBC's Annie Palmer contributed reporting.

title: Dow tumbles more than 600 points as oil prices rise and market sell-off hits most sectors
content:
The Dow slid on Friday as a sell-off in tech in the prior session shifted to other areas of the market and U.S. oil prices topped $100 a barrel amid rising fears that the U.S.-Iran conflict would flare up again.

TheDow Jones Industrial Averagedropped 652.82 points, or 1.23%, to settle at 52,215.16, while theS&P 500slipped 0.52% to 7,623.68. TheNasdaq Compositelost 0.21% to close at 25,955.34.

More defensive stocks came under pressure on Friday, with the consumer staples, utilities and healthcare sectors all lower. Dow componentAmerican Expressfell more than 3% after announcing it wascutting about 5% of its global workforce, citing the need to "prepare for AI."Caterpillaralso edged down about 2%, whileGoldman Sachslost more than 1%, adding pressure to the 30-stock index.

On Thursday, many technology stocks had pulled back as traders assessed the impact of outsized corporate borrowing and rising rates on AI and other tech names.Microsoftticked higher on Friday. However, chip stocks such asMicron TechnologyandAdvanced Micro Devicesmade a stronger move, with gains of nearly 3% and almost 2%, respectively.

"For the last two weeks, investors have been sprinting from tech stocks and data center beneficiary stocks to safe stuff, and eventually, you run out of people willing to do that sprint, and that's what today looks like and feels like," Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management, told CNBC.

Ellerbroek added that tech companies' earnings have proven strong this season, giving investors a reason to embrace tech stocks and focus less on emotion-based flights to safety.

"Emotion and fear play a really big role," the investor said. But, "we've gotten a few tech companies' [latest quarterly financial reports] and their earnings results have been good."

The10-year Treasuryyield was at around 4.999%, up more than 4 basis points on the day. The benchmark yield had fallen below the key 5% level on Thursday for the first time in a month as investors grew cautious about the massive borrowing that is underway to finance the building of AI data centers.

Oil prices also rose on Friday, further pressuring stocks.West Texas Intermediate futureswere up 3.8% to settle at $103.27 per barrel.Brent crudeprices rose 3.1% to end the session at $116.72 for the highest settle since April. The gains follow reports that the U.S. and Israel may be drawing up plans for renewed attacks on Iran as part of the regional war that started in late February. Iran has countered that it is prepared to strike back as well.

On the week, the S&P 500 lost 0.5%, and the Nasdaq shed 0.7%. The Dow gained 0.4% in the period.

The three major stock indexes ended Friday's session with losses.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 1.23%, or 652.82 points, to finish at 52,215.16. The S&P 500 ended down 0.52% at 7,623.68. The Nasdaq Composite closed down 0.21% at 25,955.34.

Shares of discount retailers are lower today after analysts at Wells Fargo warned in a note that rising diesel prices could pressure profits through the second half of the year and into 2027.

With third-quarter diesel prices up about 60% year-over-year, analysts estimate the average hit to operating margin will rise to about 27 basis points from 18 basis points in the second quarter. The drag on earnings per share is expected to more than double to 6.2%.

Dollar TreeandDollar Generalare down around 5% in midday trading whileFive BelowandTJX Companiesare both down more than 1% on the day. Wells Fargo says Dollar Tree is the most exposed, historically seeing a larger drag than peers when diesel spikes. They estimate the higher fuel costs will weigh on third-quarter profit by about $25 million, or 50 basis points of margin.

The increased costs could mean additional pressure on retail inflation.

Bank of America raised its price target onServiceNowto $180, implying roughly 15% upside from Thursday's close.

BofA analyst Tal Liani reiterated his buy rating ahead of the company's third-quarter earnings on October 28, citing growing demand for its artificial intelligence offerings.

"We believe ServiceNow's AI could see broader adoption and incremental spend, which should support durable revenue growth," Liani wrote in a Friday note.

The bank's October CIO survey showed that nearly 36% of respondents expect to allocate more than 10% of their software budgets to AI, while nearly 55% said they were likely or very likely to use ServiceNow for back-office AI applications.

The analyst expects third-quarter subscription revenue to grow nearly 21% year over year as IT, customer service, and security adopt new AI products and automation tools.

Uranium, nuclear and clean energy exchange-traded funds all fell to 52-week lows on Friday, while the largest fossil fuel producers in the nation touched all-time highs.

Global X Uranium ETFandSprott Uranium Miners ETFboth dropped to their lowest levels since June 2025, while theVanEck Uranium and Nuclear ETFwas at its lowest since May 2025. Of the stocks inside those ETFs,Centrus Energy,Oklo,NuScale Power,Energy FuelsandBWX Technologieswere also at 52-week lows Friday.

Clean energy ETFs saw losses, too.Invesco Solar ETFandInvesco WilderHill Clean Energy ETFwere at their lowest since September and August last year, respectively, while individual stocks in the group, such asNextPower,Solv Energy,Rivian AutomotiveandFluence Energy, also dropped to 52-week lows.

Meanwhile,ExxonMobil,ChevronandConocoPhillipsall traded at all-time highs on Friday.

— Scott Schnipper, Gina Francolla

In a Friday note to clients, Goldman Sachs posed some key questions about hyperscaler Oracle's AI strategy as pressures mount on the AI trade and investors grow increasingly wary to part with capital.

Analyst Gabriela Borges at Goldman said the conversation around Oracle is centering on monetization in proportion to capital expenditures; the sustainability of demand amid customer concentration; and the company's ability to execute despite political pressures facing the data center buildout.

Borges has a buy rating on the stock and a price target of $206, implying upside of 64.1% compared to a closing price recorded as $125.54.

Among the key risks to the company listed by Goldman are "intense capex investment cycle and financing needs."

"Oracle has outlined a FY27 financing framework supported by roughly $20bn of equity issuance (ATM program, already executed), $20 – 25 bn of customer prepayments ($11 bn as of 1Q), ~$20bn of debt issuance (expected in 2HFY27), with the remainder funded through operating cash flow," Borges wrote.

Stocks outside the AI trade are taking the lead.

TheS&P 500 Excluding AIindex closed Thursday up 12.4% this year, edging out theS&P 500'sroughly 12% gain. The gap has converged largely in October.

The ex-AI index is up about 6.6% in October, while the S&P 500, weighed down by concerns around AI financing, is down roughly 0.4%.

The move suggests some leadership broadening beyond AI-linked mega cap names that have dominated in recent periods. By sector,EnergyandConsumer Staplesare each up double digits in October whileInformation TechnologyandCommunication Serviceslead lower, each down more than 5%.

Morgan Stanley reduced its price target onCoreWeaveto $70 from $99 Friday, citing mounting financial pressures the so-called neocloud company is facing. The new target still implies 26% upside from Thursday's close.

Shares of CoreWeave, down 2% on Friday, havesold off over the past weekamid investor fears over its massive artificial intelligence-rated debt. Its bond yields have also jumped, while the spread on its credit default swaps — which are insurance against default — has widened to levels generally considered distressed.

Morgan Stanley believes CoreWeave's execution has been solid and said it "remains the speed and scale leader in a crowded neocloud ecosystem."

"However, growing financing uncertainty reduces visibility into the path to deploying existing contracted capacity and achieving 8 GW [gigawatts] (active) longer-term," said analyst Adam Wood, who maintained his equal-weight rating on the stock.

He sees a multitude of outcomes for CoreWeave's future financing, "though the most reasonable path forward would likely be through securing a portion of the financing via a hyperscaler agreement to obtain a more attractive rate."

Consumer sentiment changed little in October from historically low levels as inflation weighed on the economic outlook, according to aUniversity of Michigan surveyreleased Friday.

The survey showed the headline consumer sentiment index at 48 for the end of the month, off just 0.1 point from September and better than the Dow Jones consensus for 46.3. Compared with a year ago, the gauge tumbled 10.4%.

Current conditions sentiment declined 8.3% monthly but the expectations measure rose 5.4% and was off just 3% from the same period in 2025.

On inflation, the one-year outlook rose to 4.7%, while the five-year expectation accelerated to 3.5%, both 0.1 percentage point higher than September.

Wall Street firm Seaport reiterated its bearish call on Nvidia with a sell rating and its price target on the stock of $180 per share, below Nvidia's Thursday closing price of $212.

If it has to be months from now or longer than that, or another administration, before a proper deal comes into place, we will do that," he said, according to CBC.The US-Canada trade war in 5 chartsPublished31 AugustThe Wall Street Journal had reported that the exemptions, largely focused on Canadian agricultural and forestry, were made in a bid to help Collins and other Republicans in the upcoming midterm elections.The reductions could be offset by raising levies on âother Canadian goods, the Journal reported.In a statement Collins put out before the White House announcement, the incumbent lawmaker, who is trying to clinch her sixth term, said she had "secured additional tariff exemptions products crucial to Maine's agricultural industries, including blueberry, potato, apple, and seaweed producers"."Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense," she posted on X.Collins said she has asked US officials and senior administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada.âMaine's economy, as well as that of other border states, is deeply linked to Canada and they have felt the effects of the month-long trade war.Michigan lawmaker Mike Rogers, also a Republican, has called on Trump to end the standoff after spending months supporting the policy in recent advertisements airing in his trade-reliant state.Related topicsUnited StatesCanadaTrade warTrump tariffsMore on this storyUS embassy accuses Canada of election meddling ahead of midtermsPublished1 day ago

title: Trump's executive order targets mortgage insurance, refinance costs. What it means for borrowers
content:
PresidentDonald Trumphassigned an executive orderthat aims to reducemortgage costsas risinginterest ratesand inflation make homeownershipless affordable.

Theorder, titled "Decreasing Housing Costs for the American People," directs federal agencies to proactively cancel mortgage insurance on eligible future loans and expand a program to make refinancing cheaper, among other actions.

In anX post on Thursday, Federal Housing Finance Agency director Bill Pulte said "millions of Americans will save thousands and thousands of dollars."

But it's difficult to know the future consumer impact without more details, according to Keith Gumbinger, vice president of mortgage website HSH.

Trump's executive order comes less than two weeks before theNov. 3 midterm elections, with rising costs andhousing affordabilitya major concern among voters. It builds on previous orders torestrict Wall Street firmsfrom buying single-family homes, among other actions.

Homeownership has become less affordable in recent years. In 2025, the monthly payment for a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage on a median-priced home was roughly 33% of the median family's income, up from 26% in 2022, according to the Federal Reserve's latestSurvey of Consumer Financespublished in early October.

Whether you're a current homeowner or future buyer, here are some of the key things to know about the new executive order.

Conventional loans — mortgages not insured or backed by U.S. government programs — typically require private mortgage insurance, or PMI, when a down payment is less than 20% of the home's purchase price. By contrast, Federal Housing Administration mortgages require mortgage insurance on all loans.

Trump's executive order directs the FHFA to create a pilot program thatcancels eligible borrowers' mortgage insurance "proactively"once their home equity reaches a certain threshold, according to the White House. This would apply to mortgages originated after the pilot program launches.

Currently, conventional loan borrowers cangenerally remove PMIonce their loan balance is below 80% of the purchase price or once they have reached 20% equity, according to Fannie Mae. Once your balance is below 80%, you can ask your loan servicer if you're eligible to remove PMI, or they may remove it automatically when your balance reaches 78% of the original value.

In astatement Thursday, Seth Appleton, president of U.S. mortgage insurers, an industry trade organization, said: "We commend the President's focus on lowering costs for future homeowners, and the private mortgage insurance industry is proud to already be delivering on that goal."

Typically, the cost of PMI can be0.2% to 2% of the loan annually, but varies based on your down payment size, credit score, amount borrowed and other factors, according to Fannie Mae.

For example, if you purchased a $600,000 home with a 10% down payment and a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage at 7.3%, your monthly mortgage insurance could be $351, according to aprivate mortgage calculatorfrom Freddie Mac.

"Most mortgages ... are carrying PMI at this point in time, especially with the way home prices have been and down payments being as small as they've been in recent years," Gumbinger said.

During the second quarter of 2026, the median home down payment was 13.7% of the home's purchase price, or $27,100, according to aSeptember reportfrom Realtor.com.

Trump's executive order also aims to reducemortgage refinancingcosts by making permanent the FHFA'spilot programthat waives the lender's title insurance policy and allows "cost-friendly alternatives," according to the White House.

"I don't know that it's necessarily a game-changer in terms of the cost of housing, which is dictated by home price and mortgage rates at the moment," Gumbinger said. "But you know, every little bit certainly helps."

As of Oct. 23, mortgage interest rates for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages were 7.32%, according to Freddie Mac, andrefinance demand was down 59%in mid-October, compared to the same week the previous year.

Originally plannedthrough November 2027, the FHFA pilot was"limited in scope,"for refinances with a loan-to-value ratio below 80%, in a handful of states, former FHFA director Sandra Thompson said during a Congressional hearing in April 2024.

Thompson estimated that consumers could save$500 to $1,500in closing costs for loans sold under the pilot program.

Making the program permanent could save borrowers because the lender's title insurance policy, which is usually required for new loans and refinances, "has always been fairly pricey," Gumbinger said.

The lender's title and title insurance-related fees generally make up the largest share ofmortgage closing costs, according to a 2025 Urban Institute report.

title: Qatar deal to buy U.S. natural gas shows how Iran war has redrawn global energy markets
content:
Before the Iran war, Qatar was one of the biggest natural gas exporters in the world. After only eight months, the Gulf state is now buying supplies from its principal competitor — the United States.

QatarEnergy struck a deal Thursday with U.S. exporterCheniere Energyto buy 4 million metric tons of liquefied natural gas, or LNG, annually through 2054. The purchase price is indexed to the U.S. Henry Hub price plus a fixed fee. Deliveries are expected to begin in the 2030s.

"We look forward to reliably supplying QatarEnergy from both Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi into the second half of this century," Cheniere CEO Jack Fusco said in a statement.

The gas that Doha will buy is less than 1% of the global LNG trade of more than 400 million metric tons. But "in terms of an individual deal, this is about as big as you see in the U.S," said Alex Munton, director of global gas and LNG at Rapidan Energy in Houston.

The deal signals how the Iran war is reshaping global energy markets to the benefit of U.S. companies, cementing the dominance of American LNG exporters. Shares of Cheniere andVenture Global, the other independent U.S. player, have gained 26% and 40%, respectively, since the start of the war.

Qatar was second only to the U.S. in LNG exports before the war. But shipments have since collapsed in the eight months since Iran bombed its key production facility at Ras Laffan. The attack badly damaged two production lines, taking out about 17% of Qatar's LNG export capacity.

It will take about three years to repair the damage at Ras Laffan, Qatar's energy minister, Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi, has said. The Persian Gulf state has declaredforce majeure— citing unexpected, uncontrollable events preventing contracts from being honored — every month since the March attack.

"It did give us a big blow, if you will, for our production capability for the next few years," Al-Kaabi said in aninterviewon the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in September. Qatar is exporting "very little" LNG right now because "we can't export through the Hormuz Strait," he said."Very sparingly, some ships are crossing the straits but a very small amount, it's not something that would even be measurable in a percentage point," the energy minister said.

And it is far from clear what security conditions in Hormuz will look like when the repairs are done at Ras Laffan. The decades-long contract with Cheniere indicates that Qatar sees a risk that freedom of navigation will never return to Hormuz as Iran keeps attacking tankers, Munton said.

It is harder to find ways to get around Hormuz in the case of LNG because it is fundamentally a waterborne product, the analyst said.

"It's liquefied so it can be put on a ship and that requires access to seaborne routes," Munton said. "They've got to access the Strait of Hormuz. There's no other way of getting LNG to market. They're just stuck."

With its production badly damaged and Hormuz blocked off, QatarEnergy is expanding its LNG trading business through the Cheniere deal, Munton said.

It secured a $3 billion loan earlier this month from Chinese banks that could allow it to secure more U.S. LNG to honor its international delivery commitments, said Manav Gupta, a UBS analyst, in a note to clients Thursday.

Venture Global, for example, is in advanced talks with QatarEnergy to supply 3 million metric tons annually,unnamed sources told Reuters.

With the Qatar deal, Cheniere is disproving the bears' case that it will struggle to secure incremental sales which would in turn constrain capacity expansion, Gupta said. UBS has a stock price target of $340 on Cheniere, implying 18% upside from Thursday's close.

Wall Street is broadly bullish on both Cheniere and Venture Global. Nearly 90% of equity analysts who cover Cheniere rate it a buy, with an average price target of $314, implying about 9% upside from Thursday's close.

Nearly 60% of analysts recommend Venture Global as a buy with the rest rating it a hold. The average price target of $17 would amount to some 35% upside from Thursday's close.

"The U.S. once again is being called on by buyers to diversify supply," Munton said. "So much is under construction in the U.S. that you get to the point where now the U.S. is becoming disproportionately big in terms of global [LNG] market share."

title: U.S. fines Air France, KLM over flights in prohibited Iraqi airspace
content:
The U.S. Transportation Department said Friday it was finingAir Franceand KLM a total of $425,000 for operating dozens of flights in Iraqi airspace below a minimum altitude intended to protect them from threats from the ground.

The Federal Aviation Administration prohibits flight operations by U.S. operators in foreign-managed airspace where conflict, militant activity, or heightened tensions can threaten the safety of flights. Foreign airlines operating flights with a U.S. airline's code must abide by these prohibitions, and KLM and Air France both operate flights withDeltacodes.

An FAA order in place for more than six years bars flights over Iraq at altitudes below 32,000 feet.

Air France operated more than 30 flights and KLM more than 100 flights carrying the Delta code through FAA-prohibited airspace over Iraq between early 2022 and 2025, USDOT said.

USDOT said the airlines must pay $265,000 of the $425,000 within 60 days and the remainder of the fines will be payable if there are any other violations within one year.

The airlines did not immediately comment but Air France and KLM told USDOT they were fully committed to adhering to regulatory requirements at all times and took the issue extremely seriously.

Both airlines said that due to conflicting traffic, local air traffic controllers had directly instructed their flight crews to descend or refused to allow them to ascend.

Both said they believe the flights should have fallen under the "emergency situations" exemption given the safety implications of refusing an air traffic control order.

title: U.S. dropping some Canada tariffs, Susan Collins says as trade war looms over Maine Senate race
content:
The U.S. will issuetariffexemptions on several categories ofCanadianimports, Sen.Susan CollinsofMainesaid Friday.

The Republican incumbent's announcement came as voters have already started casting ballots in the pivotal Maine Senate race, one of the most competitive contests of themidterm election cycle.

PresidentDonald Trumphas waged a trade war against Canada resulting in heavy tariffs on a wide range of goods imported from the top U.S. economic partner. Many of those tariffs have putstrain on businesses in Maine, whichbuys more from Canadathan any other foreign country.

Collins, whose Democratic opponent Troy Jackson has tried to tie her to Trump's unpopular tariffs, has previously touted her efforts to push back on the president's protectionist trade policies.

In their first televised debate on Oct. 6, Collins took credit for removing some items from Trump's list of tariffs on Canadian goods, including road salt.

Jackson fired back, "What about everything else? We can't eat road salt."

In Friday'spress releaseannouncing the new tariff exemptions, Collins said she has asked U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to lower Trump's import duties.

"In my repeated conversations with Ambassador Greer, Secretary Lutnick, and other senior Administration officials, I have asked for tariff relief for these important products and stressed the burdens additional costs impose on Maine businesses and families," Collins said in a statement included in the release.

"I will continue working directly with Administration officials to seek additional relief from tariffs and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbor, ally and largest trading partner," she said.

The latest exemptions apply to tariffs on nine product categories, including corrugated paper, plastic boxes and packing bags, refrigeration equipment, multiple forms of machinery and seaweed and algae products.

"These producers are a vital part of our state's economy and support our rural and coastal communities," Collins said in the statement. "Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense."

The White House and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on the tariff exemptions, which werefirst reportedearlier Friday afternoon by The Wall Street Journal.

title: Doctors call Moderna, Merck cancer vaccine data a major advancement — despite Wall Street reaction
content:
Leaked confidential data. A major stock sell-off.

Beneath the chaos surroundingModernaandMerck'slatest dataon their personalized cancer vaccine, oncologists see something else: an important milestone in melanoma treatment.

The companies on Thursday released detailed results from a phase 3 trial on their mRNA-based shot after partial data leaked on social media platforms earlier that day.

The vaccine, known as intismeran autogene, reduced the risk of melanoma recurrence or death by 42% when given alongside Merck's immunotherapy Keytruda, compared with Keytruda alone. The combination also reduced the risk of cancer spreading to distant parts of the body or death by 38%, compared with just the immunotherapy, according to the trial on roughly 1,100 patients whose tumors were removed by surgery.

The stock market's reaction contrasted with the assessment of six melanoma specialists, who told CNBC the results represent a clinically meaningful advance that could eventually become a standard of care for patients who undergo surgery first and have not received immunotherapy before their operation.

"This has the potential to be a major breakthrough in melanoma treatment and also cancer immunotherapy in general that will open the door to greater outcomes for patients," said Dr. Sekwon Jang, a melanoma specialist at Inova Schar Cancer and principal investigator at one of the trial's U.S. sites.

Dr. Janice Mehnert, NYU Langone skin cancer specialist and trial investigator, added that "this is the first time we're seeing that when you add something to immunotherapy, you actually boost the efficacy of the immunotherapy."

The vaccine is not far from potentially entering the market for the first time and reaching melanoma patients. In an interview ahead of the results, Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel said the company is finishing a filing with regulators as it aims to get the drug fully approved next year.

"It's a very, very happy moment for the field, for patients," he said.

An immunotherapy like Keytruda wakes up the immune system to detect and attack cancer cells. Unlike preventative vaccines, which protect against infections that can cause cancer, Moderna and Merck's treatment acts like a blueprint to train the immune system to recognize and hunt residual cancer cells based on the specific mutations in an individual patient's tumor.

The significance of the phase 3 data extends beyond delaying a recurrence, doctors said. Melanoma can become much more difficult to treat when it returns after surgery and spreads to distant parts of the body, such as the lungs, brain or liver. Patients with advanced disease may require additional treatments, including immunotherapy, radiation or further surgery, and those methods are not guaranteed to work.

Preventing the cancer from returning could spare patients from ever facing the risks and complexities of metastatic disease altogether.

"If we can essentially cure more patients with earlier-stage melanoma and never have to deal with unresectable metastatic disease — that's a wonderful advance," said Dr. Michael Postow, chief of the Melanoma Service at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center and an investigator on the trial.

Ideally, patients in the future may be able to undergo surgery and receive the vaccine and Keytruda without needing further melanoma treatment, Postow told CNBC.

Still, questions remain about whether the combination ultimately helps patients live longer, what the benefit looks like over longer periods of time and which patients benefit most.

The results also leave open where the personalized vaccine would fit into a changing melanoma treatment landscape, some experts said.

The trial tested the vaccine after surgery, alongside Keytruda, rather than against immunotherapy regimens given before surgery. That's an approach increasingly used for eligible patients with resectable melanoma, where the primary tumor can be removed. The data does not show that using the vaccine approach is more or less effective than receiving immunotherapy before surgery.

The medical community will get more clarity after Moderna and Merck present the detailed results at the European Society for Medical Oncology conference on Saturday.

Moderna shares fell as much as 25% Thursday, before regaining some ground, after partial data from the trial leaked on social media. The sell-off came despite the positive results, underscoring the gap between the treatment's clinical promise and investor expectations for its commercial potential. Moderna shares are also up nearly 600% this year due to the cancer shot optimism, creating more potential for a Wall Street letdown.

Investors had hoped the vaccine and Keytruda would replicate the results of an earlier phase 2 trial, which showed a roughly 49% reduction in the risk of recurrence or death at five years, RBC Capital Markets analyst Trung Huynh wrote in a note Thursday. Huynh described the phase 3 results as clinically meaningful and likely to support regulatory approval, but said the primary efficacy result landed at the low end of investor expectations.

But there was a key difference in the studies: The phase 3 trial included patients with a broader range of risk profiles, including some at lower risk of recurrence than those enrolled in the earlier phase 2 trial, said Dr. George Ansstas, who leads the melanoma department at Washington University in St. Louis. That may have slightly tempered the results, since patients considered lower risk have less chance of recurrence to begin with.

"It's great data actually. It's overall consistent with what we've proven in the phase 2 trial," said Ansstas, who also worked on the phase 2 trial.

The combination showed little difference from Keytruda alone during the first six months of treatment, the companies said. But a separate analysis of the phase 3 data offered a more encouraging signal about the treatment's effect after the six-month mark. The vaccine and Keytruda reduced the risk of recurrence or death by 58% after that point, compared with Keytruda alone.

The 42% figure comes from the primary analysis, which included patients' outcomes throughout the trial's follow-up period. The median follow-up was about two years at the time of the analysis, so the result reflects the overall treatment effect, not just what happened before or after the six-month mark.

Ansstas said the benefit of the personalized cancer vaccine may take several months to emerge because each shot must be custom-manufactured, a process that can take roughly six weeks, while patients begin Keytruda in the meantime. After vaccination begins, the immune system also needs time and repeated doses to develop a response against tumors.

That timeline could help explain why the group that received the combination regimen saw even greater benefits around six months, Ansstas said. Still, the explanation is a hypothesis rather than proof of when the vaccine's effect begins.

Dr. Hussein Tawbi, a melanoma expert and trial investigator at the University of Texas MD ​Anderson Cancer Center, also highlighted the relatively mild side effects associated with the vaccine, including injection-site reactions, as a positive.

Keytruda and other cancer therapies can cause potentially serious immune-related side effects. Detailed safety results released on Saturday should help clarify the trade-offs of adding the vaccine to the immunotherapy regimen.

For Moderna, the stakes extend beyond melanoma. The company is working to build a business beyond its Covid vaccine, while Merck is preparing for the eventual loss of patent protection on Keytruda.

The companies have several hurdles ahead of them, including selling an individualized therapy that takes several weeks to create for a patient at scale.

"I think the downside is that it's super labor-intensive, and you're gonna have to make vaccines for each person, and so you can't just stockpile a million vaccines and then just ship it out when somebody needs it," said Dr. Adil Daud, professor of medicine and melanoma oncologist at the University of California San Francisco, who was the lead investigator on the phase 3 trial. "There is the time and expense, and it's probably going to cost like a lot of money."

Moderna and Merck have not disclosed any details about the manufacturing costs for the vaccine.

He added that most people who walk into the clinic with a tumor that has not been surgically removed may stick to receiving Keytruda before an operation because "that approach is simpler and doesn't put the patient through the delay" of creating the vaccine.

Daud said he expects the vaccine combination to be used primarily in the adjuvant setting, after surgery, rather than replace established immunotherapy regimens given before an operation. For patients who receive immunotherapy before surgery but show little or no response, the vaccine combination could offer another option, he said, though that would likely be for a smaller group of patients.

Moderna and Merck still need to validate the approach in other cancers, including non-small cell lung cancer, bladder cancer and renal cell carcinoma. Success in melanoma does not automatically guarantee that the approach will work in other tumors.

"I can dream of creating a log cabin, but we got some wood chops, and we've just knocked down one tree," Merck Research Laboratories President Dean Li said in an interview ahead of the results. "Knocking one tree does not give you a cabin or a village."
