title: Musk's SpaceX is still restricting Starlink in Ukraine and the toll is rising
content:
SpaceX'sStarlink internet systemcontinues to be throttled inUkraineas the stakes rise for the war-torn country, Ukrainian officials and a national security expert said Friday.

"Every day matters for Ukraine, because every Ukrainian life matters," wrote Denys Sienik, Ukraine's deputy ambassador to the U.S.,in a Friday post on X.

"Our people are waiting for positive news, hoping that the restrictions will be lifted and our defenders will have the capabilities they need to protect lives," Sienik said. "Unfortunately, as of today, nothing has changed. We continue to wait."

Since Oct. 14,Ukrainian officialshave accused SpaceX of undermining the country's ability to defend itself by imposing speed limits on Starshield, the military-grade Starlink offering. Any drone traveling above 100 mph lost its connection, disrupting some missions, officials said.

Despite recent comments from PresidentDonald Trumpthat indicated service was restored, Ukraine's Starshield terminals continued to experience problems on Friday, said Dmitri Alperovitch, chairman of the Silverado Policy Accelerator, a Washington, D.C., think tank focused on energy, defense tech and global trade.

"They are losing drones," Alperovitch, who is also a co-founder and former chief technology officer of cybersecurity firmCrowdStrike, told CNBC. "Ability to do mid strike to hit Russian logistics is now limited."

Ukrainian PresidentVolodymyr ZelenskyytoldABC Newsthat the Starlink system was still recording issues on Friday, and his defense tech advisor, Serhii Beskrestnov, also confirmed the restrictions were in place in a post on his Telegram channel.

"While there are isolated cases where Starlink may operate somewhat beyond the established limits, this is likely a result of SpaceX's algorithms or specific usage conditions, rather than an actual removal of restrictions," Beskrestnov said in a post translated by Google.

Musk and representatives from SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Who is ultimately responsible for the decision to limit Ukraine's service remains unclear.

TheWall Street Journalreported on Thursday that Trump spoke toElon Muskby phone about lifting the restrictions on Ukraine's Starshield terminals.Trumpsaid Thursday he didn't "want to comment one way or the other" about whether he made the call to Musk, and added, "The bottom line, he put it back."

But on Friday, Trump insisted that he hadn't spoken with Musk, and reiterated that Starshield service had been restored.

"I've heard it was fixed," Trump told reporters outside the White House. "But if it's not, I'll speak to him."

Amid the Starshield disruptions, Zelenskyy and other Ukrainian officials have floated the possibility of adopting additional satellite internet communications systems. Experts previously told CNBC that it could prove challenging for Ukraine or other countries to secure alternatives to Starlink since other options are not yet comparable to the service.

Zelenskyy wrote on Wednesday ina post on Xthat he met with Norwegian officials and Kongsberg, a Norwegian defense company, to discuss air defense systems and "launching work on new satellite communication capabilities for our warriors."

On Thursday, Ukraine's Ministry of Defense signed aletter of intentwith Nokia and ICEYE, a Finnish space intelligence firm, to "explore cooperation in space" and "support Ukraine's defense capabilities, particularly in building sovereign satellite communications," the companies said in a release.

"Modern warfare has proven that reliable communications are a matter of national security," Zelenskyy said in a statement. "We must all rely on capabilities that we can control."

-- CNBC's Eamon Javers and Lora Kolodny contributed reporting to this story.

title: AI's 'Black October': Critical PHP flaws set off global security scramble
content:
Cybersecurityteams around the globe are rushing to patchPHP programming languageflaws this week, in anartificial intelligencesafety moment that's being described as "Black October."

Nearly 70%of all websites use PHP, according to some estimates.

"In the last 2 days there have been several dozen cyber attacks which, in isolation, would each have been the worst to happen in an entire calendar year," John Milinovich, senior director of product management at Figma, wrote ina post on Xon Thursday. "Every sector from government to education to big tech and banks is being massively affected, and people are starting to freak out."

Researchers atGoogle'sWiz and the AI firm Calif discovered major vulnerabilities in PHP in August by using advanced AI models fromOpenAIand Google. But by Tuesday, the warnings had spread online, prompting governments and businesses around the globe to scramble tocontain the fallout.

Major AI companies have been warning about the technology'sadvancing cybersecurity capabilitiessince April, when Anthropic announced alimited rolloutof its powerful model calledMythos. Concerns mounted in July, when OpenAIdisclosedthat two of its models escaped containment, accessed the open internet and breached a company calledHugging Face.

Experts believe the PHP security flaws serve as the latest example of what's to come.

Jason Clinton, deputy chief information security officer at Anthropic, wrote ina post on Xon Thursday that the cybersecurity landscape is likely to get "a lot worse" before it gets better.

"Security leaders, never let a crisis go to waste: please go to your boards and ask for help right now," Clinton said. "Not for ai, for the basics. (we need to hold on for ~18 months.)"

While many large companies have access to advanced models that they can use to harden their systems, serious bugs could be more challenging for small- and medium-sized businesses to address, Chris Krebs, former director of the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency,told CNBCon Friday. He encouraged smaller companies to "constantly" scan for vulnerabilities, deploy patches as fast as possible or take legacy systems offline.

"This is a significant week or two in cybersecurity," Krebs told CNBC's "Squawk Box." "As I mentioned, 3% of all critical vulnerabilities ever discovered have been found in the last month."

Figma's Milinovich encouraged individuals to set up two-factor authentication for "everything," use a password manager, set up an identity protection app and move smart devices to their own network. He added that people should lean in and experiment with AI to understand how powerful the tools have become.

"While I still firmly believe that AI will be a net positive for humanity, it's more clear to me than ever that the societal and individual risk is very real, and is playing out NOW," Milinovich said.

Krebs added that company leaders and employees should check in on their security teams.

"Make sure they're doing okay," he said. "They've had a heck of a week."

—CNBC's Isabel O’Brien contributed to this report

title: TikTok U.S. hunts for multiple gigawatts of computing capacity, sources tell CNBC
content:
TikTok's U.S. entity is looking to secure multiple gigawatts of computing capacity, sources told CNBC, amid a global scramble for digital infrastructure deals.

The company, officially TikTok USDS Joint Venture, operates the social media platform in the U.S. and has sounded out opportunities to obtain capacity over the coming years, two people familiar with the discussions, who asked to remain anonymous as they weren't authorized to share the information, told CNBC.

TikTok U.S. is looking for four gigawatts of compute power by the early 2030s, one source said.

Companies across the world are looking to secure more compute capacity as artificial intelligence workloads become more prominent.

A company spokesperson told CNBC that the company "runs primarily on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure in the U.S. and Oracle will continue to be our primary cloud infrastructure provider."

Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, or OCI, typically runs in facilities thatOracleleases. CNBC has approached Oracle for comment.

There are signs TikTok U.S.' product plans could require extra compute going forward.

The company has numerous machine learning roles live on its website. Ajob advertposted by TikTok states that the company is "shipping a flagship B2B AI product at the frontier of large-model inference and creative automation."

TikTok USDS Joint Venture was established in 2026 in compliance with U.S. President Donald Trump's executive order mandating the divestiture of TikTok in the U.S. from its Chinese parent company, ByteDance.

In January, TikTok U.S. said it would "retrain, test, and update" its prized recommendation algorithm, which is built on machine learning, on U.S. user data. The company's recommendation algorithm will be "secured in Oracle's U.S. cloud environment," it said.

TikTok U.S. has three managing investors, Silver Lake, Oracle and MGX, each holding 15%. The Dell Family Office, the investment firm of Michael Dell, is also an investor. ByteDance retained 19.9% of the new entity.

title: American Express is cutting 5% of its workforce to 'prepare for AI'
content:
American Expressis cutting thousands of employees as the leading credit card company prepares for artificial intelligence to take over more of its internal processes.

Amex is eliminating 5% of its global workforce and taking a $336 million restructuring charge, CEO Stephen Squeri told analysts Friday on the company's third-quarterearningscall. The firm had almost 77,000 employees at the end of 2025.

Chief Financial Officer Christophe Le Caillec told CNBC in an interview that the restructuring was to make American Express "leaner, more agile, and also to prepare for AI."

"You don't want to automate processes that are not optimally structured," Le Caillec said. "So what we're doing here is to reduce layers and increase spans of controls, so that we can automate and take advantage of AI in the coming quarters and the coming years."

The Amex announcement reflects a broader trend across financial services, where banks are working to replace repetitive roles with AI automation. On Thursday,Barclays confirmed plansto trim 5,000 jobs — also roughly 5% of its staff — in another tech-driven cost initiative. The moves come even as the sector is enjoying robust profits from growing consumer spending and resilient credit.

During the analyst call, Squeri said that the charge was to improve the company's efficiency.

"We've got good momentum, but to accelerate innovation and win over the next few years, we needed to become [a] more agile and efficient organization," Squeri said.

Squeri devoted a 10-minute section of his prepared remarks to his views on AI, focusing mainly on how it will be used to personalize experiences and offers for Amex cardholders.

While the CEO emphasized the need to meetcustomers' desires to use AI,including agents, he added that Amex is "not going to let assistants run rogue through our system."

"We need to protect our customers [and] merchants, and we're only going to allow agents to access our systems that are either approved through API or MCP channels," he said, citing two ways to securely connect outside platforms with Amex systems.

Amex posted quarterly results that topped Wall Street profit expectations. Adjusted earnings per share were $4.68, topping the $4.48 average estimate of analysts, according to LSEG.

The companyraised its full-year earnings guidanceto a range of $18.30 to $18.60 per share, on an unadjusted basis, up from its previous target of $17.30 to $17.90.

That metric was helped by proceeds from Amex'ssale of its stake in Global Business Travel Group, part of which went into the restructuring plan, Le Caillec said.

Total revenue rose 9% to $20.06 billion, also coming in slightly below Wall Street's $20.12 billion LSEG forecast. Executives attributed part of the spending drag to recent exits from small business co-brand partnerships.

Shares of the card company fell roughly 3% in morning trading.

title: Fewer people are flying as airfare soars. Here's why airlines aren't worried
content:
Fewer people are flying this year, but with airfare this high andclimbing, airline executives say that's just fine.

The number of people screened at U.S. checkpoints is on track for its first annual decline since 2020. Major U.S. carriers have said capturing higher fares is more important than fully filling their planes or flying record numbers of travelers.

"We're actively prioritizing yield versus load factor and really happy as we see it. It fits right in with the premium investments that we're making,"American AirlinesChief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper said on the company's earnings call Thursday.

American's load factor, a gauge of how full planes are flying, fell to 83.4% in the third quarter from 86% in the same quarter of 2025.

The price of plane tickets has skyrocketed as airlines grapple with a spike in jet fuel prices, their biggest expense after labor, and pass more of those costs on to customers.

Fares in September were up more than 22% from a year earlier, according to the latest inflation read. Fare tracker Hopper said it expects thisholiday seasonto come with the most expensive ticket prices in years.

The averageSouthwest Airlinesfare in the third quarter, for example, was $231.69, up close to $50 from a year earlier. That doesn't include Southwest's new fees, like its extra charges for checked bags or a seat closer to the front of the plane.

The airline's count of revenue passengers, however, fell 3.2% from a year ago, to about 33.5 million people.

Still, both fares and the passenger counts exceeded Southwest's expectations.

"Passenger fares came in about $3 above what our forecast was and the more important thing is that passenger volumes also exceeded our expectations," Southwest CEO Bob Jordan said on an earnings call Thursday.

Since April — when airlinesbegan warningin earnest about profits taking a hit from the spike in jet fuel — through Thursday, about 9.3 million fewer people were screened at airport checkpoints compared with the same period of 2025, according to the Transportation Security Administration. While that's down less than 2% from last year, it follows years of growth.

With jet fuel prices more than double year-ago levels — as seen in U.S. Gulf Coast spot prices going for $4.63 a gallon, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration — airlines have been focused on recovering as much of the fuel spike as possible.

Even despite some drops, airline executives said during their earnings calls that travel demand overall is robust, especially for profitable premium cabins like business class.

And not every carrier is seeing a decline.United Airlinesflew 2.4% more passengers in the third quarter than it did a year ago, and said its unit revenue rose by 16%, the biggest increase since the pandemic.

"I've been pleasantly surprised at the industry's ability this year to raise yields and pass through much of the increase in fuel prices," CEO Scott Kirby said on the company'searnings callWednesday. "So it's possible that airlines will continue to focus on yields at the expense of load factor and that alone could get us to double-digit margins next year."

Most airlines are anticipating that fuel costs will continue to bite, but executives say they're confident in their pricing power.

United, for example, said it expects to pay an average of $4.80 a gallon for fuel in the fourth quarter, up from an average price of $3.90 a gallon in the third.

American, United,Delta Air Linesand Southwest all cut their profit forecasts for 2026 this month when they reported earnings. American is the only one of the four that expects to post a loss this year.

American and others have also reduced growth plans or warned the industry could dial back on its goals for expanding capacity, which could keep fares elevated. Reduced capacity can make bookable seats scarcer, driving up prices even more if demand holds.

The carriers said demand has been particularly strong for premium seats, which command hundreds, if not thousands of dollars, more than coach tickets.

Smaller airlines set to report results in the coming weeks, includingFrontier AirlinesandAllegiant Air, have traditionally focused on more price-sensitive customers, which could show if those travelers are pulling back at all.

One factor that could also affect air travel is the demise of Spirit Airlines, which went out of business in early May.

"Some of its customers have likely stopped flying," Bank of America said in a research note Thursday.

title: U.S. oil rises above $100, Brent at five-month high as Iran says it’s prepared for warfare
content:
Crude oil futures ticked higher on Friday, with global benchmark Brent crude hovering at a five-month high.

By 6:51 a.m. ET, front-monthBrent crude oil futureswere 1.1% higher at $114.49 per barrel. U.S.West Texas Intermediate crude futureswere up 1.6% to trade at $101.04 a barrel.

Brent futures were on track for a weekly rise of 3.3%, putting the contracts on course for their third consecutive week of gains. They were also trading at their highest since early May.

WTI futures were on track for a weekly decline of 1.1%, putting the contracts on course to snap two consecutive weeks of gains.

Traders are continuing to monitor developments in the Middle East.

On Thursday, U.S. President Donald Trump accused Iran of lying about attacks on ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz.

"Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of Oil prior to the U.S. Midterm Election," he wrote on Truth Social. "They are even making up fake hits, mines, and everything else, because more Oil is coming through the Hormuz Strait now than it did even prior to the beginning of the Conflict."

Iran's Islamic Revolution Guards Corps said Thursday that four vessels had been struck and caught fire in the Persian Gulf, according to the Iranian state-affiliated Tasnim news agency, while a further three had struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz.

Separately, Iran's army chief was reported to have said the country's military is fully prepared for "asymmetric warfare" after strengthening its capabilities.

In Saudi Arabia, oil giant Saudi Aramco reportedly told staff to evacuate its Dhahran headquarters and work remotely following a series of attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels, Reutersreported.

The Houthis have launched strikes on Saudi airports and some Aramco offices in recent weeks, resulting in multiple fatalities.

title: Russia and Ukraine trade fresh strikes despite renewed push for U.S.-brokered peace talks
content:
Russia and Ukraine continued tradingintense strikeson civilian and energy infrastructure overnight, less than a day after the parties signalled that peace negotiations were moving forward in U.S.-brokered talks.

Russia unleashed a major attack on Ukraine's energy facilities, knocking out electricity for over 500,000 after strikes on energy facilities in the Zhytomyr, Volyn, Mykolaiv, Poltava, Khmelnytskyi and Rivne regions,Ukraine's Energy Ministry saidFriday.

Work has begun on emergency restoration where the security situation allows, the ministry added.

DTEK, one of Ukraine's largest private energy companies, said an unspecified thermal power plant had stopped generating electricity after Russian shelling.

Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion in 2022, DTEK's thermal power plants have been attacked more than 230 times, the company said in apost on Telegramearly Friday.

Meanwhile, Russia's Ministry of Defense said that air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 443 Ukrainian drones overnight.

The latest attacks come after U.S. special envoySteve Witkoff met with Russian PresidentVladimir Putinin St. Petersburg on Wednesday for talks on how to end the conflict with Ukraine.

Following the meeting, Putin told Russian television that Moscow wasready to resume U.S.-mediated talkswith Kyiv in November.

"The ​goal of these talks will be to ensure the security of Ukraine and Russia after reaching ​peace agreements, in their final form, not as a result of a temporary ceasefire for some short period of time. We are ready to resume these contacts to achieve this goal," Putin said, Reuters reported.

A so-called "energy ceasefire" announced byPresident Donald Trumpon Oct. 11has failed toyield any meaningful outcome.

Ukrainian PresidentVolodymyr Zelenskyysaid earlier this week that Ukraine refrained from attacking Russian energy targets for three days but later resumed attacks, citing Russia's continued attacks on its infrastructure.

Speaking to CNN late Thursday, Zelenskyy said he was ready for a ceasefire, but that Ukraine needed strong security guarantees.

title: France is flashing euro crisis signals. This time, the fault lines are different
content:
As France's economic and political woes mount, investors are asking whether the country's debt problems risk contaminating the rest of the euro zone.

Markets are flashing alarm bells over the euro zone's second-biggest economy. Theeurohas remained under pressure, falling almost 5% against the dollar since the start of the year.

France's benchmark borrowing cost, the yield on its10-year bond, rose above 5% for the first time since 2002 this week before moving sharply higher.

Meanwhile, the spread between French and German 10-year bond yields — a closely watched metric of distress — reached more than 170 basis points on Thursday for the first time since the euro zone debt crisis of the early 2010s. The cost of insuring the French government against default, as measured by credit default swaps, is also the highest since that period.

The big concern is fragmentation, when countries that share a currency face sharply different borrowing costs, compounding market stress and risking spiraling debt repayments for the worst-impacted countries.

As the euro zone sovereign debt crisis of the early 2010s showed, market stress in one country can spread rapidly through economies that share a currency and a central bank but retain separate fiscal systems. The crisis began in Greece before spreading to countries including Portugal, Ireland, Italy and Spain.

Governments were expected to rescue struggling banks, which held large amounts of sovereign debt, creating a vicious cycle.

The crisis only eased after rescue programs tied to sweeping austerity measures, and ECB President Mario Draghi pledged in 2012 to do "whatever it takes" to preserve the euro.

Economists arewarningthat anew vicious cycle is being created— not only in France but in big economies from the U.S. to the U.K. — as investor concern over rising government debt pushes up yields and interest costs, which in turn add to the debt burden.

A slowdown in bond purchases raises "the specter that the government will be forced into default because it simply doesn't have the cash to pay interest and principal on its debt,"Nobel laureate Paul Krugman wrote in a blog on Oct. 8.

"Fear of default then leads to even more capital flight, which increases fears of default and the interest rate," he said.

France in particular has one of the highest deficit-to-GDP ratios in the 21-nation euro areaand a growing national debt pile. Its economy has slowed toa crawl, with the government cutting its 2026 growth forecast to just 0.5%.

Those fiscal strains come as political volatility and social unrest raise doubts about the government's ability to deliver measures aimed at stabilizing the public finances.

"We are deep into French crisis territory," Carsten Brzeski, ING's global head of macro research and chief euro zone economist, said by email.

"There is no risk of an imminent liquidity issue for the French government but the lack of trust of bond markets and the ongoing crisis should finally bring a high sense of urgency to Paris."

John Stopford, head of multi-asset income at Ninety One, said France has gone from being a core or semi-core European country for fixed income investors to increasingly being considered on the periphery, which he labeled "bizarre" given the history of France in relation to the EU and its economic power in the continent.

"We as investors, have just chosen for the time being to pretty much avoid all of the non-core countries in Europe – it's too fluid a situation with too much uncertainty to really want to get involved," Stopford said on a call.

Nonetheless, analysts CNBC spoke to broadly agreed that reforms meant that even if the market is behaving in similar ways to the post-financial crisis period, the contagion risk remained limited this time around.

Ninety One's Stopford said spreads would likely need to be trading "in the 200s" before the situation is broadly perceived as a genuine crisis — but, he added, that the situation in France "doesn't look great."

"French spreads are now wider than they were at the peak of the peripheral crisis of the early 2010s, but they're still much narrower than the extreme levels that we saw in Spain, Italy, Greece and Ireland back then, so... I think the market's assumption is that things will need to get worse before we get to a point where EU institutions start to look to try and limit further damage," he told CNBC.

BlackRock strategists noted the current environment is "materially different" to the one that preceded the 2011 to 2012 euro zone debt crisis, with the region now better equipped to weather financial stress, but they added that "further volatility and spillovers remain possible."

"The French bond sell-off illustrates how competition for capital is reshaping fixed income markets amid a global rate reset," they wrote. "Rising government borrowing and AI-related investment are pushing up financing costs, exposing borrowers with deteriorating fundamentals to greater scrutiny."

George Lagarias, chief economist at Forvis Mazars, said France was already in a debt crisis, citing its debt-to-GDP ratio of 119% at the end of the second quarter of 2026 — close to Greece's of 128% in late 2009.

A spillover would mean a wider French-German yield spread followed by higher credit default swap prices – the cost of insuring debt, he said.

"Italy, Spain, would see higher borrowing costs, and have to curtail fiscal expenditures, possibly raising political backlash in their own countries," he told CNBC. "The European periphery would come under tremendous pressure, even if their finances are in much better order than a few years ago."

However, Lagarias said crucial structural differences minimize the risk of a wider spillover akin to the early 2010s, which he estimated at 10% to 20%.

"Greece had a very bad trade deficit. France also has a trade deficit, but the numbers are much more benign," he said by email.

He added that the Insee, France's national statistics body, was "not likely to lie about the deficit" and contrasted this with Greece.

In 2009, Greece sharplyrevisedits projected budget deficit from 3.7% of GDP in the spring to 12.5% by October, undermining confidence in the reliability of its public finances and helping accelerate the crisis.

"[French] debt levels are worrying but known. Markets can deal with known risks. They hate surprises," Lagarias added. "What sunk Greece was a deficit that was suddenly revealed to be five-fold versus the official estimate. This catalysed a crisis."

Alex Everett, investment director for rates management at Aberdeen Investments, agreed that the current environment should be treated "primarily as French risk rather than a systemic euro-area risk."

"Compared to the early 2010s, the Eurozone has stronger banks, greater integration and numerous tools designed to limit the risk of sovereign fragmentation," he said. "I anticipate contagion to be short-lived."

title: Nvidia's Huang heads to Kazakhstan for the first time — and he's not the only one with big plans
content:
Kazakhstan may not be the first place that comes to mind when thinking about the global artificial intelligence boom, but several Big Tech companies have taken interest — including Nvidia.

NvidiaCEO Jensen Huang, who made his first visit to Kazakhstan on Friday, said the country could become a major AI computing hub serving Europe, pointing to its energy resources and plans to expand data center capacity.

Sitting in a fireside chat in Astana with Zhaslan Madiyev, Kazakhstan's deputy prime minister and minister of artificial intelligence and digital development, Huang highlighted the country's role.

He also emphasized the importance of countries developing their own AI capabilities, saying nations should have the infrastructure to deliver AI services domestically, while adapting the technology to their own languages and cultures.

The visit comes as Kazakhstan seeks to attract billions of dollars in technology investment and position itself as a regional hub for artificial intelligence.

Kazakhstan has made AI a national priority,declaring2026 the Year of Digitalization and Artificial Intelligence as part of a broader effort to develop its digital economy.

In June, Kazakhstan's governmentannounced plans for a $10 billion AI infrastructure investment in partnership with U.S.-based AI cloud company Firebird, aimed at building a computing cluster powered by 100,000 advanced GPUs, including Nvidia chips.

Nvidia intends to invest in the company, which is pursuing an approximately 2-gigawatt AI infrastructure expansion across Armenia, Kazakhstan and other market,as statedin the chipmaker's announcement.

Meanwhile, San Francisco-based AI video startup Higgsfield also has a significant presence in Kazakhstan, with more than 300 people working across its engineering and creative teams there.

The company's co-founder, Kazakhstani AI engineer Yerzat Dulat, told CNBC exclusively that "building a team in Kazakhstan was an unexpected bet for many. Today, we're backed by some of the most influential names in technology and media."

Higgsfield said Friday that Nvidia and investment firm TCV had invested in an extension of its Series B funding round, yet it did not disclose the amount. Earlier, the AI video startup company had alsoraised$400 million in a Series B funding round at a $5.4 billion valuation in August.

"The first thing and the last thing is you invest in people, not companies. And the founders of Higgsfield are visionary in the work that they do" Huang said in a fireside chat.

At the center of the initiative isData Center Valley, a planned AI infrastructure hub in Ekibastuz with 300 megawatts of power capacity is already available with plans to expand to 1 gigawatt.

Kazakhstan is promoting its competitive electricity costs, large land reserves and investment incentives as advantages for international data center developers, as demand for computing capacity continues to grow — and some of that investment push is already taking shape.

Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayevsaidearlier this month that two supercomputing clusters powered by Nvidia technologies had already been launched in the country.

Other international companies have also announced plans to invest in Kazakhstan's digital infrastructure.

Accordingto the country's digital development ministry, Singapore-based GK Hyperscale has also signed an agreement with Kazakhstan's government to develop two hyperscale data centers, with an expected investment of $1.5 billion and a combined IT capacity of 200 megawatts.

The project also includes a planned $1.2 billion investment in power infrastructure, with construction initially scheduled to begin in early 2026 and the first data center module expected to become operational in 2027.

The growing corporate interest in Kazakhstan also extends beyond the AI industry.

German'sVolkswagenhasrevampedits push into Central Asia this year, announcing in late June that for the first time its China business and factories was leading vehicle exports to another country, in this case Uzbekistan.

A few weeks later, the automaker announced entry into Kazakhstan.

The expansion illustrates how international companies are looking beyond China for new customers while using their existing Chinese manufacturing operations to serve neighboring markets.

In a "Tianjin Declaration" at the close of the SCO Summit in 2025, members of the security organizationnotedthe potential of platforms such as an AI innovation center in Kazakhstan.

This year's SCO event on artificial intelligencetookplace earlier this month in Kazakhstan's capital, Astana, bringing together representatives from member states to discuss national AI strategies, regulation and opportunities for technological cooperation.

title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI
content: Image source,Mohammed AshimImage caption,Mohammed Ashim is paid to film his hands at workByPriti GuptaTechnology Reporter,ÂReporting fromMumbaiPublished4 hours agoMohammed Ashim has been cutting hair and trimming beards for four years in Bengaluru.But recently the 22-year old has been strapping a camera to his head to record his work.The camera only records his hands and fingers - his client's faces are blurred out."The routine is simple, but you have to be disciplined about how you move. The operations team taught me that my hands always have to stay cleanly inside the frame, the lighting has to be sharp, and I can't tilt my head too abruptly while working."He wears the camera for five or six hours a day."It's good money, but honestly, the feeling of doing something this futuristic is what keeps me excited. I never imagined my razor techniques would be useful to a global tech company," says Ashim.He is one of hundreds of thousands of workers across the world paid to record their activities.Ashim's footage is collected by a local company, which might have hundreds of people filming their work.That video is then sold on to technology companies and research organisations who use it to train artificial intelligence - in particular so-called physical AI, a type of artificial intelligence that can control robots in the real world.Rashdan Technologies collects and processes such human generated data."Every robotics company, every frontier AI lab, has a specific kind of data they want: industrial tasks, agriculture, household chores, small business work like pottery, garment-making, embroidery, candle-making. We go wherever the task is," says co-founder and CEO Shahil Baig.His company pays $5 to $10 (Â£3.74; Â£7.47) for eight to 10 hours of recorded work."For a lot of these people, that's meaningful," Baig says.Making sure workers give their consent and are comfortable with the process is important, he says."We record hands, not faces, and where multi-camera rigs do capture more of the body or environment, we blur faces out. No names, no contact details, nothing that identifies them personally goes into what we hand off."But his customers are getting more demanding."Now clients are asking for four to six cameras rigged around a person's head to cover the entire scene, not just the hands."Getting someone to agree to one small camera is one conversation. Getting them to agree to wearing what's effectively a five-camera headset is a completely different, and harder, one. We pay more for that tier of data collection because of what we're asking of people."And the industry is becoming more crowded, Agarwal expects dozens more competitors to emerge in India this year.Image source,Rashdan TechnologiesImage caption,Shahil Baig expects dozens more firms to start collecting video of workersWhy is such data so important?If you want robots to navigate the real world, they can't just be trained inside computer simulations, argues Manish Agarwal, the founder of Humyn Labs, which collects and processes human-generated data.Most of that data comes from video, but sometimes collectors wear hardware on their hands and fingers to capture physical contact."Physical tasks require high-quality signals involving limb movements, fingers, wrists, elbows, shoulders and dynamic force application. For example: applying the correct grip force so a plastic bottle doesn't crumble versus a steel glass," he says.And until recently, that data was not available."There is no existing internet archive of embodied human activity - no dataset of a kitchen being cleaned, or a car being assembled by hands that know exactly how much force to apply. That data has to be captured from scratch, in the real world, across diverse environments," says Agarwal, whose company has bases in Bangalore and San Francisco.At the moment his firm has 96,000 data collectors across countries in Latin America and Southeast Asia.Humyn Labs filters the thousands of hours of video supplied by those collectors, selecting the most useful content. It's then labelled so the AI knows what it is looking at and packaged in a format that can be used by clients."You need to source across a variety of factories, a variety of tasks, in different geographies because if you want to build deployment for US factories or US houses, you'd want environments that are a proxy for that. Residential houses in India may not be the right context for building a robotics use case for the US."Figure caption,The factory workers teaching robots how to work like humansBut are workers collecting data for machines that will one day do their jobs?At the moment it's too early to tell says Bino Paul, senior professor at the School of Management and Labour Studies at the Tata Institute of Social Sciences (TISS) in Mumbai.For some workers AI might be a useful tool, but robots could automate other jobs, he says.The problem is that, if machines do start to take over, there will be little workers can do about."By the time workers realise what they have participated in, things may have gone too far," he says.Like many others, he wants governments to regulate AI."AI cannot be viewed merely as a technical system. We need to develop a socio-technical system in which ethics is upheld through human agency, ensuring that AI delivers beneficence rather than maleficence."'This is survival'Despite concerns over where AI is heading, money is still being poured into its development.Some of that trickles down to workers in India, where there is no shortage of workers prepared to wear a camera for a few dollars a day.Mohammed Arman has been working in the textiles industry in Bangalore for 10 years."Garments stitching and cutting. I know this work so well I could probably do it with my eyes closed. Cloth, thread, needle, machine after 10 years, your hands just know what to do before your mind even tells them," he says.He has recently started wearing a head-mounted camera that records his work."For me, it's simple. This is survival. I have a family back home in Bihar, and every rupee I send back matters. If someone offers me extra money to wear a camera while I do the exact same work I've been doing for 10 years, I'm not going to say no."It doesn't cost me anything. I'm already doing the stitching, already doing the cutting. Now I just get paid a little more for it," he says.Image source,Mohammed ArmanImage caption,Mohammed Arman has been filming his tailoring workWhile there is demand for such footage it will be collected somewhere."India's current role in this industry is largely as a supplier of raw material - people strap on cameras, record themselves doing ordinary tasks, and that footage gets shipped off to labs abroad," Agarwal says.But he argues the value of that kind of work will quickly become eroded, as more companies compete for collection contracts."India can't afford to stay a footage supplier. It needs to move up the value chain: from recording raw video to owning the pipeline that turns that video into something usable - cleaning it, structuring it, validating it, and ultimately setting the standards for what counts as high-quality training data," he says.Image source,Jolly ArifurImage caption,Jolly Arifur has been filming domestic work for a few hours a dayFor some people collecting data is attractive part time work.Science teacher Jolly Arifur was looking for work she could do from home that would fit around her young son."For the past seven months, I strapped a rig-mounted camera on my head while doing my routine domestic work scrubbing, cooking, sweeping tile floors, and folding laundry."Arifur, who lives in Guntakal, Anantapur, fits the recording work around her teaching."I get paid two to three dollars per hour. If I record three to five hours a day, that's a good amount in hand it's become an extra source of income for me, on top of teaching. I'm managing both honestly, fantastically."Related topicsInternational BusinessTechnology of BusinessArtificial intelligenceIndiaRoboticsMore Technology of BusinessThe virtual worlds where robots are trainedPublished18 SeptemberThe extreme engineering of aircraft windowsPublished16 SeptemberCan Europe recharge its battery industry?Published11 September

title: Defense giant Saab sees orders triple after Gripen fighter jet deal with Ukraine
content:
Swedish defense giantSaabreported better-than-expected third-quarter earnings and revenue on Friday, as new orders more than tripled from a year earlier, boosted by a deal to supply Gripen fighter jets to Ukraine.

New orders came in at 65.8 billion Swedish kronor ($6.6 billion), up from 20.9 billion kronor a year earlier, beating FactSet expectations of 56.4 billion kronor.

Third-quarter sales reached 20.6 billion kronor, ahead of FactSet expectations of 20 billion kronor. Earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) came in at 1.95 billion kronor, also beating forecasts of 1.9 billion kronor.

The results come asEuropean governments raceto turn defense spending pledges into military capability.

Saab's order intake included a 24.6 billion kronor contract for 16 Gripen E fighter jets for Ukraine, signed in June and booked in the third quarter. Deliveries are scheduled for 2029-2030.

"The growing customer demand is reflected in major contract awards, including Gripen for Ukraine, GlobalEye and an order related to Germany's new frigates," CEO Micael Johansson said in a statement.

Orders booked in the quarter also include a10.1 billion kronor orderfor its military surveillance aircraft GlobalEye to an undisclosed customer in the Middle East, and an 8.7 billion kronor order for systems for German frigates.

Saab, whose products range from Gripen fighter jets and submarines to missiles and advanced electronics, has seen exponential order growth since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022.

Even with anever-growing order book, booming sales, and increasing profitability, Saab stock, like many of its peers, has taken a hit in recent months as some investors question whether valuations have run ahead of the industry's ability to deliver.

title: SpaceX records $561 million investment gain from stake in Elon Musk's Boring Co.
content:
SpaceX said on Thursday that its stake inElon Musk'sThe Boring Co. netted the company an investment gain of $561 million during the third quarter.

The gain accounted for more than half of SpaceX's "other income" in the period and boosted its net income, which landed at just over $4 billion, the company said in its quarterlyfinancial filingwith the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Created inside SpaceX in 2017 and spun out a year later, Boring Co. says its mission is to "revolutionize transportation" by creating underground tunnels with stations where passengers can board and exit. Last month, Boring Co.raised$3 billion at a $23 billion valuation, with backing from the United Arab Emirates and a roster of other longtime Musk supporters.

Boring Co. has announced about a dozen city projects, but its only tunnels currently open for public use are in Las Vegas, where passengers can travel in Tesla vehicles between the downtown convention center and various casino resorts using its Las Vegas Convention Center Loop.

In July of last year, Boring Co.strucka deal to build about 20 miles of tunnels in Nashville, Tennessee. The Music City Loop, as it's known, is being designed to carry paying passengers between downtown and the airport inTeslavehicles. The fast-tracked projectsparkeda partisan feud when it was greenlit and has drawn new safety concerns oversinkholerisks this week.

In the UAE, Boring Co. plans to build over 150 kilometers (93 miles) of tunnels, includinga project announcedin February of last year, the Dubai Loop.

SpaceX also said in Thursday's filing that it purchased $151 million worth ofTesla'sMegapack energy storage systems during the quarter. Musk said on SpaceX'searnings callon Tuesday that he thinks it would be a "good idea" for the two companies to merge, and said they've both created special committees to discuss a potential transaction.

title: Etsy bans AI-generated recipes and patterns from its online marketplace
content:
Etsysaid Thursday it will no longer allow merchants to sell AI-generated recipes and patterns on its online marketplace, as part of a wider push to set firmer rules around the use of artificial intelligence on its platform.

Ina blog post, Etsy said it's banning the sale of "functional guides" that are created using AI, including patterns, cooking recipes and instructions. The products are usually marketed as digital downloads, such as crochet or sewing patterns. Users then "put in effort to achieve a finished product," the company said.

Sellers will also be required to show an actual item made using the instructions, not an AI-generated or simulated result, "so buyers know what to expect," Etsy said.

Etsysaidin a separate notice to sellers that it was making the changes as AI threatens to erode buyers' and sellers' trust in the platform.

"Today, many active buyers say they can't tell which items involve AI-generated content," the company wrote. "It's become a top-three barrier to shopping more often on Etsy. And you, our seller community, have told us you're concerned about your work appearing alongside items that use AI in misleading ways, and that it's becoming harder for buyers to recognize your role in creating your items."

As part of the move, Etsy said it's barring sellers from creating bot-generated listings without any human involvement. Sellers will also be required to include at least one unedited photo of the actual item they're selling.

Etsy told sellers it will continue to allow AI-generated art on its platform as long as merchants "play a clear role in what they create and are transparent about the process."

"Sellers must still disclose when an item is created using AI and cannot misrepresent AI-generated work as handmade or entirely their own creation," the company added.

Founded in 2005, Etsy is known for its mix of craft makers and artisan goods. The company has beenleaning moreinto that reputation as it has battled an influx of generic, mass-produced items from resellers and increasing competition fromAmazonandWalmart, as well as newer e-commerce upstarts like TikTok, Temu and Shein.

Misleading, AI-generated products or images present a new challenge for Etsy and other online marketplaces. Etsy has in recent years struggled to curb the proliferation of AI-madecrochet patternsand otherAI "slop."Amazon recentlyrequired sellersto label photos or videos that feature AI-generated people in response to recent legislation mandating the disclosure.

While Etsy has cracked down on the use of AI in listings, it's been infusing the technology throughout more of its website. The company has used AI to build more detailed profiles of shoppers and surface relevant products in search results.

Etsy has also partnered withOpenAIon shopping features, including launching a ChatGPT app for product discovery.

title: Trump invokes Cold War era Defense Production Act for oil production, refining
content:
President Donald Trump determined on Thursday that petroleum production, refining, and related activities are essential to national defense, a move that could open up U.S. funding for fossil fuel projects.

In a presidential memo, Trump also invoked part of the Cold War-era Defense Production Act, allowing him to provide financial incentives for oil-related activities, pipelines and storage of liquid fuels.

Prices for crude oil and diesel have surged since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in joint action at the end of February. Since then, the conflict has limited energy shipments globally, with Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries exacerbating the fuel shortages.

The surge in costs poses a risk for Trump in the Nov. 3 elections, as his fellow Republicans try to maintain control of both chambers of Congress. The Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll that closed Monday shows just 36% of Americans approve of Trump's handling of the economy.

The memo said that without taking the actions, the U.S. is not able to provide enough of those energy services in a "timely manner due to constrained financing, long lead times, permitting and infrastructure bottlenecks, and supply chain limitations."

The memo did not mention specific projects that could be funded. The U.S. averaged around 13.6 million barrels of daily crude production in 2025, making it the largest crude producer worldwide.

Last ‌week, Vice President JD Vance said the administration would use the Defense Production Act to expand capacity of a Texas refinery owned byDelek U.S. Holdings.

Trump signed legislation last year that included $1 billion in Defense Production Act funding for energy-related projects deemed critical to national security.

title: Disney’s multiplatform Super Bowl plan frustrates ABC affiliates
content:
The CNBC Sport newsletter with Alex Sherman brings you the biggest news and exclusive interviews from the worlds of sports business and media, delivered weekly to your inbox.

Subscribe here to get access today.

Disney knows that business, like football, is a contact sport. Sometimes the hits come in-house fromfeuding among executives. Sometimes they come in court, frombattling the Federal Communications Commission.

And sometimes, Disney, which owns ABC, takes hits from its own affiliates.

ABC station owners are irritated with Disney's recent decision to air the Super Bowl on many different platforms, including Disney+, ESPN2, NFL Network and ESPNU. The game is already airing on both ABC and ESPN. The aggregate of the different platforms may drop advertising revenue associated with broadcast viewership by up to 35% compared to last year, according to a station group CEO who asked not to be named because the data is private.

Disney has the broadcast rights to this season'sSuper Bowl. ABC hasn't had the Super Bowl since 2006.Disney got back in the Super Bowl rotation when it struck its most recentmedia rights dealwith the NFLin 2021.

The Super Bowl is a major moneymaker for ABC stations. Some of these are owned by Disney, but the vast majority are part of local station groups owned by companies such as Sinclair, Nexstar and Tegna.

Fox saidlast yearthat Super Bowl ads generated more than $800 million in gross revenue across all platforms. The math for the main broadcast network is simple. There are about 85 30-second spots during a standard game. At $8 million a pop on average, that's $680 million.

Most advertising campaigns are national, but some brands buy big markets only. That allows smaller markets to sell advertising locally.

An average primetime audience is around eight million viewers. So, if the Super Bowl gets 15 times the audience, advertising rates increase in lockstep. Super Bowl LX, held in February, had 125.6 million viewers.

About 3% of a typical local affiliate station's annual advertising revenue comes from the Super Bowl when the game is on its air, according to a person familiar with the matter. The number can be much higher for the owned-and-operated big market stations, which typically take in about $10 million in advertising revenue from the Super Bowl, according to a source familiar with the matter.

Local affiliate stations pay the owners of the broadcast networks — Disney for ABC, Comcast for NBC, Fox for Fox and Skydance for CBS — a so-called reverse retransmission fee for the right to carry network programming.

There's a standard process to retransmission fee discussions. Disney pays billions for live sports and then asks its affiliates for money to help pay for them. The affiliates then negotiate with the pay-TV providers and chargethemretrans fees.

This is why the broadcast affiliates are steaming. For decades, the Super Bowl was exclusive to broadcast TV. Getting access to the Big Game was a big part of that fee.

For years, media companies have made the Super Bowl available for both broadcast and streaming audiences. Still, this year, Disney has taken a wrecking ball to the broadcast exclusivity of the past.

Given the game is an ESPN production with ESPN's primary "Monday Night Football" announcing crew — Joe Buck and Troy Aikman — it's reasonable to assume the cable network will get a fair amount of viewership for the game.

Disney is also putting the game on Disney+ — a streaming service that's never been about sports. Airing the Super Bowl on a streaming service isn't new. NBCUniversal's Peacock, Fox's Tubi and Skydance's Paramount+ have streamed the game in the past. But those services allow for geofenced dynamic advertising insertion (DAI), allowing local affiliates to sell commercials to a streaming audience. Disney+, which doesn't typically air live ABC sports programming, doesn't have DAI.

Disney is also airing so-called"alt-casts" of the game on ESPN2 (Eli and Peyton Manning will do their typical "ManningCast"), ESPNU ("Super Bowl LXI Field Pass with The Pat McAfee Show"), and NFL Network ("Super Bowl LXI Playbook with Next Gen Stats").

Disney is even airing a "Star Wars"-themed alt-caston Disney Channel and Disney XD. The "Star Wars" alternative broadcast will also be on Disney+.

The commercials that run nationally will be the same on all platforms, according to a Disney spokesperson. The "Star Wars" alt-cast will be ad-free.

Disney wants to synergize its platforms to maximize viewership — and collect the ad revenue.

"The Super Bowl is the year's most-watched telecast, and our broad distribution across ESPN, ABC, and Disney+ will give fans everywhere more ways than ever to enjoy the game," according to a statement provided by a Disney spokesperson. "Making marquee live events available via streaming is a well-established industry practice. Fox and NBC have recently offered the Super Bowl on Tubi and Peacock, and we've similarly streamed 'The Oscars' on Hulu and 'Dancing with the Stars' on Disney+, for example. There's nothing unprecedented about this approach as we are meeting the modern consumer where they are."

Still, the totality of it all will certainly lower broadcast viewership. One station group CEO estimated local advertising revenue associated with the game may fall 35%. That executive declined to be named because the analysis is private.

"Any time you fragment distribution, you're destroying value for each of the individual platforms," a station group CEO told me, who asked not to be named for fear of potential retribution. "I don't have a problem with what Disney is doing — I have a problem that there's no acknowledgement that we're losing money."

This issue of lower broadcast Super Bowl viewership, and associated advertising revenue, is of so much concern that it's currently being discussed at the affiliate board — an elected body of executives across the TV broadcasting industry who act as liaisons between local stations and their parent network (Disney/ABC, in this case).

It's unclear exactly how affiliates may be compensated, if at all.

The decline in traditional TV viewership is pushing Disney to broaden its coverage to new platforms and new audiences that don't watch cable or broadcast TV.

Station executives want Disney to lean in to what continues to be a profitable, albeit declining, business. Several of those executives told me privately they think Disney is doing itself and the broader linear TV ecosystem a disservice by not banding together with affiliates to keep viewers on broadcast platforms.

"Our ABC affiliates are important partners and we always take that into careful consideration when making these decisions," said a Disney spokesperson. "We've successfully navigated similar situations in collaboration with the governing board many times before, and this is no different."

The chairman of the ABC Television Affiliates Association Board of Governors declined to comment.

title: OpenAI nears up to $30 billion funding round at $1.25 trillion valuation led by UAE investors
content:
OpenAIis closing in on a funding round that could value theartificial intelligencegiant at more than $1 trillion ahead of a potentialinitial public offering.

The San Francisco-based AI company is raising up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation, according to people familiar with the deal, who asked not to be named because the details were confidential. That valuation does not include new capital raised.

Investors from the United Arab Emirates are leading the round alongside Coatue, according to the people. The financing is being positioned as an "opportunistic" bridge ahead of a potential IPO.

OpenAI kickstarted discussions for a new funding round afterinvestors approached the companywith proposals in September, as CNBC previously reported. OpenAI told investors on Thursday that it is aiming to secure signatures by the end of next week, but the final size of the round is still being determined, the people said.

Alongside the new investment, OpenAI is negotiating a commercial deal that would secure more computing capacity from the UAE, according to one person. OpenAI told investors in February that it's targeting roughly $600 billion in total compute spend by 2030.

The companyconfidentially filedits prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, but it has not disclosed exactly when it plans to debut.

OpenAI CFO Sarah Friartold employeesin August that the AI lab "will be a public company in 2027." The following month, CEOSam Altmansaidthat "right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public."

Anthropic, OpenAI's chief rival, is also gearing up for what is widely expected to be a massive IPO. The companyconfidentially filedits prospectus with regulators in June and is activelyengaging in meetingswith prospective investors, as CNBC previously reported.

In May, Anthropic closed a$65 billionfunding round at a $965 billion valuation.

title: Nasdaq falls more than 2% for worst day since June as AI spending woes, oil prices spark sell-off: Live updates
content:
Stocks mostly slid Thursday on renewed concerns around spending by artificial intelligence companies, while oil prices jumped amid rising geopolitical tensions.

TheNasdaq Compositepulled back 2.6% to 26,008.86, while theS&P 500shed 1.21% to close at 7,663.43. The tech-heavy index suffered its worst session since June, while the S&P 500 posted its worst daily performance since July. TheDow Jones Industrial Averageinched up 11.89 points, or 0.02%, to end at 52,867.98.

Meta Platformsslipped about 7%, even as itexceeded revenue expectationsand offered upbeat guidance. Technology more broadly was under pressure as well as ongoing concerns about artificial intelligence spending persisted.Advanced Micro Devicesfell more than 8%, whileMicron TechnologyandNvidiadropped 6% and 4%, respectively.

Neocloud leaderCoreWeave, whose bond yields and credit default swapsremained elevated, declined 10% as well. The move comes as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huangtold CNBCThursday that demand for neoclouds is "off the charts." However, he added that capital is scarce and impeding growth.

Huang's commentary about a scarcity of capital is "spooking markets and reigniting the concerns around the capital markets on the credit side being full from a risk appetite standpoint," said Wells Fargo traders in a note. They also said Meta's comments about the large amount of AI funding needed caused the shares to roll over and weighed on the overall market.

JPMorgan traders noted that Wednesday's bullish "tone reversed overnight" because Meta shares rolled over in the premarket and chatter increased "over renewed Iran kinetic-risk post US mid-term election."

Additionally, "underlying price actions and feedback from our trading desk also suggested the still fragile narrative around AI financing concerns and the lack of conviction/re-grossing from the recent tech reversal," they said in a note to clients.

Oil prices, meanwhile, jumped after The New York Times reported, citing sources, that the U.S. and Israel have plans for renewed strikes against Iran following next month's midterm U.S. elections. PresidentDonald Trumpalso told reporters late Wednesday that Washington is not negotiating with Tehran and that something will happen "fairly soon."

International benchmarkBrent crude futuresrose 4% to settle at $113.17 per barrel.West Texas Intermediate crude futuresadvanced 2.39% to $99.47 per barrel.

Investors also turned to U.S. Treasurys in their search for a safe haven. The benchmark10-year Treasurynote yield dropped more than 17 basis points to 4.972%, falling to itslowest level in almost a month. The2-yearnote yield also shed more than 16 basis points to 4.659%.

The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite saw sizable declines on Thursday.

The broad market index moved down 1.21% to 7,663.43, while the tech-heavy index decreased 2.6% to 26,008.86.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average, however, traded just above the flatline, rising 11.89 points, or 0.02%, to 52,867.98.

Shares of power and energy companies tied to the AI boom plunged Thursday as investors grew increasingly concerned about the soaring costs of data center expansion.

Two major energy equipment players,GE VernovaandBloom Energy, led the declines, with each falling more than 11%. As investors sold their AI infrastructure stocks,Vistraalso shed over 10%, whileQuanta Servicesdropped more than 8%.Talen EnergyandEatondeclined 8.3% and nearly 7%, respectively.

The selloff came asMeta's latest earningsreport reignited concerns over AI infrastructure spending. The tech giant raised its capital expenditure forecast, highlighting the enormous investment required to support its AI ambitions and raising questions about how quickly those investments will generate returns.

Nuclear energy stocks were also caught in the downturn, withOklofalling more than 4% andNuScale Powerdeclining over 3%. The broad retreat shows a deeper, growing investor unease over whether the pace of AI infrastructure investment is sustainable.

Oil prices spiked Thursday as investors fear escalation in the Middle East with the U.S. reportedly planning to resume strikes against Iran.

Brent crudefutures gained 4% to close at $113.17 per barrel, the highest level for the international benchmark since May 4. U.S.West Texas Intermediategained 2.4% to settle at $99.47.

Modernashares dropped as much as 25% on Thursday following the leak of partial data on itsclosely watched cancer vaccinedeveloped withMerck.

The stock fell even though the full data, released later Thursday following the leak, appeared positive relative to Wall Street expectations. The investment comes amid a wider effort by Skydance to raise equity investments as it looks to cut costs.

title: Trump defends Ramaswamy ad with Acton's estranged mom after bipartisan criticism
content:
PresidentDonald Trumpon Thursday defended a controversialad by the campaignofVivek Ramaswamyfeaturing the estranged mother ofAmy Acton, his Democratic opponent in the Ohio gubernatorial race, calling Acton a liar.

Trump's defense of the ad came after widespread bipartisan backlash to it, which focused on the fact that Acton's stepfather,Cledith Arthur, was charged with raping her when she was a child and was married to Acton's mother, Donna Arthur.

In the ad, Donna Arthur says Acton has "lied her entire life."

"Don't vote for people who lie," Arthursays in the ad. "Don't let her become your governor. If you think she'll make your life better, you're fooling yourself. It will only get worse."

Acton has said she has not seen Arthur since she was 12 years old. Cledith Arthur fled after his arrest and remained a fugitive until his death in Pennsylvania in 2004.

Trump, in a Truth Social post on Thursday, said, "Vivek Ramaswamy put up a very powerful Ad about a mother saying that her daughter, Amy Acton, who is running for Governor of Ohio, is a liar, and much worse."

"The Press, in a concerted and well coordinated attack, is trying to get Vivek Ramaswamy to 'take down the Ad,' " Trump said. "Frankly, anybody whose mother spoke about a daughter in that way would normally lead to the daughter being precluded from serving in Office, let alone the Office of Governor."

Trump also criticized Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine for calling for the ad to be taken down, even as DeWine continued to support his fellow Republican Ramaswamy's candidacy to succeed him.

"The ad, on its face, is deeply, deeply troubling," DeWine said in a press conference earlier Thursday.

Trump said DeWine "probably wants a Dumocrat to win, and certainly doesn't want someone who will do a much better job than he is capable of doing."

"I suggested, on the other hand, that Vivek should keep it up, and let everyone listen to the mother of a defective, dishonest, and incapable Candidate, explain how the daughter is a DISASTER who, uncontrollably, lies, cheats, and steals!" Trump said.

Trump later told reporters that he had "no idea" about Acton's allegation of being raped by her mother's husband, and questioned when Acton had made that claim.

Trump's comments came a day after his vice president, JD Vance, during a visit to Cincinnati and said it was "not really my concern" whether the ad was appropriate.

But Vance also said, "I'm a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America."

"The media and the Democrats in the state of Ohio are obsessed because guess what? Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is and calls Amy Acton a liar," Vance said. "Whatever you think about any of the TV advertisements, focus on the substance and focus on the facts."

Ramaswamy's campaign has spent nearly $95,000 to air the ad so far, according to AdImpact, with more than 100 airings concentrated in Cleveland, Columbus, and Cincinnati — three of Ohio's biggest media markets.

Ramaswamy's campaign has said it committed $4 million to air the ad.

Acton on Thursday said of the ad, "It was a horrible and hideous thing to do. A sad thing. And I feel like it was an exploitative thing to do."

"My mother is not well," Acton said.

Her brother, Philip Stearns, told The New York Times in a statement earlier this week that he and Acton were removed from their mother's custody after their stepfather was arrested.

"Our birth mother stayed married to Amy's rapist until he died," Stearns said. "This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core — a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants."

Former Ohio Sen. Rob Portman, a Republican, told Politico on Thursday that the ad should be taken down.

"The increasing incivility in the political arena should concern us all," Portman said, according to Politico's Jonathan Martin. "This ad is an unfortunate example of that broader trend. It crosses the line. I hope the ad will be taken down and the final days of the campaign will focus on policy differences."

— CNBC'sLuke Fountaincontributed to this article.

title: 10-year Treasury yield tumbles below 5% to lowest level in nearly a month
content:
Treasury yields fell sharply on Thursday, with investors turning to safe havens amid a steep sell-off in stocks driven by concerns around the artificial intelligence trade and surging oil prices.

The benchmark10-year U.S. Treasuryyield — used to price mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — slid more than 17 basis points to 4.972%, the first time below 5% since Sept. 23. The yield saw its biggest one-day decline since March 10, 2023.

The yield on the2-year Treasury note, which closely tracks short-term Federal Reserve rate policy, tumbled more than 16 basis points to 4.659%. The yield on longer-dated30-year U.S. Treasury— most sensitive to geopolitical developments — was more than 14 basis points lower at 5.296%.

One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.

"It is a flight to safety," said Mitch Goldberg, president of ClientFirst Strategy. "People are all of a sudden terrified of the amount of bond issuance by AI-related companies. They see the rates going up and people want to hold on to something that they think will be there at maturity."

Others on Wall Street also sought to explain the turnaround in bond prices.

"For the first time in a while, Treasurys are enjoying haven status," said Larry Holzenthaler, senior portfolio manager for fixed income at Catalyst Funds. "You have weakness in tech, an escalation of risk in the Middle East and higher oil. On a relative basis Treasurys start to look like the safe place to hide again in the short term."

The reversal in bonds this week emerged as questions persisted about the billions being spent to build artificial intelligence networks.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huangtold CNBCThursday that while demand for neoclouds is "off the charts," capital was scarce. Neoclouds are aspecialized cloud computing providersthat focus on high-performance tech infrastructure designed specifically for artificial intelligence.

This week's rebound in Treasury prices marks a turnaround from earlier this month, when 10- and 30-year yields reached theirhighest levels in more than two decadesamid investor concern over inflation and high energy prices.

Above 5%, however,attitudes began to shiftand yields suddenly starting looking like an attractive entry point, compensating even for the risk of inflation above 3%.

Tensions in the Middle East added to risk-off behavior Thursday.Oil pricesmoved sharply higher, withWest Texas Intermediatefutures closing up 2.39% at $99.47 per barrel.Brent crudefutures, the global price benchmark, jumped 4%, rising to $113.17 a barrel.

Higher energy prices followed aNew York Times report,citing unnamed U.S. officials, that the U.S. and Israel are considering resuming strikes on Iran in a "short but intensive" operation following the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

"You always look for one risk point, and there isn't really just one at the moment, which makes it a little bit more challenging," said Gregory Faranello, head of U.S. macro strategy at South Street Securities. "But if I had to take one of those and say what's most important right now, it has to be what's going on geopolitically."

"The consumer is clearly getting pinched here in the U.S., so it becomes tricky for central bankers" setting monetary policy going forward, he said. If energy prices "stay elevated, it could force the Fed's hand to do even more, which certainly wouldn't be wouldn't be a good thing for the bond market."

— CNBC's Michelle Fox contributed reporting.
