title: Trump's approval rating on economy hits all-time low as midterm looms: CNBC survey
content:
With less than two weeks to go before the congressional elections, Americans are nearly as gloomy about the economy as they were when the nation was emerging from the pandemic, and PresidentDonald Trump's economic approval rating is hitting an all-time low, according to the latest CNBCAll-America Economic Survey.

Eight out of 10 Americans rate the economy as fair or poor, the highest number since December 2023 and one of several ominous signs for Republicans in the new polling data released Thursday that show why their candidates are facing anuphill battle in the midterm.

Downbeat views on the economy are most intense among Democrats and independents, but there's been a strong move toward economic pessimism even among Republicans in recent months. Overall, 63% of the public is pessimistic about the current state of the economy and the outlook, up one percentage point fromthe July survey. But that percentage now includes 35% of Republicans, up six points from July and the highest level of Republican pessimism of either of Trump's two terms.

"We got there not because of independents or Democrats getting more sour — it's because Republicans have," said Micah Roberts, partner at Public Opinion Strategies, the Republican pollster for the survey. "Since Trump has been president, [Republicans] have held on to a small margin saying that the current economy is either excellent or good. And now that has kind of broken and changed."

The survey of 1,000 registered voters nationwide, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1%, found Americans preferring Democratic control of Congress by a 52% to 45% margin. The seven percentage point Democratic edge represents a three percentage point gain for Democrats from the July survey.

The poll contained other foreboding signs for Republicans as well. It showed 72% of Democrats highly interested in the midterm election on Nov. 3, compared to just 62% of Republicans. Women are 10 percentage points more interested in the election than men, and they prefer Democratic control of Congress by 22 points. Independents prefer Democratic control by a wide 49% to 33% margin. And the majority of survey respondents said Democrats would do a better job than Republicans on many of the issues they singled out as their top concerns, including corruption andthe cost of food and gas.

Read the full survey results here.

In the eight states with competitive Senate races, respondents prefer Democratic congressional control by 4 percentage points. Trump carried those eight states by a combined 10 points in the 2024 presidential election.

The survey shows "things moving either away from Republicans or toward Democrats, depending how you want to look at it, in a way that would make me very nervous if I was leading Republican campaigns leading into these last two weeks," said Jay Campbell, partner at Hart Associates, the Democratic pollster for the poll.

Despite the economic gloom, Trump's overall approval rating has remained stable, though at just 40% approving and 59% disapproving. His current net approval of -19 percentage points compares with -8 a year ago.

More striking is the sharp nine-point drop in the president's net economic approval rating from just the last survey in July. The president's economic approval dropped to 34% from 38% in three months and disapproval rose to 65% from 60%. The net -31 economic approval is the lowest of either of Trump's two terms. The 65% disapproval rating is one percentage point higher than former PresidentJoe Biden's worst showing and the highest for any president surveyed by CNBC going back to PresidentBarack Obama.

Government corruption was identified as the top concern by 36% of respondents, and Democrats hold a 4-point lead on addressing the issue. On the cost of food and groceries, the second most important issue, the Democratic lead widened to +16 from +7 in the July survey. Democrats also topped Republicans on protecting democracy as well as dealing with thehigh price of gas.

Among those most interested in the election are respondents who identify corruption and protecting democracy as top issues, and they prefer Democratic congressional control by wide margins.

Republicans continued to hold a strong advantage on border security and immigration, but the lead on immigration fell to +9 from +15. Democrats, meanwhile, are seen as better at handling the issues of jobs and unemployment and Iran, which flipped from +2 for Republicans to +5 for Democrats.

The public continued to be skeptical of the value of the Iran war. The survey found just 46% of the public believe the military action was worth it to disrupt development of Iran's nuclear capabilities, down from a 53% majority in April. And just 35% say the military action was worth it given the rise in the price of gasoline.

While the survey showed continued deep divisions by party, there was near unity on the corruption issue. Ninety-three percent said elected officials, including the president and members of Congress, should not be allowed to personally own or trade stocks in individual companies that have contracts with the federal government. And 89% said companies owned by or invested in by a sitting president's immediate family members should not be allowed to recerive contracts from the federal government.

While corruption was a top issue, prices are clearly top of mind for registered voters. Taken together, concern about the cost of food, gas and housing is the top concern for 57% of respondents. Eighty percent say prices are rising, up five percentage points from a year ago, with 55% saying they are rising faster than usual, also up five points. The cost of food actually eclipses gas as a greater concern in the survey 34% to 23%. It's a top worry among most major demographic groups but is most elevated among those making $30,000 or less and supporters of the agenda of Democratic Socialists of America. Yet it's also the top issue for those Republicans who don't count themselves as MAGA supporters.

Both pollsters were cautious about how extensive Democratic gains could be. Roberts from POS said it's a battle between "the map and momentum."

"There are several indications nationally that the electorate is tilting more toward Democrats … but the movement is also fairly concentrated, each party's base is consolidating, and a 'big change' is dependent on Democrats flipping a lot of districts and states that Trump won handily just two years ago," he said.

Campbell doesn't see a "realignment" election like in 1994 and 2008, saying, "This looks like a return to the mean—young voters and voters of color returning to the Democratic fold, bolstered by independents being fed up with Trumpenomics." He adds, "At no point did anyone expect that Democratic candidates would suddenly pull 15% of the Republican vote."

title: American Express brings Airbnb bookings and rewards to Amex Travel platform
content:
American Expressis bringingAirbnbinto its travel rewards platform.

The companies on Thursday announced a new partnership to bring more than 1 million Airbnb listings to Amex's travel portal and allow cardholders to earn rewards when booking the stays. It does not currently allow members to redeem points to pay for Airbnb bookings.

The launch adds Airbnb rentals to Amex's hotel portfolio, which includes more than 3,400 properties across its Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection programs.

Amex members with either the consumer or business Platinum card can also now apply their $600 annual lodging credit — previously called the hotel credit — to Airbnb's higher-end Luxe stays and take advantage of a new $250 statement credit on eligible Airbnb Experiences after making a Luxe booking.

"We're excited to bring more choice and flexibility to American Express Card Members with this exclusive partnership. Both of our companies exist to help people travel more and better, and this partnership helps people see more of the world by making travel more rewarding," said Juan David Borrero, head of partnerships at Airbnb, in a news release.

Membership points vary by card:

The changes come ascompetition among premium credit cardscontinues to ramp up.

Last year,American Express raised the annual feeon its premium Platinum card to $895. In turn, it's been investing in cardholder perks such as new lounges in airports and atbig-ticket events and experiencesas a way to attract more high-paying customers.

Earlier this month, it announcedan expansion of its Centurion Lounges, with renovations coming to four existing lounges and new ones planned for Newark Liberty International Airport and London Heathrow Airport. The Newark lounge will be the largest in its network.

The partnership also comes as Americans continue to opt for travel and luxury experiences, even as prices for airfare, gas and hotels rise. Despite higher costs, more than half of Americans reported making no changes to theirtravel plans this summer, a recent study by travel insurance company Squaremouth found.

title: American Airlines forecasts bigger loss in 2026 on fuel spike, plans to slow growth next year
content:
American Airlinesforecast deeper losses this year as record revenue failed to help the airline recover from this year's spike in fuel costs. The carrier plans to slow its capacity growth next year as a result.

American on Thursday said it expects to lose between $1 and $1.60 a share, on an adjusted basis for the full year. In July, it forecast earnings of up to 65 cents a share to a loss of as low as 65 cents a share.

The airline's stock was down about 4% in premarket trading.

"American delivered record third-quarter revenue and the strongest year-over-year revenue growth in my career, with premium performance leading the way," American CEO Robert Isom said in a news release. "The investments we are making across the four pillars of our commercial strategy are working, and we expect another quarter of record revenue growth to close out the year."

The Fort Worth, Texas-based airline is the fourth major U.S. carrier to cut its forecast for 2026 due to a jump in jet fuel following the start of the Iran war. Rising jet fuel prices have also driven up airfare more than 20% from last year.Delta Air Lines,United Airlines, andSouthwest Airlinesalso slashed their outlooks this month.

Jet fuel is airlines' biggest cost after labor, and the spike has added billions to costs this year. American's fuel bill was up 67.5% in the third quarter from last year to $4.64 billion.

American forecast it will lose between 50 cents and $1.10 a share, adjusted, in the fourth quarter, with revenue expected to be up as much as 22.5% from a year earlier and capacity up between 5.5% and 6.5%.

Here is what American reported in the third quarter compared with Wall Street estimates compiled by LSEG:

For the third quarter, American had a net loss of $269 million or 41 cents a share, compared with $114 million, or 17 cents a share, a year earlier. Adjusting for one-time items, American reported a loss of 28 cents a share. Revenue jumped 19.3% from a year earlier to $16.34 billion.

Isom has been under pressure to boost profits at the carrier, which hasdramatically trailedprofitable rivals Delta and United. American has been investing in new lounges and revamped cabins with more premium seats.

Earlier this month, the airline named a new network chief. It was the latest move in a management shake-up that has included new hires in its operations department and its commercial team. Last year, American brought in anew commercial chief, industry veteran Nat Pieper.

title: David's Bridal plans to spin off AI platform Pearl into publicly traded company
content:
David's Bridal is planning to spin off its artificial intelligence platform, Pearl, into a stand-alone publicly traded company targeting a valuation of roughly $350 million, CNBC learned exclusively.

The company expects the deal to close in the first half of 2027.

David's Bridal filed a nonbinding letter of intent on Thursday to separate out Pearl. The AI-centered business would own David's Bridal's intellectual property and look to build on its growing AI model, while the original company would try to strengthen its physical retail business.

"We have a fast-growing, high-margin business generating positive cash flow right now in Pearl, and going public now will help us attract the talent and give us more optionality to fuel the growth that we believe that we have," David's BridalCEO Kelly Cook, who will take over as CEO of Pearl after the deal closes, told CNBC in an interview.

Cook said the companies will work hand in hand to serve customers throughout the wedding-planning process, adding that the split is "positioning both companies for strategic growth."

Pearl's services include an agentic AI-powered wedding-planning platform, a proprietary tool to streamline appointments and communications and a digital content network with original programming. It uses AI to personalize its suggestions based on its data collection for each client.

David's Bridal expects Pearl to generate an EBITDA margin of more than 30% this year and is projecting revenue growth of more than 100% in 2027, exceeding $85 million. It's expected to be debt-free after the deal closes and have positive free cash flow over the next two years, according to the company.

"Pearl has earned the right to stand on its own because it's created more value than we've expected," Cook said.

Following the transaction, Pearl will own David's Bridal's intellectual property and license it back to the chain.

"It's a very healthy business model," Cook said.

She added that the demand remains strong for both of the businesses. Grand View Research estimates the U.S. wedding services marketwill top $96 billionin 2026 — and both Pearl and David's Bridal want to be at the forefront of that segment.

The companies will continue to have a "relationship built on reciprocity," she said, sharing proprietary data and pointing customers to the other business for the next steps in their wedding planning. The split will allow each company to refine its focus, she added.

Still, the plan to go public comes at a time when AI stocks have been struggling. The initial public offering market for consumer companieshas been lackluster, more companies arepostponingtheir public debuts and investors are beginning tolose confidencein the AI boom.

Cook said the differentiator for Pearl is that the company is "not AI for AI's sake."

"Most AI companies have to find a customer," she said. "We already have her ... we have her information, and it's less about the AI side and more about modernizing this entire ecosystem for her that desperately needed modernization."

David's Bridal is no stranger to financial struggles. The company filed for bankruptcy protection in 2018 and emerged a few months later. It then filed a second time in 2023, citing a significantbusiness slowdown from the pandemicand high inflation. To save itself, the company thensold its businessto asset managerCion Investment Corp.to avoid a shutdown.

As part of the spinoff deal, Cion has proposed to invest $25 million as an anchor investor in the separate company.

Cook, who took over as CEO last year to help it transition from a legacy retailer to a more cohesive online and in-store experience, said the company has "been through a hard chapter," but those struggles led to the decision to split the business.

"That's no secret, we've talked about that openly," she said. "What's extraordinary is what came out of that process is a leaner David's, a more focused David's ... I think it's a move from strength."

title: Barclays cutting 5,000 jobs as it increases reliance on AI
content: Image source,Getty ImagesByLucy HookerBusiness reporterPublished22 October 2026, 09:00 BSTUpdated 2 hours agoBarclays is cutting its staff by around 5,000 as it introduces more artificial intelligence (AI) into its work processes.The banking group said 1,000 posts had already been closed and it expects a further reduction of 4,000 to be complete by the end of this year, amounting to around 5% of its global workforce.The bank's cost reductions are focused on its UK retail bank, but some back office functions for the UK are done in India, where a significant proportion of the job cuts are expected to fall.Barclays said the changes were the result of an ongoing modernisation plan, with the use of AI being the "icing on the cake" of its strategy.The banking group is reaching the end of a three year cost-cutting programme focused primarily on its UK retail banking arm, although the investment banking division is also affected.Barclays also revealed it made Â£2.3bn profit in the three months to September, higher than the same period a year ago, but slightly less than forecast.Economists have been watching companies' results carefully for signs that investment in new technology, and AI specifically, is making a difference in their day-to-day operations, leading to greater efficiency and lower employment.Barclays Group chief executive CS Venkatakrishnan said the job cuts were the result of significant investment it is making in technology to simplify and improve its business."AI has an important role to play and may have a more important role to play in the future."We will employ the AI at scale," he said. "But AI is the icing on the cake not the cake."Because you need to do the infrastructure build to get the benefits of AI."Barclays said around 60% of the job cuts will fall within its support functions, including among developers.Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, said Barclays was "reaching for the AI lever, expecting to cut a decent chunk of its workforce as it expands the use of artificial intelligence", but had failed to match expectations with its financial results.Will Howlett, financials analyst at Quilter Cheviot said the cuts illustrated "how significantly AI and automation could reshape the banking industry over the next few years"."Banks have spent heavily on technology for years, but we are increasingly reaching the point where that investment translates into fewer people being required to run the business," he said.Barclays said it expects its efficiency measures to deliver a further Â£1.1bn of savings in 2027.Get in touchHow has AI changed your job or the type of work your do?ÂContact formRelated topicsUK economyBankingBarclaysMore on this storyBarclays workers ask for more money to return to the officePublished17 SeptemberAI boom could trigger market shocks, Bank of England boss warnsPublished1 October

title: What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber-security scramble?
content: Image source,Getty ImagesByOsmond ChiaBusiness reporterPublished22 October 2026, 04:48 BSTUpdated 7 minutes agoFor more than a decade, serious flaws had gone undetected in the technology underpinning much of the internet.It took artificial intelligence (AI) to bring them to light and caused a global cyber-security alert.The vulnerabilities lie within a programming language called PHP, which has been used internationally since the 2000s to build websites.Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world scrambledto contain the fallout of this discoveryon Wednesday, and have urged website operators to install a new emergency fix or consider taking their platforms offline.Cyber-security firm Wiz - one of the companies whose researchers uncovered the vulnerabilities - described the flaws as the "most severe" ever detected by AI.OpenAI, whose technology was used to find the flaws, called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory".What is the flaw?Most people may not have heard of PHP - short for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor - but they most certainly interact with it daily.PHP powers a vast number of platforms, including online shops, Wikipedia and WordPress â the content management system behind many websites like blogs.When you visit a website like Wikipedia, PHP is the code that collects information you need and presents it in a way you can read on the web, Paul Spain, chief executive of Gorilla Cyber Security, told the BBC.But due to a flaw that could allow attackers to take control of affected web servers without authentication and steal sensitive data, everything built on PHP was left exposed.AI could make such attacks easier and faster, Spain said, estimating that the flaw could affect "millions and millions" of websites.It would be "disastrous" if hackers or countries weaponised the flaw and seized private data from websites, said cyber-security researcher Jill Slay from the University of Adelaide.What websites have been affected?The alert has disrupted services globally, from gaming platforms to government portals and online forums.That includes Wikimedia - the organisation behind the online encyclopaedia Wikipedia - which took down a number of its systems as a precautionary measure.Sites and pages have been taken offline by the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC, with the Netherlands' cyber-security agency also pulling its website.Image source,EPAImage caption,Websites like the University of Geneva's were taken offline on WednesdayA number of Scotland's public organisations, including councils and health boards, have also taken their websites offline.Some experts warn the vulnerability could leave poorly maintained websites, particularly those belonging to smaller organisations with limited security resources, at greater risk.More attempts to exploit these flaws are likely in the coming weeks since the technical details are now being made public, cyber-security researcher Salil Kanhere from UNSW Sydney said.What happened after the flaws were exposed?Developers of the PHP platform on Wednesday rolled out patches to fix the vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years."All PHP users are strongly encouraged to update immediately," the company said.Authorities and security organisations around the world have echoed those warnings to website operators to secure their platforms.The US National Security Agency told all organisations that use PHP to take their systems offline if they were unable to patch them immediately, adding that the flaw could provide a "direct path" to exploit a system's database."These risks are serious enough to require immediate patching across United States Government departments and agencies," the agency said.The UK's National Cyber Security Centre gave similar advice and told organisations to check for "backdoors installed by an attacker".Its counterparts in the EU, Singapore and Australia have also issued similar alerts.Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP.Image source,Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption,Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP"We have an urgent request for everyone to take action tonight," Takaichi wrote on X."If it is difficult to apply the fix patch promptly, temporarily suspending websites and similar measures can be considered an effective way to reduce risk," she said.Tech companies are also racing to secure their systems.E-commerce giant Amazon said it was targeted in multiple attempts days before the public disclosure of the PHP issue. It is unknown how the potential attackers knew about the vulnerability.How is AI finding weak spots?The vulnerabilities were found by researchers at the security firms Calif and Wiz.The researchers used advanced AI tools that are able to analyse code and find flaws much faster than humans or older systems can."Modern software is incredibly complex, and some vulnerabilities can remain undetected for years," Kanhere said."The underlying bugs weren't new; what changed was our ability to find them," Kanhere said.Details of the discovery leaked online this week, forcing the PHP platform's developers to rush out its announcement of the security flaw and its huge scale.The incident "highlights how AI can uncover security flaws" but also how it can "help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits," OpenAI said in a blog post.The ChatGPT-maker said it had released a program to check if the PHP platform is secure."Many of these flaws stem from the way software were built in the past, which were built for functionality and not with security in mind," said Ryan Ko, at the University of Queensland's Cyber Research Centre.What can people do to safeguard themselves?Website owners are being urged to secure their websites with the latest version of PHP.The PHP software patch is a small, routine fix for most tech teams, Spain said.The US National Security Agency has urged "heightened awareness" in the coming weeks and to closely monitor updates from software vendors."Vigilance in applying patches related to those systems is paramount," it said.The onus lies mainly on website operators, but users should stay alert for any security advice issued by affected services, such as requests to change passwords, Kanhere said.He warned people to be alert to any phishing messages exploiting the publicity around the incident too.Related topicsInternational BusinessCyber-attacksCyber-securityArtificial intelligenceMore on this storyKing warns malicious online actors are evolving tacticsPublished10 OctoberMake sure use of AI is safe, data watchdog warnsPublished12 October

title: Oil prices jump on Middle East worries as U.S., Israel reportedly weigh fresh Iran strikes
content:
Oil prices climbed Thursday on worries over a possible escalation in the Middle East conflict as the U.S. reportedly plans to resume strikes against Iran.

Brent crudefutures rose 1.71% to $110.67 a barrel, while U.S.West Texas Intermediatecrude gained 1.42% to $98.53.

The U.S. and Israeli militaries have drawn up specific plans for renewed strikes on Iran after next month's midterm elections,The New York Timesreported, citing unnamed U.S. officials. Planning for a "short but intensive" operation is progressing, The Times said.

The U.S. has alsoordered non-emergency government employeesand their families to leave Saudi Arabia.

State Department spokesman Tommy Pigottin a post on Xsaid the order applies only to Saudi Arabia, citing increasing attacks by Iran-aligned Houthis on civilian targets, after reports said that the U.S. had directed some staff in the wider Gulf region to leave.

The economic fallout from elevated oil prices, however, may be less severe than in previous decades, as consumers have become less vulnerable to energy shocks, according to David Wagner, head of equity and portfolio manager at Aptus Capital Advisors.

"$100 oil today is very different than $100 oil, you know, 20, 30 years ago," Wagner said, noting that crude prices remain well below their inflation-adjusted historical highs.

He pointed to U.S. government data showing that gasoline accounted for roughly 5% of the average American's disposable income a decade ago, compared with about half that today, suggesting households may be better positioned to withstand elevated energy costs.

"I think we can hold that umbrella over our head ... from the rainstorm of oil," he said.

— CNBC's Anniek Bao contributed to this report.

title: Is an 'AI war' complicating your job search?
content: Image caption,Sheeraz Gulsher says there are "huge worries" about AIByMeghan OwenLondon work and money correspondentPublished6 hours agoI have lost track of the number of people who have told me they have applied for hundreds of jobs, only to be met with rejection after rejection.Often, they said it felt like a human had not even looked at their applications.There are lots of different types of recruitment tools. Some match candidates to jobs, others grade and screen CVs. Employers use them to save time sifting through applications, but there are growing concerns that these tools could be biased.I want to find out how fair AI recruitment tools being used to help decide our futures really are - and what happens when we click "apply".What is the 'AI war' in recruitment?Image source,Getty ImagesImage caption,There are concerns about the increasing use of AI in recruitmentA London-based non-profit organisation, People Like Us, is raising awareness of people's legal right to challenge automated decisions when they disagree with the outcome.A survey conducted by Censuswide among 2,000 UK workers who had applied for at least one job in the past 24 months found that 75% were unaware of their right to challenge an automated rejection.Sheeraz Gulsher, CEO of People Like Us, is leading the campaign called Reject the Rejections, which calls on employers to improve transparency and accountability in the use of AI and automated recruitment systems.He describes the current situation as an "AI war", with candidates "resorting to AI to bolster their applications" while "employers are dealing with huge amounts of applications".Gulsher said: "We can't say for certain that every company is operating its automated or AI systems without bias. That's why we're calling for companies to audit these systems, publish the results and have them independently assessed."In our research, we foundguidance from the Information Commissioner's Office,externalstating that people subject to certain automated decisions have the right to request a human review. We're trying to remind people of that right, as many simply aren't aware of it."The research also found 70% of ethnically diverse jobseekers had altered or concealed information on their CVs, including their country of origin, religion or name, out of fear that recruitment software or AI tools would reject their applications. This compares with 57% of white candidates.Would people ask for a human review?Image caption,Vivi says she needs feedback as a jobseekerBusiness consultant Vivi, who lives in Lewisham, was made redundant earlier this year. She says she has applied for so many jobs that she's given up and started her own company."There's one instance where applications closed on Friday and I got a reply on a Saturday morning basically saying that I should work on my skills and come back in six months. But it was so obvious that nobody had assessed my skills."If she had known she could ask for a human to review her application, she might have done things differently."I would definitely go back and ask for a human to look at my application and if it is a 'no', that's fine, but feedback helps me as a jobseeker."Image source,HemaImage caption,Hema was made redundant in JuneHema, 49, from Surrey, is an HR and talent professional who has worked internationally across multiple sectors.She was made redundant in June and has since tracked more than 100 job applications and recruitment opportunities."A lot of them have been automatically rejected within 24 to 36 hours."She added: "I've always landed a job in 10 applications, so to be nearing 100 is completely out of this world."While she is "hesitant" about asking for a human review in case she jeopardises her application, she believes "a human recruiter can see the fuller picture"."If you've got an in-house recruitment team, they know the culture, they can see the type of language that you're using in your CV, in your cover letter, during a phone screen."How much do recruiters use AI?Of the 425 recruiters CV-Library spoke to, about 90 said they used AI in the CV screening stage.Alec Stanwell, director of marketing, believes there is a "perception gap"."Candidates almost universally believe that employers are using AI to screen their CVs, filter them and to screen them as they go through the process and that is happening but nowhere near as much as candidates think it is."That perception gap is a problem because candidates are now writing their CVs, and applications, through the lens of 'an AI bot is going to be reviewing this rather than a human'.He adds this is a problem because recruiters are seeing all CVs look the same because "they're all written by AI, or polished by AI".He says this creates a "perfect storm" because AI is then more likely to be used to filter through a large volume of applications."We're going to end up with computers hiring computers, but we're actually in the world of hiring people."Is there evidence of AI hiring bias?In the four years to December 2022,Stanford researchers analysed four million job applications processed by an AI hiring tool,external.Some candidates were rejected from multiple roles more often than would have been expected if they had been assessed by each employer independently.The analysis also indicated black and Asian applicants were recommended for jobs at lower rates.But the evidence is limited. They only looked at one AI hiring tool, and other factors such as education and immigration status could have also played a role.The hiring tool assessed did not respond to our requests for comment.The people I have interviewed are not talking about any company in particular, but concerns over AI used in recruitment are also playing out in the courts.One company, Workday, isfacing legal claims,externalin the US, alleging that its tools discriminated against job applicants.The case is ongoing, but Workday denies the claims and says its tools do not make hiring decisions.More generally, it says its tools "support rather than replace human judgement".Do AI tools work in different ways?Image source,Barb HymanImage caption,Barb Hyman's company grades candidates on text-based chat interviewsWhat makes this even more difficult is that AI hiring tools work in different ways, with some not even screening CVs in the first place.I spoke to one company that grades candidates on text-based chat interviews.Barb Hyman, founder of Sapia AI, said: "We don't know anything about you from a demographic perspective and we don't know whether or not you were hired or not hired for a previous role. So I think you've really got to look at the nature of the AI and how it's built. Not all AI is the same."At least in the enterprise space, every company we speak to is very conscious of the EU AI Act, even if they don't see themselves as having to comply with that yet. And that requires a level of accountability."She added: "No company ever built a high-performing culture by monitoring its people, and you won't build a fair hiring process by policing candidates either."Start by earning candidates' trust: tell them what you're measuring, how they'll be scored, and give them feedback. Fraud gets smaller when people trust the process."Can you tell when somebody has used AI on their CV?Image source,Alec SamwaysImage caption,Alec Samways says his company has seen "huge uptick" in applications, which "all look the same"Alec Samways, CEO of London-based Splendid Communications, says they usually get three to four hundred applications for three places on their annual intern programme but last year they saw triple the numbers."We saw a huge uptick in applications, but strangely, they all look the same. Our suspicion was candidates all of a sudden were using AI to make the applications themselves."Samways used two different AI tools to help the company understand how much of the content was produced by AI but they "produced such a variety of responses"."We found we couldn't trust them and we had to literally sift through those, applications in a human way in the end."It's just clear that at this point we're not prepared to trust AI for this kind of decision-making."What are the rules and regulations?An ICO spokesperson said AI and automation could "make recruitment quicker and more efficient" but "must not come at the expense of people's rights".They said: "Employers should be upfront about when automated decision-making is being used, how it works and how it could affect someone's application."Bias can appear at different stages of building and using AI products, and we expect all organisations to take steps to identify and mitigate it."A government spokesperson said that "while AI can help employers manage large volumes of applications and reduce administrative burdens, it is vital that recruitment processes remain fair, transparent and accessible".They added: "Existing legal protections, including equality and data protection law, already apply to AI systems, and we will act where additional protections are needed."There seems to be a real fear of the unknown because we are often unsure what happens on the other end once we click "apply".But given it seems AI is here to stay, how can we ensure it's fair?Listen to the best of BBC Radio London onSoundsand follow BBC London onFacebook,external,X,externalandInstagram,external. Send your story ideas tohello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk,externalRelated topicsArtificial intelligenceRecruitmentEmploymentLondon

title: U.S. pulls diplomats from Saudi Arabia as it reportedly readies Iran strikes after midterms
content:
The U.S. ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks on the kingdom escalate.

The move comes as the U.S. and Israeli militaries have drawn up specific plans for renewed strikes on Iran after next month's midterm elections, according to The New York Times, citing unnamed U.S. officials.

Planning for a "short but intensive" operation is progressing, The Times said.

The developments point to a possible widening of the nearly eight-month war, while U.S. and Iranian negotiators continue talks on Tehran's nuclear program and the Strait of Hormuz.

State Department spokesman Tommy Pigottin a post on Xsaid the order applies only to Saudi Arabia, citing increasing attacks by Iran-aligned Houthis on civilian targets. Meanwhile, Reuters reported Washington also plans to withdraw family members from other missions in the region.

A strike Wednesday on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam killed at least one person and injured eight. Two people died in a drone attack on Saudi Aramco's Shaybah oil field, the Saudi Press Agency reported, adding that operations were not affected.

In recent days, the U.S. and Israeli militaries have stepped up military exercises, including flying planes over Iraq to practice strike maneuvers, according to The New York Times. The Times also reported that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during an unannounced visit to Israel this week to discuss potential new strikes.

The renewed military strikes would likely target Iran's energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone arsenal, according to The Times, noting thatPresident Donald Trumphas yet to approve the fresh strikes and has repeatedly vetoed plans for a return to major combat this year.

Iranian officials have vowed to widen their attacks to target data centers and undersea internet cables, while refusing concessions on their nuclear program.

Despite the persistent shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, Middle East oil flows through the vital strait have recovered to near pre‑war levels according to Kpler.

AsBrent crudetopped $110 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate gained 1% to $98.12, recovering appetite for crude from China could drive oil prices higher, according to the commodity research firm.

"China's crude import demand is expected to continue recovering, driven by rising refinery throughput and rapidly declining crude inventories," said Muyu Xu, senior crude oil analyst at Kpler. The war has cut China's oil stockpiles, with the fastest drawndown on record at 1.6 million barrels a day in September, Xu estimated.

China still holds 1.1 billion barrels in reserves, about 80 days of refinery needs, Xu said. She added that with virtually all Iranian cargoes outside the U.S. blockade discharged, substantial new crude arrivals in China appear unlikely.

Chinese state-owned refiners are likely to have a stronger appetite and greater urgency to secure prompt Middle Eastern barrels as they face higher throughput and inventory-replenishment needs. Independent refiners are also seeking alternatives to Iranian crude, a shift that could limit further downside in the Dubai structure, Xu said.

title: China's stock market sinks into bear territory as CSI 300 extends 10-week rout
content:
China's benchmark CSI 300 index on Thursday entered bear-market territory, falling 20% from its June peak, as a prolonged sell-off in its equities deepens.

The index, which tracks 300 of the largest stocks listed in Shanghai and Shenzhen, has declined for 10 consecutive weeks and is down 2.6% so far this week, underscoring sustained pressure on Chinese equities, data from LSEG showed. The index was more than 1% lower Thursday.

Jordan Cvetanovski, chairman and CIO at Pella Funds, said China's equity market continues to face structural challenges, particularly as the world's second-largest economy grapples with the fallout from years of excess capacity and overinvestment.

"I think China is really struggling with reining in the problems that they've had in the past from the overbuild of capacity and other things," Cvetanovski told CNBC, pointing to challenges facing companies even in globally competitive industries such as batteries — a sector where he still sees select opportunities in China.

Chinese firms have been suffering from declining profit growth amid intense competition that has eroded margins and even invited the government to step in. In September, the country posted it's weakest growth in industrial profits this year.

The world's second-largest economy also posted its slowest growth in over three years in the second quarter, pressured by a multiyear slowdown in the property sector and extended weakness in consumer demand.

Shaun Rein, managing director at China Market Research Group, expects further selling pressure as geopolitical uncertainty, concerns over an artificial intelligence bubble and deteriorating consumer confidence weigh on investor sentiment.

China's large base of retail investors could also exacerbate market volatility, Rein said, as individual investors are prone to exiting the market faster during periods of uncertainty.

Unlike major markets such as the New York Stock Exchange, where retail investors account for about 20%-25% of trade volumes, China's retail investors drive 90% of daily trading, according to data provided by HSBC.

"For Chinese, it's about wealth preservation," Rein said, noting that investors are increasingly favoring safer assets such as time deposits amid a weakening property market and sluggish labor conditions.

While Rein expects increased pressure on markets, he said the sell-off has been excessive, pointing to resilient exports and signs of a recovery in property prices in China's largest cities.

"It's a crisis of confidence right now not a crisis in the economy," he said, predicting a strong rebound in Chinese equities in 2027.

Daniel Gerard, senior multi-asset strategist at State Street Markets, also struck a more optimistic tone, saying that China's growing capabilities in artificial intelligence could eventually draw global investors back into its equity market, even before corporate earnings recover.

title: Southeast Asia is hungry for AI — and the money isn't just in subscriptions
content:
Southeast Asia is embracing artificial intelligence at a rapid pace. But the business of making money from AI is about more than getting consumers to pay for it.

Generative AI adoption in the region has reached around 243 million people in less than three years, according tothe annual e-Conomy SEA reportreleased Wednesday by Google, Temasek and Bain & Company.

That is equivalent to 58% of the working population, with adoption occurring four times faster than the uptake of mobile internet. Yet only 1% to 2% of the region's population pays for personal AI subscriptions, highlighting a gap between widespread adoption and direct consumer spending.

Florian Hoppe, a partner at Bain & Company, told CNBC in an interview that businesses have found other ways to generate AI's commercial value from online shopping to digital advertising.

Companies have been using AI to improve e-commerce conversion rates and handle routine customer inquiries, allowing employees to focus on other tasks, he added.

Consumers may also be paying indirectly for AI when purchasing products developed using the technology.

The findings come as Southeast Asia's digital economy is projected to grow 17% to $368 billion in gross merchandise value this year, with the market expected to exceed $1 trillion by 2035, according to the report.

Hoppe also pointed to another factor driving the region's enthusiasm for AI: its willingness to embrace new technologies as consumers have shown what he described as "pragmatic optimism" toward AI, embracing the technology for its practical benefits.

The region has historically ranked among the most active users of major digital platforms on a per-capita basis.

"They're very experimental," Hoppe said, describing consumers' openness to new tools and services. He also added that in terms of individual markets, Singapore is among Southeast Asia's early leaders in AI adoption.

That openness is extending to more autonomous uses of AI, with 75% of users willing to let AI agents find the best prices and complete purchases on their behalf. The report shows that confidence is also growing, with 62% of respondents saying they trust AI tools more than they did a year ago.

Despite the rapid adoption, people in Southeast Asia still use AI far less than those in the U.S., with usage per person at just 10% of U.S. levels.

For businesses, however, the potential returns are becoming more tangible. About 69% of shoppers use AI to compare complex purchases such as electronics, while early case studies show AI helping businesses boost conversion rates by 10% year on year and increase the average amount customers spend per order by as much as 75%.

An example is Shopee, a Southeast Asian e-commerce platform, which now handles approximately 80% of customer queries through AI chatbots, helping cut its cost per customer contact by 30% year on year.

In online media, Hoppe pointed to a "significant uplift" in advertising click-through rates and conversions through AI-powered advertising and improved targeting.

But the benefits extend beyond online shopping. AI is helping travelers plan trips, making digital advertising more effective and enabling voice-assisted bookings for ride-hailing and food delivery services.

Southeast Asia's online travel market is projected to grow 10% to $59 billion in gross merchandise value this year. Online media revenue, including digital advertising and streaming, is expected to rise 22% to $44 billion, while ride-hailing and food delivery are forecast to grow 15% to $40 billion in gross merchandise value, according to the report.

title: Critical web security flaws spark global alarm as Google, OpenAI and Amazon respond
content:
The tech world is racing to implement fixes after the discovery of critical security vulnerabilities in software used to power much of the internet.

The software, known as PHP, is an open-source programming language widely used to power websites and web applications. The discovery of the flaws prompted urgent warnings from governments worldwide, while tech giants including Google, OpenAI and Amazon have been involved in efforts to uncover the vulnerabilities, detect potential attacks and protect affected systems.

The two vulnerabilities, collectively known as "PHP2Shell," could allow hackers to remotely execute malicious code on affected servers, potentially exposing sensitive data, according to cybersecurity researchers. While not every website using PHP is necessarily vulnerable, the software's widespread use has raised concerns about the potential scale of attacks.

The U.S. National Security Agency on Wednesdayurgedorganizations using PHP to prepare security updates addressing the vulnerabilities, warning that the flaws could provide attackers with direct access to server file systems and databases. The agency recommended taking affected systems offline until the vulnerabilities are fully addressed if immediate updates are not possible.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation alsowarnedthat malicious actors could exploit the vulnerabilities to execute code remotely, putting sensitive data and networks at risk.

Cybersecurity authorities inSingapore,the United Kingdom,Australia,Canadaand theEuropean Unionhave issued similar alerts, underscoring concerns about the potential impact on businesses, government agencies and other organizations that rely on PHP-based systems.

Amazonsaidits threat intelligence team had detected attempts to exploit the vulnerabilities before they were publicly disclosed, using its MadPot threat detection system, which monitors suspicious activity across internet-facing infrastructure. It said the findings suggest malicious actors were already attempting to exploit the vulnerabilities. However, Amazon said it remains unclear how the attackers obtained information about the flaws ahead of their disclosure.

Meanwhile, Google and OpenAI highlighted the growing role of artificial intelligence in identifying and addressing cybersecurity threats. Googlesaidits cybersecurity unit Wiz used AI models to help find and investigate the vulnerabilities, while its Gemini AI contributed to efforts to assess the flaws, test potential attacks and verify security patches.

OpenAIsaidresearchers working with its AI models had also helped uncover critical vulnerabilities in PHP. The company said it had spent the past two months leading a coalition of software maintainers, cybersecurity researchers and security providers to coordinate fixes and prepare protective measures ahead of public disclosure.

The ChatGPT maker described the flaws as among the most significant security issues in recent memory, highlighting both the potential of advanced AI systems to identify vulnerabilities in widely used software and the risk that similar capabilities could be exploited by cybercriminals.

Cloudflare, which provides cybersecurity and website infrastructure services,saidit had deployed protections against the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities through its web application firewall. The company said its measures were designed to help block malicious requests targeting affected systems, providing an additional layer of defense as organizations work to install software updates.

The PHP development team hasreleasedsecurity fixes, with authorities urging website operators to identify affected versions and apply the updates as quickly as possible. The episode underscores how vulnerabilities in widely used software can pose risks across industries and borders, even as AI increasingly plays a role in helping security researchers uncover and address those weaknesses.

title: Inside India newsletter: Asia’s hottest data center market aims to quell concerns over water and power use
content:
Hello, this is Priyanka Salve, writing to you from Singapore.

Welcome to the latest edition of"Inside India"— your one-stop destination for stories and developments from the world's fastest-growing large economy.

India is touted as one of the hottest markets for data centers, with several U.S. Big Tech companies investing to set up capacity in the country. But of late, some projects have faced public backlash over the use of water and power resources.

Now the Indian government is taking steps to address the situation. Will it work?

Any thoughts on today's newsletter?Share themwith the team.

Several U.S. Big Tech companiesthat are spending billionsto set up digital infrastructure in India are facing growing public anger over resource sharing and environmental concerns, prompting the government to step in and calm tensions.

On Oct. 14, Jitin Prasada, a junior minister for electronics and information technology, announced thatIndia will roll out a policyfor data centers, calling the country a "fertile ground for hyperscalers."

The minister reportedly said India wants to avoid a situation whereconsumers have to pay more for powerbecause they have to compete with data centers for supply.

Globally,data center companies are facing public backlashas communities raise concerns over electricity, water and land use. India is also grappling with similar issues that pose a threat to its ambitions tohost the whole world's data.

As per local media reports,Amazon's data centernear Mumbaiis facing resistancefrom residents who are worried that the U.S. company's facility would receive priority access to water and electricity during shortages.

Meanwhile,environmental activistshave been demanding the cancellation of permissions given to AI data centers in Visakhapatnam, whereGoogle is constructingits $15 billion project.

Amazontold CNBC that it is committed to being a "good and responsible neighbor," and said it is engaging with the community through educational sessions. They denied using water for cooling and added that their data centers "do not draw electricity from the local distribution network that supplies homes, shops and businesses."

The American firm also said it "will be a part of industry consultations with the government to advise on India's data center regulations."

Googledid not respond to CNBC's request for comments.

Experts told CNBC that the government plans to roll out a policy directive to pacify local resistance to some projects across the country.

It will also lay down clear approval guidelines that will minimize the risks data center developers face from public pushback and execution challenges, they added.

The proposed policy indicates a shift in direction from "primarily encouraging the data center investment" to now balancing it with infrastructure readiness and sustainability aspects, Jaspreet Singh, partner at Grant Thornton Bharat, told CNBC.

Last week, Niti Aayog, an Indian government think tank,shared a frameworkfor local governments to evaluate data center projects for sustainability and to provide suitable locations, based on grid readiness and water supply availability.

It underscored the need to establish guidelines "before constraints emerge," adding that data centers should get faster approvals only in cases where resource readiness, local safeguards and public value are proven.

Experts who are part of consultations expect the new policy to lay down clear and consistent rules, which will also help the industry overcome challenges around land acquisition and simplify a fragmented approval process.

"India does not have a dedicated national policy for data centers, and it is high time that this gap was addressed," Shobhit Agarwal, chief executive of real estate consultancy ANAROCK Capital, told CNBC.

He explained that projects are currently approved under existing environmental and building rules, and every state has its own "variations and incentives."

While the Indian government has been enthusiastic in welcoming the hyperscalers to invest in data centers in India,even giving them 20-year tax sops, regional governments are the final decision-makers when it comes to providing land, water and power resources.

Nikhil Narendran, a partner for technology at law firm Trilegal, who works with U.S. Big Tech companies, said local governments are proposing data center projects in locations that are already facing constraints in terms of electricity, water and other infrastructure.

He added that state governments need to be encouraged to identify locations where reliable electricity, substantial cooling infrastructure, water availability and high-quality connectivity are available, "rather than simply competing to announce large investments."

U.S. eyes refining muscle of Indian billionaire Ambani's Reliance as Rubio visits Jamnagar plantThe U.S. is looking to "work together more closely" with Reliance Industries forrefining energyfrom the "Western Hemisphere," U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in an interview with India's Network 18.

India's finance minister says market liquidity makes it easier for investors to exitThe high degree of liquidity in India's equity markethas provided easier exitsto foreign portfolio investors, according to Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman.

BlackRock, GIC among investors chasing Indian telecom major Jio's IPO as anchor bids top $26 billionIndia's Jio Platforms has seen the anchor investor quota for its initial public offering oversubscribed more than 30 times, according to a source familiar with the matter, drawingbids from top assetmanagers including BlackRock, Capital Group and GIC.

India's rupee forecast to weaken toward 100-per-dollar level even as RBI pushes backThe Reserve Bank of India's measures toslow currency depreciationwill provide short-term relief, but strategists said the rupee is expected to weaken toward the end of the year and mid-2027, and a 100 rupee-per-dollar mark could not be ruled out.

title: The 'trillion pound' oil fund the government believes Britain could have built
content: Image caption,The Jackdaw gas platform and drilling rig in the North Sea.ByFaisal IslamEconomics editorPublished2 hours agoAfter a half-century wait, the United Kingdom now has an oil fund.Chancellor John Healey announced the creation of an Energy Wealth Fund at the Jackdaw gas approval announcement on Wednesday, with Â£2bn of funding diverted from the existing National Wealth Fund.A selection of energy exporting countries, mainly in the Gulf, but also including Norway, over the years have amassed multi-trillion funds using oil and gas revenues to create epic national piggy banks.It has been a long-standing debate in UK economic policy circles. If neighbouring Norway has amassed a $2.4tn war chest from the same North Sea, where exactly did the UK's sovereign wealth fund go?It is an apposite question on the week when the national debt also hit Â£3tn for the first time."The proceeds of this oil and gas coming ashore now can be invested for the future generations," the chancellor said."If we had done this when North Sea oil was first discovered in the 1980s, we'd have a British Sovereign Wealth Fund now that would be worth probably a trillion pounds."On Wednesday, for the first time, Treasury officials actually calculated how much that missing British fund could have been worth.The trillion pound number comes from internal Treasury modelling. The assumption was that the UK's historical North Sea receipts of Â£200bn had been invested, with no withdrawals and grown at a rate comparable to Norway's."Norway demonstrates the power of long-term investment: the government wants to learn from that principle, rather than copy its model wholesale," one insider told me.It was a "missed opportunity" which "had we systematically invested those receipts, we could have built a huge national asset for future generations", they said.Burnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licencesPublished10 hours agoIt is a giant "What if?" asked often by economists critical of the Margaret Thatcher era.The peak oil revenues were, in their view, frittered away in pre-election tax cuts, which ended up being spent on 1980s garden conservatories.Others might argue that the revenues under subsequent governments were squandered on wasteful government spending. It is worth noting that Norway's fund only began in earnest in 1996.The idea of a lost oil fund has also featured in arguments from supporters of Scottish independence, and was suggested by some government advisers in the 1970s.I have met some of the officials running Norway's fund. They are sometimes lambasted by ordinary Norwegians on the Oslo commuter trains who can all check the live value of the national fund.Three percent of its value is drawn down each year to fund a fifth to a quarter of government budgets. The nation drew down on the fund during the coronavirus pandemic.It is meant to help fund Norway's post oil economy and society, as indeed are some of the equivalent funds in the Gulf. It is a gift to the future.While the UK government promises to divert new revenues into its new fund, it will be run rather differently. Norway's fund is obliged to invest abroad, and has grown hugely off the back off investments in US big tech. The UK plan is to create a fund that can invest domestically in green energy. It may struggle to match the performance.UK energy tax revenues are also forecast to dwindle as North Sea production slows. The rate of slowing may now ease, with Jackdaw and extensions to existing fields. Critically Norway's state still controls its oil companies, also giving a share of their profits.Two billion Norwegian Kroner was exactly the starting investment in Norway's fund 30 years ago. It is now worth over a thousand times that.Nobody expects the Energy Wealth Fund's Â£2bn to be worth Â£2tn by 2056. The question is: what might have been, had a similar, far-sighted idea been adopted here in decades past?Related topicsUK economyNorth Sea oil and gasOil & Gas industryOilHM TreasuryUK taxesUK government spendingMore on this storyHow much gas could Jackdaw provide? And will it cut your energy bills?Published13 hours ago

title: Airbnb hosts can no longer make guests strip beds and wash dishes under new rules
content: Image source,Getty ImagesImage caption,Washing and putting away dishes are examples of chores that Airbnb says guests should generally not be asked to doBySareen HabeshianPublished2 hours agoAirbnb has changed its rules to limit what property hosts may ask guests to do - including when it comes to cleaning.The updated guidelines state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules and can also add other "reasonable" requests.Airbnb states that guests - who are required to pay a cleaning fee - should not be asked to complete tasks normally done by a cleaner, including washing dishes and stripping beds.The new rules will apply to all reservations booked on or after 20 November on the accommodation marketplace."House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we've heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage," Airbnb told the BBC."So, we've redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises."According to the new requirements on the Airbnb website, hosts are generally not allowed to ask guests to complete tasks that "require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner, including stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes".The company said it may grant exceptions in some circumstances. For example, guests can be asked to limit shower time if there are local drought-related water restrictions.A property's rules will be displayed to guests more prominently moving forward and will appear in the guests' reservation reminders.Contracts will only be allowed in limited circumstances, including when required by law or homeowners association rules.While a host will not be able to impose fines, they remain in control of their house rules and requests, the company said.If a host's request does not follow Airbnb policies, the issue will be flagged and the owner can appeal if they disagree.Guests have for years complained about unreasonable tasks they we required to complete before departure, especially as they are required to pay cleaning fees.TikTok videos from Airbnb hosts Cassie and Jon that show them closely inspecting their rental property in the US state of Georgia after guests leave have gone viral recently for their attention to detail.One video from the couple, for example, accuses guests of "disrespecting the house rules" for leaving a television remote out of place.They have been criticised for their strict rules and high standards but said in response that their content had been misinterpretedTheir videos have inspired other content creators to parody stringent hosts.Related topicsHospitality industryTourismAirbnbTravelMore on this storyB&B resists calls from Airbnb to change logoPublished15 SeptemberAirbnb fined Â£56m by Spain for advertising unlicensed propertiesPublished15 December 2025

title: IBM beats on top and bottom lines as CEO Krishna touts 'Super Intelligence' traction
content:
IBMshares slipped in extended trading on Wednesday after the technology vendor reported better-than-predicted third-quarter results.

Here's how the company performed relative to LSEG consensus:

IBM's revenue grew about 5% from a year ago, according to astatement. Net income, at $2.19 billion, or $2.30 per share, increased from $1.74 billion, or $1.84 per share, a year ago. Adjusted earnings exclude acquisition-related adjustments.

"Our clients are now deploying 'Super Intelligence' in ways that transform entire operating models, instead of simply addressing narrow or novel problems," IBM CEO Arvind Krishna was quoted as saying in a statement.

With respect to guidance, IBM called for full-year free cash flow to increase by more than $1 billion. The forecast as of July was a bump of approximately $1 billion. IBM still sees 2026 constant-currency revenue growth between 4% and 5%.

In the third quarter, IBM generated $7.80 billion in software revenue, growing 8% and topping the $7.66 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount.

Consulting revenue, at $5.34 billion, was flat and just below StreetAccount's $5.37 billion consensus.

"AI is increasingly embedded in broader transformations our clients are undertaking, representing about 30% of our consulting revenue in the quarter and 35% of our backlog," Jim Kavanaugh, IBM's finance chief, said on a conference call with analysts.

The consulting unit's 27.4% gross margin narrowed from 28.9% in the second quarter.

"We reinvested productivity gains into digital assets, accelerating our transition towards a services as software model to capture the growing AI opportunity," Kavanaugh said.

Infrastructure revenue came to $3.70 billion. That was up 4% and higher than the $3.57 billion consensus from StreetAccount.

The company's adjusted gross margin, at 58.5%, was narrower than the StreetAccount consensus of 59.1%.

During the quarter, IBM said it agreed to buy Boeing and General Motors'HRL Laboratories, formerly known as Hughes Aircraft's research division, for an undisclosed sum.

As of Wednesday's close, IBM stock has come down 15%, while the S&P 500 index has gained 13%.

"I think the current street estimates for the year are about $32 billion of revenue," Kavanaugh said. "We feel comfortable with that $32 billion of revenue."
