title: Trump denies ordering Starlink slowdown in Ukraine, says he doesn't know who did
content:
PresidentDonald Trumpon Wednesday insisted he had nothing to do with aslowdownofSpaceX's Starlink in Ukraine and said he does not know ifElon Muskwas responsible for speed-capping the critical satellite service.

Trump's latest denial came one day afterThe Wall Street Journal, citing unnamed U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter, reported Musk ordered the slowdown and discussed it with Trump.

"I wasn't involved," Trump told a reporter when asked about the decision as he departed the White House for a campaign rally in South Carolina.

When pressed to answer if Musk, SpaceX's founder and CEO, ordered the slowdown, Trump said, "I don't know who did it, but I was not involved."

The recent disruption of Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink, rendered some Ukrainian drones effectively useless, weakening defenses against Russian attacks.

Ukrainian PresidentVolodymyr Zelenskyyon Mondaysaidhis military still faces "speed restrictions on Starlink and Starshield services in different parts of the front."

"No explanation for either of these issues has been provided to Ukraine by the American side," he said.

The Journal reported Tuesday that Musk and Trump discussed the move to throttle Starlink "soon after" the change first became public last week, citing two people familiar with the matter.

One of the people who spoke with the news outlet claimed Musk discussed the matter with multiple senior administration officials, including Trump himself, prior to imposing the Starlink speed cap.

Trump and Musk have both recently ramped up their criticism of Zelenskyy. But neither of them has yet identified who ordered the Starlink disruption.

Musk said on X last week that Starshield systems are "owned and controlled by the US government" and that any speed or usage limits are "decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."

Earlier Wednesday, Zelesnkyy said he and Norwegian Defense Minister Tore Sandvik "discussed in detail launching work on new satellite communication capabilities for our warriors."

"We will involve partners who have the capacity to provide support," Zelenskyy said in anX post.

Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday morning that he does not believe Musk would throttle Starlink without "at least the acquiescence of the White House."

title: Southwest Airlines cuts 2026 profit forecast on higher fuel
content:
Southwest Airlinesbecame the third major U.S. airline this month to cut its 2026 profit forecast due to higher fuel prices, but CEO Bob Jordan said travelers continue to book despite higher fares.

The carrier expects to earn between $2.60 and $2.85 a share on an adjusted basis this year, down from its forecast in July of between $3.25 to as much as $4.25 a share.

Here's what Southwest reported for third quarter compared with Wall Street expectations, according to consensus estimates from LSEG:

Southwest forecast per-share adjusted earnings of between 55 cents and 80 cents in the fourth quarter and unit revenue, a gauge of airfare, up as much as 21% from a year earlier. It said it expects to grow capacity by up to 4% year over year.

"Demand remained strong as we lapped last year's bag fee and other commercial initiatives, reinforcing our belief that the earnings power we've built is durable, even with significantly higher fuel costs," Jordan said in an earnings release.

The airline said its average passenger fare was $231.69 in the third quarter, up almost 27% from the same quarter of 2025. A spokesman said that number does not include add-on fees. The number of revenue passengers carried fell 3.2% to 33.47 million people.

Under pressure to grow revenue, Southwest has been remaking its longtime business model over the past several years, scrapping its old policies like two free checked bags per passenger and open seating. In its place, Southwest has started charging for many seat assignments and added a bag fee, similar to major competitors.

For the third quarter, Southwest posted net income of $270 million, or 55 cents a share, up from $54 million or 10 cents a share a year earlier. Revenue rose more than 21% to $8.42 billion.

Adjusting for one-time items, Southwest reported 66 cents a share.

Delta Air LinesandUnited Airlinesalsocuttheir profit outlooks for the rest of the year when they reported third-quarter earnings. Both of those airlines reported top- and bottom-linemissesfor the third quarter.

title: Meta posts Q3 revenue beat and strong guidance: Live updates
content:
Metareported third-quarter earnings after the bell on Wednesday. Here's how it did compared to LSEG estimates:

It was not immediately clear if earnings were comparable to the $5.75 per share expected by analysts.

Revenue jumped 26% from a year ago.

"We hit major milestones this quarter toward delivering personal superintelligence for everyone - including launching Muse and Muse Wonder, our first frontier model," said CEOMark Zuckerbergin the earnings release.

The initial success of the Muse AI personal assistant tool thatdebutedin September shot to the top of Apple's iOS app store. That AI momentum helped Meta end September withits best monthon Wall Street since 2022.

Meta isn't the first to create a digital assistant that can organize people's email and scan the web for headphone deals, but the company's empire, which includes Facebook and Instagram, has helped introduce AI agents to the masses. At the same time, Meta and its AI chief Alexandr Wang have continued rolling out new foundation models and related updates at a speedy clip, includingMuse Wonder, which was released last Monday.

Meta's third-quarter daily active people, or DAP, came in at 3.64 billion, trailing the 3.65 billion that analysts were expecting, according to StreetAccount. That figure represents all of Meta's users across its family of apps like Facebook and Instagram.

Meta said that it expects fourth-quarter revenue guidance to come between $73 billion to $76 billion. That range's midpoint is above analyst estimates of $73.73 billion.

Since Zuckerberg spentbillions of dollars overhauling the company's AI unitand placed Wang asthe division's leadersome 14 months ago, analysts at Baird Equity Research have noticed increased "positive sentiment" from investors, according to a Tuesday note that cited optimism over the Muse AI agents and related technologies.

The Baird analysts said that while Meta's AI investments will help with future AI agent and foundation model monetization efforts, they "will continue to be the bigger needle-mover to quarterly results in the near-term." That's because those AI investments will still be improving Meta's underlying online advertising platform that companies use to send targeted advertisements, they explained.

Investors havequestionedwhy Meta needs to spend that much money on data centers when it doesn't have a cloud computing business like rivals Google and Amazon. Wall Street may be more willing to cut the social network some slack because of its recent AI momentum.

As such, our ad checks are generally positive for Meta, and we expect an in-line Q3 report; we believe the street is better-informed on capex/margin pressures, and we believe a scenario where Meta raises capex guidance (2026/2027) could be received more positively (or less negatively) by investors now that the company is demonstrating a clearer ROI, despite the lack of a cloud platform.

Meta is offering $20 and $100 monthly subscription plans for Muse AI agent power users. Right now, Muse is free to use but requires a subscription to run it with Meta's latest model —Muse Wonder. The company is also charging developers $50 or $200 a month to access its most powerful Muse Wonder Full AI model via theMuse coding agentthat debuted in early August.

Meta'snascent subscription effortsrepresent opportunities for the company to expandbeyond online advertising, which is still its core money maker. Investorshave been concernedabout the Facebook parent's hefty AI investments relative to rivals likeAlphabetandAmazonthat havecloud computing businesses.

While AI-specific monetization efforts offer hope of diversification, they remains a longer-term play. Last week, Metateamedup with longtime rivalAppleto make Meta's new open-weight AI model work with the iPhone maker's high-end Mac computers. Unlike Meta's proprietary AI models, coders can download the weights of Muse Spark Openfor free.

Meta is betting that developers who try Muse Spark Open may eventually want to pay to access the company's more powerful proprietary AI systems.

"These aren't the most capable models that we've developed or released," Wang said in an interview with CNBC. "But we think that there will be a lot of companies and developers who sort of use this model and tinker with it at small scale and then seek to ramp up and scale up their usage."

Meta's Reality Labs division, which is tasked with developing virtual reality headsets and AI-powered wearable devices, is expected to post a loss of $4.54 billion while generating $513 million in sales for the third quarter, according to StreetAccount.

In July when Metareported second-quarter earnings, the company revealed that the Reality Labs unit lost $4.62 billion while bringing in $431 million during the period.

With the VR marketstruggling to catch on with consumers, Zuckerberg has since shifted Reality Labs resources to center on more on AI-driven hardware products like the Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses the company creates with eyewear giantEssilorLuxottica.

Still, Zuckerberg hasn't completely abandoned VR and its sibling technology augmented reality. The CEO revealed in September during the company's annual Connect conference for developers theMeta VR Glasses, which will cost $1,299 then they are released in the spring of 2027.

"We have built a new kind of VR device that delivers the same magical feeling of presence and immersion, high-resolution displays and views of the world around you in a form factor that is a pair of glasses for the first time," Zuckerberg said at the time.

Wall Street may be pleased that Meta's AI strategy involvessubscription pushesand potential newrevenue opportunities, but it will take a while before those efforts pay off. Until then, the company's massive online advertising business continues to be its financial anchor.

Meta is expected to report third-quarter advertising revenue of $61.87 billion. The social media giant said in July that itposted$59.36 billion in second-quarter ad sales.

The Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago continues to haunt Zuckerberg and his social media empire.

New Mexico district court judge Francis Mathew imposed a$25 billion penaltyon Meta today over a state data privacy case that derived from 2018 privacy revelations. The fine, revealed in a court filing, came after a jury in aSanta Fe courthousedetermined that the company formally known as Facebook should be held liable for misleading New Mexico residents about its data handling practices and methods to prevent harmful information from spreading on its family of apps.

Although New Mexico was awarded $219.5 billion, based on the social media company committing over 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices act, the judge reduced that figure to $25 billion.

"Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations, judge Mathew wrote in the filing, regarding the company's then pledge to examine the "data misuse."

Analysts atBank of Americawrote in a note published Friday that they expect Meta to post a sales beat, with revenue of $63.8 billion, based in part on the firm's "solid ad checks" with brands and companies that helps determine the health of the digital ad market.

The analysts don't expect Muse to contribute significantly to Meta's overall business for the rest of this year and 2027 and instead "will consume capacity w/o near-term revs.," meaning that the company's AI agent efforts will take some time to grow into something bigger.

Morgan Stanleyanalysts agree that Meta's Muse AI agent initiatives won't generate big sales anytime soon, and while they said in a Sunday research note that they are "bullish," they "encourage investors to keep reasonable adoption rates in perspective."

The analysts explained that it takes a long time for new technology habits and behaviors to normalize. In 2000, when the e-commerce boom was just five years deep, for instance, the analysts noted that online retail "only made up 4% of adj retail sales" while adding that "even ~30 years in ('26) it's still only 28%."

Meta will be the first hyperscaler to reveal quarterly financials during this tech earnings cycle, withAlphabet,MicrosoftandAmazonslated to report next week.

The four companies combined have called for roughly $730 billion in capital expenditures this year as they stock up on graphics processing units and AI systems and look to build massive data centersaround the globe.

Analysts polled by FactSet expect that number to hit around $1 trillion next year, led by Alphabet, which is projected to spend over $310 billion. The stepped up spending comes as interest rates soar andconcernsintensify that AI revenue won't justify the costs.

Alphabet and Microsoft are scheduled to report earnings next Wednesday, followed by Amazon on Thursday.

Meta's past quarter wasn't all AI agents and good vibes.

The social media giant agreed in August to paynearly $17 billion to settlea major lawsuit involving a group of state attorneys general, including California's Rob Bonta. The trial centered around allegations that Meta misled the public about the true scope of child mental health related harms caused by certain design elements of apps likeFacebook and Instagram, including recommendation algorithms.

Meta'sstate AG settlementcould cause the company to miss on third-quarter earnings per share due to the related $10 billion legal charge that "the street has not yet accounted for," Wolfe Research analysts wrote in

title: Websites taken down worldwide as critical cyber-security update issued
content: Image source,Getty ImagesByTom Gerken and Laura Cress,ÂTechnology reportersÂandÂJoe Tidy,ÂCyber correspondent, BBC World ServicePublished21 October 2026, 13:09 BSTUpdated 3 hours agoInternational governments and agencies have urged websites to address two critical cyber-security flaws in a programming language which powers much of the internet.The vulnerabilities were found within the PHP programming language, with a fix issued on Wednesday afternoon.Multiple cyber-security agencies have urged organisations unable to apply fixes in time to consider taking their sites down, leaving bodies such as the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC to take pages offline.The flaws were discovered by AI, with cyber-security firm Wiz saying they were the "most severe vulnerabilities ever discovered" by the tech, which is reshaping the cyber landscape.Finland has temporarily shut down the government's public web services, while the Netherlands' cyber-security agency said it was taking its own website offline due to the vulnerabilities.The US National Security Agencyissued similar advice on X,externalfor organisations to take their systems offline if they were unable to update with the fix."These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database," it wrote.Meanwhile, the White House said federal agencies were working with leading AI labs to speed up a fix to the issue.Andin a post on X,external, Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP.The Wikimedia Foundation, which runs the online encyclopedia Wikipedia, said it was addressing the security vulnerabilities."We have taken down a number of other systems as a precautionary measure until they can be safely patched," it said.That led some people to be unable to access parts of Wikipedia on Wednesday.Edinburgh council's website has also become inaccessible, as well as the online homes for several BBC programmes including Doctor Who and The Traitors.They have not confirmed a link to PHP - BBC News has approached them for comment.'Roughly 70%' of internetOther websites, including the art platform DeviantArt, have said they are "temporarily down for maintenance,external" without specifying the reason.The vulnerabilities were discovered by cyber-security researchers at the firms Calif and Wiz.Calif, along with PHP Foundation, were part of a program started by OpenAI called Patch the Planet.Through that program, they were given access to the AI company's advanced AI tools in order to find and fix flaws in web development language.OpenAI saidin a blog post,externalthat the discovery was "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory". It added an internal researcher at the company had also discovered the issue around the same time as the other firms.The flaws had gone undetected for more than a decade. By August, after a few weeks of using advanced AI tools, they were discovered."Frontier models were critical to making this process practical, enabling us to develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours," Wiz said in a blog post.It has estimated "roughly 70%" of the internet is affected, though the BBC is unable to verify that figure.While PHP Foundation intended to release its discovery later this month along with a complete fix for the problem, usually referred to by software developers as a "patch," details of the flaw were leaked on social media on Tuesday.It forced PHP Foundation to rush out its announcement of the vulnerability and its huge scale.The Netherlands' National Institute for Public Health and the Environment, an agency of the Dutch government, has taken down its website.Similarly the website of the Tweede Kamer, the lower house of the nation's parliament, has become inaccessible.The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), as well as its counterparts in the EU and Australia have urged those who use PHP to apply the fixes."Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organisations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated," theNCSC said in a note,external.Japan's national cyber-security office and EU cyber-security officialshave issued a similar warning,external.'Early attacks emerging'"PHP is everywhere. It âquietly powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and an awful â lot of software that doesn't even advertise that it runs PHP under the hood," cyber-security company Huntress said.Cyber-security expert Don Smith, from the Sophos Counter Threat Unit, told the BBC this would "likely be a priority target" for hackers.The immediate challenge was not simply installing a patch to fix the issue, but finding and managing every instance where PHP was running, he said."The use of PHP is pervasive, it can sit beneath public websites, content management systems, hosting platforms and third-party products, sometimes without even being obvious to the organisation using it," he said.He said it was crucial that organisations looked out for signs that an attacker "might have already have gained a foothold".The European Union Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-EU) said the risk scores given to the vulnerabilities "indicate the potential for unauthenticated remote code execution".Such a cyber-attack could potentially allow hackers to install malware and take down websites.Dane Knecht, chief technology officer at internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare,said he was,external"seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up".The NCSC said once organisations have installed the update, they should "continuously monitor for security updates from third-party software vendors, including for appliances and services that may bundle PHP".It is not yet clear which versions of the programming language are affected, but CERT-EU said it could affect all versions of it dating back to PHP 5 onwards - which launched in 2004.The PHP Foundation has issued the update only for the latest versions however - with people using PHP 8.1 or older being urged to upgrade.PHP was created for web development. It is used on servers to implement what you see when you visit websites.Not all websites use it, but it nonetheless powers a large portion of the internet.King warns malicious online actors are evolving tacticsPublished10 OctoberUK cyber chiefs say it's time to ditch passwords for passkeys - what are they?Published24 AprilSign up for our Tech Decoded newsletterto follow the world's top tech stories and trends.Outside the UK? Sign up here.Related topicsCyber-crimeCyber-securityCyber-attacks

title: Meta fined $25bn for 'lies' over user data privacy
content: Image source,EPAImage caption,Meta has been hit with numerous legal fines this yearByKali HaysTechnology reporterPublished21 October 2026, 19:01 BSTUpdated 11 minutes agoMeta, the company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp has been hit with the largest ever fine against it for its business practices.A judge in New Mexico on Wednesday ordered the company to pay $25bn (Â£18.6bn) following a two-week trial earlier this year that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data."The lies extend beyond Facebook's data practices as well," the judge said, adding they went to "the heart of Facebook's core business practices".Meta's head lawyer CJ Mahoney said the ruling made it "all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico". The company intends to appeal, a move Mahoney said will be successful.The fine is the largest to date against Meta, which has either been fined or agreed to settle several other lawsuits this year, including an$18bn deal with Californiaover child safety.New Mexico's lawsuit stemmed from the role of Meta, then still doing business as Facebook, in what became known as the Cambridge Analytica scandal.That firm utilized data and information from millions of Facebook users as part of its work in political consulting, including on work related to the 2016 US Presidential election, which saw Donald Trump elected for the first time.New Mexico had also accused Meta of intentionally misleading the public on how it benefitted from content that included hate speech, and how such rules against it were enforced. The jury found the company had intentionally misled the public on those claims, too.Meta disputed those accusations. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online," Mahoney added.Lawyers for New Mexico sued the company over many statements Meta executives had made over the years that user data was never shared with or accessed by third parties without a user's permission, when in reality it had been.They claimed that the entire population of the state, roughly two million people, was impacted by Meta's dishonesty regarding the way it controlled user data. A jury found that Meta had violated state laws more than 40 million times."For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," New Mexico Attorney General RaÃºl Torrez said Wednesday."Today's result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable."The state lawyers sought up to $40bn in fines against Meta. Meta had argued anything beyond $3.4bn would be unconstitutional.Judge Francis Mathew on Wednesday was direct in his decision to fine Meta an amount roughly equal to its profits each quarter.He said Meta's violations of law and misrepresentations to the public about how their Facebook data was used and shared were "willful" and spanned "more than 11 years", stretching from 2010 to 2021.Communications between senior executives, including Mark Zuckerberg, were "designed to mislead the public", Judge Mathew wrote in his order.While the full amount of the penalty against Meta, based on thousands of violations of state law, was calculated as $219bn, Judge Mathew reduced the penalty to the $25bn fine.It follows a $5bn fine levied by the US Federal Trade Commission in 2019 against the company over its data privacy practices.New Mexico has been one of Meta's most notable adversaries in court. The state this yearalso fined Meta almost $1bnfor misleading the public about the safety of its social media platforms for children.The judge overseeing that lawsuit ultimately compared Meta to an industrial polluter of the air, with its form of pollution being "the psychological harm and sexual exploitation of children".California and several other states had collectively sued Meta over similar issues related to a lack of child safety features on Meta's platforms and resulting harms to children.Meta and the states reached a mutual settlement deal, which did not include a fine or any admission of wrongdoing, to end that case only a few days into what was expected to be a multi-week trial.Related topicsMetaMark ZuckerbergFacebookData protection

title: GM aims to develop vehicles in as little as two years with AI, software push
content:
NEW YORK —General Motorsplans to lean into artificial intelligence and vehicle software for future growth and development amid increasing competition abroadfrom Chinese automakersand a tougher U.S. market.

The Detroit automaker on Wednesday shared new details about a proprietary AI agent it's releasing under its OnStar brand, plans for a fourth generation of more efficient all-electric vehicles and a target to cut its vehicle development time in half.

GM alsoreconfirmed that by 2028, it wants to have eyes-off highway driving, or "personal autonomy," that will let drivers take their attention off the road. The automaker said that technology would start with the Cadillac Escalade IQ EV before rolling out to other, more high-volume models.

"All of these developments are building us the car of the future," CEOMary Barrasaid Wednesday during an event laying out the plans, called "GM Forward," in downtown Manhattan.

The initiatives, which Barra, Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson and other executives discussed at the event, are designed to streamline the automaker's operations, while also improving the capabilities of its vehicles for customers.

"Over the last 12 months, we've evolved how we design, engineer and build our vehicles," said Anderson, who led the event and who has been tasked with overseeing GM's latest technology transformation.

GM said it is now targeting a vehicle development time of roughly two years from concept to production versus a traditional four- to five-year cycle. However, the company did not detail a timeline for reaching that goal.

The event comes asChinese automakersare growing outside of the U.S. with rapid development times of new technologies and vehicles. Consulting firm AlixPartners said it believes China is currently bringing vehicles to market twice as fast as traditional automakers, with 40% to 50% less investment and a 30% cost advantage.

GM also continues to play catch-up to U.S. EV leaderTeslawhen it comes to delivering technology advancements through over-the-air updates andautomated driving capabilities.

Anderson, a former Tesla executive, declined to speak specifically about how GM's technologies will compare to the EV maker, but said GM's systems will be able to visualize, or see, more things through the use of multiple types of sensors than a strictly camera-based system, which Tesla uses.

He also said the rapid development and new software architecture will help the company better compete against Chinese automakers abroad.

"There's inherent virtue to speed," Anderson told CNBC during an interview after the event. "Not just in being able to get a car out faster, it's being able to develop a system that's far more performant that you could have otherwise."

GM said Wednesday it has major plans for its next generation of EVs and traditional vehicles with internal combustion engines.

The company said those coming vehicles – regardless of type — will have 40 times the computing power and up to 50% faster cellular connectivity than prior systems.

That computing power is expected to help the automaker with over-the-air updates, onboard diagnostics and AI, as well as other technologies such as automated driving features.

The new brain of the vehicle will launch on the $130,000Cadillac Escalade IQ EVin 2028 before rolling out to other models, including its next generation of EVs.

GM said the forthcoming EVs are expected to be 25% more aerodynamic and 15% lighter and feature electric motors and battery packs that are more compact.

GM President Mark Reuss said despite lackluster consumer adoption and the automaker pulling backbillions of dollars in investments in EVs, it remains committed to producing them.

"We continue to develop our future EVs and work to reduce battery costs," Reuss said during the event. "And when the U.S. market is ready for EVs in large numbers, we will be there for them."

GM expects to achieve such targets through the use of AI in research and development.

The company said it is developing a "new operating approach for vehicle development" that leans into enterprise AI and virtualization to increase speed.

"This concurrent engineering model allows us to innovate faster, improve continuously, and scale new technologies across our lineup with incredible agility," the company said in a release.

GM used the development of its next-generation vehicles, including a new battery chemistry, as an example of how the new technologies are reshaping its vehicle development.

The company said it virtually tested more than 300,000 battery designs using its recently announcedlithium manganese rich battery chemistry,or LMR, before building a single physical prototype.

Anderson said Wednesday that LMR will be the exclusive battery tech for its fourth-generation EVs. GM had previously said it wanted to use those batteries in full-size electric vehicles such as its Chevrolet Silverado and Escalade IQ beginning in 2028.

Anderson said GM is uniquely positioned to use AI compared to other automotive companies because of its more than 100 years in the industry as well as 30 years of OnStar.

"In the age of AI, data is currency," Anderson said. "For decades, GM's engineering, manufacturing and product teams have generated unparalleled body of data that we're now using to build industry-leading AI tools."

The company is building on its internal use of AI to better shape its experiences for customers.

GM on Wednesday reconfirmed that it plans to launch a proprietary in-vehicle AI assistant through its OnStar technology brand.

The OnStar AI assistant is expected to launch in the coming months on the2027 Cadillac Lyriq EVthrough an over-the-air update before expanding to other models.

GM currently uses Google's Gemini for its in-vehicle AI assistant. The companytold CNBCearlier this year that the GM-developed AI will be more integrated with the vehicle.

The goal for OnStar AI, which will be available through a subscription, is to help customers be productive while in the car, especially if the vehicle has self-driving capabilities that don't require the driver or passengers to monitor the system.

GM on Wednesday also reiterated its plans to launch eyes-off highway driving in 2028. The automaker said a year ago that it wanted to launch that technology. It's been five years since Barra said she expected the automaker to offerpersonal autonomous vehiclesthis decade.

"Our vision is that eventually every vehicle should drive itself or its occupants anywhere, and we're investing across the self-driving stack to make that real," Anderson said.

title: Netflix has dipped its toe into theatrical. Is it ready to jump in?
content:
Netflixis making itself clear: It's a streaming-first business.

During the company'sthird-quarter earningscall on Tuesday, co-CEOTed Sarandosreiterated the streaming giant's long-held stance that its content, which it spent $20 billion on last year, is meant for its subscribers and, therefore, should be delivered to customers on its streaming platform as quickly as possible.

Yet, the company is set to have 30 theatrical releases in 2027, on par with what it brought to cinemas in 2026. And while not all of these features are expected to have wide releases or long runs in theaters, Netflix is testing the waters with projects like Greta Gerwig's"Narnia: The Magician's Nephew,"which will have a wide release and a 49-day exclusive theatrical window when it hits cinemas in February.

The company seems poised to carve a new path forward as it grapples with viewership stagnation and a stock slump of roughly 30% since January.

How its theatrical ambitions fit into a streaming-first strategy remains a question mark.

"Theatrical releases are a net positive for reach and streaming demand," Alicia Reese, analyst at Wedbush, wrote in a note Wednesday. "Netflix's more amenable attitude toward exclusive theatrical windows will not only facilitate better relationships with talent, but also add a new revenue stream and build interest in its streaming service. This follows the pattern we have seen with the major studios' streaming platforms over the past several years: theatrical releases don't cannibalize the streaming window, as Netflix fears."

Ahead of its Tuesday earnings report, Netflix restructured its C-suite, bringing in former Disney executivePeter Rice to take over as the company's chief content officer, ousting 10-year veteranBela Bajaria.

Netflix also dismissed Dan Lin, the company's head of film, according to a person familiar with the matter who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal changes. That came just days after itlaid off roughly 1,000 employeesincluding Lin's right handDoug Belgradas well asSheroum Kim, the director of independent film, according to various media reports. It's unclear who Netflix will tap to take over Lin's position.

The company aims to restore quality to the brand and utilize Rice's expertise in talent relations to lure big names in an increasingly competitive market.

Still, Netflix executives seemed to downplay the change in leadership during the company's earnings call.

"Our business and our business flywheel are working," Sarandos told investors during the company's earnings call. "There is no need for a fundamental shift in the strategy. We do need better execution in the U.S. ... It's just not growing as fast as it could or as fast as we'd like."

Sarandos said the streamer had "some really solid doubles and triples this year," but suggested the company needs more "home runs."

In an emblematic moment during Tuesday's call, Sarandos highlighted a deal withDisney,struck in October, to bring the Ice Age films and others to the streaming service, and gave a nod to that company's CEO, Josh D'Amaro.

"We already are seeing some of those benefits from the Ice Age movies. All five of them hit our top 10. That's really exciting," the Netflix co-CEO said. "And by the way, yes, Netflix just plugged a Disney movie on our earnings call. You're welcome, Josh."

In a bid to capture consumer attention and broaden its subscriber funnel, Netflix has spent years diversifying its offerings to includevideo games,live sportsand quick-turn documentaries on buzzy cultural moments.

But more recently, it's lacked some of the water-cooler-type hits like "Stranger Things," "Bridgerton" and "Squid Game" that previously boosted subscriptions and viewership numbers.

"We know there's some investor concern about our view hours growth," Netflix said in its shareholder letter Tuesday. "Engagement — which encompasses quantity, quality and variety of viewing — remains healthy."

And yet with Netflix stating plainly that it needs new avenues for growth — and against the backdrop of afoiled deal to buy the Warner Bros. film studio— investors and onlookers are once again looking at the theatrical business.

"I think there's a place for the theatrical for Netflix," Matthew Condon, equity research analyst at Citizens, told CNBC. "Especially, as the competition for time and attention just continues to increase."

"If they really want to build stickier fan bases around some of their [intellectual property], I think theatrical could be a good avenue for them to do that," Condon said. "That's one area that Netflix has historically not been all that strong in, is building like really, really strong IP. And I think building fan bases around theatrical releases and things of that nature can help with that and then also can help them get top tier talent."

Netflix is no stranger toluring in big Hollywood directors. It's worked with the likes of Rian Johnson, Martin Scorsese, Alfonso Cuarón, Bong Joon Ho, Spike Lee and Guillermo del Toro. However, none of these directors' Netflix films received a wide theatrical release or a long run in theaters.

Sarandos admitted earlier this month that the company haslost talentbecause it would not guarantee wide theatrical releases.

Most notably, the creators and lead producer behind its hit "Stranger Things" have all jumped ship in the last year. Matt and Ross Duffer signeda four-year exclusive dealwithSkydance— thenew homeof the same Warner Bros. film studio that Netflix nearly bought — while Shawn Levy joined the ranks of Disney to direct "Star Wars: Starfighter."

Sarandos said Tuesday the company's strategy is about "specialty theatrical releasing," in which each film gets its own bespoke release. In some cases, Netflix plays the film in theaters for the minimum requirement to be eligible for awards. Others appear for weekend stints as one-off events, like in the case of its "KPop Demon Hunters" smash thatran in theaters for just two days.

Gerwig's "Narnia" adaptation is among those chosen few to get longer theatrical runs and a wider reach, along with an animated film called "Charlie vs. the Chocolate Factory."

"Both films have big global IP and big global fandom, so we're very excited about how they'll play out next year," Sarandos said.

In another sign of its evolution into theaters, Netflix has said it will report box office results for films that have longer theatrical windows. Those readouts are standard for major studios, regardless of release or windowing, but the move marks a new level of disclosure for the streamer.

Incoming content head Rice could be the missing piece for Netflix in a new theatrical model.

The executive has a wealth of experience in television and film. Since 2023 he has produced films like "Saturday Night" and "28 Years Later." He's currently developing a movie adaptation of the video game "Elden Ring."

But right now, Netflix doesn't have the infrastructure for a full theatrical commitment.

"Going into theatrical isn't quite as easy as I think sometimes folks make it sound," Steven Cahall, stock analyst at Wells Fargo, told CNBC. "You have to negotiate with movie theaters, and find spots for your films."

Cahall noted that sending the occasional film to theaters, especially with a limited release, "maybe isn't so hard, but there is a muscle of theatrical distribution ... You need a team of people, and you need a pipeline of content that's intended for theatrical release, and you need a marketing department around it."

That's where buying Warner Bros. Discovery's studio assets would have come in. In the absence of that acquisition, it's not clear how, or how quickly, Netflix can bulk up its own operations.

Plus, it's previously balked at the marketing costs that come with bringing films to the cinema, which can total hundreds of millions of dollars per film. Despite a hefty content budget, Netflix has long prioritized quantity and seemingly endless choice for its subscribers over individual big-budget projects.

A shift to a multi-pronged strategy that feeds both streaming and cinemas would require Netflix to more closely mimic the companies it disrupted in the first place.

"So that becomes more of an existential question for Netflix: Is it time to become a media conglomerate rather than being a pure play streaming company?" Wells Fargo's Cahall said. "'Do we want to become a media conglomerate?'"

title: Burnham proposes plan to cut standing charges from gas bills
content: Image source,Getty ImagesByTom Espiner,ÂBen King,ÂBusiness reportersÂandÂKevin Peachey,ÂCost of living correspondentPublished3 hours agoPrime Minister Andy Burnham has asked ministers to develop a plan to remove standing charges from gas bills.These are fixed daily fees that cover the costs of connecting to a supply. They vary by region and households must still pay them even when energy is not being used.Industry body Energy UK said whether the proposed changes would make a difference to bills would depend on how or where the charges were reallocated on the bill.But an influential research foundation argued it would be a progressive move that would help those on low-incomes and knock Â£27 off a typical annual bill.During Prime Minister's Questions, Burnham said the "pragmatic decision" on giving thegreen light to the Jackdaw gas fieldin the North Sea would allow the government to increase investment in renewables and "do more to help people with bills".He said he had asked the Chancellor John Healey and Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh "to look at whether we can remove standing charges from gas bills and to report back to this house at the earliest opportunity".No details have been given on how removing standing charges would work in practice. But the suggestion has been made by research firmNesta that they could be moved to the unit rate,external, so people pay for what they use.This would probably benefit customers who don't use much gas, but heavy users could end up paying more.For nearly two years, regulator Ofgem has run a series of consultations on standing charges, with a massive public response including vociferous opposition from low-energy users who can do nothing to cut standing charges.Ofgem is running a pilot scheme on low standing charge tariffs, but is yet to draw any firm conclusions, suggesting there are no easy answers.Higher cost of electricity standing chargesAverage standing charges are 54.8p a day for electricity and 29.7p a day for gas.When asked why electricity standing charges would not be scrapped as well, the PM's official spokesman said VAT had already been cut on electricity bills.Standing charges cover costs such as transporting energy to homes via pipes and wires, and the upkeep of that infrastructure.The standing charges also fund schemes to support low-income households.Many of these costs will need to be recouped somehow, butCitizens Advice has warned,externalabout the potential consequences of reform for vulnerable customers.Vulnerable people who don't have a high income, but have high energy usage, could be penalised.But Madeleine Gabriel, director of sustainable future at Nesta, said: "Abolishing the gas standing charge and moving those costs onto the unit rate would help those worst hit by rising energy prices."Pressure remains on the chancellor to offer more fundamental, targeted energy support this winter in his Budget next week, with energy pricesforecast to rise by 16% to a four-year high in January.In addition to standing charges, Burnham said investing in renewables would also bring household bills down "substantially" by breaking the link between gas and electricity prices "in this parliament".Electricity prices in the UK are mainly set by gas prices, and this is often cited as a reason why electricity prices in the UK are higher than many other countries.Get in touchDo you have any views, comments or questions about this story?Contact formRelated topicsPersonal financeMoneyEnergy industryMore on this storyHousehold energy bills forecast to see biggest rise in four yearsPublished30 SeptemberBurnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licencesPublished4 hours ago

title: Just Eat apologises for AI food mistakes after social media ridicule
content: Image caption,A chip muffin and bacon and egg soda - menu items well known in parts of the UK, but not to the AI which made thisByLaura CressTechnology reporterPublished6 hours agoJust Eat has apologised after it was ridiculed online over a series of mistakes with AI-generated pictures for some of its restaurants' food items.The online food delivery platform had been testing out the tech to showcase food which didn't have images yet - but not all turned out as planned.Instead the AI invented several bizarre concoctions, from bacon and eggs floating in a glass of cola - a confusion between "soda" and "soda bread" - to chips poking out of muffins.A Just Eat spokesperson said the firm was "in the process of removing" the incorrect images, and would stop making more until the AI was further developed.Image caption,Salt and pepper chips usually involves frying chips with onions, garlic and chillies - a little bit more exciting than this suggests"We work with tens of thousands of small restaurants on their food imagery, including funding professional local photographers," the spokesperson told the BBC."We've been trialling AI-enhanced images, and as with any new technology, it isn't always quite right the first time."Image caption,What some parts of Manchester call a "chip muffin" - also known as a chip butty - causing the AI to invent a dish which seemingly involved baking potato into breadThe incident highlights the difficulties companies can still face when using AI to speed up or simplify work processes, especially when it is used to interpret words in a specific context.Members of the Just Eat UK subreddit have flocked to the site over the past few days to post the latest unintentionally hilarious spins on takeaway food items.Any picture generated using AI on the delivery app appears with a label indicating so, and the BBC has spotted many of the more unusual takes still up on menus.Image caption,A "cheese roll" was inexplicably turned into sushiA Belfast cafe, meanwhile, had its bacon and egg soda bread dish represented as a glass of fizzy drink with a cooked egg and bacon floating in it.Spelling mistakes on menu items have sometimes added to the confusion, with the Instagram account @uknewestfoods posting a picture of garlic bread in the shape of a plane - presumably because of a misspelling of the word "plain".This Instagram post cannot be displayed in your browser. Please enable Javascript or try a different browser.View original content on InstagramThe BBC is not responsible for the content of external sites.Skip instagram postAllow Instagram content?This article contains content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. You may want to readMetaâs Instagram cookie policy,externalandprivacy policy,externalbefore accepting. To view this content chooseâaccept and continueâ.The BBC is not responsible for the content of external sites.End of instagram postMeanwhile, a "cheese roll" - bread and cheese - instead became slabs of cheese rolled into a sushi roll.While some on social media said they found the images "hilarious", another was less interested in the AI-generated dishes, saying: "Well, that lot just helped my diet".Meanwhile, one personon Instagram,externalquestioned why customers would ever want to see AI images of a restaurant's food even if they were closer to the real thing."I want to see what the dish actually looks like as it helps me decide who to order from or what to order," they said."These 'perfect' AI versions just lead to disappointment if that's what you think your meal will look like."Sign up for our Tech Decoded newsletterto follow the world's top tech stories and trends.Outside the UK?
