title: The tech helping crack decades-old cold cases
content: Image source,Getty ImagesImage caption,Crime scene evidence is often not enough to identify suspectsByChris MarshallTechnology ReporterPublished1 hour agoRandy Gail Sperino was last seen alive on the evening of 9 November 1993, as she was getting into a pickup truck in Granite City, Illinois.The 34-year-old's body was found hours later in a field nearby, the victim of blunt force trauma.The identity of her killer was a mystery. DNA evidence found at the crime scene was tested against standard law enforcement databases, but no matches were found.For three decades, investigators from the Madison County Sheriff's Office chased leads and interviewed hundreds of people as they attempted to identify the perpetrator.The case looked like it would remain one of more than 250,000 unsolved homicides in the US.Then, last year, detectives tried a fresh approach. They sent genetic evidence to Othram, a Houston-based company that uses DNA technology to help identify the perpetrators in cold and current crime cases.The Madison County detectives had been inspired by investigative genetic genealogy techniques used to identify the Golden State Killer, Joseph James DeAngelo, back in 2018. In that case, an investigative team constructed a family tree to help identify the killer.They were able to do so thanks to DNA data that relatives had provided to commercial databases, similar to consumer ancestry platforms.Unlike traditional forensic DNA testing, which generally relies on a direct comparison between evidence and a known person, investigative genetic genealogy can identify distant genetic relatives of an unknown individual.Othram set about applying this technique to track down Sperino's killer. While the killer's own DNA profile wasn't available, profiles submitted by his extended relatives allowed the company to identify a male family member."That lead broke the case open," said Captain Tim Lawrence of Madison County Sheriff's Office, which was responsible for investigating the crime.It was a crucial clue that led the detectives to Albert "Buddy" Zigler, 70, who then confessed to the murder. He was charged in May this year.Wes Sperino, Gail's son, said at a press conference: "I finally get closure and I finally know who did this."Image source,Madison County Sheriff's OfficeImage caption,Albert Zigler was charged with murder in MayThe technique that led detectives to Zigler is credited with revolutionising how forensic cases are solved.It has been highly successful in helping solve cases involving unidentified human remains and identifying suspects in longstanding investigations.Othram claims it has helped solve thousands of cases. The company's chief executive David Mittelman likens investigative genetic genealogy to a GPS system: "The DNA profile is the GPS signal and it says 'you belong here.' But to understand where 'here' is, you need a map."Public records, obituaries, and census data build that map so Othram's scientists can establish how different family trees connect.However, Mittelman is quick to point out that DNA technology can only go so far before "a cascade of investigative steps" are needed.Image source,OthramImage caption,An Othram scientist prepares a bone for DNA extractionDNA science isn't the only technology that are helping detectives solve cold cases.One of the challenges facing detectives on major cases investigations like the hunt for Sperino's killer is the sheer amount of evidence they dig up.Officers investigating Sperino's murder realised AI could help them wade through the mountains of evidence they had accumulated since 1993.They used a platform called Centerline AI, from Florida software company CentralSquare, to analyse more than 2,000 pages of records and identify evidence for the DNA testing that helped to break the case.The AI helped them reconstruct timelines and organise witness information. "It's so much easier than having a detective have to read through 2,000 pages," Lawrence says. His team could interact with the AI like a chat bot.This also helped when it came to interviewing Zigler after they had tracked him down. Detectives were able to ask questions of the AI to help "figure out if Zigler was being truthful", says Lawrence.But the technology is "only as good as the investigator," says the captain. There comes a point, he says, "where you leave the technology behind and you have to go track people down and talk to them."Investigative genetic genealogy has its limitations too. Mittelman says: "It can't solve every case. If you have no DNA, you can't really use this technique.""But this technique is a lot more powerful and a lot more likely to yield identities than having to rely on the chance that you find a match somewhere in a database," he adds.While firms like Othram only use ancestry platforms where users have provided consent for law enforcement matching, there remain some concerns about the ethical implications of using this data."There are significant privacy concerns," says Denise Syndercombe Court, professor of forensic genetics at King's College London. While one person may have opted in to their DNA being used, genetic relatives may not have given consent.A lack of funding is another hurdle. Mittelman says: "Every law enforcement agency wants to do it. There's just not a lot of funding for it."Sometimes cases are funded through donations or crowdfunding. Othram operates a website listing cases that members of the public can help fund.While investigative genetic genealogy has been adopted in countries such as Sweden, Denmark and Australia, it is not yet used in the UK. The Home Office is conducting a study to consider whether it should be adopted in the UK but did not respond to a request for comment.The UK is already in a strong position, says Syndercombe Court. "We have such an efficient DNA database that if you can get any DNA out of a crime scene, you've got over a 65% chance of putting a name to that person, which is enormously powerful," she says.Related topicsInternational BusinessTechnology of BusinessDNACrimeForensic scienceUnited StatesTechnology of BusinessX-planes: Are they needed in the new era of drones?Published25 SeptemberThe AI telling farmers when to harvestPublished1 OctoberThe start-ups hoping to return battery making to the USPublished30 September

title: Netflix posts third-quarter earnings beat, but shares fall on advertising and revenue guidance
content:
Netflixon Tuesday reportedthird-quarter earningsthat topped analyst estimates and revenue that was in line as Wall Street eyes the company's engagement and advertising metrics.

Here's how Netflix performed for the period ended Sept. 30, compared with projections from analysts polled by LSEG:

The streamer's revenue was almost 12% higher year over year, boosted by growth in membership and anincrease in subscription pricesthat went into effect in March, the company said. Netflix said the response to those price hikes has been consistent with prior changes and with its expectations.

Net income for the quarter was $3.66 billion, or 87 cents per share, compared with $2.55 billion, or 59 cents a share in thesame period last year.Netflix said the year-over-year jump in profit was due in part to the timing of expenses.

The company expects fourth-quarter revenue to rise more than 11% to $13.44 billion, driven by growth in memberships, pricing and ad revenue, it said.

The company narrowed its 2026 full-year forecast, saying it now expects revenue to reach $51.1 billion, a 13% increase over the year prior. This is on the low end of the range Netflix provided during its previous earnings report of between $51 billion and $51.4 billion and below Wall Street's expectations of $51.2 billion for the year, according to LSEG.

Shares of Netflix fell about 6% in extended trading Tuesday.

Wall Street and investors will be looking for Netflix to provide additional details about the company's strategy following recent organizational changes and headwinds including stagnating viewership and growing competition from the likes of YouTube.

"With intense competition and an explosion of content competing for consumer attention, strategic clarity and excellent execution are critical," the company said in a shareholder letter Tuesday. "In Q3, we delivered well across all three priorities, but we see room to do even better with focused, continuous improvement."

Last week, Netflix said it waslaying off about 6% of employees,or roughly 1,000 workers, and that Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria wasdeparting from that role.

The company said Tuesday it expects its fourth-quarter results to be impacted by those reductions in head count, with a negative impact on operating margin of about 120 basis points.

Former Disney executive Peter Rice has been tappedas the new CCO, but it's not yet clear how he'll address concerns around viewership.

Netflix in its shareholder letter said, "We know there's some investor concern about our view hours growth," but added, "engagement — which encompasses quantity, quality and variety of viewing — remains healthy and … we continue to deliver strong value to members."

The company seeks to accelerate growth in those view hours and plans to do so with a three-step strategy, it said: deliver more entertainment value to members; leverage technology to improve all aspects of the service; and improve monetization.

Central to Netflix's value offering has been its cheaper, ad-supported tier. Yet, the company on Tuesday lowered its full-year revenue guidance for its ad business.

Netflix said it now expects 2026 ad revenue of around $2.7 billion, down from the roughly $3 billion the company had previously forecast. That lower guidance is due to a slower-than-expected rollout of some ad product capabilities, the company said.

"Our ads business has delivered really impressive growth since we've launched, and we do see a long road of continued growth ahead of us," co-CEO Greg Peters said on the company's earnings call. "We set big growth targets for our ads business this year. We established an aggressive product road map that was consistent with that strategy. And, just note, I think that the build-out that we've been on is the fastest build-out of a comparable ad stack in our industry, but we are currently a bit behind our aggressive target for the year."

Earlier Tuesday, Netflix announced new features for advertisers that it says will help better connect brands to the right audiences and measure the impact of their ads.

title: United Airlines slashes 2026 profit outlook on fuel prices, but travelers keep booking despite higher fares
content:
United Airlinesis slashing its profit forecast for the year as fuel costs continue to bite, but the carrier said passengers keep booking.

United said Tuesday that it expects to earn between 50 cents and $1.50 a share on an adjusted basis in the fourth quarter, well below the $1.76 a share Wall Street analysts expected. At the high end of that range, it would bring United's 2026 adjusted earnings to no more than $7.22 per share. In mid-July, United said it was expecting full-year earnings of $9 to $11 a share.

The carrier expects to pay an average of $4.80 a gallon for fuel in the fourth quarter, up from an average price of $3.90 a gallon in the third.

A surge in fuel prices this year has added billions of dollars to airlines' costs, eating into profits, despite strong demand, and driving up airfares.

Here is what United Airlines reported for the quarter that ended Sept. 30 compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on estimates compiled by LSEG:

United's third-quarter net income rose 8.5% from a year earlier to $1.03 billion, or $3.14 a share. During the same period last year its net income totaled $949 million, or $2.90 a share.

"Our employees met the challenge of our ever-changing environment and our results prove the resilience of focusing on building a brand-loyal airline for customers," United CEO Scott Kirby said in an earnings release.

United's fuel bill rose close to 62% in the quarter from a year earlier to $4.84 billion.

Revenue for the three months ended Sept. 30 rose 17.4% from a year earlier to $17.88 billion, compared with $15.23 billion the year before.

Domestic passenger unit revenue rose 14.5% from a year earlier, while international unit revenue was up 17.4%, a sign of higher fares. Passengers continue to book, United said, with passenger counts up more than 2% from last year.

Adjusting for one-time items, United reported net income of $833 million or $2.54 a share.

title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wins dismissal of sister's lawsuit
content: Image source,Minh Connors/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesByRachel ClunBusiness reporterPublished10 minutes agoOpenAI chief executive Sam Altman has won a dismissal of a lawsuit brought against him by his sister that claimed he had sexually abused her more than two decades ago.A US district judge dismissed the case after Ann Altman had refused to attend an independent medical examination, adding she was warned a failure to do so would result in the case being thrown out.Ann Altman had claimed the OpenAI founder had regularly sexually abused her between 1997 and 2006. Sam Altman has denied those accusations.The Altman family has said Ann Altman has mental health challenges and they have supported her financially, adding the claims were made as she continued to demand more funds.District Judge Zachary Bluestone said that despite multiple accommodations and multiple opportunities to do so, Ann Altman did not appear for an independent medical exam on three separate occasions, and "failed to meaningfully prosecute her case"."Because Annie has continued to violate her discovery obligations and forced this case to a halt through her intransigence, the Court has run out of options and, thus, dismisses her claims with prejudice," he said in his written order.The case was filed on 6 January 2025 in the Eastern District of Missouri.In it, Ann Altman claimed that her older brother Sam Altman began abusing her when she was three, and he was 12.However, in a joint statement released by Sam Altman along with his mother and two brothers at the time, the family said they were concerned for Ann Altman's wellbeing and have spent years trying to support her financially and to look after her wellbeing.The family said she receives monthly financial support, and her bills and rent were also covered, while also trying to assist with medical help.The statement said her claims against Sam Altman had changed drastically over time, but all of those claims were "utterly untrue".Sam Altman is the co-founder of OpenAI, which launched its popular ChatGPT artificial intelligence chatbot in 2022.If you've been affected by the issues in this story, help and support is available via theBBC Action Line.Related topicsUnited States

title: Trump sued over Canadian tariffs in latest legal challenge
content: Image source,Jim Lo Scalzo/Pool/EPA/ShutterstockByRachel ClunBusiness reporter,ÂReporting fromNew YorkPublished23 minutes agoUS President Donald Trump is facing another legal challenge on tariffs after the group that successfully sued over his so-called "liberation day" import taxes filed a new lawsuit over the latest Canadian levies.The White House imposed a 50% levy on some $20bn of Canadian goods after trade talks between the US and Canada broke down in August.The Liberty Justice Center filed a suit on behalf of US food business Gellert Global Group, urging the US Court of International Trade to find the levies unlawful and to order refunds with interest for affected importers.The lawsuit argues the White House exceeded its authority in imposing the tariffs and caused "immediate harm to American businesses".The White House has been contacted for comment.Gellert Global Group is a third-generation family business that is paying 50% tariffs on cheese exported from Canada. The New Jersey-based firm is also facing retaliatory tariffs from Canada on American-made cheese it sells north of the border.Co-chief executive Thomas Gellert said the firm had spent generations building relationships with suppliers and customers in the food industry."These tariffs disrupt those relationships overnight and create costs and uncertainty that ripple through the entire supply chain," he said on Tuesday.The Liberty Justice Center is challenging the administration's use of Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act to hit Canadian goods from wine to dairy products and hockey sticks.That section of the nearly 100-year-old Act is aimed at protecting US business against foreign discrimination, but the legal group is arguing that it does not allow the executive branch "to impose sweeping tariffs or import restrictions whenever a trade dispute arises".The US-Canada trade war in 5 chartsPublished31 AugustThe lawsuit seeks to challenge the White House's reliance on retaliatory tariffs imposed by Canada to justify its own duties under Section 338.Canada has imposed a series of countermeasures against numerous US tariffs. Last month, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carneymatched the Section 338 US tariffs "dollar for dollar"after Trump imposed them for what he called "unequal treatment" of US cars, dairy and alcohol.It also points out Section 338 requires a 30-day waiting period before levies can be imposed, but the tariff on products including cheese was added to the list just a week before tariff collection began.Sara Albrecht, chief executive of the Liberty Justice Center, said the case was not about Trump himself but about the presidency."No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required," she said.The lawsuit argues that Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 has been superseded by Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.It also argues that if Section 338 still applies, the White House has not established the legal basis for the sweeping tariffs against Canada."The case is not an objection to tariffs as such. It asks who has the power to impose them and whether the executive branch followed the law Congress wrote," the Liberty Justice Center said.The law group has also filed a motion for a preliminary injunction to block their collection.It is the fourth case brought by the group against Trump's tariffs, including its successful case against the sweeping tariffs brought in under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA)that were struck down in Februarythis year.Albrecht said the group had brought all the cases for the same reason: "the Constitution gives tariff power to Congress. The executive branch cannot keep moving the same policy from one statute to another and pretend the limits disappear".Figure caption,As Trump shares an AI goose meme amid the trade war, the BBC's Jessica Murphy examines how much Canada can fight back.Related topicsTrade warTradeMore on this storyWhat tariffs will really cost Canadians and AmericansPublished9 SeptemberWhat tariffs has Trump introduced and why?Published22 August'Half my business will be gone' - firms in Canada and US fear trade warPublished24 August

title: Housing is flashing warning signs just as the Fed weighs more interest rate hikes
content:
The Federal Reserve's inflation fight is running into a growing complication: The housing market is slumping even as broader price pressures persist.

Housing datadeteriorated further in September, according to separate reports Tuesday, adding to an already complicated policy landscape for the central bank as it contemplates its next move on interest rates.

Things appear poised to get worse before they get better. If the Fed raises short-term rates as expected over the next several months, mortgage rates that are already at 7.43% could push even higher, putting a further damper on affordability. Higher home borrowing costs have coincided with a general rise in inflation and a housing shortage.

"The housing market is about to go into a deep sleep unless Washington can do a 180 on its policies and make the cost of a new home more affordable," wrote Chris Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds. "It is not winter yet but housing is going into a deep freeze."

TheNational Association of Realtorsreported that pending sales, a forward-looking index that measures home sales under agreement but not completed, hit an all-time low in records that stretch back to 2001. The index slid 7.3% for the month and was off 11.3% from a year ago. The Wall Street estimate was for a decline of just 0.4%.

Housing starts, another important metric when evaluating the state of the market, also posted a decline well outside already-muted expectations Tuesday.

Privately ownedhousing startsfell at a seasonally adjusted annualized rate of 5.2% on the month, against expectations for a decline of just 0.4%, while building permits were off 0.2%, against the Dow Jones consensus outlook for a 2% gain, according to Commerce Department data.

Moreover, single-family permits totaled just 845,000, down 4% from August and the lowest number since 2023.

"Market conditions weakened in September due to fast-rising mortgage rates," said Lawrence Yun, the NAR's chief economist. "Although job growth and income gains can support home purchases, housing affordability is more affected by changes in mortgage rates."

The rate for a 30-year mortgage was above 7% for most of September, ending the month around 7.6%, according toMortgage News Daily. Five years ago, rates were closer to 3%, feeding into the Covid-era housing boom that saw an explosion in demand and, consequently, prices.

Outside of the pending sales number,home builder sentimentis at lows not seen in 14 years.

Under some conditions, Fed officials might respond to the housing weakness with easier monetary policy. Lower rates generally help spur demand by lowering borrowing costs.

But the Fed has a bigger fight on its hands in its effort to bring inflation under control.Readings last weekon consumer and producer prices provided few signs of optimism, with wholesale final demand goods prices rising 2.6%, the fastest pace in a Bureau of Labor Statistics data series going back to December 2009.

Fed officials have said they are tracking the inflationary effects of the robust investment in artificial intelligence, which is driving up the cost of chips and electronics. At the same time, they believe that benefits from AI investment could offset weaker sectors of the economy such as housing.

However, conditions generally point to a housing market likely to weaken further before stabilizing, Goldman Sachs economist Ronnie Walker said in a client note Monday.

"In 2027, we expect the headwind from affordability—reignited by the recent rebound in mortgage rates—to increasingly dominate, weighing further on activity," Walker wrote. "Sustained higher mortgage rates will continue to have their most pronounced impact on housing turnover, and the recent run-up in rates is likely to push existing home sales lower in the coming months."

Several data points tell the story: More than 95% of mortgage borrowers have rates below the prevailing level, and 65% are 2 percentage points below. Goldman forecasts residential investment to decline 2.5%, 4% and 1%, respectively, over the coming three quarters, with a possibility for a steeper decline if mortgage rates don't fall.

The firm sees single-family starts of just 875,000 in 2027, little changed from this year, while existing sales are forecast at 3.9 million, also about the same as 2026 but notably 26% below pre-Covid 2019 levels. Walker attributed the middling levels as a product of the "lock-in" effect in which it's too expensive for current homeowners to move and take on higher borrowing costs while deteriorating affordability weighs on new construction.

"Housing activity has remained rangebound in recent years, capped on the upside by affordability headwinds and buffered on the downside by the longstanding housing shortage," Walker wrote. "In 2027, we expect the headwind from affordability to increasingly dominate, weighing further on activity."

Markets expect the Fed to hold benchmark rates steady when it meets next week. However, futures pricing implies a strong chance of a quarter-point hike in December and another in March 2027, according to the CME Group'sFedWatchtool.

One point of optimism comes from Yun, the NAR economist, who thinks the trend of mortgage costs running ahead of Fed hikes could mean that rates are topping out.

"Given that mortgage rates have already risen much more than the Federal Reserve's short-term interest rate hikes, mortgage rates could be topping out," he said. "Buyers and sellers may simply be holding back until mortgage rates move favorably."

title: Mike Bloomberg spent $80M to boost Democrats in midterms: NYT
content:
Mike Bloombergspent $80 million in September and October to help Democrats regain majority control of theHouse of Representativesin the upcoming midterm elections,The New York Timesreported Tuesday, citing his team.

Shortly after The Times published its article about Bloomberg's campaign spending, his fellow billionaire, PresidentDonald Trump, in a social media post reiterated his vow to spend $400 million to boost Republican candidates.

The dueling announcements came asRepublicans are increasingly worriedabout retaining their majorities in both chambers of Congress.

Many political analysts expect Democrats to win control of the House, and multiple polls show Democrats within reach of winning a majority of seats in the Senate.

Bloomberg "is of the view that resources matter in campaigns," his political advisor Howard Wolfson told The Times.

Bloomberg, a former New York City mayor, "expects a result," Wolfson said.

With the $80 million in spending, Bloomberg is among the top five largest individual Democratic donors according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings for the 2025-2026 election cycle.

Wolfson did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNBC.

Before Tuesday's announcement, Bloomberg was known to have donated $23 million to Democrats and affiliated causes this election cycle, according to Federal Election Commission records through Tuesday.

As of the beginning of October,Bloomberghad put $11 million behind asuper PACsupportingMicah Lasherin New York's 12th Congressional District and $2.5 million toward Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro's reelection, according to campaign-financerecords.

Trump, in a Truth Social post, said that he and his affiliated political action committee have spent more than $300 million to help Republican candidates with advertising, voter contacts, rallies and turnout efforts. Trump promised that his spending will top $400 million by Election Day, Nov. 3.

FEC filings as of Tuesday afternoon so far show roughly $200 million in identifiable spending and ad reservations tied to Trump's political operation, leaving a gap between what's publicly visible and Trump's broader claim.

In September, Trump said he had "close to a billion dollars" in his super PAC, MAGA Inc., and planned to spend $400 million to $500 million on the midterms. At the time, MAGA Inc. reported about $403 million in cash on hand — less than half the amount Trump cited.

title: Trump sued over 50% tariffs on Canada in latest trade challenge
content:
A newlawsuitfiled Tuesday challenges PresidentDonald Trump's invocation of a Depression-era law to impose 50%tariffson a range ofCanadian goods.

Trump in July used Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to slap those steep tariffs on Canadian hockey sticks, wine, honey, wigs, and other products in response to alleged trade discrimination by Ottawa. It was the first time the 96-year-old law had ever been used to impose a tariff.

"Section 338 is a relic of the retaliation-based tariff policy" that has been "impliedly repealed" by subsequent legislation, the civil complaint filed in theU.S. Court of International Tradesays.

The suit was filed by Gellert Global Group, a New Jersey-based food importer that says its cheeses are covered by the tariffs. The complaint asks the court to declare the tariffs unlawful, block their enforcement, and order the Trump administration to issue refunds for duties already paid, with interest.

Gellert Global is represented by the Liberty Justice Center, the same legal group that dealt a major blow to Trump's trade agenda by successfully contesting his "reciprocal" tariffs.

The Supreme Court struck those tariffs down in February. The administration is in the process ofrefunding the estimated $166 billionthat the federal government collected from importers through the reciprocal duties.

The Liberty Justice Center is currently engaged in two other lawsuits against what it says is Trump's misuse of laws to impose sweeping tariffs.

"This case is not about the president. It is about the presidency," the group's CEO Sara Albrecht said in a statement Tuesday morning announcing Gellert Global's suit. "No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required."

The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on the suit.

Trump on July 20 signed three presidential proclamations targeting different sets of Canadian imports with the Section 338 tariffs in response to alleged unfair treatment in the U.S.motor vehicle,alcoholanddairysectors.

The tariffs took effect Aug. 22, after last-ditch trade talks with Canadian officials in Washington fell apart. Canada later retaliated with "dollar for dollar" tariffs on U.S. goods.

Tuesday's lawsuit argues that even if the 1930 tariff law is upheld, the Trump administration did not meet the legislation's requirements when it imposed the duties on Canada.

It says that the law permits tariff action "only upon finding 'as a fact'" that a foreign country is unequally imposing unreasonable charges or trade limitations on U.S. products, or that its customs rules otherwise unfairly disadvantage the U.S.

"Even then, the President may impose only such duties 'as he shall determine will offset such burden or disadvantage,'" the lawsuit states.

But the Canadian actions cited in Trump's proclamations "do not discriminate against the United States," it says.

Two of those actions are "Canada's responses to the President's own tariffs, including tariffs the Supreme Court has held unlawful, and retaliation is not discrimination," the lawsuit contends.

Another centers on dairy quota terms that were negotiated in USMCA, the U.S.'s trilateral trade deal with Canada and Mexico. Those terms "give American cheese better access to Canada than the cheese of most of the world receives," the suit states.

The suit says Gellert Global boasts more than $1.7 billion in annual revenue. In 2025, the company imported $71 million worth of Canadian cheese — including sheep's and goat's milk cheese, mascarpone, brie, camembert and the hybrid cheese borgonzola, the complaint says.

Gellert says it paid no tariffs on its imports of Canadian cheese under USMCA. The Trump administration said in July that itwould not renewthat trade pact for another 16-year term.

Under the Section 338 tariffs, "Gellert now pays a 50 percent duty on the entered value of its Canadian cheese, an estimated $40 million per year," according to the suit.

While it plans to absorb the costs through the end of the year, the situation is "not sustainable long term," the company says.

"If the tariffs continue, Gellert will be forced to raise the prices on its products, resulting in lost or reduced sales, decreased customer loyalty, risk of losing product placements due to higher costs, and supply chain interruptions as producers scale down or go out of business due to increased costs," the suit says.

title: UK government to make Jackdaw gas field announcement
content: Image caption,The Jackdaw gas platform and drilling rig stand east of Aberdeen in the North SeaByJack FenwickÂandÂBenjamin RussellPublished2 hours agoThe UK government is expected to announce a long-awaited decision on whether to approve the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea.It is widely believed in Westminster that Jackdaw will be approved but that a decision on the Rosebank oil field off Shetland will not yet be made.The question of whether to approve the two sites has become hugely politically significant and has been delayed for several months.Multiple Whitehall sources have told BBC News the government would make an announcement on Jackdaw on Wednesday morning with the Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh expected to address MPs in the afternoon.Prime Minister Andy Burnham has spoken repeatedly of the need for a "flexible" approach to energy and is believed to be in favour of drilling more where licensing already exist in the North Sea.Labour's 2024 manifesto pledged not to issue any new oil and gas licences in the North Sea but to honour existing ones such as Jackdaw.Jackdaw, about 150 miles (241.4km) east of Aberdeen, is a gas field which its operators say could be connected to the UK network within months.Rosebank, about 80 miles (128.7km) north-west of Shetland, is Britain's largest untapped oil field, which would also produce some gas.The controversial fields have been the subject of years of debates, legal wrangling and public consultations, with arguments from both industry bodies and environmentalists being weighed up by the UK government.Licences for the fields weregranted by the Conservative UK governmentin 2022 and 2023, which sparked legal challenges from environmental groups.The Court of Session in Edinburghruled last yearthat Rosebank and Jackdaw had been unlawfully approved because the government had failed to take into account the climate impact of burning extracted oil and gas from the sites.Environmentalists insist more drilling would be unconscionable, and hamper efforts to cut planet-warming carbon emissions as deadly heatwaves and extreme weather affect people across the globe.They also claim starting production would not protect energy security and transitioning sooner to greener technologies would be better for supporting jobs.Industry bodies argue starting production at Rosebank and Jackdaw will title: SpaceX earnings live updates: Here's why analysts are bullish ahead of the report
content:
SpaceXis set to announce third-quarter results after the bell on Tuesday, the second earnings report forElon Musk'sdefense tech conglomerate since its record IPO in June.

Here's what analysts are expecting, according to LSEG consensus estimates:

While SpaceX is best known for its reusable rockets, most of its revenue and profit in recent quarters came from the company's connectivity segment, which consists of itsStarlinksatellite internet service.

Buzz is building about Starlink's plans to build a U.S. network after SpaceX, earlier this month,announcedthat it's buying 800 MHz of low-band spectrum, and after the Federal Communications Commission approved a plan for the company to build out a 15,000-satellite constellation.

The moves strengthen "Starlink Mobile's ability to compete with major carriers by enabling broader, deeper coverage," RBC Capital Markets analysts wrote in a note ahead of earnings. The firm has a $225 price target on SpaceX stock and the equivalent of a buy rating.

In the third quarter, analysts are expecting AI revenue of $6.47 billion, connectivity sales of $4.84 billion, and revenue in the space business of $1.41 billion, according to StreetAccount.

During the third quarter, SpaceX also closed its $60 billion purchase of AI coding startup Cursor.

What you need to know ahead of the earnings report:

In its first earnings report in August, SpaceX reported capital expenditures of $18.4 billion, with 80% of that going towards its artificial intelligence division.

That number spooked Wall Street, and shares dropped following the report.

SpaceX and xAI, now known as SpaceXAI, merged in February and the company has been pouring money into its effort to become a major player in AI, a market dominated by OpenAI, Anthropic and Google.

Wall Street is sounding bullish on SpaceX ahead of its third-quarter earnings report, to be delivered after the bell on Tuesday.

Mizuho has an outperform rating on the stock and a $200 price target, per a Monday note from analyst Brett Linzey. Shares were trading around $148 as of 10:45 a.m. on Tuesday.

"AI is the largest swing factor for 3Q26 revenue and EBITDA. Consensus has AI revenue of $6.30B (+146% Q/Q from $2.56B) and AI adj. EBITDA of $3.32B (from $1.15B)," he wrote.

Analysts are expecting some conversation about deals or competitive plays with cable and telecom companies following SpaceX's acquisition of low-band spectrum earlier this month.

"We expect initial strategic commentary centers around Connectivity and how SPCX can partner/compete its way into global markets, although we think low-band distribution becomes a meaningful intelligence lever over time," Colin Canfield at Cantor Fitzgerald wrote in a Monday note. He has a price target of $246 and an overweight rating on the stock.

Oppenheimer's expectations are more measured. The bank thinks the quarter will be "in-line" with "guidance reiterated."

"Industry subscriber growth is slowing with limited room for pricing action, so focus is shifting from net adds and service revenue growth toward cost-cutting using AI, and lower subsidies/churn," Timothy Horan at Oppenheimer told clients in a Tuesday note. He expects "more rational incumbent behavior" from SpaceX's competitors.

Musk said Monday that he'llgiveevery child in the U.S. one of his SpaceX shares next year.

With 72 million children under 18 in the U.S. as of July 1, 2025, according to official census data, that would amount a giveaway of about $10.5 billion worth of shares as of the current price.

Musk, the world's richest person with a net worth of over $900 billion, said in a post on X that, "This will be the first of many," without providing further details. However, when it comes to fulfilling hisphilanthropic promises, Musk has a spotty track record.

A military tier of Starlink, marketed as Starshield, has drawn scrutiny of late as restrictions on the system in Ukraine hindered the country's ability to defend itself against intensifying attacks by Russia.

Ukrainian officials saidSpaceXand the Trump administrationrestrictedStarshield without warning last week, causing Ukraine's military forces to lose control of drones moving over 100 miles per hour, as the craft were relying on Starshield for connectivity at those speeds.

Musk said in a post on X that any changes to Starshield should be attributed to the U.S. government and President Donald Trump, though Trump later denied he ordered any such restrictions.

Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told NBC's "Meet the Press" on Sunday that the restraints remained in place over the weekend.

Investors, meanwhile, have poured capital into potential Starlink competitors,including Eutelsat.

AfteracquiringxAIin Februarywith its data centers in and around Memphis, Tennessee, SpaceX struck lucrative cloud computing agreements, establishing a new revenue stream.

Deals with Google, Anthropic and Reflection AI, as well as an unnamed customer revealed by SpaceX CFOBret Johnsenat an event last month, amount to potentially tens of billions of dollars in annual revenue for the company.

SpaceX is reportedly in talks to raise up to $40 billion to buy more Nvidia chips to support its AI ambitions.

Investors are looking for updates around this business for SpaceX as it seeks to monetize its AI capacity.

Ahead of earnings, investors are invited to submit questions for the call. One entry that got a lot of upvotes was about timing for a potential merger between SpaceX and Tesla, Musk's automaker.

Musk's companies have had business and financial relations for years, even sharing personnel and some board members.

Tesla invested $2 billion into xAI, which later converted into shares of SpaceX. The AI unit of SpaceX also spent about $430 million last year on Tesla's Megapacks, which are battery energy storage systems, and $143 million on Cybertrucks.

With SpaceX hitting the public market in June, speculation about a more permanet tie-up has been swirling. SpaceXCOO Gwynne Shotwelltold CNBC ahead of the IPO that a merger "might make Elon's life a little easier."

A demo ofTesla's next-generation Roadsterlast week stirred up further merger excitement among Musk fans. The new Roadster was developed with SpaceX and incorporates its technology, including cold gas thrusters, to enable the car to launch, hover and flip in mid-air.

title: Dow jumps 500 points as solid earnings, falling crude oil stir rebound: Live updates
content:
TheDow Jones Industrial Averagerose on Tuesday as a number of upbeat earnings reports and a drop in oil prices overshadowed recent pressure seen among artificial intelligence-related stocks.

The blue-chip index gained 523 points, or 1%, while theS&P 500added 0.4%. TheNasdaq Compositetraded up 0.2%.

Shares of industrial and safety products producer3Moffered a boost to the Dow, jumping more than 5% following better-than-expected earnings results and afull-year guidance raise. Shares of aerospace and defense companyNorthrop Grummanalso advanced 6% after it posted an earnings beat.

Meanwhile,oil pricespulled back from earlier gains, helping investor sentiment. U.S.West Texas Intermediate crude futureswere last down less than 1% at around $103 per barrel, whileBrent crude futuresfell more than 1% to roughly $107 a barrel. The moves in oil, which added to the declines inTreasury yields, come as traders continued to monitor developments in the Middle East.

The market has been weighed down as of late by worries about the sustainability of the AI trade, as debt and demand concerns grow. In fact, sentiment in tech took a hit earlier in the day after Korean AI firm Elicetumbled more than 30%overnight in its public market debut. Asia-Pacific markets declined Tuesday, after U.S. stocks rose overnight, leading to declines in the South Korean market.

However, AI-related stocks staged a bit of a comeback as the session went on.Micron Technology,IntelandSandiskall rose around 1%.Seagate Technology, andAdvanced Micro Deviceswere up 2% and more than 1%, respectively. TheVanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH)added nearly 1%, whileCoreWeavegained more than 2%.

TheS&P 500climbed 0.4% in regular trading on Monday, while theNasdaq Compositeadvanced more than 1%.Nvidiaadded 1.4%, andTeslajumped 3.8%.Alphabetshares advanced about 1%. That marked a rebound from last week's rout, which spilled over into the broader market, as concerns grew around companies borrowing too much money for their AI build-outs.

"Improving moods regarding the prospects of modern technology have Wall Street breathing a sigh of relief as participants drop hedges, after the cost of volatility protection soared intraday on Friday, ahead of the intensifying selloff," wrote Jose Torres, senior economist at Interactive Brokers.

3Mshares popped more than 5% after the producer of industrial and safety products posted adjusted earnings of $2.50 per share, more than the LSEG estimate of $2.38 per share.

Shares ofGE Aerospacewere off 2% after the company reported its third-quarter financials, where the company delivered an earnings and revenue beat.

GE Aerospace reported adjusted earnings of $2.25 per share, compared to analysts polled by LSEG's estimates for $2.01 per share. Revenue also came in above expectations at $13.29 billion.

The company also hiked guidance across various metrics for the full-year, however free cash flow at $2.04 billion was lower than expectations for $2.2 billion, according to StreetAccount.

The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite began Tuesday's session in the red.

The broad market index fell 0.2% just after 9:30 a.m. ET, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq pulled back 0.4%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average traded around the flatline.

Investor concerns overCoreWeave's credit ticked higher on Tuesday, with the spread on its five-year credit default swap rising back up near levelsseen on Thursday.

The CDS, which is a way for buyers to pay for protection in case the borrower defaults, last saw spreads over 1,121, which is up 2.22% for the day and more than 17% over the past week. Spreads of 1,000 or greater are generally considered a sign of distress.

Housing startsslumped in September, raising fresh concerns about the state of the real estate market as the Federal Reserve contemplates additional interest rate hikes.

The Commerce Department reported Tuesday that privately owned starts totaled 1.22 million at a seasonally adjusted annualized rate. That was off 5.2% from the August level and well below the Dow Jones consensus for 1.3 million.

Additionally, single-family starts weakened, totaling 859,000, off 4.6% from the prior month.

Building permits issued during the month were slightly better than expected, totaling a seasonally adjusted annualized 1.4 million, against the estimate for 1.39 million. The total was 0.2% below August.

Check out the companies making headlines before the bell:

General Motors beat Wall Street's expectations on the top- and bottom-lines as it reported its Q3 2026 earnings, delivering strong results driven by high truck sales and growing subscription revenue

The company raised its free cash flow expectations and narrowed its 2026 full-year guidance.

The Detroit automaker alsoannounced a new multiyear stock buybackof $20 billion, but didn't provide a specific timeframe for the repurchase.

"GM is performing well, and we are working hard to continue our momentum despite growing inflationary pressures through strategic investments in new products and services, and through improved quality and operating efficiency," GM CEOMary Barrasaid Tuesday in a letter to shareholders.

GM expects commodity inflation costs to be nearly $2 billion, which was the high end of its previous guidance. The automaker also said thecosts of its pullback in all-electric vehiclesannounced last year were "substantially completed."

GM stock was off roughly 7% during premarket trading despite the beats.

Shares ofSolstice Advanced Materials, which was spun off from Honeywell last year, rose more than 3% after The Financial Times reported, citing sources, that activist Starboard Value had built a stake in the company.

Starboard wants Solstice to cut about $100 million in corporate costs focus on its refrigerants and nuclear businesses,the report said. Solstice shares are up more than 24% year to date.

The company earned $7.89 per barrel, beating an LSEG estimate of $7.18 per share. However, revenue of $11.12 billion was just below the $11.14 billion consensus.

ABBCEO Morten Wierod told CNBC he sees no slowdown in the AI data center buildout in the coming years, despiteinvestors becoming wary of ballooning AI spend.

The Swiss multinational firm declined around 6% on Tuesday, even after reportingrecord third-quarter orders, which jumped 40% to $12 billion, driven by a triple-digit increase in its data center segment.

"ABB without data centers, it is a double-digit growth when you look at the order intake," Wierod told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe."

"I believe there is a strong trend...you will see a continued build-out of the data center capacity in the coming years," Wierod added.

Other data center stocks were also down Tuesday.Schneider ElectricandSiemens Energyfell 3% and 4%, respectively. Meanwhile, neocloud companiesCoreweaveandNebiuswere both down around 3% in premarket trading.

Asia-Pacific markets closed in the red on Tuesday, with South Korean equities leading the losses.

Chip stocks fell, withASMLdown 2.5%,ASMIdown 3.3% andBE Semiconductordown 3.6%.
