title: What options traders expect from SpaceX earnings after the bell
content:
It's been a busy three months forSpaceX.

The company delivered four astronauts to the International Space Station in record time, expanded its mobile network spectrum, is reportedly eyeing a $40 billion debt deal to buy Nvidia chips, and CEO Elon Musk said he plans to give shares to every kid in America next year.

Traders think all that means more gains for the stock after it reports earnings after the bell Tuesday.

Options market-makers are pricing about a 6% swing for SpaceX after the event, according to Cboe LiveVol data. That's less than half the 13% it erased after its inaugural report in August, a selloff that turned out to be the low for the shares, which rallied 60% the following two months before reversing before dropping as much as 19% the past two weeks.

While there are about as many open call contracts as puts on the stock, daily trading volume has leaned toward calls the past week, Barchart data shows.

Among the 1.1 million contracts traded Monday – 20% higher volume than the 30-day average – 665,000 were calls, with more bought than sold, according to Cboe LiveVol. Traders also bought more calls than puts, and sold more puts than they bought, the data show, decidedly bullish flow as the space giant heads into its second earnings.

The most popular call contract for Friday expiry was the 170-strike, which needs about a 14% rally, according to SpotGamma data. There was also notable buying in the 190-strike call for month-end, a 40-cent contract that needs SpaceX to rally 29% to break even.

For that to happen, SpaceX will have to rally through two more share lockup periods: a scheduled release two days after earnings, as well as another on October 26 that together will amount to over 1.6 billion eligible shares for sale. So far that hasn't been a problem for the stock, as releases on Sep. 9, 10, and 24 had no discernible effect on the share price.

Implied volatility is much lower in SpaceX going into this report compared to last quarter, as reflected in the implied move. SpaceX traded with an IV of 62 on Monday, compared to above 110 before releasing second-quarter earnings, according to ThinkOrSwim.

title: Former OpenAI exec has quietly built $1.5 billion startup, betting AI can revive U.S. manufacturing
content:
OpenAI'sformer research chief has been quietly building a startup that aims to bring manufacturing back to the U.S. using AI.

Bob McGrew's newest company, Arda, has raised $230 million at a $1.5 billion valuation, the company told CNBC in an exclusive interview Tuesday. The round was led by Altimeter Capital, Accel and Khosla Ventures.

Arda makes AI software to help automate manufacturing. McGrew, who was alsoPalantir'sproduct and engineering lead for over a decade, said Arda's AI models have already been deployed with military tech company Anduril.

"It's a user interface and an agent that does for manufacturing engineers what Claude or Cursor does for programmers," McGrew told CNBC. He pointed to the "human-intensive" nature of manufacturing, and the time it can take to adapt production to a new design for a weapon or drone.

"When a design changes, you can retrain a human in a day — but it takes three to six months in order to change the automation to reflect the new design," McGrew said. "We've built a software and AI product that basically allows manufacturing engineers to build assembly lines much faster."

McGrew joined OpenAI in 2017 and worked on the reasoning capabilities of early models before the launch of ChatGPT. He left during a 2024 wave of other high-profile exits, including chief technology officer Mira Murati and co-founder and chief scientist Ilya Sutskever.

"OpenAI is an amazing place," McGrew said. He said he remembers being in rooms with CEOSam Altman, Dario Amodei, who left to startAnthropic, and Sutskever, "talking about what it would look like when a model could write your email for you."

McGrew stayed through the famous weekend in November 2023 when Altman was abruptly fired and then rehired. McGrew said he wanted to stay to ship OpenAI's reasoning product, which he called the "last key breakthrough left before AGI," or artificial general intelligence.

"I said, if I could just ship that, I'd be happy with my career at OpenAI, and I'd be ready to move on to something else," he said.

McGrew, who hasn't spoken publicly about Arda until this week, said the company is using a combination of its own proprietary models, open-source models and some frontier models to run the software. Arda's other co-founders include Augustus Odena, who helped start Adept and previously worked atGoogleandMeta, and former Palantir engineers Alex Mark and Jakob Frick.

Altimeter's Apoorv Agrawal led the recent funding round. He met McGrew when they both worked at Palantir. Manufacturing largely happens overseas, Agrawal said, but there's a market for bringing it back.

"Manufacturing globally is a $16 trillion industry. In the U.S. alone, it's $3 trillion," Agrawal said. "We think that Arda, and the vision that they've outlined, will continue to capture a significant portion of that. Yes, the price is steep today, but the long-term opportunity is very high."

McGrew said robotics is next on the product roadmap, and automating factories could help bring more manufacturing — and more jobs — to the U.S.

"If your design changes very frequently, the only place you can really build your product is in East Asia, because you need an army of human workers who can be retrained quickly, and you can't wait for automation to catch up," he said.

McGrew also highlighted the economic opportunity as the Trump administration looks to onshore manufacturing.

"No one has ever successfully built a smartphone in the U.S.," he said. "Never successfully assembled one, and so if you can build a smartphone in the U.S. that is not taking away American jobs. That is bringing American jobs."

title: U.S. oil surges to top $110, Brent crude at five-month high amid Mideast tensions
content:
Oil prices climbed on Tuesday as investors continued to monitor simmering tensions in the Middle East and U.S. front-month futures contracts neared expiry.

Front-month U.S.West Texas Intermediate crude oil futuresjumped 6.58% by 7:38 a.m. ET, trading at around $110.48 per barrel. The contracts expire on Tuesday.

WTI crude futures for November delivery have been on a tear this month, with Tuesday's moves putting the contracts on track for their ninth consecutive session of gains and a monthly rise of almost 20%.

Global benchmarkBrent crude futuresfor December delivery were last seen trading 1.94% higher at $111.67 per barrel — their highest price since May.

Developments in the Middle East remain in focus, with attacks on commercial ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz escalating in recent weeks. At least 18 vessels have come under fire over the past two weeks,according toship tracker Kpler.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps said Tuesday that two "non-compliant" oil tankers had been set ablaze in the strait after hitting mines laid by its naval unit, Iranian state-affiliated news agency Tasnim reported.

Meanwhile, Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said at a weekly news conference on Tuesday that Tehran would respond to any American strike "in equal measure, if not more forcefully," according to Tasnim.

U.S. President Donald Trumpsaidearlier this month that American forces will not attack Iran before the midterm elections on Nov. 3.

Tamas Varga, analyst at PVM Oil Associates, told CNBC in an email on Tuesday that front-end WTI strength ahead of the contract expiry is a sign of tightness in the global crude oil market.

"It is a reflection of falling export volumes from the Middle East as tanker attacks and Houthi strikes on Saudi oil infrastructure intensify," he said. "Secondly, the U.S.decisionto exempt Russian shadow fleet from sanctions will push freight rates possibly lower, which was a prohibitive factor to increase demand for U.S.-sourced crude."

"With this hurdle removed, at least temporary, U.S. crude oil grades are back in play as replacements of Mideast crude oil," he added. "Thirdly, U.S. commercial oil stocks are expected to have declined last week."

title: General Motors beats Wall Street's Q3 earnings expectations, narrows full-year guidance
content:
DETROIT —General Motorsnarrowed its 2026 earnings guidance and raised its free cash flow expectations after beating Wall Street's third-quarter expectations.

The Detroit automaker also announced a new multiyear stock buyback of $20 billion after GM completed a $6 billionshare repurchase programthat was announced in January. GM did not disclose a specific time to complete the program.

Here's how GM performed in the third quarter, compared with average estimates compiled by LSEG:

The new guidance includes adjusted earnings before interest and taxes of between $14.5 billion and $15.5 billion, or $12.75 to $13.75 adjusted earnings per share, and adjusted automotive free cash flow of between $11.5 billion and $12.5 billion.

That compares with its raised guidance from July that included adjusted EBIT of between $14 billion and $16 billion, or $12 to $14 adjusted EPS, and adjusted automotive free cash flow of $9.5 billion to $11.5 billion.

"I think the market's been pretty consistent from what we've said all year," GM CFO Paul Jacobson told CNBC'sPhil LeBeau. "Our fourth quarter's going to be down sequentially. ... I think the fact that we're able to hold our guidance in the face of that late inflationary pressure in the year is another sign of the GM team executing really well."

GM stock was off roughly 5% during premarket trading despite the earnings beats.

Wall Street analysts were mixed before the report on whether GM would raise its guidance Tuesday amid concerns of slowing sales and rising commodity costs.

GM on Tuesday said it expects commodity inflation costs to be around $2 billion, which was the high end of its previous guidance. That includes higher costs for logistics and dynamic random-access memory, or DRAM, chipsthat are impacting multiple industries.

While the inflationary costs were at the automaker's high end of guidance, GM said its gross tariff costs are expected to be at the low end of its expected $2.5 billion to $3.5 billion range. Warranty costs are expected to be at high end between $1 billion and $1.5 billion, GM said.

Jacobson said vehicle pricing is relatively flat as inflationary costs continue to increase. He said the company would assess where consumers are in the coming year when deciding if it should pass costs along by raising prices more than normal.

"GM is performing well, and we are working hard to continue our momentum despite growing inflationary pressures through strategic investments in new products and services, and through improved quality and operating efficiency," GM CEOMary Barrasaid Tuesday in a letter to shareholders.

The automaker also said thecosts of its pullback in all-electric vehiclesannounced last year were "substantially completed," saying it has recorded $11.2 billion in such charges since the second half of last year, including paying $4.6 billion of $7.4 billion in cash through the third quarter.

The company's net income attributed to stockholders was $3.3 billion during the third quarter, up roughly $2 billion from a year earlier.

GM's North American operations continued to lead the automaker's results, accounting for $3.6 billion of its $4.1 billion in adjusted EBIT results during the third quarter.

GM's 2025 third-quarter results included $48.59 billion in revenue, net income attributable to stockholders of $1.3 billion and earnings per share of $2.80 adjusted.

title: Zelenskyy to meet with U.S. envoy as tensions with Trump mount
content:
Ukrainian PresidentVolodymyr Zelenskyyis set to meet with U.S. special envoys on Tuesday after U.S. PresidentDonald Trumpaimed a fresh spate of criticism at the wartime leader.

Zelenskyy will arrive in Norway on Tuesdayand meet with the country's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr and President of Finland Alexander Stubb in Oslo later in the day. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will also take part in the discussions.

The meetings come as tensions mount between Zelenskyy and Trump, while the U.S. has recently eased some pressure on Russia, which invaded Ukraine in 2022.

Ukraine requested that Witkoff and Kushner join the meeting in Oslo, Norway, Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said in a statement.

"Diplomatic efforts have previously taken place in several countries, and Norway and Finland are pleased to be able to continue this work. The aim is to put diplomatic efforts on a more constructive path," he said.

Trump responded to criticism on Monday that he waived sanctions against Russia recently and is on the"wrong side" of history.

"Zelenskyy doesn't know what he's talking about,"Trump said to reportersoutside the White House. "Zelenskyy is a man that should have had this war settled a long time ago."

"I think it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine," Trump said, echoing previous calls for a "new president" in Kyiv. "If he would have listened to me, he would have made a much better deal a long time ago, and he'd have a million people living from his side."

Trump also said he would meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping to figure out how to end the Ukraine war, whichreportedlycould exclude Zelenskyy. "Anything I can do to end the war, whether somebody's there or not," Trump said.

Last week, Zelenskyy hit out at the U.S. government over restrictions on access to satellite services offered bySpaceX's military satellite system, Starshield, which is critical to Ukraine's defense against Russian strikes.

"No explanation for either of these issues has been provided to Ukraine by the American side," Zelenskyy said on Monday.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk had shifted the blame to the U.S. government and Trump, who he said are"ultimately" responsiblefor any slowdowns. Secretary of State Marco Rubiodeniedthat the U.S. is responsible, and Treasury Secretary ScottBessent told Zelenskyyto be "very careful about making statements like this that aren't true."

Trump said Monday that he doesn't know who restricted the Starlink service in Ukraine, "but I'd like to find out."

— CNBC's Kevin Breuninger has contributed to this report.

title: France curfews calm unrest as Macron faces criticism over Gulf trip
content:
Curfews contributed to a "calm" night across France, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said Tuesday, even as public discontent remained high following the weekend'smass protests, looting and violent scenes.

Certain areas of several French cities were under curfew overnight, including Place de la République and Les Halles in Paris, and parts of central Lyon. Lille and Nice were among the cities to impose curfews for minors.

The unrest comes at a particularly fragile moment for France, where public anger over living costs and deteriorating services is colliding with political instability and afiscal crisisthatthreatens to turn into a debt crisisas government borrowing costs rise to the highest level in decades.

The country faces a divided parliament with no majority and presidential elections in April 2027.

In a statement on Tuesday, Lecornu said local officials would impose new curfews where required.

Meanwhile, criticism is mounting over President Emmanuel Macron's decision to embark on a three-day tour of the Middle East as France suffers its most severe riots in many years.

Riots followed weeks of demonstrations over the country'seducation system, the cost of living and other issues.

While hundreds of thousands of people marched peacefully, pockets of violence erupted, shocking the country, as protesters smashed shopfronts and set Limoges Town Hall on fire.

Political commentator Christophe Barbier on radio station RTL said on Monday there was "no longer a pilot in the plane." At the same time, newspaper La Dépêche du Midi wrote in ascathing editorialthat Macron had "to see if the misery of a reviled president is less painful in the Persian Gulf sun" as France "sinks deeper into crisis."

Macron said on Sunday he was looking to address high fuel prices and secure French energy supplies through the trip to Kuwait, the UAE, Bahrain and Qatar, while strengthening defense and security cooperation.

There is also public anger over claims that police lost control of the situation at the weekend as disorder and looting escalated. Police were earlier this month accused of excessive force in their response to student protests, after a 15-year-old ​boy's hand was blown off by a stun grenade.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez' offered to quit his post on Monday afterclaiming responsibilityfor what unfolded. Macron declined his resignation, saying immediate leadership of law enforcement was needed.

"The lack of enforcement means that more than 3,000 shops have been sacked, and for the economy today we awake with a feeling that the state cannot do the basic duty that it is supposed to do, and this is now creating somehow lack of trust," Fabrice Le Saché, vice president of business group MEDEF, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Tuesday.

"This is dangerous because we have been used to... riots in our country — remember the Yellow Vests and other movements — but this one has passed, I think, the level of the previous ones, and we cannot continue to keep going with that same type of situation every time we have social unrest," Le Saché said.

French businesses have one of the highest tax burdens in the euro area but now feel they cannot receive basic security in return, he added.

Lecornu said Monday that a support fund would be established for damaged or looted businesses, and that the government would talk with insurers to speed up assessments.

"The scale of the damage suggests this weekend's riots could ultimately prove more costly than the unrest that followed the death of Nahel Merzouk in 2023," which generated around 1 billion euros ($1.12 billion) in insured losses, Jess Middleton, senior Europe analyst at risk intelligence firm Verisk Maplecroft, said by email.

"Further violence is not inevitable, but protests linked to the underlying grievances, including cost-of-living pressures and discontent over public services and education, are likely to persist, putting continued pressure on the government to demonstrate that it can maintain order," Middleton said.

French markets came under pressure on Monday after the weekend scenes, with bonds, stocks and the euro all selling off, amid growing skepticism about the country's ability to bring down its deficit to a sustainable level.

Fierce debate is underway over the 2027 budget, with the government targeting an overall decline in the deficit to 5% of GDP from 5.4%.

title: Walmart launches joint membership with Sam's Club as it leans into delivery, gas discounts
content:
Walmarton Tuesday announced a new joint membership combining its namesake chain and its subsidiary Sam's Club, as the retailer leans further into convenience and value to win over cash-strapped shoppers.

The membership, which combines Walmart+ and Sam's Club Plus, will cost $120 per year, according to the company. That price is nearly $100 less than buying individual annual memberships to each retailer, though there is no monthly payment option for the new deal. Both stores will continue to offer standalone options.

"We're giving people a reason to expect more from their memberships," Walmart CEO John Furner said in a statement. "For $120 a year, we're raising expectations for what a membership can deliver: more money in their pockets and more time to call their own."

The membership gives customers access to Sam's Club warehouses, free delivery from both chains, a subscription to Peacock or Paramount+ streaming services, gas savings and 2% Sam's Club cash on eligible purchases. Customers who already have accounts at both stores can link their accounts to receive the discount.

While Walmart's customers often shop for routine, everyday essentials, Sam's Club warehouses offer more opportunity to stock up on bulk purchases. A joint membership could allow the store models to complement one another, according to the company.

The announcement comes as Walmart bets on convenience to drive sales, especially as consumer wallets are squeezed by high gas and food prices.

In August, as Walmart reported fiscal second-quarter earnings, the companyraised its outlookfor the year, with Chief Financial Officer John David Rainey telling CNBC that consumer spending remained strong despite higher fuel prices. Even so, its stock fell at the time as its sales outlook disappointed Wall Street.

Rainey said in August that the company was lowering prices across various categories, including beef, adding that it's well positioned to weather economic uncertainty because of its emphasis on value and its scale.

Meanwhile, Sam's Club saw a 26% increase in e-commerce sales in the fiscal second quarter, driven by increased transactions and membership growth. The retailer, which also operates its own gas stations,reportednet sales of $25.7 billion, including fuel, during that period.

The membership business — which is part of Walmart's push to grow sales with higher profit margins — is already strong. Walmart reported a 17% increase globally in revenue from its membership in the fiscal second quarter with Walmart+ net adds notching a record second-quarter high. For Sam's Club, that revenue number grew 6%.

Walmart added Tuesday that employees at both stores will also receive joint memberships as part of their benefits.

The company said any costs related to the changes in the membership program are not expected to materially impact the company's fiscal third-quarter or full-year guidance.

title: Burnham vows end to 'rip-off parking charges' under new rules
content: Image source,Getty ImagesByFaarea MasudBusiness reporterPublished19 October 2026Updated 2 hours agoDrivers will be given the right to challenge "rip-off" private parking charges and more grace when using private providers under new rules set out by Andy Burnham.The prime minister announced the changes after concerns were raised that penalties issued by private providers were too harsh and left motorists unfairly punished.The new rules include a cancellation of charges for honest mistakes such as stopping to check directions and for non-payment due to broken ticket machines. Drivers will also get a 10-minute window to leave a car park without facing a penalty.Motoring groups welcomed the changes, but said more needed to be done to stop charges when the driver had done nothing wrong.Private car parks are different to council-owned car parks and streets, but more tickets at private sites are now being issued than ever recorded.According to RAC analysis of government data, some 17 million private parking tickets were issued in 2025-26, a 17% increase from a year earlier.With each charge worth up to Â£100, the data suggests drivers could collectively face private parking charges worth more than Â£4.6m each day.In one case, a woman was taken to court in a Â£1,906 claim after taking longer thanfive minutes to pay at a car park in Derby. The charge waseventually dropped."Being a few minutes late back to your car or typing one digit of your number plate wrong shouldn't end with a hefty fine landing on your doormat," said Burnham.He added that such charges left "people feeling ripped off and out of pocket".The new rules will give drivers:A guaranteed five-minute period to decide whether to parkA 10-minute window to leave without facing a penaltyCancellation of charges for issues drivers can't control, such as vehicle breakdowns in car parksCancellation of charges for honest mistakes such as stopping to check directions, as well as for medical emergencies or broken ticket machinesMaximum charges of Â£20 on appeal for slip-ups such as forgetting a parking permit, entering the wrong vehicle registration, or forgetting to confirm the registration in the machine when parkingA freeze on the maximum parking charge at Â£100, which is the same limit as the current private parking Code of PracticeThe new code will apply in England, Scotland and Wales.Operators who do not comply risk losing access to DVLA data, making it more difficult to pursue the car's owner even if they do issue a charge.'I got fined Â£11k over a five-minute parking rule'Published1 August 2024Firm told to pay Â£10,240 in five-minute parking rowPublished5 April 2025'Increase trust'The government's Private Parking Code of Practice has been seven years in the making.In 2019, an act of Parliament was passed to create a code but the code was withdrawn in 2022, due to "resistance from the private parking industry", according to the RAC.The current industry Code of Practice, created by the British Parking Association and the International Parking Community, was introduced in 2024 andupdated last year after a review.Angela Rayner, the Communities and Housing Secretary, told BBC Breakfast that parking "shouldn't be a way of making money".Asked if the changes were an admission that motorists have been "ripped off" by parking companies for years, she said: "We're calling time on it. They have regulated themselves and they have their appeals process but we're giving it more meat now."She said the current level of fine was a "proportionate response to when people don't follow the rules".Derek Millard-Smith from the British Parking Association said the group welcomed the changes as it would "increase trust" and said "detterents work" when it came to questions over the cost of fines."We know dog fouling, rail fare dodging, littering - all those levels are around Â£100 or more because that is a level that is deemed sufficient to change behaviours."'Work to do'Both the AA and the RAC said the new code was a good first step but did not go far enough.The AA said some drivers pay up even if they have done nothing wrong, just to avoid the hassle and over fears of legal action being taken against them."There is still a huge amount of work to do, such as tackling the scourge of debt recovery fees," added Jack Cousens, head of roads policy at the AA."Ultimately, we need to stop charges being issued in the first place, especially where the driver has done nothing wrong."The RAC's head of policy, Simon Williams, called for the banning of debt recovery fees and said the current industry-run appeals bodies should be replaced by a single independent one.The government said it would be consulting on the issue of debt recovery fees, as well as other recommendations from the Competition and Markets Authority.Get in touchHave you been affected by the issues raised in this story?Contact formRelated topicsMotoringParkingMore on this storyParking rules to change after 'five-minute fines'Published12 February 2025Parking fee rises could 'desecrate' high streetsPublished4 days ago

title: Alberta votes to remain part of Canada
content:
Alberta residents voted to remain part of Canada in the province's first-ever referendum ‌on separation, in a much-needed win for Prime Minister Mark Carney as he attempts to unify the country amid a trade war with the US.

CBC News, Canada's government-funded national broadcaster, called the result late Monday after 33% of the vote had been counted. At the time of the call, 76% of tallied votes were in support of the "remain" side ​versus 23% in favor of the province moving forward with a binding vote on separation. The referendum was nonbinding.

"Albertans made a clear ​choice," Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement. "They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of ⁠each other."

"Canada is greater than the sum of its parts," he said.

Pollsters and analysts had repeatedly dismissed the possibility of a separatist victory, citing ​data that showed about one-third of residents in the western province supported a future referendum on leaving.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced the referendum in May, ​saying it was "time to have a vote, understand the will of Albertans on this subject, and move on."

Late Monday, Smith issued a statement on social media saying she was "very pleased" that early results show widespread support for remaining in Canada. She said she would address Albertans on Tuesday to discuss the results and "where our province goes ​from here."

A small but vocal group of separatists has campaigned for months for an independent Alberta, arguing that the province's energy wealth is ​subsidizing poorer parts of Canada and that Alberta would be far richer without Ottawa bureaucracy impeding its path.

Last week, Carney told a rally in Calgary that voting ‌to leave ⁠Canada would be "a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep division," and appealed to Albertans to "vote like Canada depends on it."

Carney, who grew up mostly in Alberta, acknowledged that Albertans have often felt slighted by Ottawa and said his government had approved a proposed new pipeline, adding that Alberta is critical to helping Canada reduce its dependence on the US.

Alberta's referendum follows two previous referendums on separation in the majority French-speaking province of ​Quebec. Quebecers voted to stay in ​Canada in both instances.

First ⁠Nations groups have also objected to the idea of an independent Alberta, as their land treaties with Ottawa predate the province's creation within Canada.

CBC News reported strong turnout from First Nations. One southern Alberta polling station in an ​area that is home to the Siksika Nation temporarily ran out of ballots, and then stayed open until ​after 10 p.m. ⁠MT (0400 GMT) to ensure everyone in line had the chance to vote.

Still, Monday's referendum is unlikely to end the separatist movement in Alberta. Before the referendum, some separatist leaders said they would continue to pursue another vote even if most Albertans voted to remain.

According to data released on October 16 by ⁠the pollster ​Angus Reid, 62% of Albertans believe "there will never be an end to the separatist movement" ​in the province.

Alberta's referendum also included nine other nonbinding questions on topics including immigration, access to provincial services — such as education, social care and healthcare — and voter identification requirements. Results for ​those questions were still trickling in.

title: What’s making Europe so angry? The frustration behind the protests
content:
Anger over the cost of living and pressure on public services has broughthundreds of thousandsof protesters onto streets across several European countries, with grievances ranging from expensive housing to poor conditions in schools and universities.

France saw the largest demonstrations at the weekend, withmore than 500,000 peoplemarching. Most protested peacefully, but some looted and vandalized shops, set fire to city halls and attacked police officers.

Separate protests also took place in Italy, Spain, Portugal and Albania on Saturday and Sunday. Their immediate triggers differed, although high fuel and energy costs formed part of the backdrop in several countries. The wars in Iran and Ukraine have pushed diesel prices sharply higher across the continent.

There's no one "single trigger" for the riots, Capital Economics' Chief Europe Economist Andrew Kenningham told CNBC. The increase in energy costs may be playing a role, but the increase is smaller than in 2022, at the onset of the Russia-Ukraine war, when there were no comparable violent protests, he added.

Nevertheless, the demonstrations pose a shared challenge for governments: how to improve living conditions and maintain public services while supporting households and keeping strained public finances in check.

The demonstrations in France began last month when high school students criticized poor schooling conditions, including shoddy facilities and teacher shortages. They have since evolved into broader protests over living standards and declining public services.

In Spain,housing protestsbegan in September after an 87-year-old woman, Maricarmen Abascal, was evicted following a 230% rent increase by an investment fund. She died a fortnight later.

Thousands of protesters alsotook to the streets in Portugalon Saturday to demonstrate against soaring housing costs and the cost of living.

"People obviously are protesting on the cost of living with diesel and fuel prices, but mainly on housing costs, which have been increasing substantially all over Europe, but also particularly in Portugal," Miranda Sarmento, Portugal's minister of state and finance, said Monday.

In Albania, protesters were angry about poor university conditions and high tuition fees, and called for the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama. Some threw Molotov cocktails and other objects at the police and set fire to cars and litter bins.

In Italy, a march in central Milan on Saturday over living costs also ended violently, with rioters attacking the police with stones and paving blocks and setting fire to barricades.

"The underlying problem is that politicians are not able to offer hope of a better life for many Europeans because the economy is growing only slowly and governments have built up huge debts, leaving them little scope to support higher public spending or to cut taxes," Capital Economics' Kenningham said.

The escalation of violence in France in particular is due to a "conjugation of different elements," said Douglas Yates, a professor at the American Graduate School in Paris.

"This was a storm that turned into a hurricane," Yates told CNBC's Steve Sedgwick. "There was this inflation, which has brought out the cost-of-living protesters who would have been disgruntled at any rate."

Yates said another factor is France's 2027 presidential election, as opposition parties seek to capitalize on growing public discontent with PresidentEmmanuel Macron.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has proposed a 2027 budget aimed at narrowingFrance's deficit, projected at 5.4% of gross domestic product this year. Measures include freezing the civil service pay index and tightening reimbursement for sick leave.

"Finally there's the students, the poor students who started this by making reasonable demands for having their dilapidated infrastructure repaired and perhaps getting some air conditioners installed in the classrooms, and so these three forces have come together and created an out-of-control hurricane," Yates added.

The economic backdrop has also deteriorated. In the second quarter of 2026, France's unemployment rate rose to 8.3%, representing 2.7 million people, according toInsee, the national statistics bureau. The unemployment rate among 15- to 24-year-olds climbed to 21.6%.

Consumer prices rose 3.1% in September from a year earlier, up from 2.4% in August, according to final Insee data. Energy prices jumped 21.3%. Meanwhile, purchasing power per consumption unit is projected to fall 0.7% in 2026, according to Insee figures, cited byLe Monde.

Calculations by the French Institute of Economics for Le Monde estimate that the decline in purchasing power since 2024 is equivalent to a loss of 1,200 euros ($1,345) a year for a household with two adults and two children, and 600 euros for a single adult.

Portugal's Sarmento said that the situation across Europe varies, with Portugal in a stronger fiscal position and with much less debt than France.

"Those countries [those with higher public debt] have much less fiscal margin to act, but the main issue is that we need to resolve the problem of productivity and competitiveness at the European level," he said.

"The European economy is not growing as much as the U.S., and without economic growth, it's impossible to have better salaries and to have the resources for better public services and social support," Sarmento added.

In the second quarter of 2026, Portugal recorded the EU's highest annual increase in house prices, up 16.5% from a year earlier, according toEurostat.

The Portuguese government is looking to increase the supply of housing to reduce buying and renting costs to resolve the issue, according to Sarmento.

Frenchgovernment bond yields rose and the euro weakenedon Monday as the unrest added to investor concerns over France's debt and budget.

"It will be difficult to see the budget deficit come down without painful measures," Sharon Bell, senior European equity strategist at Goldman Sachs, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Monday.

"Taxes could well go up for French businesses. I think taxes may generally go up in France. Fiscal consolidation means you need to either spend less or tax more. Those things are very tricky."

Mike Bell, head of market strategy at RBC BlueBay Asset Management, said France faced a "very real risk" of a sovereign debt crisis.

"What's needed in France is to get the fiscal position in order; they need to raise the retirement age — you can't retire at 62 if the average person's living to 84 — but if this is going on even before they start talking about that, then imagine what would happen on the streets of France if you tried to raise the retirement age... I mean, here in the U.K. it's 68," Bell added.

title: Brent crude holds near five-month high on Middle East tension
content:
Oil prices advanced on Tuesday, with Brent hovering around a five-month high as traders priced in a geopolitical risk premium from Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure and reports of vessel attacks in the Gulf.

Brent crude futuresclimbed 55 cents, or 0.50%, to $110.10 a barrel by 0319 GMT, after rising as high as $110.70 a barrel in the previous session to their highest since May 20.

TheUS West Texas Intermediate crude(WTI) contract for November delivery, set to expire on Tuesday, was up 0.24% to $103.91. The more-active December contract rose 39 cents, or 0.40%, to $98.93.

"Oil prices remain well-supported ... This suggests the market is pricing in a significant risk premium, given the situation's volatility," ING analysts said in a note on Tuesday.

"However, if flows continue uninhibited despite the geopolitical environment, the risk premium would likely erode slowly. Clearly, there are no signs of this yet."

At least 18 vessels were reportedly attacked over two weeks, which keeps the risk premium intact, shiptracker Kpler said in a note on Monday.

Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Monday they launched several attacks on Saudi energy, airport and military targets, such as an Aramco site in Yanbu, the Shaybah oilfield, Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and Abha airport.

Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the claims and Reuters could not independently verify them.

Also on Monday, a Houthi attack on a training camp for government security forces in Yemen's Shabwa province killed 58 people with more than 200 injured.

The renewed attacks heightened fears about regional stability and underscored continuing risks to energy supply from the region, keeping oil prices above $100 a barrel.

In the US, crude oil stockpiles were expected to have fallen last week along with product inventories, a preliminary Reuters poll showed on Monday.

Friday's executive order by President Donald Trump waived key Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs, including goods duties and penalties for purchases of its energy.

However, Trump said on Saturday he had yet to announce a final decision on the matter, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio said officials wanted more time to evaluate the situation.

Russia's crude oil production increased by 65,000 barrels per day in September to 8.43 million bpd, but remained about 870,000 bpd below that of a year ago, the International Energy Agency said last week.

"While the prospect of additional Russian diesel supply offers some theoretical relief, traders appear far more focused on the ongoing risk of further damage to energy infrastructure across the Gulf region," said Tim Waterer, KCM Trade chief analyst.

title: Chancellor rejects calls to raise Capital Gains Tax in Budget, sources say
content: Image source,AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption,Chancellor John Healey says he wants to avoid an investor exodus from the UKByNick Eardley & Harry Farley,ÂPolitical correspondentsÂandÂHarry SekulichPublished20 October 2026, 02:31 BSTUpdated 8 minutes agoChancellor John Healey has dismissed calls from some Labour MPs to increase Capital Gains Tax (CGT), according to Treasury sources.Cabinet ministers Wes Streeting and Louise Haigh both previously voiced support for raising CGT before Andy Burnham became prime minister in July.Ahead of next week's Budget, as first reported by theTimes,external, Healey is minded not to increase CGT - which is imposed on the profit people make when they sell an asset that has increased in value, such as shares in a company or properties which are not primary residences.The move followed warnings that it could end up costing the government money if wealthy people leave the country or defer selling off assets.If you pay income tax at the basic rate then CGT is charged at 18%. For higher and additional rate income tax payers, the CGT rate is 24%.The chancellor gave an indication of his approach last month in a speech when he spoke about the importance of businesses and self-employed people making profits."I want to see this country as a country of wealth creation. I want our government decisions and policies to raise the levels of confidence, and investment, and profit in British business," Healey said.Burnham has faced warnings against lifting CGT. His former adviser and Goldman Sachs Chief Economist Lord Jim O'Neill suggested it would send "the wrong message to business".But influential Labour figures had pushed for equalising CGT and income tax, with the former generally attracting a lower tax rate.Louise Haigh, a key ally of the prime minister, had suggested capital gains should go up to be closer to income tax, before she became Burnham's first secretary of state.Defence secretary Wes Streeting called for a "wealth tax that works" in May, shortly after resigning as a minister in former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's government.Healey already ruled out levelling the two tax rates,according to the Financial Times,external.It comes after senior banking executivestold the BBCthey expect Healey to raise taxes on the sector. UK banks have been reporting bumper profits, leading to calls from unions for higher taxes.In a pre-Budget speech on Tuesday, Tory leader Kemi Badenoch is expected to urge the government to drop its spending plans and reduce its borrowing.Related topicsJohn HealeyLabour PartyTaxMore on this storyWhat is the Budget and what could be in it?Published21 hours agoWes Streeting pledges 'wealth tax that works'Published21 MayBanks expect to be hit with higher taxes in BudgetPublished3 days ago

title: Copper is outshining gold this year. Investors say the rally can survive an AI correction
content:
Copper is becoming increasingly strategic to governments and industries as artificial intelligence, power-grid investment and defense spending increase demand for the industrial metal, investors say.

The metal — a key component in electronics, construction and transportation, and often seen as a barometer of economic activity — has outperformed gold this year, as the need to secure reliable supplies has intensified.

Copper has rallied 15.8% year-to-date, and is up more than 30% over the past 12 months. By comparison,gold futureshave slipped 4.11% year-to-date, and are down 4.52% over the past 12 months.Spot goldis 4.89% lower over the past 12 months, and 4% down year-to-date.

Speaking to CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe," Ivanhoe Electric CEO Taylor Melvin said countries, regions and industries are increasingly focused on securing access to metals for national security, economic growth and technology infrastructure. Melvin said that shift has helped support copper prices.

"It's certainly a good time to be in copper mining globally, and specifically in the United States," said Melvin, whose Arizona-based mining and exploration company focuses on copper, gold, silver, nickel and cobalt.

"We're really in a world right now where the metals that we used to refer to, and still do, as critical metals are really becoming strategic metals, in every sense of the word," said Melvin, who spoke as LME Week, the annual gathering of the global metals industry, began in London on Monday.

That shift comes as investors question the sustainability of AI spending and the hyperscaler build-out, which has led to a recent wobble in tech stocks.

But Melvin said he expects copper to withstand the recent volatility.

"It's a new pocket of demand, and it really is almost an inelastic demand for copper," he said of the tech sector's need for the metal. "It's hard to think that one of these large-scale technology companies is going to make an investment decision on a hyperscale data center based on the cost of copper."

He added: "That same inelasticity applies to another demand pocket that's emerging, which is national security, national defense budgets. So when you look at copper demand, the impact of technology, artificial intelligence infrastructure, I think we can all agree that that market is growing.

"There certainly has been a bit of a retrench, a retreat, in those [tech] valuations. But two things can be true at the same time — you can have a capital market move in sentiment on equity values… but it can also be true that those industries are growing, and they're going to be a source of incremental demand for our metal."

The rally has also been supported by uncertainty over whether the U.S. will impose a tariff on refined copper. In 2025, the Commerce Department recommended a 15% tariff beginning Jan. 1, 2027, but no final decision on the proposed levy has been publicly announced.

"Because of the potential for US tariffs, a large share of the world's copper is now stored in the U.S., and it isn't clear those stocks will be available to the rest of the market," said Iain Pyle, senior investment director at Aberdeen Investments and co-manager of the abrdn Future Minerals Fund.

"At the same time, Chinese inventories look exceptionally low and premiums there are rising."

In an Oct. 15 note, Pyle called copper the "clearest example" of a market where supply cannot keep up with demand. "Higher incentives will be needed in the form of sustained higher copper prices.

"There is still some risk of a pullback around tariff announcements, but we see the underlying fundamentals as clearly bullish, and the potential for a spike in prices has increased."

title: 'Cannot play hide and seek': Minister's warning over haze sends Singapore agricultural stocks lower
content:
Shares of several Singapore-listed agricultural companies fell Tuesday after Senior Minister K Shanmugam warned they won't "escape responsibility" for their possible role in the haze blanketing the city-state.

"Companies cannot play hide and seek" with different corporate structures, hoping that will help them, Shanmugam said, revealing that seven companies had been questioned by the Singapore Exchange.

Bumitama Agrifell as much as 6.5%, whileFirst Resourcesdropped to a low of 4.83%.Golden Agri ResourcesandWilmar Internationalslipped almost 2%.

Shanmugam, who is also home affairs minister for the city-state, said that some of the fires or smoke source points seem to be associated with First Resources, Bumitama Agri, as well as non-listed First Borneo Plantations.

"Take, for example, First Resources. It issued a detailed statement on its zero burning policy and firefighting efforts ... but statements, no matter how well drafted, are not good enough. Show us the evidence."

The other companies named by the minister were Golden Agri-Resources, Wilmar International, Kencana Agri, Indofood Agri and TSH Resources.

Thehaze has affected businesses and daily lifein Singapore and Malaysia in the past few weeks, with the air quality in Singapore hitting levels not seen since 2015.

Schools in the state of Johor Bahru in Malaysiahave also closeddue to the air quality reaching unhealthy levels.

"They should not underestimate the Singapore government's determination to act," Shanmugam said, adding, "we will use every legal and regulatory lever at our disposal to exert pressure where it matters, including on their bottom lines, including on their access to financing, and including on their standing with investors."

He also revealed that Singapore could even amend laws or introduce new laws "on an urgent basis" to ensure cooperation, if needed. Companies potentially linked to the haze would also be examined if they still meet the standards for government grants or incentives.

When asked if Singapore's actions will affect bilateral relations between the city-state and Jakarta, Shanmugam dismissed the concern, saying, "Our people are suffering. What do these experts think we are supposed to do? Shiver in our shoes before we take any action to protect our own people? That's not the Singapore approach."

He was responding to a question about an articlepublished by local media outlet CNA, which cited legal experts saying that actions taken by Singapore against haze-causing firms in Indonesia may carry diplomatic implications.

"If we think like that, there will be no Singapore, and we do not think there should be any bilateral issues. The Indonesian public is suffering as well, and it is in Indonesia's interests as much as ours to deal with the companies that are causing these problems."

He said that Singapore's actions against companies are aligned with the broad policies of Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto."In fact, we hope to get full cooperation from Indonesia in going after the companies," Shanmugam added

title: Bank Indonesia faces mounting pressure to hike after MSCI threat fuels market rout
content:
Bank Indonesia faces mounting pressure to raise interest rates on Wednesday as economists revise their forecasts after global index provider MSCI warned it may downgrade the country's stock market from emerging-market status, setting off a selloff in stocks and the rupiah.

Citibank now expects a pre-emptive 50 basis-point increase to 6.25%, abandoning its earlier call for no change. Capital Economics and Permata Bank expect a 25 basis-point hike to 6%. The central bank has held its benchmark seven-day reverse repurchase rate at 5.75% since June.

MSCI said Friday it is consideringmoving Indonesia to "standalone"from the emerging-market status it has held since 1989, causing the Jakarta Composite Index to suffer the worst two-day sell-off recorded, before recovering about 3% Tuesday after authorities announced steps to improve market transparency and price discovery, including expelling tightly held companies from the flagship index.

Meanwhile, rupiah weakened to 18,030 per dollar on Tuesday, near its June record low, falling about 8% this year.

"Not delivering a rate hike [on Wednesday] would run the risk of disappointing investors and fueling further downward pressure on the currency," said Jason Tuvey, deputy chief emerging markets economist at Capital Economics. "A decision to hold rates on Wednesday could also revive concerns among investors that Bank Indonesia is kowtowing to political pressure."

Citi's Helmi Arman said a hike would aim to stop equity outflows spilling into bonds and prompting capital flight by domestic investors. He expects it to be a "one-off" followed by other support such as government foreign-currency borrowing or another round of bilateral currency swaps with foreign central banks.

The central bank has already raised rates by a combined 100 basis points since May. Headline inflation quickened to athree-month high of 3.28%in September, within the 1.5%-3.5% target range, while core inflation eased to 2.84%. The governor, Destry Damayanti, has said foreign-exchange reserves of$146.3 billion at the end of Septemberwould be adequate to stabilize the rupiah.

"Market confidence can deteriorate much faster than economic fundamentals," said Josua Pardede, chief economist at PT Bank Permata, estimating that foreign investors have net sold about $5 billion of Indonesian stocks this year. The risk is that foreign equity withdrawals could further weaken the rupiah and trigger selling in government bonds, he added.

An MSCI downgrade could force $3 billion to $5 billion of passive outflows, with another $15 billion of actively managed foreign money exposed to reassessment, he estimates. Pardede expects the market adjustment may come in stages, from precautionary selling through the first half of 2027 and mechanical selling if MSCI confirms the move by June.

"BI can provide liquidity and reduce excessive volatility, but only credible market-governance reforms can address MSCI's fundamental concerns," he said, calling for credible free-float data, ownership disclosure and transparent engagement with international institutional investors.

"The biggest risk is not simply losing Emerging Market status, but letting doubts about market integrity become a lasting increase in Indonesia's cost of capital."

title: BlackRock, GIC among investors chasing Indian telecom major Jio's IPO as anchor bids top $26 billion
content:
India's Jio Platforms has seen the anchor investor quota for its initial public offering oversubscribed more than 30 times, according to a source familiar with the matter, drawingbids from top assetmanagers including BlackRock, Capital Group and GIC.

The country's largest telecommunications and digital services company, backed by Meta and Google, plans to raise up to 302 billion rupees ($3.2 billion) through India'slargest ever IPO in rupee terms.

According to the source, who is not allowed to speak on the matter due to legal restrictions, the company's anchor book received total bids worth 2.5 trillion rupees ($26.3 billion) for the 81.1 billion rupee anchor book portion.

Jio Platforms, in a release on Monday, said it had finalized the allocation of 72.47 million equity shares to anchor investors at 1,119 rupees a share, at theupper range of the priceband.

The anchor book is a portion of the total fundraise set aside for large institutional investors before the IPO opens for public bidding.

Some other major institutional investors who have been allocated shares include India's state-owned insurance firmLife Insurance Corporation, Fidelity Investments, JPMorgan Asset Management and Abu Dhabi Investment Authority.

The Jio Platforms IPO will be open to the public from Wednesday through Friday. Jio Platforms, owned byReliance Industries, has been positioning itself as atech company and not just a traditional utility provider. The IPO price values the company at around $108 billion — lower than the valuations of over $130 billion floated a year ago.

title: ‘Open your doors for AI’: German chancellor urges businesses to embrace AI as Nvidia announces new investments
content:
Nvidiais increasing its investments in Europe's artificial intelligence sector, unveiling plans to back four German startups as the country pushes to strengthen its position in industrial AI.

The investments are part of the U.S. chipmaker's nearly $10 billion commitment to invest in companies, universities and research institutions across Europe, asannouncedat the Invest in Germany Summit in Berlin on Monday.

The four startups are Agile Robots, Avelios Medical, Mirelo and Reflex Aerospace. However, Nvidia did not disclose the size of the planned investments.

Agile Robots develops AI-powered robots for manufacturing, logistics and healthcare, while Avelios Medical builds AI-powered hospital management software. Mirelo develops AI models that generate audio for videos, while Reflex Aerospace designs and builds satellites.

The announcement comes as Germany seeks to accelerate AI adoption across its industrial sector, with Chancellor Friedrich Merz saying the country aims to become a leader in integrating AI into key sectors.

Merz, who described the technology as a major opportunity for the country's economy, named manufacturing, machinery and the automotive industry for integrating AI. He also urged Germany's small- and medium-sized businesses to capitalize on the data they already hold.

"Please open your doors for AI to make use of your data," Merz said. "This is a real secret and a real advantage for Germany to make use of all the data which is already available in our companies."

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang echoed Merz's remarks while highlighting Germany's expertise in manufacturing, mathematics and science, saying that AI would strengthen rather than replace the country's industrial capabilities.

"AI can only augment your capability, it will not replace your capability," Huang said, describing the technology as a new instrument for businesses.

Nvidia is also expanding its collaboration with the German federal government and its "Industry 4.0 Platform,"bringing together representatives from government, industry, research and trade associations, to accelerate the adoption of industrial AI. On Monday, the government signed a joint declaration of intent with Nvidia to advance AI models for industrial applications.

Earlier in the day,Siemenshad also announced new AI solutions developed with Nvidia at its factory in Erlangen, Germany. Siemens said the technologies could reduce engineering work involved in preparing production by up to 85%, while AI-powered production planning could cut costs by as much as 20%.

Huang had alsovisitedFrance last week, where heannouncedinvestments in four French startups and met with French President Emmanuel Macron to discuss AI development. The Nvidia boss is scheduled todelivera keynote address in Berlin on Wednesday.

title: JD Vance refrains from endorsing Israeli leader Netanyahu as Trump offers praise
content:
U.S. Vice President JD Vancedeclined to endorse Israeli Prime MinisterBenjamin Netanyahu, afterPresident Donald Trumpoffered his backing for the leader's reelection bid next week.

"The president has the most effective endorsement in American or international political history," Vance said inan interview on Mark Halperin's 2WAY Tonightpublished Monday. "I endorse American candidates, and that's where I'm focused on in the midterms," he said.

Vance said he was not criticizing Netanyahu: "I'm not anti-endorsing him. I'm not pro-endorsing him," he said, adding that "I'm not getting involved in Israeli elections."

Those remarks diverge from the approach by President Donald Trump, who gave the Israeli prime minister his backing in the election next week.

Trump on Sunday praised Netanyahu, the country's longest-serving prime minister, on Truth Social as "aGreat Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combating the Islamic Republic of Iran." In a social media post, Netanyahu thanked Trump for his "tremendous support and work together."

Vance has weighed in on foreign politics before. He campaigned in Budapest in April to publicly endorse then-Prime Minister Viktor Orban's reelection bid. Orban was later voted out after 16 years in power. Last year in Munich for a security conference, Vance met Alice Weidel, the leader of Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany party, which Elon Musk was also boosting at the time.

The Israeli vote next week will be the first national election since Hamas attacked Israel in late 2023.

The comments also come as U.S. public support for Israel, historically strong among both Republicans and Democrats, hasfallen sharply. There has also been vigorous debate in America about the Netanyahu-led government's response to the Hamas attack.

In June, Vance said thatIsrael has almost no friends leftin the world and should think hard before turning on the one it has.

title: Three big takeaways from the IMF-World Bank meetings
content:
The world's finance chiefs spent last week in Bangkok debating the biggest risk facing the global economy — with debt, artificial intelligence and trade imbalances topping the list. Meanwhile, China, long a main risk factor in these discussions, was no longer at the top of the worry list.

The Bangkok meetings were the first in Asia since 2018, when the gathering was held inBali, Indonesia. Thailand last hosted in 1991, six years beforethe unpegging of the bahtfrom the U.S. dollar set off the Asian financial crisis.

Fast-forward to 2026, and anything from global imbalances to the AI boom or a massive debt buildup in the "Global North" could trigger the next financial crisis, said Kevin Gallagher, director of Boston University's Global Development Policy Center, who spoke with reporters in Beijing after attending the IMF and World Bank meetings.

The IMF was upbeat on economies positioned to benefit from the global AI supply chain, such as South Korea, Japan and China, and downbeat on those that aren't, warning that the AI build-out is widening gaps between economies.

AI-related borrowing is also pushing up debt levels and competing with governments for capital, which lifts borrowing costs further. The IMF warned that should AI technology fail to deliver the promised productivity gains, it could trigger severe global economic consequences.

Gallagher said he's watching whether the IMF, the Federal Reserve and People's Bank of China can coordinate, or end up going in different directions and "make things worse."

The U.S. Treasury is at odds with the Fund over its own debt. IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said strong growth alonewon't put the U.S. on a sustainable path, with federal debt above $40 trillion. David Zervos, a counselor to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, dismissed the warning. "It's good to remember how messy their forecasts have been in the past," he said."So take it all with a grain of salt."

There were also few signs of coordination. Chinese and U.S. finance officials were seated at a distance at Thursday's G20 finance ministers' and central bank governors' meeting in Bangkok, according to a layout seen by CNBC.

Chinese central bank Governor Pan Gongsheng told theInternational Monetary and Financial Committee Saturdaythat China supports stronger Fund monitoring of spillovers from "major advanced economies' fiscal risks." He said countries should address their own fiscal deficits, while those running surpluses should boost consumption and investment.

Russia and Ukraine returned as a central focus of the week's meetings as tensions flared. Russian officials were also back in the room at a G20 finance chiefs' meeting on the margins of the IMF gathering last Thursday.

Finance Minister Anton Siluanovattended in person for the second time this year, after an August G20 session in Asheville, North Carolina, drew harsh criticism from European leaders that forced him out of participating in a group photo.

German finance minister Lars Klingbeil reiterated his discontent over the Russian delegation's presence, saying in a statement to CNBC that "pretending that Russia's returning as a normal member of the G20 and sitting at the table again — that won't happen with me, and it won't happen with the other Europeans either."

Nearly half of IMFC delegates walked out of the room when Siluanov was addressing the group in Russian on Saturday. Ukraine's central bank chief, Andriy Pyshnyi, told Reuters that he was surprised by the large number of finance officials who expressed solidarity with Ukraine, calling it a "deep and emotional moment."

After a three-hour meeting Thursday evening, the Group of Seven announced 260 million euros ($300 million) in funding for Ukraine to repair infrastructure at the Chornobyl nuclear power plant, and expect to bring that to 500 million euros — which would pay for the whole project — at a donor conference in Paris next month.

The IMF has warned that rising public debt is squeezing governments' room to spend on priorities such as defense.

China featured prominently during the IMF meeting in 2018 as the U.S.-China trade war was just kicking off. But this year, panels and interviews had little to say about the country.

Tim Adams, president and CEO of the Washington, D.C.-based Institute of International Finance, said China has rarely come up in his conversations during recent visits to Singapore and Bangkok.

"We would have had a long discussion about U.S.-China relations, China's impact on the [exports] shock 2.0 in Europe, and China's impact on global trade and global manufacturing. [But] actually, we've had very little of that," Adams told CNBC in an interview Friday.

The reason, he said: U.S.-China relations appear to have reached "some sense of stability," leading investors to pare back worries about China as a risk.

"The perception is that the relationship is stable and solid, without much visible tension beyond the nagging set of issues that have been around for some time," Adams said.

Investors remain reluctant to commit direct investment to the country, he said, but are keen on Chinese tech IPOs in the pipeline. He also cited a real appetite for Chinese bonds, with the currency stable to slightly stronger.

"It seems just more of a standard normal assessment, like China is any other risk rather than something unique and special," Adams said.

— CNBC's Penny Chen contributed to this report.
