title: Robot factories and hypersonic missiles: JPMorgan Chase's first $5 billion of defense investments
content:
JPMorgan Chasehas made $5 billion in startup investments in the first year of its U.S. security and resiliencyinitiative, the company said Monday, a faster-than-expected pace that indicates the bank is finding plentiful opportunities in emerging defense, manufacturing and supply chain firms.

The bank, whichlast year said it would deploy $10 billioninto startups over a decade, may expand the program beyond that initial dollar amount, JPMorgan co-President Doug Petno told CNBC in an interview.

Todd Combs, the formerBerkshire Hathawayexecutive who leads theJPMorgan groupin charge ofmaking startup investments, has "hit the ground running," Petno said. "He's done a great job and put us in some really interesting companies," he added.

Most of those investments have yet to be disclosed, but two known stakes seem emblematic of the project's mission to bolster companies that are needed for a moredangerousand chaotic era of geopolitics. JPMorgan, the biggest U.S. bank by assets, has taken direct stakes in defense-related startupsHadrianandCastelion.

Wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, as well as trade disputes with China, have threatened the flow of energy and key components needed for U.S. industries and defense, which spurred JPMorgan CEOJamie Dimoninto creating the initiative a year ago.

He put Petno, widely seen asone of two key possible successors, in charge of the overall investment project. Combs, a former boardmemberof the bank, reports directly to Dimon.

The scope of the project extends beyond supply chain, defense and manufacturing to include frontier technologies and the pharmaceutical and health-tech industries.

"There's a lot of really interesting companies that have been working to solve some of these problems," Petno said.

These "early venture-stage, advanced manufacturing companies have found ways to build these capabilities in the U.S." rather than relying on overseas trading partners, he said.

In August, the bank helped lead a $1.4 billionfunding roundfor Hadrian, which builds automated factories that make parts for the defense, aerospace and maritime sectors. A California factory run by Hadrian has 10 robots for every human employee,accordingto the startup's founder.

That month, JPMorgan was also involved in a $1 billionfunding roundfor Castelion, whose flagship product is a relatively low-cost hypersonic missile called Blackbeard. Castelion was founded in late 2022 by a group of former SpaceX engineers.

"Our approach is to find generational companies and partner with them for the long term," Combs said in a statement Monday.

"Putting more than $5 billion to work in our first year shows how many exceptional businesses are building in industries that strengthen critical supply chains," Combs said.

JPMorgan making billions of dollars of direct investments in nascent companies is a departure from its usual role as a lender and advisor.

Before the defense initiative, the bank had moved away from taking startup stakes, which can be relatively risky bets on unproven technologies. JPMorganspun offits private equity business, One Equity Partners, more than a decade ago.

In its more traditional role, JPMorgan has also financed and facilitated more than $230 billion for industries that support American national interests, according to the bank.

That part of its security and resiliency project, meant to hit $1.5 trillion over 10 years, is led byJay Horine, a former co-head of investment banking.

JPMorgan built a team for the project of about three dozen bankers, who are aided by hundreds more across the firm, as itexpandedthe initiative to Europe and Canada.

Its bankers are mapping distribution lines for key products, from submarines and missiles to aircraft, to identify suppliers that may lack the capital or capacity to meet rising demand, according to Petno.

JPMorgan is also in regular communication with the U.S. Department of Defense and Department of Commerce about the government's needs, he said.

title: Bereaved families could face 'unjust' tax bill after civil service pension delays
content: Image source,Getty ImagesByBecky MortonPolitical reporterPublished19 October 2026, 12:34 BSTUpdated 46 minutes agoBereaved families affected by severe delays paying out civil service pensions could face an "unjust" tax bill, the government has been warned.Under HMRC rules, certain lump sum pension payments must be paid within two years of the pension scheme being notified of a death to remain tax-free.Conservative MP Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who chairs Parliament's Public Accounts Committee, said it was "unconscionable" some families could face a "death tax" through no fault of their own.The Cabinet Office said that if delays caused a tax charge there were existing avenues to claim compensation, such as the Pensions Ombudsman.However, the ombudsman is currently advising that standard complaints are only likely to be resolved within 18 months, with more complex cases facing a longer wait.The Civil Service Pension scheme manages the pensions of 1.7 million public sector workers in the UK.Outsourcing firm Capita took over the administration of the scheme from a company called MyCSP in December 2025, saying it inherited a backlog of more than 86,000 cases.Despite a two-year transition period to prepare for the takeover, problems have persisted and by February the backlog had grown to 120,000 cases.Retired civil servants and bereaved families have been left waiting months for pension payments, with some struggling to pay bills.Civil service pension backlog 'overwhelmed' Capita, boss saysPublished12 FebruaryEmergency loans offered to civil servants waiting on pensionsPublished29 JanuaryRetired civil servants left in pension limboPublished23 JanuaryAccording to the latest figures up to 30 September,external, 1,643 outstanding cases of bereavement or death in service are more than 100 days old.Of these, only 301 are in scope to be paid within 15 days.The PCS union, which represents civil servants, said that while not all these cases would ultimately be affected by the two-year tax rule, there were "serious questions" over how long they would remain unresolved.If someone dies before the age of 75, a pension lump sum death benefit is only tax-free if it is paid within two years of the pension scheme first becoming aware of the death, and if the value is below the deceased's Lump Sum and Death Benefit Allowance.The payment would be taxed at the same rate as the beneficiary's income tax rate.Sir Geoffrey has written to Cabinet Office Minister Louise Haigh to urge the government to confirm the bereaved families affected will not face this "unjust financial penalty".His letter came after BBC Radio 4's Money Box Live highlighted the potential tax liability.Sir Geoffrey said "the chaos currently engulfing the Civil Service Pension Scheme means that the likelihood of death benefit payments being made within two years is slim".He warned "a significant number" of family members "will be watching the clock quickly tick down to a year, as the maladministration of the scheme enters its tenth month".He added: "This is an additional stress they should not have to bear."Money Box Live: Capita, What Went Wrong?Money Box Live looks at what is going on with Capita, which administers millions of people's pensionsListen on SoundsRob Wassell, 58, has been waiting almost two years for the lump sum from his brother's civil service pension, following his death.On 22 October it will be two years since the pension scheme was notified of his death so if he does not receive the payment in just a few days times, it could face being taxed.Rob, who contacted the BBC's Money Box programme about his case, said he had been phoning Capita with increasing "desperation" as his situation dragged on."It's a bitter pill to swallow to have to pay tax for something which was not my fault," he said."It creates unnecessary worry and anguish through the process, which is already in itself difficult."Rob said he needed the money to cover the estate costs he had to pay for his brother and fill a Â£20,000 hole in his savings.However, he said it was "heartbreaking" to hear of other cases where people needed the money just to survive.Rob added that the idea that he might face "another battle" to recoup the tax through compensation made it feel like "you just want to give up".Image source,Rob WassellImage caption,Rob is hoping the government will waive the tax due for people in his situationFran Heathcote, head of the PCS union, said it would be "a profound injustice" if families faced a further financial penalty because of Capita's failures."If that does happen, the government should be ashamed that families are being made to pay the price for failures that are entirely outside their control," she said.A spokesperson for the Cabinet Office, which has overall responsibility for the Civil Service Pension Scheme, said: "The service levels following the move to Capita have been completely unacceptable and we are committed to ensuring no member is left financially worse off."We are continuing to hold Capita to account, including holding back nearly Â£10m in payments, and are doing everything in our power to ensure that individuals do not experience delays."If delays cause a tax charge, existing avenues for complaints can provide financial redress or compensation to cover losses."A Capita spokesperson said: "We are deeply sorry for the frustration that the administration of the Civil Service Pension Scheme has caused members and their families."Our teams are working tirelessly to resolve outstanding cases as quickly as possible, with particular focus on people who have been waiting the longest and those facing financial hardship or challenging personal circumstances."Sign up for our Politics Essential newsletterto keep up with the inner workings of Westminster and beyond.Related topicsCivil ServicePensionsCapitaCabinet Office

title: Elon Musk says he'll give a SpaceX share to every child in America next year
content:
SpaceXCEOElon Musksaid Monday that he'll give every child in the U.S. one of his shares in the company next year.

Musk currently owns about 4.8 billion SpaceX shares, according to an August SEC filing. That figure rises to 6.4 billion when taking into account unvested awards and stock options, representing a 48.4% beneficial stake in the company.

There were 72 million children under 18 in the U.S. as of July 1, 2025, according to official census data.

That would amount to the CEO giving away about $10.5 billion worth of shares, taking into account SpaceX's closing stock price of $146.03 as of Friday.

"This will be the first of many," Musk said in a post on X, without providing further details on how the share giveaway would happen.

CNBC has reached out to SpaceX for further comment.

Musk's financial giving has been in the news in recent weeks primarily for his political contributions.

The Tesla CEO has spent more than$276 millionin donations to Republican groups since July, making him the biggest known donor of the 2026 midterm election.

The world's richest person poured$158 millioninto the Senate Leadership Fund, the Republican Party's leading Senate super PAC, in September through an affiliated Texas PAC created to support Republican Ken Paxton. Musk's two contributions of $75 million and $83 million are among the largest political donations ever.

Musk's post came hot on the heels of Anthropic revealing that it plans tocommit 5%of its shares to a new public benefit fund, with the stake potentially increasing as the company's valuation grows.

In response to an Anthropic post on X about the fund on Sunday, Musk replied, "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public," and added that's what he'd be doing.

Subject to shareholder approval, Anthropic's fund would immediately commit 5% of Anthropic's shares, with the board adding, at its discretion, an additional 2% for every 50% increase in the company's value above a set baseline that has yet to be disclosed.

The fund may be used to "explore large donations," including to traditional nonprofits or as direct distributions for specific populations, or for "bolder approaches" to study and address AI's disruption and displacement of jobs, the company said.

— CNBC's Jennifer Liu contributed to this report.

title: Google says it can build data centers the right way. Some experts and residents are skeptical
content:
If there's one thing most Americans can agree on, it's that they don't want a data center in their backyard.

A Gallup survey conducted in March found that71% of Americans opposedthe construction of a data center in their local area. Chief among their concerns: energy usage.Half of Americanssurveyed by Pew Research Center in July and August said data centers would be mostly bad for the environment and for household energy costs.

Now Google is betting that a massive AI data center can help finance a cleaner, more reliable power grid. Its proposed deal withXcel Energywould add more wind, solar and battery capacity than the data center is expected to use.

Under the agreement, Google would help pay for the added capacity and continue paying, even if it doesn't use all of the power.

Pine Island, Minnesota, is a small town of about 4,000 residents an hour southeast of Minneapolis. Google hopes that its new 780-megawatt data center plan will build goodwill with the Pine Island community and keep the company on track to meet its goal of operating on carbon-free energy, 24 hours a day, seven days a weekby 2030.

Google — whose cloud business powers its own Gemini AI and brought in nearly $25 billion in second-quarter revenue, an 82% increase from a year earlier — says it has found a model for doing this the right way. The company plans to finance the addition of 1,400 megawatts of wind, 200 megawatts of solar and 300 megawatts of battery storage to Xcel's grid.

Those additions amount to more than the capacity of the data center itself, which Google said is because wind and solar do not generate energy at all times. Xcel Energy said the new power will serve all customers in the local area, not just Google. Xcel also said the upgrades will help advance the local grid's carbon-free energy supply.

The proposed agreementbetween Google and Xcel includes minimum demand charges and exit fees, which Google says will keep the company on the hook for the infrastructure being built on its behalf, even if the AI boom cools. Google will pay for at least 75% of its contracted capacity, even if it uses less, and would owe up to eight years' worth of those minimum demand charges if it terminates the agreement early.

"Nobody wants to have a big buildout and then have nowhere for that power to go and nobody to pay for that power," said Amanda Rome, executive vice president and chief customer officer at Xcel Energy. "That's where these protections come in."

The agreement between Google and Xcel Energy is pending approval by the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission.

New data centers will account for "most" of the projected increase in electricity demand over the next decade, according to the North American Electric Reliability Corporation, a nonprofit regulator.

The Department of Energy under President Joe Biden reported that more than 70% of U.S. transmission lines and power transformers were at least25 years oldand found that the cheapest ways of meeting future demand would require the nation's transmission system tomore than double in size by 2050.

But hyperscalers argue that they can finance badly needed grid upgrades while also making the grid cleaner and more reliable.

"The timing of this industrial revolution couldn't be more perfect," said Amanda Peterson Corio, Google's global head of energy and power. "It's right at the time when we needed capital to fix aging infrastructure in the United States."

Jigar Shah, a partner at Multiplier, a consulting firm that helps clean energy startups go public, said data center operators could be constructing smaller facilities in places where the grid already has unused capacity. That would minimize the need to build — and pay for — new generation or transmission equipment.

"If you fit the load growth that the data centers want into the existing grid, everybody's rates go down by a lot," said Shah.

That's because the existing grid has enormous fixed costs from the infrastructure already in place: power plants, transmission lines, substations. If one new customer comes onto the grid and pays a large slice of that, everyone else's bills go down.

"And so the question really is, why are people not doing these 25-megawatt data centers? Why are they doing 1,000-megawatt data centers? And it turns out people are just lazy," Shah said. "They're like, well, it's easier for me to contract one data center that's one gigawatt in size than figuring out how to do something on the order of 40 data centers that are 25 megawatts each."

Industry watchdogs also warn of another reason that utilities often prefer to build new infrastructure, rather than make more use out of their existing grid.

"When [utilities] build something new, they fund part of that investment with dollars from their investors on Wall Street, and they enjoy incredibly high, exorbitant returns on those investments, typically around 10%," said David Pomerantz, executive director at the Energy and Policy Institute, a utility watchdog agency.

Building a data center that fits neatly into an existing grid provides little opportunity for a utility to make new money.

What if a hyperscaler offers to pay for those grid investments?

"One way to leverage data centers to lower people's bills is for data centers to provide that capital at much cheaper rates than the utility," said Pomerantz. "But that's a big problem for the utility. And this fight is actually already emerging."

Still, Shah said, the Google/Xcel project in Minnesota is a good example of a data center project acting as a catalyst for newer, greener technology.

"Google came in and said, well, here's a new way of doing things, using new technologies. How about we do it that way? And then that helps ratepayers. And the utility was like, yeah, that makes a lot of sense."

Watch thevideo above for the full story, including an interview with Google's global head of energy and power.—CNBC's Jeniece Pettitt and Lora Kolodny contributed to this report.

title: Women may be at greater risk of AI job losses. Telephone switch operators and PCs show why.
content:
Decades before Siri or Alexa or ChatGPT, there was a real person, almost always a woman, at the center of the information world. She was so vital, most long-distance communication could not happen without her.

She was the telephone switch operator, and at one time she was part of the single largest occupation for white, U.S.-born women under age 20.

The world is struggling to figure out what the dawn of artificial intelligence means for society, culture and the economy. A lot of ordinary Americans are just wondering what it means for their jobs.

The history of technological progress — from automated telephone switches to the introduction of the washing machine and the personal computer — can offer some guidance. And that guidance suggests women are likely to be among the most affected by AI.

"AI is focused on routine tasks and numbers and finding patterns, and those types of jobs are the clerical, administrative jobs that a lot of women hold,'' said Ariane Hegewisch, a senior research fellow at the Institute for Women's Policy Research. "It's still 90% of secretaries and clerical workers who are women."

New research backs this up. The International Labour Organization in March concluded that nearly one in 10 women in high-income countries works in occupations at the highest risk from AI.

In the 1940s, nearly 95% of America's telephone operators were female. It was a relatively well-paying job for women at the time, and a complicated one: It took months of training to be able to handle the several hundred calls an hour that could come in at peak times. Operators were expected to be speedy, precise — and polite.

These womenwere hit hardwhen AT&T introduced the automated telephone switch. It was one of the largest automation investments in history — a close analog to the massive AI investment now underway — and created one of the biggest technological shocks the nation had ever seen.

In the decades after the automatic switch was popularized, an estimated 75,000 operator jobs vanished.

Economists James Feigenbaum from Boston University and Daniel P. Gross from Duke University's Fuqua School of Business studied census and paycheck data from the time and followed local employment trends along the path of AT&T's rolling investment in switches across the nation.

"The effect of this shock on incumbent operators was to dispossess many of their jobs and careers,"they wrote in 2020. Many switchboard operators wound up in lower-paying jobs — or dropped out of the workforce entirely, they found.

Economist David Autor says this outcome reflects the reality that many workers are already in their highest and best-paying occupation. When the job goes away, the next step is often down.

"Most people are not changing careers very often. They make their career decisions early, and they stick with those careers," he said. "If those careers, if the value of that work … suddenly goes out of fashion, becomes technologically obsolete, they're going to, in general, do something not as good."

But Feigenbaum and Gross also discovered that the next generation of women fared better.

"Future workers found work in other fields, often taking up similar-quality jobs," they wrote, as the younger workers were "more adaptive to an evolving labor market … Anxiety over the opportunities available to future generations proved to be somewhat misplaced."

In other words: One type of job went away, but other work emerged over time that was just as good.

By the 1950s, another technological innovation would come along and have a profound effect on women: the washing machine.

Dubbed "engines of liberation" in a seminal paper on the topic by University of Pennsylvania economist Jeremy Greenwood and others, washing machines and other appliances dramatically reduced the time women spent on unpaid housework.  That meant time could be reallocated to a paycheck outside the home, even as women's responsibility for the home remained.

From 1950 to 1980, as gender norms changed, the number of employed women in the U.S. grew by more than 25 million. Their participation rate, or share of the female population in the labor force, grew to 52% from 34%. At the same time, 16 million more men found work, though the male participation rate dropped by 5 percentagepoints.

The relevant question for the AI boom today: How did the economy suddenly find jobs for these women? If AI creates a vast new pool of available workers, can the economy put them to work?

First, the very entry of women into the workforce meant demand for tasks once done at home moved into the paid economy, services like childcare and food preparation. Second, as the nation grew wealthier, other employment opportunities for women emerged in the service economy — in retail, restaurants, leisure and hospitality, and even some professional services.And third, as American businesses grew, they needed more people to handle the paperwork — everything from payroll to customer accounts.

Changes to the economy and businesses were partly related to the entry of women into the workforce, but it was also partly random luckthat the U.S. was booming and businesses were changing to need more office workers.

"Between 1940 and 1980, there was a ton of new work created in the U.S. economy, and it was in office and clerical work that was accessible to people with a high school education,'' Autor said.

The next big revolution affecting women in the workplace was the personal computer.

Before PCs arrived on the scene, women were the backbone of office infrastructure. According to the 1980 U.S. census, nearly 4.7 million Americans worked as secretaries, stenographers and typists. More than 98% were women.

When IBM introduced the personal computer in 1981, followed by the advent of Microsoft Word just two years later, some of the middlemen, or in this case, middlewomen, became obsolete. It didn't eliminate writing, filing or editing. It simply shifted a big chunk of those tasks from dedicated clerical workers to others in the office — executives could type their own reports, book their own travel and print their own papers.

But the PC wasn't entirely bad news for women in the workforce. Studies show women were already more likely than men to be using a computer at work at the dawn of the PC era. The PC put new tools at their fingertips: spreadsheets and databases and general computing power. While many roles were eliminated, many women adapted and found new ways to use the emerging technology to make themselves indispensable to their employers.

That's a potential outcome for AI. In some cases, it will eliminate tasks but not entire jobs, enhancing the time and ability of a worker to do the remaining value-added jobs that only humans can do.

A 2022 paper by Marcus Dillender and Eliza Forsythe found that when companies adopted software to do office and administrative work, it resulted in a 1% decline in employment in the sector but a 3% increase in wages for college graduates.

Many more women have earned college and advanced degrees, and hold managerial jobs, than when other technologies ripped through the economy, offering some potential protection from automation. But maybe not for long: One of the promises of AI is that it will move up the value chain of the jobs performed by humans.

Whatever capabilities the new technology may have now, the outlook is unclear because, Hegewisch says, somewhat ominously, "AI can learn."

title: In pictures: More than 500,000 took to the streets as France protests erupted into violence
content:
Protests in Franceagainst rising living costs and declining public services turned violent over the weekend, with more than 500,000 people taking to the streets.

Hundreds of thousands of people marched through various cities and protested peacefully but others set fire to the city hall in Limoges, gutting the 19th-century building.

Lyon's city tourist office was also set ablaze, supermarkets were looted and there were attacks on police officers and vehicles and luxury boutiques, in what was described as the country's worst unrest in years.

Officers used tear gas to restrain the crowds. One protester died of a heart attack, and another lost a hand.

"Those who looted will have to pay back for the damage, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable," French PresidentEmmanuel Macronsaid in a televised address to the nation on Sunday.

He blamed "unrestrained violence" on "insurrectionist elements from radical far-left groups, joined by numerous criminals."

The demonstrationsbegan last monthas high school students across Paris lamented poor school conditions, including teacher shortages and unsatisfactory facilities. The demonstrations evolved into a nationwide protest.

title: China's growth accelerates as AI export boom outweighs domestic weakness
content: Image source,VCG via Getty ImagesByOsmond ChiaBusiness reporterPublished19 October 2026, 03:03 BSTUpdated 48 minutes agoChina's economic growth picked up in the three months to the end of September, rebounding from a three-year low as the artificial intelligence (AI) boom helped boost exports.The world's second largest economy grew by 4.5% in the third quarter, up from the previous period but below the 5% expansion recorded from January to March, according to official Chinese data.The latest figure is at the bottom end of Beijing's annual growth target of 4.5%-5%, which analysts have said gives policymakers room to address the country's economic challenges.While exports have helped offset weak spending at home, global trade tensions and uncertainty over AI investments are clouding its outlook.China's National Bureau of Statistics said on Monday that the economy "sustained steady development against pressure" and showed "momentum with new growth drivers and improving structure".With exports climbing, China's trade surplus - the amount of goods and services it sells abroad compared to what it buys from other countries - is on track to overtake the record $1.2tn (Â£900bn) seen last year.But property investment fell by more than 20% in the first nine months from the same period last year, official data also showed.Oxford Economics researcher Sheana Yue said manufacturing and high-tech exports have boosted China's growth, despite weak investment and domestic spending.China's economy has struggling to shake off a long-running property slump, after years of overbuilding and excessive borrowing by private developers.There are still no signs that this trend will end soon, Yue said.Trade uncertainties and geopolitical issues have also made Chinese consumers more "pessimistic" and unwilling to spend, she added.'Investing in people': Can China's new push to boost spending revive the economy?Published10 MarchFaisal Islam: Why China and AI are worrying global finance bossesPublished2 days agoThe effects of Beijing's targeted support measures for businesses have yet to be seen, said Dave Chia, an economist at Moody's Analytics.Several risks stand out from the data, including China's reliance on a "single external engine" in exports, he added.The technology industry has been a key driver of China's growth in recent quarters.Global demand for computer chips and other components used to build AI data centres has helped to ease pressure on Beijing and cushion the impact of sluggish domestic consumption.Chinese businesses have leaned heavily on exports as a prolonged property slump, weak wage growth and high youth unemployment have weighed on consumer spending at home.In September, Beijing unveiled a raft of support measures, including lower interest rates for some businesses and subsidies for property buyers, in an effort to boost the economy.But Beijing is facing a backlash from Western economies - including the US and European Union - as manufacturers struggle to compete with large amounts of cheap Chinese goods.There are also concerns over the billions of dollars being spent on AI infrastructure and whether the companies making those investments can deliver on their promises of generating huge profits.Related topicsInternational BusinessChinaGDPArtificial intelligenceTradeMore on this storyWhy is China spending billions to get people to open their wallets?Published18 March 2025Huge data centres rise at 'China speed' to power its AI ambitionsPublished22 September

title: OpenAI bugging suspect WhatsApp'ed Saudi royal days before arrest, feds reveal
content:
TheSaudinational charged with planting a recording device in a sensitiveOpenAIexecutive conference room inSan Franciscowas "in frequent communications viaWhatsAppwith a member of the Saudi Royal Family" throughout 2025 and 2026, prosecutors revealed in a bombshell court filing Sunday.

The defendant,Abdulrahman Alfozan, communicated with the Saudi royal as recently as Oct. 5 — four days before he was arrested, theU.S. Attorney's Office in San Franciscosaid in the filing, which requests that he be detained without bail.

Prosecutors did not identify the Saudi royal, or say in the filing how Alfozan, who then was working as an engineer at OpenAI, knew that person.

"Among other things, the individual [the royal family member] told the defendant [Alfozan] that anartificial intelligenceinitiative was being launched in Saudi Arabia and wanted the defendant to join it," prosecutors wrote in their filing.

"In May 2026, the individual told the defendant, 'Saudi needs you more then [sic] the US!' to which the defendant responded '100,' indicating he agreed," prosecutors wrote.

"The individual repeatedly tried to recruit the defendant and asked when he planned to leave OpenAI," prosecutors wrote. " At the time, the defendant said he wouldn't leave until his stock vested."

The filing does not say that the Saudi royal directed Alfozan to install a recording device at OpenAI or steal information from that AI giant.

Alfozan, who lives near the San Francisco airport, is a venture partner atRaed Ventures, a Saudi venture capital firm. PrinceKhalid bin Bader Al Saud,a member of the Saudi royal family, joined the firm as a venture partner in 2025. In their filing Sunday, prosecutors did not mention that prince by name, or say that the unidentified royal who communicated with Alfozan had ties to Raed.

Prosecutors in the same filing said that the Saudi government and then, shortly afterward, a member of the Saudi military, booked separate flights for Alfozan's wife, Lujain Alassaf, and their three-month-old baby son to fly out of the United States after his Oct. 9 arrest upended plans for the three of them to fly as a family to Saudi Arabia on Oct. 12.

The wife and son flew from San Francisco to Doha, Qatar, on Oct. 10 on a business-class flight paid for by the unidentified member of the Saudi military, the filing said.

The filing asks that a judge order Alfozan, 35, detained without bail when he appears in U.S. District Court in San Francisco on Monday morning.

Alfozan has been in jail since his arrest on a charge of using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.  He faces a maximum possible sentence of five years in prison if convicted. OpenAI fired him after his arrest.

Alfozan's lawyer, William Pernik, in a separate filing asked that the defendant be released with home detention and GPS monitoring, and a bond co-signed by others, and "supported by the written undertaking of the Consulate General of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia."

The Saudi embassy in Washington, D.C., has not responded to CNBC's requests for comment on Alfozan since his arrest was announced on Oct. 13

Prosecutors said that in the days around the time that Alfozan allegedly installed the recording device on Sept. 28 in the back of a television in the conference room, "OpenAI executives met with government officials in that very room."

"Defendant's conduct could pose a danger to the national security of the United States," prosecutors said in the filing.

FBI Director Kash Patel, when Alfozan's arrest was announced on Oct. 13, said he allegedly concealed the recording device to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company's artificial intelligence technology.

Prosecutors in their new filing also argued that Alfozan is a flight risk because of his access to "ample resources ... and what appears to be considerable support from a foreign government that has (i) no extradition treaty with the United States; (ii) limitless resources; and (iii) the ability to provide extraordinary travel assistance, including based on similar circumstances in this District," the filing said.

"He has the connections needed not only to flee, but to build a new life in Saudi Arabia. The Court should order the defendant detained pending trial," prosecutors wrote.

Alfozan has spent about 15 years in the United States, working at various tech companies, including Meta, and obtaining a master's degree from the University of California, Berkeley in 2025. He is a legal permanent resident of the United States and has applied to become a naturalized citizen.

For his most recent job, as an OpenAI engineer, Alfozan was hired in July 2025 with an annual base salary of $325,000, which was later increased to $385,000, prosecutors said in their filing. He also received a new hire equity grant of $2.2 million in profit participating units, the filing said.

Alfozan planned to take two months of parental leave after the birth of his son, according to the filing. He and his family were scheduled to fly one-way to Saudi Arabia on Oct. 12.

"On or about September 28, 2026 — about two weeks before their scheduled flight—the defendant inserted a surreptitious audio recording device into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive OpenAI conference room, where the device remained for at least multiple days," the filing said.

The conference room is frequently used for "discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, as well as nonpublic information about OpenAI's technical progress and strategic decisions, capabilities, priorities, government engagements, and commercial relationships," the filing said.

The filing also says that Alfozan's iPhone, after his arrest, was found to contain photographs dated Sept. 22 to 28 depicting "at least one additional concealed device as well as what appear to be the input/output panels on televisions and other electronic devices in various locations in OpenAI buildings, including another conference room where sensitive meetings frequently occurred."

"The defendant's residence contained several electronic components similar to those in thecustomized devices the defendant installed in the OpenAI conference room," the filing said.

OpenAI also found another recording device in a bag Alfozan inadvertently left behind in a printer room on Oct. 5, the same day he was seen on camera checking behind the TV where the first recording device had been left in the conference room, prosecutors have said. The camera was installed after OpenAI discovered the recording device on Sept. 30, prosecutors said.

His cellphone also contained a deleted note from September 2026 "with links to various recording devices, including devices made by Seeed Studio, the manufacturer of the devices OpenAI found in its offices and the devices FBI agents found in the defendant's residence," the filing said.

Another note, entitled "OpenAI leave," suggests that Alfozan planned early pickup "of the devices he had installed or intended to install and then extending his planned parental 'leave to full,' " the filing said.

In addition to being in contact with a Saudi royal, Alfozan "was pursuing other opportunities in Saudi Arabia, including participating in the Misk Foundation's '2030 Leaders' program, which would have required his in- person participation in Riyadh," prosecutors said.

A day before she left the U.S. with her baby, Alfozan's wife told FBI agents who interviewed her that "her U.S. visa was expiring and that she and her son were permanently moving back to Saudi Arabia — and that her husband, the defendant, eventually intended to do the same," the filing said.

Alfozan's lawyer, Pernik, in his request that Alfozan be released into home detention, said, "nationality is not evidence of flight," and that his planned travel to Saudi Arabia was for "family and immigration reasons."

Alfozan's wife's 60-day post-employment grace period for her own visa was expiring on Oct. 12, the originally scheduled date of their flight, the lawyer said.

"Mr. Alfozan was made aware of OpenAI finding the device per its own filings and OpenAI'spublic statements, approximately eight to ten days before he was arrested," Pernik wrote. "If his intention was to flee, he would have done so at that time."

The lawyer also said that Alfozan, who had booked a one-way ticket to Saudi Arabia for himself and his family, regularly bought one-way tickets because he has learned they are more cost-effective than changing his flights at the last minute.

Pernik also wrote that the Saudi Consulate General confirmed in writing to the U.S. Pretrial Services Office on Thursday that it "'will not issue any travel documents' to Mr. Alfozan during his release and that, if he requests one, it 'undertakes to promptly notify U.S. Pretrial Services.'"

The attorney argued that prosecutors have not shown that Alfozan is a serious flight risk.

"Mr. Alfozan has lived in the United States for fifteen years and in the Bay Area for roughly ten," Pernik wrote. "Fifty-four people, at least twenty-seven of them in the Bay Area, have written to the Court, and they describe someone who organizes dinners, welcomes newcomers, mentors students, and shows up for friends' weddings, birthdays, and moves."

"That is not the profile of a person with one foot out the door," Pernik said.

title: Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi rejects criticism around weak yen and high interest rates
content:
Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has rejected criticism that she was on one hand responsible for a weak yen and on the other for pushing up interest rates in the country.

Speaking in parliament,Takaichi said; "I have been repeatedly criticized for 'Takaichi's weak yen' and 'Takaichi's high interest rates,' but I clearly deny that," according to aReuters translationof her remarks in Japanese.

She was responding to a question from an opposition party lawmaker Yoshifumi Hamano, who asked about the compilation of a second supplementary budget for the country.

Takaichi also said that her administration will increase confidence in the yen by building a strong economy.

Under her administration, yields on Japanese government bonds have risen to multi-decade highs, while the yen weakened to its lowest since 1986, promptingTokyo and even Washingtonto step into the forex market to support the currency.

In January, Takaichi hadreportedly saidthat a weak yen presented an opportunity for export industries and acted as a buffer against U.S. tariffs, thoughshe quickly clarifiedthat she held no specific preference for the currency's direction.

Japan's exports have beenpartly boostedby yen's depreciation, as a weak currency makes exports more competitive.

For bond markets, Takaichi said that "We intend to appropriately control the amount of government bond issuance," at a time when yields have been rising as Japan's central bank raises its policy rate and continues to normalize its monetary policy.

Earlier this year, Takaichi had announced a plan tocut the country's food taxand unveiled asupplementary budgetearlier this year, raising the possibility that Japan might need to issue more bonds to sustain its government spending.

Takaichi has said that the total bond issuance for calendar year 2026 would remain unchanged from the original budget plan,according to Bloomberg, although experts were skeptical.

Jesper Koll, expert director at Monex Group told CNBC back in April — whenthe supplementary budget was announced— that "Bond markets are a lot of things, but they're not stupid. You cannot increase spending without increasing debt."

title: Putin reportedly suggests summit with Trump and Xi to decide fate of Ukraine
content:
Russian President Vladimir Putin had reportedly suggested a summit between himself, U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping for a deal to end the Ukraine war.

The meeting was mentioned in a phone call to Trump on Oct. 9, theWall Street Journal reportedon Monday, citing a former Russian intelligence officer briefed on the matter. The call also produced a deal for Moscow to sell diesel oil on the global market.

The summit is not confirmed, but if it takes place will not involve Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and may take place at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in November in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.

The report comes amid mounting tensions between Ukraine and the U.S., its largest military backer. The Trump administration's recent steps that seem to be taking a pro-Russian turn have caused alarm among European allies and prompted criticism even from some members of Trump's own Republican Party in the U.S.

Over the weekend, U.S. President Donald Trumphad defended his decisionto temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports, as well asan executive orderon Oct. 18 to waive new Russia sanctions from a bill introduced by the late Senator Lindsey Graham.

In a post on X,Zelenskyy said that ″the decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me."

Trump accused Zelenskyyin a post on Truth Socialof not wanting to end this war, and said his decision for sanctions relief on Russia was to not "do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table."

"Trump's October 16 Executive Order does not support Trump's stated foreign policy objectives of ending the war in Ukraine and will only enable Russia to continue financing and protracting the war in Ukraine without any proper incentives that may force Russia to engage in any meaningful peace negotiations," the Institute for the Study of War wrotein a report.

The latest move comes after Trump told Ukraine to stop striking Russian energy infrastructure, claiming that it was driving up diesel prices.

A so-called"energy ceasefire"announced by Trump on Oct. 11 saw Moscow continuing strikes on Ukraine's infrastructure. Ukraine had then paused strikes for three days, but resumed attacks again last Thursday.

"America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements. On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting," the Ukrainian president wrote on Sunday.

On Sunday,he also told Bloombergthat "steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate."

"I am not saying that this is the goal our partners are pursuing. I don't want to think that our American partners believe the war" against Russia "could be ended sooner at Ukraine's expense. But that's how it looks."

Over the weekend, both Kyiv and Moscow traded strikes, with Ukrainelaunching a strike of over 1,000 dronesinto Russia, setting fires at an oil export terminal and refinery in the city of St Petersburg, while Moscow pounded Kyivwith ballistic missiles.

Last week, Kyiv also accused Washington of ordering restrictions on its Starshield networks, the military grade version of SpaceX's Starlink which it uses to control military forces and defend against Russian strikes.

Trumpdenied on Friday that the White House had ordered restrictions onStarlink satellite internetservices provided to Ukraine's armed forces.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk pinnedresponsibility for any restrictionson the U.S. government and Trump, writing on X that, "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government."

The restrictions meant that platforms that traveled above 160 kilometers an hour (100 miles an hour), such as interceptor drones, had lost connectivity.

Ukrainian media reportedZelenskyy as saying that the restrictions were a "planned operation," as Ukraine had sent cars with Starlink to EU countries to test Starlink's connectivity, and discovered that there were no such restrictions in those countries.

Reutersreported on Thursday, citing two U.S. officials, that the call to restrict Starlink in Ukraine came from the White House, but did not say who made the order.

The Telegraphreported on Fridaythat Musk "approached Donald Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine," and both had a hand in imposing the restrictions.

—CNBC's Lora Kolodny contributed to this report.

title: People playing loud music on buses could face £100 fine
content: Image source,Getty ImagesByMarc Ashdown,ÂBusiness correspondentÂandÂNick Edser,ÂBusiness reporterPublished48 minutes agoPassengers who play loud music on buses in England could be fined up to Â£100 under an attempt by the government to crack down on antisocial behaviour.The measures also seek to tackle littering, vaping and threatening behaviour to help improve journeys on all forms of public transport.Offenders on buses could be issued with the fines under new powers for local authorities.A national campaign asking rail passengers "share the carriage, not the noise" is also being launched. The proposed crackdown has been welcomed by campaigners, but some have questioned how it can be enforced."We've all been on the train when someone starts blasting music or videos from their phone. It gets on your nerves and can quickly spoil the journey," said Prime Minister Andy Burnham.Under existing powers, those who are asked to stop and refuse could be removed from a train or fined up to Â£1,000.The phenomenon has been given many terms - including loudcasting or sodcasting - and in recent years, Ofcom, YouGov and Transport for London (TfL) have all published polls showing the vast majority of people dislike it.Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said small changes in behaviour "can make a massive difference to people's experience on public transport".The government said it had issued new guidance to local authorities on powers - which were introduced earlier this year - to help them crackdown on loud music and other antisocial behaviour on buses in England.These new powers allow them to impose new rules on buses, but still need to be signed off by the Transport SecretaryThose who commit offences could face fixed penalties of up to Â£100.The government says bus drivers will not be responsible for enforcing the new rules. It says authorised officers, including Transport Safety Officers and the Police, will deal with the incidents.Meanwhile a new national campaign aims to remind rail passengers to "share the carriage, not the noise", to improve journeys for everyoneThe campaign will be launched across operator websites, social media, and in carriages. The government said this would end the current "patchwork" of approaches across different rail operators, and help create "a clear, consistent message across the network".The general secretary of the TSSA transport union, Maryam Eslamdoust, said tackling antisocial behaviour on public transport was "a step in the right direction".However, she added that the government must also "urgently confront the violence, threats and abuse faced by passengers and transport workers"."Increasing the budget for British Transport Police is vital to protect people, respond to incidents and bring violent offenders to justice," she said.Michael Solomon Williams from the Campaign for Better Transport told the BBC antisocial behaviour could be a "real deterrent" to people using public transport, especially those with different accessibility needs.He also questioned how the new measures will be enforced. "When local authorities are required to do the enforcement there are perhaps some question marks about how a local police force might be called upon on bus services, for example, where we don't tend to see British Transport Police."Richard Holden MP, Shadow Transport Secretary, said: "After we led the charge against antisocial behaviour on public transport last summer, Ministers have worked out that nobody wants to endure pounding techno or blaring hip hop on a packed train or bus."But passengers and railway staff face far more serious problems. Assaults against rail staff have risen by 68%, while prosecutions have slumped under Labour. It's time for Andy Burnham to get serious about enforcement, tackling violence and protecting those who work on our railways."Liberal Democrat Transport spokesperson, Olly Glover MP said: "Tough talk means nothing without enforcement."Unless the Government funds transport safety officers on the ground, these new rules won't be worth the paper they're printed on."Independent watchdog Transport Focus said research it had published in June showed personal safety and security was now fundamental to passengers' confidence in the railway."Four in 10 passengers say that anti-social behaviour has made them feel vulnerable when travelling," said Alex Campbell, Transport Focus's director of policy and insight."Measures that reduce nuisance behaviour, such as playing loud music and vaping, can help improve people's experience and encourage more people to choose public transport."Related topicsTransportMore on this storyWhy phones on loudspeaker may become just another noisePublished6 AugustReported assaults on Britain's rail services rise by more than a thirdPublished24 SeptemberSafety concerns put Londoners off buses, say ToriesPublished11 July

title: EU tariffs aimed at China hitting Ukraine, steel boss says
content: Image source,Getty ImagesByMichael Race,ÂBusiness reporterÂandÂSimon Jack,ÂBusiness editorPublished1 hour agoThe boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies has called on the European Union to drop import restrictions on products made from the country, arguing it has been "bundled together" in measures aimed a curbing cheap imports from the likes of China.Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, told the BBC the recently-imposed tariffs on imported steel to the EU were "unfair" and had been put in place "without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in".He said he wished to see "at least a carve out" for Ukraine to access the EU market.A spokesperson for the European Commission said the EU "took into account the difficult situation" of Ukraine when deciding its steel policy.The trading bloc has recently imposed restrictions on steel imports in an effort to protect steel manufacturers of member nations.It has capped the amount of steel which can enter the EU tax free at 18.3 million tonnes per year - a 47% reduction from 2024 levels.There are some country-specific quotas in the policy, but the overall aim is to cut the amount of steel that can be imported due to member nations struggling to compete with cheap imports from the likes of China and Turkey.Despite a free-trade agreement (FTA) being in place between the EU and Ukraine, the FTA does not stop the EU from introducing separate trade protection measures."Ukraine has been bundled together into those measures without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in," Ryzhenkov said, pointing to the war with Russia."Access to the European market is crucial for survival," he added. "The restrictive measures that have been put in place by the authorities in the European Union, they don't help."I think it's unfair that Ukraine has been treated in the same way as all of the other importers into the European Union."The Ukraine steel industry estimates steel exports to the EU could ultimately fall by about 50â60%.The EU said Ukraine's specific steel quota guaranteed exports of the metal, but acknowledged this was at a "level lower than in the past years"."Despite the war effort, Ukraine remains an important exporter of steel to the EU," a spokesperson said, adding it had "offered compensations" to its largest suppliers, which included Ukraine.Image caption,Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, says EU steel quotas are "unfair" on UkraineSteel products are a foundation in Ukraine's economy. Before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, metallurgy and mining accounted for roughly 10% of Ukraine's national income and a third of its exports. The EU is its top customer.But the industry has suffered from the continued Russian bombardment.All of Ukraine's steel mills have been bombed at points since the conflict began in 2022, but Ryzhenkov said strikes had "intensified significantly recently".At one point in September, there was "no single tonne of steel produced" in Ukraine for the first time in about 150 years, he added.Almost 800 Metinvest workers have been killed since the war began.Ryzhenkov said the company had "improved the covered areas" at its mills where workers can shelter during air raids."The only thing we can do is to design procedures to keep people safe and just obey those procedures and try to minimise the risks.""Unfortunately, you cannot cover a whole steel mill to avoid it being damaged."Ryzhenkov said he expected the coming winter to be "one of the hardest in our history"."We are in a dire situation when we don't have logistics to access any other market apart from the EU and cutting our available market by 60%, that doesn't help for the industry to survive."Related topicsWar in UkraineSteel industryEuropean UnionTradeUkraineInternational Business

title: Don't fall for this - how to protect yourself from AI scams
content: Image source,Getty ImagesByKevin PeacheyCost of living correspondentPublished1 hour agoBe careful where you buy from, shoppers are being warned as criminals use AI to supercharge scams.Some fraudsters have made websites for fake retailers that claim to be family-owned firms selling quality UK-made products. Images may show a UK High Street with Union Jack flags in shot.If you order you're likely to find a product either never arrives, or is a cheap, mass-produced item from a country such as China, trading standards officers say.AI-generated images like this, as well as voice cloning and deepfake videos are increasingly being used to trick people out of their money, according to National Trading Standards.For the first time, it has drawn up anAI scam watchlist,externalhighlighting some of the tools and techniques criminals are using.What are the tricks to look out for?Tricks include:Cloned or new websites that look polished and professional in rapid time and at a low costRomance scams in which AI is used to remember victims' personal details and keep conversations going over weeks or monthsAI-generated deepfake videos and voice-cloned audio is used to impersonate family members or close friends asking for money in an "emergency"Error-free, personalised phishing emails, text messages and social media posts can be generated by AI on a huge scaleHow can I protect myself?Some of the old scam-avoidance techniques may now be less successful due to the benefits of AI.Typos or grammatical errors can no longer be relied on to spot scams, says consumer group Which?.Some of the ways to protect yourself, according to trading standards, include:Never sending money, gift cards or personal or financial information to someone you have not met in personDoing your research - such as checking whether a shop's address is real, using theFinancial Conduct Authority's Firm Checker,external, to ensure a company is authorised to give financial advice, and contacting a business directly to check whether a job advert is realNot assuming someone is genuine just because you've heard their voice or seen them on a video callIn general, they say stop and think before paying, sharing personal information or taking action. You should be especially wary of pressure or urgency because criminals want you to act before you have time to think.Fraud and scams can be reported toReport Fraud,externalor by calling on 0300 1232040, or you can call the Citizens Advice Consumer Helpline on 0808 223 1133 for advice.Related topicsPersonal financeMoneyCost of LivingFraudTrading StandardsArtificial intelligenceMore on this storyRoofing scammers con homeowners out of thousands of poundsPublished7 days ago'Add me on WhatsApp' scam calls to be investigatedPublished9 OctoberLego fraudster among last year's most high-profile insurance scammersPublished6 October

title: India’s Finance Minister blames easy exits and excess liquidity for equity market's underperformance
content:
Excess liquidity in India's equity market has contributed to underperformance and may continue to do so, according to Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman.

"Because of the ease of liquidity, ease of availability, people are even exiting easily" from equities, Sitharaman told CNBC in an exclusive interview on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank meetings in Bangkok on Friday. However, the fundamentals of the Indian economy are "fine," she said.

Since January, India's key benchmark indexes have slipped nearly 12%, as per LSEG data, even though thecountry's economic growthhas been resilient amid trade uncertainty and geopolitical shocks. India has beenhit with record outflowsby foreign investors from its equity markets, and Sitharaman said that continued capital outflows are one of the biggest risks for India in 2027.

Still, domestic capital continues to flood the market. Indian equity mutual funds have recorded net inflows every month since March 2021, according to data released by industry body Association of Mutual Funds in India earlier this month.

Multinational companies,private equity funds and foreign investors have been able to make partial or full exits from their investments at a premium. Between 2021 and 2025, Indian initial public offerings collectively raised $60.4 billion, of which "a staggering" $37.7 billion, or 63% of total proceeds,went to existing holderswho sold their shares to the public, an EY report in August said.

Foreign portfolio investors havesold direct Indian equitiesof over $33 billion so far this year, as per Indian depository firm NSDL. India has gained a reputation as an anti-artificial intelligence trade, while markets like Taiwan and Korea, with AI champions, have attracted strong investment flows.

The flight of capital toward AI and the U.S., which otherwise moves toward different countries for different sectoral investments, is "a concern," she added.

Taiwan now has the largest market weighting in the MSCI Asia Pacific ex-Japan index at 29%, while Korea has moved into second place at 22%, as per a report by Goldman Sachs on Oct. 8. India's share has compressed from 19% a few years ago to 10%, it added.

But with the globalAI rally showing cracks, Sitharaman said India wouldn't be "hurt" from any spillover if the bubble burst. India has not received the "AI kind of investments coming into different jurisdictions," she said.

Sitharaman, who is India's longest-serving finance minister to hold the office continuously, added that the South Asian country was "no longer a laggard" in the frontier tech space and investment was being made to set up semiconductor manufacturing.

title: Anthropic commits 5% of shares to new public benefit fund that could address AI job disruption
content:
Anthropic said Sunday it plans to commit 5% of its shares to a newpublic benefit fund, with the stake potentially increasing as the company's valuation grows.

Subject to shareholder approval, the fund would immediately commit 5% of Anthropic's shares, with the board adding, at its discretion, an additional 2% for every 50% increase in the company's value above a set baseline that has yet to be disclosed.

The fund may be used to "explore large donations" — including to traditional nonprofits or as direct distributions for specific populations — or for "bolder approaches" to study and address AI's disruption and displacement of jobs, the company said.

An August Pew Research Center report found that 71% of adults think AI will lead to fewer jobs in the U.S. over the next two years.

The fund will be established as a wholly owned limited liability company rather than a 501(c)(3) tax-exempt nonprofit or other format to adjust between different forms of giving, the release said. Equity held by the LLC will not be used for lobbying or political giving in the U.S. or internationally, Anthropic said.

Anthropic told investors its third-quarter revenue stands at $16.8 billion ahead of its planned initial public offering reportedly slated for November,CNBC reported.

The timing of Anthropic's public fund announcement is both mandatory to prepare for an initial public offering, and "beneficial from an image perspective," especially as AI reshapes the jobs market, Lise Buyer, partner at IPO advisory firm Class V Group, told CNBC.

Buyer said Anthropic's move could be seen favorably if the funds support retraining or help workers find alternative employment when the technology disrupts their jobs.

"Of course, it is also to burnish their reputation at a time when AI is coming under significant scrutiny," she added.

Anthropic said it will share more about the fund structure and governance in the coming months, including valuation milestones that may increase the stake. It said it will also share progress on the fund in an upcoming public benefit report.

In response to Anthropic's announcement,TeslaandSpaceXCEOElon Musk said on Xthat he "recommend[s] giving the shares directly to the public."

title: Brent crude hovers near $109 a barrel as Ukraine resumes energy strikes, tankers attacked in Middle East
content:
Crude oil prices hovered near recent highs on Sunday as traders weighed a Ukraine bombing of oil facilities in Russia and more tankers coming under attack in the Persian Gulf.

Brentcrude futures, the international benchmark, shed $1.04 to $108.82 per barrel. U.S.West Texas intermediatelost 26 cents to $101.15 per barrel.

Fires broke out at an oil terminal and depot in St. Petersburg after Ukraine launched a massive wave of drone strikes on Sunday, St. Petersburg Gov. Alexander Beglov said in a post on Telegram.

The terminal in St. Petersburg exports about 120,000 barrels per day of refined products, mostly fuel oil, according to data from Kpler. It is unclear how bad the damage is at the facility.

Ukraine briefly paused strikes on Russian energy facilities after PresidentDonald Trumpdeclared on Oct. 11 that Kyiv and Moscowhad agreed to a truce.

But Russia continued to strike Ukrainian energy infrastructure after Trump's announcement. PresidentVolodymyr Zelenskyysaid last week that Kyiv wouldresume strikeson Russian facilities in retaliation.

In the Middle East, meanwhile, two tankerswere attackedoff the coast of Saudi Arabia in the Persian Gulf on Friday, according to incident reports from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre.

A small boat fired a rocket-propelled grenade at an unidentified tanker 78 nautical miles northeast of Al Jubayl, according to UKMTO. Another tanker, the ST3, was hit by an unknown projectile, UKMTO reported.

Iran has escalated attacks on tankers in the Persian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman in an effort to choke off crude oil exports from the region.

title: Nasdaq futures gain as investors buy the dip in the AI trade: Live updates
content:
Stock futures rebounded on Sunday night as traders cautiously dipped a toe back in following last week's rout in shares linked to the artificial intelligence trend.

Nasdaq-100 futuresadded 0.4%.Dow Jones Industrial Average futuresticked 0.2% higher, or 110 points.S&P 500 futuresgained 0.2%.

Stable oil prices early Sunday also lent the equity market some support.

The S&P 500 lost nearly 2% last week, its biggest weekly decline since late June. The Nasdaq tumbled 4.5%, snapping a four-week winning streak.

Concerns around the health of the AI trade took center stage after CNBC reported, citing sources, that Anthropic'sthird-quarter revenue totaled $16.8 billion. And while that's up from $11.6 billion in the second quarter, it raised flags among investors about the pace of growth with the AI build-out.

Neocloud stock CoreWeave, which uses large amounts of debt to build data centers that it rents out to tech companies, was at the center of those fears. The AI-linked name plummeted 25% last week — its largest one-week drop since November 2025. Investors in the corporate bond market have started to shun CoreWeave, with the company's credit default swapsreaching distress levels.

It's not just CoreWeave whose moves in the credit market are concerning. Goldman Sachs traders noted Friday: "AI Credit Spreads and hyperscalers specifically are at the widest levels of the year. The last time spreads were nearly this high, the underlying equities were 15% lower."

"The widening across the complex has forced investors to confront what happens as AI spending growth slows. AI Capex has likely peaked and financing, sustainability, and returns on capital have become the debate rather than the next near term earnings revision," they said. "Pessimism is increasing, market breadth is low, and [Friday] we saw the second highest amount of puts traded (right behind June of this year)."

Traders were also keeping a wary eye on oil with ship attacks in the Persian Gulf picking up and Ukraine and Russia trading attacks on energy infrastructure. Ukrainehitan oil terminal in St. Petersburg, Russia on Sunday. Longer-dated oil futures have begun to ratchet higher on expectations energy infrastructure disruptions may last well into 2027.

On Sunday however, Brent and WTI crude futures were both trading a tad lower.

A slew of earnings from major companies such as Meta Platforms and Tesla hit the Street this week with optimism those results will stabilize the market.

Oil prices fell slightly in early trading Sunday even after Ukraine attacked crude facilities in Russia, while more tankers along the Persian Gulf came under attack as well.

Brent crudeslipped 1% to $108.80 per barrel.U.S. oil priceslost 0.2% to $101.18.

Fires broke out at an oil terminal and depot in St. Petersburg after Ukraine launched a massive wave of drone strikes on Sunday, St. Petersburg Gov. Alexander Beglov said in a post. Meanwhile, two tankerswere attackedoff the coast of Saudi Arabia in the Persian Gulf on Friday, according to incident reports from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre.

title: France's Macron vows to hold accountable those who 'sought to bring down the Republic'
content:
French President Emmanuel Macron on Sunday voiced the public's "anger" and "shame" over rioting and looting during nationwide protests against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools. At least 1,800 people have been arrested.

"Those who looted will have to pay back for the damage, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable," Macron said in a televised address to the nation.

He blamed "unrestrained violence" on "insurrectionist elements from radical far-left groups, joined by numerous criminals."

Macron has earlier held an emergency meeting with senior government officials, a day after masked groups set fires and attacked public buildings, including city halls, in several cities. He said he had instructed prefects to work with mayors to protect public buildings and businesses in the coming weeks, including by banning protests when necessary.

Flames engulfed the 19th-century City Hall in Limoges, central France, causing its roof to collapse and nearly destroying the building.

Hundreds of protesters gathered again on Sunday at the Place de la République in Paris amid a heavy police presence. Officers used tear gas as tensions flared sporadically in the neighborhood, with small groups of people trying to set bicycles and trash bins on fire.

"The right to protest is a fundamental right. Deliberately and collectively sowing disorder through violence is not," Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez wrote on X, citing the looting of hundreds of businesses in cities including Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Bordeaux.

About 550,000 people took part in protests across France, according to authorities, while organizers put the figure at about 800,000. Demonstrators answered calls from a labor union, student organizations and activists hoping to revive the "yellow vest" movement, which emerged in 2018 to protest social injustice.

Mass protests in France are often marred by violence on the fringes of otherwise peaceful marches, leading to clashes with police. The arrest tally reported Sunday approached the nearly 2,000 recorded nationwide during a single day of yellow vest protests in December 2018.

One person died of a heart attack, Paris police said in a statement, without providing details. The Paris prosecutor's office said it was investigating.

Dislodged cobblestones, shattered storefronts and broken glass littered the area around Paris' Place de la République on Sunday. Looting and damage were also reported in other tourist and shopping districts.

Paris police said they arrested 855 people in the capital region. The city's prosecutor's office said police kept 557 in custody.

"I am actually stunned by the level of destruction and violence that was expressed," said government employee Marie Peyreigne, 57, wondering what had led to the mayhem.

Parisians inspecting the damage photographed the partially dismantled base of the square's central monument, a statue of Marianne, a symbol of France.

Jean Foissy, 74, said he wanted to join the protest but hit "a wall of riot police and fires everywhere" and went home.

"I was very scared," he said. "I've been a Parisian since I was born, so when I got here, it almost made me want to cry because I find it so bad, it hurts me."

Margaux Eude, 26, said she supported the protest movement but "didn't think it would escalate like this."

"It's the troublemakers who came, and it breaks my heart because it delegitimizes the movement," she said.

Political leaders across the spectrum sought to parlay the fallout from Saturday's riots into political capital, ahead of next spring's presidential election.

Far-right leader and presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen criticized Macron's centrist government as "exhausted, disoriented and seemingly incapable of doing anything other than commenting on its own powerlessness" in a video she posted on social media Sunday.

Far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, for his part, accused Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu of "playing with fire," alleging that "by banking on degradation, you have only succeeded in uniting all youths and workers' unions."

Mélenchon, who joined the Paris march Saturday, insisted, "My message is clear: those who share our fight have no business in looting or destruction."

U.S. President Donald Trump posted "France is burning!" on his Truth Social platform, apparently linking the unrest to "the immigration of people from an entirely different world."

"Close your Borders and take control, before it is too late!" he wrote.

French authorities and police have not linked immigrants to the rioting and have repeatedly attributed some of the violence to "radical far-left groups" and other people who joined to loot.

"The scale of the damage is considerable and unprecedented," Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire wrote in an open letter. "Paris is a city of freedoms, debate and demonstrations. It must remain so. But it must also be a city where everyone can work and run a business safely."

Police said groups of hundreds of people formed unauthorized marches across central Paris on Saturday. "By late afternoon, a new phase began with the arrival of large numbers of people whose sole aim was to steal and loot, taking advantage of the unrest," police said.

The mayors of Paris, Marseille and Lyon, the three largest cities, requested a meeting with the prime minister in the coming days "given the extent of the damage and the seriousness of the situation."

In the southern port city of Marseille, some protesters briefly forced their way into the lobby of City Hall and a group of people wearing hoods and masks damaged a police station. In Lyon, a fire broke out inside a tourist office.

In Limoges, a group of "radical troublemakers" broke into City Hall while there were elected officials, employees, security personnel and members of the public inside, Maurice Barate, prefect of the Haute-Vienne region, said. "Despite the presence of so many people, they deliberately set the building on fire. It is an extremely serious and unspeakable act."

In eastern France, the Mulhouse prosecutor's office said an investigation has been opened after a 17-year-old girl was injured during the protests and lost an eye. On Saturday, another investigation was opened after a young protester lost a hand in Saint-Étienne.

The injuries come as police have drawn sharp scrutiny over their use of grenades and other riot-control weapons during recent demonstrations.

title: Microsoft pulls out of UK's largest AI data centre
