title: Bessent warns Zelenskyy to 'be very careful' about claims U.S. is throttling Starlink
content:
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned Ukrainian PresidentVolodymyr Zelenskyyon Sunday to "be careful" in public statements about U.S. support forUkraine.

U.S.-providedStarlinkinternet was recently restricted in Ukraine, hindering the war-torn country's ability to respond to Russian assaults. Ukraine uses Starshield, the military and government-controlled version of the commercial Starlink, to conduct military operations.

In an earlier interview on NBC's "Meet the Press," Zelenskyy said he believed the U.S. government was responsible for the slowdown, and that Ukraine was "blocked" from U.S. intelligence for a period of time. Zelenskyy said Starshield-linked vehicles and drones are still being restricted in speed.

Bessent cautioned Zelenskyy about making those claims.

"President [Donald] Trump and Secretary [Marco] Rubio have categorically said that no one under the Trump administration did that, and I think it is very reckless for President Zelenskyy to make such a charge," Bessent said on "Meet the Press."

"President Zelenskyy should be very careful about making statements like this that aren't true," he added.

Starlink, high-speed satellite internet provided byElon Musk'sSpaceX, is critical to Ukraine's defense. Musk himself said in apost on Xlast week that the U.S. government and PresidentDonald Trumpare"ultimately" responsiblefor any slowdowns to the military version of Starlinkknown as Starshield.

"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," Musk wrote. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."

Reuters reportedlast week that the White House ordered the technology restrictions, but Trumphas denied responsibilityfor the slowdown.

"Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," the president said last week. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been."

The U.S. relationship with Ukraine has been highly scrutinized throughout Trump's second term, as he has frequently antagonized the war-torn country while pushing for a peace deal.

Trump has recently expressed frustration over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries as he faces pressure from voters over sky-high gasoline anddiesel pricesahead of the U.S. midterm elections. The president has even personallyblamed Zelenskyyfor the rise in energy prices: "He wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel," Trump said.

Soaring energy prices are largely due to the U.S. war with Iran, which severely disrupted the Strait of Hormuz and choked oil shipments from the Persian Gulf. The national average for a gallon of gas in the U.S. was nearly $4.30 on Sunday, according toAAA. Diesel was roughly $6.32 per gallon, about 20 cents off September's record high.

Trump has tried to offset the energy pinch by importing Russian diesel. In apost on Truth Socialearlier in the month, he said: "Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!"

Many U.S. lawmakers, including Republicans,have condemnedthe president's plan to buy Russian diesel. Congress recently sent Trump an overwhelmingly bipartisan sanctions package aimed at crippling Russia's energy industry. Trump signed the bill into law, butwaived portions of itover the weekend, citing the national interest in an explanation to Congress.

"Beyond irresponsible. What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand?" Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said in apost on X. "It's unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day."

This story is developing. Please check back for updates.

title: Iran says it has a 'new operational plan' if the U.S. resumes attacks, as shipping vessels report strikes
content:
A senior Iranian security official warned Sunday that Tehran has prepared a new response plan for any renewed U.S.-Israeli attack, as maritime authorities reported several separate attacks on commercial vessels around the Arabian Peninsula.

"Iran's armed forces have prepared a response to any new act of adventurism that would be far more devastating than the 12-day and 40-day wars," Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said in aposton X, referring to attacks by Israel in June 2025, and the conflict triggered by the U.S. and Israel in February.

"Iran's new operational plan will not follow the rules with which they are familiar," Rezaei said in comments translated by Google.

PresidentDonald Trumpsaid last week that hedoes not intend to use nuclear weaponsagainst Iran or foresee deploying ground troops in the country.

Speaking inan interview with Newsmax,broadcast Thursday evening, he said: "I wouldn't use nuclear. We don't have to. We're the greatest nuclear power in the world."

The right-wing cable outlet asked Trump about reports thatWashington was consideringusing the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast, or MOAB, widely known as the "Mother of All Bombs."

Iranian state media agency IRNA quoted Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi assayingthat while Iran would not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure, it remains ready for dialogue.

Meanwhile, shipping vessels operating in waters around the Arabian Peninsula reported coming under fire in recent days.

The British Navy-affiliated UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said a tug traveling south northeast of the United Arab Emirates washit by two unknown projectileson Sunday.

On Saturday, a master of a liquefied natural gas tanker southwest of Yemen reported "being approached by a small skiff with seven persons onboard," UKMTOsaid. The skiff fired twice, and the tanker's security team responded with two warning shots, it said.

Another tanker northeast of Saudi Arabiareportedbeing hit by a rocket-propelled grenade fired from a small boat on Friday.

Crude oil prices rose sharply Friday amid rising tensions in the Middle East, while Ukraine vowed to keep striking Russian refineries.

Brentfutures hit a session high of $110 per barrel for the first time since May before easing slightly to settle at $109.86, a 3.7% gain.

U.S.West Texas Intermediaterose 3.5% to settle at $101.41 per barrel. WTI added more than 10% last week while Brent advanced nearly 5%.

Saudi Arabia intercepted several missiles fired over the Red Sea on Friday, including one that was heading toward the oil export terminal Yanbu, amilitary spokesmansaid. Three drones were also destroyed in the kingdom's Riyadh and southern regions, the military said.

Iran-allied Houthi militants in Yemen repeatedly fired at Saudi Arabia last week. The kingdom's energy ministry said oil giant Aramco came under attack when militants hit one of its administrative buildings in Dhahran on Tuesday.

title: I've studied over 200 kids—parents who raise resilient, successful children teach them these 6 lessons early on
content:
When we talk about raising successful kids, we tend to talk about what they can do.

Are they getting good grades? Are they going to basketball practices and winning games? Did they clean their rooms and set the table? Are they motivated? Responsible? Social? Can they solve problems, make good choices and eventually become independent adults?

But after years spent working with more than 200 families, I've seen that some of the most important lessons children need to live successful, happy and fulfilling lives — and to build healthy relationships — have very little to do with action or achievement.

Children absorb crucial messages in ordinary moments based on how we respond when they struggle, fail, disagree with us, disappoint us or simply become someone different from who we imagined they would be.

In my experience, there are six things parents of the most successful, confident,resilientand well-adjusted kids teach them early on that have nothing to do with accomplishments.

Children notice what happens between you when something goes wrong. They see your face when the grade comes back. They notice whether you seem prouder after the win and more distant after the loss.

A child should be able tofail without feeling they have fallenin your eyes. For example, instead of immediately asking "Why didn't you study more?" try "I know you wanted a different result. How are you feeling about it?"

When children know a bad result won't change how we see them, they don't have to be so afraid of getting things wrong. Failure can become something they learn from instead of something they feel they need to hide.

If being "good" means pleasing other people, someone else's disappointment can start to feel like proof a child did something wrong. They may learn to read the room before they learn to read themselves.

We can show them a different way. You might say: "Someone else can be disappointed in your choice, and it can still be the right choice for you."

Your child needs to know that you can disagree with them and they can still trust themselves. That matters later, too, with friends, partners and bosses.

Even positive labels can feel like pressure. If adults keep saying:

A child can quietly start to hear:This is who I have to keep being.Then a B isn't just a B. Getting cut from the team isn't just disappointing. Struggling can start to feel like losing a piece of who they are.

Instead of making the achievement their identity, noticewhat went into it. You might say: "You kept going even when that got difficult."

When we separate what children accomplish from who they are, we give them room to become more than whatever they happen to be good at today.

Children need to disagree with us sometimes and discover that the relationship is still okay.

That doesn't mean they make every decision. We are still the parents. We can hold a boundary with our kids and stay connected to them at the same time. You might say: "You're allowed to be angry with my decision. The answer is still no, and we're still okay."

A child shouldn't have to choose between having a voice and feeling close to us. If they feel like they have to give up their voice to stay connected at home, saying no can become much harder everywhere else too.

Our instinct as parents is often to make our children feel better. We fix, reassure, distract or tell them everything will be fine.

Sometimes they need something simpler: "This is hard. I'm here."

Children need to learn that feeling bad doesn't mean something has gone wrong. They can be embarrassed and get through it. They can be nervous and still walk into the room.

We don't have to rescue children from every uncomfortable feeling. Sometimes staying beside them as they experience those feelings is how they discover:I can handle this.

Children already live in a world that measures them: grades, teams, rankings, likes and eventually college admissions, job offers and performance reviews.

The outside world will keep asking: "What can you do?" Home should answer a different question with an emphatic yes:Do I still matter when there's nothing to celebrate?

Sometimes it helps to say it directly: "I love watching you succeed. But you never have to impress me to belong here."

Achievement should add to a child's life. It should never become the only reason they feel worthy.

Reem Raoudais a certified conscious parenting coach, speaker and author dedicated to one core idea: that loving your child and making them feel safe are not the same thing. She is the founder of The Safe Mom and creator ofThe Safe Mom Masterclass, helping parents raise emotionally healthy children through emotional safety, connection and self-awareness. Find her onInstagram.

title: Hurricane Trudy brings heavy rain and strong winds to Mexico’s Pacific coast
content:
Hurricane Trudy lashed parts of Mexico's Pacific coast with heavy rain and strong winds Sunday as the U.S. National Hurricane Center warned of potentially life-threatening flooding and mudslides.

A hurricane warning remained in effect from Manzanillo, Colima, to Cabo Corrientes, Jalisco. The latest NHC data showed the Category 2 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 105 mph (165 kph) moving northwest off Mexico's Pacific coast at 10 mph (17 kph).

Meanwhile, Typhoon Champi was moving away from Guam as a Category 4 super typhoon.

Trudy's center was expected to remain near the Mexican coast through Sunday evening before moving south of the Baja California Peninsula on Monday and Tuesday. A tropical storm warning remained in effect for Las Islas Marias. The warning for the coast east of Punta San Telmo to Lazaro Cardenas was discontinued.

The Mexican Navy urged mariners and coastal residents to exercise extreme caution because of high waves, heavy rain, and the risk of rising rivers, flooding, and landslides in vulnerable areas.

Colima authorities said risks remained low but warned that heavy rainfall could cause damage because successive storms had already saturated the ground along the Pacific coast.

Trudy was expected to bring 4-8 inches (10-20 centimeters) of rain through the weekend, with isolated totals of around 12 inches (30 centimeters) along and near the coast in Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco. The hurricane center warned of potentially life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas with steep terrain.

Also in the Pacific, Champi moved away from Guam on Sunday after passing near the island's southern tip, with sustained winds of 150 mph (240 kph). Late Sunday afternoon, it was 200 miles (320 kilometers) west of Guam, moving west at 14 mph (23 kph), according to the U.S. National Weather Service.

The storm was forecast to weaken through Monday but remain a major typhoon. All tropical cyclone watches and warnings for Guam, Rota, Tinian and Saipan had been canceled.

The governors of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands requested emergency disaster declarations on Friday.

On Saturday, U.S. President Donald Trump approved an emergency declaration for Guam authorizing the Federal Emergency Management Agency to coordinate all federal disaster relief efforts. FEMA announced that federal disaster assistance was available for the territory of Guam to supplement local response efforts following Typhoon Champi.

Airports, harbors and some health facilities in the territories were closed. FEMA said resources were unlikely to reach the islands for three to five days, according to Saturday updates.

The territories are still recovering from super typhoons Sinlaku and Bavi, which struck in April and July, respectively.

title: Top Wall Street analysts are bullish on the growth potential of these 3 stocks
content:
Fears around the artificial intelligence trade and higher pressure on oil prices are weighing on global markets, but a few stocks offer investors solid growth prospects even in choppy times.

Investors with a long-term horizon can look beyond the ongoing volatility and track the recommendations of top Wall Street analysts to pick attractive stocks with strong long-term growth potential.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Health insurerUnitedHealthdelivered better-than-expected results for the third quarter of 2026. The company also raised its full-year earnings outlook, reflecting continued progress on its turnaround plan.

Following the Q3 print, Morgan Stanley analyst Erin Wright reiterated a buy rating on UNH stock with aprice target of $529. "UNH's beat & raise reinforces turnaround momentum, with improving MA [Medicare Advantage]/Optum Health supporting a higher '26 EPS baseline & upside to '27 consensus," said Wright.

The five-star analyst added that better-than-expected performance in the UnitedHealthcare and Optum Health businesses supported another upgrade to the company's 2026 adjusted earnings per share outlook to at least $20.50. Wright noted that UNH raised the earnings guidance despite incremental investments planned for the fourth quarter of 2026.

Furthermore, Wright highlighted management's view that the consensus 2027 EPS of $22.63 was too conservative. Reaching even the low end of the company's 13% to 16% long-term EPS growth target would imply an EPS of $23.17.

Wright raised her 2026 EPS estimate to $20.65 from $19.82 and 2027 EPS to $23.24 from $22.54, reflecting the latest upside and an improving 2026 medical loss ratio to 87.4% from 88.1%. Overall, she believes that UNH's operational performance continues to improve, increasing her confidence in its UHC strategy and Optum Health turnaround execution.

Wright ranks No. 264 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 15%.See UnitedHealth Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Social media giantMeta Platformshas been making headlines since the launch of its Muse AI agent, which isseeing solid traction. Investors look forward to updates on the company's AI strategy when it announces its third-quarter results on Oct. 21.

Heading into Q3 earnings, Guggenheim analyst Michael Morris maintained a buy rating on Meta stock and increased hisprice target to $850from $700, reflecting higher estimates for 2027. He expects Muse usage momentum and engagement levels to shape investor sentiment into the Q3 earnings call.

Specifically, Morris highlighted that, according to Apptopia, Muse reached 1.3 million daily active users in five weeks versus 300,000 in the first week. Given that Muse's current adoption represents less than 0.05% of Meta's 3.6 billion daily active user base, the analyst expects management to prioritize boosting usage over near-term monetization.

"Over time, we believe Muse monetizes primarily through businesses paying to reach consumers through their agents, consistent with the economics of Meta's core advertising business, rather than consumer wallets," said the five-star analyst. He added that the checkout integrations with Shopify and PayPal reflect this framework.

While there are concerns that a rival could overtake Muse or the recently launched Muse Wonder and push Meta into a prolonged cycle of overinvestment, Morris remains bullish due to the company's strong record in scaling WhatsApp and competing strongly with TikTok via Reels as well as free distribution to an extensive user base.

Morris ranks No. 629 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.2%.See Meta Platforms KPIs on TipRanks.

Next is semiconductor companyMarvell Technology. Earlier this month, Marvell held its Investor Day, where it raised its total addressable market estimate to $400 billion by 2030, reflecting solid AI-led demand tailwinds.

After hosting a non-deal roadshow withMarvell's senior management following the Investor Day, Stifel analyst Tore Svanberg reiterated a buy rating on the stock with aprice target of $370.

The five-star analyst said that a major focus of the roadshow was the XPU and XPU Attach mix, as Marvell's Custom business expands toward its FY31 revenue target of $30 billion. In this regard, management reiterated that it expects a balanced mix of XPU and XPU Attach revenue in FY31, though it noted that either segment could grow rapidly enough to shift the mix toward 60/40 or 40/60.

While XPU drove most of the nearly $1.5 billion Custom revenue in FY26, Svanberg expects Marvell's XPU Attach business to grow substantially through the end of the decade, leading to a more balanced mix in this business. At the Investor Day event, the company raised its FY29 Custom target from more than $10 billion to over $12 billion, mainly driven by strength in the XPU Attach business.

Svanberg said that another key topic in the roadshow was whether Marvell can secure enough capacity to meet its raised targets. Management said that it met with suppliers ahead of Investor Day to share its five-year goals and received commitments to support these targets. The analyst believes that Marvell's supply chain commitments give it a competitive edge over rivals as customers seek reliable partners for large-scale infrastructure buildouts.

Svanberg ranks No. 91 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 58% of the time, delivering an average return of 31.8%.See Marvell Technology Statistics on TipRanks.

title: Always on, always listening: New AI devices are pushing legal limits and could put users in jeopardy
content:
Chris Thomas is all-in on AI gadgets.

Thomas, 43, wears a pair ofMeta's camera-equipped glasses, aFieldynote-taking pendant around his neck and a wristband fromAmazon's Bee, all of which record his daily life. A Pittsburgh-based business owner and a livestreamer, Thomas relies on the devices to help him stay organized, pay bills on time and set reminders.

"I'm forgetful AF," Thomas said in an interview. "My life is so crazy that not having to remember to remember is fantastic."

Not everyone is on board with his lifestyle. Earlier this week, a bystander at a local bar noticed his Meta Glasses.

"He was like, 'I don't feel comfortable,'" Thomas said. "I don't turn it off, I take it off completely because people don't really believe it's off."

It's the type of interaction users are increasingly navigating as more tech companies introduce AI-powered, always-listening devices and features, which have been marketed as useful tools to transcribe meetings, keep track of conversations, set reminders and offer personalized recommendations.

The latest example of these gadgets arrived Thursday with Amazon'sBee Frontierwearable and Bee Eclipse, a card-shaped device that attaches to a smartphone. Both devices are designed to record, transcribe and analyze a user's day.

Apple's latest Apple Watch Series 12, unveiled in September, will have Siri Recap, which "ambiently" takes notes throughout the day and generates summaries of conversations. Another feature called Live Rewind can recap 15 seconds of a conversation via a text transcription.

Meta's popular smart glasses can take photos, capture video and record voice notes or reminders. Startups including Plaud and Pocket also developed card-sized note-taking devices, while Friend offers an AI necklace.

The devices have fueled concerns that they could erode privacy, by enabling covert recording without obtaining bystanders' consent and collecting sensitive data that's potentially accessible to others.

Amazon, Google and other makers of voice-activated smart speakers faced similar privacy concerns when their devices first hit the market, in some cases leading to lawsuits and regulatory fines.

But this new generation of AI devices is also testing the limits of privacy law.

Unlike earlier smart speakers that were activated via a so-called "wake word" and sometimes stored recordings or sent audio to the cloud, some of these products can continuously listen, interpret speech, and extract its meaning without retaining the underlying audio. This capability has raised a largely untested question about whether that processing itself can amount to an unlawful interception.

"With new technology like this, my statement is always to embrace with caution," Karen Panetta, dean of graduate education at Tufts' School of Engineering and a fellow at the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, said.

She added, "If I'm giving permission for myself to be recorded, or for everything I look at to be recorded, that doesn't mean everybody else around you has given that consent."

Apple and Amazon appear to have sidestepped some of the privacy concerns that dogged earlier voice assistants.

Applesaysthe feature does not store audio, send recordings to its servers, or involve human review. Amazonhas saidit doesn't store audio from Bee devices, and conversations are processed in a secure environment "where no one, including Amazon, can access your data."

But that may not resolve the legal question.

Many state wiretap and eavesdropping laws are written around whether a private communication was intercepted or its contents were acquired — not simply whether a conventional audio recording was created.

Colin Zick, a privacy and data security attorney at Foley Hoag, said Apple appears to have learned from the first wave of litigation over voice assistants. But the new technology raises questions those earlier cases never had to answer: Can a system that is continuously listening, interpreting speech and turning it into a summary still amount to an interception if it never saves the underlying audio?

Some state laws define interception broadly. Massachusetts, for example, defines an intercepting device to include equipment capable of "transmitting, receiving, amplifying, or recording" a communication, while the "contents" of a communication can include its substance and meaning.

In Zick's view, a device that continuously receives speech and produces a written summary could potentially fall within that language even without retaining an audio file.

And in some states, the bigger legal risk may fall not on Apple, Amazon or other AI gadget makers but on the person wearing the device.

"A non-wearer did not buy the watch, agree to Apple's terms, or choose to have their conversation summarized in the app," Zick said.

Daniel Pi, an associate professor at the University of New Hampshire Franklin Pierce School of Law, said New Hampshire's statute is broad enough that he believes the Watch's new audio-intelligence features would qualify as an interception. The law covers not only recordings, but the "aural or other acquisition" of the contents of a communication.

That could create an unusual situation in which an ordinary consumer turns on a feature built into a mainstream device and, at least technically, runs afoul of state law by using it during a private conversation without everyone's consent.

Pi said a user in New Hampshire could potentially face civil or criminal liability for doing so, though he stressed that the practical risk of prosecution is far lower. It could be difficult to know whether someone had the feature enabled in the first place, and he said he would be surprised to see prosecutors pursue cases involving a bare statutory violation where no one was harmed.

The legal questions are also different from those raised by earlier smart speakers and voice assistants. Those cases often centered on devices mistakenly activating or capturing speech that was not intended as a command. Here, the feature is designed to acquire and interpret the substance of a conversation — and the user has deliberately opted in.

That changes the analysis, Pi said, and could also shift responsibility toward the wearer rather than the technology company itself.

The broader privacy concern extends beyond who is legally responsible.

Michael Stokes, a former CIA officer and senior vice president of emerging technologies at Veilant, said the bigger shift is that people can be swept into AI-powered surveillance without owning or knowingly interacting with the device doing the collecting.

"I think the bystander problem is really the concern I have — that you can be surveilled without owning the technology," Stokes said.

He pointed to the growing number of cameras, microphones, and sensors embedded in consumer devices, from smart glasses to watches and AI recorders. The difference now, he said, is that AI can rapidly interpret what those devices collect and draw meaning from far larger volumes of information than earlier generations of consumer technology.

For Stokes, that makes the Apple Watch part of a much larger change in the privacy landscape. During his time at the CIA, he helped develop the concept of ubiquitous technical surveillance, describing a world in which everyday devices continuously generate information that can reveal identities, locations, and associations.

The concern is not simply that more data can be collected, he said, but that the cost of making sense of it has fallen dramatically.

In the past, Stokes said, intelligence collection could require thousands of hours of work to gather, sort and analyze information about a person. AI increasingly automates that process, making it cheaper and easier to extract useful information from data that may have been gathered incidentally.

That creates a new kind of exposure for people who never opted into the technology in the first place — whether it is a private conversation picked up by a nearby wearable or information collected by a device they do not own.

"We no longer have these pockets of small privacy that we thought we did in the past," Stokes said.

Aida Baradari, founder of the startupDeveillance, is trying to give some control back to people worried about being recorded without their consent.

The company created a hockey puck-shaped gadget, called the Spectre I, that uses AI to scan for nearby devices and sends out "adversarial signals" that scramble a person's speech before microphones can process it.

Baradari said she watched as more AI wearables hit the market and felt users should have a greater say in how they interact with them.

"We need to be able to use technology while not giving up our core values or rights," she said.

title: Vance faces tough questions on Iran war, immigration and more in CBS town hall
content:
Vice PresidentJD Vancefaced tough questions from voters about the Trump administration's policies on data centers, high costs, immigration and his own rhetoric in a town hall on CBS News that aired Saturday night.

The string of sharp questions, some from voters who said they had supported him and PresidentDonald Trump, previewed the rocky path he may face if he runs for president in 2028 and has to answer for the administration's record.

Vance, who said during the town hall there's "of course" a chance he doesn't run for president, faced an especially pointed question about "a failure of leadership" posted by the widow of one of six U.S. soldiers killed by an Iranian drone strike in Kuwait, which occurred the day after Trump started the war with Iran.

"This literally is the first time I've heard of this," Vance said in response.

As he went on, he said, "This job is an amazing honor, but you live in a bit of a bubble and sometimes information doesn't filter up."

After telling the vice president about his late wife, Master Sgt. Nicole Amor, who was killed on March 1, Joey Amor asked about mistakes and fundamental failures that led up to the deaths of those soldiers and how leaders would be held accountable.

Vance seemed taken aback by Amor's questions, saying, "This literally is the first time I've heard of this," and said he wanted to talk with Amor afterward to learn more.

But as Vance went on, he acknowledged mistakes were made and said, "There were issues with where troops were located that we realized was a huge mistake that we could do better on, and we have changed that."

A Michigan man who said he voted for Trump and Vance in 2024 but now plans to vote for Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed pressed Vance about the high gasoline prices resulting from the war. In response, Vance said he recognized that gas prices were too high, and said, "I think it's important to be honest about why they're so elevated."

He said it was because of "what's happening in the Middle East" and that the administration was taking steps to lower prices.

"We've never had a situation like this where you have effectively the largest state sponsor of terrorism that's trying to choke off world energy supply," Vance said, without acknowledging that situation occurred because of the war Trump launched.

He also blamed former PresidentJoe Biden, saying that during his tenure, America's refining capacity was diminished.

But when Vance was pressed on whether the Trump administration owned the current situation, the vice president suggested that looking backward for blame wasn't the way.

"Fundamentally, we are where we are, and you have to, in my view, I'd like to know what is Abdul El-Sayed's solution for the problem that we have right now," Vance said. "It's easy to criticize something that happened seven months ago."

A nun who spoke to Vance about their shared Catholic faith questioned the administration's hardline immigration enforcement tactics, including children who are separated from their parents when the adults are swept up in sweeps, and how that squared with their values.

"We're trying to strike the right balance," Vance said. When moderator Tony Dokoupil asked Vance if the administration is not striking that balance, Vance replied, "I think that is constantly a work in progress."

He admitted that, "Sometimes you have some people who made mistakes. Sometimes you have some people who really screw up."

When Dokoupil asked for specific examples, Vance said the administration has investigated several cases that resulted in further training or discipline for immigration enforcement officers, but they don't advertise them publicly to let investigations play out.

Another voter, who said she became an immigrant five years ago and voted for Vance after becoming a U.S. citizen, asked him pointedly about his recent remarks referring to H1-B visa holders as "foreign indentured servants," and accused him of "scapegoating immigrants for the issues you're supposed to be solving."

"To the extent that my rhetoric has been imperfect here, that's on me," Vance said, before explaining that he was trying to criticize the companies that bring in the workers, not the immigrant workers themselves.

Dokoupil pressed Vance on whether Trump and others in his administration profited from the presidency, including the nearly $1.2 billion the president took in from his crypto businesses last year, according to a federal filing. When asked if he'd seen anything in the White House that made him squeamish, Vance said, "I've never seen anything like that from the president."

He said, though, that there is evidence of corruption in Washington, but he doesn't see evidence of it from the president or the administration.

Vance said he's read articles about allegations, but he investigates claims himself and finds they are not true.

Dokoupil asked Vance about the president's crypto profits, as well as the recent resignation of his ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, over allegations she denies that she leveraged her position for benefits.

"If somebody's selling access to the White House, that's disgusting and despicable, and they should suffer consequences," Vance said.

title: Deaths confirmed after 'serious incident,' fire at Canada military base in Alberta
content:
People were killed and injured in a serious incident that resulted in a fire on one ofCanada'sbusiest military bases in Alberta, Defense Minister David McGuinty said on Saturday.

"I'm saddened to share that there have been both fatalities and injuries as a result of an incident" at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, McGuinty told reporters in Ottawa.

He did not say how many people were killed or injured, or what caused the "tragic" situation at the base in the east-central part of the province, about 210 km (130 miles) east of Edmonton.

A major fire was still burning on Saturday evening, he said, adding: "I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory."

The Canadian military and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are investigating the incident, McGuinty said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney posted on social media that the national government was "working closely with the Government of Alberta and local authorities."

CFB Wainwright had 1,310 military and civilian personnel stationed there as of 2021, according to census data. The town of Wainwright, population about 6,600, is just north of the base.

The municipality posted on social media that the fire had crossed the base fence into the nearby district but no evacuation orders had been issued.

General Jennie Carignan, the chief of Canada's Defense Staff, said on social media that the Canadian forces are fully engaged with federal, provincial and local authorities.

"Our priority remains the welfare of our members, their families and their community," she said.

title: Why hedge funds could be making a bond market shock more likely
content:
Hedge funds' increased presence in global bond markets makes the likelihood of a broader market shock "greater than what it was," Bank of England deputy governor Sarah Breeden told CNBC Thursday.

Breeden — the central bank's deputy governor for financial stability, and a member of its rates-setting Monetary Policy Committee — said the changing mix of bond market investors, and their increased use of leverage, raises the risk of localized market turbulence turning into broader financial stress.

"One of the things that has become increasingly apparent over the last several years is that the investors in our core government bond markets globally have changed," Breeden told CNBC'sSri Jegarajahin an interview Thursday.

"It's not the real money investors, the insurance companies and pension funds, in the way it used to be. It's increasingly hedge funds, and those hedge funds are price-sensitive, leveraged, international. That, of course, means that the likelihood of a shock in one market transmitting to another is greater than what it was."

Breeden was speaking on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand.

With gross assets now standing at about $13 trillion, hedge funds have become an increasingly important part of the global investor landscape, the IMF said on Tuesday.

In its latest Global Financial Stability Report, published Tuesday, the IMF acknowledged hedge funds' role in supporting market liquidity and efficiency.

But it also warned that the hedge fund industry's use of leverage to boost returns, and its tendency to pursue crowded trades, could turbo-charge market stress in times of turmoil.

That, in turn, could spill over into broader financial markets, and areas such as banks' prime brokerage businesses, according to the IMF.

"The source of the shocks are bond markets, and the likelihood of a spillover is higher than it was," Breeden said.

Hedge funds' presence in the global government bond market— particularly their use of so-called "basis trades" — has come under sharper scrutiny this year, following the sharp sell-off in sovereign debt.

Hedge funds held a record 7% of the $30 trillion Treasury market at the end of 2025, according to U.S. Office of Financial Research data published on Aug. 19.

Basis trades are an arbitrage bet in which hedge funds are positioned long in cash Treasurys while shorting their corresponding futures contracts, with the aim of profiting from the price gap. While the price differential between the two is relatively small, hedge funds often employ large amounts of leverage to further inflate returns.

Earlier this month,10-yearand30-year Treasuryyields hit their highest levels since 2002. Across the Atlantic, yields on10-year U.K. government bonds, known as gilts, also touched multi-decade highs.

Yields on France's government bonds, known as OATs, have moved sharply higher in recent weeks amid rising concerns about thecountry's fiscal outlook— fueling fears of a fresh sovereign debt crisis impacting the euro zone.

title: AI rapidly improving, could vastly boost U.S. GDP, Anthropic's Clark tells policymakers
content:
Rapidly improving artificial intelligence capabilities will drive much faster change across all fields, Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark said on Saturday, with one of the company's internal models forecasting that, under certain conditions, it could increase U.S. economic output by almost 50% by 2030.

Clark, speaking at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, said international cooperation was needed to set "unusual and serious rules" for transformative technology, and that policymakers had a shrinking window to act.

Clark said the estimated potential U.S. GDP of $44 trillion, compared with the current level of just over $30 trillion, "sounds very outlandish, I know." But he added that AI was vastly increasing scientific discovery.

He said the forecast assumed "the technology continuing to get better. And if GDP were to grow this much, then economic doctrine suggests that new industries and inventions would need to have been created to power such a major economic expansion".

Clark's remarks come as the company prepares for an initial public offering expected in November that could value the firm at up to $2 trillion.

Clark issued a wake-up call to policymakers about the speed of AI development, saying growing evidence points to a "singularity" in which AI development outpaces human control.

"We should expect that in the coming years, the whole pace of progress of not just AI but science as a whole will speed up, and this will feel confusing and disorienting, and will bring with it great wealth and potentially great peril," he said in a lecture to hundreds of government and finance officials.

AI was a major topic at IMF and World Bank meetings, both as a source of growth that could offset high energy prices and as a potential threat to stability if it falls short of its promise as a productivity game-changer and stock valuations crash.

Officials also expressed worries that AI could destroy certain jobs and leave some countries behind.

But Clark, a former journalist who serves as Anthropic's "head of public benefit," painted a picture of a rosy future where AI was a force multiplier for scientific discovery, solving mathematical, engineering and biological problems, including new drug discovery, as human researchers are supplemented by hundreds or thousands of AI assistants.

More countries can join the AI revolution by helping build the data center computing capacity needed to power AI, he said.

Clark cautioned that global leaders need to understand how powerful AI will become and make urgent choices about how to regulate the technology.

"Being able to use AI for science opens us up to the misuses of science as well, biological and cyber weapons and things we cannot yet imagine, and we have many choices to make," he said.

Biological research, where AI has already created new viruses, is an area "where we want the strictest human oversight and transparency to maintain safety."

Despite recent high-profile incidents in which rogue AI systems escaped testing environments and hacked websites and databases, he said AI remained under human control. But the window to impose safeguards was shrinking as AI became more capable and was now "a small number of years."

Clark also acknowledged that AI was causing job losses in some fields with "high AI exposure," such as call centers and customer service. But in other fields, such as scientific research, he said AI was boosting employment, and a major unknown was its potential to create jobs in entirely new industries.

title: Trump touts his power at Kentucky rally to energize voters ahead of midterm elections
content:
PresidentDonald Trumptouted his power in his second go-around in the White House Saturday while rallying in Kentucky to bolster Republican turnout as his party struggles in the midterms, saying, "I can do stuff that is unbelievable."

Trump, who spoke in the city of Highland Heights to boost Republican candidates including Ed Gallrein for the U.S. House, was riffing on his decision to change how the U.S. government refers to the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America.

"I don't think I could have done this in my first term. This is a much more powerful term," Trump said. "Google wouldn't have taken my call in the first. Now, they kiss my ass."

"Well, I also changed the name of a lake in Canada to the Lake America," he continued, referring to Lake Ontario.

Trump's self-proclaimed power clashes with voter frustration over how he's wielded it, with tariffs and the Iran war driving up prices and more Americans seeing the president as looking out for his own interests, not the country's.

With control of both chambers of Congress on the line, and with it the prospects of Democratic-led investigations of his administration should they win, Trump has put himself at the fore for voters even as Republicans privately worry he's a liability.

Trump nominated one of his personal lawyers to serve as attorney general, ordered military strikes on accused drug smuggling boats, is trying to put his name on the Kennedy Center, and has enriched himself and his family while he's been in office.

While meandering through topics onstage in Kentucky, Trump touched on gas prices, saying the war with Iran would end soon — an assertion he's made many times over the nearly eight-month conflict — and that gas prices would drop to lower than before. The crowd cheered.

Trump rehashed his dubious promise that if Republicans win the House and the Senate, then every adult American would get $5,000. That would most likely cost more than $1 trillion and require congressional approval, while exacerbating the country's nearly $1.8 trillion annual budget deficit.

At Saturday's rally, Trump added a new conditional promise for Kentucky. That if Republicans win, he said, the Department of Defense would invest in revitalizing a drug manufacturing facility in the state.

title: Semiconductor market to remain solid ‘at least through next year,’ South Korea finance minister says
content:
The semiconductor boom will last at least through 2027, South Korean finance minister Lee Hyoung-Il said on Saturday.

"For now, our view is that we can sustain this growth at least through next year," Lee told CNBC on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok. "That's because the gap between demand and supply for semiconductors is still very wide, and supply is still being expanded."

His comments come aftersemiconductor stocks fell sharplythis week, hurt by investor concerns about interest rate hikes and rising competition from Chinese companies. South Korean chip stocks likeSK Hynixand Seoul Semiconductor were part of the sell-off, along with U.S. giants likeNvidia.

Chip stocks have fueled volatility in South Korea's stock market this year, Lee said. He attributed the market's wild swings to the semiconductor industry's larger share of the economy than in other countries. Despite the market swings, South Korea's economy is "solid," Lee said.

On Thursday, an opinion column inMaeil Business Newspaper, a prominent South Korean publication, urged the country's government to prepare for the coming slowdown in the artificial intelligence boom. The author said two experts expect a "flood of new supply" of semiconductors that will turn the memory market "into a red ocean" by 2029, according to aCNBC translation.

While South Korea's semiconductors may be driving volatility in its stock market, the industry has also fueled tax growth. Lee said the country expects to collect more taxes than initially projected this year.

South Korea will ultimately be in a stronger fiscal position because of the chip boom, he added.

title: Investors are buying up vast tracts of timberland across U.S. in one of market's longest-term bets
content:
When the economy andthe marketlook shaky,goldandgovernment bondsare the traditional places to park money. Lately, some investors have also been looking at something more rooted: timber.

The pitch is easy to like: a back-to-basics, natural asset that grows on its own, matures into a harvest and can be cashed in all while you use it to hunt, pitch a tent, or forage.

Institutions have been buying timberland at a rate of one million acres per year, according to Bank of America, and some financial advisors say individual investors, includingyounger Americans priced outof the housing market, are also taking a look at the asset class. But it is far from a rush, and investors who already own timberland caution that it may not be very profitable in the short term.

"Timber is a very low return investment. I have curtailed my investments," said Pat Dorn, founder of Anchor Investment Management, a fee-only advisory firm in Columbia, South Carolina, and a former chairman of the South Carolina Forestry Association. Dorn owns 2,500 acres of timberland in South Carolina's booming upstate region. Dorn said the problem is that right now more timber is being grown than is needed in a sluggish housing economy.

"Supply beats demand, and that causes flat prices. Timber is not an investment I would make currently," Dorn said.

Nationally, the Bureau of Labor Statistics'producer price indexfor logs, bolts, timber, pulpwood and wood chips ticked up in September, but prices have been mostly on the decline since summer 2022. This measures prices received by producers for those products, rather than timberland values or investment returns. Over the very long-term, prices have climbed substantially.

Financial institutions point to the asset class as one of interest specifically for the long-term investor.

Ken Shepard, head of specialty asset management at Bank of America Private Bank said that timberland is not a tactical asset class that can be easily entered or exited in response to short-term market conditions. "We view it as a strategic, long-term investment supported by several favorable secular trends, including the continued expansion of the timber industry in the U.S. South and growing demand for wood products beyond traditional construction uses," Shepard said.

For example, he said, demand forwood pelletsused in bioenergy, whilecontroversial, has increased significantly. In addition, timberland values are benefiting from strong demand fromrecreational and lifestyle buyers, providing support for land prices beyond the income generated from timber harvesting.

The National Council of Real Estate Investment Fiduciaries' Timberland Property Index, which tracks privately held U.S. timber properties owned at least partly on behalf of institutional investors, posted a total return of 0.95% in the second quarter of 2026, comprising 0.34% income and 0.61% appreciation.

Bank of America's 2026 outlook reported that the one-million-acre annual pace of buying is a three-year streak of dealmaking it expects to continue.

According to Bank of America, timber managers acquired 55% of all acres that changed hands in 2025 against just 15% sold. Institutions are playing the long game. Large timberland managers buy for pension funds and endowments that can wait decades, and that can make bets on a longer-term recovery in a currently slumping U.S. housing market that will be good for lumber pricing. But a private owner living through today's market sees things differently.

Dorn pointed out that timber companies buy less mature trees for pulpwood, which goes into paper towels or notebook paper, and those trees can take 12-14 years to mature. The chip-and-saw variety of trees take a little bit longer, while the big prize, timber cut for houses, can take 25 years. "That is where the top value is," he said.

According to Dorn, what landowners are paid for standing timber varies depending on what the trees are used for. Pine pulpwood consists of trees ground into paper and packaging, while pine sawtimber is made up of larger trees cut into lumber for homebuilding. Meanwhile, hardwood sawtimber, consists of oak and other big trees used in flooring, furniture and pallets. Each product feeds a different set of buyers, so one can climb while others fall.

South Carolina Forestry Commissiondatashow statewide average pine pulpwood stumpage prices, what buyers pay landowners for standing timber, fell from $5.67 a ton in the third quarter of 2025 to $3.79 in the third quarter of 2026, a decline of about 33%. Pine sawtimber prices fell about 6% over the same period, from $22.78 to $21.47 a ton, while hardwood sawtimber prices rose about 40%, from $16.04 to $22.52.

Historically, pulpwood has been as high as $12 to $18 a ton, according to Dorn, and twenty years ago, soft timber was in the $35-$40 range. He said those prices could make a comeback if the housing market ever recovers, because pine sawtimber is cut into lumber for new homes, so its price tends to follow home building.

Strategically placed, timber may not be a bad investment, according to Dorn, though that would be because of the land itself more than the timber. "The return is in the land, not the timber," Dorn said.

He advises anyone thinking of investing in timberland to scout for prime parcels of land located outside growing metro areas that may be poised to pop as the local population keeps spreading. "If one hopes to buy land near growing metro areas and holds on to it, timber is a reasonable way to keep it earning something — a very low return — while you hold that land," he said.

Michael Martin, a timber owner in western New York and vice president of market strategy at brokerage firm TradingBlock,says timberland can be a good long-term investment but the reality of being an owner belies the romantic image of acres of untouched timberland. It is not as passive an investment class as it may seem to be.

Direct ownership is highly illiquid and comes with management costs, property taxes, harvesting expenses, exposure to local timber markets, and risks including wildfire, pests, disease and trespassers hunting or cutting trees.

And when it is time to harvest timber, you need to make sure you are getting the best deal. "If you simply go with a small local outfit without getting competing bids, you don't always know if you're getting the best price," Martin said.

He also said timber prices are very local and can impact whether it's a solid investment.

"I am constantly checking stumpage reports because timber prices are extremely local. An oak tree in western New York may have a completely different value from one in the Adirondacks," Martin said.

In addition, partial timbering every ten years or so has barely covered the property taxes. "At the end of the day, I barely break even," he added.

Some in local real estate and investing markets say younger buyers are curious, though firsthand evidence is hard to find.

"As a millennial and a realtor, I understand the appeal. I've thought about buying timberland myself," said Jake Kennedy, a Nashville-based realtor, noting that his generation has lived through the dot-com crash, the Great Recession, a pandemic, huge swings in housing and now inflation. "One lesson from all of that we have learned is that scarcity matters when it comes to places to park your money," Kennedy said, adding as examples that more IPOs can be announced or new crypto created.

"But you can't manufacture another 500 acres of land," Kennedy said. "Timber itself is a resource that takes decades to grow. And there is something reassuring about owning an asset that is tangible," he added. But he also cautioned that timber's durability doesn't mean profitability. Trees can be temperamental and subject to many variables.

The people Kennedy has spoken with see timberland as a relatively safe place to park money, he said, because demand for timber products isn't going away. "In the meantime, yes, hunting is a common activity while owners are waiting for the investment to grow and mature, literally," he said.

"I don't think my generation is suddenly giving up on houses and becoming timber barons. However, I do think we are a lot more interested in alternative places to store wealth than previous generations might have been," he added.

For many millennials, homeownership has become increasingly difficult due to elevated home prices, higher mortgage rates, and limited inventory in many markets. "As a result, some investors are looking for alternative ways to participate in real assets and potentially build equity without purchasing a home directly," said Nadeem Kassam, chief investment strategist at Marnoa Private Wealth Counsel.

Outside direct or institutional fund ownership, there are timber ETFs and timber-focused funds that provide exposure to a theme that is closely tied to long-term housing demand and construction activity, though they remain highly niche investments in an ETF market now valued in the trillions of dollars.

Kassam pointed to the iShares Global Timber & Forestry ETF (WOOD), with roughly $260 million in assets, and the Invesco MSCI Global Timber ETF (CUT), which has roughly $30 million in assets.

"The investment case is supported by persistent housing shortages across many parts of the U.S. and growing bipartisan support for policies aimed at increasing housing supply and improving affordability. If these efforts lead to increased homebuilding over time, demand for lumber and wood products could benefit," Kassam said.

title: Berkshire shares buck market sell-off, rally to highest since Buffett said he would step down as CEO
content:
(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign uphereto receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)

Berkshire Hathaway shares closed Friday at their highest level since Warren Buffett told shareholders at the May 2025 annual meetinghe planned to step down as CEO at the end of that year.

The day before that Saturday surprise, both theClass AandClass Bshares had closed at all-time highs.

Over the next three months, they lost more than 14% of their value as investors worried a "Buffett premium" was dissolving.

It's been more than a year since their post-meeting low in August of 2025, and the recovery has not been a straight line, but BRK.A ended Friday at $798,000, just 1.4% below its all-time closing high of $809,350.

The B shares finished at $532.02, also 1.4% under their all-time closing high of $539.80.

A loss Thursday broke a 10-session winning streak that added 5% to Berkshire's stock prices but they rebounded with gains of more than 1% Friday.

CNBC Prothinksinvestors may be happy Berkshire is spending some of its big cash pile under CEO Greg Abel, with$4.5 billion of buybacks in Q2, investments inAlphabet,Taylor Morrison Home,Lennar, (although there haven't been any buys of that stock since October 2), and now,Bending Spoons. (More on that below).

It also notes Keefe, Bruyette & Woods analyst Meyer Shields believes higher short-term interest rates are helping to lift the shares.

Berkshire still has roughly $360 billion in cash, "a good symbol of continued patience under the new CEO," and those higher rates mean "they'll be making more money" on that money.

In addition, its insurance operations have benefited from aquiet hurricane seasonso far.

Higher oil pricesare good for its $19 billion stake inChevron, which closed Friday at an all-time high after gaining almost 36% since the start of July. Berkshire's energy-relatedsubsidiariesare also getting a tailwind.

And recently, Berkshire may be getting a boost as investorsshift away from high-flying AI and tech stocksand turn to"old" economy names.

For example,Coca-Cola, a long-time Buffett favorite and now a$37.6 billion holding, also closed Friday at an all-time high, perhaps with some extra help fromKFC's switch from Pepsi to Coke. It's up 34% year-to-date.

Berkshire's position has gained $2.4 billion since last Friday, overtaking Alphabet to become the third largest stake in its portfolio. (See the full top 10 below.)

Berkshire's B shares have cut their June 1 deficit of 17.5 percentage points versus theS&P 500by almost two-thirds.

They are now 6.0 percentage points behind the benchmark for the year.

Berkshire Hathaway's surprising bet of close to $1 billion onBending Spoonsis paying off big, at least in the short term.

The Italian company, whichbegan trading on Nasdaqin the U.S. in July, buys cast-off internet names like AOL, Evernote, and Vimeo, uses AI to cut costs, and deploys the savings to make more acquisitions.

In late July,CNBC Pro said, "Wall Street is buzzing," and "analysts ... see big gains ahead."

The tech stock is decidedly not a typical Berkshirevalue play, trading at a large multiple to its earnings.

But before Wall Street's open Wednesday morning, a Bending Spoonsnews releaserevealed Berkshire is investing a "further" $330 million in the company by purchasing 10 million newly issued shares at $33 per share in aprivate placement.

That was already an almost 12% discount from Tuesday's closing price of $37.86 and thenews sent Bending Spoons shares even higher.

They hit an intraday high of $58.56 before closing up 41% at $53.46 on Wednesday.

Bending Spoons shares are up 24.3% over the three trading days since the revelation, after giving up a chunk of their earlier gains inFriday's tech sell-offto end at $47.07.

That's a solid 42.6% higher than Berkshire's $33 purchase price for a profit, on paper, of nearly $141 million.

But what's that "further" in Bending Spoon's statement?

The release also disclosed, apparently for the first time, that Berkshire invested $600 million at Bending Spoon's IPO more than three months ago.

The release doesn't specify how many shares Berkshire bought in July, and Bending Spoons wouldn't confirm my math, but assuming Berkshire paid the $29 per share IPO price, that initial purchase would have been almost 20.7 million shares.

That puts Berkshire's holding now at close to 30.7 million shares, which would be worth more than $1.4 billion at Friday's close, a gain of 55.3% for its overall investment of $930 million.

Bending Spoon's release also says the "new investment brings Berkshire Hathaway's ownership to 4%."

The company told me in an email it hasn't "specifically disclosed" how manyoutstanding sharesit has now, "but we had 635 million fully diluted weighted average shares outstanding in Q2, we issued 34 million shares as part of the IPO, and we will be issuing an additional 10 million as part of this transaction."

Using those numbers, Berkshire's presumed 30.7 million shares are a 4.5% stake, and that's what I've put in theBerkshire Portfolio Trackerfor now.

We may learn more next month about exactly how many shares Berkshire bought in the IPO when its portfolio snapshot as of September 30 is due to be disclosed.

Another unknown: who at Berkshire made the call to take a stake in Bending Spoons.

Bending Spoons CEO and Co-Founder Luca Ferrari shares Wall Street's enthusiasm about Berkshire's investments, saying in the news release the Omaha company "has been among the finest and most respected capital allocators in the world, and is a longstanding inspiration for Bending Spoons."

Morningstar'sGreggory Warren (who was one of the designated analyst questioners at Berkshire shareholders meetings from2014to2019)writesthe Bending Spoons buy, along with Berkshire'snow $36 billion stakeinAlphabet, show "the firm is finally moving out of its comfort zone to find places to put capital to work, which should be viewed as a positive for long-term investors."

AtBarron's, Andrew Bary says, "Many Berkshire holders would like to see the company invest more heavily in stocks given the company's $350 billion-plus in cash, but Bending Spoons was a surprise" given its high valuation.

Some links may require a subscription:

Warren Buffett defends Coca-Cola, a big and long-time Berkshire Hathaway holding, against health concerns over sugary beverages.

WARREN BUFFETT: Yeah well — people have been drinking Coca-Cola since 1886, so I imagine that there's been some —

I don't know of any study that's been made on the lifetime of heavy users of Coca-Cola versus people who drink nothing but water.

But speaking for myself, I'm 84, literally one-quarter of all the calories I've consumed in the last 30 years have been Coca-Cola. And I don't see how anybody can feel any better than I feel.

I am one-quarter Coca-Cola, and I can tell you, I haven't missed a day of work, you know — since I had the prostate cancer — radiation — three years ago. And I don't think the prostate cancer was caused (laughs) by Coca-Cola.

So — I — and all my friends drink it like crazy.

So there's 1.9 billion eight-ounce servings of Coca-Cola products sold around the world today, and there will be more than 1.9 billion a year from now, and more than that five years from now, and more than that ten years from now.

And that's been true.  And some people will like other things, and — and if they like broccoli and Brussels sprouts, God bless them, you know, but don't invite me for dinner.  (Laughter)

Also, Buffett's annual letters to shareholders are highly recommended reading. There are collectedhere on Berkshire's website.

-- Alex Crippen, Editor, Warren Buffett Watch

title: How to get a same-day personal loan
content:
Getting approved for a personal loan doesn't always mean the money will be available right away.Same-day fundingis possible, but it depends on the lender, when you accept the offer and how quickly your bank processes the deposit.

Here's how to get your loan funds the same day you're approved.

Many online lenders offer same-day funding. Traditional banks and credit unions may take longer, but some do offer same- or next-day funding, especially for existing customers.To qualify for same-day funding from any lender, you typically need to submit your application, get approved and electronically sign your loan agreement by a specific time of day, often between 2:30 p.m. and 6:00 p.m. ET on a business day.

OneMain Financialsaysfunds can be available in as little as one hour, provided your loan application is approved by 12:00 p.m. local timeand the money is disbursed to a bank-issued debit card. (If it's issued by check or ACH, it may take one to two days.) It considers borrowers with bad or fair credit, and has no minimum credit score requirement.

OneMain Financial allows borrowers to use their vehicle as collateral to improve approval odds and unlock better rates and larger loan amounts.

See if you're pre-approved for a personal loan offer.

We like that OneMain accepts borrowers with bad credit and offers secured loans and fast funding. However, its minimum APR is on the high side and the $30,000 financing maximum may be too low if you need a larger loan.

*You must complete a loan application and continue to meet any criteria used to select you for a loan offer. Not all applicants are approved.Loan approval and actual loan terms depend on applicant's state of residence and ability to meet OneMain Financial credit standards such as a responsible credit history, sufficient income after monthly expenses, and if applicable, availability of eligible collateral.

Not all approved applicants qualify for larger loan amounts, lower APRs, or the most favorable loan terms.For example, larger loan amounts typically require a first lien on a motor vehicle that is no more than ten years old, meets our value requirements, and is titled in applicant's name with valid insurance. APRs are generally higher on loans not secured by a vehicle.

Example Loan:A $6,000 loan with a 24.99% APR that is repayable in 60 monthly installments would have monthly payments of $176.07.

OneMain charges origination fees allowed by law.Depending on the state where the loan is opened, the origination fee may be either a flat amount or a percentage of the loan amount. Flat fees vary by state, ranging from $25 to $500. Percentage-based fees vary by state, ranging from 1% to 10% of the loan amount subject to certain state limits on the fee amount.

For information about these fees and minimum and maximum loan sizes available in certain states, visitomf.com/loanfees.
