title: U.S. presses China on Mastercard, Citigroup market access in bilateral Bangkok talks, official says
content:
BANGKOK – U.S. officials pressed Beijing on market access issues forMastercard IncandCitigroup Incduring at least two bilateral meetings with Chinese counterparts in Bangkok this week, according to a U.S. Treasury official.

The Treasury delegation, led by Deputy Secretary Francis Brooke, held bilateral meetings with officials from the People's Bank of China and the finance ministry on the sidelines of the Group of 20 finance meetings and the IMF-World Bank annual gathering this week, the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss the closed-door meetings.

The talks included market access for U.S. companies, including Mastercard,Visaand Citigroup, the official said, adding that regulatory approval was part of the agreement reached during the meeting betweenPresidents Donald Trumpand Xi Jinping during the latter's state visit in Washington last month.

The sideline meetings in Bangkok continued discussions on implementing these deals, the official said.

The PBOC, China's National Financial Regulatory Administration, China Securities Regulatory Commission, Chinese embassies in Singapore and Thailand, the U.S. Treasury Department press office and Visa did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment. Citigroup and Mastercard declined to comment.

The progress follows China's Oct. 13 approval for Visa Inc. tobegin preparing a wholly owned domestic card-clearing business. Visa has up to a year to prepare before it applies for an operating license,the PBOC has said.

China has opened much of its financial sector to foreign firms since 2018, gradually lifting foreign ownership caps on services such as securities, futures and fund management. It still limits cross-border capital flows and has kept state-backed domestic players dominant in payments.

Mastercard currently operates yuan card payments in China through a local joint venture with NetsUnion Clearing Corp., which began operating in 2024. The pending approval would allow it to operate as an independent entity, the person said.

Citigroup — which has hired several dozen employees for its China unit — is seeking a wholly owned securities license to conduct A-share brokerage, underwriting, research and principal trading businesses in the onshore market, two people familiar with the industry said, requesting anonymity for discussing private matters.

One of the two people close to Citigroup said the bank planned to increase its China securities staff to about 100.

The bank applied in late 2021, andReuters reported lastmonth that approval could come soon.

Trump and Xi are expected to meet in person for the third time this year in Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in November.

"The move suggests the US-China trade environment remains benign, and Beijing is keen to keep up the momentum," said Dan Wang, China director at Eurasia Group.

Licensing U.S. financial firms is a "limited concession" on market access, she said, though it signals China is continuing to open up, and "this should marginally bolster investor confidence in Chinese assets."

title: OpenAI Saudi national bugging case shows threat to U.S. leadership in AI: DNI Clayton
content:
U.S. companies and the Trump administration both "need to be wary" of foreignespionageattempts as the race forartificial intelligencedominance continues, Director of National IntelligenceJay Claytontold CNBC on Friday.

AI "amplifies" existing cybersecurity risks toward U.S. digital infrastructure, which is interconnected with critical systems related to everything from public goods to the national defense and global communications, Clayton said on "Squawk Box."

It's "why we're focused on hardening those systems" and using "our commitment to continue to lead to stay ahead of those nefarious actors," said Clayton, who leads a newWhite House AI task force.

Clayton was asked how concerned Americans should be with the threat of foreign spying in light of the recently revealed case charging Saudi nationalAbdulrahman Alfozanwith allegedly installing a recording device in anOpenAIexecutive conference room. Alfozan has not been charged with espionage; the federal charge involves alleged interception of oral communications.

Alfozan, who was an OpenAI employee, had booked aone-way plane ticketto Saudi Arabia with his wife and another family member prior to his arrest, according to federal prosecutors.

"The short answer to your question is espionage, both commercial espionage, and I would say state-sponsored espionage, are realities," Clayton said.

"It's something that our private sector companies need to be wary of. We, as a government, need to be wary of," he said.

The OpenAI incident "shows the lengths that people will go to try and supplant our leadership in this, or at least stay close to us in this emerging technology," Clayton said.

An ex-CIA official, who asked not to be named because they were discussing information that is not public, told CNBC this week that the case is "probably the tip of the iceberg."

Clayton, who was appointed AI czar earlier this month, said that the task force's "very good" inaugural meeting at the White House on Thursdaybuilt on the accordsigned by PresidentDonald Trumpand a number of AI leaders at the White House last month. Trump had described the agreement, which includes industry pledges to police AI risks itself, as "morally binding."

The task force also established three subcommittees that are focused on different AI-related issues. One is tasked with reporting and response, another with assessing critical infrastructure and working with the private sector, and a third with law enforcement and responsibility, Clayton said.

The DNI reiterated to CNBC that the Trump administration is intent on staying ahead in the AI race.

"We're not the only ones developing it. There are vectors in this technology that are coming from some of our known adversaries and competitors," he said. "The Chinese, the Russians, the Iranians, the North Koreans all have significant technical capability. We need to stay ahead of them."

title: Schwab to create 'tax-aware' strategy that's been attracting billions from wealthy investors
content:
When Charles Schwab released its quarterly earnings on Thursday, it wasn't the quarterly earnings per share print inthe numbersthat caught the attention of those who manage money for wealthy stock investors — it was a $60.7 billion figure. That was reported in a detail about margin loan balances which increased 14% quarter-over-quarter to $187.9 billion, including a whopping $60.7 billion related to what are known as "tax-aware" long/short strategies used by many registered investment advisors.

These strategies have been booming as a way for the wealthy tosuper-charge tax-loss harvestingapproaches to stock gains and losses. According to one estimated provided byTax Alpha Insiderto CNBC in September, total assets in TALS surged to more than $170 billion this year from $2 billion in 2022.

Now Schwab is planning to take a bigger piece of that action. Onthe earnings call, Schwab CEO Rick Wurster said in response to a question from UBS analyst Mike Brown that the broker will launch its own version of the tax-aware long-short strategy.

"Obviously, the tax advantage long/short products have been a meaningful driver of client demand and asset gathering across the industry. There is an increasing number of funds coming to market, and so given Schwab's positioning and client interest in the category, do you see an opportunity to launch a proprietary solution?" Brown asked.

"I do expect us to have an offering," Wurster said. "We already have a great direct indexing capability today that has had wonderful performance in terms of tax alpha and delivering for clients, and I expect us to be able to deliver an extended version of that on long/short. ... Certainly another way we can deliver monetization, but more importantly, it is a way we can deliver sustainable long/short strategies to our clients in a way that is operationally and financially manageable over the longer term," Wurster said.

With the stock market posting big gains for multiple years in a row, the wealthy are looking for more ways to shield capital gains from taxes, according to a recent report from CNBCInside Wealth's Robert Frank. The situation is similar for business owners cashing out and executives with hefty stock compensation packages, and for employees at firms that have gone public in recent years. For the brokers and investment advisors, the products offer relatively high fees and attract new wealthy clients.

Wealthy investors already use direct indexing strategies on platforms including Schwab to pair up stock gains and losses in a tax efficient way. The issue that wealthy investors run into with standard tax-loss harvesting is that fewer and fewer losses become available to harvest over time, according to an overview of TALS from advisor research platformKitces. "Because on average, the market tends to rise, and so in a diversified portfolio most positions will eventually rise far enough above their cost basis that even subsequent downturns don't result in taxable losses, while for positions that do continue to decline there's only a finite amount of losses they can actually generate (because their market value – and cost basis – can only go down to zero)," it wrote.

Tax-aware long-short strategies get around this by adding leverage on both the long and short side of an existing portfolio, with the investor buying more positions and increasing the number of potential losses to harvest. That allows the portfolio to remain "economically neutral ... And because short positions can theoretically generate an infinite amount of losses (since they decline when markets rise), TALS portfolios are less likely to run out of losses to harvest over time than standard long-only portfolios," Kitces noted.

Brent Sullivan of Tax Alpha Insider noted ina post on Xon Thursday that advisors will have many questions about the Schwab products, which he noted should not be referred to as "funds" — UBS analyst Brown used that terminology in his question. Sullivan wrote that it is reasonable to speculate that a Schwab product could "meaningfully lower" the assets under management minimum requirement typical on these products, but it is also an open question as to whether the products will only be available to Schwab advisers and only on Schwab's platform.

Wurster provided few details, and no timeline for a launch. "We are thrilled about that, working on it, and we will give more updates in future calls as to when that may launch," he said.

The government has been takinga more aggressive stanceon tax avoidance strategies and some though not all "tax alpha" strategies of the wealthy, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and the IRS recently issuing a notice over the use of sophisticated ETF strategies to shield capital gains from taxation. The notice also expressed interest in "tax-aware" strategies typically structured as partnerships or separately managed accounts, but according to ananalysisfrom law firm Ropes & Gray, it also made clear that "tax-aware" itself is not a cause for concern and year-end tax loss harvesting is a well-established practice.

title: SpaceX AI policy leader grilled by NYC Council on Grok safety, sexualized images
content:
SpaceXartificial intelligence policy leader Gabriela Castillo Madrid faced a tough line of questioning from NYC Council Speaker Julie Menin and other members on Friday as part of a council investigation into AI safety.

When Castillo Madrid claimed that the company had appropriate "safeguards" in place around its AI products, Menin immediately confronted her.

"I'm going to completely push back on that," Menin said. "I mean, just this morning — myself and my team — we put our own names, my own name, into Grok, and there's absolutely a sexualized image of myself. So then, how is it that within a second, I could find a sexualized image of myself using Grok?"

Castillo Madrid responded that the company has "strict controls" and would have the safety team look into that specific instance.

NYC Council Member Carmen De La Rosa, who leads the council's tech committee, told Castillo Madrid that "it is disgusting" that Grok enables users to easily "sexualize" images of real women without their consent.

"I just don't understand how you can say that there are these safe models," Menin said. "It's just unacceptable."

Castillo Madrid appeared in front of the council's tech committee by video.

Elon Musk'saerospace, defense tech and AI company originally evaded requests and a subpoena from the city council toappearalongside leaders fromOpenAI,Anthropic,GoogleandMetaon Oct. 5. SpaceXagreedto testify earlier this week after the council threatened to have its subpoena enforced by a judge.

The council opened its probe following a month of intense debate surrounding the risks posed by advanced AI models, and is aiming to use testimony and information unearthed through the investigation to guide new regulations.

Before Castillo Madrid took a role in government affairs at SpaceX earlier this year, she worked at X, Musk's social media company that's now owned by SpaceX, according to herLinkedIn profile. Prior to that, she spent almost three years at the U.S. Department of Commerce.

De La Rosa asked Castillo Madrid how many whistleblowers the company has fired, to which Castillo Madrid said she was "not aware" of any.

"I just want to interject for a minute because Devin Kim, one of your former employees, was reportedly fired after he sounded the alarm about serious safety concerns," Menin said.

"I'm not aware with that specific case," Castillo Madrid responded, adding that the company has a culture where "everybody has a an ability to say something when they see something."

Kim is now President of the nonprofit Center for AI Safety, a think tank focused on AI risks and safety.

Kim began his testimony before the council by outlining his experience as one of the first employees at xAI, saying that he "built the systems that researchers use to train and evaluate Grok." Kim said that he started raising concerns in January 2025 and those worries were shut down by his manager.

"My supervisor responded that AI safety was useless, and that AI would kill us and all anyways," he said.

Kim appeared by video, along with his attorney, following Castillo Madrid's questioning.

Kim said under prior standards at the company, "tasteful nudity was acceptable and is the goal."

"During my time there, there were only three employees working on AI safety, many of whom left after I resigned," Kim said. "And I think in large part due to the frustration with how safety was being handled."

The council also pressed Castillo Madrid about other areas of misuse with Grok and the types of safeguards that were in place.

Councilmember Mercedes Narcisse asked why the company promoted the idea of users uploading X-rays to Grok, asking if that was safe and if HIPPA protections applied.

SpaceX's Castillo Madrid said Grok is "not meant to be a clinician, a doctor," adding, "in terms of privacy, users decide whether their Grok conversations are used to train our models or not."

Narcisse said it was dangerous to tell people "openly on X, to put their MRI, X-rays," into Grok and expect "a definite answer" on health matters. The council member then upbraided the SpaceX representative for the vagueness of some of her replies.

"You're supposed to give us answers, you're not," she said.

In merging SpaceX with xAI in February, Musk combined his AI and social networking business with his rocket launch company, which also owns the Starlink satellite internet service. The merger put SpaceX in control of AI model Grok, which is used by some federal agencies, including thePentagon.

SpaceXwent publicin June and is now valued at about $2 trillion. In August, SpaceX completed a $60 billion acquisition of AI coding startup Cursor.

In skipping the earlier NYC Council hearing, SpaceX avoided direct questioning from a member of the U.K. Parliament, Jess Asato, who testified about experiencing AI-enabled online harassment.

Asato is suing xAI in the U.K. after Grok users created and distributed sexualized images of her online without her consent. She's seeking damages, alleging misuse of her private information and breaches of European data protection rules.

According to theBBC, Asato criticized SpaceX for its "arrogance" in not appearing last week.

SpaceX didn't respond to a request for comment ahead of the meeting.

title: Blue Origin plans $330 million Florida expansion to ramp New Glenn launches
content:
Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin said Friday it plans to make extensive upgrades to its Florida launch facilities with the goal of supporting multiple flights per week by the end of the decade.

The company will add two more launch and landing pads for New Glenn, its heavy-lift, partially reusable rocket. A $330 million expansion to its Rocket Park campus in Cape Canaveral, expected to be complete in the summer of 2027, will enable it to produce up to 150 upper stages of its New Glenn rocket annually, Blue Origin saidin a blog post.

"These investments are centered on one goal: building the capacity to support more missions, more reliably, and more efficiently," Ian Richardson, Blue Origin's senior vice president of operations, wrote in the post. "As we look ahead, this infrastructure is designed to support multiple flights per week by the end of the decade."

Blue Origin is working to ramp up its launch cadence as it vies to compete with its chief rival,Elon Musk'sSpaceX, for commercial and government customers.

Blue OriginCEO Dave Limptold CNBC's Morgan Brennan last month that the company's first outside funding round is "oversubscribed." The company had raised $10 billion for the round, valuing it at $140 billion,The Wall Street Journalreported.

The company is also recovering from a setback in May, when one of itsNew Glennrockets exploded on the launchpad.Blue Originhas been aggressively restoring the launchpad with a goal of returning New Glenn to flight by the end of 2026.

As part of the upgrades, Blue Origin said it's building a new customer integration facility with the U.S. Space Force at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station that will enable it to "prepare multiple missions at once" when it's up and running.

Blue Origin has invested more than $3 billion in its infrastructure and facilities in Florida, which now spans more than 20 sites across the state's Brevard and Orange counties, with more than 5,000 employees, Richardson said.

The space industry is also grappling with a launch capacity shortage, as SpaceX has stopped offering commercial rides on its workhorseFalcon 9rocket to prioritize its massive Starship rocket. That's spurred a flurry of investment, with $92.5 billion invested in the commercial space sector in the first three quarters of 2026, according to a report this week by venture capital firmSpace Capital.

Blue Origin, SpaceX and other rocket providers are seeing increasing demand from companies and governments trying to deploy satellites into orbit. Both Blue Origin and SpaceX have their ownsatelliteinternet services, and they're launch partners forAmazon, which is in the process of standing up its fullLeolow Earth orbit satellite constellation.

SpaceX'sStarlinkcurrently dominates the market with more than 11,000 satellites in orbit.

title: Here's how the CoreWeave sell-off is affecting OpenAI vs. Anthropic valuations
content:
The spread is widening between AI leaders OpenAI and Anthropic as a sell-off in CoreWeave leads neocloud stocks lower.

OpenAI's valuation is down more than 4% the past 24 hours after briefly slipping under $1.5 trillion, according to perpetual futures pricing on decentralized exchange Hyperliquid. Meanwhile, Anthropic perps are up 2.4% over the same time period, recovering an overnight dip and indicating a valuation of just over $2 trillion.

Perpetuals are bets that never expire. They maintained by "deployers" on Hyperliquid's blockchain infrastructure that determine a funding rate for going long or short the futures based on a spot "oracle" price that uses third-party data like private funding rounds and secondary market transactions to estimate private-market prices.

Open interest, defined by Hyperliquid as the sum of long and short positions on a contract, is more than five times bigger in Anthropic than OpenAI — more than $41 million, compared to less than $7 million in OpenAI.

Right now the deployer behind these pre-IPO contracts – the developer building the exchange – is Entropy IO. TradeXYZ, the most prominent developer on the platform, typically does not list pre-IPO perps until S-1s are public, according to David Schamis, CEO ofHyperliquid Strategies, the publicly traded treasury company that invests in the HYPE token that powers the exchange.

"Liquidity will probably be deeper once TradeXYZ lists these companies," Schamis said in a call. "Generally these will trade at a premium to the IPO price but they do a good job predicting where it will be post-IPO."

The bigger price drop in OpenAI perps reflects the company's closer ties to GPU rent-a-center CoreWeave, whose shares touched a new one-year low Thursday, extending a decline over that period to 54%, as concerns mount over the company's debt-financing strategy.

In April, CoreWeave announced a deal with Anthropic to power the company's Claude products, but did not disclose the value of the deal. The company's relationship with OpenAI stretches back further, and as of September 2025 was worth at least $22 billion including a 5-year agreement to provide datacenters and technology.

While OpenAI perps are falling more than Anthropic the past 24 hours, the two are both down about 15% from highs last month, according to Hyperliquid pricing.

title: Elon Musk cash infusion helps GOP Senate super PAC raise record $273 million
content:
TheSenate Leadership Fund, the Republican Party's leading Senate super PAC, posted the largest quarterly haul in its history and entered the final weeks before the Nov. 3midterm electionwith more than $155 million in cash, according to a new Federal Election CommissionfilingThursday.

The SLF brought in $272.9 million from July through September, including $209.7 million from donors — including.TeslaandSpaceXCEOElon Musk, who supplied the bulk of that money

Musk poured $158 million into the SLF in September through an affiliatedTexas PACcreated to support Republican Ken Paxton. His two contributions of $75 million and $83 million are among the largest political donations ever.

Musk's contribution alone also exceeded the Democratic Senate Majority PAC's entire third-quarter fundraising. That super PAC reported raising a record$151 millionduring the period and ended September with $111.8 million in cash, which the group said was its third-quarter record. The super PAC's FEC filings are not yet available.

The SLF's haul shattered its own previous records. The group brought in nearly$116 millionin the third quarter of 2024 and$111 millionin 2022. In 2020, when it filed monthlyreports, SLF took in roughly $157 million fromJulythroughSeptember. Its previous quarterly high was roughly $216 million in the final three months of 2020, according to a CNBC review of FEC filings.

The record influx gives Republicans a sizable financial cushion as they fight to preserve their53-seat Senate majorityacross the country that has become increasingly defensive in the closing weeks of the election.

The SLF paused additional advertising in perennial battlegroundNorth Carolinathis month after spending more than $30 million there — according to AdImpact data — and redirected resources towardKansas, where Republican Sen. Roger Marshall faces an unexpectedly competitive challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton.

In Nebraska, SLF has committed $15 million to defend Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts, including $7 million through the affiliated Cornhusker Majority,The Wall Street Journalreported this week. Trump carried Nebraska by more than 20 percentage points in 2024.

The super PAC has also been central to the Republican intervention in Texas, where DemocratJames Talaricohas turned what had been expected to be a safe GOP Senate contest into one of the most expensive races in the country.

Republican groups spent roughly $122 million in Texas in September alone and had another $66 million in advertising reserved through Election Day as of the beginning of October, according to AdImpact data.

Talarico announced Thursday that he raised$64 millionin the third quarter, the largest third-quarter haul on record for a Senate candidate. Paxton raised$10.2 million, according to a FEC filing.

title: I watched Nvidia's Jensen Huang work the room in London. He brought big checks — and a blunt message
content:
This report is from this week's The Tech Download newsletter. Like what you see? You can subscribehere.

Nvidia'sJensen Huang draws a crowd wherever he goes.

In an old converted church in West London on Wednesday night, Huang stood on a pop-up stage in front of politicians, investors, tech execs and journalists, announcing the chip giant was taking stakes in five U.K. startups.

"We're not your largest investor, but we are your best investor," he proclaimed. "I'm gonna invest in you, I'm gonna invest in you," he shouted, pointing at the founders. His appearance in London was part of a European tour ahead of Nvidia's GTC event in Berlin next week.

Earlier, he'd searched out U.K. neocloud Nscale CEO Josh Payne in the crowd, declaring, "last year you were zero."

"Now look at them," he said. "We invested in you, I attracted a whole bunch of investors to you." Nscale could be the most valuable British company in a decade, Huang said to cheers from the crowd.

The Nvidia boss certainly doesn't lack for confidence.

The warm reception Huang regularly receives is a sign of just how much sway he holds in the AI industry.

Nvidia has a near monopoly over the most powerful AI chips and Huang courts tech execs and world leaders with ease. He's a near constant presence at U.S. President Donald Trump's side at state dinners and visits.

In London, after the pomp and ceremony of Huang's speech, he emerged around 40 minutes late to a media huddle outside the front of the church.

"The Prime Minister [Andy Burnham] and I had a nice whiskey together. He's a whiskey man," he told reporters. Later, Huang said he'd be meeting German Chancellor Friedrich Merz "in a couple of days."

Huang spoke to journalists for nearly an hour that evening — a fair effort considering he'd only eaten a "quarter of a quarter" of a sandwich that day — dishing out praise and criticism to Europe with a bombastic assuredness.

"Nothing pains me more, frankly, than to see one of the most technologically advanced countries to be left so far behind in technology," he said, referring to Germany.

And the U.K. didn't escape scot-free. "If you tell an entrepreneur there's one in a million chance they can succeed, that entrepreneur says, 'So you're telling me there's a chance?' But in the UK, somehow there's 999,000... reasons to fail."

The CEO was also bullish on Europe's chances of succeeding with AI, not least, presumably, because Nvidia now has stakes in so many of the region's most promising startups.

On Wednesday those lucky startups were biotechs Prima Mente and Boltz, project delivery platform Foresight, algorithm discovery startup Hiverge and quantum company Riverlane. Those companies, alongside others in the U.K. that Nvidia isn't naming, will be the recipients of $1.16 billion of Nvidia cash.

Earlier in the week the chip giant announced it was taking stakes in a number of French startups.

It's all part of a major push by Nvidia to build out holdings across the AI stack. Among the recipients of funding from Nvidia have been the likes of OpenAI, Anthropic, Intel and XAI.

The chip giant has participated in 116 investment rounds in 2026 so far, according to Dealroom, up from just 12 in 2022.

Anthropic's third-quarter revenue is said to hit $16.8 billion ahead of IPO, according topeople familiarwith the matter.

AppleandMetateam upto makeMuse AI modelrun on Mac computers.

CoreWeavecredit default swaps hit distress levelsasinvestors souredon AI debt.

TSMCposted record profit for a sixth straight quarter,beating estimates.

ASMLsays it's getting order interest through 2030asprofit smashes expectations.

SpaceX'smilitary satellite system, Starshield, has drawn renewed attention this week as Ukraine has grappled with restrictions on the tech. My colleague Elsa Ohlen has written thismust-read explaineron how it works and differs from Starlink.

title: Trump says he won't use nuclear weapons or send ground troops to Iran
content:
U.S. President Donald Trump has said he does not intend to use nuclear weapons against Iran or foresee deploying ground troops in the country.

Speaking inan interview with Newsmax,broadcast Thursday evening, he said: "I wouldn't use nuclear. We don't have to. We're the greatest nuclear power in the world."

The right-wing cable outlet asked Trump about reports thatWashington wasconsidering using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast, or MOAB, widely known as the "Mother of All Bombs."

"The mother of all bombs is not nuclear. It's not nuclear at all. This is just an extremely large bomb. It's like a tiny nuclear bomb. But the mother of all bombs is one big bomb, but it's not nuclear," he said, without specifically confirming or denying the reports.

When asked if he would put "troops on the ground," Trump said: "No, I don't see that, I don't see it."

The MOAB is the largest non-nuclear bomb in the U.S. arsenal. It was used in combat in 2017 againstISIS militants in Afghanistan.

Earlier on Thursday, CNN reported that the U.S. military has developed new strike plans to target Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites.

The strikes could take place if Trump orders combat operations to resume, either before or after the midterm elections, the outlet reported. The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

Trumpsaid onOct. 8 that he would not order a resumption of military strikes before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

Merchant shipping through the Strait of Hormuz faces heightened risks after a series of attacks in the critical waterway.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operationssaid that the threatremains "severe" in the Strait of Hormuz, afterthe Singapore-registered container ship GFS Pridewas struck by an unknown projectile, caught fire and later sank.

The UKMTO added that "deliberate hostile action" was highly likely and said it had recorded eight attacks in the critical waterway since Oct. 11.

title: Fed's Warsh withholds rate signal, praises recent global tightening with 'no free riders'
content:
BANGKOK — Federal Reserve ChairmanKevin Warshrefrained from signaling whether there will be another interest rate hike again this month, while acknowledging a "synchronous tightening" by central banks around the world and there's "no free riders."

"I don't prejudge meetings. I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year," Warsh said, reiterating his opposition to the use of forward guidance for markets that should rely on interpreting data.

He also acknowledged that stance may disappoint anyone who had hoped for a steer ahead of the central bank meeting later this month. "It's a new chapter at the Fed [and] we're not in that business anymore. But we can go in any direction you'd like," he said.

Warsh spoke at a fireside chat with the International Monetary Fund's managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, as part of the weeklong IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok on Friday.

"Alongside other recent comments from FOMC participants, Warsh's comments indicate that the FOMC is set to pause in October," Goldman Sachs economists led by Jan Hatzius wrote in a note. "We continue to expect a second and final hike in December."

S&P 500 and Nasdaq futures edged higher following the speech, while stock market indexes in Asia and Treasury yields were largely stable.

Warsh described the global shift toward tighter monetary policy as a common fight on prices. Central banks made their own choices under their own mandates, he said, but the result was "a synchronous tightening in monetary policy in most places around the world," which means "there's no free riders."

Surging energy costs stemming from the Iran war and artificial intelligence investment boom are stoking inflation and pushing up borrowing costs around the world, just as global public debt is on pace to exceed 100% of the world's GDP, a level last breached in the aftermath of World War II.

The U.S. government has insisted that strong growth would be the best way to grow out of its rising debt pile,dismissing IMF's warning that the plans of relying solely on growthwon't work as something that needs to be taken "with a grain of salt."

Warsh also expressed optimism about how AI will make economies that use it well more productive and wealthier, while warning the road there may be "very bumpy," and its near-term effect on employment is still uncertain.

"I want you to hear from me optimism, but optimism leavened by the seriousness of purpose," Warsh said.

A decade from now, he said, people will look back on the developments and "say this was hugely consequential."

The Fed raised rates to a range of 3.75% to 4% last month,its first hike since 2023. Traders see a 72.3% chance for the Fed to keep the interest rate unchanged at the Oct. 27-28 meeting, according to CME FedWatch, while the majority expect a 25 basis point hike at the December meeting.

title: Marco Rubio to visit Indian billionaire Ambani's refinery in Gujarat as U.S. diesel prices surge
content:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is set to visit the world's largest oil refinery in Jamnagar, India, owned by billionaire Mukesh Ambani'sReliance Industries, asdiesel pricessurge ahead of U.S. midterm polls.

The International Energy Agency has warned that constraints on the diesel market will likely keep prices elevated into the next year. To ease diesel prices, which affect American truckers, farmers, and shippers, U.S. President Donald Trump earlier this monthpaused sanctions on Russiato allow supplies from Moscow in the global market.

The Trump administration is using this trip to focus on business deals rather than policy and politics as Americans remain focused on the economy ahead of the midterm polls, experts told CNBC.

Not only is Ambani's flagship company Reliance investing in a U.S. refinery and is a key buyer of Venezuelan oil, but its strong ability to supply diesel has put Jamnagar on the map during Rubio's visit, they added.

On Tuesday, the U.S. Department of State announced that Rubio will be traveling to Samarkand in Uzbekistan and from there toMumbai and Jamnagar in India, with no mention of a stop in New Delhi, between Oct. 17 and 22.

Rubio, who is on his second trip to India this year, will meet with some senior Indian officials and with business leaders "to promote opportunities for commercial investment and economic cooperation," according to the release.

US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor said Rubio will travel to Jamnagar to visit Reliance's refining complex and hinted thatAmbani would meet the U.S. official, according to Bloomberg. Given Ambani runs Reliance, "I'd imagine he'd be there," Gor said, according to the report.

Later in an interview with Indian media outlet NDTV, Gor said that the visit to Jamnagar was scheduled givenReliance's "incredible" investmentin the U.S. refinery project. Reliance did not respond to emails sent by CNBC seeking details on the visit. The State Department did not respond to CNBC's queries sent outside of working hours.The U.S. is facing exceptionally high diesel prices ahead of its November midterm elections, and the Trump administration has been looking for ways to increase fuel availability, Arpit Chaturvedi, South Asia Advisor at strategic advisory firm Teneo, told CNBC.

Jamnagar has "considerable export-oriented refining capacity," making a strong case for the U.S. to explore refined-product supplies, including diesel, he added.

Ambani, who SpaceX founder Elon Musk referred to asthe real boss of Indialast week, has been developing ties with the Trump administration. In March, U.S. President Donald Trump thanked Reliance for its "tremendous investment" in the first new refinery project in the U.S. in the last 50 years.

Reliance, which is majority-owned by the Ambani family, has also emerged as the second-largestbuyer of Venezuelan crude outside of the U.S., even as Indian state-owned firms remain largely unmoved by Trump's appeal to buy more of it.

Rubio will also use the visit to highlight "Reliance's plans for a large, new refinery in Texas, which is the site of heated midterm U.S. election races drawing national attention," said Atman Trivedi, a partner at Washington-based DGA Albright Stonebridge Group.

Reliance's is also "well-positioned to sell diesel," and other refined petroleum products to the U.S., he added.

The Jamnagar refinery is the world's "largest and most complexsingle-site refinery" with crude processing capacity of 1.4 million barrels per day, according to Reliance.

title: One Singapore ship was sunk, but here's why others are still transiting the Strait of Hormuz
content:
Commercial vessels are likely to continue navigating the perilous Strait of Hormuz despite the sinking of a Singapore-flagged container ship this week, as strong demand for Middle Eastern energy and lucrative shipping opportunities keep some operators willing to brave escalating attacks, maritime experts said.

The latest attacks on two Singapore-flagged container ships have heightened concerns over the safety of commercial shipping through one of the world's most important maritime chokepoints. But analysts say the incidents are unlikely to bring remaining shipping activity through the Strait to a halt, even as major container lines largely stay away.

Collin Koh, a senior fellow at Singapore's S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, said shipping companies were likely to continue seeking opportunities to transit the strait despite heightened security threats.

"I don't see in the short term, that Singapore flagged ships or Singapore shipping companies would necessarily avoid taking the transit if there is an opportunity," Koh told CNBC.

His comments follow attacks on two Singapore-registered container ships, GFS Pride and GFS Giselle, this week. GFS Pride sank after being struck by a projectile and catching fire, while GFS Giselle was damaged. Crew members from both vessels were reported safe.

Crossings through the Strait of Hormuz fell to 131 in the week ended Oct. 14, from 176 the previous week, according to maritime analytics firm Kpler, although the decline cannot be attributed solely to the latest incidents.

Dimitris Ampatzidis, maritime risk and compliance manager at Kpler, said the attacks underscored Iran's continuing ability to threaten commercial vessels, with the risks extending beyond oil and gas transportation.

Koh said shipping companies around the world have continued looking for opportunities to navigate the Strait since the conflict erupted, with some operators prepared to accept higher risks and costs.

Strong demand for oil, particularly from Asia, continues to provide an incentive for tanker operators to transport energy supplies from the Persian Gulf, even as security threats complicate voyages.

Some operators may be willing to take their chances even if doing so involves paying a premium, Koh said.

Singapore Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan offered an example of how higher oil prices could make voyages through Hormuz commercially worthwhile despite the dangers.

Speaking at the Milken Institute Asia Summit last week, Balakrishnan recounted a conversation with an unnamed Gulf counterpart who said his country was earning more from oil exports than before the war by operating a so-called "Hormuz shuttle" involving about 20 very large crude carriers.

The vessels were effectively self-insured against attacks, according to the official's account, with higher crude prices making the voyages financially worthwhile despite the risks.

"Sometimes you get hits, but it is still worthwhile to run the 'Hormuz shuttle,'" Balakrishnan quoted the official as saying.

Despite the risks, vessels continue to transit the Strait, reflecting its commercial importance, particularly for energy shipments to Asian markets, Ampatzidis said.

However, further attacks could deter more operators from making the passage, with the impact likely to differ depending on vessel type and individual companies' assessments of the risks, he added.

The Singapore Shipping Association also played down the prospect of a broad withdrawal of commercial shipping from the region, suggesting operators would instead adapt to changing trade conditions.

"Rather than signalling a broad withdrawal from the region, these developments are more likely to result in adjustments to trading patterns as markets respond to shifts in the supply and demand of goods and energy," said association president TS Teo.

Shipowners would continue weighing commercial considerations against security developments and crew safety when making operational decisions, he added.

While some operators remain willing to transit Hormuz, much of the global container shipping industry has already adjusted its networks to avoid the strait.

Jayendu Krishna, a director at Drewry Maritime Advisors, said none of the major container shipping lines had resumed services through Hormuz since suspending operations following the outbreak of the war in February. Only some regional operators have continued sporadic services, generally using smaller feeder vessels.

That means the immediate impact of the latest attacks on container shipping could be limited, he said.

However, a further escalation into the Gulf of Oman could pose a more serious threat to regional supply chains, particularly if it disrupts alternative ports like Khorfakkan in the United Arab Emirates and Oman's Sohar that have become critical gateways for cargo entering Gulf countries.

"If the Gulf of Oman became a zone of kinetic activity, a significant part of supplies to the Gulf countries would be cut off, since Khorfakkan and Sohar have been a lifeline for them," Krishna said.

title: The IPO drought is driving private equity-owned companies to the debt market to pay investors
content:
Private equity funds are increasingly pushing their portfolio companies to take on more debt to return cash to their investors, data suggests.

It comes as the typical ways of monetizing private equity investments — selling company stakes via IPOs, or offloading them to other PE funds or buyers — have dried up in recent years.

While investors get paid, the practice of private equity sponsors adding more debt to companies — known as dividend recapitalizations — risks weakening their ability to invest or weather future downturns in trading.

"Dividend recap" activity has surged since 2022, and Moody's Ratings expects it to remain high in Europe, the Middle East and Africa as private equity firms look for ways to return money to investors while company sales and IPOs remain subdued.

The ratings agency estimates that private equity-owned companies in the EMEA region could take on a further 41 billion euros ($46 billion) in debt before reaching leverage levels that typically prompt a downgrade.

New Moody's analysis indicates the practice remains limited to the strongest-performing companies with the greatest capacity to take on new debt, indicating this "significant releveraging capacity" could support a further ramp-up in dividend recaps.

Still, it does not address the exit backlog weighing over private equity, where funds are now having to hold onto companies for much longer than the typical period of around five to six years.

"The fundamental problem is that exits are few and far between – the European IPO markets have been muted, and the capital that would generally fund strategic purchases by large corporates has become a lot more expensive after the last rate hike cycle," said Moody's analyst Mayank Mallik. "Generally, we are more focused on the impact that the general PE ecosystem has on corporate credit quality — and this is one of the key transmission mechanisms currently."

Moody's said PE sponsors have remained "disciplined" in choosing dividend recap candidates, with services, consumer products and manufacturing the most active sectors.

Mallik noted most dividend recaps have involved companies that outperformed their original business plans, with the new debt generally returning leverage to its initial level without "materially" affecting exit opportunities.

"It is true, however, that companies preparing for IPOs like to show a track record of solid deleveraging for a couple of years before approaching the market," he told CNBC via email.

"There is indeed a risk that, if an IPO window unexpectedly opens, issuers that have recently done a div recap may not be able to jump on the opportunity. Any company doing a div-recap is likely taking a forward-looking view that the IPO market will be closed in the short run."

Distributions to investors have fallen sharply in recent years. Moody's, citing PitchBook data, said private equity distributions dropped from more than 30% of starting net asset value in 2022 to about 12% today.

"The risk is that if PE exit backlog is prolonged, sponsors may start looking at relatively weaker credits to monetize, which may lead to credit deterioration across the portfolio," Mallik added.

He said that those risks are greater than a decade ago, partly because documentation has become "quite permissive" for issuers looking to raise additional debt.

Portfolio companies' recaps are typically funded through the broadly syndicated loan market, where several investment banks will club together to lend money to a borrower, thereby spreading the risk. Alternatively, funding is raised by high-yield corporate bond issuance or private credit borrowing.

Sunaina Sinha Haldea, global head of private capital advisory at Raymond James, said there is still "meaningful capacity" to fund recaps, highlighting how tight spreads and scarce new loan supply are helping support appetite.

"Weaker earnings, wider spreads or investor withdrawals could tighten availability, while a recovery in acquisition financing would give lenders more alternatives to funding shareholder payouts," she said.

Haldea noted that dividend recaps provide liquidity, relieving the pressure to sell without ultimately resolving the valuation gap.

"Investors get some cash back, but the asset remains in the fund and still needs an eventual buyer," Haldea told CNBC via email.

"A dividend recap need not derail an exit if earnings growth has created genuine borrowing capacity, but borrowing against hoped-for growth is a different proposition. More debt means less financial flexibility and, at the same enterprise value, less equity value left for shareholders when the business is eventually sold."

title: Russia returns to G20 table in Bangkok on U.S. invitation that angers Europe
content:
Russia's finance minister attended a Group of 20 meeting in Bangkok on Thursday, his second in-person appearance at the event since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, testing how far Washington'srapprochement with Moscowwill strain ties with Europe.

Anton Siluanov and Bank of Russia Deputy Governor Elizaveta Danilova were listed as Russia's delegates at the finance ministers and central bank governors' meetings on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, according to a seating plan seen by CNBC. Siluanov was in the meeting, according to a person familiar with the matter.

According to the layout document, Russian delegates were seated between attendees from South Korea and the United Arab Emirates.

German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil was also listed as an attendee. At the August G20 finance meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, he told Siluanov that Moscow must end the war and declined to pose in a group photo with him. The traditional group photo was ultimately taken without the Russian delegation after European officials protested.

Klingbeil has pushed back on the U.S. efforts to bring Russia back on to the international stage,reportedlysaying after the Thursday meeting that "there will be no pretending that Russia is now returning as a normal member of the G20 and simply taking its seat at the table again — not with me, and not with the other Europeans."

Russia's seat at the table tests how far Washington can ease pressure on Moscow without breaking with its European allies. The U.S., which took over the G20 presidency this year, welcomed Russia's finance minister back to the finance talks after years of isolation over the invasion of Ukraine.

The Trump administration also introduced a deal to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel imports until April, drawing criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European allies. Dombrovskis told CNBC on Wednesday that"now it's not a time to ease sanctions on Russia."

In a statement issued after the Thursday meetings, Australian Treasurer Jim Chalmers said Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on commercial vessels "must end." Those impacts "are exacerbated by Russia's unprovoked and unjustifiable war in Ukraine," he said, adding that Australia calls for Russia to end the war and respect Ukraine's sovereignty.

The finance chiefs ended the meeting without a joint communique, underscoring persistent divisions among members over the Middle East conflict, trade imbalances, and Russia's war with Ukraine. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who would normally chair the talks, skipped the meetings to stay in Washington.

The Asheville meeting also ended without a communique, after Chinaobjected to language on several issues, including efforts to rectify excessive global trade surpluses. The U.S. instead issued a chair's statement backed by every member present except China, withBessent calling China "the dissenter."

Delegates started the day with a plated breakfast of baked goat cheese, spinach and egg soufflé with chutney made from locally grown Bijin tomatoes, according to a menu card at the venue. The bread basket came with "Nam Dok Mai" mango jam. Every card carried the U.S. presidency's stars-and-stripes G20 logo and its "Freedom 250" tagline,marking America's 250th anniversary.

The finance ministers' meeting Thursday could have helped lay the groundwork for improved coordination on a raft of global challenges, including energy problems stemming from the Middle East conflict and concerns about record public debt in advanced economies. Leaders are expected to convene at the next G20 summit in Miami in December.

title: Order to limit Starshield for Ukraine came from inside White House: Reuters reports
content:
The order to limit a satellite system used by Ukraine for battlefield communications and drone operations came from inside the White House, according to two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter.

The officials said leaders at the Defense Department received a message that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military needed to be slowed.

The officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, did not specify who in the White House made the decision or who was responsible for implementing the order. The Pentagon is the biggest customer of Starshield, which is the military-grade version of the Starlink service.

Ukrainian officials said this week that military-grade Starlink receptors stopped working in Ukraine when mounted on fast-moving objects, interfering with the performance of ‌Ukrainian drones that rely on them for onboard guidance systems over Ukrainian territory.

A person in Ukraine's Defence Ministry said on Thursday that the receptors were now working when in motion, but only at speeds of up to 100 miles per hour (160 kph).

The move to temporarily restrict the vital communications system came as President Donald Trump has pressured Kyiv to stop its attacks on Russian refineries, which he has blamed for the soaring energy prices that are denting his Republican Party's prospects in the November midterm elections.

But experts say that surge in energy costs is mainly the result of the US-Israeli war with Iran, which brought Iranian attacks on energy facilities and has largely shut the vital Strait of Hormuz.

In response to a request for comment about the order to limit Starshield, a senior US official said: "No such request was ever made by the president."

The White House did not respond to questions about whether other administration officials might have made the request.

Starshield was developed by SpaceX specifically for government and national-security customers, particularly the US Department of Defense. Starshield uses the Starlink constellation as its backbone.

Ukrainian officials said the restrictions complicated strike missions against Russian forces and logistics in occupied territory and slowed interceptor drones used to shoot down incoming Russian Shahed drones.

Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX, said on X on Wednesday that because Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government, any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military or the president.

SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.

The Department of Defense and the Ukrainian embassy in Washington also did not respond to requests for comment.

Relations between Kyiv and Washington have deteriorated in recent days following a meeting in Miami on October 9 that convened representatives from both countries as well as Europe and the World Bank.

Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, the Trump administration's Middle East envoy, struck a tough tone with Ukraine in the meeting, according to a separate person familiar with the matter. They told Ukrainian officials that the US was frustrated with Kyiv's continued strikes on Russian refineries despite repeated requests from Washington to stop.

The US delegation also explained Washington's decision to strike a diesel deal with Russia, saying the White House hoped it would soften Moscow's stance on peace talks.

That deal, under which Russia will supply more than 2.25 million barrels of diesel to ​US and global markets, has triggered a backlash from some US lawmakers, who say it will give Moscow cash to pursue its war without forcing Russian President Vladimir Putin to make concessions to end the conflict.

In the days that followed, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy and Trump criticized each other, with Zelenskiy calling the US decision on the Russian diesel deal "weak." Trump called for elections in Ukraine and Zelenskiy's ouster.

Behind the scenes, American officials threatened to stop providing intelligence to Kyiv about Russian missile launches that Ukraine uses to thwart attacks, as Reuters previously reported. Trump said on Tuesday Washington was still sharing intelligence with Ukraine.

Following the move to restrict Ukraine's access to Starshield, the Ukrainians made calls on Tuesday and Wednesday to find answers from senior officials at the White House, State Department and Pentagon, a senior Ukrainian official said, adding that Kyiv was told it was a White House decision.

The Pentagon has spent billions of dollars on the Starlink and Starshield services. It has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft ​for missile-warning missions and a spy ​constellation for the National Reconnaissance ⁠Office, Reuters reported in 2024.

title: India's rupee forecast to weaken toward 100-per-dollar level even as RBI pushes back
content:
Fund outflows and a rising energy bill are expected to keep putting pressure on India's rupee, even as the central bank works to slow depreciation.

Over the last several days, the currency has recovered from 96.79 rupees per dollar to the 95-level, aided by the Reserve Bank of India'slatestmeasures. But while those will provide short-term relief, the currency is expected to weaken toward the end of the year and mid-2027, and a 100 rupee-per-dollar mark could not be ruled out, strategists said.

The RBI's steps will slow the rupee's depreciation, but they cannot "fully offset the fundamental pressures stemming from elevated oil prices, a wider current account deficit, and a challenging global capital flow environment," Hanna Luchnikava-Schorsch, head of Asia-Pacific economics at S&P Global Market Intelligence, told CNBC.

Her firm sees the Indian currency trading around 97 per US dollar by end-2026 and at 98 rupees by mid-2027. Singapore-based Mizuho Securities also expects the rupee to slide to 98 rupees against the greenback by late 2026 and early next year, Vishnu Varathan, head of macro strategy for APAC at the firm, told CNBC.

"The RBI is determined to dowhatever is necessary to ensureorderly movement in the foreign exchange market," Sanjay Malhotra, the governor of the RBI, said in an interview with local Indian media outlet Moneycontrol on Tuesday.

On Saturday, the central bank announced measures that will make it expensive totake speculativebets on the rupee and restrict rebooking of cancelled foreign exchange derivative contracts.  It also opened a special window to meet theentire daily dollar requirementsof three public sector oil marketing companies, ring-fencing this trade from spot markets.

The steps offer "short-term to medium-term stability, not long-term structural support," Devarsh Vakil, head of research at HDFC Securities, told CNBC,

These steps come just months after the central bank in June launched a special scheme, known as the Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) deposits, that offered incentives tonon-resident Indiansfor making foreign currency deposits in Indian banks.

While this boosted the RBI's foreign exchange reserves by $105 billion, global adverse conditions forced the central bank to make "aggressive" intervention in spot markets to counter the pressure on the rupee, global brokerage Nomura said in a report on Saturday.

Since the close of the program on Aug. 30, the rupee has fallen 1.9% against the dollar, and the RBI's interventions to curb the decline "through dollar sales" have resulted in foreign reserves falling by $51 billion as of Oct. 2, Indian brokerage Ambit Capital said in a report on Wednesday.

FCNR-B, along with other currency swap measures announced in June, has led to forward dollar commitments of $200 billion that reduce the RBI's effective reserve cover, "leaving the rupee vulnerable to further depreciation," the report said.

India's import cover stands at around 6.2 months, its lowest since the U.S. taper tantrum in 2013, it added.

India, which remains the world's fastest-growing major economy, is among the countries mostvulnerable to supply disruptionscaused by the Iran war. The South Asian country meetsnearly 85% of its fuel needsvia imports, withthe Strait of Hormuzbeing a key supply route before the war.

High energy costs, coupled with record exits of foreign investors from its capital markets due to risk aversion and the lack of artificial intelligence play, have kept the rupee under pressure.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modiappealed to citizens last monthto avoid foreign travel and buying gold, to ease the pressure on the local currency. He had made asimilar call in May, amid the growing risks to the economy from the Iran war.

A move towards 100 rupees per US dollar cannot be excluded, Luchnikava-Schorsch said, adding that the scenario could play out "if oil prices rise further, portfolio outflows resume and the current account deficit widens beyond current expectations."

Foreign portfolio investorshave sold direct Indian equitiesworth $32.5 billion this year through Oct. 13, according to the data of Indian depository NSDL.

The rupee is likely to remain under pressure for the financial year ending in March 2027, Harsimran Sahni, associate director and head of treasury at Indian firm Anand Rathi Global Finance, said.

"Businesses should strengthen their hedging strategies and stress-test their foreign currency exposures," Sahni said, adding that RBI interventions can moderate volatility but cannot offset external imbalances "indefinitely."

If sustained capital outflows coincide with elevated crude prices and a widening current account deficit, the rupee could move toward the 100 per dollar mark, he said.

title: Gasping for clean air: Singapore battles relentless haze as Prime Minister Wong warns of action
content:
Singapore continues to grapple with severe haze as smoke from wildfires in neighboring Indonesia drifts into the city-state, with Prime Minister Lawrence Wong warning of action against companies responsible for the fires.

Air quality in Singaporeremained unhealthyon Thursday, as smoke from widespread fires in Indonesia's Kalimantan region continued to drift toward the city-state, accordingto the National Environment Agency.

Singapore's air quality first deteriorated tounhealthy levelson Sept. 4, the first time in nearly three years, according to government data. The worsening haze has cast a shadow over the city-state, disrupting daily life and threatening businesses as air pollution continues to worsen.

In a post on X Thursday night, Wong said the government waslooking into companiespotentially responsible for the forest and peatland fires in Indonesia. He said authorities could take legal action under Singapore's Transboundary Haze Pollution Act where warranted, while also exploring joint action with other countries.

Singapore's Seletar Airport has seen 16 diversions due to low visibility, spokespeople for Changi Airport Group and the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore told CNBC in a joint media reply.

The prolonged haze is taking a toll on daily life and businesses, with some outdoor dining establishments, including outdoor dining restaurants and hawker centers, reporting a drop in business,accordingto the local media.

A spokesperson from Marina Bay Sands told CNBC via email that "certain outdoor experiences that involve prolonged exposure to the outdoors have been temporarily suspended" and the hotel is providing masks and air purifiers to guests.

Singapore's Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" on Thursday that the haze was "not the best way to welcome our international guests," as the city-state hosts Singapore International Cyber Week. The event has drawn a record turnout of more than 15,000 visitors from over 100 countries.

Teo said the government had begun preparations weeks earlier to support residents, including distributing masks to those most in need. While it remains unclear when the haze will improve, she said Singapore has been in close contact with Indonesian officials to understand their needs and stands ready to provide assistance.

A spokesperson of ride-hailing and delivery platform Grab told CNBC via email that they have been distributing masks and have issued advisories to their platform workers as well.

The haze has extended beyond Singapore, affecting neighboring Malaysia as well.

Malaysia's Second Finance Minister Amir Hamzah Azizan told CNBC on Wednesday that the worsening haze requires a coordinated response across Southeast Asia, saying the country has offered to deploy water bombers and other resources to help tackle the issue. "It is an issue that needs an ASEAN solution," he said.

title: People in China are spending nearly as much of their income as Americans on healthcare
content:
BEIJING — High healthcare costs are a big factor driving people in China to save, rather than spend, their money, the International Monetary Fund pointed out in anew booktitled "Toward a New Economic Growth Model for China."

In rural China, 8.7% of disposable income is spent on healthcare — just second to the U.S. among 20 major economies, the research found. The U.S. ranks the highest in the world with nearly 9.9% of disposable income spent on healthcare.

Urban China ranks third, at 5.4%, slightly more than Canada, the data showed.

The level of the healthcare burden in China grows starker when consideringper capita disposable incomein the U.S. was $68,289 as of the end of last year — more than 10 times more than China's 43,377 yuan in U.S. dollar terms (around $6,400).

The gap widens further when looking at China's countryside, which only officiallyemerged from extreme poverty in 2020.

Urban China recorded more than twice the disposable income as rural areas, at 56,502 yuan versus 24,456 yuan, according to official data accessed via Wind Information.

Targeted measures to raise government spending on health and social security in rural areas can significantly reduce the savings rate in rural households, the IMF said, citing prefecture-level analysis.

"China's social spending is low compared with international peers, and increasing that spending wouldlift consumption," wrote Yizhi Xu, economist in the north Asia division of the IMF's Asia and Pacific Department, and Fan Zhang, the IMF's deputy resident representative in Beijing.

They recorded a savings rate of around 14% for people from rural areas working in China's cities, and about 6% for people with urban "hukou" residency rights, which give them more social welfare benefits than migrant workers from rural areas.

"Declining house prices in recent years continue to weigh on consumption and contribute to elevated household savings," Xu and Zhang wrote in their section of the IMF book.

title: Trump says 'if Ken Paxton loses' Texas Senate race, blame Cornyn and Karl Rove
content:
PresidentDonald Trumpon Thursday said that ifTexasSenate nomineeKen Paxtonloses, it will be the fault of incumbent Republican Sen.John Cornynand conservative commentatorKarl Rove.

Trump accused Cornyn and Rove of "doing everything possible to make it hard" for Paxton, the state's attorney general, to beat Democratic nominee James Talarico. Cornyn lost the Republican primary to Paxton, whom Trump controversially endorsed.

"If Ken Paxton loses, it will be because of WEAK and INEFFECTIVE Political Hacks like John Cornyn and Karl Rove, who have ineffectively opposed me for my entire political career," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Trump's preemptive blame-casting came as Texas has surprisingly become one of the most competitive battlegrounds of the 2026 midterm cycle.Most recent pollsshow state Rep. Talarico maintaining a lead in the low-to-mid single digits over Paxton.

The reliably red state has not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1988. In 2024, Texans voted for Trump over Democratic presidential nomineeKamala Harrisby nearly 14 percentage points.

Cornyn's office and Rove did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment on Trump's post.

Trump's decision to back Paxton in the GOP primary delivered a major blow to the four-term incumbent Cornyn, whom the president viewed as disloyal. The move was also seen as a major gamble, as Paxton's history of scandal and opposition within his own party has made him a polarizing figure.

Hoping to stave off Democrats' goal of winning majority control of the Senate, groups backing Republicans have poured hundreds of millions of dollars into the Texas contest, making it the most expensive race of the cycle.

GOP spending in the race has topped $370 million so far, eclipsing Democratic spending by nearly $235 million, according to AdImpact.

Trump has repeatedly lashed out at Rove, calling him a "loser" and urging Fox News to stop putting him on air.

Rove, who was a senior advisor to former President George W. Bush, "is so bad for the Republican Party, and completely wrong so often," Trump wrote in a Sept. 14 Truth Socialpost.

In a Wall Street Journalop-edtwo days later, Rove said that he would back a Democratic candidate in a different race in Texas, voting blue for just the second time in his life.

title: CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt
content:
CoreWeave's credit stress continued to spiral on Thursday amid a broader sell-off in AI-related names.

CoreWeave — a so-called neocloud company — has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure build-out. It's now facing a rebellion from stock and bond investors as concerns mount about AI overspending and debt levels.

Yields on CoreWeave debt have continued to climb, with the yield to maturity on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 reaching 15.78%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Meanwhile, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, at one point soared above 1,140 basis points. It last stood at nearly 1,038 bps — a 16% week-over-week jump and 164% higher than a year ago.

Credit concerns are spreading into AI equities too. CoreWeave's stock dropped during trading Thursday before recovering and closing 5.94% higher. The moved followedWednesday's 15.5% nosedive.

Other neocloud stocks were under similar pressure.Nebiusalso sank before climbing higher to close 1.29% and andIrenultimately ended the day down less than 1%.

Anxiety about AI overspending is also spreading. For instance, shares ofMicron TechnologyandAdvanced Micro Devicessold off following a big sell-off in South Korean chip stocks. Micron closed up 1.87%, while AMD fell 1.5%.

While AI debt worries have been rising steadily, investors have suddenly grown skittish about the underlying finances of companies borrowing heavily to buy chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power.

Coreweave's credit default swaps are one place to see that stress.

Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CoreWeave's CDS means investors view the debt as riskier.

The market is "basically saying 'no mas' to AI debt without operating cash flow support," the Evercore ISI trading desk said.

A spread level of 1,000 basis points or above is generally a sign of credit distress, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.

No one is questioning whether demand for CoreWeave's services is real, since the company has contracts with all the big hyperscalers, Nolan said. The question is whether the cash flows will ultimately arrive.

"It's obviously heavily negative free cash flow at the moment, and it needs that cash flow to arrive really to justify all the capex that it's spending," Nolan said.

CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves on Wednesday, according to a memoobtainedby CNBC.

"When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations."

The backlog is over $100 billion, with around two-thirds of it with investment-grade counterparts includingMicrosoft,Meta,IBMandCaterpillar, Deutsche Bank said in a note Thursday. The firm reiterated its buy-rating on the stock Wednesday, calling the dislocation a buying opportunity.

"The problem is this kind of concern can prove to be a self-fulfilling prophecy, and risks triggering broader issues in other AI-related names," said Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research.

Domino effects may already be happening.Oracle's five-year CDS spread also spiked this week. It was last at 282 basis points, a roughly 10% increase in one week.

"A downgrade from its BBB rating would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," Reid said.

title: Democrat Talarico says he raised record $64 million over summer in Texas Senate race
content:
DemocraticTexasSenate candidateJames Talaricoraised $64 million in the third quarter, his campaign announced Thursday, setting what the campaign said is a Senate fundraising record asRepublicanspour outside money into the race to bolster GOP nomineeKen Paxtonin the2026 midterm election.

The haul was the largest ever reported by a Senate candidate in the July-through-September quarter, according to the campaign, surpassing the previous record of $57 million set bySouth CarolinaDemocrat Jaime Harrison, who unsuccessfully ran against Republican Lindsey Graham in 2020.

Talarico has raised more than $134 million since launching his campaign last year, according to his campaign ahead of the quarterly filing deadline with the Federal Election Commission.

“Grassroots contributors from across Texas are coming together to end billionaire control over our politics and bring down costs for working families,” Talarico said in a statement.

The campaign said more than 1.3 million people have donated and that 97% of contributions were $100 or less. Paxton, by comparison, announced earlier this month that his campaign and two affiliated fundraising committees raised a combined $18 million during the quarter.

The candidates' full financial picture will become clearer after their quarterly reports are filed with theFEC.The filings will show how much each campaign spent and how much cash they had left entering the final stretch.

But the gap in direct fundraising tells only part of the financial story. Republican outside groups have spent more than $175 million since Sept. 1 supporting Paxton or attacking Talarico, according to AdImpact, helping offset Paxton's weaker campaign fundraising. Overall political advertising in the race has surpassed $500 million.

SpaceXandTeslaCEOElon Muskhas emerged as a major force in the race, giving $10 million to a pro-Paxton super PAC, according to figures confirmed Monday by a spokesman for Musk's America PAC, while hisAmerica PAChas spent about $9.4 millionattackingTalarico and another $1.8 millionsupportingPaxton, according to FEC filings.

The source of that money matters as federal law guarantees candidates lower broadcast rates for television advertising than super PACs, allowing Talarico's campaign dollars to go further in buying TV exposure than outside Republican groups.

No Democrat has won statewide in Texas since 1994, and the party has not won a U.S. Senate race there since 1988.But Talarico leads Paxton 48.5% to 45.2% inFiftyPlusOne's polling average, a 3.3-percentage point advantage, forcing Republicans to devote significant resources to what has traditionally been safe territory.

Talarico's fundraising also eclipses previous high-water marks for Texas Democrats. Beto O'Rourke raised $38.1 million in thethird quarter of 2018during his challenge to Republican Sen. Ted Cruz.
