title: How high inflation became a 'fact of life' in the U.S.
content:
U.S. consumers are in the midst of one of the longest stretches of elevatedinflationof the past century. Some are beginning to act like it's a new normal, raising alarm bells for members of theFederal Reserve.

Wednesday'sconsumer price indexrelease showed a 3.7% increase year over year in September.CPIhas now registered around 65 months — that's more than five years — of consecutive annual readings above 2%, a widely accepted target for inflation in the U.S.

This yearslong spell of high inflation has cast a dark cloud over everyday Americans' view of the economy, and could shape everything from how they budget to how they vote in next month's midterm elections. At the Fed, leaders are left questioning whether consumers' inflationary expectations are becoming too entrenched to rein in.

"They're starting to accept high inflation as just a fact of life," Cleveland Fed PresidentBeth Hammackwrote in a social media post last week. "That's concerning."

The current streak of stubborn inflation ranks among the most persistent in modern U.S. history.

The uninterrupted string of above-2% monthly CPI readings is the longest of the 21st century, according to a CNBC analysis of data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The U.S. has seen longer periods on only two other occasions going back to the late 1940s.

Since inflation started running above 2% in early 2021, the average CPI reading has sat around 4.5%. The last time a streak had a mean reading that high was during a period ending in the 1980s.

Consumers are expecting inflation to accelerate. The one-year inflation outlook in September rose three-tenths of a percentage point to 3.9%, its highest reading inmore than three years,according to the New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations released last week.

One of the main worries of central bankers is that businesses and consumers may start permanently adjusting their behaviors to account for high prices. That can have ripple effects through the economy.

Businesses anticipating rising costs can preemptively hike prices for consumers. Workers expecting sticky inflation will ask for steeper pay raises to get ahead of any sticker shock.

All of this can make inflation a self-fulfilling prophecy, rendering the monetary policy tools at the Fed's disposal less effective in slowing price growth.

"Inflation expectations have to be anchored for monetary policy to affect the economy in an effective and predictable manner," said Gary Richardson, an economist and former historian at the Fed. "That's got to be number-one goal of any central bank."

At this juncture, Fed officials are closely watching to see if and how consumers respond to inflationary pressures.

During an event last month, Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari said he heard from a labor union leader that inflation was"worse" than a recessionfor their members. Kashkari said that conversation influenced how he views the trade-off within the Fed's so-called dual mandate, which calls for stability in prices and maximum employment.

At a gathering of economists in Ohio this week, Hammacktold the audiencethat she did not take the fact that long-run inflation expectations have stayed anchored "for granted." With each month that inflation comes in high, she warned that the risk grows of an "inflationary mindset" getting entrenched.

Economists widely view interest rate hikes as the Fed's main mechanism for slowing demand and, in turn, putting downward pressure on the annual pace of price growth. After hiking interest ratesin September, Fed funds futures traders anticipate the central bank will raise borrowing costs further in December and in 2027.

In the long run, Diane Swonk, chief economist at consultancy KPMG, said interest rate hikes can benefit consumers by getting inflation under control. But in the near term, Swonk said consumers can feel more pressure due to higher borrowing costs.

"Inflation is like a cancer, and if you let it metastasize and go further, it's even worse," Swonk said. "Even when the cure hurts, it's better than letting it metastasize."

In Hammack's district, the Cleveland Fed chief said via social media that she's found evidence that residents are "choosing" rather than "trading down." For instance, she said they need to pick whether to pay for groceries or essential bills.

Consumers have lamented the cumulative price increases they now see in everyday life after the years-long run of high inflation. Adding to their woes is the fact that year-over-year inflation has run at afaster clip than wage growthin recent months, meaning the average consumer has lost purchasing power.

The University of Michigan's closely followed consumer sentiment survey earlier this year fell tothe lowest levels ever seen. The highest share of respondents citing high prices as a reason for having worse personal finances surpassed 50% for the first time on record in 2026.

High prices are "dominating consumer thinking," said Joanne Hsu, the director of Michigan's survey. "They still consider it an unacceptable fact of life."

Compared with Democrats, consumer sentiment has tumbled more sharply among Republicans and independents this year. The question now is if voters angered about the rising cost of living will shift control in Washington away from Republicans and PresidentDonald Trumpin themidterm election.

Despite those glum outlooks, economists say that everyday Americans shouldn't bank on prices coming down from current levels. Deflation — which is when annual price growth falls below 0% — could put the national economy on a downward spiral.

Instead, their hope should be that inflation's 12-month growth rate can cool to levels below the pace of pay increases. If that happens for a long enough period, the higher wages and increased purchasing power would leave shoppers better equipped for today's prices.

Olena Nicks, an analyst and local lawmaker in Long Island, New York, is one of those consumers tightening the purse strings in the face of lofty prices. Nicks said she's specifically noticed steep price increases over recent years in thegrocery store produce aisleand when looking atairline flightsfor vacations.

In response, the 34-year-old said she's cut back on purchasing meals at restaurants or from fast-food chains. Her friend group has forgoneleisure activitieslike bowling, opting instead for less-costly nights spent in someone's home.

"Frustrated is an understatement," Nicks said. "It feels like you're stuck."

title: Fannie Mae sharply raises mortgage rate forecast for 2027
content:
Economists at Fannie Mae are now predicting much higher mortgage rates through the end of 2026 and into 2027. It now puts the average rate on the 30-year fixed at 7.4% for the fourth quarter of this year and 7.5% through all of next year. It previously forecast 6.8% for the fourth quarter and 6.7% for all of next year.

The average rate on the 30-year fixed stood at 7.46% Tuesday, according to Mortgage News Daily, but will likely move higher today. Bond yields are rising after a hotter-than-expected inflation report.

Mortgage rates have been rising sharply since the start of September, as inflation remains stubbornly high and bond markets sell off due to several factors. The Federal Reserve also raised its benchmark rate for the first time in more than three years. Mortgage rates do not follow the Fed's rate exactly, but they do react to how the central bank sees inflation going forward.

Mortgage rates loosely follow the yield on the 10-year Treasury, which has been rising sharply on higher oil prices and growing concerns in the global economy.

CNBC's Property Play with Diana Olick covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, delivered weekly to your inbox.

Subscribe here to get access today.

Higher rates have already put the housing market in an early deep freeze this fall. Pending sales, counted by signed contracts on existing homes, were down 8.5% in September year-over-year, according to Zillow.Mortgage demandcontinues to drop sharply, as buyers face higher prices and weakening affordability. Not only can fewer buyers now afford a home, but fewer can qualify for a mortgage.

Fannie Mae did not respond to requests for comment on its latest forecast.

title: BlackRock's Larry Fink warns a data center moratorium could trigger a recession
content:
BlackRock CEO Larry Fink warned that a halt to data center construction could trigger an economic slowdown.

"If we have a moratorium of some sort in this country, we will be in a recession," Fink told CNBC Wednesday, after BlackRock reported better-than-expected third-quarter earnings early Wednesday.BlackRock advanced about 1% in late morning trading.

"So much of our economy is based on the buildout of this capex," Fink added, referring to the massive investments made to develop artificial intelligence infrastructure.

Fink's warning comes as strong, local opposition to data center construction has emerged as a key issue in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, as communities struggle with rising utility costs, water use, environmental damage and questions over investment transparency.

While Fink acknowledged fears about the data center buildout, he also noted "most of it is on misinformation."

The stakes are high. Wall Street analysts estimate total AI capital expenditures could climb above$1 trillion in 2027and total in excess of$5 trillion by 2030.

"Data centers are not the problem. They're creating more new jobs than ever before," the BlackRock CEO explained. The scale of investment has created demand for construction workers, physical digital infrastructure, AI compute hardware and energy infrastructure to secure grid power, he said.

title: Toilet paper and secret recorders: What we know about the arrest of the Saudi OpenAI engineer
content: Image source,Reuters/DOJImage caption,A recording device (R) was wrapped in toilet paper and plugged into a TV (L)ByLaura CressTechnology reporterPublished3 hours agoA Saudi national who worked for OpenAI appeared in court this week for allegedly planting a secret recording device behind a TV in one of the tech giant's meeting rooms.Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer, was arrested by the FBI and charged with using or attempting to use a device "to intercept oral communications".As yet, it is not clear what he was planning to do with the recordings.But, here's wedoknow so far.Help from a chatbotThe engineer asked AI to help him listen in to discussions about AI, according to an official complaint (the document filed in court).Between 17 August and 16 September, Alfozan had reportedly asked a productivity AI assistant several questions about meeting rooms and their availability.Some detailed in the complaint include "how about external partners, where would they usually meet with OpenAI at" and "can you list today's meeting in this room".The complaint also claimed that in September, Alfozan used a chatbot associated with his spouse to ask how to build and install a recording device and how to access it remotely.Alfozan had worked at the firm for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant a recorder.The room where the device was found was regularly used to hold meetings to discuss "highly confidential technical, commercial and strategic information" as well as OpenAI's "government engagements and commercial relationships", the complaint stated.Alfozan had no authority to access or be involved with meetings in the room, the complaint states.But CCTV footage recorded him near the conference room on eight separate occasions in September.Hiding in plain toilet paperOn 30 September, OpenAI staff discovered a "surreptitious audio recording device" behind a television - which had been wrapped in toilet paper.A camera was placed in the conference room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering the room and appeared to look behind the television where the device had been inserted.The complaint also stated that same day he allegedly left an unattended bag in a different room.When security personnel opened it, it was found to contain "another recording device" similar to the one discovered, as well as Alfozan's wallet and ID.In apost on X,external, OpenAI wrote it had used its own AI models to "understand the device and where it had come from".It also said: "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data."Image source,Reuters/DOJImage caption,Alfozan was captured looking behind a television where a device had been insertedWho is Abdulrahman Alfozan?Alfozan had been employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025. The complaint said he was educated in the US and has been a legal permanent resident since 2020.He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI has been terminated.Alfozan's lawyer William Pernik told the BBC: "Like countless Americans, Mr Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream."These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible and any possible reasons why."Pernik added: "In the meantime, we respectfully ask everyone to withhold judgment until full facts become known. Like every one of us, Mr Alfozan is presumed innocent, and what has been made public is an accusation, not a finding of guilt."On Tuesday, Alfozan made his initial appearance in a federal court in California. A detention hearing is scheduled on 19 October to determine whether he should remain in custody while proceedings continue.The FBI investigation is ongoing.If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (Â£190,000) fine.Sign up for our Tech Decoded newsletterto follow the world's top tech stories and trends.Outside the UK? Sign up here.Related topicsArtificial intelligenceFBI

title: Social Security Administration announces 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment for 2027
content:
TheSocial Securitycost-of-living adjustment will be 3.6% in 2027, the Social Security Administrationsaidon Wednesday.

The cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, provides an annual inflation adjustment to both Social Security and Supplemental Security Income, or SSI, benefits.

Social Securityretirementbenefits will increase by $75 per month on average, the agency said.

"Social Security will implement this cost-of-living adjustment for 76 million Americans, giving them greater financial stability," Social Security Commissioner Frank Bisignano said in a statement.

Around 72 million Social Security recipients will see the benefit increases in January, according to SSA. About 7.3 million SSI beneficiaries will receive higher payments starting Dec. 31, the agency said.

The 3.6% COLA for 2027 is in line with Social Securityexperts' projections, which last month forecast an increase of 3.5% to 3.6%.

The 3.6% COLA for 2027 is the largest increase to benefits since 2023. That year, beneficiaries received an8.7% benefit boost— the highest in four decades — in response to rising inflation.

New government inflation data released on Wednesday shows consumer price increases are accelerating. The consumer price indexrose 3.7%over the past 12 months, as gas prices jumped.

About 40% of Social Security beneficiaries ages 65 and over rely on the program for at least half of their income, according to theAARP.

A recentAARP surveyfound 76% of respondents said a 3.5% COLA wouldnot be enough.

The Social Security COLA is "critically important" because it helps millions of Americans cover rising everyday costs, including groceries, routine bills and health care, AARP CEO Myechia Minter-Jordan said in a statement.

"There's a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans: one in five have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last," Minter-Jordan said.

Beneficiaries can multiply their current monthly benefit amount by 3.6%, or 0.036, to estimate the increase to their checks for 2027.

However, keep in mind that increases to Medicare Part B or Part D premiums for 2027 — which may be deducted directly from benefit checks — can affect the size of beneficiaries' monthly payments.

Standard monthly premiums for Medicare Part B are projected to be$209.50 in 2027, up from $202.90 in 2026, according to a report from Medicare trustees. Some beneficiaries may pay extra surcharges, known as Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amounts, or IRMAAs, if they have higher incomes. Medicare Part B covers medically necessary and preventive services.

Meanwhile, Medicare Part D prescription drug plans may see modest premium increases in 2027, according to ananalysis by KFF, a nonpartisan health policy research group.

The Social Security Administration will send beneficiaries notices about the COLA changes. The notices will include specific information about their 2027 benefits, including exact payment dates and dollar amounts, as well as any deductions.

Individuals who have created onlineMy Social Securityaccounts can access that information starting in late November, according to the agency. Beneficiaries without an online account who want to see their COLA notice online must create an account and opt into paperless notices by Nov. 18.

Beneficiaries who have not signed up to receive online notices will receive mailed COLA statements in December. Those individuals should make sure the address the agency has on file is up to date, according to SSA.

Medicare premium amounts for 2027 will also be available online through the My Social Security message center starting in late November, the agency said.

The COLA is based on the percentage increase of one specific government inflation measure — the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, or CPI-W — from the third quarter of the previous year to the third quarter of the current year.

The CPI-W is a subset of theconsumer price indexthat tracks the average change in prices for goods and services purchased by urban households.

The CPI-W rose 3.9% over the past 12 months, according toSeptember datathe Bureau of Labor Statistics released on Wednesday.

Policymakers and advocates have proposed alternatives to the CPI-W for calculating the annual COLA. One alternative is the chained CPI, an index that accounts for changes in buying habits as prices rise. However, arecent AARP analysisfound that switching to that measure would "substantially lower benefits over time."

Others have proposed using the Consumer Price Index for the Elderly, or CPI-E, an experimental index that tracks spending for individuals ages 62 and over. However, some experts say the CPI-E does not necessarilygrow much fasterthan the current measure used to calculate benefit increases.

Switching to a different COLA measure is among the changes lawmakers may consider in upcoming Social Security reform.

"Social Security's future is on the ballot this November, and that includes the size of annual COLA adjustments," said Nancy Altman, president of Social Security Works, an advocacy group focused on expanding Social Security.

title: Netflix to lay off roughly 1,000 employees, or 6% of workforce
content:
Netflixsaid on Wednesday it will lay off roughly 6% of its employees, or roughly 1,000 workers, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.

The job cuts will largely impact the product, tech, legal and HR teams.

"Our mission - to entertain the world - is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritize our people and resources," Netflix co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters wrote in the email to employees. "Our business is strong and growing, and we remain on track to deliver our full year forecast. We'll continue to invest aggressively in high impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation.

"Doing that means making focused choices across the business so we can keep delivering for our members, partners, employees, and investors," the note said.

Netflix said it did not have additional comments beyond the co-CEOs' memo. The company is due to report quarterly earnings on Oct. 20.

The layoffs come just a few weeks after Sarandos told attendees at theBloomberg Screentime conferencethat the company was "not growing as fast as I want."

Netflix has faced a paradox in recent months. It continues to post solid profits and remains the biggest player in the streaming realm, but its viewing time has stagnated and the main driver of new subscriber acquisitions has been its password-sharing crackdown and the launch of a cheaper, ad-supported tier.

Netflix's biggest threat has been YouTube, but looming on the horizon isSkydance. The combined entity of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery has plans to integrate the two companies' streaming platforms, Paramount+ and HBO Max.

Netflix has diversified its content in recent years, expanding into live sports, documentaries and video games in order to compete for share of consumer attention. At the same time, it's lacked the water-cooler-type hits like "Stranger Things" and "Squid Game" that previously boosted subscriber growth and viewership.

And Netflix is not the only company looking to cut costs in the media space. Last month,Disney said it would lay off around 300 employees, with the majority of cuts coming from human resources and technology roles.

— CNBC's Julia Boorstin and Stephen Desaulniers contributed to this report.

title: Iran says it’s ‘counting the moments’ until it can strike U.S. warships; Saudi Aramco facilities attacked
content:
Saudi officials said Wednesday that an administrative building belonging to oil giant Saudi Aramco was targeted overnight, as the Tehran-backed Houthi militants step up their attacks on the kingdom.

The strike caused a fire, but no injuries were reported at the site in the city of Dhahran on the country's eastern coast, according to a statement from the Saudi Arabian Ministry of Energy.

The Houthis, a Yemen-based militia group backed by Iran, have launched a series of strikes on Saudi Arabian targets over the past week. Airport attacks in the capital city of Riyadh led to multiple fatalities, flight cancellations and property damage. Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport remains closed until Saturday.

Yemen's civil war has returned to full-scale fighting between the Houthis and the country's internationally recognized government amid a wider regional escalation linked to the U.S.–Iran war.

Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) chief Ali Ozmaei said Wednesday that Tehran is "counting the moments" until it can sink American warships, according to Iranian state-affiliated media.

"If the Americans think the Strait of Hormuz is open, let them come closer. We are impatient to sink American warships," Ozmaei reportedly said in a televised interview.

"We are waiting for U.S. warships to approach the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz so we can sink them. We are counting down every moment until this happens."

CNBC has reached out to the White House for comment.

The Wall Street JournalreportedTuesday that the Islamic Republic has been strengthening defenses around sensitive locations like nuclear sites, and telling regional officials that Tehran will respond to any new U.S. strikes with retaliatory measures across the Middle East as itprepares its populationfor renewed war in the coming weeks.

U.S. President Donald TrumpsaidTuesday that American forces would not attack Iran before the midterm election, which will take place on Nov. 3.

On Wednesday, reports emerged that a cargo ship caught fire and sank in the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a naval mine as it attempted to transit the waterway. CNBC was not able to independently verify the reports.

Later on Wednesday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations — a Royal Navy-sponsored maritime security organization — said a "verified source" reported that a container ship had been struck by an "unknown projectile."

In aposton X overnight, U.S. Central Command refuted Iranian claims that the strait is under Iran's control.

"IRGC's navy commander has no navy. American forces and regional partners clearly control the Strait of Hormuz," Centcom said. "Just yesterday U.S. forces assisted Gulf partners in shipping more than 19 million barrels of crude oil through the strait."

title: Here's the inflation breakdown for September 2026 — in one chart
content:
The inflation rateincreased in Septemberon the back of higher gasoline and energy prices amid the Iran war, further squeezing households' budgets and perhaps putting pressure on the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates, economists said.

The consumer price index rose by 3.7% in September from 12 months earlier, the Bureau of Labor StatisticsreportedWednesday. That's up from a3.4% annual pacein August.

Economists may be more concerned about the reading for "core" CPI, a measure that strips out food and energy prices, which can be volatile, and is often used to examine underlying inflation dynamics in the U.S. economy. That reading jumped to 2.6% in September from 2.4% in August.

"The overall report shows inflation is uncomfortably strong," said Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's.

"The war's fingerprints are all over the report," he said. "It's driving a lot of the inflationary pickup."

The inflation reading comes less than a month before the upcoming midterm elections, in which affordability is widely seen asa primary issue for voters.

In addition to rising prices for goods and services, Treasury bond yields haveincreased sharply in recent months, puttingupward pressureon rates for mortgages, auto loans and other types of consumer debt.

The Fed — the U.S. central bank, which uses interest-rate policy as a lever to control the trajectory of inflation — may choose to increase its benchmark interest rate at upcoming policy meetings to rein in persistently high inflation, economists said. That benchmark ratehas a direct impact on credit card ratesand influences other borrowing costs, too.

The central bank aims for a long-term annual inflation target around 2%. Inflation has been above that target for more than five years.

Wednesday's CPI report "gives more support to the argument that the Fed is going to continue raising rates," Zandi said.

Inflation pressures will likely push the Fed to hike rates between now and spring 2027, according to a Wells Fargo Investment Instituteanalysispublished Tuesday.

Barometers of consumer sentimenthave plunged to multiyear lowsamid rising prices. The University of Michigan's index of consumer sentiment sunk to itssecond-lowest reading on recordin September.

"Frustration over cost-of-living continues to mount, as consumers across the political spectrum believe that the trajectory of the economy has weakened since the beginning of the year," University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers Director Joanne Hsusaidof the data.

The Social Security Administration on Wednesdayannounced a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustmentfor benefits in 2027. The Social Security COLA calculation is based on a subset of the consumer price index, known as the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, or CPI-W.

However, a recentAARP surveyfound 76% of respondents said a 3.5% COLA wouldnot be enough.

The Iran war — which began at the end of February, when the U.S. and Israel launched strikes on Iran — has pushed up oil prices.

In turn, prices for fuels like gasoline, diesel and jet fuel, which are refined from crude oil, have also increased, generating higher costs across the U.S. economy, economists said.

Inflation is an "oil story," said Michael Reid, head of U.S. economics at the Royal Bank of Canada. "That'll be the story for a few more months."

The war severely crimped oil flowing through the Strait of Hormuz, a key transit artery in the Middle East through which a large volume of the global oil supply passes. The conflict has damaged the region's refining infrastructure and restricted supplies of other materials like fertilizer, putting upward pressure on global food prices.

Russia's war in Ukraine has also contributed to higher diesel prices, largely because Kyiv has bombed Russian refineries, economists said.

"Crude oil is moving through the Strait of Hormuz but remains below its pre-war pace. Even after key waterways fully reopen, lost refining capacity and distribution problems may delay lower energy prices until mid-2027," according to the Wells Fargo Investment Instituteanalysis.

Gasoline prices rose by 9.1% in September alone, accounting for more than half of the monthly increase in the consumer price index, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Wednesday. Gas prices are up 34% over the last year, it said.

The average nationwide price at the pump was $4.33 per gallon on Wednesday, up 45% from $2.98 per gallon on Feb. 27, right before the Iran war began, according toAAA data.

While higher gasoline prices have pinched drivers,high diesel pricesare pressuring consumers more broadly.

Diesel is a fuel used by trucks, trains and ships that transport goods to stores. It has many uses beyond transportation, including farming and manufacturing, as well as residential and industrial heating.

Average diesel prices were $6.30 per gallon on Wednesday, up about 68% from $3.76 per gallon before the Iran war, according to AAA data.

"Somebody has to pay for that," Reid said.

But higher fuel prices don't trickle through to consumers quickly — it's a process that may take a few months, he said.

As the winter holiday shopping season approaches, when retailers typically offer enticing discounts to draw consumers, Reid said he'll be looking to see whether businesses offer smaller discounts than usual, or none at all.

Airline fares are up 22% over the past year, according to CPI data, largely reflecting higher jet fuel prices, economists said.

But travel prices are also up because of strong consumer demand, economists said.

For example, hotel and motel prices are up more than 4% over the past year, too, according to CPI data.

"I think a lot of that goes to high-end demand [for travel]," Zandi said. "A lot of wealthy Americans are traveling more because of the runup in stock prices and their net worth. That's powering a lot of spending."

The Iran war and energy prices aren't the only sources of inflationary pressure, economists said.

"It's tariffs on top of that, adding slightly and layering on energy prices," Reid said.

A combination of tariffs and transportation costs is starting to show up in the price of recreation commodities, according to an RBC Economics research note on Wednesday.

"Toys and other recreational goods — products that are largely imported — posted their largest-ever monthly changes," the note said of the September CPI report.

The build-out of data centers supporting artificial intelligence is also a contributor, economists said.

That's because it has increased demand for — and scarcity of — the computer chips used in AI data centers. Manufacturers use those chips in all types of consumer electronics, including in laptops, video game consoles and cars, economists said.

For example, in June,Appleannounced higher pricesfor MacBooks and iPads, citing surging memory and storage costs.Microsoftsaid shortly afterwardthat it's increasing Xbox game console prices for a similar reason.

One bright spot in the inflation report, Zandi said: Grocery prices fell over the month by 0.1%, despite higher diesel prices.

Beef prices fell 1% during the month, according to CPI data, which Zandi said was at least partly attributable to atemporary reprieve on beef tariffsthat President Donald Trump announced in August.

title: Driving test waits fall to two-year low - but still average 20 weeks
content: Image source,Getty ImagesPublished1 hour agoWaiting times for driving tests have dropped below 20 weeks for the first time since November 2024, according to official figures.But learner drivers in September still had to wait an average of 19.7 weeks, or around five months, for a practical test.The Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) has been trying to cut waiting times and clear a backlog which began during the Covid pandemic in 2020.Commenting on the agency's progress, one driving instructor told the BBC: "I don't think this is anything to boast about."The DVSA initially had hoped to reduce the average waiting time to seven weeks by the end of last year.Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander pushed the target back to summer 2026, but subsequently admitted even that would not be possible - with waits not expected to fall to seven weeksuntil next autumn.The DVSA conducted 191,682 practical driving tests in September, with more than half of those passing.Learner drivers have repeatedly told the BBC how a lack of access to driving tests has limited their freedom, education and job prospects.Until earlier this year, many learner drivers chose to pay inflated prices to access driving tests being resold by third party providers who'd used automated programmes, or bots, to block book tests before learners could access them.But a number of changes were made to the test booking system earlier this year by the DVSA to stop the system being exploited. Now, only the learner driver is able to book their driving test.Image caption,Sophie Stuchfield, a driving instructor in Watford, previously showed the BBC hundreds of driving tests being offered for sale by resellers on messaging groupsSophie Stuchfield, a driving instructor in Watford, told the BBC: "Whilst the re-selling of tests does seem to have stopped, which is a massive positive, they've still failed to recruit enough examiners to cope with demand."She didn't believe that the slight fall in numbers for waiting times "is anything to boast about", adding that in many areas the wait for a driving test when booking is 21 weeks."On many occasions, my drivers wake up at 5.45am on a Monday, only to not end up with a test as when they click on something, by the time they put their details in, they are told the test has already been taken."Sophie added that the waiting time to get a test meant that many learner drivers "who haven't even started driving lessons will book a test knowing it's 5 months away", putting themselves and the instructor under a lot of pressure.Justin Madders, the minister for roads, said the government "inherited record waiting times and a significant backlog"."While driving test waiting times are still not where we want them to be, these figures show real progress is being made," he added.A DVSA spokesperson said the agency was "committed to reducing waiting times" and that "examiner numbers are at their highest level since November 2017"."But we know there's more to do and we won't stop until every learner can get a test slot when they need one, wherever they're learning to drive," the spokesperson added.Related topicsUK driving licence

title: Trump's diesel dilemma — by the numbers
content:
Diesel pricesare surging as midterms approach – and they are likely to stay high in the near future, according to analysts.

The International Energy Agency'smonthly report for October,released Wednesday, was the latest to predict that constraints on the diesel market will likely keep prices elevated into next year. The group warned that even if refineries step up production of diesel into the year-end, inventories will likely remain strained until the second half of 2027.

Last Friday, President Donald Trumpunexpectedly paused sanctions on Russian diesel fueland announced that he reached a deal with PresidentVladimir Putinin which the Kremlin would release4.8 million metric tons of diesel, or nearly 36 million barrels, to the global market.

Over the weekend, he took to Truth Social to announce an"energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine, but Ukrainian PresidentVolodymyr Zelenskyylater accused Russia of attacking the country'senergy facilities.

The foreign policy developments come asrising fuel prices—particularly skyrocketing diesel— have become a major flashpoint ahead of this year's midterm election. But releasing Russian diesel to the global market is unlikely to drop prices in the near term.A note from Goldman Sachs last weekeven predicted that diesel prices will remain high through 2027 as refineries struggle to meet demand.

Here's what the numbers tell us so far:

Wholesale diesel prices have more than doubled since the beginning of 2026 through the end of September as both the war in Iran and Russia's war in Ukraine have dramatically cut global supply.

Trump has insisted that the war in Ukraine is to blame for high diesel prices. On July 8, Russia banned diesel exports after Ukraine struck its refineries. In the U.S., the price of a gallon of diesel rose nearly 40% between July 6 and Sept. 22.

However, the price of diesel had already jumped after the Iran war started and was still 20% above its prewar level when Russia instituted its export ban, making thattightening of supplyfeel that much more acute.

Indeed, both conflicts have created major ripple effects across global energy markets causing major swings, sometimes daily.

title: Faisal Islam: What surprise praise for UK economy tells us about the Budget
content: Image source,Sirachai Arunrugstichai/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption,The managing director of the IMF, Kristalina Georgieva, has praised the UK's approach to debt reduction.ByFaisal IslamEconomics editor,ÂReporting fromin BangkokPublished14 October 2026, 12:03 BSTUpdated 4 hours ago"Get your fiscal health in order," is a key message at the the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) annual meeting here in Thailand.The IMF is worried about the debts of the world's biggest economies. It is doing its job as a watchdog, looking for and warning about financial vulnerabilities.In the meantime, the finance ministers of former crisis countries are boasting about how little their borrowing costs have gone up, compared to the world's biggest economies, such as the US.On three occasions in the past 24 hours, top IMF officials havepraised the UK's plansto reduce its annual levels of borrowing, bucking the trend of the rest of the G7 group of countries, which includes Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the US.The IMF clearly seeing the UK in a different light to these major economies is very interesting."The UK is actually one country where action to reduce debt and deficit has been taken decisively and we see the UK in that sense enjoying a bit of a better growth prospect," managing director Kristalina Georgieva said earlier.Her comments followed those of the IMF's chief economist Silvana Tenreyro who told me that UK borrowing reductions "stand out".Three things we've learnt about the UK economy from the IMFPublished1 day agoUK growth forecast upgraded but higher energy prices to hit economy next yearPublished1 day agoThe IMF's twice-yearly assessment of global countries' economic prospects showed only the UK among the G7 having a serious plan for consolidation of its annual borrowing over the next few years, worth nearly 4% of the size of the economy. The US, Germany and Japan are increasing borrowing. Canada and Italy are keeping borrowing at the same level.It appears the UK is now the IMF's model pupil - at the top of the G7 table for reducing deficits.Leaning into austerityThis matters because for the past half decade the UK has been on the bond market naughty step, often having the highest borrowing rates among the G7 since the Liz Truss mini budget, as political and economic crises afflicted different governments.While this is good news for the chancellor and the Treasury, it also points to the sort of Budget we will get in a fortnight's time. To keep its plans to reduce debt on track, John Healey is likely to have limited room for extra spending. He will want to marry this with limited tax rises. There could be a modest decrease in the margin for error around meeting debt rules - so-called headroom. If so that will be tied to providing a cushion against an expected rise in energy prices due to the ongoing Middle East conflict and the impact on the cost of living overall - the so called global inflation shock.This is likely to mean disappointment for many public services expecting cash injections to account for rising inflation, as suggested this week by think tank the Institute for Fiscal Studies. It will mean tough public sector pay discussions.It won't be "austerity" but the chancellor is likely to lean into the IMF framing of a government with austere plans, relative to other advanced countries. The initial prize is to avoid the direct gaze of the bond markets, whose full glare is on others, such as France now. The bigger prize could be lower relative borrowing costs for government and households.Ultimately forecasts mean nothing without the underpinning of solid plans. Those plans will be here for everyone to judge soon enough.Related topicsInternational Monetary Fund (IMF)EconomicsEconomy

title: Bank of America is set to report third-quarter earnings – here’s what the Street expects
content:
Bank of Americais scheduled to report third-quarter earnings before the opening bell Wednesday, just one day after the bank was hit with a$1.2 billion penaltyby the U.S. Treasury Department.

That charge, which cut net income by 17 cents a share, will inevitably spark questions as to whether CEO Brian Moynihan has a handle on controls at the second-biggest U.S. bank by assets.

content: Image source,Getty ImagesByMitchell LabiakPublished14 October 2026, 10:24 BSTUpdated 35 minutes agoWayfair is among three firms which have been fined Â£6m in total by the competition watchdog over misleading sales tactics â with some customers set to receive refunds.The Competition Markets Authority (CMA) has fined the online furniture retailer Â£4.8m and electronics retailer Appliances Direct Â£1.2m for misleading customers with time-limited offers.Meanwhile, Gold's Gym has been fined Â£48,000 for not telling customers the total price of memberships.Appliances Direct and Gold's Gym have been ordered to refund customers a total of Â£440,000. title: Ukraine warns Starlink limits are disrupting military operations as Russia pounds its energy infrastructure
content:
Ukraine has accused Elon Musk'sSpaceXof imposing new restrictions on its Starlink satellite internet service without warning, disrupting Ukrainian military operations.

It comes as Russia intensifies attacks on the country's energy infrastructure despitePresident Donald Trump's proposed "energy ceasefire."

Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to PresidentVolodymyr Zelenskyyon defense technology, said Wednesday thatSpaceXhas implemented a speed limit on Starlink terminals in motion without notifying Ukrainian defense forces, disrupting some missions.

Meanwhile, Russia unleashed an attack on Ukrainian energy infrastructure overnight, leaving at least 600,000 people without power in the Kyiv and Kharkiv regions, raising further questions about the "energy ceasefire" announced by Trump on Sunday.

"There is significant damage to facilities and equipment – at 26 facilities of our power system and four facilities in the oil and gas sector," Zelenskyy said in aposton X early Wednesday.

He highlighted a targeted ballistic missile strike against the energy infrastructure that Zelenskyy said should have been covered by the"energy ceasefire"announced by PresidentDonald Trumpon Sunday.

"The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States," Zelenskyy said.

The attack comes after the Ukrainian president on Mondayaccused Russia of violating Trump's proposalthat the adversaries stop attacking each other's energy facilities to help bring down the cost of oil and diesel.

Both Russian and Ukrainian authorities initially denied any knowledge of an energy ceasefire agreement. Ukraine has since welcomed such a deal, while Russian authorities said talks are ongoing, without confirming whether they have reached an agreement.

Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Monday: "Regarding the status of this agreement, we can refer to Zelensky's reaction. When asked the same question, he said he had not heard of such an agreement, would welcome clarification and was ready for a ceasefire,"according to the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Zelenskyy also said that for the second time this week, Ukraine received no advance warning about Russian ballistic missile launches. The latest unflagged strike on Kyiv damaged a residential building and killed one person and injured six, Zelenskyy said.

Ukraine's Beskrestnov said that the Starlink speed restriction currently applies to the StarShield military service package and is set at 100 mph, or about 160 km/h.

"It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation," Beskrestnov said on Telegram. "SpaceX is likely to have taken such measures at the request of the Trump administration," he added in a separate post.

SpaceX and the White House have been contacted for comment.

title: Scott Bessent's growth plans aren't enough to tame surging deficit and debt pile, IMF chief says
content:
BANGKOK — The head of the International Monetary Fund has urged Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to trim the deficit, warning that his plan to lean on growth to tame U.S. Government debt isn't sufficient.

"Growth of course helps, but it cannot deliver fast enough the necessary adjustments," Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said at a panel Wednesday at the IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok. "Some [fiscal] measures would be necessary."

Georgieva said Bessent recognizes that federal deficits and overall debt have grown "too high," and that measures to improve the budget balance and reduce the debt are necessary. But "the authorities very much rely on strong growth in the United States" to bring them down, she said.

Bessent and Trump administration officials havetouted resilient economic growth, driven by the artificial-intelligence build-out, reshoring manufacturing and tax cuts for consumers, as crucial tools to improve the U.S. fiscal posture.

"With 3% growth, we grow our way out of this," Bessent said last month. He has argued sustained growth above 3%, combined with spending restraint, could lower the debt ratio and bend the debt-to-GDP curve.

U.S. federal debt has exceeded 100% of gross domestic product, once an unthinkable threshold, with the country's publicdebt load surpassing $40 trillionandon track to break a recordset in the aftermath of World War II.

The U.S. government has historically spent more than it collects through taxation, committing to unbalanced spending in the decades since President Bill Clinton briefly managed to balance the budget in the 1990s. But debt-financed spending has sharply accelerated in recent years. Trump cut taxes in his first term and signed the first Covid relief packages in 2020, which Joe Biden followed with a $1.9 trillion stimulus in 2021.

That federal spending helped stave off a recession but also fueled inflation that still weighs on American households and businesses.

Before his appointment, Bessent had said he wanted Trump to cut the deficit to less than 4% of GDP by the end of his term, and said in August that the U.S.budget deficit had likely peaked.

The U.S. Treasury market has been battered this year with yields climbing to multidecade highs, as investors bet that surging energy costs and heavy AI spending will keep borrowing costs higher.Benchmark 10-year yieldshovered near their highest level since 2002, standing at around 5.2% on Wednesday.

Although the budget figures for the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30 have not yet been released, the deficit is expected to top 6% of GDP,compared with 5.8% in fiscal 2025.

"With the government running an annual budget deficit of 6 percent of GDP, the debt will rise another $7 billion by the end of today—and each subsequent day," Benn Steil, senior fellow and director of international economics at Council on Foreign Relations, said in a Sept.25 note.

Steil also warned that it could be "reckless" for Washington to declare the debt crunch solved by supporting unsupported projections, pressing for spending and revenue reforms.

The IMF, which released its October World Economic Outlook on Tuesday, forecasts U.S. growth of 2.3% in both 2026 and 2027, and projects U.S. gross government debtreaching 142% of GDP by 2031.

IMF chief Georgieva has also urged governments to set credible medium-term plans to control deficits instead of relying on stronger growth alone, as global public debt heads toward 100% of GDP before the end of the decade, the highest since World War II. Bessentreportedlymissed this week's meetings to attend to "domestic engagements."

title: ASML says it's getting order interest through 2030 as profit smashes expectations
content:
ASMLsaid Wednesday that some of its customers are expressing interest in placing orders for its critical semiconductor tools for 2029 and 2030 as the company reported third-quarter profit that beat expectations.

The comments will likely comfort investors who have been looking to assess the longer-term demand outlook for ASML's lithography machines.

"Our customers continue to increase their short- and medium-term equipment demand forecasts with us, driven primarily by their views on the size and duration of AI-related investments," CEO Christophe Fouquet said in a press release.

"In light of their demand visibility, some customers are expressing an interest in placing orders with us for 2029 and even 2030."

ASML is the only company in the world that produces extreme ultraviolet lithography machines, a key tool used by the likes ofTSMCto make the world's most advanced semiconductors.

Investors closely watch the Dutch company's earnings for signs of AI-related chip demand.

Fouquet said current supply planned for 2027 and 2028 will not fully meet the demand of its customers. The company is "investigating ways" to increase capacity for 2028 beyond the 30% increase it had previously forecast.

ASML has now updated its guidance three times this year,upping its full-year forecastfor the second time in July, and on Wednesday it raised the lower end of its sales forecast for 2026.

The company now expects net sales of between 44 billion euros and 45 billion euros ($49.3 billion to $50.4 billion). The previous lower end of the forecast was for 43 billion euros.

ASML also said it expects fourth-quarter net sales of between 14.2 billion euros and 15.2 billion euros. The upper end of the range is ahead of LSEG consensus estimates of 14.2 billion euros.

ASML's stock was around 2% higher in early trade in Europe. Shares of the company have rallied 56% this year.

During the quarter, Samsung and TSMC, the world's two biggest chipmakers,committed to usingASML's High NA extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines. High NA EUV is ASML's next-generation tool, which analysts see as key to the Dutch firm's future growth.

For the third quarter, here's how ASML did versus LSEG consensus estimates:

The semiconductor equipment maker said it expects China sales to account for 20% of its total business, sticking to a prior forecast.

While ASML holds an effective monopoly on EUV machines, a July report fromThe Informationsuggested an unnamed Chinese company hadbegun manufacturing an immersion deep ultraviolet lithography(DUV) machine, citing people familiar with the matter.

ASML dominates the manufacturing of DUV machines, which are less advanced than EUV. China has been ramping up its domestic semiconductor supply chain, with some investors concerned it could challenge the European and U.S. dominance. However,analysts raised questionsabout China's ability to ramp up its own DUV technology.

ASML meanwhile has faced challenges in China over the last few years. The company is restricted from selling EUV and some DUV tools to China.

title: Not building third runway would be 'huge missed opportunity', warns Heathrow boss
content: Image source,Getty ImagesByMichael RaceBusiness reporterPublished21 minutes agoNot building a third runway at Heathrow Airport would be a "huge missed opportunity" for the UK, the boss of the country's busiest airport has warned.Thomas Woldbye told BBC Radio 4's Today programme it would be "good to know" the government's position on the project, after Prime Minister Andy Burnham refused to say whether he backed expansion.The airport's chief executive said if its owners could not invest in a third runway, the money "will be invested somewhere else in the world", suggesting a decision would be made in the new year.The Department for Transport said it was reviewing responses to a consultation and was "considering the appropriate next steps".A spokesperson added that the government supported airport expansion "across the country where this can contribute to growth and opportunity, while meeting the tests on the environment".They said expanding Heathrow had the "potential to deliver around Â£40 billion in economic benefits across the country".Building a third runway at Heathrow has been debated for decades. The project has proved controversial, facing steep opposition from local residents, politicians and climate campaigners.Last year, then-chancellor Rachel Reeves announced the government-backed expansion, saying that "a third runway is badly needed", and that the government could not "duck the decision any longer".Heathrow Airport is owned by a consortium of investors, the largest of which is French private equity firm Ardian. Others include the Qatar Investment Authority, Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund and the China Investment Corporation."If they cannot invest in Heathrow... then that money will be invested somewhere else in the world," Woldbye said."It's not about allocating this money elsewhere. It's private money. It's not public money. So hence, it will not go into the UK. I think that would be really a sad, huge missed opportunity for this country."A third runway would mean demolishing hundreds of homes, diverting rivers, and rerouting the M25 motorway between junctions 14 and 15 through a tunnel under the new runway. It is estimated it would cost Â£33bn to build.Heathrow serves more than 80 million travellers a year with its four passenger terminals and two runways. The number of flights, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000 - or nearly 2,000 a day on average, if a third runway is built.This additional traffic would potentially lead to a huge surge in revenue for the airport's owners, and Heathrow has argued the expansion would provide a "huge economic boost" and create jobs.The new runway was scheduled to open by 2035, subject to plans being submitted and approved, but Heathrow has sincesuggested it would be delayed by four years to 2039 due to planning and regulatory issues.Whether the new-look government still backs a third runway is not yet clear. Burnham, who as Mayor of Greater Manchester opposed the scheme, said he believed the matter was "for London and Londoners"."I think we ought to hear the voice of people there first. It's not right for me to just jump straight in on the back of the consultation," he said,speaking to the BBC last month.Woldbye said he hoped the prime minister would "will come along" with the project, pointing out it was backed by the unions.Image caption,Thomas Woldbye, seen here speaking to the BBC last year, has stressed the importance of Heathrow's third runway'Heathrow not just for Londoners'He added that a third runway was "not just for Londoners". "Benefits will be felt all over the country because our supply chain reaches all the way from the north all the way to the south of the UK."Downing Street declined to comment on Woldbye's remarks.Questioned about the noise impact on nearby communities of more planes taking off and landing, Woldbye claimed Heathrow had seen a "stark" reduction in noise over the past 40 years and said the "trend will continue"."My biggest concern is actually the years of uncertainty. And I think it's time that we give them certainty on what we want with this project so that we can move on and they can move on in their lives," he said.Andy Burnham refuses to back third runway at HeathrowPublished27 SeptemberWoldbye told the Today programme he had not yet met the current Chancellor John Healey, but if he did, he would outline that the airport "contributes dramatically to the economy" but that "we are now full"."That means we will stop contributing or stop growing that contribution. If we want to avoid that, we need to now take this decision, move forward and continue the work of the previous government to move at speed and deliver this," he said.The Department for Transport said it was still finalising its Airports National Policy Statement, which provides the basis for deciding whether to grant a new runway at Heathrow. It was last updated in 2018.Woldbye said Heathrow was working on a planning application which has planned to submit in the next couple of years, but said any decision would be guided by government's the national policy statement.Related topicsUK economyHeathrow Airport expansionLondon Heathrow AirportAndy Burnham

title: Oil rises amid growing Mideast tensions between Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia
content:
Oil rises Wednesday, amid worries over supply disruptions as tensions continue to escalate in the Middle East with fighting between Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia.

Futures for international benchmarkBrent crudefor December delivery gained 0.61% to $106.33 a barrel. U.S.West Texas Intermediate futuresfor November advanced 0.63% to $94.73 per barrel.

Fighting between Saudi Arabia and Iran-backed Houthis continued to escalate, following a deadly attack on Riyadh's main airport by Tehran-backed Houthis in Yemen.

According to Al Jazeera, Houthi energy terminals and fuel reserves in Yemen were struck by a Saudi-led coalition, though a spokesperson said that precautions were taken to avoid "collateral damage on civilians."

Meanwhile, tensions also continued to simmer between the U.S. and Iran.

U.S. Central Command rejected claims by the commander of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy that the Strait of Hormuz is under Iran's control and that any approaching U.S. Navy warships would be "sunk."

"RGC's navy commander has no navy," CENTCOM said in an Xpost, adding that "American forces and regional partners clearly control the Strait of Hormuz."

Oil mayrally another $20-$25due to the Iran conflict, hedge fund manager and noted commodity trader Paul Tudor Jones said on onCNBC's "Squawk Box."

"I am long oil... bullish oil...I think it can rally another $20 or $25 bucks," said the founder and chief investment officer of Tudor Investment.

"If something to ameliorate the situation was going to happen, it would have happened already before the midterms," he added.

title: Taiwan agrees to buy 30% of gas from Alaska LNG project, Trump says
content:
U.S. PresidentDonald Trumpsaid Tuesday that Taiwan had agreed to buy 30% of the gas from a proposed liquefied natural gas project in Alaska.

"Taiwan has just agreed to buy 30% of the gas coming off the pipeline for the next 20 years," Trump said at a rally in Alaska. "That guarantees a success."

His latest remarks follow repeated claims earlier this month that South Korea hadagreed to jointhe $50 billion Alaska LNG project, even as Seoul maintained that its participation had not been finalized. "We'll also invest $4.4 billion into the project, on top of $50 billion already committed by South Korea to Alaska," Trump said.

However, the terms of the Taiwan deal cited by Trump were not immediately clear.

Last year, Taiwan's state-owned energy company CPC Corpreportedlyreached an agreement with Alaska Gasline Development Corp to purchase LNG and invest in the pipeline project.

Taiwan, home to critical semiconductor giant TSMC, has seen energy demand climb due to AI-related growth. However, the island relies on imports formore than 90%of its energy supply and this summer projected its average electricity demand growth rate through 2035 would exceed that of Japan and South Korea.

Taiwan's economic affairs ministrysaidthat growth rate would climb by about 2.5% a year, the second-highest forecast in its history. The democratically self-ruled island is still waiting on major new arms sales from the U.S.

Beijing considers Taiwan part of its territory.

Glenfarne, the developer of the Alaska LNG pipeline,toldthe U.S. government in a report this month the project aims to deliver its first gas in 2029.

Trump has alsostepped up pressureon South Korea over its participation in the project, warning earlier this month that he would charge the country more and threatened to double the charges if Seoul failed to sign soon, without specifying what would be doubled. That prompted speculation in South Korean media that he was referring to higher tariffs.

The White House, Taiwan's energy ministry and CPC Corp. did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment.

title: Bank of America hit with $1.2bn fine for money laundering failings
content: Image source,Bloomberg via Getty ImagesByPeter HoskinsBusiness reporterPublished3 hours agoBank of America has been fined $1.2bn (Â£910m) for failing to detect potential money laundering and other illegal activity, the US Treasury Department said on Tuesday.The banking giant failed to report over $5bn in suspicious activity to the government, $1bn of which posed national security and illicit finance risks, the Treasury said.Those failures included not flagging transactions that possibly involved Chinese money laundering networks or trade-based laundering "with a substantial nexus to the southwest border", according to the Treasury."Our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators," Bank of America told the BBC.The announcement came less 24 hours before Bank of America was due to announce its quarterly earnings on Wednesday morning."Our third-quarter results will include a non-tax-deductible charge of $1.2 billion impacting net income by approximately 17 cents per share," the bank said in an emailed statement."We have already dedicated substantial personnel and resources to our ongoing remediation efforts, and those costs are in the current expense base," it added.In announcing the fine, the third-largest the department has ever imposed, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said: "When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire US financial system to significant illicit finance risks."The Treasury said the bank overly relied on inquiries from outside parties like law enforcement and other financial institutions instead of its own internal controls.This meant that it "effectively outsourced to third parties a substantial portion of its proactive detection and reporting obligations," the department said.As part of the settlement, Bank of America admitted that it "willfully violated" the Bank Secrecy Act by failing to maintain a compliant anti-money laundering programme, conduct required due diligence on foreign correspondent accounts and file suspicious activity reports, the Treasury said.The $1.2bn fine included penalties imposed by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC).The OCC's $750m fine marked the biggest penalty it has ever levied.OFAC said its settlement with the bank was tied to 475 apparent violations of sanctions programmes including those on Russia and Iran, narcotics, and global terrorism.The settlement amount of $11.6m reflected the determination that Bank of America's apparent violations were "non-egregious", OFAC said.Related topicsInternational BusinessBank of AmericaMoney launderingUnited StatesBanking

title: South Korean carmaker Hyundai plans 'strategic' investment of $15.5 billion in India by 2032
content:
South Korea'sHyundai Motor Groupon Tuesday said it plans to invest $15.5 billion from 2026 through 2032 in India, a market it considers core to the company's emerging-marketgrowth and expansion.

"India remains one of Hyundai Motor Group's most important and strategic markets globally," Euisun Chung, the executive chair of Hyundai Motor Group, said in a release following his meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

He added that this investment "reaffirms" the company's commitment to the Indian market for the next 30 years and beyond.

Over the seven-year plan, Hyundai said it will invest across manufacturing expansion and in developing research and development infrastructure, local supplier cultivation for parts localization, and future technology innovation.

To execute these investments, Hyundai will set up a dedicated investment entity in India, it said in the release.

The Indian car market has been hitting new records every month, driven by strong demand. In August, passenger car sales hit a new monthly record with sales of 439,000 units, over 36% higher year-on-year, as per data from industry body Society of Indian Auto Manufacturers.

Hyundai is the third-largest car company in India and sold 247,980 passenger cars in the country between April and August this year, according to data released last month.

Japanese carmakerMaruti Suzukiwas the top seller in the country over that period, followed by India's Mahindra & Mahindra, as per SIAM's data. However, in the financial year ended March 2026, Hyundai came in fourth,edged out by M&M and Tata Motors.

Hyundai has a total production capacity of 1.4 million vehicles across India and exports cars from these locations.

In 2024, the South Korean company listed its India business unit,Hyundai Motors India, raising $3.3 billion in thelargest-ever initial public offerin the country.

title: Stock futures are little changed as traders await consumer inflation report: Live updates
content:
U.S. stock futures were little changed Tuesday night as the release of September's consumer inflation report loomed.

S&P 500 futuresandNasdaq-100 futuresdipped 0.03% and 0.1%, respectively, after the spot gauges dropped for a second straight session on Tuesday.

Bank of Americashares declined over 2% in extended trading after the firm was hit withmore than $1.2 billion in federal penalties, with regulators saying the bank failed to report more than $5 billion in "suspicious" transactions.

In Asia, Australia'sS&P/ASX 200was down 0.62%. Japan'sNikkei 225added 0.32%, while South Korea'sKospirose 0.82%.

A drift downward in chip stocks weighed on the major averages Tuesday, with theVanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH)falling for a sixth straight session over growing fears of an AI spending bubble and rising anxieties around competition out of China.

A swath of big banks posted strong quarterly results, but shares ended the day lower, withGoldman SachsandCitigroupfalling. The market's reaction suggested businesses have a higher bar to clear during the third-quarter earnings season — especially in tech where semiconductors are expected to be the largest contributor to year-over-year earnings growth.

S&P 500 companies are expected to post a blended earnings growth rate of roughly 30%, while semiconductors and semiconductor equipment are set for growth of 130%, according to FactSet data.

"The business fundamentals are very strong. It's very hard to argue with the demand side of the story for chips," Marta Norton, chief investment strategist at Empower, told CNBC's "Closing Bell: Overtime." "I don't know if we necessarily question how good those business fundamentals are as much as we question how much valuation is left in the space."

Investors are awaiting the September reading of the U.S.consumer price indexWednesday morning. Economists polled by Dow Jones anticipate inflation to have risen by 3.6% on a year-over-year basis, up from 3.4% in the prior reading.

The results arrive as oil prices remain elevated and consumers pay more for gasoline, which is averaging at $4.34 a gallon, compared to $3.08 per gallon a year earlier, according toAAA. Last week President Donald Trump announced he wouldtemporarily ease restrictionson Russian diesel fuel exports, but analysts don't believe the deal will do much tolower fuel pricesfor truckers and farmers.

Earnings season continues, with more big bank results from Bank of America and Morgan Stanley out Wednesday morning U.S. time. Dutch semiconductor company ASML also reports.

Asia-Pacific markets opened mixed on Wednesday. Australia'sS&P/ASX 200was down 0.62%.

Japan'sNikkei 225added 0.32%, while the Topix declined 0.11%. South Korea'sKospiadded 0.82% while the small-cap Kosdaq declined 0.45%.

The September reading of the consumer price index is set to release Wednesday morning.

Economists polled by Dow Jones anticipate inflation to have risen by 3.6% on a year-over-year basis, up from 3.4% in the prior reading.

Asia-Pacific markets were set for a mixed open Wednesday as investors awaited a key U.S. inflation report that could offer fresh clues on the Federal Reserve's interest rate outlook.

Futures for Hong Kong'sHang Seng indexstood at 24,340, marginally lower than the index's last close of 24,345.22.

Australia'sS&P/ASX 200was down 0.52% in its first hour of trade.

Japan'sNikkei 225was set to rise at open, with its Chicago and Osaka futures contracts last at 68,055 and 68,100 respectively, compared with the index's previous close of 67,777.52.

Bank of Americawas hit withmore than $1.2 billion in federal penaltiesTuesday after regulators said the nation's second-largest bank failed for years to report more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions and fix longstanding anti-money-laundering problems.

More than $1 billion of the unreported activity involved national security and other high-priority risks, including Chinese money-laundering networks and activity tied to the southwest border, Treasury said in a press release.

The action also lands less than a day before the bank reports quarterly earnings Wednesday morning.

— Luke Fountain, Kevin Breuninger

Check out the companies making headlines in extended trading.

Stock futures opened near the flatline Tuesday night.

Dow Jones Industrial Average futures lost 17 points, or 0.03%. S&P 500 futures and Nasdaq 100 futures both dipped 0.01%.
